Uniform Title: Pauṣkara Saṃhitā Main Title: Pauṣkara Saṃhitā, One of the Three Jewels of the Pañcarātra Editor: Śrī Yātirāja Sampatkumāra Rāmānujamuni

Publication year: 1934 Publication city: Bangalore Publication country: India
Śrī Hari Om. Salutations to Śrī Hayagrīva.
The First Chapter of the Śrī Pauṣkarasaṃhitā:
When one who has completed his vow stands before the Guru, who desires his welfare— [the reading "cīrṇa" is correct].
And then, O Lotus-born One, he should command the disciple who has arrived.
One should cause that very thing to be given at the proper time to a worthy recipient endowed with a multitude of virtues;
indeed, go, my son, to wherever he may command you for the sake of wealth.
However, for the purpose of the sacrificial requisites by which you shall attain peace, that which has been obtained should subsequently be offered to the Guru. (3)
"O Blessed One, by your grace this has been obtained; please accept it from me. Have compassion for me, who am without a protector and submerged in the ocean of existence. (4)
When such a compassionate collection of words as this has been spoken,
the Guru should then proceed for that purpose to the worship of the maṇḍala.
Having outlined it according to the prescribed rule and filled it with auspicious powders,
or having written upon it with saffron and other substances, or having drawn it with water-clocks and such instruments.
On the ground, due to a lack of wealth, one should diligently worship with golden needles and the like, or with fruits, flowers, and other forest-born items that are always available.
One should show that which is worshipped to him; know that it is fourfold.
The first is named Padmodara (Lotus-Born), and it is not characterized by numerical count.
The second is proclaimed as containing many lotuses;
and the third would be a wheel-lotus of various kinds.
He whose manifold divisions are also many is indeed the one born from the lotus today;
the mandala named Miśracakra, moreover, possesses many divisions.
That is declared to be the fourth, wherein one who has been obstructed is liberated;
it is called "Great," possessing nine navels, and exists through the differentiation of the *bimba*.
By seeing, worshipping, or likewise by meditating upon Him in the fire,
liberation occurs swiftly for devotees through that alone.
Having observed the sequence according to the time divided [into months] as desired, then,
on the twelfth day of each fortnight until the end of the year, he should [honour] a twice-born man.
He becomes a *samayin*, a devotee, and a *putraka* by another means—namely, by seeing [the image], by worshipping it, or indeed by meditating upon it within the heart. (14)
By such a period of time, his fitness arises;
furthermore, [the deity] should be worshipped with devotion both at the commencement and at the completion. (15)

The two arrays, beginning with the twice-born and ending with the last, [are completed] by the remaining [elements] over the course of a year. When a living being, whose impurities have been destroyed, attains the status of a "son" (putraka), then even his residual faults proceed toward those two. || 17 ||
Then the Guru should employ him as the means of accomplishment;
having performed the rite in the third mandala, he should cause him to enter therein.
Having meditated upon that worshipful one through many different forms, worship Him within the field of perception for a period of three fortnights minus five days. (19)
One should worship each wheel one by one until the lotus is fully worshipped;
O twice-born one, the fruits of those acts indeed accrue to him in succession.
Therefore, the Guru should strive to show this to the practitioner;
for by means of the fourth, the Great Sacrifice (mahāyāga), one attains the status of an Ācārya.
Having first determined that time by means of a statement, one should reflect upon it;
O twice-born one, one should indeed complete each of the remaining days one by one.
O Brahmin, he who performs sacrifice through this rite for four years reaches the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra, which is otherwise difficult to cross.
If one should perform a single great sacrifice consisting of nine centers, these lamps of knowledge are thereby established within this wilderness of saṃsāra. (24)
For devotees who are self-restrained, there are indeed various sacrifices; for Brahmins who possess faith and practice self-control, there is always constant [worship].
For the ocean of existence is indeed impossible to cross by any means other than sacrifice;
having boarded the ship of sacrifice, one should recognize the goal as the further shore.
He who, being possessed by supreme compassion, truly delivers [others] even without material assistance—that wise man is remembered as a guru. || 27 ||
Having recognized a devotee who is helpless and submerged in an ocean of sorrow, he who lifts them up with the hand of sacrifice is remembered as a Guru equal to Me. (28)
Of sacrifices, sacred fords, holy fields, and those who serve the Siddhas—
all of which have been honored and worshipped with flowers, garments, and ornaments— (29)
Likewise, O great sage, amidst the sounds of Vedic chants from the sacred sites and hermitages, while the sacrificial fire was being offered oblations; || 30 ||

Indeed, for men whose minds are utterly deluded, who are hostile, whose reasoning is corrupted, and who are nihilists, [this occurs] always and even from a mere sight [of it], quite unexpectedly. (31)
Bad tendencies, evil intellect, the collection of fallacious arguments,
wicked dispositions, false reasons, and atheism shall all go to their destruction.
An emotional state (*bhāva*) arises swiftly within that [person], endowed with faith;
by its power, what need is there to mention those beginning with faith? (33)
Therefore, a disciple who is devoted, endowed with a multitude of virtues, absorbed in that [reality], ever-disciplined, and whose mind is free from conceptual construction, should be fully known.
Whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, remaining in his own station—whether a student or a householder—who has fulfilled his duties according to the prescribed rule; 35.

Then, whether he be a forest-dweller or one who subsists on alms, or a woman possessed of true discernment—one who is steadfast, pure, well-contented, and desirous of perceiving the ultimate reality. (36)
Having abandoned his circle of kinsmen, being energetic and possessed of firm resolve,
and having found a worthy recipient, he completed the initiation for the sacrifice.
Then, O Lotus-born One, the Guru should offer into the fire the ordinary bonds belonging to him—those of the past, those of the present, and those yet to come. (38)

When the circle of kinsmen has completely perished, what remains for the embodied being? It is the persistence of the family of the body, as well as the reality pervading both that which is spoken and the speaker, according to its true state. 39.

But that which resides in the heart, all-pervading, endowed with the mirror of the intellect, appearing as everything yet without appearance, is characterized by consciousness, existence, and eternal bliss. || 40 ||
Released from the states of manifest and unmanifest, untainted and like the sky—by that [Self] this world is manifested, and abiding therein, one attains equanimity. (41)
But having recognized that the goal is accomplished and having reflected upon the reality of knowledge,
you must certainly and constantly [act] for those who are terrified by the fear of saṃsāra. (42)
And the application [of the self] to the supreme reality should be performed after thorough investigation;
having placed the knowledge of the Self within the vessel, one should cast off the physical body. (43)
Since it does not vanish, it acts as a seedless seed for the world;
it is the supreme purifying knowledge that dispels the darkness of ignorance. 44.
Pauṣkara said:

Through time, by means of initiation for sacrifices and other rites as prescribed by you, [the goal is attained] for those who are timid and unawakened, once the unstable state has been conquered. || 45 ||
If they should perish in the interim, what would become of them?
O Lord, [this concerns] those who have attained knowledge from you but whose practice remains incomplete. (46)
The Blessed Lord said:
Know, O dear one, that for men the fruit resulting from the completion of an action is more intense than that which arises merely from the prior intention (saṃkalpa) of an unaccomplished act. (47)
As soon as my intellect is fully adorned, I shall cast myself upon the serpent-couch;
thus, having crossed the shoreless ocean of existence, I shall attain the supreme state of the ascetic.
By that very means, he has attained the eternal and imperishable state;
there are three types: the perfected one (siddha), the one currently attaining perfection (sidhyamāna), and the third, the seeker who desires to ascend (arurukṣaka). || 49 ||
Know that these [three] will indeed become equal after some interval of time;
just as one who has previously eaten the food of the perfected ones remains satisfied alone. (50)

Moreover, O Indra, the time for his meal has arrived; he remains without food. It is taught that for all beings, there is no lack of virtue in their insatiability at the conclusion [of their tasks]. || 51 ||
Thus, O Lotus-born One, for those devoted to the yoga of mantra-rituals, in the course of time, there are two teachers of their own school in that imperishable state. (52)
For men endowed with devotion and faith,
the undertaking of the mantra is a constant deliverer from saṃsāra, provided they are led by a twice-born who knows the truth.

The culmination of the intellect and the object of knowledge, unobscured even by conceptual constructions, [are attained] together with birth from those who abide in radiant meditative absorption. 54.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Characteristics for Examining Disciples," in the Pauṣkarasaṃhitā, a Mahopaniṣad of the glorious Pāñcarātra. || 1 ||
Now begins the second chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
"O Blessed One, please explain to me the characteristics of the mandalas."
But among these, Ananta has been described as both that which undergoes transmigration and that which is itself [the transmigrator]. || 1 ||
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Lotus-born One, having reached a meritorious place that is renowned and frequented by the Siddhas, there are many kinds of locations therein."
When the characteristics of the portions of ground upon which grain depends have been thoroughly examined, sacrificial rites proceed; those [characteristics] I shall now describe to you. (3)
And on a mountain peak, in its midst, on a plateau suitable for the twice-born,
or in a delightful forest on the ground, thick with trees and medicinal herbs.
Indeed, today in the auspicious and delightful Bhadrecopavana, which is praised and filled with lotuses, and on the banks of rivers as well as at their confluences— || 5 ||
Near sacred fords, in a stable place teeming with cranes,
in the vicinity of a temple, in cow-pens, or in the hermitages of Brahmins.
In a place free from harmful creatures and devoid of fear such as the terror of thieves, one should first examine the ground—ensuring it is rich in auspicious characteristics and well-defined. (7)
For the sake of the gods' abode, for the sake of the village among the Brāhmaṇas and others, for the sake of sacrifice for the rituals, and for the sake of a home for householders; || 8 ||
O Brahmin, without doubt, there are indeed merits and demerits on the earth;
listen as I describe them to you in brief. || 9 ||
Since the earth, when free from defects, always performs its purposeful function,
that same earth, if possessed of defects, would produce many obstacles.
O Lotus-born One, by the power of the mantras of the weapons, that forest which was filled with peaceful trees and abounding in fruits and flowers is abandoned by the Piśācas.
It was strewn with lush young grass, covered with soft blades of turf,
pleasant to the touch, abounding in clear water, rich in fragrance, and sweet-smelling.
For it is free from marshy ground, unburnt by the flames of fire or the rays of the sun, liberated from great defects such as foul odors, and bestows happiness and peace. (13)
Free from wicked beasts and frequented by noble birds, where indeed cows and other species of deer shine (or take delight) there. (14)
Where indeed tigers and elephants rejoice together with human beings, their very sight quickly produces delight, as if one were beholding one's own beloved wives. || 15 ||
That ground is always auspicious for all people during worship and other rites;
it is crowded with white water-lilies, blue lotuses, and kalhāra lilies, as well as cranes and other birds.
To its east is a lake, and to its west is a grove of mango trees; on the left is a great thicket of reeds, and on the right is a mountain. (17)
A site that is uniform in color and free from serpents and other such creatures is also praised; likewise, one for whom there is a pond, a well, or similar excavation in the northeast or the north.
That auspicious earth, endowed with favorable characteristics, brings about all accomplishments;
even in the heat of summer, that blessed ground has a touch as cool as the rays of the moon. (19)
That which is excessively hot in winter, or possesses flavor during the arrival of the clouds;
the sound of a bell-metal vessel, and the auspicious sounds of the lute and the flute. (20)
The sound of clay drums and kettledrums bestows the fruits of all desires;
having dug a pit of equal or half-measure, one should fill it after removing the earth.
With an excess [of qualities], it becomes excellent; with an equal amount, it is middling;
know that which is incomplete to be inferior; one should abandon that which is full of faults.
That soil in which a seed sprouts within three, five, or seven nights is proclaimed as superior, middling, or inferior, respectively.
O twice-born one, this [seat] is always praised when it slopes toward the northeast; it is unsuitable if it does not slope at all.
It is fit and very auspicious when it is elevated like the back of a tortoise and has a surface like a mirror.
Having the form of the conch, discus, mace, lotus, śrīvatsa, and garuḍa,
as well as the form of a garland and a crown, this earth bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
Therefore, any other [practice] that is contrary to this always yields undesirable results;
since it causes the loss of accomplishment, it must be avoided from afar. (26)
If a site endowed with the characteristics previously described cannot be obtained,
one should accept a site common to all, honor the mantras, and perform the sacrifice with them.
In that very place, let one perform the supreme [offering], even if it lacks the correct number; one should offer with much clarified butter where there is no ghee, in the middle region as it stands.
Having abandoned a tree that has indeed grown tall, as well as one produced from a shrine, a wall, or a palace—
having cast off that double-bodied self— one should fear it like a fetus in the womb. (29)
Then, on an auspicious and favorable day, one should perform the ritual acquisition of the ground (bhūmiparigraha) with unblemished meat, parched grain flour, and water.
When it has been fomented with oil and alkali combined with fruits and flowers, and with a collection of tactile substances along with curd, milk, and molasses; || 31 ||
With black sesamum mixed with the powder of turmeric,
one should offer the bali-oblation in the cardinal and intermediate directions as well as in the center, while reciting this mantra.
May those cruel beings for whom this portion of the earth is a refuge grant me satisfaction and proceed to the supreme abode. (33)
Having meditated upon the body as resembling a weapon and made it radiant with the Astra-mantra,
he should thereafter command the spirits and bury the earth down to the water-level.

This person is unknown; having summoned those who are equal, or perhaps one who is equal to Śama, from the street—those who are very pure, rich in fragrance, and endowed with consciousness—[he should do so]. (35)
Having filled that pit with earth, he struck the ground with a measure of one āṭhaka;
thereafter, he leveled it with even grass and the sprouts of trees, filling it with rice.
Having prepared it, he should cause a herd of cows to stay there for three days;
then, on the fourth day, having purified the ground by turning it over with ploughs, [he should proceed].
Then, it should be touched on all sides with a glowing brick;
thereafter, with gold dust, [silver dust], copper dust, and likewise with silver dust.
It is produced from jewels, enriched with perfumes and garlands, endowed with crops, rice, and fruits;
it is abundant with flowers, parched grain, and fried rice, and joined with white mustard seeds and sesame seeds.
One should sow Śrīkaraṇa seeds everywhere on the ground with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
whether the pit has been dug or not, it becomes pure at that very moment.

In whatever place one may properly perform [the rites], such as those involving grain and so forth—for the sake of purification, for the sake of auspiciousness, and specifically for the sake of purifying the site—[in that very place one should act]. (41)

But for those who perform sacrifices such as the *yāga* and *yajña* for the sake of visible and invisible fruits, when [the time] has been equated from that point until the submergence in the east, [then... 42.
Furthermore, it should be crushed repeatedly with broad pestles made from the wood of sacrificial trees.
Having made it resemble the touch of rainwater by using clay, cow dung, and water,
one should smear it and then sweep it with the hand or with a cloth.
Then, on an auspicious day and under favorable conditions, one should perform the rites for success in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Examination of the Ground," in the Pauṣkarasaṃhitā, a Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the third chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
"Tell me, according to the established tradition, that which is called the 'Characteristics of Success in the Directions'."
For the benefit of all the worlds, and especially for my own sake. || 1 ||
The Blessed One said:
O twice-born one, on a single level plot of land that slopes toward the northeast,
the east and west should be determined either by common consensus or by specific characteristics.
(6) That which is well-known,
whether acquired from a temple, a great pillar, a street, or on walls,
or inherited from one's ancestors, should be obtained.

Through the conjunction of the sun and the gnomon, with effort, the east and west are to be known for the sake of defining the directions; the center, indeed, is the means for accomplishing everything.
And I shall declare that clearly to you: wherever one may be situated and at whatever time, one should construct a sacrificial hall and so forth upon ground that is free from obstructions. (5)
One should fashion a probe from gold or other metals, four finger-breadths long,
or up to twelve mānas in length, with a head shaped like that of Nahuṣa at both ends.
Alternatively, having abandoned one-third of that measurement at its end,
one should fashion a mallet-shaped piercing on both sides at a single point.
Having understood the cloudless sky on the equinoctial day, one should join the corner of the firmly stretched thread at both ends with a gnomon. (8)
It should be as round as the little finger, made of strong wood or of very sharp metal, sixteen fingers in height, and is thus commended.

Having fixed it twelve finger-breadths into the ground and extending it twelve [finger-breadths] upwards, one should place that cord with its pins, reaching as far as the base of the *śaṅku* (the central peg).
O Pauṣkara, by means of the method for binding the girdle, the auspicious moment indeed shines forth;
then one should stretch that thread, either half of the equal measure or exactly equal.
One should mark the ground with a stylus using that thread in all directions;
it should be even with an even cubit, subtle, and possessing the characteristics of Sāketa.
And one should observe that shadow of Śaṅkavī on the circumference of its circle, O twice-born;
wherever it enters, there one should mark a point.
In the western direction, O twice-born one, and likewise in the eastern direction,
when the increase proceeds in this manner until the end of the outer sequence, || 14 ||
O twice-born one, in whatever region day and night are always equal, there alone—neither before nor after that time, nor elsewhere—does that [phenomenon] occur. || 15 ||
Where day and night are equal on a single equinoctial day,
there the east and west must be known by this specific method.

O twice-born one, when the sun has reached the equinoctial point (viṣuvatī) at the meridian line, moving from south to north, its eastern and western portions are to be discerned by means of its shadow.
Likewise, one should diligently observe whether it is situated in the western part, or in the eastern part, or located within that [area]. || 18 ||
Under its influence, the eastern quarter of the world was filled with apprehension;
likewise, in their respective lands and in other regions as well, it took on the form of a widespread rumor.
Then, having determined the sixth part from the day and night for those [places] situated on high ground, low ground, in the middle, or at a distance, one should establish the indicator.
One should employ even a small image that is consistent [with the ritual requirements] at dawn;
however, when there is a single moment of copper-colored light in a cloudless sky, one should act at that time. 21.
If the well-defined midday does not coincide with the meridian,
know that place at all times to be situated between the eastern and western junctions.
If, at midday when it is full, such a thing indeed occurs for one of that kind, then those of the Śāṅkava lineage are seen to be likewise. || 23 ||
When the eastern portion is greater, the region is to be determined by that [portion] which is grasped. || 24 ||
In Aries, the midday shadow is to be known as eight finger-breadths;
likewise, when joined with two [fingers], it becomes six in Taurus, and five finger-breadths. || 25 ||
In the sign of Gemini, it should be three finger-breadths less than four;
in Cancer, it should increase by one, two, and two finger-breadths respectively. [26]
Know that in Leo it is like Gemini; in Virgo it should be like Taurus;
in Libra it is similar to Aries; and in Scorpio it is twelve finger-breadths long.
Listen, O Brahmin, regarding the bow: it is joined with twenty-eight [fingers] and two fingers;
it is eighteen fingers long, O Brahmin, when ten fingers and two are subtracted.
In the sign of Pisces (Jhaṣa), it is twenty fingers minus thirty-two fingers;
in Aquarius (Kumbha), it should be equal to a bow; and in Pisces (Mīna), it should be as in Scorpio (Vṛścika).
That which is known as the twelfth part of the śaṅku is an aṅgula;
its sixth part should be understood as two aṅgulas.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, on this very earth,
one should first understand the middle, western, and eastern regions exactly as they are situated.
Just as previously in one's own country, one should observe the western and eastern directions;
having set up the gnomon as before and likewise drawn the mandala, (one should proceed).
O Pauṣkara, O twice-born one, one should likewise determine the western portion known as Īśa within that circular field by means of the midday shadow at its very center.
Having reflected as before, O Lotus-born One, one should then stretch a thread toward the east, and having fixed it with two threads for the east and west.
Having abandoned that [measurement] from the two directions—east and west—near the thread, the measurement is the shadow at midday; this is the divine [method] based on the directions.
One should clearly mark two points within the interval of that circular approach;
from there, one should determine the cities and other locations, O Lotus-born One. (36)
One should cast various markers at the eastern, western, and middle points;
however, when there is a difference in location, the cord should be fixed by means of the east and west.
Having fixed that thread, one should subsequently [draw] the south-north line;
then, having smoothed out that thread which was previously placed in the center of the circle.
Even if that thread were to have that same form externally as it does within that region, it would have existed there previously; [if you say] "that thread exists," [we reply: no. (39)
If one wishes to know the event that occurred on the day of sunrise by observing its position at the midpoint of that interval, using exactly the elapsed time, [then this method applies]. (40)
O Lotus-Seated One, together with the gods, by this very method, one will surely perceive the eastern quarter exactly as it is, without any doubt.
Having first filled the surface of the earth externally, in due order, with very fine lines that are numerous, distinct, and continuous, according to the previously stated measurement.
And as far as the end of the earth, one should likewise observe the shadow;
and the lines enter as if directed toward that very place. (43)
Furthermore, as for that [shadow], even by means of other shadows;
but on which [day] the ground is marked by lines, and it is truly long. (44)

One should clearly mark that spot toward the northern direction of the lines; then, having uprooted the stake, it should not move from the earth as before. Then, from the mark made by the stake situated in the northern direction—
O Lotus-born One, even for a mark situated at the base of the sacrificial post (śaṅku), [the same applies].
Having stretched out a long thread smeared with lime above,
one should [mark] the south and north directions, or from that, the east and west.
It must be thoroughly understood with diligent effort when performing rites such as the construction of temples.
Pauṣkara said:
O Lord, I wish to understand that which has been described by you:
whether it flows from east to west, from north to south, or from west to east. (48)
The Blessed One said:
Having divided the peg-thread into two parts, there will clearly be an obstacle in the middle;
having fixed the thread right there, one should not rise up from it, being of a single-minded intent.
O twice-born one, with that second thread used for covering, he should mark the rotation of that wheel with his hand by means of two points in two directions.
Within those two, with a long thread stretched between them,
he should mark each one— the southern and the northern— with both hands.
O Brahmin, it should be like the tip of a vajra, having the form of two joined parts.
A thread of the desired length should be cast into the middle of that;
thus, O Pauṣkara, the measure of the center for the four directions is produced.
Then, by means of the desired measurement, one should construct the square,
which is the progenitor for the house, the mandala, the lotus, and so forth, for the practitioner.
One should again mark it with the central thread and the directional threads;
then, having placed the measurement of the threads for the marks corresponding to the number of directions.
Having marked the cardinal directions and the intermediate points with the previously mentioned marks,
one should then cast four lines connecting each mark to its opposite.
O Great Sage, for one who is uncertain, the field should be made quadrangular by means of the subsequent laying of the thread,
for the sake of accomplishing the construction of the sacrificial altar (sviṣṭi).
O Brahmin, a person standing there according to the prescribed rite is worthy of worship; furthermore, O sage, there is the shadow that arises from the omnipresent Lord Viśvarūpa.
And having divided the ground of the sacrificial hall into nine equal parts in all directions with threads smeared with lime, (59)
Having thus diligently fashioned that [mandala] consisting of eighty-one parts, one should,
for each [square], draw a lotus using a fourth part of that [area].
There should also be a pair of eight petals, provided with a pericarp and filaments,
as well as [petals] in the outer corner positions of Agni, Īśa, Rakṣas, and Vāyu.
That which is a set of four lotuses consists solely of four petals;
one should perform worship beginning from the lotus at the foot of Īśāna.
In the lotuses of the outer rows, one should place the gods, the celestial beings, and the sages in sequence;
within the pericarp of the lotus at the foot of the Bull-bannered Lord, however, one should place Brahmā.
One should place Īśvara, Tapana, Diti, and likewise Aditi,
beginning from the eastern petal and proceeding as far as the northern one.
Having thus worshipped the pentad upon that lotus-foot,
one should then properly worship the seven deities.

Successively, upon the pericarp of the lotuses situated at the seven steps, one should place Ravi and the deity Satyātman; then, in the lotus-foot of Agni, one should again firmly install Pitāmaha in the center and [the other deities] on the eastern petal.
Having thus worshipped the pervasive Gagana in the south, west,
and north, one should likewise worship the four [deities] situated upon the petals within the corner lotuses.
Then, one should worship seven lotuses extending to the south-western corner:
Savitṛ, Sāvitra, Svastyayanī, and Grahakṣama.
Vivasvān, the god of Dharma, is remembered as the lord of the Gandharvas;
he is situated in the lotus located in the southwest corner (Nairṛtakoṇa), further within the interior of Brahmā.
(9) Bhṛṅga, Bhṛṅgarāja, and then the Lord of the Pitṛ-gaṇas;
the two deities known as Dvāparikas—[variant: the two Parighas and Kās]—occupy the four eastern petals. (71)
Then, having sequentially placed the seven deities within the eight petals of the lotus—
starting from the pericarp and extending as far as the quarter of Vāyu— [72]
Indra, and he who is called Indrapada, Sugrīva, Kusumadvija, the one named Mitra, Varuṇa, and you again as the Lord of the Gods (Surādhipati). 73.
In the lotus-petal of Vāyu, one should place Prajāpati in the center;
in the petals starting from the east, one should place Śeṣa and Adharma.
Then one should worship me, the Lord, and immediately after that the King of Nāgas;
thereafter, one should worship the group of seven deities as before.
Pūrvākhya, Rudradāsa, Mukhya, Bhallaka, Somaka, Dhārādhara, and those known as Matsas—these are the hosts of deities. (76)
After having performed worship, one should thereafter worship the Lord of the Site (Vāstunātha), who resides within the center of each individual lotus, by means of his own name.
One should worship him beneath the filaments of the lotuses situated in the corner sections;
one should worship with the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ) followed by "Salutation to the Lord of Vāstu" at the end.
There, one should fill [the vessel] with the eightfold lotus and worship it according to the prescribed rite with the eight syllables, using flowers, incense, and other offerings. (79)
Having first thus worshipped the host of gods with curd, milk, water, and various foods including fruits and roots, within both the external and internal faculties; 80.
Then, starting again from the northeast corner (Īśakoṇa), one should [place] the lotus-feet of those intermediate quarters,
with Brahmā [at the center], in a clockwise direction like a serpent’s coil.
Having filled as far as the central lotus-petal with eight syllables,
according to the distinctions of the Mātṛkā letters in the sequence beginning with the letter 'a'.
Up to the letter ṛ, one should worship the host of deities in each lotus and upon its petals according to that very same sequential method.
And now learn from me regarding the second enclosure and the intermediate space:
Dhātṛ, Yantṛ, Dhruva, Kālamān, and Kartṛ—one should worship them there. 84.

He is the living soul, the one who causes the breaths to move, the sacrifice, the unchanging, and the primordial source; he is indeed the Lord of the worlds, the Ordainer, the Blessed One, the Creator, and the Restrainer.
O Lotus-born One, those who are not virtuous, as well as Indra, the Viśvedevas, the creators, and Viśvakarman—these are the ones [who follow]. 86.
The deities within the intermediate space are to be worshipped in the number twenty-four;
listen further regarding these in the third enclosure.
Then, from that [number], the count of the sixteen groups of deities, the oceans, the other continents, the months, the channels, and the stars [is derived]. (88)
The Viśvedevas, the Apsarases, the Manus, and likewise the Ṛṣis;
the Vasus, the Maruts, the Siddhas, the Nāgas, the Sādhyas, and the Mi[...]. (89)
At his feet and so forth, however, in the middle of the petals of nine lotuses— || 90 ||
One should worship the Lord of universal form, situated upon the petals in the central lotus, whose circle of deities is thus accompanied by mounts and weapons. (91)
It remains joined within the body of every great-souled being, together with the *praṇava*, one’s own name, and a salutation. (92)
One should worship each deity individually, as well as each syllable of the twice-born (the mantra),
in this manner, O Lotus-born One, either in the northern direction or in the eastern one.

One should extract the field that is secluded; field after field, field after field, one should bring it into the state of the Fourth (*turya*) through the path of the sons. Because the field of the site (*vāstukṣetra*), which is the glory of the Fourth, bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*). 94.
(10) All supernatural powers (siddhis), whether manifest or unmanifest, are always operative for men;
through universality or through the absence of modification, there arises eternal peace. || 95 ||
For this very reason, that field must be cultivated with great effort, since it is from it that the perfections (siddhis) are established for the sake of liberation. 96.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Attainment of the Directions," in the *Pauṣkarasaṃhitā*, a great Upaniṣad within the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Pauṣkara said: "O Lord of Gods, for what purpose was the square (caturaśra) described by you?"
Therefore, specify by measurement the temples and other structures for the sacrifices.
The Blessed One said:
Having ascertained that the measurement of the mandala is well-prepared, or else, having taken a measurement from the mandala even if its dimensions are not yet prepared; || 2 ||
Furthermore, what is the proof for its being called "bhūti" (prosperity) in that sense? It is simply the measure of the whirling of those who have become powerful.
Having understood this, one should subsequently construct either a wall or a mandala.
Pauṣkara said: O Teacher of the World,

please describe in detail the extent of the ground for the sacrificial rites, beginning with the placement of the weapons, as well as the common rules regarding the measurements of the *praṇītā* vessels.

The Blessed One said: When the sun shines through a lattice window, there appears a mass of dust; that is what constitutes an atom (paramāṇu). Eight of those atoms are traditionally reckoned as one aṇu.
O Lotus-born One, eight of those atoms (aṇu) make one nit (likṣā);
know that eight nits make one louse (yūkā), and eight lice make one barley-corn (yava).
An *aṅgula* consists of eight barley-corns (*yava*) produced from their standard measure;
indeed, two such *aṅgulas* shall be known as a *golaka* and a *kala*.
And the *tāla* known as *ṣaṭkala* is prescribed for the performance of the *madhyanīna*;
O Brahmin, it consists of twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) of the hand.
By that same measure of a cubit, arising from the teacher and the disciple, one should everywhere establish the conceptualization at the beginning of the mandala and so forth. 9.
The measurement for the various sacrificial altars (*pramāṇayāga*) is proclaimed to be twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) for the first [type], according to the single standard of the earth. || 10 ||

The second [section] consists of eighteen and twenty-four [verses], and the following is supreme. From one finger-breadth (aṅgula) there are trembling and other states; from three finger-breadths there are four finger-breadths. 11.
According to the measurement of sixteen finger-breadths, the sacrificial offering (naivedya) for the virtuous is superior;
then there are those measuring one and a half cubits, two cubits, and likewise one and a half cubits.
The pathway for the sacrifices is declared to be of very little width;
it is the lowest type when two cubits long, the middle when [two cubits], and that which is three cubits long is the highest.
An altar measuring one and a half cubits is considered most auspicious;
it should be made for various types of extensive sacrifices that differ in form.
The circumference of the wheel called *yuga* is known to be four cubits, or else six *golaka*s; its diameter is remembered as two [cubits]. || 15 ||
One should prepare a ground for them that is distinct from the sacrificial offerings and flowers, which are twelve finger-breadths in height and lack the annual [measure]. || 16 ||
One should prepare the weapons, as ordained by me for you;
one should fashion them on the ground, each distinct from the others. || 17 ||
And for the sacrificial canopies, it should be equal to the height of the entire [structure];
one should also construct the extent of the ground, beginning with the weapon-mantra (astra) and ending at the circumference of the circle.
The measurement of the sacrificial ground (yāga) is appropriately from one cubit up to five cubits;
however, a measurement exceeding six cubits results in deficiency or excess for this [rite]. || 19 ||
Know that the medium size is up to twelve cubits, whether it be slightly less or slightly more; beyond that measurement, it is recorded as large.
Having carefully considered the dimensions for the sacrificial hall and so forth, one should then construct it according to its defining characteristics.

O Brahmin, for houses with very small mandalas, one should calculate the width of the walls as one cubit, or perhaps one and a half cubits. (Note: The four half-verses beginning with "vaipulyam" are missing from manuscript *kh*.)
O Lotus-born one, for the middle class of practitioners, the wall of the sacrificial hall should be two cubits in height and its width should correspond to the breadth of the walls.
One should construct it with a height of four, five, six, seven, or eight cubits according to one's desire; this earth [altar] should be used during the conjunctions (saṅgava) as well.
O best of the twice-born, it should be nine cubits high, or ten, or eleven;
having always prepared the assembly of devotees, one should perform the central measurement.
One should likewise fashion the span of the outstretched arms as twelve cubits long, or even one more than that,
or fourteen cubits in height.
For this mandala master, there may always be either a deficiency or an excess;
however, the measurement of the wall is threefold, depending on that [measurement] at midday.
O Lotus-born One, Māyā is to be conceptualized by means of number, and indeed along with its successive increase in magnitude. (28)

The construction of a sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa) made of wood, baked bricks, and mixed materials, and plastered with lime, is sattvic; it is highly praised and bestows all perfections (siddhis). || 29 ||
One should perform [the rites] at the proper time and in the proper place according to one's wealth;
for small sacrificial halls, one should provide a single door.
In the middle, in the eastern quarter, and likewise in the western;
by abandoning the intermediate directions, it becomes a door that grants success.
Therefore, one should diligently establish [the deities] from the center toward the directions;
for houses of medium size, there are two doors, one in the east and one in the west. (32)
One should likewise arrange four gates in each direction for the various types of very extensive enclosures.
For those [temples] that are deficient by three [parts], one should make the height one and a half [times the width];
for the middle [category], it is prescribed as being increased by a fourth part of its own width.
One should determine the height of the door by the rear portion of the others; its width, moreover, should be known as one-third of that height. (35)
The width of the pair of door-frames and the pair of udumbara-beams shall be less than their height by one-eighth.
The thickness of those [objects], such as the śaṅku and so forth, should be made one-fourth for the middling ones and one-third for the superior ones, according to half of their width. 37.
That [mandala] is endowed with nine branches according to the sequence of five times seven;
at each door, it is established with two branches at the fourth part.
One should establish the two-fold stability everywhere [in the sense that "the two-fold situated" exists everywhere], according to the sequence of one's own directional sectors;
[specifically,] Vajranābha and Harīśa in the east, south, and north.
He holds a conch and a discus, as well as a vajra and a cane-staff;
he is engaged in the gesture of prohibition (niṣedha), with his hands placed upon the slope of his hips.
One should fashion the multitude of eyes, which resembles the nature of the oblation,
as being cruel, endowed with wondrous vision, and having a vajra at its center.
In the same way, one should represent Hariśa as devoid of the gesture of prohibition,
but marked by the hand known for the gesture of entry.
For here, one indeed effects the exclusion of those who are not devotees, while another grants entry to the devotees. (43)
At every door, there is this purpose for a pair of doorkeepers.

"The Superintendent of Dharma and the Controller [are on the right, and the one on the right and the north]"—these syllables are seen; this has fallen into error, belonging to the final quarter of the immediately preceding half-verse. 44.
In one [hand], he should hold an arrow and a bow; on the right upper arm, he should fashion two arms resembling those of Antaka (Yama), adorned as before. 45.
But [the two] holding staff and mace in their hands, devoid of the thunderbolt and discus, [represent] Śuddhākṣa and Amṛtānanda, starting from the south in the western direction. (46)
In one hand he holds a bow and arrow, and likewise a noose in another;
his other four hands remain undisturbed as before. (47)
Indeed, in form they were always like the Lord of Waters;
to the north and south of the Lord of Wealth, [there were] Sudhānanda and Udak. 48.
With sword and mallet in their hands, the remaining four [deities] are as previously described; the form of these two hands should be made identical to that of the Moon.
Then, accompanied by cranes, lotuses, and water-fowls, with rows of conch shells,
and joined by the Yamunā— the mistress who protects Rāma—
she was endowed with the splendor of full jars and attended by lordly serpents and cranes. || 51 ||

O twice-born one, one should adorn the two door-posts with an udumbara fruit placed above; according to this view, the udumbara is decorated with figures of serpents, lions, elephants, horses, and so forth. || 52 ||
One should never perform what was previously mentioned [if it is] improper;
the door should be elevated by one-third [of the height], and its triple ornamentation [should be] half of that elevation. || 53 ||
Having fashioned such a multitude of windows with branches and other ornaments for Dvāravatī,
one should complete it with a count of two, four, and six, including the directional pillars.
One should fashion two very beautiful pigeon-cornices for the doors equipped with latticed windows, arranged in rows and decorated with various paintings, or alternatively, let them project outward.

O twice-born one, having determined the construction of the walls, one should gradually investigate the doors and other features, as well as the parts made of wood or iron, along with the surrounding enclosure.
Now, learn of the arrangement of pillars for pavilions;
that which is very small for the assembly of sacrificial halls is devoid of pillars.
I shall tell you how one should construct the remaining pillars;
[they should be] all around the sacrificial ground that is adjacent to the ground for the offerings (balibhūmi). || 58 ||
Having abandoned the ground from the site of the earth-jewel, the placement of the pillars is prescribed;
according to the *Pauṣkara*, the four directions beginning with the east are determined by the central thread.
Having inspected them all, one should place a row of pillars there for the purpose of worship; for one who has sat down, it should be done with the pillar according to the proper sequence.
One should worship continuously between the pillars according to the following numbers:
four, eight, four, and twice eight.
Having ascertained the extent of the pavilion, there should be twenty-four pillars, or thirty-two, or even double that number plus half.
And the pillars, O twice-born one, should be well-rounded, or else eight-sided,
twelve-sided, or sixteen-sided, and they may be endowed with various decorative motifs.

O twice-born one, it should be half the width of the remaining space, or equal to its splendor; furthermore, the thickness should be according to availability and in consideration of the expenditure. || 64 ||
Then, having entered through the wall, he beheld the group of maidens, adorned with seats and other furnishings, numbering four more than the pillars.
Is there a fixed rule? O Pauṣkara, this rule applies everywhere;
however, wherever pillars exist that have not been conquered by men, there [the rite] should be performed together with pillars.
Like sixty-four pillars in a square, one should place the other full abodes, the group of four, and the maidens. 67.
O Mahāmati, for the arrangement of the pillars and so forth, one should perform the expansion of those [pillars] with a measurement of two and a half parts. 68.
O Lotus-born one, its thickness should be one-third of its own width;
in this manner, groups of pillars in pairs were formerly arranged by the Saṅgha.
Having done that, one should subsequently place the collection of weights upon it;
now listen as I describe how the covering for the top should be made. (70)
Having first constructed a wall-enclosure for the group of maidens by means of skillful artifice,
he bound them with fetters of black iron and other materials, just as he had previously brought about the dissolution of his elder brother.
Just as necklaces, earrings, and bracelets cannot be uprooted [from their places], so too the measurement of four, five, or three cubits is fixed as the four-cornered [area]. || 72 ||
Then, in front of the pillars of the sacrificial ground, a Garuda-banner (or a Brahmin banner,
if one prefers) should be firmly held up by strong, very clear, and well-secured bamboo poles.
Having carefully bound the head of the pillar-maiden with a *vetula* [reed], one should first place the root-mantra upon the wall; nothing else, O Goddess, should be placed there. (74)
Having pierced the root [of the pillar] from that point, one should place an arm upon that wooden beam;
this is the characteristic of the thick fourth part of the vertical line hanging from the wall.
Likewise, O twice-born one, with many thick pillars made of solid wood, equal in size to the columns and the pilasters.
And one should provide a binding with iron vessels, as well as with many pegs, chains, and the like, so that it may become immovable. (77)
Then, O Pauṣkara, at the region of the root of the balance (tulāmūla),
one should construct a great mass of head-stones (śīrṣagaṇa) above the jointed section using bricks and plaster.
Then, is it like the form of the moon, or like the essence of the *aṅka*? Is it the sky appearing in various ways as it unfolds? Above that is the void, the courtyard of the radiant one. (79)
One should construct the path known as *trimaṇī* (or *kramaṇī*), which extends from the wall to the base of the pillar;
all that rises above the beams should be completed down to the level of the wall-base.
Together with the groups of clay and wood, it does not perish by means of powder;
such is the condition of the one whose mind is balanced, having established this state for a year.
One should further establish its position in front; it should be firmly fixed upon the pillars, the base-sections, and the necks (or ears), being highly meritorious and stable. 82.
And that end of the balance which has gone out, one should place upon his head;
together with the balance, one should generally bind his arm with a weapon. || 83 ||
Together with kinnaras, uragas, gandharvas, yakṣas, and vidyādharas,
they should be depicted as holding scales while sporting with their beloveds.
Then, O Lotus-born One, having placed a slightly elevated series of pillars well-fastened at the edge of the scales, all around— (85)
One should provide a million-fold weight for the pegs, the covering, and that which stands upon it, as well as for the upward-extending pillars. || 86 ||
One should place that equal-weight [object] upon the raised arm, which has been extended while bent;
it should rest first upon the scale through the very nature of its fragrance.
For him as well, one should apply the binding as before, together with the balance; let it be adjusted by means of the two upper arms joined crosswise. (88)
First, one should again place [the image] with its forearms extended at the tip of the balance;
thereafter, for those who are peerless, [one should place it] in front of the lineage succession.
One should gradually contract the tip of the silver [tube], like a lotus that has not yet fully blossomed,
by means of very light bamboo rods extended obliquely in succession.
That [space] should then be filled up to the edge and covered with thin,
light, and firm wooden panels.
Alternatively, what [should be used] for the support—whether made of bricks or of stone?
One should employ four or three [units] on each wall, and likewise apply the *pralayas*. (92)

In the midst of the moons upon his heads and of the sandalwood paste not yet fallen away, there was at times the scent arising from clouds, or rather, for the sake of the vehicle of the cloud [the reading "for the sake of the vehicle" applies everywhere]. || 93 ||
In a place endowed with the back of a foot [a sacred site], at a time duly acquired,
for the sake of the swift accomplishment of the rite, one should prepare an auspicious image made of reeds and wood.
One should construct a wall provided with windows and adorned with gateways, covered at the top by a canopy.
For those who have performed sacrifices free from passion, there is the direction [of the quarters], like the offering of one whose self is tranquil;
and for women, there are various distinctions made with red chalk, saffron, and other substances. || 96 ||
For those intended for long-term use,
however, one should construct a high, very firm, and large enclosure wall made of baked bricks and similar materials for the purpose of protection.
It should be square, well-rounded, or triangular, pleasing to the mind, appropriate for the worship of the sacrifice, endowed with the knowledge of that [mandala], and firm. (98)

Having thus constructed the pavilion by means of proper technique, one should then prepare within its center a firm, level surface, shaped like the pavilion itself and slightly sloping toward the northeast.
And the ground should be especially elevated and like a mirror,
so that the earth beneath the pavilion does not appear level.
O Pauṣkara, for those eager to perform worship, [the measurement] should be made starting from one finger-breadth and increasing up to eight finger-breadths in height. 101.
For those with small chambers, one should always construct a platform (sthalāgaṇa) by increasing [the height] by one unit,
from a height of nine finger-breadths up to fifteen finger-breadths.
The elevation of the raised platforms and the central chambers should range from sixteen finger-breadths up to twenty-four finger-breadths. (103)
And as before, the form of the Gaṇa’s elder brother should be made with increasing proportions;
this height has been described by you for the various sites.

First, one should construct the foundations with bricks and other materials, extending a quarter, a half, or a full cubit in width in all directions. Then, after that, [the structure] should be built up.
Having filled its interior with clay mixed with a small amount of sand,
and having subsequently examined it for hair, insects, and the like, one should ensure it is free from impurities.

One should examine the site for seven days—having specifically observed whether it possesses the previously mentioned characteristics or other particular qualities—and ensure it is situated in the center of the ground, delightful, and elevated. (107)

O Brahmin, one should not give [the materials] in such a way that a division occurs; rather, having first established [the image] upon a pedestal provided with an altar and archways, it shall then become fit for sacrifice.
Outside, near the four corners and not far from them,
there should be a structure provided with four legs, even if it possesses many pillars.
O best among those who know the Vedas, one should place the foot-steps at the four cardinal directions from the center of the fourteen [squares], within equal intervals. 110.
It consists of four times twelve quarters, endowed with twenty feet;
or it may consist of a continuous succession of quarter-verses increased by eight times eight.
In that sacrificial hall, a beautiful row of pillars was formerly erected, consisting of twenty distinct supporting members produced from the expansion of *kṣamā*.
Having fixed four archways in this [mandala] in the four directions,
one should properly place three in each individual direction.
Having understood that the width of the pavilion should be five or seven [parts],
in a house devoid of pillars, it should be provided with a pedestal and arches.
One should perform [the rite] endowed with the proper characteristics; understand what that is:
first by means of general measurement, and then indeed by means of specific measurement. (115)
With purifying sacrificial wood—firm, straight, and even—the staffs on the scale were raised up, each increased by its own respective proportionate parts. || 116 ||
O best among those who know the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, it should be auspicious in its height;
by that same proportion for its length, one should make it with an increase of one-quarter.
The height of the archways (toraṇas) is such that their width is one-third of that;
this includes the entire collection of pillars, excluding the group of upper pillars.
Having divided [the space] into three equal parts, the upper portion should be circular;
that which is second, situated below it, one should complete as an octagon.
The third, however, is square and situated below each of those respective parts;
all of them have handles to be held and are circular on all sides.
Or one should make them square, endowed with various ritual functions,
and provided with flowers, flower-clusters, leaves, and birds.

Due to the thickness being three, four, five, six, or seven [parts], it shall be eight finger-breadths; however, if it exceeds by one-eighth, one should subtract that from the earth [the height] by means of the Vedas (four). 122.
One should place another arch of equal size on the ground, consisting of a portion of the twice-born;
thus has the general measurement and its defining characteristics been duly described.
O sir, listen to the specific details of the Veda-staves:
having set aside one-sixth part from above the base of Hari, it should measure five parts.
O Lotus-born One, the measurement of the arch (toraṇa) is one-twelfth of this;
its middle third is equal, and it is fixed to the ground upon all the staffs.
O Lotus-born One, one should construct the height of the archway upon the principal, elevated, and essential parts of the walls or the houses,
within a palace provided with pillars.
One should make it equal to the height of the pillar; one should place that staff upon the ground.
Indeed, by measuring from the top of the pillar with a slightly greater length, that very same [measurement] is obtained.
Having determined the measurement by means of a height equal to one-quarter of the pillar,
the width of the arches (toraṇas) is established as being situated within the pillars.
O best among the knowers of the Vedas, that [form] should be fashioned in the likeness of the Lord of the Gods,
situated between two wheels and adorned with a circle of eyelashes.
At every archway, one should fashion a Garuḍa standing upright;
then, one should have the Tūperaśramapāra painted with its various colors. (130)
By sages, perfected beings, and immortals who witness many wonders;
by the guardians of the quarters, forest groves, and many leaders of deer herds.
One should diligently make the entire sacrificial hall pleasing to the eye, either by smearing it with lime-plaster or by decorating it thereafter. (132)
With mirrors, chowries, garments, and various brilliant silk cloths; with bells, crescent moons, and other ornaments, and with beautiful parasols. || 133 ||
One should decorate the area above the altar with a variegated canopy, either pure white or brilliant,
provided with a lattice of lotus centers.
From the north-eastern direction as far as the north-western corner,
one should fix there banners arising from the distinctions of colors such as white and so forth.
Thus, by means of the division of passion (rāga) and again from the western portion,
the rule for the southern direction extends up to the second group of four.
One should construct both with a single [measure], and all [the other parts] as well; one should arrange the archway and the canopy in a uniform manner. || 137 ||
Listen attentively to how the eight banners are to be installed,
beginning from the southeast corner and extending as far as the northeast corner.
One should make the four colors white, reddish, yellow, and black;
furthermore, O twice-born one, from the northern quarter as far as the western direction.
A group of four such [flags] is proclaimed as the *dhvajas*;
it has the luster of the color of royal stone (*rājapāṣāṇa*) and is approached by the Lord of Birds (*cakrapakṣīśvara*). 140.
One should fashion three Vaijayantī banners on the arch situated in the eastern direction;
that on the south should have the luster of crystal, while that on the west should have the brilliance of vermilion.
And on the northern archway, one should place three banners with a golden luster,
joined by four pennons of white and other colors.
At each gateway (toraṇa), there should be three or five [arches];
and the length of the banners shall be half the width of the gateway.
One should always make the width of those banners one and a half parts;
as for the height of the banners, O Lotus-born One, it should be as previously described.
One should make it equal to half the height of the archway; its width should be one-third of that very [height].
It should be provided with banners, weapons, and vehicles in the respective sections, but without the attendants.
All the deities of the directions should be fashioned according to their respective positions;
in this very manner, they are likewise placed at the well-proportioned doors.
The eight external groups of attendants begin with Caṇḍa and end with Subhadra;
the supreme eight elemental spirits (bhūtas) are the internal group beginning with Kumuda.
The height of the archways (toraṇa) is declared to be one-fourth of their length;
and the length [of the arches] is one-fourth of the width. || 148 ||
One should meditate upon Purandara, who resembles a hundred suns and has four arms;
one should remember the red-hued Hutāśana (Fire) mounted upon a goat, holding a spear in his hand,
filled with thousands of rays, and as radiant as a thousand suns.
One should meditate upon the Lord Īśvara as being seated upon a great buffalo, possessing a luster like a mountain of collyrium, most terrifying, and holding a staff in his hand. 151.
One should meditate upon the Lord of the Rākṣasas, who has a face made terrible by fangs, whose splendor is like a black cloud, who is formidable, who sits upon a corpse, and who wields a sword. 152.
The lord of waters, resembling the luster of pearls, with his noose of frost uplifted in hand, seated upon a makara and surrounded by thousands of nāga maidens. (153)
One should meditate upon the god Samīraṇa, who resembles a dark blue cloud, is marked with a great banner and a footprint, and is seated upon a deer. (154)
One should meditate upon the Moon, accompanied by hosts of stars, white as a conch shell or cow’s milk, seated upon the back of a large hare, the maker of night. 155.
One should meditate upon Īśāna, the wise one, whose limbs are smeared with white ashes, who has three eyes, whose vehicle is a bull, and who holds a trident as a weapon in his hand.
One should meditate upon Halāyudha, situated in the direction of Pātāla, mounted upon a tortoise;
he is white, possessing a thousand hoods, and is the king of serpents named Ananta.

One should meditate upon the Lord, the eternal, unborn, and all-pervading Prajāpati, who is mounted upon a swan, established in his own state, holding a staff in his hand, and causing the earth-circle (or the two circles) to revolve. 158.
All these have four arms, are adorned with rosaries, always contemplate the supreme reality, and grant boons and fearlessness with their hands. (159)
O twice-born one, they have their limbs smeared with divine ornaments, are endowed with celestial garlands and garments, possess divine forms, and waft a divine fragrance. (160)
O Brahmin, from these [four], the bull-bannered Lord is known as four-armed;
others have two arms, holding weapons in their hands, or bestowing boons and fearlessness.
Thus has it been stated regarding the Lords of the World (Lokeśvaras); now the meditation on Caṇḍa and the others, as well as that of the external retinues, is correctly described in due order.
Resembling the rising sun, broad-chested, and four-armed;
tall with elevated shoulders, his limbs were well-proportioned yet not excessively fleshy. || 163 ||
He had a thick belly, a deep navel, and was adorned with a line of body hair;
his face was formidable with fangs, and his beard and eyes were tawny.
With eyes honey-brown and joined by curved, creeper-like eyebrows, with long and swaying ears, a broad nose, and a smiling face; || 165 ||
Adorned with earrings, decorated with necklaces and armlets, his forehead bound with a turban and graced by dark hair; || 166 ||
Wearing white garments and adorned with garlands, one should meditate upon his right pair of arms as holding a raised discus and a blazing mace in the other. 167.
And she is seated upon the slope of her hips, resting on the surface of the earth;
in her left hand she holds a conch shell, and in the other, a rosary of beads.
Thus the fierce Lord of the Gaṇas, unconquered by valor, being enraged, is capable of gradually destroying tens of thousands of obstacles. || 169 ||
Having invoked [the deity] at the archway standing in front of the Lord of Mantras,
one should place it there so that it is to the right of the Sovereign.
Indeed, he should always be on the left side of the Guru or the sacrificer;
in that very same place, on the other side, one should likewise install Pracaṇḍa (or one resembling Pracaṇḍa). || 171 ||
However, there may be a reversal by means of the left and right arms;
for Caṇḍa, it is proclaimed that [the mudrā] is formed with both arms on the left side.
On the right, one should likewise visualize the two attendants of Pracaṇḍa;
they resemble the interior of a lotus and possess such formidable prowess.
Wearing red garments, adorned with red garlands and red unguents,
the two deities Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ stand as attendants on the right side.
Dark as the flax flower, adorned with yellow garlands and garments, wearing yellow turbans, fierce, and possessing arms adorned as before. (175)
And one should likewise place the two attendants named Jaya and Vijaya on the western side—those who bear fierce forms, are difficult to behold, and are hard to overcome. (176)
And [the two] are as white as milk-jars, dressed in blue silk garments, their bodies adorned with flowers having the hue of dark blue clouds. || 177 ||
One should place Bhadra and Subhadra, who resemble the previously mentioned groups and are so named,
from the two pillars of the archway toward the northern direction of the Mantramūrti.
These eight lords of the Gaṇas are indeed identical in the form of their bodies and faces, as well as in their ornaments and weapons, except for their radiance, flowers, and garments. (179)
They are both intent upon severing the web of obstacles for their devotees—which stands in every direction and yields the fruits of saṃsāra. (180)
All of them stood facing one another in uniform postures,
accompanied by tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands of Gaṇeśas who bore bodies of various colors.
Surrounded by those solely devoted to the propitiation of Acyuta,
there were then two leaders of the Gaṇas, worthy of worship, standing before the Lord of the World.
Kumuda and Kumudākṣa, with serene faces and eyes, resembled the snowy mountain and were in the prime of their youth. (183)
O twice-born one, their limbs were smeared with various ornaments, they were adorned with various earrings,
endowed with various garlands, and wearing various crowns.
With their limbs smeared with various perfumes and adorned with various garments, the right hand of the Lord of the Gaṇas named Kumuda should be meditated upon in the right hand. 185.
Adorned with a fly-whisk resembling a ray of the moon,
one should meditate on the second right hand as bestowing fearlessness.
For others who have taken refuge in the teaching of his virtues out of a desire to destroy worldly existence, there is his very first left hand, with a fully blossomed lotus raised up. (187)
One should meditate on the supreme hand of the one situated outside, which is silent and indicative of fear;
these two hands of Kumudākṣa should be visualized in reverse order.
With two hands each, it is exactly the same for the others;
both Puṇḍarīka and Vāmana possess a splendor like that of the consumer of oblations (Agni).
Having made the two hands hold the *garuḍadhvaja* (the Garuda-banner), and having performed the remaining [rites] as previously described—
whether by meditating upon them or by performing the ritual placement (*nyāsa*)— one should place them in the southern shrine of the Lord.
The one named Śaṅkukarṇa and Sarvanetra of Pauṣkara—these two, who have the luster of campaka flowers, are both intent upon raising peacock-feather fans. (191)
Of the Lord Mahāvibhūti, Sumukha and Supratiṣṭha are situated on the western and northern directions, respectively, on the left side of the All-pervading One.
The two [deities] Mudgaphala and Śyāma are to be visualized holding parasols in their raised hands;
know that for the remaining hands, whatever was not specifically mentioned, they hold up night-lotuses.
O Brahmin, these inner qualities of the Blessed One have been described by me;
with their minds absorbed in his being, they [serve him] through action, mind, and speech. (194)
It was filled with millions of supreme beings endowed with the six qualities beginning with knowledge, as well as with infinite perfected ones (siddhas) who were seeking the highest state. 195.
When this has been done, thereafter, having smeared the altar together with the arches using fragrant substances such as sandalwood and other scents brilliant in color, in due order.
Having anointed it with sandalwood paste, he should place it in the northern direction;
having prepared a pedestal with milk, sandalwood, and saffron.
With hrivera mixed with the powder of rajani and water,
along with the two auspicious herbs, he [should sprinkle] the doors and the interior of the pavilion.
Then, O twice-born one, he should fumigate [the area] with many various incenses until it takes on the appearance of the world of Vairāja or resembles Śvetadvīpa. (199)
Having thus prepared the excellent sacrificial grove for the mantra-form [of the deity],
for the purpose of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) of the devotees, ending with the ritual ablution (abhiṣeka).
One should complete everything there, up to the enjoyments and liberation taught in the scriptures;
this is appropriate by entering through a single [door], except for the direction facing the foremost part of the sacrificial altar.
One should construct the sacrificial pavilion in one of the three desired directions, provided with exits for the smoke and adorned with various sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas). 202.
It was provided with clarified butter and palāśa leaves, joined with arches and other ornaments;
it was fashioned from three kinds of silk and adorned with a girdle-string.
O Lotus-born One, having wrapped all the reed-staves of the altar with *darbha* grass whose roots and tips are unbroken, [one should proceed]. 204.
(19) At the site of Bhauma, according to the respective divisions, with *darbha* grasses having many tips,
he seemed to shake his very self on all sides with the spotted deer. (205)
Having smeared [the ground] with earth mixed with cow dung according to the prescribed rite,
one should fumigate it with guggulu resin combined with clarified butter and then perform the fire-oblation (homa).
Then, being the very essence of the mantra and being well-pleased, he utterly consumes all worldly misfortunes as well as those of his devotees, like fire in the midst of a flame.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Sacrificial Pavilion," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, which is a Mahopaniṣad within the glorious Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Pauṣkara said: O Lord of the gods of gods, please describe in due order the sacrifices beginning with the Bhadra.
By seeing which, the initiate (samayin) perpetually attains the status of a spiritual son (putraka). || 1 ||
The Blessed One said: "The mandala called Sarvatobhadra, which brings about welfare, is remembered as the first;
the second is named Aghanirmocana, by the mere sight of which [one is liberated from sin]."
Furthermore, the impurity accumulated over many lifetimes goes to destruction;
the third [aspect] is the true essence, which reveals the path of Dharma (or the path of action).
The fourth is called Dharma, for through its worship one bestows righteousness;
the fifth is Vasugarbha, which increases the wealth of devotees.
The sixth sacrifice, which grants all desires and bestows the fruits of one's wishes,
is declared to be the slayer of enemies and the destroyer of the hosts of adversaries.
O Pauṣkara, the "Aṣṭaka" (the group of eight) is proclaimed everywhere as that which bestows long life; by the mere sight of it, one attains supreme longevity and abandons untimely death.
The ninth is Balabhadra, which brings about an abundance of strength and energy;
the tenth is named Pauṣṭika, which indeed bestows nourishment through worship.
Then there is the twelfth [chapter], named Viveka, which bestows health, destroys all diseases, and produces results consistent with its name.
Beyond this, there is the supreme sacrifice known by the name Vāgīśa;
by the mere sight of which the power of speech is set in motion.
The fourteenth is the mental [offering], which produces joy through vision;
thereafter is the fifteenth sacrifice, named Jaya, which bestows victory.
The sixteenth, O Brahmin, is called Svastika; by worshipping it, one becomes a maker of well-being (svastikṛt).
Furthermore, the name of this supreme sacrifice is proclaimed as Ananta.
The eighteenth name, "Nitya" (the Eternal), bestows eternal satisfaction; by its mere sight, it swiftly grants the attainment of infinite bliss.
O twice-born one, because it is the dwelling place of the spirits, this mandala is named Bhūtāvāsa; by seeing it, living beings shall eternally achieve mastery over the spirits.
Beyond this, there is the sacrifice known as Amogha, by which,
when it is performed, the sense of "mine" in embodied beings is indeed turned away from the ocean of existence.
Therefore, he who has been properly honored by someone,
upon being seen with supreme devotion, shall indeed attain peace of mind. (15)
Therefore, it is declared that the intellect is the support; for by worshipping it, one attains the firm establishment of the intellect and Brahman in its own state.
It should be known that the mandala where the Puṣkara resides is called Guṇākara;
by meditation and worship, the multitude of qualities within the heart comes to an end.
Another great sacrifice of this [tantra], known as Dhruva, is also proclaimed;
by the mere sight of which a transmigrating being may attain [liberation]. (18)
Established correctly within its own self, it shall not return to primordial nature (prakṛti) again;
this mandala of supreme bliss is the highest state.
Having seen and having worshipped which one may attain the supreme state—O Brahmin, now attend to the characteristics of these in their proper order. (20)
Having made the field square, one should divide it into seven parts; thus, forty-nine squares are produced. (21)
One should fashion a lotus in the center with nine divisions;
by means of two rows [of lines], the doors and the six corners are indeed formed.
One should likewise cleanse from the vicinity of the Padmakṣetra by means of the Dakṣas;
[this extends to] half the neck of the door of the enclosure, and three [units] each outside of that.
Indeed, the doors are thus formed for the sake of establishing the vicinity;
one should erase six squares at a time in each corner. (24)
In this way, one should fill the auspicious void that has been erased with dust;
it is joined with the circular movement of the sky, and in its center a lotus is situated.
Likewise, all the lines should be drawn with black and white [pigments], as should the joints of the lotus petals and likewise those within the intervals. (26)

But indeed, I shall describe the filling of all [the channels] by means of the *rajas* element, starting from the exterior of the sphere of space (*vyomavṛtta*) and proceeding in due order, exactly as it exists.
The space between the two necks is colored with a pale red dye;
their corners are brilliant red, while the interior of those two is yellow.
Having thus completed [the ritual], there will be auspiciousness; now listen to the liberation from sin.
Having properly divided the field into eight parts, there are sixty-four sections.
One should draw a lotus in the center with four compartments;
outside of that, one should clear away a single row of squares for the sake of the pathway (vīthī). || 30 ||
The doors are outside the street, each pair being half the size of the previous;
half of the neck (kaṇṭha) is to be omitted, and four [parts] are indeed from the neck-protuberance (upagalāt).
In the locations adjacent to the doors, according to the number of the previous mandala,
one should first erase [the lines] and then color the ground-jewel with black.
The remainder, however, should be like that of Bhadra; now the *sadadhva* is described.
Having divided the field into nine parts, it shall consist of eighty-one portions.
They arise according to their respective parts; one should draw a lotus like that of Bhadra.
Outside of that, in a row, one should clear away the beautiful pedestal. || 34 ||
Therefore, having established three parts situated at all the intermediate directions (vidiś),
and placing one part in each of the cardinal directions, there shall be the doors and their supports.
Listen: they arise only by means of two external rows [of squares], and not otherwise.
One should fashion the neck of the door (dvārakaṇṭha) with parts equal to the corners of the pedestal (pīṭha). || 36 ||
Having cleared away the area of one-fifth for the vicinity and six parts (or six limbs) for its corner,
one should subsequently fill it with colored powder so that it shines resplendently.
The space between the two celestial seats (vyomapīṭha) should be radiant with yellow and red;
likewise, the portions situated at the directions of the seats should be radiant with dark blue.
One should fill the corners of its pedestals with yellow;
the doors with very white, and the base with pale red. (39)
I have already explained the six paths; now that which is called Dharma is being described. By dividing the field into ten parts, there shall be one hundred divisions.
One should prepare the central pedestal with four *puṣkaras* in a row; there, O Lotus-born One, one should purify the surrounding sections. (41)
One should lay down the diagonal threads so that they form four squares;
one should then fashion the circumambulatory path (bhramaṇī) in a row, and the door by means of a pair of those.
One should wipe away six portions from the throat and its vicinity;
then, beginning from both sides, one should massage two portions on each side.
Having subtracted three, two, and then one [unit] from each corner,
one should color the center of the two celestial seats with pale red pigment.
One should fill the two front and back portions from the pedestal with yellow;
one should fill the two locations adjacent to the neck of the door with yellow as well.
Just as there is an interval between the sky-seats (vyomapīṭha), so too are the four corners;
this has been described as Dharma. Now hear about Vasugarbha.
Having divided the field elevenfold into one hundred and twenty-one parts,
the central lotus is produced by nine of those parts.
Having cleansed it for the sake of the pedestal, one should prepare a single row;
listen now to how that is done according to the rule for laying out the lines.
Having placed [the thread] at the corner position at the end of the two lines,
one should strike that thread across both sides at every corner.
By this method, the cardinal directions become like the pericarp,
the corners like the tips of ploughs, and then the walkway follows in a row.
O Lotus-born One, one should perform [the rite] with exactly two rows of remaining [units],
having purified the collection of parts at the gates according to the six paths.
One should clear [the space] from the two doors through the middle and from the region of the corner;
one should then establish each corner by means of three parts.
Having done this, one should afterwards fill the external space with various kinds of passion and with dust that is like a tranquil fire.
Beginning from the northeast corner, one should fill it with white and other colors;
likewise, one should cast the colored powders into the corners starting from the west and ending with the north and east.
One should fill the area outside the pedestal with a color resembling the belly of a fish;
the doors with reddish-orange, and the space between them with white.
The remainder, however, one should color with black lead at the ten-foot boundary.
Thus has been described to you the *Vasugarbha* [mandala], which grants all desires; now listen. (56)
Having divided the field into twelve parts by means of that same thread, O Pauṣkara,
