one hundred and six minus six (one hundred) [squares] are then produced.
In the center, one should fashion a lotus with sixteen squares, complete with its characteristic features;
the pedestal (pīṭha) is formed by a row of squares, and from there, two squares each are placed in the cardinal directions.
Thus, two parts are purified; then, three by three [units] are placed upon the corners.
One should rub the *bhramaṇī* line with the remaining two rows.
Having thus made twenty-two [lines] from corner to corner here among the six necks and sub-necks,
one should fill the space between the two void-seats as before.
One should fill the pedestal from the corner with a color resembling royal blue;
then, one should dye the central regions of those corners with a golden luster.
Then, O twice-born one, one should color the pathways with a white pigment;
the doors with a crystal-like luster, or the bases with a red dye.
By performing this rite which grants all desires, one is called a slayer of enemies;
having divided the field into thirty parts, there arise one hundred divisions.
Within the center of the wheel, there is a lotus consisting of sixty-nine squares;
outside of that, the pedestal (pīṭha) consists of twenty-five squares arranged in rows.
There, three [squares] each from the middle, and likewise on the corners;
outside of that, a path in a row by means of a pair [of squares] starting with the gates. (65)
The neck should be made with three parts, and up to the ear-circles with five;
from the middle of the two sides of the door, there should be eight parts for each of the two ornaments.
Then, with six [lines] and six [lines], one should form the four corners;
having done so, one should manifest the outer space with a deep red color.

All the corners of the pedestal should be made with that same extremely brilliant material, or with a substance resembling the wings of a bow; thus, the four directions of the pedestal are established.
Then one should fill the circular path with the likeness of a royal gem;
the doors with the luster of silver, and within them, the white quality.
Just as there is an interval between the celestial seats (vyomapīṭha), so too is the corner (koṇa) traditionally defined.
This has been stated; now that which destroys enemies and bestows long life is being described.
Having divided the field into fourteen parts, one hundred and ninety-six squares arise;
the lotus, however, is formed within sixteen squares.
In the middle row, outside of that, one should fashion the support for the lotus;
there, two units each are placed in the cardinal directions, and three each at its corners.
With two rows [of squares] around it, there should be a path on the outside;
then, one should complete whatever remains with two rows of squares. (73)
The door-ear (dvārakaṇṭha) should be two parts, and the secondary ear (upakaṇṭha) should be four parts;
then, from near the ear, one should clear away three parts for the sake of ornamentation.
And thus there should be eight such beauties approaching the vicinity;
then one should purify [the site] in the four directions of the mandala and in its corners.
O Brahmin, one should then color ten parts at a time;
one who desires the lineage of the Kulikas should fill [the space] from outside the void.
Then, one who desires emerald [green] should color the corners of the pedestal;
one should completely fill the entire assembly of directions with a reddish-amaranth hue. || 77 ||
The pathways were like gold or possessed a golden luster, and the gates were brilliantly white;
adorned with precious stones, they shone as if they were part of the exterior of the sky itself.
This has been declared as the rite for longevity; now hear the procedure for Balabhadra.
Having divided the field into fifteen parts, there shall be two hundred squares.
It may be twenty-five units more; one should act like the destroyer of enemies (Amṛtaghna).
The pedestal (pīṭha) is made with lotus-shaped parts, and the secondary pedestal (upapīṭhaka) likewise with rows of parts.
The learned should construct the *upagala* and the assembly of ornaments as before;
O Pauṣkara, one should subtract eleven parts from each corner.
One should fill the area from the sky downwards with white and red [pigments];
the throne should be of such a kind as the king, and so too is the throne of the yantra.
Listen attentively to the procedure by which it should be given:
one should fill [the area] starting from the northeast corner with four [substances], beginning with white.
The corners of the pedestal (pīṭha) are marked with red [lines], starting from the west; then, by that same [method], up to the southern direction, the secondary pedestal (upapīṭha) is described.

Starting from the southern direction with white and other colors, continuing until the eastern limit, one should draw the circumambulatory paths (bhramaṇī) in white and red; thereafter, the four doors [are to be made]. 85.
O twice-born one, afterwards, with [a portion] equal to Jāmbūnada gold, there is the eighth beauty;
then, in sequence, with an emerald-like [portion], and for the remainder, with a red quality.
Now, this powerful and nourishing [rite] is being described.
Having divided the field into sixteen parts, there are two hundred portions. (87)
One should then arrange fifty-six [units] in the middle;
with thirty-six [units], however, one should form the kahlāra seat by means of two rows.
Two parts each should be removed from the middle of the directions, and five parts each from the corners;
then, for the sake of the upapīṭhas, one should further subtract those parts.
There are three [squares] in each of the corners and six in each of the directions;
outside of that is the path (mārga), arranged in a row with two doors and so forth.
Is it one by one, through the two, four, and the recollections (smṛtis) such as the galopa and gala-śobhā?
Likewise, the upaśobhā is formed by the reversal of the śobhā with those same [elements]. 91.
And near the *śobhā*, one should erase the corners with six [lines];
thus, O Brahmin, there are eight *śobhās* as well as eight *upaśobhās*.
Having cleansed it, one should then fill the four directions with colored powder;
the exterior of the circle of space being filled with a reddish-orange hue.
One should fill all the corners of the pedestal with a golden luster,
and one should fill the limbs with a pale-red hue.
One should color the corners of the upapīṭha with that same [color],
its limbs with white, and the exterior of it with black.
One should adorn the doors with very white [pigment] and the beauties [ornaments] like the exterior of the sky;
then one should decorate the secondary beauties and the corners with yellow.

"O Brahmin, by one desiring emerald-like luster, whether dark or radiant—having spoken thus, I shall describe the nourishing sacrifice (pauṣṭikayāga) known as the 'Health-bestowing' (ārogyaka). [In some versions: "I shall describe the sacrifice known as the 'Health-bestowing'. 97.
Having first divided the field into seventeen parts, three hundred and eleven parts arise from the center.
One should then form a lotus with twenty-five [units], and from that, a support for the lotus with two rows; one should then expand it in the cardinal directions.
Near the lotus-field, there are six [parts] among them on the exterior;
having thus fashioned the limbs so that they are equal in beauty, [one should proceed]. (100)

One should erase portions on all sides, specifically one part in each corner; one should then clear away two rows of squares that have been formed for the sake of the five spokes and for the sake of the circumambulatory path. || 101 ||
O best of the twice-born, one should then create the beauty of the doorway and other features by means of two [units];
three [units] for the half, and five parts for the neck (kaṇṭha) and its vicinity starting from the door.
In each of the primary, secondary, and corner [sections] of the ornamentation, having cleared away three times seven [squares] with powder and filled them with various colors, || 103 ||
Outside the perimeter of the space,
however, there are four legs for the pedestal, resembling the bandhujīva flower and white as cow’s milk.
Then, with all his limbs resembling stone and like fine Chinese powder, the king should smear the pathway.
The doors and other features should be of golden color, well-established within as dark blue,
adorned with white, and the remainder with reddish-orange.
Thus has the section on health been declared; now attend to the section on solitude. Having divided the field into eighteen parts, there are three hundred subdivisions.
O Lotus-born One, it indeed arises as twenty-four [squares];
in the center, there is a lotus with sixteen [squares], and the pedestal (pīṭha) consists of three rows. 108.
There, for each of the limbs, there are indeed two sets of four parts;
two [parts] are from near the lotus-field in the row, situated in the middle of the directions.
Having arranged four in the middle row and two in the outer row according to the interval, one should thus form the group of limbs; then, from those two, in the middle space: || 110 ||
The wise one should construct a quarter-measure using exactly thirteen parts;
there should be seven in the outer row and one part in the middle row.
Then, having unified [the parts], one should form the image with five portions,
so that its limbs are slightly shaped from those two rows.
One should leave a pathway for movement from the remaining two rows;
O Brahmin, one should then erase ten squares at a time in each corner.
From the remainder, one should cause the primary ornaments (śobhā) and secondary ornaments (upaśobhā), as well as the doors, to be made by means of [specific] divisions;
having then filled the pericarp-sections (karṇikā) with all [the remaining parts], listen to how that is done.
Immediately after the area of the pedestal, one should smear the limbs with white [pigment] resembling the flower of the pomegranate tree, while the dark parts are smeared with black.
One should fill the corner formed by the eight parts with material resembling ruby, and the area outside the pedestal with material resembling royal stone (sapphire). || 116 ||
(24) That tetrad beginning with the gate, which was described by means of the four [deities] starting with Sitā, is called Viveka; now Vāgīśa is being described. 117.
Having divided the field into nineteen parts,
O twice-born one, there arise three hundred and sixty-one lords (īśakas).
The lotus is formed with twenty-five [petals], and the pedestal (pīṭha) with three rows;
starting from the east and ending in the northern direction, there are seven [sections] in sequence from that.
One part [should be] in the first row, and likewise those five in the middle;
then one should accomplish it joined with the third part.
Then, by means of the remaining set of parts, one should [mark] the entire collection of lines;
starting from the corner adjacent to the lotus-field, there is a group of five in the eastern row.
Then, having divided the portions into twelve parts from the two [sides],
the pathway (vīthī) is formed by two parts, while the doors and so forth are formed by two parts each.
There, the portion for the neck is by that same measure; the upakaṇṭhaka is with five parts;
the corners are with a tenth part (or ten parts according to the *kh* manuscript); and the remaining portions are for the *śobhā*s and so forth.
Then, having filled the external space from the circle of the sky with that very same blazing red light,
one should next fill the interiors of the feet with a golden luster.
One who desires all-embracing emerald should first fill the four directions with [the color] ending in radiance; one should then complete the remainder of the area by foot-measure.
One should color the path of movement with the passion of the form of the *dvirepha* (bee), using white, red, and deep red [pigments], and likewise gold and vermilion in succession. 126.
O Pauṣkara, the fourfold [mandala] should be completed starting from the four gates;
this has been described as Vāgīśa, and now I shall tell you about Mānasa.
Having divided the field twelvefold—meaning by ten doubled—it shall become four hundred [squares].
Therein, in the very center, one should draw a lotus with thirty-six parts.
Then, one should erase that support by means of three outer rows;
two from near the lotus-field, two on the outside, and four in the middle.
One who is endowed with the practice of movement should erase the parts from the middle of the directions;
understand this here by means of eighteen parts plus a fraction. 130.
From the two limbs, one should again join three, one, and three;
likewise, starting from the outside, one should join two sets of six with their respective parts.
One should merge the six [squares] from the corner with the outer and middle rows;
then, as before, one should erase the pathway using the two outer rows.
The remainder should be of that same measurement; therein, the placement [of the deities] consists of six.
O Brahmin, listen likewise to the group of six for the neck and its vicinity. (133)

In the remaining space, one should create two types of beauty (śobhā) and one ornamentation (upaśobhana); then, one should fill [the spaces] from the center, the doors, and the corners with colored powder (rajas).

The area of the ground beginning from the pedestal should be colored like Chinese ink (cīnapiṣṭa), and their limbs with a beautiful yellow; that which is between them, however, [should be colored differently]. 135.
One should fill that interval with a very white [pigment], produced from one-twelfth part, resembling lapis lazuli, and arising from six parts.
One should color the circular path with reddish-orange and the continuous row of doors with white;
the ornaments near the doors should be colored like the exterior of the sky.
O Pauṣkara, some [ornaments] are adorned with gold, while others are beautiful;
the remainder should be like the previous ornamentation, resembling the belly of a fish.
Thus has been described the mental sacrifice; now hear of another called Jaya.
Having divided the field into twenty-one parts, it is produced. 139.
The lotus consists of one hundred and ninety-six parts,
and outside of that, the pedestal (pīṭha) is formed by twenty-five rows.
Then, O Brahmin, one should erase three parts each in the four directions of the limbs,
and likewise on the corners.
Outside of that, one should construct the *upapīṭha* (subsidiary pedestal) by means of three rows;
from that, seventeen parts are to be subtracted for each limb.
p. 25) Thirdly, one should arrange seven [syllables] each in the middle row, and then form the feet [of the verse] from the two rows consisting of the beginning and the end. 143.
O Brahmin, one should rub each corner [of the grid] with thirteen parts;
once the group of quarters is established, one should construct the pathway with two [parts].
Then, with the second [part], one places six units each for the twenty and so forth upon those corners;
the door is formed by eight parts, and the remaining portions are used for the ornaments and other features.
Having done this, one should subsequently dye it; listen now to that, O Pauṣkara: one should make that which ends with one's own conduct bright white.
First, the assembly of the pedestal's feet is like the whiteness of cow’s milk;
from that [arise] four [feet] shaped like emeralds situated in the intermediate directions. (147)
One should fill the limbs of the pedestal with that same [color],
and then from the feet [onward] with a form of broken ruby.
The exterior [of the mandala] is like lapis lazuli from the pedestal; outside of that, one should fill the continuous series of corners with a golden luster, and then with a deep red glow.
Having filled the secondary ornaments with white,
one should then color the doors with a broken hue resembling gorocanā.
This which has been described is called Jaya; now hear about Svastika, O twice-born one. By dividing the field into twenty-two parts, it is produced. 151.
There, the central seat for the Mūrti consists of thirty-six squares, while the total area is four hundred and eighty-four squares.
One should then fashion its support by means of four rows of squares; thereafter, for the sake of accomplishing the limbs, one should erase [the lines] from the center toward the directions. (153)
O Lotus-born One, twenty-four degrees from the vicinity of the Padmakṣetra, there is a division of four parts arranged in a row. (154)
Then, one should purify the second [deity] in the second row;
having thus fashioned the partial image, it shall be like a doorway. || 155 ||
There, in the third row, one should omit two parts;
furthermore, one should omit four from the outside of that, as in the previous diagram. (156)
O twice-born one, with the remaining portion of the parts, one should fashion two such [deities] for the animal realm,
occupying the limbs and having the form of a door-panel.
Next, it is explained how one should fashion the four feet, each foot having the shape of a limb and consisting of sixteen parts. (158)
However, each of those images should consist of four parts;
two images, resembling doorways, are situated in the eastern direction from the pedestal.
Thus the northeast direction has been described; one should erase that [first] contact, and beginning from the southeast corner, one should wipe away the second.
O twice-born one, one should first fashion two bimbas situated at the feet in the western direction;
then, through their conjunction, one should fashion them in the northwest and northeast corners.

O Lotus-born One, one should place two images each in the north and south, leaving aside the supreme position; [and likewise] from the northeast, in the southeast, northwest, and southwest corners. (162)
O Lotus-born One, by this purified method, a second pair of images arises directly from the two limbs. 163.
O Lotus-seated One, having thus fashioned it joined with eight svastikas,
one should likewise create the path for circumambulation on the outside by means of two outer rows.
It is now explained how one should perform the remainder using exactly two rows [of squares]:
the door, joined with the neck and sub-neck, is constructed from six parts. (165)
One should construct a *śobhā* (ornamental projection) near the door, measuring four parts;
the *upaśobhā* (sub-projection) adjacent to the *śobhā* should be made as before, measuring six parts.
Near the secondary door (upadvāra), one should likewise construct a corner of such beauty with a sixth part; having thus removed [the excess], one should complete it.
(26) With pale-red pigment, one should draw two images resting on the body, positioned in front of the central lines and beyond the perimeter known as the sky (vyoma). 168.
In a beautiful emerald [stone], or likewise in one that is red and crimson,
when that reflection moves obliquely, this sequence occurs in all its limbs.
Then, one should cast [the measure] for the feet which are endowed with four images;
it is equal, having fourfold forms according to their respective positions through the division of the feet.
When the foot is situated in the northeast corner, it is pale-red in the eastern image;
it is white in the south, and like sapphire in the west.
Listen: in the northern image it is gold-colored; in the southeastern position, you should know it is likewise red in the east, and then yellow, black, and white in sequence.
Now, the protection for the regions of Yama, Apas, and Soma will be described in the section on protection:
starting from the east and ending in the north, [the directions] are colored black, yellow, reddish-brown, and white. (173)
Having filled that [space] with its reflection, I shall now speak regarding the wind at the feet:
from the direction of Indra to that of Kubera, they are white, black, and red by others. (174)
Having thus filled the entire pedestal with groups of red [dots],
one should fill the pathway with six-petaled lotuses and the door with white [dots].
The *śobhā* should be colored with deep red, and immediately thereafter with yellow;
one should color the *śobhā* situated at the corners and the middle of the side-doors with dark blue.
One should fill the corner with passion (rāga), which is like a smokeless fire; this is called the Svastika. Now I shall describe to you the Ananta. 177.
O twice-born one, having divided the field into twenty-three parts, there would be five hundred and twenty-nine parts. (178)
In the center, joined with twenty-five *aṃśakas*, is the lotus;
the pedestal (*pīṭha*) consists of three rows, and the minor pedestal (*upapīṭhikā*) consists of one row. || 179 ||
Having subtracted seven parts from each of the limbs,
there shall be one part in the directions in the eastern row, and five in the middle.
Then, from one part of that same row of forms, one should construct each foot with seventeen parts; thus it is called the *upapīṭha*.
One should erase five squares in each of the cardinal directions,
and then, having thoroughly cleared the intermediate directions, erase seven squares in each.
One should [draw] the Bhramaṇī with two rows, but the doors and so forth with three;
there, the neck with three, and from the neck-region (upakaṇṭha) five.
O twice-born one, one should fashion the base (ādhāra) for the neck (kaṇṭha), and outside of that, the ornament (śobhā) reaching to the door, with seven parts of the neck. (184)
Therein, one should rub the portion adjacent to the base and the three portions adjacent to the neck;
then, from the region of the neck, one should massage five parts along the row toward the north.
Then, one should subtract twenty-seven degrees from the corner region;
having done so, it should be filled on all sides with a network of passion (rāga). || 186 ||
The other sacred seat (pīṭha) is situated within the field, reddish like a ruby;
then, the four legs of the seat are radiant with gold.
One should then fill the limbs with something like snow;
likewise, the king should fill the limbs of the pedestal with something like stone.
One should color his feet with red *kiṃśuka* flowers;
the path of his movement with white, and the doors like the exterior of the sky.
Resembling the autumnal sky and endowed with splendor,
one should adorn the lattice of its corners with a pale-red hue.
Understand that what is called "the infinite" is designated as "eternal";
having divided the field twelvefold, one should then divide it again into two.
There are five hundred and seventy-six parts;
one should construct the lotus in the center with thirty-six parts.
The pedestal (pīṭha) consists of four rows; two of these are in the middle, while in the cardinal directions there are two each from the first and last rows, and likewise four each from the middle.
O twice-born one, having thus purified it from the two rows, there shall be the *gātraka*;
then, joined with a twelfth part, one should calculate the *pāda*.
Dividing [the area] into twenty-eight parts, one should draw a very beautiful and well-proportioned figure.
From the corner adjacent to the lotus-field, five [squares] are to be taken in the first row toward the east. (195)
Then, having combined the two groups of twelve from the middle rows separately,
one should subtract the eleventh parts from the outer row in due order.
Having thus completed the quarters with two rows [of squares] for the path, listen now, O Pauṣkara, to what remains to be done with the third row. 197.
One should divide two [units] from the throat and so forth according to the sequence of four and six;
then, starting from the outside, one should erase one part, three, and five. || 198 ||
O Lotus-born One, there should likewise be a beautiful *śobhā* near the door;
one should then construct the *upaśobhā* using a portion consisting of four parts.
Outside the vicinity of the Jyeṣṭha-śobhā, there are indeed two rows;
then, one should erase seventeen parts at each corner.
Afterwards, one should fill it with colored powder; listen to how that is done, O Pauṣkara.
One should apply that powder, red as blood, on the exterior of the sky (the dome) using the finest powder.
One should adorn the limbs with the splendor of various colors—white, black, and yellow—from the beginning to the end of the body. (202)
Having filled the quarters from their respective portions, one should fill the path with gems that are radiant,
and the splendor at the gates with yellow stone.
One should fashion the *upaśobhā* arising from its side with the luster of emerald;
know that the *śobhā* reaching the corners, however, is brilliant white.
The corner shines with a dust that has the luster of nectar;
thus has that which is known as "eternal" been described. Now hear about the abode of the elements (bhūtāvāsa). || 205 ||
Having divided the field into twenty-five parts, six hundred and twenty-four degrees, including the quarters, arise from the center. (206)
Having drawn an auspicious lotus with forty-nine [squares],
one should fashion a pedestal with four rows of squares, adorned with feet and limbs.
One should fashion the body with twenty-four parts and endowed with five images; therein, one should eliminate certain portions.
O twice-born one, from the two fourth rows, one part each is in the intermediate directions;
however, three parts each are in the middle from the two rows.
In this way, the first image produced from eight parts of the body should have its horizontal dimensions made up of four parts each.
Of which there are four bimbas that indeed have a beautiful form;
then, three each in the first row, on the exterior of the lotus-field. || 211 ||
In the second row, there should likewise be two images for each;
however, in the third row, one should omit one part from each.
In the fourth [line], there are three and three [syllables]; from the cleansing [of the previous line], it becomes the body (gātraka).
Beyond that, each quarter-verse (pāda) consists of twelve parts (aṃśakas).
There, starting from one square, then five, then seven, and again seven,
one should erase [the squares] in the front row until the very end.
One should make the path for movement by means of two rows of parts;
as for the three remaining parts, they are produced from fifteen portions.
One should first make the door; one should wipe three [units] at the limit of the neck (grīvā);
five from the vicinity of the throat (upakaṇṭha), and seven for the support of the door (dvārādhāra).
Then, near that [central area], one should prepare the place for beauty and sweep it;
[dividing the space] from the region of the neck (kaṇṭha) onwards in sequence into five, three, and likewise one part.
In this very manner, one should perform the embellishment, but in the reverse order.
Then, the fifteen parts situated in the inauspicious [directions] are to be subtracted.
Having thus effaced [the previous form], one should then color it with delightful tints such as these;
then, one should indeed make that which resides within the field and the sacred seats radiant white.
One should make the limbs white, with a continuous series of images situated in the middle;
that image, located near the lotus-field, is like a mountain for men, O King.
Then,
with a red and blazing dye, one should color those two external mandalas; likewise, with a golden-hued dye, one should color the pedestal and the walkway.
Everything has the luster of emerald; the doors are like the exterior of space, the corners resemble the feet, and the intermediate parts of the body are like the joints.
That which resembles crushed collyrium and possesses a multitude of ornaments is called Bhūtāvāsa; Amogha is now described.
Having first divided the field thirteenfold— [meaning in two ways and then thirteen ways, resulting in twenty-six ways]— one should divide that into two parts,
consisting of six hundred and seventy-six portions.
From that center, a lotus arises with sixty-four parts;
it is adorned by four rows of pedestals and by the limbs and feet depicted in various colors.
The first and middle sections of the body consist of twenty-eight parts each;
therein, from the two rows situated at the beginning and end, two parts each are taken from the intermediate directions.
Likewise, from the two middle rows, there are again two by two;
thus, this consists of twelve parts, and in the center, there shall be an auspicious image.
And on both sides of that, near the lotus-field,
two parts each should be cleared away from the two middle rows.
O Pauṣkara, having combined two parts in the outer row, each [part] shall consist of eight divisions; in this way, there will be two images (bimba).
Thereafter, one should form two squares, each consisting of twenty parts;
then, from the outside of the lotus-field, one should erase six parts.
The foot-print becomes one; that which stands outside should be stationary.
Arising from fourteen parts, the path (vīthī) is formed by two rows.
Then, one should indeed construct the neck and other parts on the outside in three rows;
starting from the throat, the door consists of two, four, and six parts respectively.
Then, O twice-born one, one should fashion a *śobhā* of nine parts near the door as previously described,
and likewise fashion an *upaśobhā* in the vicinity of the *śobhā*.
Then, one should fashion a subtle ornament (*upaśobhā*) using four *aṃśakas*;
indeed, two pairs [of ornaments] should be placed near the *upaśobhā* from the two rows.
Then, O Pauṣkara, one should construct the corner with a thirteenth part;
from the beginning to the middle there are six parts, while in the outer row there are seven.
Having unified it with one's own *rajas* and filled it with various [substances],
one should offer that which is white and radiant upon the lotus-shaped ground.
Into the central mandala, one should scatter gold-colored powder for the limbs;
the remaining portions of the limbs should be like the petals of a blue lotus.
One should fill the circles situated within the feet with brilliant white,
and the area outside of those, all around, with blazing red.
One should fill the pathway with an emerald luster and the door with white;
the *śobhā* with a brilliant red and the *upaśobhaka* with a golden luster.
Having filled that corner which stands there with a subtle beauty, like lapis lazuli and with a pale, brilliant luster; 240.
This which has been spoken is unfailing; therefore, listen to this well-established [instruction]:
having divided the field into twenty-seven parts, it is produced.
One hundred and seven parts should be joined together as the *pauṣkara*;
with twenty-nine parts, one should fashion the lotus in the center.
The pedestal (pīṭha) consists of eighty-one parts by means of two rows;
there, one should polish the limbs (gātraka), which consist of thirty-two parts.
There, from the first and last rows, one should remove three parts each from the intermediate directions;
likewise, from the two middle rows, one should remove one part each.
The image of the body itself should thus consist of eight parts and so forth;
then, by means of twelve divisions, two images are established therein. (245)
For that purpose, one should create two rows each from the inner [lines] and so forth;
therein, by means of the two middle rows, one should erase and merge the eight [squares]. || 246 ||
Having thus divided the body, one should make a quarter with twenty squares;
understand how the first image is formed within that quarter.
O Brahman, starting from the *ka* field at the corner limit, one should erase three by three [squares] in sequence from the three rows. (248)
The first footprint (pādabimba) should be constructed with nine squares;
for the sake of accomplishing the second footprint, there should be eleven corner squares.
Having purified the two outer rows, one should [purify] the second group of nine in sequence;
the *bhramaṇī* with two rows, and the remainder with three rows.
One should quickly fashion the triad beginning with the neck, then the pentad and the heptad;
near the door, one should construct the ninefold ornament as previously described.
Then, one should fashion a side-door near Śobha;
from that neck and so forth, one should wipe away two, four, and six parts.
Then, from each corner, one should erase five squares in every row; having done this, O Lotus-born One, one should subsequently color it with pigments.
One should place within the center of the lotus pond a radiant white [image],
with the central parts of the limbs [marked] with very white powder.
Then one should color the remaining images with a blazing red;
thereafter, the image situated between the feet should be colored with the luster of emerald.
One should fill its exterior with a luster blazing like refined gold,
and likewise the pathway with that which resembles the autumn sky.
The main gate possesses a splendor like that of the kunda flower or the moon, while the side gates are beautifully filled with a brilliance resembling the campaka flower or gold.
The corner [is] like the belly of a fish and resembling the bright fortnight;
this is declared to be the well-established [foundation], and now the support of the intellect is described. (258)
Having divided the field into seven parts and having further divided the fourth part, there arise seven hundred shares with an additional [portion]. || 259 ||
One should fashion the central lotus with eighty-four parts, the [central] space with one hundred,
and the pedestal with four outer rows, possessing excellent characteristics.
That single limb should consist of twenty-eight words;
provided with three images, one should erase them from its center toward the directions.
Two each, situated at the beginning and end of the rows, [are combined] four by four with those in the middle;
in this way, one should extract the central diagram from the portions of the twelve triangles.
On both sides of that [central line], one should mark the image with divisions increased by one-eighth;
from those two, the first and last rows, one should eliminate three squares each.
One should give one foot each from the two intermediate positions and [the remaining] feet from those equal to them;
one should create two beauties like a reflection—listen to how that is done.
O twice-born one, beginning from the vicinity of the lotus-field, one should wipe away three squares each across the three rows. 265.
Having unified [the parts], there shall be one ninth-part for the first foot-image;
from the outside of that, one should erase nineteen parts.
O Brahmin, excluding the first row, from the remaining three rows, one should [draw] for the purpose of the second quadrant-image and for the sake of its path; beyond that is the next [part]. (267)
Two rows are to be wiped away, while the remainder is [cleansed] by three rows;
two, four, and six parts [are removed] from the directional regions in sequence.
One should fashion the two, the *śobhā* and the *upaśobhā*, as before, arising from nine parts; then the *bimba* consists of five [parts], and the corner arises from twenty-seven squares.
One should act so that it is understood everywhere; listen closely to me as well:
near [the center], by means of two beauties (*abhyupaśobhā*), there are two beautiful parts (*śobha*) devoid of divisions. (270)
Having swept and opened [the door], the image should first be prepared;
one should then beautify the image from the outside, starting from the seventeenth square.
Having erased three [syllables] in the second row, as well as the seventh and those belonging to the outer row, one should fill [the grid] with the net of passion arising from the divisions. 272.
First, the area outside the surrounding circle of white lotuses should be made radiant with red;
however, the central orb of the limbs should be made radiant with white.
One should fashion that pair of images white, as pale as cow’s milk;
but between them, one should fashion the foot-image with the luster of emerald.
Outside, the path is made of gold with the luster of royal stones;
the doors are like nectar, beautiful like the exterior of a lotus.
O best of beings, the secondary ornaments (upaśobhās) are equal to three-quarters of the side;
those within the corners are equal to one-quarter of the side.
All [the channels] are equal in their middle sections and circular in their external parts;
this is declared to be the support of the intellect (buddhi). Now, the "mine of qualities" (guṇākara) is described.
Having divided the field into thirty-one parts, it arises with one hundred and eight portions consisting of four squares each. (278)
Starting from the lotus-field (*padmakṣetra*), one should arrange the lotuses with exactly one hundred and twenty-one, and then the seats in two rows.
On that [mandala], one should indeed fashion the body-part situated upon forty squares;
it is beautiful, endowed with five images, and one should erase half of that in the cardinal directions.
From the two rows at the beginning and the end, three squares each [are taken], and one square each from the two middle rows; thus, it arises as eight compartments.
The torso should be the central image, and the remaining eight parts should also be situated at its sides; listen, O Pauṣkara, as to how they are to be made. 282.
O best of the twice-born, one should erase the portions near the center of the circle, both at the beginning and the end; specifically, three parts each from within that interval.
Then, from those two images, there should be another pair outside;
one should erase them by smoothing them away from the vicinity of the eastern and northern images. (284)
Two [units] each from the first and last rows, and likewise from the two situated in the middle;
having thus formed the two limbs, one should then establish the feet.
O twice-born one, the twelvefold arising from two images consists of two images and a quarter;
from the vicinity of the corner of the lotus-field, there is a fifth part, which is half of that [quarter]. (286)
Having purified it from two rows, there is first a triad in the first row;
then, in the second, there should be two words. Thus, the first image will become clearly manifest.
Then, one should clear fifteen parts from the exterior of that;
in the second row there is one part, and in the third there are five parts.
Then, nine parts [should be left] for the second row (vīthī), and likewise for the two rows [above it];
whatever remains by the third [row], there the door is located, with three [parts] at the neck (gala).
Five and five [units] from the throat, and seven from its support;
one should create the genitals in the front row, beautiful and born from nine parts.
The private parts and the door-adjuncts; therein, on the path of the throat, are two.
From the vicinity of the throat, there are four, and one should cleanse the group of six outside of that.
From that, one should hear of the two bodies; then, constructed from three times seven [twenty-one] steps, one should sweep away the six [units] of the two rows near the excellent path.
One should subtract the two sets of constituent groups from that which is external to the two rows;
one should wipe away two by two from the first and second rows respectively. (293)
The third [layer] should consist of seven [circles], having been wiped all around;
and outside of that sky, it should be white and radiant.
One should indeed fashion the central orb of the father (the Sun), surrounded by one part; it should have the luster of emerald, like frost situated within it. (295)
The reflection within the interior of the feet is indeed equal in radiance to the sun;
it is reddish-orange externally, while the pathway is like the exterior of the sky.
In this [palace], the gates are white and should be as beautiful as the bandhujīva flower;
the side-gates have the luster of gold, and those on the interior are black. (297)
One should indeed fill their exterior with the luster of emerald;
know this to be the source of all virtues (Guṇākara). Now hear about the one called Dhruva.
Having divided the field into two parts of fifteen [squares] each, O Lotus-born One,
one should draw the Puṣkara in the center, consisting of nine hundred parts.

Then, outside of that, by means of four rows of one hundred and fifty-five [squares] less six, there is the pedestal (pīṭha); then, by means of two [rows] of body-squares (gātragapada), [the limbs are formed].
There are forty parts plus four more; having subtracted twelve from the middle circle for the sake of the [inner] circles, [the remainder is as follows]. (301)
In the first row there are four [units], and likewise in the last row;
from each of the two middle rows, there are again two and two.
Then, having combined those, one should place two images each outside, produced from eight parts,
and one image each from the two rows at the beginning and end, consisting of two parts each.
Having thus placed three [units] on each side by means of the two intermediate positions, O twice-born one, two images of him should be made at his eastern and western feet.
With a middle number of words, one should place each of these between the two;
thus, when the collection of limbs is established, it is then endowed with five images.
One should fashion the feet joined with four images;
each individual foot should be composed of twenty parts.
Then, from the space adjacent to the corner, one should clear away seven parts;
one part in the first row, three each in the next two rows, and two in the following.
Having thus [placed] the image in the middle of the foot, now hear from me regarding the three:
two on each of the two sides, and three below those two. || 308 ||
Having taken one part from the second row,
and again two from the third row, one should color [the remaining] one part on the outermost row.
Know that the two mandalas of the wings are thus established in four ways;
one should arrange their fivefold mandala according to the outer row.
Then, one should form two rows for the *bhāga* (share) and the remaining three for the *vīthī* (pathway);
here, the door consists of two, four, and six squares, starting from the neck (*kaṇṭha*) in sequence.
The *śobhās*, *upaśobhās*, and *śobhās* are nine parts as before; just as for each individual direction, there shall be four *śobhās* in each quarter.
One should likewise polish those two *upaśobhās*;
then one should create two *bimba*s and a corner situated between the *śobhā*s.
One part [of the measurement] should be in the front row, while in the second [row] there should be four;
omitting the tip by means of a single square, the image shall be situated in the corner.
Just as it is described when situated externally, joined with five parts;
so too, there are nine portions in the outermost [circle], while the second indeed has a square (pada).
Having thus performed the ten-fold portion, one should fill it with a web of passion;
one should make the lotus at the corner like a full-blown red lotus.
The central images of the limbs should have the luster of yellow pigment (piṣṭa),
while one should fashion two images for its private parts resembling emeralds.
And when that [lotus] is remembered as being situated outside [the body], shining with refined gold,
then its central orb, which is the feet, should be made to shine with silver.
Resembling the Bāhlīka flower, it should be like the center of a *bhāga*;
that which is situated nearby should have the luster of an emerald. || 319 ||
O twice-born one, when that [wind] has gone outside, a third [wind], resembling the pomegranate flower, arises for him who has accepted the cold. (320)
One should make the pathway as white as jasmine or the moon and fill in the doorways;
the beauty should be like that of royal stone, extending from the middle of the body.
That which is situated near it should have the luster of an emerald;
and that which is situated at its very beginning should be beautiful with the radiance of a campaka flower.
From the corner, a beautiful image should be fashioned, radiant with red; then,
one should adorn its exterior with a hue resembling sapphire.
It is said that what is called Dhruva is termed supreme bliss;
by properly establishing the field with thirty-one words, it indeed arises. (324)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Sarvatobhadra and Other Mandalas," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, a Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pañcarātra.
Now begins the sixth chapter.

One should divide it upon the ground; from that, one should divide it again. Having made both parts clearly demarcated, [one should establish] the mark [of a fathom], as was done before for the cattle-pen.
Then, having omitted the eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh,
and twelfth parts in succession, one proceeds for the sake of accomplishing the tips of the petals.
Of each of the five [sets of] five [petals], starting from the three-petaled one up to the last;
with the remainder, [one should draw] the filaments and petals in the area of the pericarp.
O Lotus-born One, this sequence for the purpose of accomplishing the tips of the petals is indeed taught as having the form of a perfectly blossomed lotus within the fields of lotuses. (4)
I shall describe the method for forming the bud-like shape at the tip of a lotus petal,
dividing it starting from the pericarp and ending at the middle mark.
(33) By means of fourfold divisions arising from [the proportions], whether they be equal or unequal—
I shall explain that to you so that you may become free from doubt. (6)

The field [of the lotus] may consist of nine, eight, seven, six, five, or four parts; I shall describe the construction of each separately, beginning with the three-petaled and ending with the eight-petaled [lotuses]. (7)
Starting from the central region (madhyadeśa) up to the end of the field,
the pericarp (karṇikā) should be made in the center of all [the petals] by means of a single part for each.
Of the remaining thirty in number, the first three in each group are elongated; the filaments are half as long as those parts, and the pericarp is half the length of the base of the petals. (9)
Alternatively, having conceived them as being equal in height to the pericarp,
they are situated everywhere within the middle of the petals in groups of two or three.
Having divided the remainder of the petals into two, the first is said to be in their middle;
that which is at the tip of the lotus petal from the center is proclaimed to be at the base of the edge.
Such is the rule for lotuses beginning with three petals and ending with eight petals;
from nine petals onwards, it continues up to twenty-seven petals.
I shall tell you how the measurement of the pericarp, along with its filaments, should be:
the pericarp of the eight-petaled lotus is one-twentieth less [than the total]. (13)
One should extend the measurement of that pericarp by increasing it by one unit;
according to this rule, one should lead the pericarps of the lotuses forward.
One should fashion the filaments (kesara) as before using the remaining material;
however, for the filaments of the oblong pond (dīrghikā), one should increase their length by half the size of the pericarp (karṇikā).
Furthermore, O Brahmā, this very same procedure is prescribed for the worship of the deities of the other lotus-petals when they are being consecrated.
In the arrangement of the forms and so forth, there is the expansive space for couches and beds upon lotuses with well-established bases, following the path of the golden mountain and other features.
One should fashion the petals with a fourth part of that measurement,
and the pericarp (karṇikā) with three parts, enriched with filaments (kesara).
That [pedestal] should be raised by half a petal or by the measure of a petal;
one should fashion the fallen [petals] between them, having a length equal to half a petal.
Or else, O Brahmin, know that the filaments should be made equal to one-third of those [petals],
or they may be fashioned as resting upon the pericarp.
With hundreds of thousands of such lotuses of twice-born ones, which have arisen perfectly with the previously mentioned heights and measures.
Having observed what is appropriate for its beauty, one should fashion a series of petals;
then one should also make a pericarp, which may be of the prescribed measurement or even larger.
This is the prescribed method for the formation of lotuses that are round or elongated;
having reflected thus, one should ensure that the sky [the space] is neither deficient nor excessive.
Know that the four circles, when rotated, with the one situated in the center, constitute the pericarp (karṇikā);
the second is called the filaments (kesara), and the third is the middle of the petals (dala).
In the case of a woman, however, the end of the petals should be like the proximity of a mark;
subsequently, it remains within the interior of the circle situated at the end of the petals. (25)
The lotuses previously mentioned are to be placed outside in the east according to the number stated before;
or, even regarding those not explicitly mentioned, they are fixed by rule for those situated above as well.
Or rather, O Lotus-born One, the common portion is reckoned among all those others that have arisen, such as the three-petaled [lotus] and so forth. (27)
One should cast a ray of light before whichever lotus shines;
and by means of the expansion or contraction of its petals, the bestower of boons [is revealed]. (28)
Therefore, among those with narrow petals, the long one shines preeminently; likewise, among those situated within the interior of the reflection, that which has many filaments indeed excels.
O Lotus-born One, having thus completed this collection of threads with a portion of the leaves of the *sāgra* tree,
he then cast half of the portions of crystal into it.
By means of the mental thread at half a petal, and by that which is established at the tip of the petal,
the portion of the petal [is determined]; let the middle [line] belong precisely to the portion of the petal.
Having properly produced the intersection by means of two fish-marks (matsyacihna),
one should then cast lines through them in the middle of the petals for the sake of their successful accomplishment.
Indeed, this Sūtra remains renowned even among the petals;
for the remaining two Sūtras would mutually serve as its means of accomplishment. || 33 ||
Thus has been briefly described the laying out of the lines for the lotus sacrifice;
now hear in brief the arrangement of the petals and their continuous sequence.
Alternatively, by means of the moon’s mark and so forth, together with the threads, his desired worship is accomplished; [thus] one should draw the petal by circumambulation.

For the purpose of filling [the space] with lotus petals joined at the seven cardinal and intermediate directions, there is that which resides within the heart of the petals; meanwhile, the interval between the petals consists of threads.
Starting from the end of the fourth line, one should draw a mark (lāñcha) and touch it with the two lines of accomplishment; in the middle, there is a level ground.
The two threads of the moon [should be positioned] like the two closed throat-veins; then, having placed a thread at the location of the tip of the moon's crescent, || 38 ||
Having completed it up to the tips of the petals, or alternatively, by means of this procedure, it shall take the form of withered leaves. (39)
Between the initial and final sutras, what is the non-attainment of the names of the mantras?
It is within the interval of the fallen leaf of the perfected one, at the half-measure of the bark-fragment. || 40 ||
Having prepared the thread and brought it near the vicinity of the previously offered portion, O Lotus-born One, one should likewise fix that very thread at that limit. (41)
And when one sprinkles divine sandalwood paste upon the moon-marked stone,
it becomes sharp at the tip like a vajra, while the space between the middle teeth and the petals remains soft.
Now, this is the means for those with overlapping petals;
and for those with non-overlapping petals, it is the state of being a thread (*sūtratva*) without the [central] circle (*bimba*). || 43 ||
Without the *śakti*, one would be unable to act;
therefore, I shall now explain it to you for the sake of dispelling your doubt.
First, having drawn a lotus joined with its petals, even without the accomplishment of the petals... [45]
Having abandoned half of the space near the middle of the thread,
and having understood the third part or the quarter within the lotus of the square, one should maintain mindfulness of the position.
This half-moon on the moon, however, is in the middle of the petal as before;
the parasol is located in the region of Brahmā by the laying down of two threads. (47)
Of one whose back has not been seen and who is surrounded by a retinue. || 48 ||
The presence of the Lord should be conceived by resorting to the southern portion;
for the supports of the Bhūtas and others, the heart is indeed the direction and the intermediate directions.
From the front, the eastern and then the south-eastern [directions] are established;
likewise, in the northern part, the deity of the north-east is traditionally remembered.
Then, regarding "dalatā devamasya" (the deity of the petal): it is said that wealth is given.
Having extended a thread from the center toward the junction of the eastern petal and the [central] direction, || 51 ||
One should bring the leaf of the two lords of Āpya and Ṛkṣa up to the Siddha [stage]. From the eastern quarter onwards, that which is called the Lord (Īśvara) is marked as before. 52.
O Lotus-born One, this is the definition of the network of petals existing in the state of a row for lotuses composed of leaves.
The procedure for the pericarp, which is common to all [mandalas], has been proclaimed; now hear it.
It should be made with half the diameter of the base, or with that increased by one-quarter.
Alternatively, O Brahmin, one should make the height of the pericarp twice that;
one should likewise fashion the width of the faces together with the seed-syllables by this same measure. (55)

Having set aside the edge of the hibera-karṇikā for the sake of the girdle (mekhalā), one should divide the remainder at the site of the Brahma-sthāna into two parts for the sake of the seed-syllable (bīja). || 56 ||
One should write the eight seed-syllables in the cardinal and intermediate directions in the center of that [mandala];
O twice-born one, the end of the perimeter is the interval between the seed-syllables.
Now, a slight depression should be made, and the seed-syllable is indeed placed there as it is described:
it may be made from substances such as gold, or from sacrificial wood, or even from stone. (58)

One should fashion the mantra as hollow and shaped like a pericarp (karṇikā), possessing a distinct division. By that means, it becomes elevated like the pericarp of Indra’s ear, reaching up to the karṇakela. || 59 ||
Śrīveṣṭaka mixed with a little milk and honey,
colored with saffron and well-prepared yellow resin—
by means of that, one should apply it to the face, which is like a double-bodied sun, and to the lotus-like eyes. || 61 ||
Having removed the door-panels and having become a solid mass,
he then entered his own field as he had come, which was endowed with gold, jewels, and other riches.
Indeed, they are said to be situated in the middle, like a sphere resting within water. 63.
They are like the frontal globes of an elephant and resemble the eggs of a bird;
they are situated both externally and internally, and are elevated and reddish like the goddess Śoṇa.

Gradually, one should proceed toward the lower ground until reaching the excellent portion of the earth; having well-supplied the base of the body and its extremities, one should fill the middle parts.
The filaments are likewise equal to the tree-bark and the ground respectively;
having prepared them in this manner and worshipped them, O twice-born one,
within the others [one should worship] according to the sequence of the adhyātma, the adhideva, and the adhibhūta.
The mantras, the one whose form is mantra, and all the principles (tattvas). || 67 ||

For the mantra is declared to be the internal self; the deity is the form of the mantra; and the principle (tattva) is remembered as the elemental sphere (adhibhūta). Thus it is performed, O twice-born one. (68)
In that manner, the state of the mantra itself exists as gross, subtle, and supreme;
or, having established it within oneself, one should proceed together with each subsequent stage.
One should apply the continuity of mantras through the yoga of their origin and dissolution, as well as the Vedas, which are non-different from one another yet exist individually. (70)
Indeed, by means of the sequence of the path and through reasoning, he enjoys the fruit of the sacrifice;
for know that whatever object is expressed by mantra has bliss as its defining characteristic.
Because it transcends all entities, one should apply it to all [mantras]; likewise, in the petals of the lotus-yāgas of the *smasta*, at both the beginning and the end. (72)
Because it is the substratum of all and because it is, in reality, the reflection of that [p.
36], we should place the *lāja* grains upon the filaments; for that is the power (*śakti*) in this ritual action. (73)

Pervading all bodies, though divided into many different parts, that which is the Lord (Aiśvara) is distinct from the collection [of elements], beginning with the knowledge of the six limbs of that [body]. || 74 ||
By means of which, through the power of bliss (ānanda-śakti), one attains grasping;
sprinkling it, one should truly place [the seed-syllables], which are distinct, resembling the tips of filaments. 75.
The mantra which bestows grace, together with the adhibhūta and adhidaiva, is the Lord who is to be worshipped in the middle of the petals; indeed, its limbs are also to be worshipped there.

From the tip of that [central point], one should perform the mental visualization of the intermediate directions; then, having performed the visualization of the intermediate directions, one should worship the Astra-mantra there, beginning with the Hṛdaya-mantra and the others, along with the Sahya-mantra in the four cardinal directions. || 77 ||

O best of the twice-born, having meditated upon the Netra-mantra alone—because it possesses the power of a second [eye]—in the middle near the mantra, one should then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and worship it. 78.
Thus has been declared this supreme nyāsa of the mantras belonging to the Self,
which was revealed in twenty-six distinct parts beginning with the Fourth State (turya).
O twice-born one, the great mantra-vow residing within the body through its various locations consists of the *piṇḍa* [mantra] equal in number to the mantras,
as well as the collection of *pada*-mantras.
For he indeed functions by means of his power and likewise by means of his sovereignty over the previously mentioned arrays, locations, movements, and mantras in their entirety. (81)

Whether by means of the principles of meditation on that which stands today, or through the methods of the objects of meditation, one should contemplate the various locations of the seats (pīṭha) and the deities designated as the seats. || 82 ||
Through the two gatekeepers and their followers, as well as in other locations and supports, there are various [deities] situated both outside and inside the sacrificial rites. (83)
O Lotus-born One, these [teachings] must indeed not be revealed by you to those who lack devotion, nor to those whose souls are thoroughly scorched by speech and action. 84.
This classification of yoga, which I have declared, should be spoken for those beings who grasp at sense objects, who desire knowledge and its objects, and who seek the highest good. 85.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Lotus," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, a great Upaniṣad within the illustrious Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
O Blessed One, O Lotus-eyed One, you who know the vows of the world!
Having understood that the world of living beings is beginningless, the classification of their manifestations has been set forth in this aphorism.
O Supreme Lord, I desire to hear from you correctly concerning its essential nature, its measure, its means of accomplishment, and its ritual placement.
The Blessed Lord said: Listen attentively, O Brahman; with a concentrated mind I shall speak.
One attains one's true nature, O Brahman, and the bliss of liberation from various wombs.
O twice-born one, [this concerns] the doors and the corners from within the ancient city,
specifically regarding the various circular worlds.
Or else, from the center of the four tips joined by the pedestal-path,
one may [place them] according to one's desire within each one of all those previously mentioned.
With the division of lotus petals, [the mandala] arises from a single root;
in the center of the gateway at the front of the path of the active pedestal, there is a four-petaled [lotus].
Outside that lotus are three triple-tiered pavilions and lotuses;
listen as I describe them according to their fourteen-fold proportions. || 7 ||
And for this [mandala], first, within the triangular world of the fourfold array (caturvyūha), there are lotuses arranged in a square; the remaining portions are circular in the center.
The primary array should consist of four lotuses; in its center, however, is a four-petaled lotus. Outside of that, there are three triple-tiered lotuses.
The second [mandala] consists of five lotuses with five petals within the heart;
then, outside of that, there are four vessels in the four directions.
The third [layer] consists of six lotuses; having drawn a six-petaled [lotus] in its center, it is surrounded by five [petals], each with five faces, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise.
O Pauṣkara, there are three arrays above that, and seven lotuses;
among them are lotuses with seven, eight, and nine petals respectively.
There are six and seven [petals] situated externally, and eight petals in sequence;
then there are three arrays (vyūha), and finally, ending at the top, there shall be a lotus of eight [petals].
There are seven layers of filaments in each of those; likewise, there is a third layer on the outside.
But, O Lotus-born One, each inner layer contains a single auspicious lotus.
Furthermore, O Lotus-born One, there are three sets of nine arrays;
in the center of each of these, an eightfold group is situated in the eight directions.
Having accomplished the eleven lotuses through the arrangement of thirteen petals—one as previously described within that [central lotus], and the remaining ten outside of it. (16)
And then, from the beginning of the seventh array, there is a lotus with eight petals, extending up to one with seventeen petals... || 17 ||
Within the first [mandala], one should fashion a ten-petalled lotus.
One should conceive each of those [petals] in turn by increasing them, until there are seventeen petals within them. || 19 ||
Furthermore, one should likewise arrange those situated outside, beginning from the ninth petal (*navapatra*) as before, increasing by one each time. (20)
O best of beings, each of those [lotuses], as well as the sixteen-petaled lotuses situated outside, [should be drawn] separately. || 21 ||
"Thus, O Lotus-born One, this arrangement of the sacrificial pavilions along with the lotus-design has been described by me to you in brief. (22)
The division of the directions for the lotuses should be as previously stated regarding the petals;
thereafter follows the measurement of the course starting from the lotus situated within the womb.
Together with the street and the lotuses situated outside, the first field is eleven [units]; the circular array of the *vyūha* is thus formed in sequence.
Beyond that, the second [mandala] should be twelve cubits;
one should fashion each subsequent one by this same sequence, increasing by one cubit at a time.
Indeed, by means of twenty-four hands, the completion of the array is achieved;
a field arises, circular in all directions, expansive and level.
O Brahmin, first take the measurement of some square enclosure;
then, using that measurement as the radius for a half-cord, draw a perfect circle from the center.
Now listen to the method for the measurement known as *kṣetramāna*, which follows the previously stated logic; first, divide the eastward direction and so forth into twelve equal parts. (28)
Starting from the Middle Country with threads equal in measure to the wings. || 29 ||
Having first filled that which was previously made circular and named "the Array-Bearer" (*vyūhabhṛt*),
one should then [proceed] from the lotus-pedestal with twelve equal parts at the beginning. (30)
One should mark all the lines until the field is reached;
beginning from the Brahma-sthāna, one should [mark] that group starting from the first part of the field. || 31 ||
Indeed, one should not perform [the measurement] from the edge of the field using the partial divisions;
rather, having first drawn a circle with five parts in the middle, one should proceed.
Then, having set aside one part and half of the path outside of that,
[one should place] the series of outer circles around that middle circle on all sides.
O Brahmin, above the [central] threads, one should rotate [the cord] by means of a thread measured in four parts,
while remaining equidistant from the central axis.
O twice-born one, when the circles have been rotated, two degrees of the circumference known as the field remain in the middle of the expansion.
The external location of the outer thread from the center is the Pauṣkara; its own extent is...
Furthermore, whatever space is remembered as being between the outer circles,
that should be equal to one another by means of an indefinite measure.
For that which is included within the *vṛtta* [is as follows]:
having arranged it manifoldly within a single [unit], one places the final [element] in the intermediate spaces. (38)
When the circle has been thus delineated, situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions, [one should draw] the circular forms... || 39 ||
They possess both gross and subtle forms and are endowed with various leaf-divisions.
Now listen to those previously mentioned sūtras which were set forth for the purpose of establishing the existence of external objects. (41)
Likewise, two equal lines should be drawn toward the east, west, north, and south.
Having rotated [the compass] by a measure of two parts of the sūtras, one should mark the center at the *pauṣkara*;
there, having drawn a lotus as before, [one proceeds with] the center... [43]
Having first established the seat (pīṭha) and so forth, one should [construct] the four petals by means of division within that [mandala], with the mandala outside the doors.

Then, Padmā is to be accomplished; otherwise, there is no accomplishment of the goal. This is due to the remainder of the three parts of the division of sixty [degrees] for my means of accomplishment. (The letters within the brackets are missing in manuscript *kh*; in *g* and *gh*, they appear as "śaṃvāsanastyame"). || 45 ||
Having unified that which remains within and having divided it, [one should proceed]. (46)
Rotate it with four well-proportioned parts, and with one part it is unequal;
having thus rotated three fields, one should then construct the pedestal (pīṭha).
Understand how that is done through the division of the limbs of the feet. 48.
In the first watch of the night, facing the seed-syllable,
one should first cast four lines according to the sequence of the Brahma-position.

Then, from the two circles of the directional thread according to the Paiṭhīya tradition, [one should draw] a circle situated outside by twice the measure of a person's body, and inside by half that measure; it is not by that same measure alone, O Pauṣkara. (51)

The portion, however, is established by means of both the mark and the circle; likewise, having drawn a thread between those two, there is indeed a state of being twice-heated for the small one, O Lord. (52)
(39) One should divide the sixteen-fold area of the courtyard into sections by means of two lines;
then, one should mark the Brahma-position with a line in the shape of a fish. || 53 ||
By means of the two circular lines drawn [from the corners],
and by means of the previously mentioned line representing one-sixth, [the center] of the two middle sections is determined in brief.
Then, one should mark two moons facing each other at the cardinal lines.
Listen to how each one reaches dissolution through the *pīṭha* and the *vṛtta*;
indeed, one reaches dissolution at the peak through the signs of intoxication (*matta*). || 56 ||
O twice-born one, before the two previously struck lines [of the lunar path] meet at the circumference, one should mark it in such a way that the union occurs according to the prescribed rule. 57.
One should mark the half-moon situated in the middle with the center [of the line];
I shall explain the procedure by which that is done for the sake of success in the lineage (*gotra*). (58)
One should avoid my [measure] by means of the two lines, the proximate and the distinct;
having fixed the line there, the width of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) should be determined. 59.
First, one should mark the center facing the foot with the instrument;
by this method, the side-gauge (gātraka) shall be formed on both sides. 60.
O twice-born one, it is like the mouth of a serpent, spread out and without interior;
from that middle part, the two limbs of the beings and then the feet [emerge]. (61)
Know this to be the procedure for the pīṭha; now listen to the construction of the door.
It should meet the directional line that extends beyond the doors and so forth. 62.
Having laid out the cord and returned, one should mark the side doors;
the width of the doors should be marked with a thread equal in length to the breadth. (63)
Then, having made a cord and stretched it out from the palate (*tālva*) to the lips (*oṣṭha*),
one should then mark the intersection of the circle with the directions within the circle.

O best of the twice-born, having thus stretched the thread for the purpose of establishing the door-posts and the feet of the door, one should [fix] that which stands within the space of the doorway along the directional thread.
Having divided it into four parts, one should mark them with clear signs;
leaving two signs outside that, the thread should be drawn on the third.
Then, he should lead it near the opening of that door; O twice-born one, he should mark it with a circle like that of the moon.
One should carefully join [the threads] with the two previously struck lines;
then, with that same floral offering, one should mark it extensively.
Are the horns and other parts of that thread situated with the slanted thread?
Just as the two horns are joined by the half-moon [mark] of the twice-born [the thumb-nail]. (69)
Then, in that very same manner, having drawn the thread from outside the door and [the point of] delusion,
one should lead the thread, once it has reached its completion, as far as the tip of the moon's horn.
O best of beings, having brought that [image] from its place at that time, it should be observed like a fish, until it reaches the outer limit of the door. 71.
The space between the two doorways, which is similar to the opening of a conch, should be known as the corner-ground area; it is divided into four parts within the circular mandala.
Having placed or drawn there four equal parts,
one should thus produce the middle circle in the center of the mandala.
One should fashion those same forms upon the external circle within the mandala according to the prescribed rule; now hear from me the specific details.
With two shoulder-lines [of the mandala], a lotus, and two [lines] for the pedestal and so forth, one should draw a thread facing the center and a thread right through the middle. (75)
Having observed that which was previously given and remains among them, one should proceed to another;
for by means of the middle thread of the circles, they appear divided into four parts. (76)
Having drawn the limbs [of the deities] with those threads as before, one should draw the doors;
O Pauṣkara, this applies to the center of the maṇḍala lotus and to those situated outside.
(40) There would always be an absence of lotuses for the mandalas;
for the arrays being drawn, the central mandala (or central circle) would be outside. || 78 ||
This characteristic of the maṇḍalas and their arrays has been described by me;
now the specific details regarding the lotuses alone are being stated. (79)
From this, one should arrange and conceive the measurement of the field according to its proportions; having measured all [the parts], excluding the outer mandalas. 80.
But should one make that sevenfold, or twelvefold as before?
The field [is divided] into petals and paths, with the arrangement of parts as previously described. (81)
One should determine the extent of the outer arrays of cities— whether triangular or otherwise— by taking one-eighth of the entire area of the field.
O Brahmin, today the adornment of the corners and the means for the doors of the city, or rather of the array (vyūha), come into being.
The field consists of fourteen cubits, with a measurement of six finger-breadths;
one should likewise visualize its array as thirty cubits in extent.
This measurement of the triangle of the world from the center is appropriate for the three directions, yet it exceeds [the space] from the corners. || 85 ||
Therefore, in this mandala, the two primary directions do not reside in the corners;
now, O best of the twice-born, I shall tell you its ritual procedure—listen.
As it has been stated, that which is being accomplished succeeds when its width is as described;
however, from the circular field of the array, it should be twice as wide as the object to be accomplished.
Having constructed a square city outside of that as before, he did so by means of that path-mastered [mantra] for the sake of first achieving the triangle. 88.
Then, for the sake of the field, having laid a cord in the middle commensurate with that field,
one should subsequently drop it as it is held fast by the two side-cords.
After that, one should lay down two threads, and then cast down the third,
avoiding the interval between the two previously struck threads.
From the circumference of the circle, a triangle is clearly drawn outside;
by this sequential method, one should again touch that circle.
Within the triangle, one should cast three lines;
[this is done] upon a circle that is tripled and increased by one-eighth.
O Pauṣkara, when that measurement is established from corner to corner, then indeed, O twice-born one, the interval between the directions and the corners is from the center. 93.
Determine the dimensions and the construction of the doors and so forth;
one should place the thread facing the center, and the thread in the direction of the quarters.

One should mark each [point] on the middle line—both from the outer side of the wing and likewise from the inner side—using a measurement that is doubled. Or, one may mark them using a doubled [measurement]. || 95 ||
One should divide the interior of those two into sixteen parts;
then, using the central thread as the core, one should lay down the threads there.
In this way, the thread extending horizontally is cast into that [square] for the purpose of making it such; [thus it is said: "one should cast it with compassion"].
In this manner, there are sixteen squares, doubled. || 97 ||
O Brahmin, in each direction, from door to door as before,
one should purify six [sections] at a time for the sake of attaining mastery over the throat and its vicinity.
With the remaining parts, the primary and secondary ornaments (śobhā and upaśobhā) are formed according to the proportions of the doors;
the door, accompanied by two primary ornaments, shall consist of twelve parts.
Each one that remains should be led from the two corners to the destruction;
likewise, there are two upaśobhās and four śobhās. || 100 ||
Know that there are thirty-two parts as before, with two parts each for the corners;
having made two parts each for the *śobhā* and *upaśobhā*, the remainder consists of five parts.
One should place the two corner mantras within thirty-two squares;
by this procedure, one should construct the triangular world outside.
O Pauṣkara, for those magnificent arrays that have been perfected,
and for whatever has indeed been completed, the lotuses and other elements are drawn. (103)
The characteristic of that [mandala] is stated according to the measurement of the ground in its center:
from the square, one should produce a triangle using three cords as before. 104.
Then, having first drawn a thread from the corner to the center, one should mark two lines above the wings using that same thread. (105)
O twice-born one, one should likewise form two remaining corners, with two [lines] on each side;
one should mark the lines until they reach the corners.
Understand the measurement and the construction of the doors and so forth, as well as the one hundred and fifty principal forms of the mantras. (107)
Formerly, for the sake of the attainment of worldly enjoyment and liberation for living beings in this world, you indeed manifested yourself through two deficient forms. || 108 ||

Precisely because they are established by the assembly of forms (mūrtisaṅgha), the forms are worshipped in sequence starting from the primordial form (ādimūrti) up to the number thirty-seven. || 109 ||
The lords of the years, the seasons, the months, the fortnights, and the days are recorded respectively, each one individually. || 110 ||

At the beginning, the lord of the year was declared; and who are those others, the leaders of the solstices? Six have been enumerated by the officiating priest as the lords of the seasons, and likewise the lords of the months. (111)
O Brahmin, twelve are said to follow in succession from Meru as the lords of the wings;
these forms are reckoned as the twelve suns by means of the triple verses (*tṛca*).
Whenever and wherever a sacrifice is performed by whatever means—
whether it be a single lotus, many lotuses, or a wheel with lotuses— 113.
The two [lines] fall outside the pedestal, upwards toward the lineage of gurus;
first, the Lord of the Year (Abdeśvara) is worshipped, and immediately after, the Lord of the Solar Return (Ayaneśa).
O best of the twice-born, for these six months— whether the southern course or otherwise—
one should worship the Lord of the Seasons and the sequence of the Lords of the Months according to their respective times.
O best of the twice-born, among the fortnights of the year, that which is to be worshipped immediately after [the month] is one specific lord of the fortnight.
Having worshipped their respective Sun-gods immediately after the Lord of the Fortnight,
they should daily offer oblations of parched rice and other foods, as well as libations to the fire.
Does one who has been worshipped at the time of worship ward off the Lord of the Form? This subject regarding the entire collection of forms has indeed been declared by me. (118)
From the fourfold form and so forth, one should arrange the conceptualization of the manifestations (vyūha) in sequence by number,
up to the seventeenth.
In that [mandala], by virtue of his sovereignty, he is the King of Mantras of the primary form;
