and having assigned the others to the petals in sequence for the sake of the forms, || 120 ||
O best of the twice-born, listen as I shall explain that in brief: regarding the fourfold manifestation, the four lotuses, and the four forms.
I shall proclaim the arrangement which is all-pervading for all:
one should place Vyūheśa within the pericarp of the central four-petalled lotus.
One should place the four forms, adorned with the six limbs, in sequence upon the respective petals in the southeast, south, and west.
Having established the forms situated upon the petals of the central lotus in sequence, starting from the eastern lotus and proceeding in a clockwise order, [verse 124].
The primary form is in the center of the pericarp, and [the others] are in the second circles (or, according to k, g, gh:
in the second abodes), situated in the directions of the east, the southwest, and the northwest. || 125 ||
In that very same [mandala], one should place [the mantra] from the center of the pericarp into another lotus;
indeed, this is the second Mantra-form, with two [mantras] each within the preceding petals.
Those two forms [arise] respectively from the leaves of Nairṛta and Anila;
then, in the third lotus, the third [form arises] within the pericarp (karṇikā).
The second [form] is the first form, and the fourth is from the middle of the petals;
the forms beginning with the chowrie-form (cāmara-mūrti) are to be placed upon the lotuses.
(42) And furthermore, O Lotus-born One, the arrangement should be performed with the true forms and so forth;
however, in the case of the multiform [images], it is done for all the other lotuses except for the central lotus. || 129 ||
O Lotus-born One, by means of which the Antamūrti may indeed attain preeminence among all [the forms], one should establish the Niṣṭhāmūrti in the center of the pericarp.
In this manner, one should install the four forms upon those three lotuses,
according to the previously described method, for the purpose of filling the petals.
Then, one should place that which is the second lord of the array above them; by whatever rite belongs to oneself, one should thereafter worship the assembly of forms.

Then, by this very same application, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) from that [deity] which is the assembly of the upper array (ūrdhvavyūha), situated within the five lotuses and so forth. || 133 ||
When, indeed, by way of circumambulation from left to right, one moves among the lotuses and their petals of the outer array into the interior of the pericarp (karṇikā), || 134 ||
O Lotus-born One, this is the ritual of placement (nyāsa) for the secondary forms and so forth;
the procedure for designating the primary form is in every case as previously described.
One should perform the second [rite], the *mūrtinyāsa*, as previously described;
this is remembered as the procedure for all *vyūha* sacrifices. || 136 ||
O Lotus-born One, for the purpose of the placement (nyāsa) of that which constitutes the primary minister,
one should place the Lord of the Vyūha as the twenty-fifth in the thirteenth Vyūha, as previously described.
Among the lotuses situated inside and outside, the outer lotuses are destroyed at the end;
thus it is in this collection of arrays, numbering one thousand.
One should perform the placement of the mantra-multitude in a counter-clockwise direction (apasavya) according to the sequence;
listen now as it proceeds from the first array until the very end. 139.
Then, as before, one should assign the four mantras to the Lord of the Array (vyūheśvara) in the center;
thereafter, they are assigned to the four petals located in the outer row starting from the east.
One should worship Vyūheśa in the center of the pericarp, and likewise in the other two [lotuses];
beginning from the eastern petal, one proceeds as far as the petal in the northwest.
Having placed the fifth mantra in sequence,
one should likewise place the sixth and seventh in the lotus of the Nairṛta direction according to the lotus-order.
Having placed the eighth and ninth [syllables], and having established the tenth— the king of mantras— from the tenth abode,
one should place it upon the lotus situated in the northwestern direction and then set down the vessels.
Having assigned the eleven-syllable mantra, the one called twelve-syllable, and the thirteen-syllable mantra to the four lotuses of the first array, there are thus thirteen mantras.
Now, regarding the second five-petalled lotus, I shall describe to you the placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa).
Within that five-petalled lotus, one should place Vyūheśa upon the pericarp (karṇikā).
Beginning from the eastern petal, one should place the five mantras therein:
starting from the fourteenth mantra up to the eighteenth, in successive order.
Now, the description of the four lotuses situated outside that will be given, starting from the eastern lotus up to the northern lotus. (147)
Having placed Vyūheśvara in the center, one should then assign the sixteen powers of the mantra to the petals according to the sequence of the four-fold manifestation (caturvyūha).
From the nineteenth up to the thirty-fourth,
the king of mantras [is arranged] in this very same sequence as a continuous series of petals for the arrays.
Beginning from the central lotus and filling it with the collection of mantras,
[one proceeds] as far as the array of ten lotuses, up to the thirteenth primary array.
O Lotus-born One, one should indeed place as many measures (mātrās) as there are leaves in the number of the arrays (vyūhas), and distribute them accordingly in each of those places.
O Brahmin, this Sahavyūheśvara [tantra], consisting of one thousand mantras, is completed without the six and five mantras. 152.
Whatever is in excess among the thirteen arrays,
that one should place in the tenth array, within the eleventh lotus.
Beginning from the central lotus, within the pericarp of all [the lotuses], one should place that [mantra] three times upon the petals of the central lotus. || 154 ||
Starting from the eastern petal and proceeding again to the tip of the inner petals,
one should do exactly the same for those on the outside, each with their own respective mantra.
But the third [line], having been turned back, [is placed] quickly within the pericarp;
and as before, having deposited the weapon-mantra at the tips of all the petals. (156)

Just as the arrangement of the primary forms (agramūrtis) in their respective parts has been declared by me, so too shall be the arrangement of the thousand forms of the divine manifestations (vyūhas). || 157 ||
One should not place the mantra located at the pericarp into the middle of a petal;
rather, one should place it in the center as before, through the application of the movement [of the breath]. 158.
But having first installed the Lord of the Array (Vyūheśvara) as before, one should then place him within the mantra,
and likewise install him upon the petals as has been described by me to you.
This single form of ritual placement (nyāsa) is proclaimed along with that [other rite];
it must not be performed in two ways, O best of the twice-born, as if it were a separate image.

Having determined the number of mantras according to that procedure when there is a desire, one should worship oneself as desired; indeed, in the ritual of the sacrificial array (vyūhayāga), it is what is sought.
O twice-born one, for the sake of attaining desired fruits, one should always perform with supreme devotion the rites of installation and so forth within the forms of Ruci.

In the year ending with Vatsara, the first letters of each group appear in sequence; for each [letter], its corresponding state arises from the sequence of birth and so forth, depending on the accomplishment of one's will. (163)

He should proceed with the *sohayā* form; otherwise, he should not worship another. Or rather, for whomsoever the path of mantra is complete with its limbs (*sāṅga*), that is supreme even over the eight petals. 164.
Having the nature of the essence of sound and enveloped by the greatness of the six qualities (ṣāḍguṇya), she,
as if desiring the final completion, moves above the pericarp and filaments.
She is the nature of the final vowel, all-pervading, and characterized by Brahman;
she resides within the lotus of the [central] portion, her form being the mantra, blazing with radiant light. || 166 ||
One should then recollect her with form above the pericarp and meditate upon her;
then one should worship her limbs upon the filaments, and without those [limbs], one should worship thereafter.
By means of the reality of mere sound (*śabdamātra-tattva*), as before, on the petals;
thus indeed has the sequence for the worship of the mandala of the Threefold Form (*trimūrti*) been described. (168)
O best of Brahmins, even for the Trimūrti who assumes forms by his own will, there is this specific distinction:
in that case, the lotus-stamen (karṇikā) should be above the water. (169)
The second [line] is situated above the filaments, and the third goes to the region of the petals;
indeed, in the worship of the preceding [deities], there are five, six, or seven objects.
One should fashion a collection of lotus petals equal in number to the forms;
one should worship each form with a petal, indeed, in due order.
And in the center, O lotus-eyed one, she who resides in the middle should be fashioned according to the rule; and outside of that, it is likewise in fire, in water, and here in the heart.
Through the distinction between the higher and the lower, one desires auspiciousness by worshipping the great host of mantra-forms along with their general retinue. || 173 ||
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Vyūhas," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, a great Upaniṣad within the illustrious Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
"O Lord of the gods, I have not heard the characteristics of the lotus of the disc."
Tell me now that which was previously indicated by you. || 1 ||
The Blessed Lord said:
This wheel-and-lotus is known in many ways as the hundred-thousandfold;
listen to me as I explain how this one has become manifold.
The deities who have gone, those who are present, and those who will go—from the beginning of the Dvirātmā onwards, there are hundreds of them whose number is not known. (3)
The paths to liberation proceed forth out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds;
they ferry living beings across the terrible ocean of existence.
They constantly bestow their grace upon devotees, those who have taken refuge [in them], those who rely on purity, and those who follow the path of the righteous.
Those who are portions of me, whose nature is power and who are endowed with the glory of the six attributes, are devoted to their welfare; having taken refuge in them, they worship and they triumph.
Praising aloud, bowing down, meditating, and constantly recollecting [the deity],
they are honored within the lotus-centered wheels and grant their desired boons.
For this reason, O best of Brahmins, I have been born from you— the supreme wheel, the support of all,
the source of transformation, and the cause from which all things dissolve.
From that excellent, circular disc, which resembles a thousand suns,
which is eternal, and which is directly devoid of parts— [from that] the eight winds [emerge].
I create the Cakras, such as Dvārakā and others, according to my own will; and wherever they are situated, the Vyūhas and other manifestations are worshipped by devotees. || 10 ||
Three, two, and one [of these] were not attached to a hub; likewise, they were all adorned with rims, covered by felloes, and beautified by axles.
Listen now to the means of accomplishment for all [deities], preceded by this first wheel, and those various forms which have been described by me in sequence. (12)
O Brahmin, I shall describe the ninefold division beginning with the *uttama* (superior),
as well as the distinctions of form in brief, and likewise the increase of the *māna* (measure).
Then follows the procedure for laying out the lines, as well as the calculation of the portions (aṃśaka);
thereafter, the construction of the spokes and the filling with colored powders (rajas).

O twice-born one, likewise [one should perform] the worship of the deities presiding over the parts of the wheel, as well as their etymological explanations; having assigned [the deities] to the axle and so forth, up to the rim (nemi), one should also worship the deities themselves.
Understand from me all this: the wheel and the fruit of worship.
He who, for the sake of worshipping the Lord, [offers] this foot and this wheel... || 16 ||
Now, O twice-born one, I shall explain in brief how that is to be drawn for all the mandalas, beginning with the Bhadra.
Then, in the middle ground, all that is brilliantly radiant along with the lotuses;
indeed, twelve parts from the two fields always reach as far as the seat of the Āgama.
That circle of space (vyomavṛtta) has been rotated outside the lotus of the wheel;
likewise, one should leave out a second part within the circle of space.
Then one should distribute the remainder; indeed, this is the description of the lotus-wheel and the lotus-mandala, as well as the characteristics of the lotuses alone, as told by me. (20)
Thus has been briefly described [the procedure] for those with overlapping petals, beginning with the three-petaled [lotus],
O Lotus-born One, just as it is for those with overlapping petals.
Now I shall describe the characteristics that increase prosperity for those who possess wheels,
concerning the site which I previously divided into five parts for you.
p.
45) Having properly divided it according to the sequence of rotation, one should fashion the axle;
then, by means of two rotating wheels, one part shall be the wheel-base.
And having thus broken it in various ways and caused the wheel to revolve, O twice-born one, [the image] should then be made from white or other precious gems, or indeed from metal. (24)
"Or else, O twice-born one, with a pure and shining substance born of minerals; [this half-verse occurs everywhere].
Thereafter, he should fill it with pure and shining powder. (25)
On the field of the eyes, one should draw a lotus with its pericarp properly raised;
the seed-syllable in the pericarp should be perfectly pure, resembling the stainless clarity of crystal. (26)
One should make the other seed-syllables dark blue and the pericarp the luster of gold;
one should fashion the series of filaments in the form of a tranquil fire.
One should make the cluster of lotus petals very white, as well as the white [markings] and so forth;
within this lotus, one should make [the center] resembling sapphire (indranīla) amidst the intervals between the petals.
One should cause all to be delighted by means of a white wheel-turning [monarch],
who is like a magnet or resembles a precious stone.
O Brahmin, one should fill the wheel on all sides with very beautiful powder,
and likewise polish its sharp edge until it is like the surface of a mirror.
And he should color the ground of the maṇḍala like a mass of sunbeams, with powder having the luster of yellow orpiment and resembling rubies. (31)
Then, having filled [the space] with yellow [light], either resembling thick flour or like fire,
one should draw a mass of rays.
O best of Brahmins, one should first prepare the site for the wheel;
then, having understood the mandala, one should color it as before.
Thus, this auspicious, white, circular abode of the wheel, dear to me,
has been duly described by me to you, along with that which is named Padmagarbha.
He who is named Vāsudeva, whose form is that of Māra and whose body is sound—within this [space], upon a worshipful eight-petaled lotus, he is to be honored one above the other. || 35 ||
Out of devotion, one who possesses the quality of purity (sattva) should place [the deity] above the three abodes, or [worship] the three abodes;
then, as before, one should assign the six limbs within the petals of the lotus.
Furthermore, O Lotus-born One, having worshipped that other form of mine which is indeed human, using one's own name preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) above the wheel.
The worship and the retinue should indeed be understood as before, through action, mind, and speech joined with the ending word "namaskāra. (38)
And the worship of the support for the ritual action and so forth, as set forth by Padmayāga—thus has that previous lotus-wheel been correctly described. (39)
And this multitude of its rays, which brings about the destruction of the gods Brahmā, Indra, and Rudra,
as well as of the Āpabhṛts and the Lohitas, even from being observed from a great distance.
O twice-born one, it is therefore renowned by the name Durdarśana, because it is always easily accessible to those devotees who bow down before it. (41)
Because it grants its vision to them, it is remembered as Sudarśana;
indeed, [its power extends] from the seventh netherworld (pātāla) up to the very limit of truth (satya).
This one, whose essence is vigor, constantly effects creation and destruction;
and within him, the cycle of existence revolves, together with gods, asuras, and humans.
For it constantly causes the wheel of saṃsāra to revolve for all those who do not know the Self; therefore, the gods and others call this by that name.
At the end of the kalpa, O best of the twice-born, he withdraws this entire multitude of beings by means of the splendor designated by me at the proper time.
In sequence, the wheel of the lotus-stream, indeed the wheel of the digits (kalācakra), and that which is fourfold—this is remembered as the unmanifest causal wheel (kāraṇacakram). || 46 ||

(46) Now hear from me about the transformed effects, such as the *dvārakā* [discs] and others; listen to the various forms of the discus (*cakra*) which bestow manifold supernatural powers (*siddhi*). (47)
O twice-born one, has this wheel ever arrived anywhere in such a sequence? Its first division, indeed, is declared to have two spokes. (48)
In the same way, another division with three spokes has been well-proclaimed later;
likewise, there is another with twice that number of forms, namely five spokes and six spokes.
Within these two wheels, there are indeed wheels having seven spokes, or eight spokes, nine spokes, and ten spokes. (50)
Those wheels are worshipped in the three worlds by the gods and others;
and the triad of wheels is common, consisting of the superior, the middling, and the inferior.
Now, listen as I explain how each of these three is further divided;
I shall describe the assembly of wheels individually and in detail.
Know that the first is the supreme wheel among the group of wheels;
another is declared to be the wheel called "supreme-middle. (53)
Likewise, the third is proclaimed as the superior-inferior; then there is the middle-superior wheel, and likewise the middle-middle. (54)
Likewise, the middle and the little finger—this indeed is the triad of the middle.
The triad of the third [finger], along with the properly placed little finger, is remembered as being from the hand. (55)
The lesser should be known as the middle, and the lesser than the lesser as the minor;
I shall describe for each one the indicative mark of auspicious characteristics.
O best of the twice-born, there is a supreme wheel with three naves and three rims;
there is a wheel with three naves and two rims; and now hear of the second and the third. (57)
The object of knowledge is to be understood as having three hubs and one rim; the third is remembered as the first.
The wheel with two hubs is said to be joined with a triad of rims. (58)
It has been stated that the second of the three wheels would be as described; listen now to this pair.
That is said to be joined with two hubs and provided with a rim. (59)
Therefore, I shall describe the second [mandala], which has two hubs and one rim and is adorned with three groups;
and I shall also explain the third, which consists of a triad of wheels.
The first is known as having a single hub (*ekanābhi*) and a circular rim (*vṛttanemi*);
however, that which has the form of two rims and one hub should be understood as belonging to the second type.
"There may be one hub and one rim; this third [wheel] has three [spokes].
Thus, that ninefold wheel, which is all-pervasive, has been described by me. (62)
One should determine the dimensions according to one's wealth;
O Brahmin, it may be as large as a six-spoked divine wheel, possessing excellent characteristics. (63)
Know that there are three sets of three; one should lead them from the finger to the ring finger.
Thus, the radiant wheel known as the month shall consist of twelve spokes.
Therefore, know that one should lead two and a half finger-breadths in succession until the number reaches thirty-six, which is the total count for the king of wheels.
This is the calculation of finger-breadths for the wheel known as the Saṃvatsara;
one should determine the equal measure for both those who are united and those who are divided.
Starting from one cubit, one should increase [the measurement] by a sixth part in succession, up to the procedure for the thousand-spoked wheel; such is the calculation of their parts.
(47) This is declared for the accomplishment of the *kalpa* known as the Yuga, when it has been fully worshipped;
[it applies] always to the wheels and lotuses that have arisen from equal finger-breadths. 68.
The arrangement of the seats (pīṭhas) and so forth should be performed, ending with the outer gate;
one should arrange twenty-five [units] for the purpose of the body including the limbs and feet.
One should carefully construct the city with four gates and five lines, devoid of legs or limbs, equal in size, and radiant with five colors.

But prior to the establishment [of the mandala], having determined the collection of lines for the neck by means of the directional threads extending to the east, south, west, and north, one should likewise stabilize them externally with threads.
One should determine the measurement from half the area of the wheel up to the extent of the lines of the elephants;
that shall be equal to the area of the pedestal of the field.
The width of the doors should be twice that [of the door-frames], measured according to the width of the hall;
alternatively, one may arrange these [proportions] there using a sixth or an eighth part.
With a young woman who is common among Brahmins yet possesses special qualities—having thus properly prepared the portion for the pedestal—one should cast eight threads. (74)

The limbs and feet [and the weapons, according to manuscripts g and gh] are formed by the portions situated in the cardinal directions, while those situated in the intermediate directions form the doors;
having divided the measurement of the door's width into two parts and then into three.

By dividing it into equal parts, the four-cornered [mandala] shall be successfully accomplished; having divided it, one should subsequently lay out the lines for the accomplishment of the doors, the ornaments, and the corners. 76.

Should he look outside at will? According to what is appropriate for the occasion and for the sake of beauty, [he should look] through the doors and corners, which are likewise beautiful, as if they were windows.
Are they being adorned with due ceremony as before?
For there is no lack of countless parts upon the edges of the cleansing cloths. (78)
O best of Brahmins, may the throat region [and so forth] of men be [purified] in due order by means of the feet and other [limbs]. (79)
Having made the outer part of the four corners of the threads into a single sacrificial thread (yāga), [one should proceed]. || 80 ||
Having performed the conceptualization of its mandala of light as being like a field of white water-lilies, one should then divide all directions of it into equal parts by means of squares. 81.
By the measure of the *vītabhāga*, the extent of that very mandala is indeed equal to a lotus (*abjakalpa*). || 82 ||
O Brahman, one should first draw a square with a single thread and then cast it outward.
Having fixed it with a cord and marked it with a split, as before, one should erase the seats and other features in various forms. || 84 ||

One should again discard from the rim-circle a portion equal to the circumference of the void. [Note on textual variants: In the manuscripts *k*, *g*, and *gh*, the sequence following "parilopayet" is as follows: "evaṃ cakrāravindānāṃ saṃsādhanamatho vakṣye cakrakṣetrāt" (three half-verses), followed by "vyomavṛtte evaṃ hi vyomavṛttādau yadā yacca nadyādau". In the manuscript *kh*, which follows the aforementioned body of the text, the reading "yadā yacca" is followed immediately by the single quarter-verse "nadyādau", suggesting that the intervening half-verses were dropped due to a scribe's error; this is considered the more sound reading. One should discard from the rim-circle a portion equal to the circumference of the void. Once again.
For in this way, one who has been deluded by the arguments concerning space and so forth is led astray from the authoritative means of knowledge. || 85 ||

When and whatever wheel one should draw, [provided it is] joined with the syllables *ra-ra-ka* and so forth, [it should be done] in the eastern direction at a riverbank or similar location... || 86 ||
Thus, I have described the dimensions of the wheels and lotuses;
now, for the benefit of practitioners, I shall indeed explain the excellent method of accomplishment.
One should determine the area of the rim (*nemi*) as one-sixth of the area of the wheel (*cakra*).
On the eastern side of a river or similar feature, where the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) resides, [one should perform the rite] for the destruction of the twice-born (*marakadvija*).
Having divided it equally according to the fields and gates, one should then clearly mark it with numbers.
One should first perform the folding of the allotted portions;
once the fold is made, one should then drop the central thread through the middle of all of them.
Thereafter, one should divide each of the petals eight times over.
Then, according to the sequence of the clear lines, one should strike down the thread.
Having divided a single portion between the two sides of the spokes,
one should always effect the accomplishment by means of six parts of the spokes.
Thus, O tiger among the twice-born, has this arrangement of the parts for the wheels of the *adhvara* and other [chariots] been declared; now hear the means for their swift movement.
In the middle of that [space] called *ara*, one should likewise mark the appearance of the *arākhya* [space];
having made a thread equal to the interval between the two peaks, one should indeed [use] that thread.
One should cause the two full moons to revolve in both directions;
for him who runs about with those full [moons], they are the most excellent. || 95 ||
One should perform the circumambulation starting from the *siddhisthāna*, while the thread remains fixed at the *brahmapada*;
or else, having divided the field with threads increased by one in each successive direction starting from the east.
Then, one should divide each pair [of spaces] sevenfold;
subsequently, there are six and six [sections] on the outer [perimeter], at the portion of each spoke among the lines.
The accomplishment of the spokes is by means of the middle lines; the eastern covering is according to the measurement of the circumference.
By two spokes, one part [of the space] within is thus distinguished. 98.
O Brahmin, by performing this rite at all times according to this procedure, this joining together of broken chariots has been described by me. (99)
And [I shall explain] the designation of the *varasīkī* and of the *kevalā*s in brief; I shall now proclaim the characteristics of the *kartarī*, the *antarī*, and so forth. 100.
When the eastern part was previously divided into eight parts, and the western part into twelve,
it is recorded that by dividing [the former] into six parts, the eastern gateway is established.
When the spokes have been thus established, one should perform the gathering (sañcaya) at the hub;
and from both sets of spokes, that which remains is the triad and the pair.
On the side of the *aṃśakas*, the *kartarī* is to be accomplished by that;
the planets are clockwise, and the thieves have the form of axes everywhere, with the letters being uniform in form. || 103 ||
Having drawn it up on the northern side according to the orientation of the eastern form,
one should lead it around and thus accomplish the protection of these deities.
The accomplishment of the *kartarīs* is performed precisely by way of circumambulation;
for the purpose of that accomplishment, the number of threads is recorded as remembered in the oral tradition (*vāgama*). 105.
Having placed [the cord] at the junction of the east-west and middle-east lines of the circle,
one should lead another cord from the center, having bowed to the middle.
From the root of the second spoke, one should bring the tip of that same spoke to meet with the two [other] spokes;
thus, the middle [point] is marked, and then one should lead it to the tip of that spoke.
From the center of the grove, having fixed [the marker] at the third point where it perfectly aligns with the full moon, one should then bring the cord; now understand that location. 108.

O best of the twice-born, from the center of the fourth spoke of that which is to be drawn along the tips of the spokes, there is a meeting of six; from that point, the position is like that of a fish.
One should mark it down to the base; thus the scissors are clearly manifested.
This is indeed the general definition; now the specific [details] are being stated. (110)
O Lotus-born One, by virtue of its lack of contraction or expansion, does the practice of the *kartarīs* ward off even a diminished serpent? (111)
O Pauṣkara, having likewise taken the measurement from the root to the tip of the spoke by means of two circles, one should fix the length of the cord therein.

Indeed, one should again touch the threefold state with great reverence; for that very union occurs when, in the confusion of the interval between the fourth state and the others, there is a rapid contact.
Being impelled toward that limit, one should join it with the previous mark,
so that the spokes of the spokes (kartarīs) may clearly have their roots aligned equally. (114)
I have already explained the means for those [beings] who are obstructed by a creator; now, the means for others, known as the "surrounding" (paridvitīya), will be described. 115.
O best of Brahmins, within the interval of the rotation at the base of the speed,
one should rotate that [line] evenly, starting from the fourth part of the *nemi*-field.
That wheel, however, should be understood as being slightly more than the body of the hub;
one should conceive of it as being divided by a fourth part of the circumference-field. || 117 ||
O best of the twice-born, you should worship the navel-field according to the power of the wheel;
in the field known as Nābhinemi, which is circular, a woman [attains] duality in due order.

Is it not the case that the field beginning with the navel is called the gross "field" (kṣetra)? This conceptualization of the field belongs to that passion for one's own [limited] nature which is known as the "outer" (parā). || 119 ||
One should indeed perform [the ritual] starting from the circle of space (vyomavṛtta) and ending with the sense-organ (akṣa);
one should perform the conceptualization (kalpanā) starting from the sense-organ and ending with the circle of space. || 120 ||
In that [region], the *vallikā* and *jaṭharā* mountains are shaped like citron fruits, while others are as broad as lotus petals and have the form of blue lotus blossoms.
Now listen to the method for accomplishing these three types of *yavodara*:
having divided the field into twelve parts according to the sequence known as "the rotation. (122)
In the middle, the axle is made with three parts, while the nave is made with two parts;
between the nave and the axle, there is one part known as the wheel (cakra).
One should indeed divide the non-field portion of the rim into two parts;
one should completely set aside one part from between the rim and the non-field portion.

Having divided the non-protective field (arakṣetra) into two parts, one should rotate [the cord] immediately thereafter; at the junction of the central cord of the spokes and the non-returning [cord]. 125.
Then, having placed a cord measuring one-third [of the width] at the distance of three [units],
one should mark two sides of the middle cord, starting from the middle cord itself.
Having placed another [mark] in the same manner upon this marking-line,
one should indeed make the fish-mark from the base up to the top with that very line.
Indeed, from the tip of a spoke to the rim, it is exactly the same as the second [spoke];
this is what is described as the connection of spokes resembling a citron fruit. (128)
Having marked the thread produced from two parts at the junction of the middle thread called *ara* and the root of the *tvara*,
and having lowered it, || 129 ||
Having placed a thread from the base to the tip, like the shape of a half-moon, so that it touches the circumference of the base,
one should likewise place the thread at the moon’s horn.
Likewise, O twice-born one, the tip of the spoke should be struck so that it extends like a lotus petal;
this characteristic has been fully explained as it was previously indicated by me. (131)
O Brahmin, listen to the method for drawing the tips of the blue lotus petals, the spokes, and the two circles—the outer circle from the root and the second circle. (132)
O twice-born one, having made a thread that reaches the junction of her slender-waisted belly,
and having drawn threads from the sides through the center,
one should then lead a thread from the mark at the center to the tip of the spoke.
From that, one should mark the center down to the root known as *arā*;
when the other marks are made, it will resemble the petals of a blue lotus.
Having first divided the field into three parts, one should draw a circle evenly;
then, one should mark each spoke according to the sequence of clear lines.
One should lay down six lines upon the squares of the lord of the twice-born (the eight),
and one should lead [the lines] so as to possess eighteen compartments and single spokes.

O tiger among the twice-born, one should erase the two square boxes containing the letters *a* and *va* (or *ca*) which are uniform in form everywhere; likewise, one should rub them out from the root. 138.
Then, two by two from the center and on both sides as well;
when these have thus been deleted, one should quickly delete the other spokes on the exterior.
(50) O twice-born one, for the sake of success, one should erase the four squares from the base as well as those in front, and likewise two squares from the middle. 140.
And that which is known as "the interior of an anthill" (*valmīkudara*) is not actually an anthill;
it is like the space between spokes that has been obliterated from the tip, the root, and the middle. (141)
That [seed] is devoid of spokes and external; its root, middle, and tip are in rapid succession.
For it is indeed like the interior of a barley grain, yet not merely the appearance of the interior of a barley grain.
Having divided and rotated it fourfold, or [divided] twelvefold as appropriate, [one should take] from the middle portion between the two anthills and from the middle of the two wings. (143)
The sequence of four, four, two, and two from the base to the tip has been previously stated.
Then, by means of this sixfold division according to one's own conduct and so forth, one should erase the clear lines within the akṣa and other parts [where the 'daṃta' ending occurs]. || 145 ||
One should perform the purification of the six twice-born classes as they manifest;
indeed, for each wheel among the wheels, it is situated in the middle of the field of the rim (nemikṣetra).
Listen as I describe how one should display the various [divisions]:
that field should be marked out evenly, with spokes equal and doubled. (147)
One should likewise drop the threads facing the tips of the spokes and along their sides, as appropriate,
according to their respective positions.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, this is known as the measurement of the wheels' peripheries (pradhina),
just as the head, the feet, and the body are held together by the sinews.
In the same way, their first station on this wheel is fixed;
they are not seen anywhere else except within the region of the rim.
"This is declared to be the wheel;
one should demonstrate it twice, with many [parts], on the outer limit. (151)
Having abandoned two within, and for that which is turned by three spokes, on the third [spoke] the first [operation] should be performed according to the enumeration as before. (152)
O tiger among the twice-born, the method for the accomplishment of wheels with two spokes and so forth has been described; thereafter, one should worship them during the rāsa dance.
One should fill all the circular designs (cakravṛtta) with white [pigment], having placed those called "efforts" (yatna) and the "pendants" (lamba) within the insignia (lāñchana). 154.
And upon well-proportioned lines that resemble the edge of a sword,
one should fashion a white lotus as before, with petals that do not touch one another.
Within that [space] between the rim and the nave-joined [center], one should fashion a lotus; its interior petals should be made black. (156)
O twice-born one, the dust of the three-naved wheel (the sun) appears in sequence like a sprout of golden durvā grass;
likewise, the dust of the single-naved wheel (the moon) is like gold, dark, and even reddish. || 157 ||
O Lotus-Seated One, the coloring of the wheel was previously described; one should completely fill all the spokes with red pigment, just like the rim. 158.
O best of the twice-born, the space between the spokes is considered equal to the surface of the wheel;
it is yellowish-white, white, and also white with three rims.
One should fill the single-rimmed wheel with yellowish-red dust, with very white dust, and with pure white dust alone. (160)
One should color it with all the [petals] having the luster of a hundred naves and rims, or otherwise;
the inner and outer parts of the principal [lotus], from those [petals] which are contracted. || 161 ||
Then, by the very method of mutual approach, one should fulfill [the rite] with the syllable 'A' from the *vibhītaka* leaf, along with the collections of the limbs and deities. || 162 ||
(51) All the primary constituents (pradhayas) are perfectly white, resembling masses of snow;
thus has this filling with *rajas* been described by me. (163)
One should bestow the seed-syllable situated within the lotus, along with the three abodes; one should assign the color according to Maya himself, joined in sequence to the pericarp and other parts.

Therefore, the deities of the sense organs and so forth, along with the ether, are established as complete within that [Supreme Self], just as gold is present in its dross; however, the eye itself is proclaimed to be the "akṣa. (165)
The three naves of the wheels are, in sequence, presided over by Madhu, Ajita, and Samadaiva;
and the rims of the wheels are, in sequence, equal to the end of the aeon wind (Kalpāntānila) and its presiding deity, Sārasa. || 166 ||
O Brahmin, Kālavaiśvānara is within the centers of the Siddhacakra;
there resides the goddess Sarasvatī, the patient one, the controller, worshipped by the gods. 167.
Having gathered these deities of the three rims together with their presiding lords, come forth from the ocean, encompassing everything all around. || 168 ||
And for the sake of nourishing the two worlds of seven realms situated on both sides of the region of the wheel, he stands facing the Lord of Waters as they set forth.
Having spoken thus, one should worship all the deities at the proper time,
duly honoring them in these locations with flowers, incense, and other offerings.
Because it is without beginning, the axle is equal, situated in the center between the rim, the spokes, and the nave;
for, O Lord, it consists of the three Vedas, arising from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman.
O twice-born one, having entered the range of the Daityas' ears, that sound quickly pierces them;
and having entered the hearts of the Daityas' wives as well, it does the same.
Whenever the embryos situated within the womb reach a certain stage, then by that sound—which bestows fearlessness—those enemies of the gods are torn asunder. || 173 ||
The pure sound residing within the heart is born from the sacred revelation (Śruti);
therefore, it destroys all that is inauspicious for those who constantly follow the path of the virtuous.
Therefore, for this reason, no specific designation is proclaimed for what is external to the senses;
for they shine exceedingly at the end of time when they have been fully augmented.
Within the circle of rays, through various distinct forms, the bodies are thus designated as situated within the navel and the eyes. (176)

Just as the wind flows through the various divisions within the channels, O twice-born one, so too do the syllables remain uniform everywhere throughout the spokes of the navel; meanwhile, the heat remains steady and difficult to endure.
O best of the twice-born, how does that which issues from the channels of the wheel [of the body] experience the three Vedas?
And why, O supreme among the twice-born, does it not [experience them] where there is the manifestation of light? 178.
In this context, the channels (nāḍīs) are first mentioned because they constitute the nature of the sacrificial staff;
they are that light which has proceeded in manifold ways through the paths and has emerged from the wheel.
As that fourfold wheel revolves externally, its function, such as the state of functioning and so forth, proceeds; and for a moment, one should cause it to revolve around [the center]. || 180 ||
O twice-born one, it was as pure as the ocean and radiant with splendor,
surrounded by eight blazing, smokeless fires.

Just as a firebrand (*alāta*) revolving in the sky appears as a white circle when it moves separately from its own path, so too does that [sun] appear as a circle of fire. (182) *Note: The commentary notes that the word "firebrand" (*alāta*) should be connected here with the phrase "the vow of the seven [planets]" (*saptalātavrataṃ*), though this seems to be a scribal or interpretive gloss on the term's usage in this context.*
Likewise, this form of the wheel is remembered by the Arakartaris; O twice-born one, this circle born of fire should be drawn with effort and devotion. (183)
Then this threefold form is endowed with the word "kadā-rūpa" (of what form?).
When? At that time, the radiance which is the wheel is of a flickering nature. || 184 ||
His splendor and vital energy shall be established under this designation;
therefore, will there not be a destruction of the Jayantīs and Pitṛs in the years following the second Nemī? || 185 ||
But that which arises from fire, being mixed, is known as having a circular rim (*vṛttanemi*).
Now, listen to the ritual placement of the mantra (*mantranyāsa*) in brief. (186)
O best of the twice-born, that collection of mantras for all the forms, beginning with the Puruṣa, along with their six limbs, which was previously revealed by me to you; || 187 ||

Having properly laid out the threads starting from the east by circumambulating clockwise, and having established them according to the sequence of the ritual procedure, listen to me regarding that [mandala] beginning with the red [color]. 188.
By means of the mantra consisting of the soul of the male nature (puṃprakṛtyātman), it is recorded as being beyond the previous wheel;
likewise, there are the [wheels] called Pauruṣa, Prakṛti, and Pradyumna. (189)

Having thus placed the fourfold self in the prison and likewise elsewhere, one should sequentially place the wheel consisting of all mantras (or, according to k, g, gh: the previously mentioned mantras) as far as the prison itself.
O twice-born one, this indeed is the Koṇa [mantra] consisting of a thousand forms and mantras.
One should fill two thousand hands with the six limbs;
when the wheel at the gateway is worshipped, the double-self becomes worshipped. || 192 ||
The threefold self is in the three-spoked [cakra], and likewise the fourfold self in the others;
this continues up to the cakra of ten spokes, following the sequence beginning with the previous mantra.

Now, its nature as that very number is explained by means of the mantra of the active form (pravṛttimūrti) through the division known as the "twice-self" (dvirātman), within the wheels and the gateways.
O best of Brahmins, he who, having formed a mental resolve within himself, performs worship with devotion to the thousand-fold form of the Self for a thousand horse-sacrifices; || 195 ||
The man who worships in a wheel with two thousand spokes— || 196 ||
He remained there, established in the form of a doorkeeper (or teacher). || 197 ||
O twice-born one, for all [of them], in the center of the wheel is an eight-petaled lotus.

Likewise, at the beginning, as before, one should worship the supreme syllable of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-paramākṣara) during the rite of the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa), in the infinite jar (anantakalaśa), in you, in the sprout (aṅkura), and in the ritual procedure (vidhi). || 199 ||

Indeed, through the festival of the *vinoda*, during the rite of establishing what was already established (*sthitasthāpana*), one should worship the causes, the means, and the weapons upon the seat (*viṣṭara*) and other such items. (200)
O Lord, one should draw them upon the foundation-pile in their respective places;
the three worlds of the world-protectors are on the walls, the cows, and the sky. || 201 ||
Then, one should worship that [deity] on the ground according to the prescribed visualization;
this very same rite is remembered for the mixed wheels as well. || 202 ||
O Lotus-born One, this placement for the worship of all deities has thus been revealed to you in brief. (203)
Having first meditated upon and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of one's entire body within the heart,
he who worships the cakra while tasting the nectar shall become a partaker of the fruit of liberation.
Whoever worships the second [image] comes into my proximity;
he who worships the third attains residence in the same world as me.
He who worships the fourth [deity] is honored even in Satyaloka;
he who sacrifices to the fifth remains for an imperishable period of time in Tapoloka.
He who worships the sixth wheel goes to the world of knowledge;
and he by whom the seventh is honored shall attain his own world.
In heaven, he shall become worthy of worship by Vāsava and the other gods, and he shall attain immortality; by him I am worshipped in the ninth [birth], and he shall go to Śvetadvīpa. (208)
By whomsoever it was worshipped with devotion for a period equal to a lifetime, or even for the tenth [birth],
it became the object of attachment for the serpents dwelling in the seven netherworlds.
And you, O best of the twice-born, are worthy of honor by the beautiful women of the netherworld (pātāla).
Thus, all this auspicious fruit of the worship of the discus has been recounted to you.
Regarding the wheel of the perfect cause and so forth, it has a single hub and a single rim;
O Lotus-born One, one should worship you at its very limit. || 211 ||
"Reveal [this] always to your own devotees and to those who possess faith.
Pauṣkara said:
"O Brahmin, having been addressed thus in the past by Viṣṇu, whose form is manifest,"
Everything concerning the characteristics of your wheel has been correctly described by you. || 213 ||
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Discus-Lotus," in the Pauṣkara Saṃhitā, a Great Upaniṣad within the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
The sages said:
"O Brahman, best among the knowers of Brahman, what indeed is the Miśracakra (the Mixed Wheel) like?"
Out of a desire for the welfare of the sages, explain this doubt.
Pauṣkara said: "O Lord, it was exactly in this way that in former times, prompted by the doubts of the Brahmins and for the sake of the welfare of all the worlds, I was urged by Viprabuddhi. (2)
Arise, O delighter of Lakṣmī! Tell me that which was spoken by you in the past:
the characteristic of the mixed wheel-sacrifices (cakrayāga). || 3 ||
The Blessed Lord said:
Just as various conceptualizations were previously described for the wheels according to the divisions of *uttama* and so forth, in the same way they are proclaimed for the mixed types.
The primary, the intermediate, and another which is known as the lowest—thus it is remembered. The primary number is unnameable; indeed, the intermediate one is threefold.
And likewise, O Lotus-born One, it should be understood that in those called "mixed," there is indeed a first conceptualization which is ninefold and accompanied by the presiding deity.
Now I shall speak of that; listen with attention as I describe it in brief:
first, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with its petals unattached [to one another].
Outside of that, one should fashion a six-spoked wheel with mixed colors;
O Pauṣkara, that which is to be accomplished by means of wheels should be done with red wheels, O King of Wheels.
One should write "parasvam" (another's property) and "pathihīranisūtam" [the syllables are the same everywhere] as "nisu";
or alternatively, one should demonstrate it by means of the two wheels preceded by the sixth.
As before, on the rim-ground (*nemibhūmi*), the four central [sections] are to be excluded;
or, when [the design] is situated outside the circle, the spokes (*pradhayaḥ*) are said to be in one [section]. || 10 ||
p.

54) The presiding principle (adhyakṣa) is perceived within those wheels of diverse forms when they are established in their arrangement according to the relationship of the covered and the coverer. || 11 ||
The purpose for you has indeed been declared by me previously regarding the spokes, from the beginning of the supreme wheels up to the interval in the middle. (12)
Listen to this mixed Cakrayāga, the first [rite], O Amara?
Beginning from the highest and the middle, it is produced as far as the Cakra and so forth. || 13 ||
The wheel of the youngest is the second, while the king of the mixed is the third;
by this sequential method, one should perform the mixing.

As long as each successive circle is smaller than the preceding one, and the middle of each circle is properly aligned with the middle of the next, when this is correctly done, the sixfold wheel becomes auspicious. || 15 ||
The ninefold collection of mixed wheel-sacrifices has been enumerated;
thus has the supreme arrangement of mixtures been declared by the Equal One.
Now I shall describe the second type, which is indeed called "the middle" (*madhya*) and is of three kinds:
it has either three naves and one rim, or likewise, one nave and three rims.
One should first draw the wheel according to one's desire outside the lotus,
that wheel-lotus being provided with a hub and a rim, and [furthermore] with half a rim.
And gradually, one should indeed draw a lotus outside the circles;
O Brahmin, one should then draw it surrounded by that [lotus], provided with a rim.
Therefore, by means of this sequential application, one should lead the metal from the rim of the previous wheel to the group of spokes at the nave.
Now, for the sixth of the five-and-a-half cakras, one should fashion the rim as before with effort; this is remembered as their middle arrangement. (21)
Now, understand the mixed varieties among the lotus-wheels:
one should construct a wheel with three hubs and a lotus, or indeed one that is curved at a single point. (22)
But outside of that is a group of four; those [circles] are devoid of spokes. And the desired circles to be accomplished are provided with rims on the outside. || 23 ||
And it is adorned? It is proclaimed as being deficient by the channels (nāḍīs) and by others;
and for that which is situated, there are many divisions according to those two, the gods, the Vasus, and the moving ones (caras). || 24 ||
O twice-born one, this [measurement] of the spokes has been proclaimed and established;
one should fashion the thousand-spoked [wheel] in three ways, beginning with the best. (25)
Listen now to how it is by means of the three qualities (triguṇa), from the triad, or from the womb (garbha).
First, the superior and the inferior have been proclaimed. (26)
The second [wheel] is the thousand-spoked one belonging to the middling and the superior;
the third is declared to be inferior, extending up to the end of the middling. || 27 ||
O Pauṣkara, listen now in due order to their primary field;
indeed, those wheels which were previously mentioned as being both principal and minor. (28)
All [the altars] are nine cubits in size and provided with six pegs; I shall now describe their arrangement according to the divisions, beginning with the maiden [altar]. || 29 ||
O twice-born one, it should be understood that there are one hundred and fourteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
now the division [of the area] consisting of those [fingers] is being described.
For all [the deities], half a lotus is to be known as fifteen finger-breadths; for the sake of the success of the navel, the vital breaths, and the siddhis, there are three powers (*balas*).
That field which is preceded by the navel [should be marked] with three sets of six limbs;
one should draw a circle, half of a wheel, in the place of the excellent *praṇava* and the twice-born.
(55) Specifically, among those [spokes] which possess hubs, rims, and wheels,
there is a binding at the root of the spokes within that [structure]. || 33 ||
This measurement indeed has been proclaimed for the *cakrabandha* [stūpa]; however, it is always common to all of them with respect to the outer wheel. (34)
Alternatively, having made a thread [measuring] the wheel-born [deity], one should perform the demarcation of their fields;
then, one should effect the establishment of the nave, spokes, and rim here in due order.
When the wheel together with the lotuses— the abundance of lotuses— has been thus fashioned,
[one should place] the enemy's wheel outside of that wheel alone.
Then, the measurement of three finger-breadths is to be applied;
it is established by dividing the fields starting from the center. (37)
In this manner, one should determine the measurement for all the external wheels;
however, the measurement for the inner wheel should be increased by three finger-breadths in successive order.
O Lord of Brahmins, the desired area up to the hub of the outer wheel becomes equal and uniform when all parts are combined. (39)
This measurement is prescribed for the naves, rims, and wheels;
now listen to the rules for those of the highest and middle sizes.
Having made the lotus twenty-four finger-breadths in measurement,
one should then eliminate the measurement of the navel and the previous measurement, as well as whatever is deficient.
The measurement of the hub and the rim should be carried out by oneself and remains beyond words;
furthermore, the measurement of their lotus-base should be known as eighteen finger-breadths.
Thus has been stated the measurement of the field in three ways for the mixed age; now understand the common support for the gods who possess the portion of the Brahmins. 43.
One should visualize a six-spoked wheel outside the lotus; then, one should fashion that wheel like the petals of a *parilla* flower. || 44 ||
Alternatively, one should draw an eight-spoked wheel within a barley-shaped enclosure;
then, one should construct a twelve-spoked wheel for that lotus-cakra using those vowels.
Beyond that, within the belly of an ant, one should fashion a sixteen-spoked wheel;
then, one should make a twenty-four-spoked wheel with parts resembling citron fruits.
Then, O twice-born one, when joined with the agent and conjoined with the Kevalas,
one should fashion a wheel with thirty-four spokes known as the Paraśu.
When this has been performed in this mixed manner, the wheel-sacrifice (*cakrayāga*) consisting of a hundred spokes is accomplished;
its body is said to be of two forms over the course of a year.
Then one should ascertain the six seasons within the six spokes;
they are outside the door of the enclosure, constituting the sixteen months.
Those twenty-four fortnights are established therein; O enemy of Māra, they exist everywhere.
Then there are the sixteen fortnights known as months, and those of the year. (50)
In that regard, know that there are two solstices (*ayana*) and two transits (*saṃsthā*);
these two are designated as southern and northern, and they are common to both types of years. (51)
And where this [system] is called "Bondage" (bandha) despite its lack of fragmentation, that [system] remains;
it belongs to the one known as Miśra, consisting of a hundred [verses], and comprising various divisions. (52)
Thus, O sinless one, this means of accomplishment has been declared to you in its entirety;
previously, the thousand-spoked [wheel] was indicated as existing in three ways through its mixture.
I have heard from you the measurement of the field, as well as that of the spokes, and their division;
it is proclaimed that the circumference of the hub is exactly one hundred and twelve [units]. (54)
One should fashion half of that lotus with thirty-one finger-breadths;
then, outside of that, the regions of the nave, spokes, and rim should be ten finger-breadths each.

The rim and spokes of the wheel situated outside that [mandala] reach the earth; heaven extends for one finger-breadth on each side of the twice-born [the spokes], measuring sixteen finger-breadths in total. (56)
The third layer from the ground is said to be nineteen finger-breadths;
then, the earth [layer] of the fourth quarter-measure is twenty-two finger-breadths. (57)
We shall now describe the measurement of the fifth [section], which is the previously mentioned barley-measure (yava).
Three cubits (hasta) consisting of twenty-five finger-breadths each shall constitute the triad.
O Pauṣkara, the sixth wheel should consist of twenty-eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
its rim and hub should each be half of that, and this should always be so.
That which has been stated for each individual wheel proceeds in three ways;
then, having understood it as either threefold or single in nature, one should perform it with equal portions.
Excluding that which belongs to one's own field, the hub, and the rim—[the others are those] by which [the wheel turns];
the wheel is the excellent abode of wandering, and the wheel is also as described before. || 61 ||
If you do not desire the full moon [or the first day of the lunar fortnight] from a field of twelve equal parts,
one should indeed contract the ground when the destruction of the navel and the rim occurs.
Then, one should accomplish a thousand *arakas* in this sequence;
having drawn a lotus circle, one should first inscribe the *tāra*, and then the King of Weapons (*hetirāj*).
Then, one should draw five other wheels outside of that in sequence; hear, O Rāma, the names for the spokes according to the method of the previous enclosure. || 64 ||
With those hundreds and hundreds arranged in sequence, and with thirty and thirty joined in order,
as well as forty joined in sequence, one should likewise construct two wheels.
One should fashion three wheels in sequence with two hundred and fifty [units] and then with sixty more, so that there may be a thousand spokes.
That which is called the "Yuga" is said by the Siddhas to be the "Mixed" (miśra), which is highly honored;
for these [rites], including the limb-sacrifice (aṅgayāga), are to be known in sequence as eighteen.
O Brahmin, my success through vigor today does not depend on those [ordinary means], just as the movement of the wheels beginning with the *uttama* has been proclaimed. 68.
Outside the grain, there are white [elements].
In that place where the two of you [were] at the end, one should cause life to flourish;
having produced a lotus petal, one should fashion a blue-lotus petal.
One should join those [petals], shaped like the petals of a blue lotus, in their proper places; outside the field of the enclosure petal, there is a shining leaf.
For some, the wheel appears on the outside of the parasvāra;
and in the case of the Cakra and Sadevacakra, the virtuous perceive it as being at the very beginning.
It is dark, and just as before; listen then to that... [kh:
reading] ...and having abandoned us, he would then cause it to revolve among the spokes.
For whom [the internal and] external [offerings] have been presented with glory... and so forth.
[The verse is fragmentary: "O young woman...
this [world] is not truly enlivened by its own life-force. Because of the lack of connection to the movement of that [life-force], those tips of lotus petals which stand outside the lotus... (69)
Would you two live in that place, a difficult region at the end of time?
Having become as delicate as the edge of a lotus petal, would you endure the harshness of a blue-lily leaf? (70)
One should join those [petals], shaped like the petals of a blue lotus, in their proper places;
outside that is the lotus of the supreme speech, with its shimmering petals.
When someone’s wheel is on the outside by four finger-breadths,
then that person is a base sinner within the circle of the gods.
p.
57) [The question] "What next?"—listen to how that should arise, just as before: O twice-born one, having first struck the middle thread called *ārā*, || 73 ||
But at the very tip of the spokes of the inner circle,
having left aside a portion of a minute fraction for the sake of creating a separation, there is also an outer circle of spokes.
Having laid the thread across the center of the spokes, one should mark the half-moons; having brought the thread to the position of Brahmā, one should bring it to its peak. || 75 ||
O twice-born one, having divided that circular region into six equal internal sectors by means of rotation, you must establish the boundaries of the regions.
Then, having laid down the threads according to the sequence starting from the east, you should indeed accomplish the attainment of the goal;
for your friend is truly the god himself.
O Brahmin, when the procedure for the wheel— both the outer and the inner— is being performed,
once the collection of spokes has been successfully completed, one should fashion it according to the remaining area.

The wheel-field (*cakrakṣetra*) is indeed perfectly circular, with its dimensions as previously described; each one should be measured separately according to the very same procedure mentioned before. (79)
And for the sake of removing discord, O best of Brahmins, one should perform the laying out of the lines;
likewise, one should carry out the construction of circles and the accomplishment of the spokes. (80)
Thus, I have described all this—the practice of the mixed [mantras] and the wheels (cakras) in brief; now hear from me their specific distinctions.
As it has been said: "That measurement belongs neither to the hub nor to the group of spokes;
rather, it belongs to all the wheels. Therefore, one should perform the movement [of the ritual] accordingly. (82)

O Pauṣkara, having understood the contraction and expansion within the terrestrial fields—from the field [known as] Ekanābhīya and likewise from that which was born of Ekanābhi—[one attains liberation]. 83.
Having grasped half the name or one-third, one should cast it out; [it is] gone to the beginning, middle, and end by means of the three naves and the two wheels of the field. || 84 ||
Then, regarding the varieties of passion (*rāgabhedam*), he spoke with haste from the beginning; first, as before, is the lotus-born *kahlāra*, and likewise the succession of the *bhramas*. (85)
The spaces between the bowls were like lapis lazuli;
then, with a dye of uniform color, they became like the petals of a blue lotus. || 86 ||
Having filled it, [one should place] within that Brahman, which is white and radiant like the interior of a barley grain; immediately after that, [one should place] the black [syllable]. 87.
One should prepare [the vessels] with chosen yellow pigment; they should be like the likeness of citron fruits.
With a brilliant red dye, one should fill their centers. (88)
Then, one should color the outer segments with a powder resembling royal blue, and the space between those spokes with a yellow pigment like *rocanā*. (89)
O twice-born one, these [ornaments], together with the movements of bees and filaments, should be filled in accordance with the beauty of the stage for the entire assembly of the circle. 90.

O Brahmin, having completed the great collection of sacrifices with supreme devotion, one should accomplish the gateway, the streets, and so forth, as previously described for the attainment of all perfections.
Among those with passion, he who has become desire itself, whose limbs are like a wheel, and who is discerning;
whose navel, head, and flanks are well-proportioned, and who supports his sons—such a one is a true sustainer of progeny.

And one should enter into its center, O knower of policy, O twice-born one—[the text here appears to contain a corruption regarding "nava"]. O Brahmin, we shall explain how that center is to be traversed.
With sacrificial wood of similar appearance, why do you restrain your speech so intensely?
Today, the three, the first, the eight, and the fourfold [groups] take the forms of an elephant, a horse, and a bull. (94)
Having established four well-proportioned, stable pillars rich in joints, they should be placed in the four directions;
either on the outer side of the doors or likewise within the intermediate walkway (vīthī).
Then, having bound it with very long and firm bands upon the shoulders, they fastened it firmly with ropes starting from the base, which were moderate in length and even. || 96 ||
Having placed those others behind him, he should indeed ascend from there;
having covered [or, having moved] everything in due order, he should then worship all of them in the proper sequence. || 97 ||

In the same way, by means of this application, one should place many bamboo-rows; having indeed provided the syllables of a single form everywhere in the intermediate directions, one should now establish the central wheel.
Having purified [the disciple] with the very water drawn from the *arghya* vessel, and having bound his own mudrā and touched him, he should gaze upon him with the vision of the mantra. (99)
O twice-born one, the group of mantras there should be honored with royal rites;
they should enter by the path of entry, and Pūrṇā should go outside from there. 100.
He should perform the second [offering] as before, having performed the consecrations;
in this very manner, he should carry out the remaining rites as well.
By this [rite], O Brahmin, the circle is mentally constructed upon the ground like a wheel,
through the ritual of sprinkling and so forth, ending with meditation and ritual placement.
There is no fault here in the transgression of the wheels, because there exists no path between the wheels and the lotuses. (103)
Because no fault arises for the practitioner who has disciplined himself, seated within the center of the wheel, by means of massaging the limbs from the navel onwards. (104)
In the center of the hundred-spoked wheels, there are two pericarp-like centers (karṇikās) in sequence:
the deity Puruṣa in the north, preceded by Parameśvara.
Thereafter, one should place two [deities], including the Puruṣa, at the limit of the filaments;
and on the petals, beginning from the east, one should place the eightfold Prakṛti.
The sixfold self resides in the six-spoked wheel, and likewise the eightfold body in the eight-spoked;
the twelvefold self in the twelve-spoked, and that same self in the sixteen-spoked.
Furthermore, there is a division of the twenty-four principles (prakṛti-tattva);
likewise, on the two sets of twelve spokes in the east, there are three powers (śakti) in successive order.
In that which is reckoned as having thirty-two spokes, the remainder is indeed the pair of powers (*śakti*).
And in the two intervals between the spokes (*ara*), the "non-accumulation" (*anicayā*)—as previously described regarding the navel and the rim—is present.
Just as the lotuses of the Ṛgveda and the others have been previously described in their proper sequence,
so too has this great collection of mantras known as the "Thousand" (Sahasranāma) been declared.
One should place that very [mantra] upon me;
[it is] eternal, pure, and free from the conceptual constructions of ritual procedures and defects, by means of the pairs.
Gradually, having brought [it] down to the heart very slowly...
What is the purpose of wandering along the path of the hot-rayed sun?
O Lord, one should proceed with divine implements as they are obtained;

from the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*) until the bath, for as long as desired, according to one's wish. One should indeed apply the mantra, having unified [the elements], beginning with the first...?
Having performed sacrifice in this wheel of the body, within the interior of the lotus, in former times.

(59) By means of the eternally pure ritual injunctions, through the various forms of visualization and offerings, one should gradually and very slowly cause [the deity] to descend into the heart. 112.
While rotating along the path of the hot-rayed sun,
one should place the entire collection of mantras, blazing like a mass of lightning, within the wheel.
O Lord, one should offer divine requisites as they are obtained; and the rite may continue until the conclusion of the dismissal, for as long as one desires.
One should contemplate him as entering the lotus of the body-cakra,
that great collection of subtle elements whose body consists of the twenty-one sounds.
One should establish them each in their respective places by means of the path of the marriage with the nectar;
the dismissal, the invocation, and the descent are not otherwise.
There is neither acquisition nor indeed relinquishment of my own mantra for practitioners, because it is eternally not something belonging to me.
When the knower of the Self says "Come" while addressing himself with the mantra, even for the sake of people, he thinks: "O Blessed One, I am becoming one with you. 118.
This is the invocation; furthermore, one should respectfully perform the external dismissal at the conclusion of the worship, saying "Go," and then deposit the sacrificial fee (bhṛti). || 119 ||
"I am going, O Blessed One; I consider my task to be appropriate. And this is what must be done: the invocation and dismissal of the deities along with their powers. (120)
For those who are all-pervading and without mantras, it is liberated; indeed, it is not so for others.
For them, go to the non-going, as it stands in their respective actions.
"Having understood this, one should subsequently perform sacrifice in the circle of deities situated on the ground.
Pauṣkara said:
"O Blessed One, this body has been understood; but how is it that [knowledge is] thus, and how is it that [it is] thus?"
What has been accumulated by me even until today, and what has been accumulated by you even until today—[I shall give] that to you and to this other world. || 123 ||
O Lord, in this body composed of the great elements, there is likewise a structure beginning with the axle and ending with the rim, consisting of parts such as the lotus.
The Blessed One said:
"O Brahmin, as before, this body is composed of the elements; O man, it consists of space, air, fire, water, and earth."
The essence of the wheel (*cakrasāra*), known as the body of Māta with its lotus, has been remembered. The perfected eightfold intellect is the middle one, known as Kamalā. (126)
But outside of the three qualities (guṇas), everything is established in that [foundation]. || 127 ||
The number of the thousand-fold wheel of flames near the Vaiśya may be according to one's own wish; the number may be according to one's own wish. || 128 ||
And by the power of the form of Brahmā, the supports are each established in their own respective abodes;
therefore, leaving aside the group, know that it has arrived with haste within the wheel of the body.
The water, bearing the wheel of streams, is established even within the two fires;
and indeed, by means of an uninterrupted pervasion, it extends from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
That which is to be known as each group in the form of a thousand channels should be understood;
one should constantly perform the visualization as if worshipping with the power of will.
O Pauṣkara, by virtue of its growth through all the channels of doubt, it stands enveloping the water; outside, there is a stream consisting of five groups.
By this diversity of inclinations, know that wheel-rim (*nemimaṇḍala*),
through the distinction between the manifest and the unmanifest, and by means of the qualities beginning with intellect (*dhī*). (133)
O twice-born one, although it was repeatedly severed by me through the power of the physician,
that which is to be established in the marshy region remains ever-present and all-pervading within Devamiśra.
Through the division of exterior and interior, like the islands and oceans in succession—all this has been told, as I was urged by you. (135)
Having understood the wheel of the body (*dehacakra*), one partakes of the nectar through Acyuta himself,
whose essence is imperishable and who possesses a form composed of the six qualities.
O Great-minded One, this body must be understood as being presided over by the all-pervading Lord, the Supreme Self, and as transcending material form.

And that which stands above the great gate, beyond the senses and superior to the faculty of cognition—that great knowledge of its attainment, which is the supreme state of non-dual oneness—is the most excellent. 138.
O best of the twice-born, in this world, the activity of the knower and the agent is extensive;
O Abhaka, O Mahānemi, you are the imperishable one whose senses are renowned. || 139 ||
Possessing a radiance like that of the fire of universal dissolution, he is the foremost leader of those who possess such power;
the source of the bliss of union, he is the primordial net, the Supreme Lord. (140)

O Supreme Person, for those devotees who delight in constant practice, who cultivate faith and self-restraint, and whose inner disposition is [purified], their prosperity becomes equal [to Yours]. 141.
The living soul of the Lord of Mantras resides in that great temple;
having thus mentally installed him, one should fashion [the image] out of gold and other precious materials. (142)
On the path of the rim (nemipatha) of that [mandala], one should indeed extend the measurement arising from all the necks;
then, the measurement for the pinnacle-altar (śikharavedī) is to be abandoned by one neck. 143.
From the neck to the ears, another [measurement] is recorded as equal to the divine pedestal (pīṭha);
the width of the door, the interior, and the water-line are likewise equal, and from that, the rim and the ground are of equal measure. 144.
One should fashion the characteristic of the crescent moon's horn by marking the eastern position,
using that field as a measure of one and a half or double [the length] of the cord.
One should mark the circular space between the two teeth with a thread first, at the center of the two lotuses;
then, on the western side, not too far from the center, for the worship of Dhruva.
Having placed the thread between the two middle threads within the protected area,
it should be positioned facing the northwest corner and in proximity to the sun.
And on the side of the *nemi* [the outer rim], one should also apply a gentle curve;
by that [curve], one should mark that field from its own limb up to the limit of that *pada*.
In this manner, one should proceed from one's own corner toward the southern direction up to the square, marking the moving point with a thread. 149.
To him whose splendor is gentle through perfection—[who satisfies those three which are inexhaustible]—and to the face of the one who possesses the splendor of the wheel and so forth... || 150 ||
Indeed, it possesses a rim established exactly as it is,
for the sages, the perfected ones, the immortals, and all those dwelling in the worlds.
By the inevitability of gentle radiance, she gladdens the quarters;
that interval between them is the measure of the rim of the wheel of prosperity.
Having given and divided the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) into seven parts,
one should establish the four-limbed [structure] with four [parts], and in the center, a twelve-petaled lotus.
(61) One should lead a petal from the fifth portion by a fourth part onto the ground of the petals;
having completed the auspicious circle at the tips of the petals with that same measurement.

That wheel, expanded by the remainder, with its stars raised by two parts of the circumference, should be made twice the size of the leaf-extension, possessing the previously mentioned characteristics. 155.
Is it called "the petal of the blue lotus," or is it like a citron?
Should that pure [form] located therein be made, or is it called the "axe" (paraśu) arising from the other? || 156 ||
Having established the measurement of the rim (nemi) within that interval according to the previously stated rule,
it should be raised by one-third or reduced by one-fourth, depending on whether the middle portion is considered inferior or superior.
Having applied the overlapping petals, one should draw a lotus with excellent characteristics;
its four directions are inexhaustible and joined by two wooden sticks.

And that which is devoid of the *prabhā* and *nemi*, having concealed with the word *hindi* [the universal common letters] for the sake of the slow (*mandin*), that which stands at the tip of the crest (*culikāgra*) is equal to the diameter of the wheel (*cakravyāsa*). 159.
One should give one part of the silver to the Brāhmaṇas who are to be served through their wives;
one should provide a fifth part or a fourth part for their livelihood outside of that [inner circle]. 160.
If it were to be expanded by that [measure], it would be like a wheel; however, according to the measurement of the rim, it should again be subject to the proportions of height and base.
Whether equal, deficient, or excessive, there should be a beautiful wrapping around the core. || 161 ||
Relying upon the middle of the axle, adorned with two moons, his two arms should be made capable of grasping that which is to be grasped. 162.
Likewise, one should bring about for him a healthy wife whose limbs are not yet fully developed;
indeed, her form must be exceedingly subtle and stainless.
Having brought him from the abode of karma by means of his power and as the cause, and having caused him to enter the sacrificial hall, he established him in the appropriate place. || 164 ||
Having meditated upon it with the very form of the conceited one (abhimānika), and having remembered it along with the hosts of weapons,
one should perform everything for the sake of its stability, just like the image of the Blessed One.
