Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Mixed," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, a great Upaniṣad within the illustrious Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
O Lord of the World, you have previously described the first manifestation within the ninefold self.
Tell me, how can that which is to be worshipped for the sake of attaining success in this world and the next be established? || 1 ||

What is the defining characteristic of sacrifice (*yāga*), and how is it established through its divisions? What are those nine lotuses of yours, and what is the accomplishment of the peaceful and fierce [deities]? || 2 ||
The Blessed One said: He who indeed presides over the sovereignty of Brahmā, established in the fourfold manifestation (cāturvyūha),
beginning with Vāsudeva and ending with Aniruddha.
Then, O Pauṣkara, the form of Nārāyaṇa— the Virāṭ self—
stood as the sovereign lord, Viṣṇu, bearing weapons in his embodied form and radiant with splendor.
O Lord, because of the destruction of the form of the sentient being (*sattva*), there are Nṛsiṃha and Dharaṇīdhara.
These nine fundamental natures (*navaprakṛti*) are established as Śaktis. (5)

Intent on bestowing grace upon those submerged in the ocean of existence— [upon those who are] inconceivable, immeasurable, all-pervading, and stainless— this [teaching] is like a great mass of sparks from a mighty fire. (7)
From that [Self], which is throbbing with light, the powers likewise emerge,
just as bubbles indeed arise from undisturbed water.
Those powers of that great-souled Lord of Power (*Śaktīśa*) which manifest His power—those powers of Yours are indeed of the nature of the unborn (*ajā*). || 9 ||
O twice-born one, all those [deities] beginning with Vāsudeva exist in manifold forms;
therefore, for the sake of attaining one's desired goals, they should always be worshipped by those who are self-restrained.
At that time, the individual manifestations do not accept worship without a support;
therefore, at the outset, one should diligently perform the visualization of the seat.
The lotus seat situated in the center of the pedestal is common to all;
however, within the ninefold self, the multitude of images specifically resides within the assembly of pedestals.
Having fashioned a lotus, one should invoke [the deity] there and worship in due order;
listen as I describe those forms which constitute the support of the lotus.

Or rather, the entire course of conduct is proclaimed within the manifestation known as Vāsudeva, because he is of the nature of knowledge and, being like a sphere (*golaka*), pervades all directions. (14)
Through her individual manifestation, she is known as Saṃkarṣaṇī; she has eyes like lotuses, wears a garland of lotuses, and is eternally fond of the lotus seat.

Everything exists for the sake of its subsistence, and all proceeds from His will; even the subtle characteristic of manifestation arises from the lotus-like source, like the kinship of the mud with the lotus. || 16 ||

O dear one, having seen [the deity] within the interior of the lotus, adorned with five lotuses and excellent garlands, one should meditate; then, having praised Him, O Brahmin, He indeed grants liberation. || 17 ||
Or rather, he is always the illuminator of all states of existence, such as time and the rest;
he is worshipped within the support known as Kālakāla (the Time of Time). || 18 ||
From that which arises as Pradyumna—the form whose manifestation is the earth characterized by light—and because it is followed by everything, it then exists within its own essential substratum. (19)

When the solar orb, which is the sign of that [state], has indeed moved into the principle of Power (śaktitattva) known as Aniruddha, he who is worshipped shall bring about complete liberation. || 20 ||
The power known as Nārāyaṇī, who is the supreme sovereign and his own form,
having become the foremost [goddess], nourishes the entire world through her various dispositions.
Then, upon the white support resembling a half-moon,
one should place the worshipped [deities] within the enclosure and join them in the supreme abode.
She is the power of the gift of Brahman and of forbearance, bearing the bow of Lord Śiva;
she is to be worshipped within the three-tiered mandala, for she is to be known as consisting of the triple Veda.
Just as a tortoise withdraws its limbs out of fear when it is spread out and situated in all directions, so too is the Lord honored when he remains encompassing everything. || 24 ||
In the Kūrmādaraga [kalpa], within the Padmani-yuta [manvantara] which is devoted to ritual action,
the Lord Viṣṇu, whose essence is Śakti, appears bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace. (25)
And that power of the Lord, which is his embodied form and which points toward knowledge—
by means of which he, with ease, produced a sound of deep resonance through the *mayas*.
Therefore, she is always worshipped in the form of the *praṇava* within the interior of the conch,
and in the lotus-bosom of the image characterized by its essential nature.

O Goddess, you who are the support of existence, the swift destroyer of sin, whose power is expended in the limbs of sacrifice—may I worship the lotus situated within the belly of the pot (Kumbhodara). 28.
Does it become a sacrifice that bestows the desired fruit when performed correctly according to the rules?
Having observed the expansion of the reality and having conceptualized it, [you have asked this]. (29)
Outside, establish the Āgneya support of Agni in that very manner;
likewise, O twice-born one, having made the nature of Dhruva firm, perform that [rite]. || 30 ||

Then, having entered into the midst of that, he beheld the principle of earth (kṣamātattva) established in austerity, which, by its own power, had made itself a thigh for the virtuous woman dwelling in the water. || 31 ||
Having destroyed the defects arising from the water-born [creation], he performed the creation of the earth;
thereafter, one should resort to the ritual procedure according to the law of Prajāpati.
For this reason, O Brahmā, Vārāhī—the manifestation of the Blessed One who resembles a dark blue cloud—is worthy of worship within the lotus of Kumbhodara’s belly. (33)

In this way, the powers of the weapons (astra-śaktayaḥ) should be worshipped together with their retinues on the nine-seated great sacrificial altar; and I shall describe that entire procedure to you.
By the mere sight of which the bondage of existence shall be destroyed:
having divided the field into sixteen equal parts starting from the eastern direction— (35)
One should subsequently distribute these and mark the portion into six parts, so that thousands of divisions arise without obstruction. || 36 ||
I consider two hundred to be one hundred; I consider sixteen to be a single enclosure (goṣṭhaka).
O twice-born one, having thus worshipped your own extended field, [one should proceed]. 37.
Having made twenty-four spokes for the purpose of sacrifice within the ninefold self,
one should perform it in the center of the self according to the sequence of the nine mandalas.
They are endowed with the splendor of beautiful gateways and possessed of vigor;
in their center they are joined with the field of meditation (dhyānakṣetra), and therein they are both even and uneven.
O twice-born one, one should fashion the first maṇḍala in the center of the field with one hundred minus fifty— that is, fifty— of the hundred parts.
One should first clear away thirty-six parts from the center, [forming] a mandala adorned with four gates, enriched with sacred seats (pīṭha), and embellished by the field of Vaimbha. 41.
That [line] of Bimbā should also be known; it is outside that, along the row of seats (pīṭha).
Therefore, one should erase [the lines] from the middle of the portions of the non-gamā-fractions in the cardinal directions. || 42 ||
In the corners of the northeast, southeast, southwest, and northwest, there are three [units] each;
likewise, the doors together with their corner portions are formed by two rows of lotuses.
In the intermediate directions between the four cardinal points, two squares are for the purpose of the corners;
and outside of that, a group of four is for the purpose of establishing the sub-corners (upakarṇa).
Having thus made the two groups of three parts for the beauty located at the fourth corner, one should erase that from the outside of the center of the mandala. || 45 ||
Six rows for the purpose of the streets run east-west and north-south;
then, does the eastern mandala of the field lie in the middle? No, it is beyond.
One should indeed erase it in the same manner using the previously mentioned number of divisions;
thus, O Lotus-born One, it shall be endowed with beauty in the four directions.
While establishing the position of these, O twice-born one, determine the placement of the ornaments; one should fashion two auspicious ornaments on both sides of the entrance. (48)

For that purpose, in the outer row, one part [is taken], and from there three parts inward; thus, the *sāṃpakoṣṭhaka* (the square for the union) is reached, which becomes inverted in the same manner [with identical letters throughout]. (49)
One should fill the corner of the adjacent beauty with the letter *pa*;
from both rows, the six-cornered figure (*ṣaṭkoṇa*) is as before. || 50 ||
One should first sweep the six rows of the *tukā* stones in the three directions—east, south, and north—for the sake of accomplishing the path. (51)
By this method, one should perform the division and effect the omission such that the count established as the "nine seats" is not diminished. 52.

O Pauṣkara, having prepared these according to this rule, if one transgresses the ritual injunctions regarding the weapon and that which has entered through its opening, [the following occurs]. || 53 ||
One should construct four doors in the directions of the six corners of the two rows of sectors, as well as eight *śobhās* and likewise eight *upaśobhās*.
There are four corners and three lines on the outside;
one should erase one hundred and eight [squares], including the door and the area beyond the door.
One should erase from the eighty-first *bhaga* for the sake of establishing the *upaśobhās*;
that much is traditionally taught as the *aṃśaka*.
One should wipe each corner one by one in sequence, and those three as well;
having first performed the visualization, one should then carry out the ritual practice.
From the outside of the pathway of the door, one should subtract three rows;
this shall be one-sixth of the parts, as from eighteen parts.

O Brahmin, one should first produce a symmetrical, elongated square with the door as its corner; then, outside the corner, for the sake of establishing the secondary corner (upakarṇa), [one proceeds].
Three rows should be wiped clean, provided with twelve divisions,
so that indeed thirty-six parts are wiped away.
Then, O Lotus-born One, one should fashion the door-support outside the *upakarṇa*, which is beautiful and similar to the *upakarṇa*. 61.
And when there are three rows of parts joined with eighteen portions, it is to be pierced;
that [line] which has fifty-four [parts]. || 62 ||
Having thus omitted it, the gateway becomes "tripura" (threefold city) and so forth;
therefore, one should construct the side-ornaments adjacent to the gateway and omit them from that central beauty.
And from near the door-ears, there are three rows consisting of fifteen degrees each; O Brahmin, they extend for forty [units] in due order.
O Pauṣkara, they arise with a numerical measure of fifty-five;
thereafter, it is provided with a ninth part near the ear.
And one must carefully elide three [syllables] from each of the two lines;
thus the total count arises as twenty-seven parts.
However, starting from the vicinity of that support, three rows joined with three parts are to be purified, so that there may be a group of nine squares for it. (67)
Having completed the outer ornamentation (*śobhā*) and so forth,
and the inner secondary ornamentation (*upaśobhā*), one should indeed perform the purification of the corners (*koṇaśuddhi*).
In this manner, from the three rows [of squares], one should erase ninety-nine squares, consisting of the first, middle, and outer [sections]. (69)
As long as there remain three hundred parts less three, by that [amount] outside is the support for the door; however, by three rows of parts, [the remainder is formed].

[Yaṃ aṃ khaṃ, like a garland of sun-disks; aṃ, the disk of the sun, with its garland...

One should show him both nostrils with the dark [wind],
and one should cover what is outside the wall with a color equal to lapis lazuli.
Is it possible? Or rather, one should display the path with a blue comparison;
having filled everything up to the corners of the fourth [square] as before, [one draws] the lotus.
Having thus prepared and worshipped the seat of Garuḍa in the center according to his means, for the sake of attaining worldly enjoyment and liberation, the wise one [should proceed]. (48)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Tortoise Image," in the Pauṣkara Saṃhitā, a Great Upaniṣad within the Śrī Pañcarātra.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:

The great sacrifice of Śaṅkhodara was for the purpose of worshipping Nṛkesarin.
The field is divided into thirty-two small parts; having extended it in thirty-two ways, it is equal in all directions. One should lay down the half-threads—thirty, plus two, plus one. (2)
Understand that the number of sections for these has been established according to the number of sūtras:
in the first thousand there are twenty, and another four.
In the center of that, one should fashion an image named Pāñcajanya with auspicious characteristics; first, O best of the twice-born, one should devoutly lay out the lines starting from the east.

Among the forms (bimba) both mentioned and unmentioned, this is indeed remembered as being thus; by means of these two aphorisms, the "Valiant in Truth" (Satyavikrama)—[which may be an address to Pauṣkara]—is the reality for all. 7.

That which is remembered as the fifteenth sūtra, extending from south to north,

One should lead the cord toward the western direction and then strike the middle;

In the southern direction from the place of sacrifice, there should be a line in the form of a conch shell;

Having made a thread from the ninth [mark] of the middle [line] at the navel—[having measured it from those two]—at their junction, one should extend that thread from there as far as the middle, O best of beings? [it should be the seventh]. || 22 ||
What kind of fish-marked banner should be made for the proponent? In that regard, he should join with it a previously established horn, which has the luster of the moon's peak. (23)
On the eighth [mark] from the middle line, at the junction known as the "fifteen arms," one should fix the thread; by that means, the fourteenth [line] is established in sequence.

One should join its northern horn with the horn of the fish;

One should perform the well-characterized grasping of the hands below the navel;
listen now to that practice in brief, which I shall explain hereafter. (27)
From the middle of the seventh [line] and the fifteenth arm [line],
having placed a thread in the center and extended it according to that sequence, || 28 ||
As far as the Niṣādas of the middle thread in the western direction,
one should strike that thread for the sake of establishing the marriage alliance.
Then, having fixed the thread at the junction of the seventeenth arm and the eighth pillar, and having led it as before, one should strike [the mark]. (30)
In the middle there should be two threads; one should fashion a collection of half-moons. Their measurement shines forth according to the sequence of the field. || 31 ||
O best of the twice-born, there is no absence of the mark of the moon;
at the portion of the barley-corn, one should rotate the half-moon and the crescent moon in proximity to that portion.
By what means does the leaf not become too black? [It is by using] a waxing disc. Now listen to the calculation for the number of the completed mark. || 33 ||
One should draw five lines in the middle, forming hundreds of squares;
that which extends from south to north is connected to the three worlds.
The three threads [or three vajra-threads], with effort, should be like a face and a half-moon;

Therefore, one must sweep the inner and outer courtyard;
that by which the unmanifest center of the square is made manifest.
When one should perform it without a mandala-array (vyūha), then one should imagine for it:
the door-ornaments and secondary ornaments are formed by two-by-two rows of parts. (37)

Two, four, six, and likewise eight; the doors, the necks, and so forth—these should be subtracted for the primary and secondary ornaments from the lines numbering seven, five, and three respectively. (38)

thus, the eastern and western doors are eclipsed, yet endowed with a slight splendor.
The remainder shall remain unbroken according to the previously stated rule for you;

Thereafter, one should dye it with red; how this is done is explained here: [the threads] are mixed with thread from a mark [of cloth] that is pale-red. (41)
And in all directions, within the lines, they should be gradually filled with a pale pigment that resembles cow's milk. || 42 ||
Having filled the interior like the surface of a mirror, just as before,
he performed the piercing of the center of his face with black-colored pollen.
One should, according to one's own wish and in accordance with the rules, fashion it well-rounded and of beautiful form;
then, one should color it black, resembling lapis lazuli.
O best of the twice-born, having thus prepared the image and so forth, one should worship it;
being absorbed in meditation, one should meditate upon the Man-lion within the interior of the conch. (45)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Conch and the Image," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, a Great Upaniṣad within the Śrī Pāñcarātra. || 17 ||

The Blessed Lord said: Now I shall fully explain to you the interior of the sacrificial pitcher (kalaśodara) regarding the sacrifice.
Where practitioners here worship the deity who bears the limbs of sacrifice. || 1 ||
Having divided the field into forty parts, one should lay down the lines;

The measurement of six parts has been explained; now understand the laying down of the lines:
forty lines are established from east to west, and likewise beyond that. (3)
One thread is proclaimed for the northern direction, and likewise for the southern;

From the center, from that which is called the fifth, and from the ninth to the south and north—[one should place] one peak of the half-moon; in that, one should bind and restrain.
And having blocked the southern horn of the middle one among those numbering thirty-three,
as well as the other horn in the junction-part (sandhyaṃśa), it should likewise be suppressed.
Having placed the thread at the junction, one should extend it from there to each respective point,

as far as the middle— [as it is said, "as far as the middle," the latter three half-verses beginning with "the sacrifice from the middle" have been lost]— from the junction of the seventeenth and the tenth.
Thus the first mark has been described; now I shall tell you the subsequent one:
[it is] at the eighth part of the line that comes from the center.
Having placed the cord at the junction and drawn it out from that position,

Therefore,
O best of beings, when the two marks have been successfully established by this rite, one should close the eyes while [the water] is being marked with the color blue.

With the *rucimantra*, with a cloth, or with the entire collection of mantras, one should cause all directions to resound; therefore, one should lead [the thread] to the seventeenth [line] in the middle.

extending from the fifth point from the center to the ninth point to the south and north.

At the junction of the twilight portion, having suppressed the horns on the right side, that [mark] should be a crescent moon as the branding; this indeed is the pitcher-mark of the water-pot.
Likewise, O twice-born one, the day is to be calculated; after that, the twenty-seventh [digit] of the ninth sūtra from the middle remains unexhausted.

Having joined [the hands] at the joint and extended them, one should touch the fifth finger from the middle; then, leading it like a fish while being marked, one brings it to its union with that [other hand].
The emblem that is proclaimed for the ninth [tithi] from the middle of the forty-third [day], located between the directions of Vāyu and Varuṇa, is as follows. 19.
One should make a mark in the middle between the western and southwestern [sections];
its base is established, and it is raised to the height of a neck-measure. || 20 ||
Then, one should fashion a beautiful neckpiece from the middle of the tenth thread up to the first thread on the opposite side. || 21 ||
Having placed the thread at the junction, one should touch the eleventh from the middle;

O lotus-eyed one, from the center [the text beginning with "madhyāda" is lost], that thread [is drawn];

Having indeed made a junction with that [line], one should touch the tenth from the middle;

For one known as the ninth of the midday [period], for a being, and for a woman—that [face] is achieved by him through this method; indeed, his face is perfected thereby. (25)
And having placed the thread at the junction of the ninth pillar and the one heated by the arm,

or rather, it would certainly be the third arm of the ninth [digit]. || 27 ||
In this manner, one should make a mark in the northern direction or on the right side;

derived from the middle of the thirteenth and the seventeenth among the fingers.
Having placed the thread at the junction, one should then extend it from there,
from the middle of the second [section] and from the junction of the tenth of the two seventies.
Having laid down that thread,
one should then begin the marking for the seventeenth [deity] called Saṃvarta, by means of the seventh arm.
Having made a thread at the junction point, one should bring it together there,
where in the three arms and where from the fixed point (dhruva) there is the seventeenth.
That spot should be marked while the drum is being struck with the hands closed;
thus has the first marking been described, and now I shall tell you the subsequent one.
From the center, having made the previously mentioned sūtra and a portion of the eighth [sūtra] meet at their junction, and having extended [the sūtra] from that point; || 34 ||
O Pauṣkara, one should bring it near the second [mark], which is like the autumnal flood; from that point, one should close the mark being delineated, which resembles the appearance of sesame seeds.
O best of men, when these two marks have been perfected by this method,
the face shaped like an elephant's trunk and the emergence of water are accomplished.
Then, one should perform its circumambulation with the portion situated above,
using either the Ruci-mantra, the Astra-mantra, or the entire collection of mantras.
For one who desires to know the means for attaining all the Vedas among those seeking knowledge, and for the sake of attaining the state of being a master of all branches of learning— 38.
Having always cleansed the mantra in the center among all objects,
the seven destroyers perish for the sake of attaining the state of Pātāla.
O Brahmin, for the pacification of all faults and transgressions of the pledges (samaya), one should offer this water-vessel; indeed, one should not perform worship elsewhere than here.
One should mark with the thread placed on the ground the two lines situated in the mouth (center) that run toward the south and north, and also the first line, using the thread to be fixed.
O Lord of the Twice-born, beginning from the east and so forth, one should draw lines for the sections;
by means of those, one should construct two circles so that the neck-line (or ear-line) may be properly formed. (42)
One should create four hundred squares from the center;
one should then clear away the remaining nine to form a lotus endowed with eight petals.
In the three rows of divisions, starting from the outside, one should arrange them like a conch shell;
for the *śobhā* and *upaśobhā*, there are two, four, and six parts respectively, proceeding from the door.
After that, one part for the women; then listen to the twenty-seven [parts]:
four for the secondary ornaments (upaśobhā), and likewise the group of ornaments (śobhagaṇa) in the intermediate directions.
By this procedure, omitting the eastern and western [lines], it is produced;
having subsequently filled [the space] with powder, I shall now describe that. (46)
The petals, along with their markings, were exceedingly brilliant,
and the space between them was colored with a golden-hued, red pollen.
Then, by means of the "young" (aruṇa) and "white" (sita) syllables, which resemble a king's gem, the metrical group situated at the throat should be filled up in due order. (48)

One should color the entire surface of that which has arisen from the water, standing upright and having the form of a round coral, with a red dye; having thus made it endowed with these characteristics.
Then, one who desires sovereignty over the seven islands— or, if free from desire, one who is capable— should worship Varāha in the center of the square.

Furthermore, that conceptualization of the centers of the circles and so forth in the middle, for the purpose of accomplishing the lotus through its divisions, occurs without a nine-fold pedestal (navapīṭha). || 51 ||
O twice-born one, if one should arrange the paths and other features within a single field,
one should place them inside those [paths] and create a collection of lotuses.
Having first understood that the representation of the lotus of Nirvāṇa is too small,
one should subsequently draw the remaining multitude of lotuses using that same measurement.
"O lotus-eyed one, thus have you spoken, for I have been urged by you regarding that which has the nine mandalas as its core and resembles a city with nine gates. (54)
For devotees who desire to ascend, this is generally the bringer of welfare for men;
indeed, I consider there to be nothing else superior to this. (55)
And it exists as the preeminent among all sacrifices;
yet that is unspeakable for those who are not devotees, for the deceitful, and for those who are enemies of the Self. (56)
But for those who are nihilists, the sinful, followers of other doctrines, those who have abandoned the sequential ritual practice, and even those who hate the twice-born; (57)
"O Prajāpati, it must certainly be stated whether even one of these is the procedure for the Navagarbha sacrifice as enjoined by the scriptures. (58)
But he who should later worship this [image] according to his own capacity or with his wealth, obtains infinite auspicious fruit pertaining to both this world and the next. (59)

Indeed, for whomsoever this is being recited, their speech reaches the exhaustion of existence (*bhavakṣaya*)—if it be said that "eloquence becomes inexhaustible"—and by whomsoever the great sacrifice has been seen even once and honored. (60)
The mental afflictions arising from thousands of lifetimes will undergo dissolution;
through that, you shall gradually reach the end of the body—thus, what need have you for a multitude of places? || 61 ||

Therefore, O Brahman, this auspicious rite known as sacrifice—which bestows the fruit of attaining Brahman—should be honored according to one's capacity, even if it is performed without [external] worship. 62.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Nine Naves," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, a Mahopaniṣad within the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
O Lord of Lakṣmī, tell me by what cause one is deprived [of merit].
By which there is indeed always an exceedingly firm disposition toward you and toward this [teaching]. || 1 ||
The Blessed One said:
"Even by resorting to deceit, one should—out of sport—behold, worship, or even from afar pay homage to that which is most precious. (2)
O Pauṣkara, however, the sovereignty of the universal monarchs is attained here by those possessed of desire; [therein] the Blessed One, whose nature is Brahmā-Nārāyaṇa, [is present].
Without a state of true devotion, however, the desired fruit is not attained by the Brahmins for a long time;
therefore, among the gods, she is the one to be worshipped at the very root of all things.

Those by whom he was gratified within the fire through the power of accomplishment and with faith, and who were honored with supreme devotion, have attained a state of worshipfulness here in this world. || 5 ||

O devoted wife, as long as a man who performs the immediate sacrifice remains within the body, he belongs to the lineage of the Siddhas—those such as Brahmā, Āditya, Indu, and Rudra—who are not born from a womb. || 6 ||
Listen now to me regarding the further fruit of one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta):
he indeed attains a full lifespan, being entirely freed from untimely death.
Free from disease, joyful, contented, strong, and without thorns [to his side],
he attains incomparable sovereignty that is beloved at all times.
Together with his sons, wife, kinsmen, servants, forces, and vehicles,
one who is endowed with discernment and righteousness prospers moment by moment.
There he performs the great sacrifice through mere intention alone;
he obtains vast renown and flourishes through the True Dharma. || 10 ||
Whatever impurity has been accumulated previously through action, mind, or speech since childhood— all that perishes instantly.

How much more so, then, for one who is thoroughly proficient in this matter at all times with his whole being, who seeks the fruit of the fourfold aims of life, and is firmly established on the path of the virtuous? || 12 ||
From every family—past, present, and indeed future—even those belonging to it who reside in hell go to the world of Brahmā. (13)
He was being praised by Gandharvas and sung of by Kinnaras, traveling in vehicles as radiant as the moon that illuminated the ten directions.
Mounted upon a vehicle made of lotuses and surrounded on all sides by chowries and celestial nymphs, this very same great-souled one appears immediately after the fall of the body. (15)
Possessing his own body, he may move at will everywhere like the Blessed One;
having previously enjoyed the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, he may descend again according to his own desire. (16)
Relying upon the excellence of his birth through the power of that past karma,
he was born into a family of virtuous and perfected beings, in a land auspicious and devoted to the Dharma.
Therefore, he was born endowed with glory, wise, and possessed of true valor; devoted to compassion, he acted for the sake of setting others, who are subject to existence, upon the right path. (18)
But always enjoying sense objects that are not contrary [to his purpose],
the wise one, whose intellect is well-pleased, remains truly devoted to knowledge and action. (19)
One whose mind is liberated from passion may remain in saṃsāra as long as desired;
finally, having cast off this body composed of the elements, one abides like Vāsudeva.
Even if the deity is worshipped but once in a new lotus within the supreme mandala, when the seed-syllable of the vidyā has arisen and is fashioned as mere presence; || 21 ||
The Soul of the Universe, who maintains the nature of true bliss despite the diversity of forms, [is worshipped] with stainless and liberated mantras that reveal Brahman. || 22 ||
There shall be no further rebirth for him in this world, which is crowded with fears; for he has begun that desire which is final and leads to liberation.
Pauṣkara said:
"O Lord, the forms which were previously fully understood by me here—I now desire to know the characteristic of the mantras known as 'knowledge' (vidyā). (24)
O Lord, by means of lotuses that have been prepared, the visualization of the lotus is to be performed;
now follows the characteristic of the mantras that reveal Brahman.
By whom the worship in the great sacrifice within the nine-petaled lotus was thus prescribed.
The Blessed One said:
"O you who grant all desires, you are like the support of one's wishes; you are the abode of the splendor of a multitude of glories, and the very ground of the sacred field."
In the central lotus, a group of nine words is proclaimed:
"O you whose essence is reality, who have transcended the world, O great-souled one, in whom does the salt-water ocean reside? (27)

One should know the entire unmanifest nature of lightning as being indeed composed of the three qualities (guṇas). It is the immeasurable Śabdabrahman, the Blessed One, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāya). || 28 ||
Then, O Lotus-born One, upon the third lotus—the foot that is indeed a stairway to Brahman—situated within Prakṛti, which possesses many forms, and likewise resting upon Pradhāna; || 29 ||
O Great Buddha, you whose objects are accomplished by mere resolve, who reveals all things, and who are imperishable; from whom the eightfold emanations arise? || 30 ||
In the fourth lotus, which consists of illusion (māyā), the state is said to be hidden, perceptible, formless, the support of all, and the abode of bliss. (31)

O Prajāpati, within the living sheath (jīvakośa) and the subtle body (liṅgapuryaṣṭaka), the objects of the intellect arise from the consciousness-intellect (cidbuddhi) which is manifest through space, location, and time; they are the spheres of perception for that intellect. || 32 ||
But in the Dharmodaya, according to the tradition, it fulfills all desires;
whether it be of limited measure or universal form, these are clearly [manifested] as the lotus and so forth. || 33 ||
Is he eternal yet incomplete? Is he the auspicious abode of all fortune?
O Lotus-born One, does he possess manifold divisions through the many varieties of sound and other objects, which are of diverse forms? || 34 ||
The powers of Brahman are "Prabhava," "Chidya" (or "Chādya"), and "Saptama"; these are the sequential stages.
From those [stages], Māyā and Vidya arise, which cause the manifestation and expansion of the manifest.
In the eighth lotus, from the foot, there is the severance of the continuum (*cchinnasantāna*).
Then, the past, present, and future manifest through their respective measures. (36)
(82) "The Great Wheel, the Great Vortex, which bestows the fruit of accomplishment upon the accomplished"— thus has the nature of the words of the Vidyā been revealed. (37)
Now, understand the characteristics of the Brahma-planes:
they are characterized by a single division, they are the True Brahman, well-established, and unstruck (anāhata). || 38 ||
O Ānanda, you possess great majesty; you are firm, eternal, and the unchanging syllable.
You are unborn, endowed with the sixfold perfections, inconceivable, wonderful, and absolute.
O All-powerful One, unmixed, perfectly tranquil, Supreme Person!
O Eternal, Immovable, Unchanging, and Stainless One among all! 40.
The intrinsic nature, belonging to Vāsudeva, is waveless, possessing the three lotuses;
it is the acceptable, incomparable, well-illuminated, and stable nectar. (41)
Immediately after that is the "Haṃsa," whose nature is consciousness, ungraspable and infinite;
it is imperishable, beyond thought, immovable, stainless, boundless, and the truly Great One.

O Lord of the World, indefinable, profoundly peaceful, Supreme Sovereign! (46)
In that which is unwavering and free from conceptual construction—what? The Great Dharma, the Great Thought (or Great Self).

By means of those [names], whether remembered or worshipped, a person attains Brahman.

He is worshipped with offerings such as water for the guest (arghya) and flowers, using words that denote the eternal Brahman, which are preceded by a single division [of the mantra], begin with the syllable Om, and end with "namas. || 60 ||
Now its characteristic is described according to the sequence of its manifestation:
having placed the tip of the nose upon a lotus situated in the center of the center. (61)

And another [method] is the "Prabhātayaṣṭa" and so forth; the eastern petal from the southeast quarter is that which was previously described by the rule of rotation, but not in that manner [as in the other method]. (62)
In this regard as well, one should always rely upon the eternally perfected eastern portion during the ritual of worshipping the feet with lotuses and lotus petals. (63)

Then, having brought her down and worshipped her there according to his own will in her embodied form, he—whether as one form, two forms, or three forms—attains that which is beyond the three forms. (64)
Starting from the lotus in the center up to the lotus of Īśāna, one should then perform the worship that bestows the principle of Vidyā (vidyātattva). 65.
Beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (Om) and ending with *svāhā*, one should proceed in order from the central lotus and its pericarp onwards, until the completion at the outer petals.

From that [starting point] and looking toward the east, proceeding clockwise until reaching the center, one should arrange eight lotuses according to this very same method used for the lotus-born [Brahmā]. (67)
The central lotus should be filled by means of two sacrifices, as well as that which stands outside;
the central form is all-pervading, with eyes, heads, and faces on every side.
Having meditated upon and then deposited [the deities] wherever and in whatever manner possible,
one should invoke them elsewhere and deposit their forms facing [the practitioner].

Then, when the occasion for worship has arrived, O Pauṣkara, one should perform the rite of facing [the deity] together with oneself, according to the sequence of both the embodied and the unembodied forms.
Thus it has been said: for those who possess desire, there is the ritual placement (nyāsa), the worship, and the attainment of liberation;
however, whichever practitioner first requests [the goal], that alone shall be accomplished.

By means of the foot-mantras known as the Vidyās, as before, the visualization of the lotus-born [deity] is to be accomplished, joined with emanation and reabsorption; from that, indeed, liberation is attained.
One should perform worship in sequence and then sacrifice to the group of deities (mūrtigaṇa);
furthermore, one should perform the adoration of Brahmā from the lotus situated in the center.
[Is it] by means of the circumambulation performed as worship? Listen also to its characteristics:
one should utter the word called "ignorance" (avidyā), and whatever was previously stated in its entirety [should be applied]. (74)
"Know that all of this, along with its ritual procedure, is a reversal [of the previous].
Pauṣkara said:
Previously, the nine forms beginning with Vāsudeva were described."
For the sake of worship, there is a supreme mandala consisting of a new lotus together with an image.
Now, from that [central point], one should lead the fire as it stands in the middle;
likewise, there may be one, two, three, four, or five forms according to one's desire.
Instruct me on how these nine lotuses are to be worshipped.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Regarding that mandala consisting of a nine-petaled lotus together with the image, pedestal, and so forth,
which was indeed previously described— in that [mandala], I shall abide as the nine forms."
Together with their limbs and their retinues, they should be deposited one by one;
the image should be endowed with the nine [features], beginning with the ritual pedestal and the doors.

Then, having constructed a nine-lotus mandala— either according to the calculations of geometry or abandoned by all such measurements— it should be made as extensive as possible, in accordance with one's means.

O twice-born one, know that the sign (nimitta) worshipped in this manner with mantras consisting of Vidyā and Brahman is the single common ground for all the forms, beginning with the One Form (ekamūrti). 80.
And there is proximity, especially of the ninefold form, within the pervasion.
Pauṣkara said:
"I have previously understood here the dissolution of the ninefold form,
beginning with the single form and ending with the eightfold form."
Now, O Lord of the World, the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of the mantra is prescribed.
The Blessed Lord said:
One should place the six limbs and the single form, each one consisting of a group of nine;
the limbs of those nine are to be placed upon the pericarp and on the petals.
For the *dvimūrti* [temple], the first [lotus] is in the center and the second is in the eight directions in sequence;
for the *trimūrti*, having placed the second [lotus] in the four cardinal directions and then [in the intermediate directions] starting from the southeast lotus. || 83 ||
In the eight sets of four intermediate directions, endowed with the third [syllable],
one should place the excellent [seat] of the fourfold form using two lotuses facing east and west.
The third [line] is in the southwest and northwest corners, divided fourfold;
then the second [line] of the five-fold form is in the two lotuses of the east and southeast.
The third [lotus] is with the southern [line], while the fourth is with the western and northern [lines];
one should place five lotuses with those directed toward the north and the northeast. (86)
Having placed the second [form] of the sixfold deity in the lotus of the eastern direction, and the third [form] between the east and north, as well as in the positions of fire and wind; || 87 ||
The fifth is in the west, and the sixth is situated in the south, having emerged from Nirṛti; she who is beyond the seven forms of the lotuses located in the northeast and the east.
O Lotus-born One, when the third [digit] is situated on the fire-pada, the fourth is on the southern lotus;
with the Rakṣas and Varuṇa lotuses, the fifth [is formed], O Lotus-born One. (89)
Then, one should install the remaining forms in the northwest and the northern lotus; likewise, in the lotuses of the northeast, east, southeast, south, southwest, west, and northwest.
O Lotus-born One, regarding the two winds— the northern and the southern— of the Eight-formed Lord, it has been stated here that,
having accepted their placement of feet, they are indeed of two kinds.

One should worship with the mantra prescribed by one's resolve, pervading with the *savyāpti* [breath] and the self; thus one attains the Brahman of the Moon, the desired fruit from the well-sacrificed oblations. || 92 ||
This general worship of the forms has been briefly described;
I shall now explain the specific arrangement in the ninefold mandala.
Furthermore, O Lotus-born One, by means of the merit arising from the distinction between stationary and moving [forms],
one should install the Primordial Form in the center above the hollow.

Then, having placed the unexhausted digits of that [moon] in their respective positions as the limbs (*aṅga*), one should worship the venerable deities beginning with Saṅkarṣaṇa in due order upon the eight petals. (95)
Then, O twice-born one, one should worship Saṅkarṣaṇa in the eastern lotus above [the central one],
having first established Vāsudeva and the rest, along with the remaining seven forms.
In the same manner, one should worship the eight petals in sequence as the veils;
likewise, one should worship the group of forms (mūrtigaṇa) ending with Varāha in due order.
But by Koṭarī, having installed the primary image of that great-souled one—the embodiment of the mantra—in brief, like Tālaketu; 98.
In this way, one should install the nine forms upon the lotus for the sake of attaining the fruit of all desires, [and] for one who is terrified by the fear of saṃsāra. (99)
And by reversing the order of the words, the worship as previously prescribed—from Vārāha up to Vāsudeva—becomes effective according to the specific fruit [sought]. 100.
When the general space of the forms of the root mantra exists,
one should indeed perform the *tanunyāsa* of those forms by means of the group of limbs (*aṅgagaṇa*) that has been obtained.
In these non-common [temples], having first arranged the garlands, one should then place five and seven images in the third [section]. || 102 ||
The twenty-second, the fifty-seventh, and the first among them are of the nature of light;
they possess form, are supreme, and are characterized by the name of meditative absorption.

Furthermore, in one's own respective lotuses— or in a single lotus, or in a *pauṣkara*— by means of the application of the lotus-deposition (*padmanyāsa*), [one should place them] either at the base of the petals or upon the ground.
It should be deposited and worshipped, characterized by various meditations,
and endowed with the forms of the rites of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal.
For the sake of accomplishment, the placement (nyāsa) of the Lord of Mantras together with his limbs is required in two ways for all rituals preceded by worship, indeed as a constant practice. (106)
The placement of the form (mūrtinyāsa) was indeed prescribed previously from the group of primary limbs (mūlāṅga);
for it bestows the fruit of the sixfold qualities upon those who know the mantras.
Then the limbs [of the mantra] bestow upon the great-souled ones powers such as *aṇimā*;
however, the fruit born of the qualities of the Lord of Mantras is not distinct from their forms.
Then they offer their limbs, O Lotus-born One, with indistinct intoxication;
for the sake of stability, the state of being an external limb is sometimes resorted to through various forms. 109.
For the sake of favoring devotees who long for both worldly enjoyment and liberation, O Lord, you alone are indeed the innermost self of those devoted beings. || 110 ||
O Brahmin, you yourself have accepted this for the sake of their peace from saṃsāra;
having thus deposited [the mantras] and worshipped them, one should perform [the rite] preceded by devotion.
Listen as I describe to you that special mode of worship:
[one should offer] gold-measured silver and the finest golden lotuses. (112)
Adorned with rubies, sapphires, and diamonds, and decorated with genuine coral, great pearls, and excellent emeralds, it was worshipped. (113)
Then one should worship with other very beautiful flowers that bloom according to the season, scented with camphor, salt, anthill-earth, sandalwood, and saffron.
With fragrant and sweet incenses, with silk garments and ointments, with variegated armlets, bracelets, crowns, and likewise with bangles; || 115 ||
Having worshipped with supreme devotion the Lord who dwells within the interior of a fresh lotus, using highly precious and beautiful necklaces, rings, and anklets, (verse 116).
With fans, chowries, umbrellas, mirrors, couches, banners, bells, and with tinkling small bells, with stationary parasols and canopies; || 117 ||
With banners of various colors, crescent moons, and beautiful bubbles;
with cows, auspicious elephants, and many vehicles adorned with numerous ornaments.
One should worship Hari with gifts such as footstools, sandals, and shoes, as well as with uninterrupted offerings of ghee and other substances and great lamps. (119)
Then, with pure offerings of flowers, with the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and with divine, purifying fruits produced in the six seasons; || 120 ||
With purifying, cool, sweet, and fragrant drinks, and with many kinds of foods consisting of balls and sugar-candy, as well as ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa). || 121 ||
One should worship the unborn and imperishable Lord with fresh milk from cows of the Ābhīra breed, with well-boiled milk, and with a mind purified by faith.
Vessels made of gold, silver, and copper were spread out,
along with gold, sesame seeds, fine rice, and juices mixed with seeds.
Having placed the meaningful mantras within them so that they are fruitful and well-filled, [the vessel] is perfumed with cloves, *takkola* berries, cardamom, cinnamon bark, and camphor.
At the end, bowing down, one should offer much betel leaf (*tāmbūla*) endowed with *jāti* and *pūga* fruits, and possessed of a very fragrant covering, to the Lord of the World. 125.
One should properly bring satisfaction to the imperishable, lotus-eyed Lord with various kinds of musical instruments, as well as with dance, song, hymns of praise, and so forth.
Whatever is most desired, whatever greatly delights the mind, and whatever is appropriate and not contradictory—one should provide all of that. || 127 ||
O Janārdana, you who are the mantra-form residing in the center of the Kumbha-maṇḍala, now,
for your pleasure, [I offer] gifts such as golden cities and so forth.
In the same way, one should worship that with a purified inner self;
for within this mandala of nine lotuses, everything from the world of Brahmā downwards is contained.
He drinks and stands there uninvited; outside the enclosure called the mantra, by the power of the mantras consecrated with mantras, that [water] becomes inexhaustible. || 130 ||
And for one's own benefit, for the successful accomplishment of sacrifices, there are sacrificial enclosures (valayas) consecrated by mantras not far from this [place]. 131.
O twice-born one, at the conclusion of the sacrifice of Kīrtinātha, the Siddhas go forth, accompanied by all the Lords of Mantras (Mantreśas), bestowing boons upon the enemy of the enemy. 132.
The lords of the worlds and the worlds themselves, along with the Īśvaras, bowed down and offered praise;
likewise the deities, the Vasus, the Sādhyas, the Agnis, and the Vāyus. (133)
Huts and other dwellings, the limbs and so forth; time consisting of the past, future, and present;
all the lunar mansions and stars, and all the zodiacal signs and planets. || 134 ||
The Ādityas, Maruts, Rudras, and mortals, as well as the two Aśvins, the Viśvedevas, the seven sages (Saptarṣis), the ancestors (Pitṛs), and likewise the Munis. || 135 ||
The Gandharvas, Apsarases, Kinnaras, Cāraṇas, and Uragas;
the Devas, the Vidyās, and the Manus; Svāhā, Siddhā, Svadhā, and Dhruvā. || 136 ||
Dharma, Sarasvatī, Soma, the sky, the Prajāpatis, the Yugas, the Ṛg, Sāman, and Sūkta hymns, the meters, the worlds, and the ten directions; || 137 ||
The continents, the rivers, and the earth together with its oceans; the mountains, the trees, the creepers, and all juices and medicinal herbs—[all these abide within it]. (138)
All sacred fields and abodes are, in manifold ways, part of the Yoga-pīṭha;
likewise, the cows that yield the milk of immortality, as well as all that is moving and unmoving. 139.

Thereafter, one should satisfy each member of the Gaṇas one by one in sequence by their own names, preceded by a salutation and containing the *praṇava*, for the attainment of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (140)
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Worship of the Nine-Naveled [Disc]," in the *Pauṣkarasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pañcarātra*.
(Total number of verses: 143) Now begins the twentieth chapter;
the Blessed One said:

O best of the twice-born, when the mantras have been worshipped, especially when they have been gratified, and when they have been employed in their proper place within the ritual, [one should worship] Gaṇanātha.
When the worship of him who is named Viṣvaksena has been performed according to the prescribed rite, including the libation and the ritual dismissal; || 2 ||
Then, one should perform their preliminary service (prāksevana) in accordance with the prescribed conduct;
likewise, O Pauṣkara, for the sake of attaining the desired success, one should prepare the arghya vessel.
Pauṣkara said:
For what purpose, O Blessed One, did [the Lord] speak of the Master who cuts through obstacles, who is the supreme cause of all the lords of obstacles? (4)
But when Acyuta has gone to the realm of enjoyment (bhogabhūmi), Viṣvaksena is to be worshipped.
By what substances, by what rite, and what does he accomplish when he is fully honored?
The Blessed One said:
"For those subject to existence, there are many obstacles that hinder the true Dharma; I do not consider any auspiciousness for worldly beings to come from sacrifices, rituals, or religious duties."
But when that [wheel] proceeds, all those obstacles which hinder one's enthusiasm perish, afflicted by the fear of the wheel’s blazing flames.
Even when there is no opportunity for them in the midst [of the practice], or even when their [power] has diminished, by the power of their presence, where is the fault and where is Vināyaka? (8)
(88) Trifling obstacles, intent upon finding flaws, wait for those established in the performance of good deeds;
having been driven outward, they watch for the moment when the sacrificers attain their fruit.
O twice-born one, by means of some previously acquired karma, he now experiences its fruit; furthermore, through sacrifice, he enjoys his own various rewards that stand before him. (10)
For the sake of its protection, one should indeed invoke Viṣvaksena at that very time,
or on the second day at the time known as the conclusion of the sacrifice.
Having made the mind free from agitation, one should perform the sacrifice for the sake of attaining the fruit;
this is done by completing the rite with the remaining seats, preceded by the offering of water (arghya).
With all types of offerings consisting of ritual services, such as ornaments and the like, and with food offerings, honey-mixtures, and so forth, presented to the principal image; || 13 ||
With the remnants of what was given to the twice-born, which were not consumed by himself,
and likewise with those offered on the following day that had remained within the vehicle.
Therefore, O Lotus-seated One, having first offered [the food] cooked with spices, seasoned with heat, and drenched in sweet ghee into the center of the maṇḍala; 15.
One should first meditate on the group of five or nine, beginning with Dharma and ending with Ananta, as being covered by Sattva; thereafter, one should meditate on the lotus alone.
Or else, in the middle of the directions between Īśāna and Soma (the northeast and northwest), within a square city, excluding the door-ornaments at the corners and adorned with three lines; || 17 ||
In the interval between those two, upon a lotus with eight petals situated on a half-moon,
that which was employed by Acyuta for the sovereignty over obstacles— || 18 ||
By worshipping according to the prescribed rite, the practitioner perpetually attains his desired goal;
therefore, having bathed according to the previous injunctions, he should worship with mantras dedicated to that deity. (19)
Having washed his hands and feet or having sipped water (ācamana), he should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa);
by means of meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās), he should [identify] his own body as being presided over by that [deity].
Having purified [the deity] and then re-installed him, beginning with the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) and the germinating sprouts (aṅkura),
one should likewise bring down the Lord into the abode of bliss as before.

Having performed the sacrifice within the lotus of the heart, one should worship externally after meditating upon that very same Self— which is essentially partless (niṣkala) according to one's own perspective— as having attained the state of being with parts (sakala).
Resembling the sprouts of fresh dūrvā grass and possessing a slightly yellowish luster, he has four tusks, four arms, four testicles, and four modes of movement. || 23 ||
His limbs were complete, his hair was dark, and he was adorned with broad, expansive chest;
he was graced by a navel cavity that was deep and spiraled to the right.
His arms reached down to his knees; he was majestic, wearing matted locks with tawny-red flames;
his eyes and chin were the color of molten gold, and he possessed a broad nose. (25)
Adorned with rows of long white nails, possessing curved eyebrows,
decorated with pearls in the middle, and embellished with a great jewel.
And on the right side, one should fashion the auspicious Śrīvatsa mark, created with ascetic merit (*tapas*),
in the middle of which is the abode of Kamalā.
The sacred thread (brahmasūtra) should be double-stranded and positioned so as to circle the navel from left to right;
his face and cheeks were broad, and his [teeth] resembled the curve of the young crescent moon.
His body was completely covered with hairs that were as bright as fresh sky-blue and reddish [saffron],
beautiful, long, broad, and elevated.
He was endowed with two ears adorned with ruby earrings,
possessed a lofty crown, and was graced by necklaces and other ornaments.
Clad in garments of variegated silk and adorned with diverse garlands,
he possesses a radiance equal to a thousand times the light of twelve suns at the time of universal dissolution.
With eyes cast slightly upward and sideways,
his teeth possessing the luster of jasmine and the moon, his face was somewhat smiling. (32)
Naturally gentle and stainless, yet colored by illusory wrath;
abiding in a posture with playful, moving steps. || 33 ||

Meditating upon the supreme state by means of one's own internal organ alone, one should form three creeper-like gestures with the fingers, starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger. || 34 ||
Bending one [finger] upward and applying it to the nose—endowed with this mudrā, which bestows fear of all obstacles. (35)
Holding a discus and a conch in his hands, and bearing a mace hanging down, with one hand resting nonchalantly upon the slope of his hip; (36)

Thus, one should visualize the god bearing such a form, possessing manifold and wondrous prowess, situated in the center of the pericarp, accompanied by the primary mantras beginning with the heart-mantra. || 37 ||
And [the deity] is situated within the interior of a lotus-petal, devoid of that [specific] form and luster;
however, meditation on the limbs as white and so forth is prescribed everywhere. (38)
Gajānana, Jayatsena, the mighty Harivaktra, and the fourth, known as Kālaprakṛti, O Lotus-born One. (39)
For these four fierce-bodied lords of the Gaṇas wait for his command, holding aloft white chowries.
And likewise Vināyaka and the others who are the foremost among the Lords of Obstacles—of these Lords of the Gaṇas, who are ever obedient to his command. (41)
One should place those situated outside the lotus in the corners starting from Īśāna,
gazing at the face of the Lord and remaining in postures corresponding to His own.
In that same way, all were marked with hand-prints, yet they were devoid of seals;
understand that their meditation was distinct from their bodies.
Terrible, with the face of a lordly elephant, four tusks, and three eyes;
with a neck like a conch shell, four arms, and the splendor of ten thousand full moons.
Adorned with necklaces, anklets, armlets, girdles, and strings of pearls;
enriched with various garlands, perfumes, and garments; and possessed of incomparable prowess. (45)
One should meditate upon Gajānana and then remember Jayatsena,
who has the face of a great horse and possesses the luster of a mountain of rubies.
Then one should meditate upon Harivaktra, whose eyes are like molten gold, who possesses manifold and wondrous prowess, and whose head is covered with a mane of hair.
O Brahmin, it resembled molten gold, possessed a terrible gurgling roar,
had the face of a lion-king, and was as swift as the wind at the end of an aeon.
One should meditate upon him named Kālaprakṛti as being like a mountain of collyrium, with a face formidable with fangs and tawny hair and eyes. (49)
With fish-like earrings, fierce, and with a sunken nose like that of a fish—these lords of the hosts of Gaṇas indeed possess the marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa). || 50 ||
O Brahmin, one should remember all the ornaments from the feet up to the neck—whatever articles of decoration there may be—as having been mentioned previously in the three [sections]. (51)

One should perform the worship of these [deities] by their own names, preceded by the *praṇava* (OM) and ending with "namaḥ," for the sake of attaining the fruits of various supernatural powers (*siddhi*), O Lotus-born One. (52)
Pauṣkara said:
Who indeed is this one of incomparable prowess, before whom obstacles capable of uprooting the three worlds flee from afar in a mere twinkling of an eye? (53)
The Blessed Lord said:
"O twice-born one, that form of the all-pervading Turyātman which is known as Kālavaiśvānara—this very deity is proclaimed as Viṣvaksena. (54)
Established through the distinctions of the *āhavanīya* and other sacred fires for those who sacrifice in the ritual,
he takes up the fallen oblation and satisfies the entire world. (55)
Thus, from the sattvic sacrifice consisting of mantra, which is permeated by Brahman, having obtained the transmission from the form of the Guru, he attained that which is consecrated by mantra. (56)
And out of a desire to bestow grace upon them, he quickly distributes [his gifts] himself to all the immortals and inhabitants of every world, even though they have not been invited.
Pauṣkara said:
Among all the forms consisting of mantra, you have pointed out one principal and supreme form, characterized by the name Vāsudeva. (58)

The worship of Viṣvaksena, as instructed by those remaining after that [offering], is performed; O Lord, just as a separate sacrifice for each individual form is effective, so too is this [worship] effective. 59.
Or one should perform the worship of the assembly of mantras by means of a specific array, [placing] the mutual limbs of the three principal tantras with the *phāla* [mudrā]. 60.
If one should indeed offer flowers and so forth to that by which [the deity] has been worshipped.

The Blessed One said: "O Brahmin, how will you bestow [the fruit] of the Absolute everywhere and at all times? Having first propitiated the Lord of Mantras who existed in the beginning, [you must do so] from the midst."
Because he is the primary one for external expression, and not any other,
his state of transcendence alone remains everywhere through the power of worship.
O Lotus-born One, due to the influence of their respective portions of existence and also by the power of various karmas, there arise the arrays of mantras and of those whose form is mantra.
In the same way, O Lotus-born One, the "higher" status of all principles has been declared as merely adventitious;
in reality, there is nothing higher than the ultimate principle.

Except for the one called Vāsudeva, who is the internal witness, eternally manifest, of two forms, consisting of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha), and characterized by origination and dissolution. || 65 ||
Indeed, there is always equality among these four even when they are distinct;
for they are here unified by their sovereignty over Brahman, like leaves upon a stalk.
In your mind, which possesses the characteristics of the six perfections from the time of its initial activity until the end of your own existence, [there is] the Lord. (67)
In whatever space there is no opportunity for obstacles—that is the knowledge; indeed, wherever the mandala of deities stands far off, that is where [the obstacles] never exist.
But at the time of propitiation, what need is there to speak of Indra and the other gods?
In that regard, the lineage of the sacrificial gifts (*dāyānvaya*)—which is established and bestows liberation even against one's will—is [the means]. (69)
O twice-born one, that which is rooted in Brahman from its very foundation and is liberated from all others—
no worship is prescribed for it within its own manifestation.
Yet there may be a slight attachment at times toward the deities of the sciences (vidyās),
and likewise toward Viṣvaksena, who is surrounded by his multitude of attendants.
From this most subtle array beyond all others,
which is endowed with form and eternally arisen for the sake of movement, [the mantra] joined with [the deity] bestows all accomplishments.
O twice-born one, if each one is worshipped individually for the sake of attaining desired goals such as liberation, or if two or even three are worshipped with distinct meditations; (73)
In that regard, without the stages beginning with the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and ending with the worship of Vighnāri,
no success arises from a sacrifice even in ten million aeons. (74)
Pauṣkara said:
From the proximity of these three arrays, there arises the eternal [principle];
I now desire to hear this logic that is eternally manifest through differentiation.
The Blessed One said: This which has been pointed out is incomparable and beyond the senses;
it is the nature of being, eternally arisen, characterized by supreme bliss and perfect tranquility.
The second [state], known as the Subtle (sūkṣma), possesses a splendor equal to ten thousand flashes of lightning, suns, fires, and full moons; it rises and sets. (77)

Through the mutual distinction of marks, garments, colors, and so forth, which were individually established by time, one becomes fulfilled; being liberated from the impurities such as disease and the like. (78)
Endowed with sovereign power, yet with all things completely subsided;
O twice-born one, in the supreme abode within the assembly of sages, you are like the sky of conceptual thought. (79)
Pauṣkara said:
"In the maṇḍala sacrifices, by means of the worship of Viṣvaksena and other rites,
you indeed always destroy the entire multitude of sins that lead to the destruction of the Name."
Therefore, he who gives to others while eating himself, or he who, out of delusion, neglects [to give], is base and goes to hell. || 81 ||
The support, purpose, and function must always be provided;
for that deity, who possesses two deities as his lords, it is indeed just so. 82.
O Pauṣkara, [this applies] to that which was previously intended by oneself, or even to that which was performed with faith according to his command, consisting of various forms of rejoicing.
Especially so for one who eats curd, fruits, and the like, or divine food.
Pauṣkara said: "O Lord, what is *devadravya*? And what is called *devasva*? O lover of devotees, why is the food of the Gaṇas forbidden, as is the food of the devotees? (84)
The Blessed Lord said:
Whatever exists within your treasury, including leaves, ornaments, and so forth, and whatever is attached to the form of Bhava—that shall be within my own presence through my grace. (85)

Know that whatever is in his marketplace or in his possession is indeed the property of the deity; likewise, cattle, elephants, and so forth, within the territory extending to the cities and villages [belong to him]. || 86 ||
Rice crops, sugarcane, flowers, and so forth; female and male servants, householders;
a virtuous alliance, trade, along with sons, livestock, and kinsmen. (87)
That which is the property of the gods is forbidden; it brings sin even to those who have attained perfection.
Whether it be given by oneself or given by another, one should avoid it with great effort. (88)
And since it causes faults and bestows the hell of Dakṣayya,
one should therefore first establish a binding [of the image] in that temple of the deity.
And why must he be nourished with effort? Surely it is because of his failure to perform the duties already undertaken, and because of his absence from the temples of Viṣṇu. || 90 ||
A king incurs a very great fault regarding his royal status;
yet, as there is extensive fame, so too is there imperishable happiness in this world.
At the end of the body, one attains auspiciousness by virtue of protecting what was previously undertaken.
Pauṣkara said:
"O Lord of the World, you previously declared that the consumption of the food of the gods is a form of giving; why is its prohibition now being stated? (92)
The Blessed One said:
That which was previously prepared with effort for the sake of the sacrifice for the deities, up until its complete satisfaction, is called the food of the gods. (93)
O twice-born one, if its consumption has been performed otherwise through delusion,
a person attains purification only after performing hundreds of penances.

O best of sacrificers, at the conclusion of the satiation with mantras, for those who have abandoned the conceited mind while performing sacrifices, this consumption brings about total purification. (95)
Although the consumption of the food offering (naivedya) is always obtained, it is purifying, bestowing purity, meritorious, and granting prosperity, service, and increase. (96)

O Lotus-born One, for the Guru and others, as well as for other devotees and even for practitioners (sādhakas), salutation is strictly prohibited in reality, with the exception of [the specific case of] vanda. 97.
Alternatively, apart from the use of cloth, [this applies] to the daily and occasional worship.
Pauṣkara said: "O Blessed One, for what reason is the food offering (naivedya) purified by mantra forbidden for the practitioner? I have a great doubt regarding this matter. (98)
The Blessed One said:

"One should never accept even a single flower that has not been offered. Indeed, it should be accepted from one who possesses wealth according to the mantra; some say it may be taken from one who possesses the skin of a wild animal."
The preceptor should repeatedly offer prayers to the Lord of Mantras for all the offerings, such as the food oblation (naivedya), and for all the enjoyments intended for those of purified soul. 100.
Because he is entirely independent and because that [independence] is established for him, he does not incur any fault;
just as a minister who has gained an interval [of safety] from a king when [the king's power] is directed toward everyone. 101.
He indeed is not afflicted; such is the mantra-lord of that guru for whom one who is intent on service has reached the culmination of the fruit.
One should not make a request of the king even for a very small matter;
if he is pleased, he may grant it himself, provided he is already disposed to do so out of his own satisfaction.
One should say, "I have attained serenity," while bowing one's head in greeting;
the wise person should not perform the *nābhi* [gesture], for it brings about the fruit of great purpose. (104)
In this way, the practitioner who is devoted to the mantra-vow and performs this discipline attains accomplishment before long, through the grace of the one whose form is the mantra. || 105 ||
Pauṣkara said:

O Lord of the World, regarding the mantra for the food offering (naivedya) to the deity to be propitiated, what is the application and the great knowledge thereof? And what is the course for that which remains [unexplained]? || 106 ||
The Blessed Lord said:
That which has been given when there is the means to do so, to the lords of the divisions of the mandala, along with their external supports and powers, and to the Gurus beginning with Kālanātha.
One should give that which has been offered to the limbs, beginning with the heart and extending to the range of vision, to the celibate students who are devoted and of purified soul. 108.
This is always prescribed for the sons in the rite of giving away the images of Śrī and the other consorts, as well as those known as the Vyūha-forms.

That which pertains to the collection of weapons such as the discus, the ritual implements for mantras, and those descended into the places of enjoyment, is known as *sāma* (conciliation) through its power. 110.

Whatever has been given to those standing at the center of the *gaṇacakra*, to the lords of the directions, to the gatekeepers, or to the *kṣetriya*—that shall be distributed among the Vaiṣṇavas, beginning with the *kṣetriyas*. (111)

O Lotus-born One, prior to this dismissal, whatever was prescribed or prohibited for all becomes forbidden once the circle of mantras has been dismissed [or, in the case of the field, when the field is dismissed]. || 112 ||
O Lotus-born One, because beings by the millions immediately follow after those who were formerly attendants of Viṣṇu for the sake of that very goal.
Is their purity not due to that power? And they adorn themselves out of compassion for the multitude of beings born in the water. || 114 ||
Whatever remains after being given is all considered given, for it becomes inexhaustible and imperishable;
having gathered it together and ground it with effort, one should cast it into deep water.
For those whose mantras are obstructed by the image (arcā), the giving of gifts is always prescribed;
likewise for the beings who depend upon it and possess prior forms. || 116 ||
And likewise for his servants, who were devoted to dance and song, even though they entreated him on behalf of the devotees living in the Brahmin village. (117)
Therefore, O Lord of Mantras, the food offering (naivedya) purified by the gaze [of the teacher] is supremely sanctifying;
it effects the purification of the body, and through that purification, there is lightness regarding time.
For those who have abandoned the faults regarding wealth, auspiciousness arises before long;
even though it may be great in this way, O Lotus-born One, so it is. (119)
Indeed, renunciation is superior to both giving and incitement;
for by it, greed does not arise in the world, nor can any fault prevail. (120)
For those who are free from greed for that, the intellect becomes exceedingly pure;
it is that intellect which knows each action that yields the fruit of attaining the supreme, eternal state.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Worship of Viṣvaksena," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Pauṣkara Saṃhitā. || 20 ||
(Total number of verses: 123) Now begins the twenty-first chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
O Lord, the collection of powers (*śakticaya*) was previously proclaimed by you.
I desire to hear about it, along with its ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) and its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). || 1 ||

The Blessed Lord said: Lakṣmī bestows all prosperity; Puṣṭi grants supreme perfection; Kānti, Prabhā, Mati, Śakti, Kriyā, Icchā, Mahimā, and Unnati— Śrībhagavānuvāca | sarvasaṃpatpradā lakṣmīḥ puṣṭiḥ paramasiddhidā | kāntiḥ prabhā matiśśaktiḥ kriyecchā mahimonnatiḥ || 2 || The Blessed Lord said: Lakṣmī bestows all prosperity; Puṣṭi grants supreme perfection; Kānti, Prabhā, Mati, Śakti, Kriyā, Icchā, Mahimā, and Unnati.
Svadhā, Vidyā, Niṣā, Māyā, Mūrti, Hrīṃ, Śrī, Tulā, Dyuti, Kalā, Dyuti, Niṣṭhā, Ṛjvī, Ruci, Ceṣṭā, Śobhā, Śuddhi, and Vibhūti—[these are the powers] thereafter. (3)
Vṛtti, Vyāpti, Gati, Supti, Bhāgā, Vāgīśvarī, Rati, Siddhi, Nati, Pluti, Krīḍā, Saṃpat, Kīrti, Śikhā, and Mati. (4)
O Lotus-born One, one should first meditate with the intellect upon Gāyatrī as the boundary and the creation, as the very body of the mantra existing as an attribute of the Self. (5)
Indeed, this entire [universe] is always filled by these formless [energies].
This is the common conjunction, O Pauṣkara, the power of the wheel, O Pauṣkara.
Now, the specific procedure together with the collection of mantras is being stated:
one should place the unsatisfied primordial form (ādimūrti) to the south and the north.
One should place the eight [syllables] known as Lakṣmī and Puṣṭi, which have been diligently gathered from the heap of refuse,
in the eight directions starting from the tips of the filaments, according to the sequence of the Vedas.

Whether within the heart and other centers or externally, depending on the desired accomplishment, the supreme state exists within the primary portion of these [energies]; otherwise, there would be destruction. (9)
By means of contact with the limbs, one obtains whatever enjoyment one desires, even that which exists outside;
indeed, by sitting firmly in the lotus posture (padmāsana) above the space enveloped by the remainder, [one attains it]. 10.
Thus indeed, by means of thorough application, those who behold the Supreme Lord perceive that it is exactly the same for the mantras descended from various separate sacrifices.
The eight Śaktis should be installed, excluding Lakṣmī and Puṣṭi;
then the remaining deities of that array, arranged as before, [should be installed] in the order of their attainment.
In a lotus other than the eight-petaled one, within the continuous series of filaments at the base,
there arises a group of eight resembling the pericarp.
And in this way, O Lotus-born One, there should be the ritual placement (nyāsa) of all sacrifices upon the deities,
with the exception of the single Miśracakra, which belongs to Śarada.
There, the eightfold [mantra] is in the Kahlāra [lotus], while in the remaining wheels it is like [the letters] *bhaḥ* and *sva*.
O Brāhmaṇa, I shall now describe the meditation-mantras in their proper order, exactly as they exist. (15)
Lakṣmī has the luster of the color of a red lotus, with eyes like blue water-lilies; Puṣṭi is white as a flood of milk, her face filled with bliss. 16.
O Brahmin, this group of thirty-four auspicious characteristics of the Śaktis— beginning with beauty and ending with eminence— is as pure as crystal. (17)
By means of the yoga of intermittent practice, one should meditate on that which resembles gold,
radiant with rubies, and endowed with incomparable qualities.
All of them had clear eyes and lotus-like faces bright with smiles;
they were endowed with mutual beauty, grace, and auspicious fortune.
All of them wear garlands and garments, adorned with every ornament, and are marked by fly-whisks resembling the rays of the moon. || 20 ||
With the left hand—and with the other [hand], one should meditate on those who grant desired objects;
like the mantra[-deities], they move in succession and likewise bestow all fruits. (21)
But at the time of propitiation, out of compassion for their devotees,
they assume their universal form (vaiśvarūpya) and cast their glances in all directions.
Thus, the external activities—
including the placement (*vinyāsa*), worship (*arcana*), and meditation (*dhyāna*) along with the mantras and lotuses— bring about the complete accomplishment of the practitioner for the Goddess.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Retinue," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Pauṣkara Saṃhitā. || 21 ||
Now begins the twenty-second chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
O you who are worshipped by the immortals, I desire to understand this correctly from you.
For the benefit of the foremost practitioners, that is the seat of the Arhat.
It has been established together with its secret meaning, unconfused, including the presiding deity, exactly as it exists.
The Blessed One said:
O Lotus-born one, that which is to be placed within is situated in my own unchanging essential nature;
it stands aloof at its beginning and end, like a multitude of gems upon a thread.
First, as the nature of the support, and then as the form of the universe;
then, indeed, as the nature of various mantras above, for in reality he is waveless.
And for the sake of quelling the karma of those performers whose latent impressions have been cultivated,
and for the sake of accomplishing both worldly enjoyment and liberation for those whose [actions] are manifested by that desire.

O Pauṣkara, for those whose minds are governed by beginningless ignorance, there is no higher reality regarding the true nature of things, nor is there any such thing for those who lack right vision. (p. 96) Or rather, [it is not perceived] in its true essence.
There is no conceptualization of "to be abandoned" and so forth, whether preceded by the horizontal [realm of desire] or preceded by the Brahma [realm];
