for that which has its defining characteristics completely subsided through the conceptualizations of particularities.
The power of the Lord Viṣṇu is called "the common" (sādhāra);
having taken up the seed-syllable, which possesses the capacity for the seat as before, by means of His will.
And she possesses both unmanifest and manifest forms, like a cluster of suns,
because she is the nature of the spreading of light and the seed-heap of the universe.
Now, the state known as the "Tortoise" (kūrma) is described for one whose limbs have been gathered together, who at the end consumes the universe by means of the fire of time (kālavaiśvānara). (9)
The Lord, worshipped by the worlds, who has assumed the form of a tortoise, is his deity;
moreover, that power and capability of the Lord remains unabandoned by him.
That which is infinite, the inexhaustible sprout of the universe for all conceptual constructions,
draws [the mind] upward, just as a tortoise withdraws its neck into itself.
That which is called Śeṣa has the serpent as its deity; indeed, it is sung of as Ananta, O Mahāmati, and as the support for the four elements that serve as seeds.
From that, the branch of fragrance attains manifestation as before;
it is the Lord whose self is the earth, in whom resides the deity known as Abhimāna.
Therefore, its fruit consists of essence, manifesting the characteristic of nectar;
its conceited form is the eternal Ocean of Milk.
Therefore, O Lotus-born one, the splendor arising from that infinite jewel belongs to him whose power is clearly manifest and eternal, characterized by burning light.
Know that to be the divine, white, fully blossomed lotus with infinite petals,
distinguished by the supreme and the prior, and consisting of one, two, or three qualities.
O Lotus-born one, having remained together with those eight transformations (*vikāra*), speech exists there as the deity, wherein animals and others are the modifications of speech. (17)
Likewise, those four modifications of time that were previously established—among them, form (rūpa) is indeed remembered as the supreme essence of existence for all. || 18 ||
Furthermore, that other [meditation] consists of the contemplations on manifestation (*vyakti*) together with their limbs;
the third is called "conceit" (*abhimāna*), characterized by the body of the deity. (19)
Therefore, indeed, it is the subtle element of touch, whose deity is Vāyu,
from which his manifest appearance arose, characterized by various wheels and limbs.
Therefore, O Lotus-born One, sound was produced with space as its deity;
it is that in which the manifestation of pure form is withdrawn from all limbs into the wheel.
That is celebrated as the celestial sphere, the primary abode of Kamalā;
within it abide all beings, and upon it everything is established. (22)
Therefore, the expansion of time—which begins with the unfolding [of consciousness] and ends with the great dissolution—proceeds, creating differentiation among all things. (23)
Of the fourfold Brahmā, who in reality is non-different even though differentiated by mere speech, and who possesses a multitude of qualities such as knowledge; || 24 ||
Because it is eternally risen, because it is eternal, because it is all-pervasive,
because it is complete, and because it possesses the six qualities, time finds no scope within that supreme state.
From sound, O great-minded one, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) having the sun as its deity arose;
and from that, the mind (manas), also having the sun as its deity, came into being.

The arrangement beginning with the Sun and so forth—which extends from the petals to the pericarp—belongs to the pervasive Lord whose nature is manifest bliss and whose deity is the light of the intellect. (27)
This form of the primary lotus is known to consist of the qualities (guṇas),
and it is the imperishable cause of the principles beginning with the intellect (buddhi).
O one of great intelligence, that which is called the Unmanifest (avyakta) indeed bears a form whose constituent qualities (guṇas) are undifferentiated;
having set aside its own qualities, it proceeds established in itself. (29)
Having withdrawn all internal mental modifications characterized by the inner self into the heart,
O best of the twice-born, it is indeed from this that all states of being arise. (30)
Beings indeed perish here; therefore, this lotus is supreme.
It is a web of rays from the sun of consciousness, characterized by the grasped and the grasper.
Wherever one's own abode and one's own capacity have been transferred, even into the object of cognition,
that stainlessness called "Vimalā" is the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), the state of being the Knower, O Lotus-born One.
That which is called "origination" is origination; that which is called "truth" is truthfulness;
that which is called "eternal" is eternality; and that which is called "illumination" is luminosity. (33)
O Lotus-born One, that which is called "the infinite" is indeed the infinite portion;
it should be known as the supreme state of grace, together with the power of grace. || 34 ||
That which consists of the two groups of four digits exists indeed as self-supported; it revolves, and having reached the supreme, it returns once again. || 35 ||
O Lotus-born One, these Kalās of the worshipped Self have been declared according to their division into higher and lower; they possess supreme infinity. 36.
Having established it through one's own power by means of the nature of one's own self-nature, [it is] for the sake of the form of the grasped and the grasper; thus is the unmanifest lotus.
O twice-born one, you remain only as the pure Samā for a brief moment;
having previously been merely the universal whole (sāmānya), you have now become the powers (śakti) and the constituent parts (kalā).

O twice-born one, when one correctly perceives one's own inherent nature, which is characterized by the sense of "I-am-ness" (asmitā), that [state] proceeds; and from the removal of that [notion], incomparable bliss arises. (39)
One should desire that mantra, which is self-luminous, incomparable, and imperishable;
it abides in the space of light, beyond all spatial dimensions such as the directions and so forth.
O Lotus-born One, having immediately assumed and relied upon a partial form (kalāmūrti),
he then departed from the central region of the luminous sky.
Then, having sat comfortably upon his own seat through the power of fortitude,
[he should proceed] with his subtle body of knowledge (vidyā-deha), which conforms to the physical body of the elements.
Now, that very nature which is the cluster of bliss, once differentiated, should be colored by the perspective of the scriptures as it enters into worldly transaction. (43)
One should perceive them as well-established and arisen through their own respective objects of focus and the characteristics of the deities, within friends and others, as [multiple] cognitions. 44.
Just as the marks, ornaments, and so forth are to be placed upon the body, so too, therefore, the pure [deities] such as Hṛdaya and the rest are to be established in their respective locations. 45.
Then, one should perform the sacrifice according to the ritual procedure exactly as prescribed in the scriptures;
likewise, in the offering of the seat, [one should contemplate] the lineage of the principles (tattva) from the Supreme.
O Lotus-born One, when the instrument is presided over by that [power], it should bring about the dissolution of what has arisen;
however, once the purpose of the person (puruṣārtha) has ceased, [dissolution occurs] either internally or externally.
Having sequentially recollected the multitude of mantras, one should cause them to dissolve into the Lord of Mantras (Mantreśvara);
or else, by the power of one's own volition, one should bring the power of the mantra to rest.

Then, together with the power of his volition, he should dissolve his own form as the embodiment of knowledge (vidyāmūrti) into his own creative powers (kalās), and likewise dissolve the entire web of those powers into the Self.
But by withdrawing [the breath] through the process of emanation (sṛṣṭikrama) into the previously mentioned support (ādhāra), one becomes nourished by a mass of bliss, just as before. (50)
O one of great intelligence, these [impurities] fall away by their very nature from those wise ones who know reality,
who are partless, and who have perfected their virtuous deeds.
And it brings about the expansion of others who delight in constant form,
who are devoted to the practice of mantra, and who, though diverse, possess an equal self.
O twice-born one, this conviction regarding the nature of the sixfold conceptualization is indeed established by the power of the Imperishable (Acyuta) through his unswerving essence. 53.
Although it is sustained and pervaded by the Lord through His own power,
even there [He exists] within the bodies of those living beings who dwell therein. (54)
O Great-minded One, having taken hold of those who have been graced by his own power,
he abides within that manifold self in the form of various mantras.
For those of small intellect who are filled with pride, it proceeds toward the partial accomplishment of worship; indeed, by such action, their true nature does not abandon them.
But Vrahayajñotpalādya and Danāvṛnda are in Pauṣkara;
Prabhavajñopalādya and so forth are in [the other]. || 57 ||
O Lotus-born one, is this mantra likewise intent upon bestowing grace?
And does it indeed manifest its own great essence, characterized by qualities such as knowledge and the rest? (58)
Until the attainment of the state of supreme bliss, those who exist throughout time remain;
yet at the conclusion of their employment, even they indeed depart together.
Or [it leads] to dissolution, O Vasu; and for the sake of their sport alone, having projected his own consciousness into others for the sake of pacifying worldly existence (bhava-śānti). 60.
Thus, O Lord, that supreme mantra belongs to the Sovereign of All;
it abides, O Lotus-born One, for the sake of liberation from the source of all beings. 61.
Pauṣkara said: O Lord, how is it possible for the inactive, all-pervading, undecaying,
and immutable Self to exist in a state of distinctness as the essence of mantra?
The Blessed One said:
Just as when grass is not gathered, a woman proceeds [to weave], so too does the inherent power of a *puṣyarāga* gem manifest even in its expansion. (63)
In the same way, the multitude of powers belonging to the Blessed Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, proceeds from that mantra whose body is the syllable *gaṃ*.
Having taken up the nature of karma, she returns once again;
she is that great power called Acyutā, consisting of tranquil consciousness from of old.
Thus is the state of the self whose nature is action, which is sustained by knowledge and awakened, with respect to the powers directed toward the objects of the senses.

For just as one who is well-trained, standing upon a leather bag filled with air, crosses over a very narrow place without his senses becoming agitated, even though it has been lost [to the current]. (67)
O Pauṣkara, why do you laugh at one whose intellect is trained in the principles of *sattva*? You remain agitated, having cast him down while your own mind is distracted. 68.
Thus awakened, he disregards the other sense-faculties, which are capable of the activities of existence, mantras, and ritual actions. (69)
And he remains composed of pure consciousness alone, like a waveless ocean; yet, because he is not deluded, he again perceives his own vibration as supreme bliss. (70)
Having superimposed [the world] by means of the powers (śaktis), one should partake in the state of the known and the knower;
thus indeed does the stability of the earth arise from the nature of the supreme substratum.

From the thorough knowledge of that, there arises the destruction of the effects of actions; as well as the establishment of their arising and passing away, and indeed their state of inner dissolution. (72)
(99) Thus, indeed, the mantras of those whose form is wind [always],
having encompassed the middle region, should enter by way of the central path. || 73 ||

Having clearly manifested myself within the intermediate space before you as previously described, I shall remain here maintaining this established order until that ancient teaching [is fulfilled]. 74.
Thereafter, that state [of consciousness] exists externally for the sake of sacrificing the various differentiated objects.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Foundation and the Seat," in the venerable Pauṣkara Saṃhitā of the Pāñcarātra.
(Total number of verses: 75) Now begins the twenty-third chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
Having thus established the configuration of the foundation,
one should subsequently arrange [the syllables] in order from the field and region of Ā-ka-ja up to the ground of the door.

The presiding deities of those [mandalas] exist in the cardinal and intermediate directions in their respective order, by virtue of the relationship between the supported and the support, and through the influence of prior necessity. (2)
The divine (aiśvara) is in the east, and the Prajāpati-related (prājāpatya) is the third.
Among these, the first is beneficial for ritualists (karmiṇaḥ) as a means for attaining liberation and other goals.
Because it is the means for accomplishing that [attainment], the syllable *a* is remembered as the source of all;
it enters into the state of being a limb for both those who possess mantras and those who do not.

O lotus-born one, this third [method], well-known to those who have accomplished their desires, has been taught for the sake of achieving the heart-sacrifice through the power of one's own intellect, O stainless-eyed one.
One's own mantra, which is eternally present within reality,
is brought to manifestation through the power of the elements, the form, the mind, and the sensory organs.
Does it bear fruit quickly as a reality for one who knows only the mere "Tva-saṃ" (the syllable *tvaṃ*);
since you, O Bhava, have been restrained solely by the power of devotion and faith? || 7 ||
Thus, that which is indeed illuminated by the net of rays from the mantra-sun is the primordial volition of those whose minds possess eternal certainty. (8)
For those who take sole refuge in mantra, however, there is benefit even in external worship.
Whether internal or external, it originates from the lotus, situated in the directions and waters starting from the support (ādhāra).
And that in which a web of rays descends is known as *pauruṣa*. It belongs to the Blessed One, for those who sacrifice to their own deity among all beings and states of being. || 10 ||
The qualities within these [elements] are manifold and diverse, both external and internal, according to their respective lords;
that which was previously determined by you through the force of established tradition remains so even now.
And that third function of it is well-known, O Mahāmati, for those who look toward the directions with desire and whose nature consists of one door and so forth. (12)
(100) And, Mahāmati, when bowing to shrines of deities, to those who are prostrating,
to couches and seats, and when placing incense and other offerings; 13.

On account of that [power], the abiding state of the guardians of the world such as Indra, as well as of sacrifices and the like, must be established according to the characteristics of dharma and so forth. (14)
It is solely by virtue of the specific purpose that [the rites] for the vessel, the fire-pit, the yantra, and the worship are performed by those who are slow, middling, or devoted. (15)
In this very manner, O Brahmin, the worship of Lokeśāna is to be performed here in this dense forest, within the interior of a cave of an excellent mountain.

In an underground chamber or on a sacrificial ground, for those whose minds delight in worldly dharmas, there is always the establishment of the world’s teachings, the meaning of the treatises, and the mantras. (17)

O Lotus-born One, one should indeed perform the rite with the visualization of the Samaya-mantra; one who knows the reality of mantra should practice that which arises from the lotus, free from untruth. 18.

Having first correctly understood the determination of the cardinal and intermediate directions for all locations, such as cities and dwellings, which are firmly established in every direction; || 19 ||
And for the sake of his own final liberation through the power of perfect fitness alone, he should then perform the ritual procedure of the mandalas; listen to it as it is.
O Brahmin, the power (śakti) always exists within the Self whose nature is Being; thus, both the gross and the subtle exist together with that which is of the nature of Being.
The aggregate of individual powers, however, persists within the subtle self;
it is conjoined with the essential nature called "Being" (sattā) for those possessing subtle bodies.
She is indeed always established within the gross self;
here, she may be conceived as being either outside or inside, depending on the perspective. (23)
The deposition of the wings is prescribed near Padmāvanī;
for indeed, O God, the form of everything consists of a twofold nature of existence. || 24 ||
In the vicinity of the sacrificial ground, they were established for the rite of ritual deposition (nyāsa);
indeed, the great form of all [deities] is twofold through mutual affection.
O Lotus-born One, because there exists a twofold arrangement of the images of the deities with ten bodies upon the seats within the maṇḍalas, [this is so]. (26)
That which is accompanied by its own substrate is clear; the other, which is solitary, is very clear.
Having understood this thoroughly and correctly from the beginning, O one of stainless vision, [act] as it truly is. (27)
As before, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) on the perimeters of the mandalas;
at all times and for all sacrifices, [this is done] from the petal to the space between the petals.
One should certainly place the manifestation of one's own deity as mere sound within the syllable *Śab* (the seed-syllable of space).
Outside of the void (*vyoma*), however, one should place the seats starting from the southeast corner.
The fourfold group beginning with Dharma has the nature of the Yugas as its form;
it is established in that manner, being composed of those very elements, yet possessing qualities that are their opposites.
Together with the commonality of the *ṛk*, preceded by the *pūrvā* and conjoined with the distinction of time;
thereafter, in that very manner, the indication of those seats (*sapīṭha*) in the region. || 31 ||
At that very moment, one should indeed place the space of sound (*śabdākāśa*) as the fourth, which is truly one and the same,
possessing the essence of the splendor of a digit of the autumn moon.
One should arrange the eight images of the seats in a clockwise direction,
beginning from the southeast for the sake of the fourfold group and ending in the northeast corner.
O Lotus-born one, O one of pure vision, knowledge of dharma, detachment,
and sovereignty are at the beginning in the east, while adharma is at the end in the north.
Ignorance, lack of dispassion, and lack of sovereignty follow immediately after;
one should install these in the four sections of the Kevala-pīṭha as previously described. || 35 ||
The root of sovereignty over dharma and the other [puruṣārthas], according to the sequence already indicated,
is located externally in the *upapīṭha* by means of the characteristics of the state of space (*vyomabhāva*). || 36 ||
The first [mantra] arises from the fourfold rotation immediately after the placement of the feet; that which arises from the single image of the seats belongs to the limbs, O Lotus-born One. (37)
But for those who move within the two-fold reflection, they are to be known there within, in sequence, along with the reversal of Sahadharmā and the others as before; then, outside of that.
And the four beginning with Kṛta are respectively on the limbs;
they belong to the limbs together with their feet, from the center of the images that consist of those [limbs]. (39)

Thereafter, one should place the [deities] of the southeast (Āgneya) according to the division of higher and lower (parāpara) upon the two frontal and rear images; and Dharma should be placed right there, outside of that.
O twice-born one, through its southern and northern parts, it bestows sovereignty and power;
for there, in the north and south, it assumes the form known as Adharma.
To the east and west, however, one should likewise [visualize] Adharma twice as being like oneself;
and in the south and north, one should visualize the Yuga known by its name Kṛta, likewise as being like oneself.
In the south, east, and west, one should place Tretā; ignorance in the south and north;
lack of dispassion in the west; and [the remaining two] in two ways in the east and west. (43)
Having placed Dvāpara on the southern side of the lower [floor], one should place Anaiśvarya on the northern [side]; thus, in the two directions starting from the south: || 44 ||
In the case of two images, however, it is performed with the [deities] starting from the east and so forth; then, in the Vidhānakalika [rite];
in the case of three images, on a pedestal (pīṭha); and in the case of five images, on the body (gātraka). || 45 ||
The dharmas of the feet are within [the body], and those of this [body] are outside them;
however, the eras such as Kṛta and the rest are made to have a common support for the subtle [elements].
The limbs, beginning with Adharma, should be placed [on the body] according to their characteristic forms;
furthermore, on the pedestal in front of a single image, or on the pedestal of a fivefold image, the limbs are to be placed.
Thereafter, with half [a verse], focus one-pointedly:
"And in their respective fields, Dharma and the others, whose characteristics are manifest, are to be placed. (48)
O Lotus-born One, from the center of his bodily forms arise such things as Adharma and the rest; likewise, from his right and left forms [proceed] those same qualities.
The single [Veda] became twofold as the Ṛgveda characterized by subtlety;
thereafter, its essential nature was established within those two wings.
Thus, in the southern quarter is the Yajus-traitā-yuga; in the west is the Dvāpara, in the east is the Tretā, in the north is the Atharva-yuga, and Kali is at the end of this configuration.
O Lotus-born One, listen now to me regarding the arrangement of the pedestals that have two reflected images and those whose bodies possess two reflected images. (52)

In the mantra-forms, from the feet up to the position of Īśa (Īśvara) in Agni, there are the principles beginning with Dharma, which are of a supreme nature, very gross, and consist of the Kṛta and other ages. || 53 ||
In the center, within the images of the limbs, are the deities beginning with Dharma, whose nature is the Supreme Self;
on both sides of them, however, are the various assemblies of Śruti-deities, possessing forms and arranged in manifold ways.

On a pedestal with two images and feet, or otherwise with five images, according to the distinction of the *parasthalī* [or *parasthūlī*], and on those beginning with *Dharma*, the [deities] are worshipped. || 55 ||
Then, the gross [deities] beginning with Adharma are in the middle of the limbs;
however, they are near the lotus and the earth on the two sides of the central disc.
The *Ṛg* and other Vedas should be deposited as two, according to the dual nature of the essence of existence (*sattāsvarūpa*).
Others also, having this same form, are likewise [deposited] externally for both [the teacher and the disciple], as before.
But one should place the *kṛta* and other [yogas], which possess forms, by means of both self and non-self—O Great-Minded One—upon the four images, the feet, and the seats themselves. 58.
102) Otherwise, the sequence of placement (*nyāsakrama*) upon the images is now described.
In that regard, first, the [deities] beginning with Dharma are composed of the supreme and subtle [levels] in succession. (59)
Having established those two within all internal spaces and outside them at every fresh step, one should then likewise establish the external pair of images.
From that, by way of coarseness, further such pairs of ages (*yuga*) of that same form should be placed in pairs so that the four become eightfold.
But he who is of a righteous nature, having arrayed himself from the midst of his limbs, stands perfectly established upon the reflection of the wings of the formation. || 62 ||
Due to the absence of clothing, each one is again as before;
from the threefold arrangement, the two-fold states such as the Ṛgveda and so forth should then be deposited.
Listen now to how the placement [of the lotus-born] is performed upon the limbs, the eight images, the four images, and the corners.
Beginning with the inner image (antarabimba) and so forth, up to the outer enclosure (bāhyabimba), [the deities] are placed upon the feet;
then, from that point, Dharma and the others are assigned in sequence according to their division into the supreme (para) and subtle (sūkṣma) levels.
In that very place, having established the form characterized by the face and the army-bearing [elements] joined with the pair made from the two parts of the side; || 66 ||
The gross elements, their own inherent qualities (dharmas), and so forth, are situated within the limbs; yet, by way of their subtle essence, they abide both within and outside the central image.
The gross self (sthūlātman) is the entire Ṛgveda; one should place it in two parts upon its two wings.
Then, with the subtle self (sūkṣmātman), one should likewise place it upon its two secondary wings.
O Brahmin, this very being, through its two feet situated outside that [body], belongs to those whose nature is that state; indeed, it should be diligently projected there. (69)
In this manner, O best of the twice-born, one should place the [Vedas] starting from the Yajurveda up to the Atharvaveda, proceeding from the southern quarter toward the north.
Just as the instruments—the eye, ear, hand, and foot—are indeed everywhere modified by the sentient being who possesses them, so too, O Viśva, are these [senses] dual from that [source]. || 71 ||
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Installation of the Deities of the Seat," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Pauṣkara Saṃhitā.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter.
The Blessed One said:
Through the eastern and western gates, one should worship Suparṇa, whose prowess is truth.
One should indeed perform the placement (nyāsa) of all the locations there, behind the Lord.
Leaning slightly against that door-post in the golden palace,
he stood facing him at the entrance, with his hands joined in reverence upon the ground.
O Lotus-born One, on the southern and northern sides, at the two doors, the mace and the discus— blazing in form and dedicated to that [Supreme Reality]— are placed.
He stands at the four gates of the eight cities beginning with Caṇḍa;
they are situated on the earth during the services and sacrifices of those whose stations have been revealed. || 4 ||
Gradually, however, the group of eight consisting of the eight Śobhās of theirs was reached;
for that which begins with Vajranābha is indeed present in the sacrifice endowed with the eight Śobhās.
O twice-born one, this third group of eight, pertaining to the sacrifices whose purpose is the eightfold adornment, should now be deposited in due order.
Lohitākṣa, Mahāvīrya, Aprameya, Suśobhana, Vīrahā, Vikrama, Bhīma, and Śatāvarta is the eighth.
O twice-born one, all three [deities] follow the eightfold beauty of another;
there, one should sequentially place this other eightfold [set], which is the fourth.
The irreversible one, the destroyer of great pride [or the slayer of serpents], the all-conquering, the steadfast;
the victorious one, the remover of fear and ailments, and the eighth is the lotus-born Tvaṣṭṛ.
At the sub-gates of the sacrifices, this group of sixteen [deities] is placed in sequence;
starting from the eastern side and proceeding clockwise, two by two, like Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa.
Firm in his vows, many-headed, large-bodied, and possessed of great strength;
one who has conquered anger, invincible, highly energetic, and possessing the three strides. || 11 ||
The Wind, the Destroyer of Evil, the Radiant, the All-Seeing, the Unsurpassable, the Uneven, the Impenetrable, and the Cloud—by these sixteen, fear is aroused. (12)
O Brahmin, within the four squares of the sacrificial altars, this tetrad of Vahni [Agni] extending up to the quarter of Īśa (Īśāna) should be deposited in due order.
"Ūrjita, Amṛtāṅga, Sarvāṅga, and Sarvatomukha—these, O lotus-eyed one, are said to be for the single images at the corners. (14)

Because of the constant mention of the two images, one should again apply the four [syllables] ending with their feet on the outside at the time of placement; O twice-born, this is the great [method].
Śubhāṅga, Varada, Vāgīśa, and Śabdavikrama—
know these to be the specific varieties of conch-shells, categorized as subtle and gross respectively.
This which was previously indicated by me regarding the mandalas has now been explained:
the array of the foundational deities, together with the groups of divine beings of the sacred seats (pīṭhas).
Accompanied by the lords of the gates and the host of Śrīnātha, O brahmins, he who is endowed with devotion and the heart performs the worship of all. || 18 ||
Accompanied by their own seed-syllables and the syllable *praṇava*, and followed by words of salutation;
furthermore, that which is called "gross" and "subtle" is joined with the word of others. (19)
In the rite of fire-oblation (homa), the mantras are provided with the word "ātmane" and end with "svāhā";
this is for the purpose of the mind's proper application, and it is the support for the worship of the Lotus-born One.
In due order, for all [the yogis], there is the stainless activity of the path of meditation;
it is peaceful, having abandoned all that remains, and it abides inwardly directed. || 21 ||
One should meditate upon the Lord known as the Support (ādhāra), who possesses the form of that which is to be supported (ādheya) inscribed [within him],
who is endowed with the tortoise-mudrā, whose face is like a tortoise, and who has the luster of refined gold.
One should meditate upon the tortoise, bearing a conch and a lotus, standing in the svastika posture, incessantly emitting from its body a terrifying and intense radiance. (23)
Then one should meditate upon that support as extending horizontally and upwards, blazing like a garland of flames,
resembling infinite moons, and itself infinite.
(104) Rich with a garland of a thousand hoods, adorned with a thousand hoods,
he beautifies his own body and the surface of the earth with his very palms joined in a hollowed gesture. (25)
[He is] endowed with a white lotus, a conch, a rosary, and a discus in his hands;
[this is for one whose mind is terrified by the fear of falling, or indeed by the fear of battle with the Nāgas. 26.
Saying "Do not fear," he bestowed fearlessness upon her, as well as upon everything up to the realm of Brahmā;
she shone intensely like the splendor of the rainy season, possessing a luster entirely like that of red gold.
One should meditate upon the Earth goddess seated in the lotus posture with palms joined in reverence,
white as a full-blown kunda flower, and bearing matted locks that are white and glossy.
He was meditating upon a white conch shell, adorned with strings of pearls, its every limb expansive, and it stood with its opening cast upward. || 29 ||
One should also remember the ocean with its knees and feet outstretched,
radiant with the palms and soles of the hands and feet, dark like the fruit of the ripe mango.
And then, O Brahmin, he saw him with blood-red eyes, disheveled hair, and a white face,
seated in the lotus posture and occupied with a rosary of beads.
One should meditate upon the lotus, accompanied by the lotus-mudrā, with very long petals, possessing the luster of frost, clear crystal, pure pearls, and the moon. (32)

The four [deities], Dharma, Jñāna, and the others, have shoulders and faces like those of the king of beasts; they are radiant with excellent pomegranate fruits and [jewels] such as rubies and corals. || 33 ||
Know that these four, who resemble the lords of the kings of kings and are colored by internal compassion, are like those sixteen years of age and are preceded by righteousness. (34)
Resplendent like the golden campaka flower, lightning, and yellow orpiment,
the Vedas are known as horse-faced, possessing the complete characteristics of a human being.
O Brahmin, thus are the ages, beginning with Kṛta, characterized by faces like those of the lordly bull;
they resemble a well-ripened mango, linseed flowers, blue lotuses, and parrots.
All are endowed with excellent garments, fine flowers, and beautiful ornaments;
all indeed hold a conch and a lotus, with hands granting boons and fearlessness.
For the sake of their own self-realization, they have surrendered their inner faculties to the Supreme Cause of Mantra, placing their heads upon the wheel that is to be established [within].

The King of Weapons should be visualized standing in the midst of a circle of birds resembling the fire of the sun at the end of an eon, with his hands occupied by his own mudrās, and leaping forward.
One should contemplate that unmanifest lotus, radiant as snow, gold, and fire;
it is peaceful, gentle, eight-armed, and situated in the form of a svastika.
One should meditate upon the formless Sun of Consciousness, which possesses the luster of a crystal stone, is a mass of consciousness, unborn, imperishable, and the treasury of all powers.
In all things, O All-pervasive Lord, that which exists within the state of becoming is situated there as the supporting Self;
it is a reality manifested by its own existence, distinct from the quality of *sattva*. || 42 ||
O best of Brahmins, know that manifestation is like a mass of flames arising from the tortoise-self;
it is the self-enjoyment of the Lord of Nagas, like gold that has been worn away by time. || 43 ||
One should fully understand that the divine nectar of the shore, endowed with floods of waves, is the inexhaustible glory of the Ocean of Milk.

The seed-vessel, together with its pericarp, which is indeed the non-delusion of the sequence of the lotus endowed with petals; my own power is the manifestation of the activities, which is not a natural state produced by me. 45.

This entire network of digits beginning with Vimalā, which is the manifestation of the Supreme Person (puruṣa), is known as the glory of the Lord whose nature is mantra; it is worshipped by the immortals and by all the cities [of the body]. (46)
Indeed, that multitude of various mantras belonging to the Great Lords of Mantras,
which is endowed with its own collection of powers, belongs to Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self. (47)

O best of the twice-born, having thus understood one's own manifestation as originating from the lotus, one should then worship those previously mentioned deities situated outside the pedestal and the altar.
Now hear of the meditation that follows this for Lohitākṣa and the others:
Lohitākṣa and the other seven are radiant with their own splendor by virtue of their color. || 49 ||
With flaming axes in their hands and joyful minds, they followed that which is indeed the fourth group of eight, preceded by the subsequent [verses]. 50.
Then know that it brings about infinite benefit for oneself, like the rising of a river;
Dṛḍhavrata and all the others are the sixteen secondary entries. || 51 ||
With great mallets in their hands, possessing the radiance and characteristics of their own abodes, those beginning with Ūrjita likewise hold clubs; they are indeed glorious.
O Lotus-born One, by their splendor they occupy the corners of the earth; by their characteristics, they all possess beautiful garments, have two arms, and wear lovely earrings. (53)
With serene faces and gentle countenances, they are capable of uplifting the three worlds;
they are resplendent with necklaces, anklets, armlets, and other ornaments. || 54 ||
They were observers of his commands and pacifiers of the faults of the wicked;
by their great power, they cast down the gods, asuras, and great serpents.
And as solitary heroes without companions, they are capable of perpetually revolving everything up to the realm of Brahmā effortlessly and with ease. 56.
O Great-minded One, since the mace, Garuḍa, the discus, Caṇḍa, and the others have already been described correctly in the past, what is the use of speaking further? 57.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Deities of the Foundation and the Seat," in the venerable Pauṣkara-saṃhitā of the Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
"O Blessed One, [please describe] the stations of livelihood for those whose souls are devoted to your teaching."
For my own benefit, I now desire to learn from you.

The Blessed Lord said: "O best of the twice-born, I shall describe the array of truth (satyavyūha) along with its divisions, as well as my other forms, my manifestations, and the various sub-manifestations."
If it has the form of another deity, then it bears the mark of a crane;
this is indeed forbidden for Vaiṣṇavas and for ordinary people during regular worship. (3)

How much more so, then, for those great-souled ones who know the reality of mantras, whose essence is the supreme devotion to Him, and who have been initiated for the sake of attaining success through His propitiation? (4)

One should pay homage to a portion of the Lord's glory—whether seen, heard, or remembered—as well as to those worthy of worship, permission, and adoration, even when they are outside [the formal ritual context]. || 5 ||
Sometimes, for the sake of accomplishing what has been seen, one's own limbs are smeared with ashes;
however, when these are used as independent offerings, they cause no fault for one who is pure.
Pauṣkara said:
O Lord of the Universe, I desire to learn from you specifically regarding the distinctions of the objects of refuge—what is to be accepted and so forth—and how they are to be worshipped. (7)

The Blessed Lord said: O best of Brahmins, listen to me regarding the sources of livelihood that are to be adopted by those who speak and those who are spoken of, for the sake of successfully performing constant worship.
From the elements, the triad arises; prior to that is the general characteristic. Furthermore, the earth is like a pedestal, distinguished by the division between the mobile and the immobile.
Likewise, there were water-pots made of gold and various other metals, as well as those produced from clay, wood, and stone, and even those fashioned from the bones of rhinoceroses.
And the water that has been strained and remains in vessels of auspicious color and leaf-bowls, held with palms joined;
and that which is in earthenware cups and basins, whether stationary or mobile in form. (11)

A fire that is blazing, free from smoke, and provided with fuel is recommended when it arises from the various substances previously mentioned and possesses the characteristics of being square and so forth.
Or, O Lotus-born one, on a simple auspicious pedestal (bhadrapīṭha) with lotuses and other designs in the center;
likewise, on pedestals of such forms that are slightly smaller in measurement.
Upon various pedestals, in diverse proportions, and in different bases, as well as upon large coral, excellent jewels, and great pearls; (14)
Or, O Lotus-born One, when a subtle collection of them has come into being, [it should be placed] upon a white,
unwashed web of cloth made of linen, cotton, or silk.

On the path—that is, on the skin, namely the black antelope hide (kṛṣṇājina)—or on the ground, or on a woolen blanket (kambala) or a goat-skin (kutapa), O Lotus-born One; or alternatively, when these are spread out separately by the Goddess Lakṣmī herself. || 16 ||
With all the village and forest rice, ground together with fragrant substances and properly spread out according to the ritual rules by groups of elderly villagers. || 17 ||
With various coarse powders of incense scented with perfumes, or with [Darbha] grass, covered over with flowers and leaves from the Śāḍgala tree, [one should cover] the place. || 18 ||
With independent colors such as white and red, free from lines, and with foods consisting of honey, milk, clarified butter, curd, and cooked rice placed upon the surface of the vessels. || 19 ||
With fruits, roots, as well as prepared vegetables and sugar-candy, in the mandala known as Nivṛtti and designated as Caitya, which possesses seven ridges (saptamekhala). || 20 ||

I do not see it on my four-horned [liṅga], nor on the liṅga within the interior of the thunderbolt, nor on the tips of the trident’s prongs, nor upon the fruits of the three-eyed one for three days. || 21 ||

O Lotus-born One, regarding other flowers that are unfit for worship, such as those beginning with the *karañja*, and especially those unknown varieties beginning with the *unmattaka*—(p. 107)—in these cases indeed... || 22 ||
When the leaves have been discarded and the water contained in the *kamaṇḍalu* has been used,
having established the source of merit (*śreyoni*) there, one should remain steady in the mandala and other rites.
O Brahmin, without a conch-shell fragment or likewise a piece of mother-of-pearl, there can be no leaf in the form of a skull when the hand is defiled by impurity. (24)
In this regard, that which is corrupted by sound—such as in dancing, on sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*), and so forth—is [rejected].
Just as the four-faced Lord (*Caturātman*) and others are worshipped by the gods within their own respective abodes, [so too should one worship here]. || 25 ||
They cannot be reached for worship by ordinary people, even by those who are devoted,
nor by those who have been diverted by the various lotuses of the heart-chakras.
The Mantra-soul bestows what is beneficial upon those who accept beneficial instructions and their foundations, as well as upon those engaged in ritual action who desire the fruits thereof.

O Brahmin, whatever fruit arises immediately according to one's conduct—whether from what is common or uncommon, from that which is illusory, or from the characteristic of the world—[is indeed the fruit corresponding to that conduct]. || 28 ||
Is it the attainment of immovability, or the attainment of supernatural power? Is it imperishable?
Furthermore, that which has the nature of transformation is characterized by mobility. (29)
From an añjali-offering accompanied by abundant [water], the attainment of rain occurs;
however, O Pauṣkara, the rain will be very slight for as long as one lives.

For the mantra-practitioners, the fire is eternally free from defects when it functions; on pedestals produced from gold and other such materials, O Lotus-born One, the practitioner [should perform the rites].
One shall obtain from kings the highest honor for a group of practitioners,
and through foundations such as coral and other gems, an unsurpassed state of radiant energy.
O lotus-eyed one, by constantly propitiating her, one obtains steadfastness, prosperity, and honor from the collection of garments she has conquered, as well as from the wealth she has acquired. (33)
When the practice of meditation is constant, the lineage-increasing activity always flourishes;
for men, inexhaustible wealth arises from their wife and food based on rice. (34)
From the *gandhādhāra* comes good fortune; from the *kulādhāra*, great happiness.
By worshipping [the deities] on the back of the *kuśa* grass and other materials, the King of Mantras is indeed always present. (35)
O one of stainless gaze, the mantra residing in the locus of passion bestows incomparable delight upon the mind and unsurpassed sensual enjoyment. (36)
He restrains [the mind] in a non-contradictory manner, provided it is endowed with wealth,
and in all possible supports, beginning with honey, milk, and clarified butter.
The worship of the Lord of Mantras bestows long life; likewise, it grants vast fame that is capable of establishing the certainty of the Dharma. || 38 ||
Furthermore, O Mahāmati, these fruits arising from the lotus-born [Brahmā] surely attain various purposes through their initial exertion and so forth. (39)
Depending upon the place, the time, and likewise the substance, as well as its magnitude and other such factors,
it becomes an auxiliary to liberation for great-souled ascetics who have reached the final stage.
This indeed belongs to the liberated living beings (jīvanmuktas), the devotees whose selves are purified.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Examination of Conduct," in the venerable Pauṣkara-saṃhitā of the Pāñcarātra. || 25 ||
(Total number of verses: 40) Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter;
the Blessed Lord said:

O twice-born one, whatever has been ordained for that state of existence—which, by virtue of place and time, constitutes an unbroken web of enjoyments, purifying and increasing delight—[is to be experienced]. (1)
Having first offered water for the guest (arghya), he should then devotedly and with faith present the gifts known as clothing and ornaments, ensuring they are perfectly complete.
But a meal consisting merely of rice accompanied by condiments, along with excellent food and the like, is for the sake of the satisfaction of the guests. (3)

O Pauṣkara, in the same manner, the characteristics of those called linctuses (lehya), drinks (peyā), drying agents (śoṣya), and roasted grain flour (dhānā) have been prescribed from pure rice. || 4 ||
Furthermore, according to the rule, from the path of those purifiers who have arisen from the six classes, there is a manifoldness for each one, arising through the power of devotion and faith. (5)
Whether it be prescribed for a special sacrifice or for the daily rite, provided it is possible,
one should first make that imperishable power of enjoyment one's own.
Immediately thereafter, one enjoys that which has been made manifest through the mouth of the Guru and others;
for from this eating, the state of enjoyment (*bhogatva*) is established as a figurative designation (*upacāra*). || 7 ||

In that [city], for the pleasure of the Lord of the Entire World, one should perform worship according to one's ability—either as a regular duty or on specific occasions—with a mind purified by faith. (8)
O Lotus-born One, for the attainment of enjoyment, one should offer each individual object of enjoyment;
therein, one should worship that which resides in the manifest through manifest objects of enjoyment, such as seats and the like.
Having sequentially [visualized] those numbering two times eight times eight, like a lord of men, one should—
either at the beginning of the mandala or elsewhere— recall the body consisting of mantra.
Having mentally united the manifest [deity], characterized by its application and enjoyment and possessing form,
and having placed it in the palm of one's hand, one should worship it with water for offering, garlands, sandalwood paste, and other such items.
O Lotus-born One, O All-pervading Lord, these— ointments, ornaments, and eye-cloths— should indeed be applied above the pericarp, excluding the eye-cloths.
O twice-born one, having offered and deposited [the remnants] elsewhere outside the sacrificial ground,
one should always place [the offering] within the fire together with fuel-sticks (samidh).
All varieties of food, as well as sandalwood and other such items, along with tooth-sticks and betel—provided they are free from pungent alkaline substances. (14)
In the Lakṣahoma, however, the seats and other items that are to be offered should be devoid of honey, salt, drinking water, and pungent oil. (15)
Having first performed the sacrifice according to the scriptures, including the worship of the mantras in the fire,
one should afterwards satisfy [the deities] with clarified butter, as well as with fruits and sesame seeds smeared with ghee.

In the midst of water in ponds, lakes, rivers, divine reservoirs, and the like, O twice-born one, one should offer handfuls of water together with fruits, garlands, precious objects, and fragrant scents.
The lords of mantra, free from sloth, should worship as they desire;
having collected the water that has been empowered within a vessel or a jar, [they should perform the rite]. 18.
There, having worshipped like a mandala with faith when the assembly has gathered,
one should offer garments, ornaments, eye-salve, and so forth, and place them outside.
One should place there the powder of camphor and sandalwood, infused with saffron and agallochum, as well as various kinds of flower garlands, and the object to be accomplished (sādhya). || 20 ||

O Lotus-born One, [the Lord] is also to be worshipped upon seats made of minerals, stones, clay, wood, jewels, or medicinal herbs, provided they are adorned with lotuses or marked with the [Śrī]cakra.
Likewise, when [the temples] are situated above by means of two [parts], they are indeed provided with doorways, half-śrīs, and verandas and pedestals. || 22 ||
And likewise, O best of the twice-born, on auspicious seats that possess various forms arising from distinctions such as being square and so forth, or even on those that are simple.
Having meditated upon the deity as being like a mandala, one should worship him according to the ritual;
likewise, [one should worship] him mentally within the solar disc and similarly within the lotus of the heart.
However, listen as I explain the specific distinction regarding that:
when there is a lack of external materials consisting of the various classes of elemental beings, [O Lord of the Earth]. (25)
Then, an offering was made with soft words born of his own resolve,
directed toward the All-pervading Lord, whose body is the manifestation of consciousness and bliss distinct from the ordinary.
Having meditated upon the form consisting of the embodied mantra, which grants the fulfillment of one's resolve,
[one experiences] enjoyments— provided they exist— as a multitude of consciousness and bliss.
Having recollected, one should utter the mantra in two ways with a perfectly pure mind;
one should worship with similar enjoyments that are formless and characterized by sound.
One should remember that [deity] as it attains growth through those [stages] meditated upon in sequence;
and when the distinction between the meditator and the object of meditation has vanished, one should then indeed [meditate] upon that which is desired.
Having dissolved one's own mind into the intellect, that [intellect],
joined with it, should itself— having cast aside the senses— make the Self one with that Supreme Self.
O Lotus-born One, by means of his form alone—which is composed of all powers—and by the Person distinguished by consciousness, [he was gradually transformed] from that state. 31.
By remaining in a state free of waves, one attains sovereignty within the Great Three;
indeed, by one's own will, one may once again differentiate one's own consciousness.

For the sake of accomplishing external sacrifice, for the perpetual attainment of the fruits of enjoyment, for the acquisition of the powers such as *aṇimā*, and likewise for the attainment of the nature of mantra; (33)
Recalling it as having a form as before, with the great forms produced from the seven worlds, which are abundant and endowed with most excellent characteristics. || 34 ||

Having worshipped him with enjoyments, dances, songs, instrumental music, and adorned with shouts of "Victory! and so forth, and having subsequently recollected him—once he has been recollected and worshipped—[35]
But externally, on a chosen support, the Lord of Mantra—the great radiance—is to be visualized as a reflected image; it is like a mirror, its function being internal. || 36 ||
This very thing is the object of the intellect of one who has reached the ultimate state; indeed, faith is the domain of the seeker.
Having dissolved the meditation characterized by beauty as before, it is to be absorbed into the "Good Footstep" (supada). || 37 ||
By means of the union of the signified and the signifier, one should draw out one's own mantra— the treasury of splendors—
by way of the apasavya path and place it within the heart.
Together with his own wind, he is perfectly established upon the seat of faith;
O Lotus-born One, for the sake of the ritual substances, he is present everywhere in a well-characterized place of worship.
Without that, O twice-born one, one should remember the Lord of Mantras arisen elsewhere from that [place], assuming a manifest form, complete with his limbs and retinue. 40.
Having dissolved [them] according to the sequence of propitiation as before, and by means of the simultaneous entry together with all [the others]. (41)
Having made the intellect follow along with the wind residing within one's own body, O Pauṣkara, one should constantly draw forth that which resides in the intellect through the middle path.
One should cause [the mind] to rest in consciousness within the hollow of the sky of the heart-lotus.
Thus, the threefold sacrifice is described as culminating in the Heart (hārda). (43)

First, with substances characterized by knowledge that resemble both consciousness and unconsciousness—supreme, difficult to obtain, most auspicious, small in quantity, refined, and established externally—[the image is fashioned]. (44)
O Lotus-born One, the third [stage] occurs through the sequence of that intuitive realization;
he who performs the heart-sacrifice attains liberation through union with the enjoyments of that state. || 45 ||

Furthermore, O Brahmin, that external manifestation bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those who have renounced action, as well as [the fruits of] action upon those who perform rituals.
Wherever the Lord of Mantras, having been summoned, enters face-to-face, one should first establish the placement of Dharma and the other elements in relation to that point. (47)
Since our Supreme Lord faces [us] directly, that seat is indeed of the nature of consciousness; this is established by his own vehicle. 48.
Regarding that portion of the ground for the sacred seat (pīṭha) within the mandalas and other ritual applications,
the worship is performed by the practitioner himself, starting from the northwest corner as previously prescribed.
This is the place for the feet of those beginning with Vighneśa;
one should perform this rite for sacrifices accompanied by ritual procedures along the path.
O Mahāmati, pearls that are outside the lines of the elephant [design] and are properly joined do not come forth with external defects when the worship is performed. (51)
In this manner, one should perform the rite at the station of the Rakṣas; however, the worship of the Lords of Time (Kālanāthas) and others is according to the authority of the Bhagavats.

Then, for the worship of the lords of the directions—beginning with Śrī and the others, who are beneficial and have their respective marks—one should perform the Paiṭhīya offerings in due order, starting from the door-keepers. || 53 ||
O Great-minded One, because they act as guardians of the directions, the stability of those infinite mantric forms of the Blessed One remains firm from the beginning of creation until its end.
Remaining in their own places, they pay homage, worship, and recite [the mantra];
they also properly attend upon them with services such as banners and other offerings. || 55 ||
For the sake of attaining liberation, they eternally protect [the world] together with many followers, and they bestow strength and vigor upon their devotees.
They incessantly destroy the flood of obstacles for those who employ mantras,
and they protect the mantra-fruit as it increases in its manifold forms.

This [power], which is the beginningless authority of the Lord of the Universe existing as His very power, possesses a tenfold nature for the sake of establishing the directions; thus, she is tenfold in essence.
If, at some time, the knowledge of the directions is lost while outside or within the inner chamber,
one should worship them as before from behind and perform their ritual adoration.
Thus, when the directions and the site have been determined by one skilled in yoga,
the worship of Viṣvaksena is beneficial, whether it be for a specific rite or for the daily obligatory one.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Varieties of Enjoyment," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā of the glorious Pāñcarātra.
Thus far has been sent; now begins the twenty-seventh chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
Having thus performed the divine rite for the lotus-born Brahmā according to the scriptures in ancient times,
one should thereafter perform the ancestral rite (pitrya) by means of the ritual action prescribed by rule.
Pauṣkara said:
O Blessed One, I wish to know how the śrāddha for the ancestors should be performed by those abiding by your teaching, beginning with the preceptor.
For whom and for whom is that [work] intended; and for each one, what kind of task does he perform?
For he performs exactly five for each, which must be properly accomplished. (3)
The Blessed One said:
"O Lotus-born one, [this] should indeed always be performed as a duty by those who have renounced action, as well as by my devotees who are initiated into liberation."
And likewise for those in the fourth stage of life (caturthāśramin) whose sequence is not specified,
as well as for the wise (jñānin) who desire to attain the state of the Blessed One.
O Pauṣkara, it is for the delight of the mantra-perfected ones and the practitioners,
for the constant attainment of auspicious births, and for the accomplishment of the favorability of the mantras.
Out of compassion, the preceptors and others should indeed always perform the duties for those sons who know the samaya, for the sake of the increase of the true Dharma. || 7 ||
For the sake of obtaining further good births and for the attainment of true knowledge, it is likewise for one's kinsmen and other devotees. || 8 ||
Out of compassion, one should always practice this for the immediate pacification of misdeeds;
[the practitioner] is one who has renounced actions, is matured, and takes refuge in the vow.
One who is greedy for enjoyments during initiation is not led to the state of nirvāṇa;
indeed, without intense devotion, one does not attain perfection through the practice of mantra.

"O best of the twice-born, even a practitioner who lacks a lineage does not enter the sphere of accomplishment; this is certainly [the case] for those established on the true path and devoted to ritual action. (11)
For they must always be favored by means of hospitable treatment;
having attained this here, they go to the supreme divine state. 12.
But for the initiated and for all those who perform the sacrificial session (sāmayājin), this must not be spoken;
yet it must be spoken for the sake of its fulfillment.

But at the time of the śrāddha, O Lotus-born One, even after they have been released, [the rite is performed] by them elsewhere, without the knowledge of mantras, mudrās, ritual actions, meditation, and so forth. (14)

O twice-born one, it should not be practiced nor should it be undertaken by devotees who follow the conventional rules and the like, having relied upon specific causes such as place, time, and so forth. (15)
Whatever is performed for the ancestors, by that a man becomes free from his debt; through that very act, even by the power of karma, he attains incomparable satisfaction accompanied by great joy.
Upon its arrival, they attain a state endowed with joy through faith;
though it occurs but once, it manifests in many ways throughout the duration of time until the signs of death appear.
O Pauṣkara, it is joined with the lunar day-count (*tithigaṇa*) and the annual count (*vātsarīya*),
preceded by the attainment of the field (*kṣetrāpti*), and indeed with the food and the collection of favorable signs (*sannimittagaṇa*). (18)
For the sake of pacifying the suffering of saṃsāra and for the exhaustion of misdeeds,
one should perform the funeral rites for the manifest wheel of the senses and for the wheel of the three cakras.

O Lotus-born One, whatever evil deed has been committed by the self of karma, arising from suffering and based upon the body of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), that must be experienced for infinite eons; for this is the reason why you are called the Lotus-born.
Therefore, O Lotus-born One, this body composed of the elements is indeed a conceptual construction for the immediate perception of suffering. (21)
Suffering is extinguished by suffering, just as for men who have committed evil deeds, the burden of the aggregates is heavier than the aggregate itself. (22)
O Pauṣkara, just as [the soul] emerges from its own body while overcome by sleep and, having resorted to a body of latent impressions (vāsanā), performs various activities; || 23 ||
Without the aggregate of the elements, they find no peace;
likewise, the vital breath (prāṇa), which previously supported the food and gathered the senses [the syllable *praṇava* and the senses], [does not find peace]. || 24 ||
O Lord, it has indeed not been manifested for embodied beings by way of a physical body;
O Great-minded One, how then can there be the exhaustion of their karma? (25)
For the sake of attaining that internal state, one should accomplish it through action preceded by knowledge;
by virtue of which, infinite happiness quickly increases. (26)
Now the common procedure for Vaiṣṇavas, and especially for those beginning with the Guru, known as the "General" (sādhāraṇa) or "Principal" (saṃpradhāna), is being described. || 27 ||

Whether invited, or arrived spontaneously, or even one who has been constantly accepted—a preeminent twice-born man who knows the five times (pañcakāla) and is devoted to the six duties (ṣaṭkarman). || 28 ||
O Brahmin, having first performed his ablutions and other rites, he should become pure and then lie down again,
having purified his hand with arghya water himself.
Having struck [him] with the flower-arrow empowered by the mantra-weapon, and while reciting the eye-mantra empowered by the meaning of the mantra; || 30 ||
Then, while reciting the eye-mantra, having looked [at her] with the *ka* and *dvi* syllables,
and having seated her before the Blessed Lady on a seat presided over by the *praṇava*, || 31 ||

Having placed it upon a consecrated, spread-out, and pure seat, facing either toward oneself or toward the north, and likewise having positioned it so that it gazes toward the northern direction; || 32 ||
Just as it is pervaded by the spreading rays from the Lord of Mantras and the others,
one should worship him with the mantra, meditate upon him, and speak with restrained speech.
O Lotus-born One, having meditated upon the Lord of the World like the sun in the sky of the heart-lotus, one should then [quickly, O g, gh:
with a worthy vessel, or by means of two vessels] offer [the oblation] from the vessels or by means of two vessels.
Having thus established the foundation with great effort in this rite,
one should offer a gift within the inner altar, dedicating it to the ancestors.
That which has been established for the lord of the twice-born, even though it abides in conduct (or manifestation), is the king of mantras;
that indeed should be known as the inner altar (antarvedī), for it is internal to those two.
Whatever offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) one may make to the ancestors as a gift,
that becomes divine and stainless because it is supported by consciousness.
O Lotus-born One, they remain there at that time, sharing [the merit];
O Lotus-born One, what is given is effective by the power of the donor's intention (saṅkalpa). (38)
One should place it upon the seat for either one person or many;
furthermore, the seat should be made of darbha grass, free of knots, and woven from many blades of kuśa.
The body of the pervasive Lord, whose limbs are the sacrifice, is said to have the *kuśa* grasses for its hairs;
these very hairs are all the channels (*nāḍīs*) that extend throughout his body of elemental beings.
In the body of the living being, however, all the powers of the Conscious Form are present as rays.
For this very reason, O best of Brahmins, there is the seat of kusha grass for the ancestors.
But at the time of a śrāddha rite, whatever is given with devotion after those who have been invited—whether it be food or anything else—that becomes identical with Brahman. (42)
O Lotus-born One, it was indeed for this reason that, in ancient times, a network of kusa grass was prescribed here for the ritual actions of men who do not know the Self.
For those for whom the Lord Acyuta, in the form of mantra, is omnipresent as the reality residing within their own being, there is indeed no need whatsoever for those [external means]. (44)
Then, with ashes consecrated by the recitation of the weapon-mantra, or with one's own sacrificial post,
or with smooth powdered stone, [he should strike] as in the case of iron clubs.
Outside that, on the seat, one should fashion [the area] in front, which is more than half a śama in length;
its width, however, being half a śama, should be made pure as before. || 46 ||
O twice-born one, he should also place there blades of kuśa grass with unbroken tips and facing north,
because the northern quarter is divine and the southern quarter is designated as ancestral (pitrya).
O twice-born one, under the very guise of the darbha grass path, those immortals constantly cause the ancestors to flourish with their own immortal vigor.
The host of ancestors dwells within, resorting to the southern portion; likewise, they reside in the northern portion of men in the form of a fraction of the *cit*-power. 49.
You are the stainless, eternal, and imperishable digit known as Amṛtā;
therefore, O twice-born one, whatever has been perceived by those who know up to Brahmā is indeed so.
And that which is offered to the ancestors is done with the left hand;
those who, having taken as their authority the Source of the World, worship Hari as the very essence of the mantra. (51)
And they offer libations of water to the ancestors;
because that [the body] is their support, what has been said is not without cause. (52)
And for those, O Mahāmati, for whom the culmination of what is to be done regarding the subject at hand flashes forth from within, preceded by the propitiation of mantras—
[that occurs] through the power of their own superior [practice] and by virtue of the direction facing the presence of the mantra.
And that which is performed with a non-conceptual mind becomes inexhaustible. || 54 ||
But, O Puṣkarasambhūta, those in whose minds this remains firmly resolved—that sentient beings are difficult to find upon this earth—[they are truly wise]. (55)

Having brought it to the state of truth, one should indeed place it upon a heap of *kuśa* grass; then, one should scatter sesame seeds over it, which have been consecrated with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*). || 56 ||
"O twice-born one, because these two, along with the tips of *darbha* grass, are the Kuruvinda;
they are the progenitor of the entire web of enjoyments in the three worlds. (57)
Because of the specific nature of the substance offered to the ancestors and the gods, which is purified by faith, the Lord himself, whose essence is peace, appears in the form of Agni and Soma. 58.
Manifested for the sake of establishing the selfhood of those whose nature is action through their formal embodiment,
he exists for the great increase of the ancestral, the human, and the divine activities.
That splendor exists as the essence of sesame seeds, while bliss exists as its own nature (*svātmanā*).
For this very reason, O twice-born one, it is present for both the unawakened and the awakened. (60)
Through the water with sesame seeds, one attains the state [of purity] during the rite of ancestral offerings (śrāddha);
and the supreme protection for the śrāddha belongs to those two [mantras], which are always for the uninitiated. 61.
And for those who know its true nature, there is a distinction for those who know the mantras;
one should place there vessels that have been consecrated with the Astra-mantra and upon which the ritual placement (nyāsa) has been performed. 62.
p.

114) Among those, the first [type of] circular vessels may, if available, be made of gold and other such materials; otherwise, they may be made from the leaves of the *pālāśa*, the plantain (*kadalī*), or the *tamāla* tree. || 63 ||
One should place vessels made of auspicious leaves, purified with water and weapons, for the purpose of washing the feet; one should pour water starting from the right foot.
Thereafter, one should worship [the deity] from head to foot with water for the guest-offering (arghya), flowers, and unguents;
and with garments, garlands, incense, and lamps, as well as with curd-rice and fruit-water.
O Mahāmati, with wealth consisting of betel leaves, according to one's ability,
having intended for all the ancestors and kinsmen, in the proper sequence.
But when there are many Brahmins, one should perform the rite for the ancestors in this manner, [regarding] the nature of sound, the state of the knower, the locations, and the forms. (67)
O Brahmin, where two twice-born men have been appointed for the sake of the ancestors, the presence of one's own ancestors must then be effectuated in that single [recipient]. (68)
In the second [case], if the single authoritative [text] of all others, including those born of the mother [tradition], is employed for the sake of satisfaction, it establishes them accordingly. (69)
One should first utter the word "om" for oneself, and immediately thereafter, for the ancestors;
then one should remember "this is the arghya," "this is the pādya," and at the end of that, one should recite "svadhā."
At the conclusion of every ritual service, one should thus remember the Mantra; one should utter "Namaḥ" (Salutation) or "Svadhā," or else utter "Svadhā" ending with "Namaḥ."
In this very way, O Pauṣkara, whoever should perform [this] as a duty toward those who are equal and of one's own kin, let there be salutation only to him.
O twice-born one, when there is a reversal of the truth, the *svadhā* offering is eternally ordained;
for the renunciant himself indeed bestows it upon those who seek its fruit. (73)
Therefore, a salutation must always be performed at the end of the *svadhā* [mantra];
for he who desires fruit bestows upon seekers the eternal fruit. (74)
At the conclusion of the utterance of *svadhā*, one should always offer salutation for his welfare;
thus, O twice-born, having distributed [the offerings] to the ancestors according to his own desire.
Having asked again and again through the opening of the vessel whether they were fully satisfied,
he then placed a handful of water, which was like nectar, into his hand with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
One should bestow that which is equal to the full moon; it is to be meditated upon while reciting its sixteen digits, distinguished by the sixteen vowels beginning with 'a' along with the anusvāra.
"And that which ends with the sound 'tvaṅkāra' and is preceded by the syllable 'sa' along with the star (u) is said, O Lotus-born One, to be the mantra expressive of the full moon. (78)
Before washing one's hands, that [water] should be drunk as before,
by which the imperishable potency of the food remains within the vessel of nectar.
O Brahmin, you too should perform the act of nourishing the assembly of ancestors and gods;
having washed your hands from the wrist downwards with black gram flour and other substances.
Having sipped water and properly withdrawn the remnants according to the rule,
and having purified the ground, he should place water with sesame seeds in his hand.
Then, having first arisen, one should perform the act of pleasing the Blessed One:
"O Blessed One, may you be pleased first, and likewise may the host of ancestors be pleased. (82)
The bodily array of deities is established beginning from the feet;
thus one should perform it in the well-expanded abode of ritual action and worship. 83.
Furthermore, in a situation of distress, the king of mantras, having honored [the deity] and purified the site through preliminary striking and other rites, should depart elsewhere. (84)

One should repeatedly recollect the mantra, which rests upon the power of pervasion (vyāpti-śakti) and is situated within the reservoir of water; then, preceded by worship, one should perform everything else in its presence. || 85 ||

One should perform the visualization with that which is contained in the vessel, while intent on smelling the vessel, using honeyed oblation together with blades of darbha grass and sesame seeds. (86)
Having rendered it faultless with fire using the heart-mantra and the tip of a blade of darbha grass,
one should meditate upon the Great Radiance, whose nature is consciousness, as a vast abode in the form of a tree. (88)
O high-minded one, that food which is intended for the satisfaction of the deities and the ancestors completely consumes, on all sides, the entire aggregate of material defects. (89)
And that means of accomplishment was previously ordained by the consecrated fire;
O Lotus-born One, this subject pertains to both the preceptor and the disciple. (90)
Therefore, at that time, the offering of other [substances] is indeed beneficial for him;
always, by this very rite, it is performed for that purpose for the sake of attaining auspicious success. || 91 ||
However, due to the power of various karmas, one should contemplate the diversity of a single foundational seed through the intellect, because of the ancestral rites performed previously. 92.
By that very [means], it should be satisfied by itself, for it is self-arisen through its own nature;
one should contemplate the two [offerings] within the vessel of food as being situated within, like the flow of my own stream. 93.
Having consecrated two *darbha* blades, each as long as a palm and containing within them the essence of the *arhaṇā* mantra, one should extract [the deity] together with those two.
That [essence], having the nature of rasa, has attained the state of food by becoming gross;
O Mahāmati, one should consume it in morsels of only four finger-breadths each. 95.
And [the worship] of the host of ancestors who previously resided in the abode of Agni and Soma.

[The half-verse beginning with *pitṝṇām* is missing in manuscripts *k* and *kh*. In manuscript *g*, after the word *tattvataḥ*, the syllables *dadyāt* are present, followed by the half-verse beginning with *anyat piṇḍadvayam*. Therefore, what is being transcribed here is not inconsistent. By joining the word *dadyāt* to the word *anyat* in the phrase *anyat piṇḍadvayam*, the sentence becomes complete; without the word *dadyāt*, the meaning of the sentence is not fulfilled. Furthermore, immediately after *tattvataḥ*, at the beginning of the half-verse under discussion, the form *anyāt*—a corruption of the syllable *anyat*—is observed. Thus, due to a scribal error, the word *dadyāt* has been corrupted into the syllables *anyāt*; this is the judgment of the wise. || 96 ||
One should offer two pindas arising from Agni and Soma;
indeed, those two blades of darbha grass, which are of the nature of the channels (nāḍī), are there together with the pinda.

Having brought [the mind] to dissolution by means of the second [method], one should then arrange the offerings for the ancestors with that [consciousness]; now, with another [method], one should fashion the *piṇḍas*.
Gradually, by means of the heart-mantra and the designations of their names for those previously unseen, one should thus clearly understand their true nature and their state. (99)

O Brahmin, as before, with mantras beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *svadhā*, adorned with the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*) and accompanied by the appropriate names, [he should offer oblations]. 100.
Thinking, "I offer the funeral ball (piṇḍa)," one should then perform the rites as before;
indeed, the worship is carried out with services such as collyrium, ointment, and so forth. (101)
Then, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) in due order with water mixed with sesame seeds;
having bowed the head and placed both knees upon the ground. (102)
With both hands placed upon the forehead and with a one-pointed mind, he should recite this:
"Oṃ, salutations to you, O ancestors; salutations to you, O Supreme Person. (103)
Salutations to those who dwell at the feet of Viṣṇu; Svadhā to you, O ancestors, salutations!
Salutations to Hari, the lord of the ancestors, whose self is Agni and Soma. 104.
O Viṣṇu, obeisance to you whose self is the drinker of true soma; obeisance to you whose self dwells upon the sacrificial grass (barhis).
O Acyuta, the Agniṣvāttas are those who have been born throughout the entire cycle of saṃsāra.
You are the grandfathers who drink the Soma; you are the other great-grandfathers. Salutations to you, the Blessed One, the embodiment of the ancestors, and to Acyuta.
O Lord, to Nārāyaṇa, to Haṃsa, to Viṣṇu, whose self is the three Puruṣas—
apart from You alone, I neither bow nor do I worship anyone else.
"O Lord of All, I do not offer libations to anyone else; I invoke no other," having thus praised the assembly of ancestors with supreme devotion once again. (108)
When possible, one should perform the joining of the mass-form (piṇḍamūrti) for the host of ancestors seated before it, in due order. (109)
O best of the twice-born, having indeed investigated [the matter] through both [means], or through one [of them],
and having meditated upon the ancestral host of Pitṛs situated at the beginning of the sibilants (ūṣman) in due order, [one should perform the rite].
Then, having arisen by itself through the Praṇava into its own true nature,
it stands positioned transversely in the center, neither too far nor with the gaze of others fixed upon it.
O twice-born one, facing either north or south,
one should place the heart-mantra from the heart according to that northern orientation.

One should [worship] that which begins with the *praṇava* and ends with *namaḥ*, whose form is wind and space, located at the tip of the *piṇḍa* of a twice-born man seated there, or of his vital energy (*prāṇaśakti*). 113.
Or, having meditated upon her as having emerged outside through the effort of many [channels] by virtue of her independence, one quickly attains oneness with her. || 114 ||

Having brought it into dissolution within the power of the self (or the tortoise-power), if that which is characterized as "heat" is thus made, and having likewise [dissolved] the collection of vital breaths into the body of the Brahmin who represents the ancestors; 115.
Having restrained them on their seats as before, one should feed them as previously described [in some versions, "having assumed the form of the ancestors"]. Then:
"Oṃ, may you lead this food to the state of nectar, O you who are preceded by Viṣṇu! (116)
The gods, the rivers, as well as the cows, the sun, the moon, and the lord of the forest;
Oṃ Mādhava, the Great Blessed One, who consists of the very form of the mantra. 117.
Remaining in another state as the essence of honey, may it indeed grant you satisfaction;
