and for the gratification of the ancestors, it should be made without abandoning its seat. 118.
Am I indeed in that very same spot, having beheld those objects and those funeral cakes? O Lotus-seated One, tell me now the current state of all my ancestors. || 119 ||
As long as the collection of morsels of food from those who have relinquished their lives has not been properly gathered, including the remnants, they continue to wander until that end.

O twice-born one, having bestowed blessings upon those who are healthy, the performer of the śrāddha, with his mind directed toward them, [offers] food mixed with nectar, water, and sesame seeds in their proper place through the power of the mantra. (121)
The secluded and open path for returning once more,
and the ritual of the excellent mantra called Nārāyaṇa, performed by one who has mastered the recitation of the Brahman.
Having mounted their respective senses as chariots, they departed satisfied for the abode of Acyuta.
This is declared to be the Prājāpatya [rite], endowed with its traditional transmission.
One should always perform the offering to the ancestors, which increases the previously mentioned fruits, by arranging the mantras through the ritual application of mantras.
O Lotus-born One, this [mantra] should always be employed in the plural or in the dual;
and if even this is bodiless (anaṅga), then indeed it should be used in every ritual act.
O Lotus-born One, the limbs should be joined to the heart and other parts as before;
for the eyes of those to be worshipped, the syllable *oṃ* is used in the interval of that ritual action.

In this context, however, the modification that was previously stated in the mantra—preceded by the mantra—is the *samaya* for the *putraka*s and others who have cultivated their own selves. || 127 ||
O high-minded one, this mantra of mine belongs to my guru, the supreme adept;
it is forbidden for him to bestow it, whereas for anyone other than you, its application would not be prohibited. (128)
O twice-born one, [this applies] to the initiates (samayin), the spiritual sons (putraka), and others, even to the Vaiṣṇavas;
likewise to the four [classes] ending with the Maudgala, and indeed to those belonging to the various stages of life (āśramin). 129.
O great sage, for those who have been consecrated and initiated, this [mantra], when complete with its limbs, is everywhere effective, perfected, and highly honored. || 130 ||
Listen now to that arrangement of mantras which is to be taught to them:
the twelve-syllable mantra is the armor; "Oṃ, salutation to Brahman. (131)
Thus, "viśvātmane" for the eye and "paramātmane" for the weapon;
all these, accompanied by the Praṇava, are suitable for Śūdras according to their fitness.
For those who have been duly initiated, the [mantras] are indeed devoid of the Praṇava;
and they are likewise prescribed for women according to the requirements of their virtuous conduct.
But for Śūdras who have practiced incorrectly, O Mahāmati, one should not break the mantras; rather, there should be a salutation (namaskāra). 134.

In the same way, for the twelve-syllable [mantra], as well as for the eight-syllable and the six-syllable [mantras], the [preceding syllable] should first be employed for the purpose of completing [the count]. || 135 ||

When it is said that [the mantra] has been brought down by means of the eight-syllable [mantra], and the eight-syllable [mantra] has likewise brought it down, then the preeminence of the twelve-syllable mantra is established. || 136 ||
The primacy of the six-syllable mantra may also arise through the power of one's disposition;
however, the eight-syllable mantra should always be employed at the time of binding the topknot.
And the primacy of the Praṇava; furthermore, the mantras consisting of twelve, eight, and six syllables, beginning with the Hṛdaya-mantra, are to be understood in their proper sequence. 138.

If it is postulated that the mantras preceded by the armor-mantra (varma) are the objects of expression, then their identity [with Brahman] is established, as is that of the *praṇava* in their place. (139)
The deity, having been brought under control by the *jitantā* mantra, is made present while remaining within the mind;
there, the sixfold mantra of the limbs should be applied exactly as it stands. (140)

That which was proclaimed as the third, preceded by the twelve syllables, and the third preceded by "Brahman," is indeed the designator of dharma and the others [or, according to k and gh: of all things]. 141.
The Praṇava is for all mantras, as well as in the rite of offering a seat;
it is likewise for those rites common to mantras that begin with the twelve-syllable [formula]. || 142 ||
In each ritual act, a fiery tranquility arises from the substances such as darbha grass, sesame seeds, and water once they have been offered and released.
Therefore, O Lotus-born One, the accumulation of enjoyments already consumed becomes contradictory when applied again toward another action. (144)
Since their manifestation is secondary, it proceeds from its very root as presided over by consciousness;
it exists depending upon that Supreme for the sake of the agent’s attainment of the fruit.
For those parts of the mantras that are devoid of the commonality of consciousness are unfit, like a body [without life];
however, the stable portions of the mantras again attain fitness.
"O twice-born one, sometimes through the power of mantras or through the cultivation of knowledge.
(Thus ends the procedure for the daily śrāddha.
Now follows the procedure for the occasional śrāddha.
Therefore, understand this rule for the occasional śrāddha,
which bestows a favorable rebirth upon the ancestors and grants abundant success in one's actions.
One should never perform it without the immediate attainment of a worthy recipient;
O Lotus-born One, the śrāddha is thus devoid of such [faults]. 148.
And if he remains for the sake of bestowing grace, then, as requested,
he shall observe the discipline [beginning with] the wooden staff and so forth.
All defects such as pride, envy, miserliness, anger, greed, and the like, must indeed be abandoned from afar until the day of final accomplishment. (150)
That which is offered with a mind of great effort and according to the ritual preceded by purification—such as fruits, roots, and so forth—shall be superior even to nectar. || 151 ||
(118) O Lotus-born one, when the excellence [of the rite] is present by virtue of the place and the recipient,
one should perform that with faith for either a single day or up to seven nights. || 152 ||
O Lotus-born One, having resorted to that auspicious time for a single day,
he passes it with supreme joy, unlike any other time.
Relying upon these three, you have performed this ancestral rite with a compassionate mind, established in the quality of goodness (sattva), and with pure wealth according to your ability. || 154 ||
It inevitably leads that which is sought after to Satyaloka before long;
however, depending on the place and time, it also bestows Tapoloka.

A śrāddha performed based on the [right] place and recipient bestows the world of humans; however, when performed under the influence of the [right] time and recipient, it yields the fruit of rebirth in Maharloka. (156)
A gift bestowed merely by reaching a sacred place bestows heaven;
whereas that which is performed by relying on the specific time leads one to the Bhuvarloka, O twice-born. || 157 ||
A śrāddha performed for one who has taken refuge in a gentle recipient bestows rebirth in the world of the living;
this, however, is the fruit of the triad consisting of the ordinary [recipient], the place, and so forth.
In that regard, O Lotus-born One, the body is well known as the nourishment (*puṣṭi*) of the lotus;
time consists of the eclipses and so forth to be grasped, and the recipient (*pātra*) is composed of that very essence, O Lotus-born One. (159)
Likewise, one who possesses self-restraint acts correctly for the sake of the *śrāddha* and not otherwise;
for that triad which was mentioned regarding the *śrāddha* is indeed characterized by specific distinctions. (160)
O Blessed One, is that Vaiṣṇava region—which by its very renown delivers men through their conscious birth—considered by me a worthy recipient? || 161 ||

O one of great intelligence, these three—the period known as the twelfth day, the Great Time (bṛhatkāla), and that which is refined by the transits [of the sun] and so forth—are indeed particularly distinguished. (162)
O Lotus-born One, it is surely a deliverer for those dwelling in other bodies, by means of the self-manifested, all-pervading Lord who possesses a single form and so forth. (163)
For that particular region, which was presided over by Him at the beginning of creation along with the waters in one part, brings about the accomplishment of all rites. (164)
If, at that time appropriate for the twice-born known as the twelfth day (dvādaśī),
there should be even a single muhūrta endowed with an auspicious asterism, it would indeed become sacred to Viṣṇu.
It is accompanied by the *prottāraka* for the ancestors and endowed with the left arm;
it is fully possessed of the threefold perfection and is devoted to the five times (*pañcakāla*). || 166 ||

O twice-born one, he who has attained the target in the supreme reality is a vessel for the single path; and because he is endowed with self-restraint and other virtues, he is indeed a vehicle for the Great Purpose.
Indeed, the attainment of a happy rebirth for the ancestors occurs perpetually;
and by that [offering], through its great momentum, [the desired result] is produced. || 168 ||
In an auspicious land, there is an auspicious birth accompanied by knowledge and virtuous action;
from the triad of ancestors, there arise fruits that are increasingly distinct and more auspicious in succession.

Having understood this, one should know that in the giving of gifts by the faithful, the place, time, and so forth are virtues; likewise, purity of mind and the like are proximate through clarity. (170)

Indeed, all this assistance regarding ritual actions is achieved through [the power of] weapons and the like, solely for those who are purified by devotion and whose souls delight in worldly dharma. (171)
O Lotus-born One, [this is for] those twice-born who are qualified, who delight in knowledge and ritual action,
and who are devoted to the five times (pañcakāla) in their own duties.
Do they go by means of the *vyāghāra* mantra and by circumambulation? Then what of their state of being the continuous syllables of Brahman? To them, the Blessed One Hari [says]: || 173 ||

The Lord is the embodiment of the sixfold policy; he is self-existent, both the source and the dissolution, and is never fallen from his true nature, even while associated with the multitude of qualities that are themselves free from attributes.
(119) For it is precisely from the sixfold group that the emergence of Time and the other factors occurs;
they do not perceive that which is beyond them as being anything other than Acyuta, except for him. 175.

Therefore, those devoted to the Blessed One, intent upon the knowledge of His mantra, [seek] that which is other than this—namely, the subtle element of Time (kālādi), the substrate, and the stainless. 176.
O Lotus-born One, for them, everything that exists, beginning with Time, shines clearly as abiding within all, by virtue of His power. (177)
Furthermore, because this [universe] is both external and internal, and because you previously elucidated that the entire universe constitutes the body of the Lord (*adhīśvara*), [it is so]. 178.
Indeed, by means of the instruction on the paths [or: the practice of the half-instruction], those very [principles] are explained in detail;
for they abide in the knower of the body, who is devoted to right action, possessed of knowledge, and established as a Vaiṣṇava. || 179 ||
The ancestors desire a pure male descendant in their own lineage who will deliver them; thus, depending on place, time, and other factors, one should strive with equanimity. || 180 ||
O Lotus-born One, having first prepared with faith food that is dehusked, radiant, pure, mixed with milk, and accompanied by excellent side-dishes; || 181 ||
Or indeed with the twelve-syllable heart-mantra, [one should sprinkle] into new vessels,
or when they have emerged from cooking, having been further sprinkled with oil.
Or rather, O twice-born one, it should be accomplished thus: through the self of a son or a disciple;
through the path of a sister, a wife, a friend, or a kinsman. || 183 ||

The sacrificial porridge (caru) for the sake of the ancestral rite (śrāddha) should be prepared by one who wears white garments, who is devoted with inner faith, who is of his own caste, and who is skillful and pure in body—free from physical disease and devoid of hunger and thirst. (184)
[By those suffering from] cough, asthma, and so forth, and by those who are naturally devoid of sight or hearing, or are dwarfs;
likewise, by one who is free from defects and intent upon devotion with inner feeling. (185)

The *caru* for the purpose of the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*) should indeed be prepared by one of the same caste; the preparation of the *caru* for the castes is ordained according to the natural order (*anuloma*). || 186 ||
O Lotus-born One, in the case of divine or ancestral rites, one born of inverse unions (pratiloma) causes defect;
however, in the absence of such [a person], one purchased by trade is not defective, provided the artisan is pure. || 187 ||
O Lotus-born One, is that [state] also free from the aforementioned defects? Or is it for those whose minds are solely devoted to greed and who are shaken by decay? (188)
Especially for those who are menstruating, for eunuchs, and for those such as priests (or the like);
and likewise indeed for dogs, pigs, cats, and monkeys. 189.
But for those sky-dwellers preceded by the village-pig, the jackal, and the vulture,
therefore with every effort, in a place where the sky is covered and shielded from the wind— || 190 ||
In a place that is free of thorns, with a paved floor, well-smeared, and whitewashed,
one should perform the worship of the mantra and the practice of the deity of the gods and ancestors.
And when it is possible, O twice-born one, this is always ordained for all of them: the sequential arrangement of all the food, condiments, and vessels. (192)

At the time of the inner movement of the breath, however, sesame seeds along with kuśa grass, honey, and clarified butter should be cast [into the fire] with the twelve-syllable mantra, which has been further perfected through the rite of collection (saṃgraha). 193.
Then, O Lotus-born One, one should carefully cover them with a cloth of eight syllables, so that no vapor arising from elsewhere escapes to the outside.
When the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) has been applied, smeared, and washed away from the heap of earth [or the pair of earthen mounds],
and when it is covered with armor or a cloth and made internal from the eastward direction, [one should proceed]. || 195 ||
Having placed a guardian in that row, one should perform the bathing and other rites;
O Pauṣkara, this applies to the fire, the Brahmin, the dwelling, and the place of worship. 196.
Having first made an allocation of the vessels according to their shares and of the assembly of virtuous companions, one should always perform the ritual until its completion. 197.
[He should place] a counter-cloth over the water;
beneath that cloth, however, he should wrap his body with a lower garment. || 198 ||
That which is unreal, stainless, clear, and produced from bark and the like; that which is adorned with blue, whatever exists such as garments and so forth—[199].
Having cast out all objects everywhere from the world outside,
one should then, through the intellect, focus upon the Supreme who has entered the form of the mantra.
And indeed, for the sake of showing favor to the ancestors once again, I shall perform the sacrifice;
having seated the twice-born ones on their seats in order, as before, and having summoned them. (201)
Prior to them, two most excellent brahmins should first be seated in the east and the southeast;
they are the twelve-spoked Dharā and Dhāman, established upon a seat presided over by the triad.

Then, having applied the six limbs as previously described—which are common to all [deities]—to the twice-born [mantras] ending in *vāsva*, one should, in due order, be joined with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) and the crest-mantra (*śikhā*), and likewise endowed with the six [limbs]. || 203 ||

Having directed [the disciple], for the sake of attaining identity with the body, he should [perform the rite] by means of his own designator (svavācaka) together with the true abode, which consists of the single form and so forth, while [the two] stand facing east. 204.
The array of deities should be installed, conjoined with the syllables *phaṭ* and *vauṣaṭ*, which constitute the two forms of the mantra known as Nṛsiṃha and Varāha. 205.
Indeed, for the sake of protection, one should always install the deity named Agniṣoma on the northern side without looking at it, and others should be installed beyond that.
There, first, having placed the [mantras] of the heart and so forth in the bottom row,
one should likewise place the groups of those born from the excellent syllables with the [mantra] *dṛśā*.
To its south and above is the lineage of the Mother (jananīyaka); another [lineage] should be joined with the Armor (kavaca), which is entirely composed of the Blessed One. 208.
And with the name of the father, [and] then to the south of him;
the third is the performer of attainment, and the fourth is indeed by means of the heart.

O twice-born one, the fifth [libation] should be joined with the name of the grandfather using the *mūrti-mantra*, and the one for the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*) should indeed be joined with his name, following the single path.
In the progenitor (janaka), by means of the state of being the living soul (jīvabhāva), those three which have passed away should be placed in sequence;
and by means of those mantras, the dyad likewise exists in sequence. || 211 ||
One should place the three ancestors beginning with the great-grandfather;
this is stated to be done either by means of the general six-limbed [mantra] or by one's own [specific mantra]. || 212 ||

The application of the mantra in the offering of *śrāddha*, in the worship of the twice-born, and according to the authority of the four forms (*caturmūrti*), is now described as existing in two ways. (213)
Both worldly enjoyment and liberation are obtained from the first mantra;
and absolute isolation alone is obtained from the second, O one of stainless vision. (214)
The King of Unmanifest Mantras should perform the placement (nyāsa) for the group of mantras together with his friends;
for the three [deities], starting from Pradyumna and ending with Vāsudeva, in due order.
(121) That indeed is not qualified; furthermore, listen again to me:
for the designator of those who are preceded by friends and mixed with others is unobstructed. (216)
From the group of mantras of Pradyumna, by means of two [mantras] starting with Kāma, one obtains a pair;
then, by means of the Praṇava, one obtains the Great-Grandfather, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman.
O Great-minded One, that satisfaction which is attained by a face filled with great joy is now described as being of three kinds, according to the section on the nine forms.
Out of affection for his friends, Viṣṇu should place [the seed-syllables] of the twice-born;
then, O Pauṣkara, he should place those of the group of Mothers with the Vairāja mantra.

Know that through the three [offerings] beginning with Nārāyaṇa, the triad of ancestors beginning with the father is pierced in due order; this is indeed called "piercing" (viddha), and it is the knowledge of Śrāddha that bestows its fruit. (220)
Indeed, for the ancestors of the sacrificer, even without attaining a physical body, [the rite] begins from the Vairāja mantra up to the end of the Sāṅkarṣaṇa, O Lotus-born One. (221)

Know that the four-and-a-half verses beginning with "samantrapañcakam" and ending with "* * * * * * * * * *"—that which is the *śrāddha* for those whose lineage culminates in the great-grandfather, O Pauṣkara. (222)
Indeed, through the power of the mantra, it bestows the attainment of self even upon the ancestors of the performer of the śrāddha, for they are the supports [of that attainment].
The assignment of the five foremost of the twice-born to the śrāddha rite,
beginning with the circle of friends— this indeed is the supreme Vaiśvadeva offering.

When endowed with all the necessary components, it grants supreme Nirvāṇa to the performer and the assembly of ancestors; for what then need be said of its full and complete bestowal? What more can be said? || 225 ||
O Brahmin, when it is possible, one should live out one's lifespan with a mind purified by faith and with compassion for one's equals, O Pauṣkara. (226)
In this optional performance of a Śrāddha offering, however, one should not join [others] except in a single row;
first, a single group of Brahmins should be seated facing north.
Then, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) for all [the deities] with the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*), [specifically] for those born from the lotus [Brahmā].
With the *praṇava* and their own names, one should know [the placement] starting from the heart and so forth. || 228 ||
One should place the weapons, ornaments, and missiles within their respective spheres according to the preceding mantras;
or likewise, facing east, one should join them with power by means of the *cakra*-mantra. || 229 ||
One should join a single Brahmin facing north with the principal mantra;
and there, one should join two facing north, connecting them with the heart-mantra.
O Lotus-born One, one should remember without exception one's friends and allies, as well as both the maternal and paternal lineages, even when they have passed into another body. 231.

In the maṇḍala, one should worship either the Cakra or Nṛhari situated in a water-vessel; (one should install a single Brāhmaṇa facing north as the presiding priest with the principal mantra). || 232 ||
For the satisfaction of the assembly of ancestors and likewise for that of the maternal family, and for the gratification of all other people, he should act according to his own capacity. (233)

Having picked up a morsel of food for the cow, one should offer it soaked in ghee and honey, mixed with *darbha* grass and water containing sesame seeds; it should not be alkaline nor pungent with salt. (234)
One should act in this manner on account of one's own lineage; otherwise, one may do so out of compassion or affection for another, such as a priest or anyone else. (235)
For at the time of its production, its lineage was indeed established beforehand:
from the feet up to the knees, from the knees up to the navel, and from the navel up to the crown of the head. (236)
Having placed the four mantras beginning with Aniruddha from the feet up to the head, and from the heart up to the head; (237)
O Brahmin, for the sake of attaining a happy rebirth and for the eternal satisfaction of the ancestors,
one should indeed offer [the remnants] from the feet up to the crown of the head of Vāsudeva and the others.
Furthermore, O Mahāmati, the four unceasing ends should be joined;
or else, O Brahmā, one should contemplate within the heart the peaceful state consisting of pure consciousness by means of the syllable Om. || 239 ||
One should sequentially place the four [deities], beginning with Vāsudeva and ending with Aghora, pervading the wind, fire, water, and earth elements respectively.

Then, O twice-born one, having established Nṛhari for the sake of protection within the four [elements] beginning with earth— which are unceased in relation [to one another]— he established the supreme [form] of the ninefold manifestation.

Then, one should sequentially place the eight [syllables] starting from the head, throat, heart, navel, secret place, and the two knees, down to the feet and ending at the earth-supporter (the soles). 242.
In the sky of the heart, however, is the Lord Vāsudeva, also known as Adhokṣaja;
and [therein reside] Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others, corresponding respectively to the elements ending with earth and to the functions beginning with intellect. (243)
Or rather, O Brahmin, it should be stated in the sequence beginning with the earth;
the group of seven, ending with Saṅkarṣaṇa, is indeed called the "support of the earth" (bhūdhārā) and the "neck" (kandharā).
Then, O twice-born one, one should meditate upon Vāsudeva within the substratum of consciousness—that is, the substratum of the intellect—within the fluids, blood, flesh, fat, marrow, and bones. 245.
One should gradually install the seven deities beginning with Saṅkarṣaṇa and ending with Varāha at the end of the white quarter (śukladhātu) for the sake of accomplishing the gates. 246.
O Lotus-born One, beginning from the mantra of Varāha and ending with Saṅkarṣaṇa, one should place the vessel as before for the purpose of dispelling evil spirits. (247)
The Lord is all-pervasive like the sky, both externally and internally;
and Sāṃkarṣaṇa, like the individual soul (jīva), is the seed within the lotus of the heart. (248)
By means of the yoga of creation and dissolution, there is a heptad within the seven elements.
Pauṣkara said: "In general, when one's own mantra is indeed present..."
In the case of the two forms of the verb, when they occur in a compound, [the suffixes] are like those ending in *jvalat* (or as appropriate). || 249 ||
How is it appropriate for mantras that have been liberated through nyāsa, arcana, and so forth, to be employed in the ritual action of mantras—whether as four or as nine? || 250 ||
The Blessed One said: "Indeed, the mantra together with its six ancillaries is always prescribed as common to all;
however, for the practitioner, the mantra may become like poison and create obstacles. (251)
O Great-minded One, whatever belongs to the fourfold self-nature and so forth is authorized for all; here, in the case of one's own mantra and the like, it is the will of the Guru.
In that regard as well, for the sake of distinction, he is said to be present at the *śrāddha* through both [means].
Previously, when the collection of mantras had been arranged according to the wish of the Brahmins, || 253 ||
Having withdrawn one's own mantra and, with a mind established in its own abode through the prescribed rite,
having thus performed the foundation and so forth, one should be pervaded by the meditation on Brahman.

(123) That array of mantras which was distributed among the bodies of the Brahmins should now be joined together within one's own self, preceded by the ritual of the hands and following the previous procedure. || 255 ||
In this regard, O Brahmin, listen to the specific rule prescribed therein:
first, the Lord [should be worshipped] by pervading both the left and the right. (256)
One should place the second [syllable] upon the five fingers of the right hand;
indeed, the third is on the left hand, following the sequence beginning with the thumb. (257)
On the two bases (or on the two families, starting from the south), one should place Aniruddha;
or else, according to one's will, one may place only one [deity] ending with Vāsudeva. 258.
When the Navātman mantra is on the two thumbs of the hands, Acyuta and the eight mantras ending with Varāha are placed in sequence from the forefingers onwards, as before. (259)
Having placed the syllable "Vāṃ" at the end of the *tarjanī* (the index finger) mantra, or ending with Vāsudeva,
and having inserted "Svāhā" in the middle, one should perform it in the essence of worship, and likewise in the fire during the rite of adoration.
Even that which has been offered into the fire, as before, one should lead to the state of a purifier;
in this way, the transformation of mantras occurs solely by the power of one's desire. || 261 ||
Easy to propitiate for those established in the ninefold path, yet causing obstruction at the time of ancestral rites (śrāddha);
having thus performed the assignment and now worshipped with the head [of the mantra]. || 262 ||
The teaching is a cluster within a flower-vessel consisting of the Blessed One;
in its midst is the moving water, which is the mind endowed with the five sense-faculties. (263)
One should perform that [rite], situated on the seat of mantras, either in the center, at the boundary, or in the heart;
for the purpose of my grace, until the conclusion of the ritual rinsing of the mouth. || 264 ||
Even for an omniscient being, when in the presence of brahmins and a blazing fire, one must remain strictly self-restrained.
Thus, by those best of the twice-born, with a very pure intellect and a compassionate heart, everything of his was to be accepted with faith.
For this reason, the measure arising from the lotus, which possesses a dual nature,
has been repeatedly applied to all entities, especially in the rite of faith (śrāddha).

At the proper time, that which completes it should be employed; for that completion is the purifier and the producer of satisfaction for all rites—how much more so, then, in the rite for the ancestors? (268)
Having taken with his mind the mantra-related command along with his head,
and having brought it into his heart, O twice-born one, the śrāddha arises from the material substances by virtue of that.
Indeed, it would be fruitful for the ancestors, for it is truly rooted in knowledge;
otherwise, by what cause could it grant them that state and bestow praise upon the ancestors? (270)
Just as the root of trees does not grow without the earth,
so too knowledge bears fruit quickly through the path preceded by joy.
Having indeed caused the entire collection of sense-faculties, which had been engaged in external activity, to dissolve of its own accord within oneself in the space of the heart-lotus; 272.
Having now become fully filled by the power of its own nature,
one should perform salutation to the Lord, the Sovereign of All, from his true essence.

One should indeed remember the unceasing vibration of consciousness belonging to you, whose nature is peaceful awareness and whose essence consists of the bliss of movement, as having spontaneously transformed [into the world]. (274)
Blazing with the radiance of a thousand moons, suns, and fires, it is steadfast,
its interior filled with consciousness in the form of a wheel of rays, and facing in all directions.
The state of the Blessed One is perfectly tranquil, abiding within the expanse of consciousness;
for it is indeed far more distinct than that power which is the channel of knowledge and its manifold variety.
One should visualize one's own assembly of ancestors, shimmering for the sake of pacifying karma, as a mass of innate bliss situated within the corner of a mirage. (277)
Just as the power of fire, characterized by burning, which resides within a great mass of wood, emerges externally upon reaching a spark, O Pauṣkara; so too does it emerge from the external. 278.
In that very same way, he indeed emerges not from the determination of external time, but from the determination of conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*).
Having taken recourse to Agni and Soma, and by the will of the Lord, the ancestors likewise [emerge] by the will of the Lord. (279)
The King of Mantras, Prakāśa, is external—[O twice-born one, he is like the space of Māyā].
Whatever arises from that in due order for those of their own [kind], whether it be pleasure or even greater suffering, || 280 ||

Then, with the very internal organ (antahkarana) ending in the root-mantra, together with the sense organs and born from the lotus of equanimity, and enveloped by the space of Māyā, one should cause the heart-mantra to revolve. || 281 ||

For the sake of pacifying that suffering, O Lotus-eyed One, through some ray of light, by means of knowledge, he [the practitioner] [should focus] again upon that limit of space, which is like the sky. || 282 ||

O twice-born one, at that time, by the power of its inherent majesty, that very mass of consciousness (citpiṇḍa), born of that lineage, comes to reside within the substratum of Agni and Soma in due order. (283)
But the seed of the internal organ, freed from the power of great delusion, abiding within the end of knowledge and the end of space, is exceedingly subtle and eternally manifest. (284)
It is presided over by those beginning with Nārāyaṇa and ending with Kṣa, or alternatively, by those beginning with Vāsudeva and ending with Prāṇa-Brahman, in due order. || 285 ||

By means of the five limbs of mantra, which are the nature of consciousness, devoid of the eyes, and pervaded by the intellect according to their actual state as characterized by origination and persistence; || 286 ||
Because of which the practitioner’s performance becomes perfectly clear;
therefore, by virtue of this arrangement, [the rite] for the libation to the ancestors is performed within this heart. || 287 ||
Remembering the emergence of the mantras through the power of one's own practice— whether formless or embodied according to the arrangement of the presiding deities— 288.

O Great-minded One, one should meditate with the Praṇava, which possesses an indivisible characteristic, upon that which was previously described as having a dual nature— the support for the accumulation of the seeds of consciousness— having attained the state of a seed within the ground in the center of the pericarp of consciousness. (290)
One should meditate upon that which has emerged from it—unpolluted by the qualities such as sattva and the rest, which are inseparable from it—and colored by the triad. 291.
O Pauṣkara, that which is known as the Great-Grandfather (Prapitāmaha), being consciousness itself, has attained the state designated as deep sleep (suṣupti) and has become slightly turbid. || 292 ||
One should remember that [the consciousness], having come to rest within the interior of the sun of consciousness in the space of the pericarp, then emerges from that very region of pure awareness.
One's own grandfather is colored by one's own internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) alone;
and by means of the letter *e*, by one's own name, and by a dream, he is made manifest even for one who has not been seen before. || 294 ||

One should recollect the abiding state of that [Self] which has two aspects— the dependent and the [pure] consciousness— as well as the portion of consciousness, in the region of Vaikuṇṭha and within the space of the navel. (295)
Then, O Lotus-born One, one should recollect the Father as Consciousness, colored by the intellect, the mind, and the ego, yet undisturbed by the waking state.

In the space within the Brahma-nāḍī, on the ground of the path of the Brahmarandhra, in the dual-natured sheath of the individual soul (jīva), which is the causal state characterized by the Fourth (turya). || 297 ||

The two deities known as Viśva should be understood as having Vāsudeva as their presiding divinity, appearing either with form like the solar disc or as being of the nature of that [divinity] itself. 298.
For that is the root from which all the ancestors of those who perform ritual acts are gathered;
indeed, it may exist presiding over that which is known as the great-grandfather.
O Lotus-born One, this consciousness of Brahmā is indeed like the midday sun in form, or it is embodied as the bearer of the form of knowledge. 300.
One should meditate upon [the form] presided over by Pradyumna as previously described in its own place;
thereafter, one should recollect Aniruddha in the form of the presiding deity of the father.

But when [the deity] enters through the aperture of the crown—whether formless or indeed embodied—one should, having propitiated [the deity] with the mantra, make the place richly endowed and presided over. || 302 ||

O Brahmin, one should meditate upon the other [mantra] with the heart-mantra, that supreme one with the head-mantra, and indeed always meditate upon the fourth as the presiding deity of the crest (śikhā). || 303 ||
One should contemplate the subtle body as accompanied by the Heart-mantra, following the Śakti-mantra;
likewise, one should contemplate the [mantra] called Astra together with the Head, and the Eye together with the Tuft (Śikhā). 304.

The fourfold group of the nine-formed Lord exists solely as the nature of consciousness within the heart, distinct from the powers of the qualities which consist of the nature of pure existence alone. || 305 ||

With "Oṃ tat sat," one should clearly manifest [the syllable] within the interior of the dense pericarp, extending from the throat downwards to the region of the navel, by means of the [mantra] beginning with Garuḍa (Gādi) in the belly of the sky.
One should meditate on [the deity] as a boar, a man, and a lion situated at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
For when there is a state of division, it arises within that which is one through the cognition of difference. || 307 ||
One water is naturally cool, while the other is hot and sweet; these two waters are distinct.
Thus, those who would act contrary to this for the sake of attaining enjoyments—[what could be more perverse]? (308)
O Brahmin, that which bestows liberation should be known as the constant giver of liberation for those who do not seek worldly fruits;
these mantras, consisting of armor, weapons, and the gaze, extend from the heart to the crown of the head. 309.

The heart and the other [limbs] are to be deposited as the presiding deities and as the powers (śaktis), because the three—beginning with knowledge (jñāna)—are indeed the objects of enjoyment, while the [remaining] three, beginning with power (bala), are the enjoyers. || 310 ||
And those six, beginning with the *hṛdaya*, have indeed been determined previously;
thus, one should [visualize] the group of ancestors (*pitṛgaṇa*) in sequence as the root cause within the body.

Having placed [the offerings], together with other desired ancestors who are of the nature of consciousness, one should then perform the satiation (santarpaṇa) to the side, preceded by the Viśvedevas. || 312 ||
Having first gratified those two with the syllable Om, which possesses the characteristic of gnosis,
he [should worship them] with that which has the supreme bliss as its essence and possesses a thousand rays.
One should meditate upon the Praṇava arising at the root of the vital energy (prāṇakalā) within the heart—
an ambrosia resembling a bubble of milk, cool as snow.
And that great sequence of the channels of knowledge (*jñānanāḍīkrama*), which is the essence of the stars (or:
which causes the stars to taste), and depending upon which the Viśvedevas and others abide. || 315 ||

One should meditate upon that [light] as having the form of the Pitṛs, possessing the form of the Blessed One, and having the shape of fire, spreading upward as far as the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). || 316 ||

O twice-born one, one should meditate upon that mantra dedicated to the ancestors and the gods, which is situated above the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) and has attained the state of the full moon. (317)
One should meditate upon her vital power (prāṇa-śakti) as having a blazing form above his head,
situated in the center of the solar orb like the fire at the end of an eon.
One should meditate on that nectar-filled maṇḍala, absorbed by that radiance.
Then, having reversed the flow through the aperture of Janaka’s hand, one should again meditate with a pure mind upon it as it gradually reaches the root. || 319 ||
(Here there appears to be a gap in the manuscript: One should meditate with a pure mind, step by step, upon that which is rooted in the source.
Thus, having transcended weariness and thirst for objects as previously described, one should utter the syllable Oṃ. || 320 ||

O best of the twice-born, one should not proceed to the fourth stage with a mind intent on meditation for the dissolution of the ancestors and so forth; rather, one should repeatedly perform this for the attainment of enjoyment.
The Śrāddha is the nectar for the ancestors, bestowing the destruction of all suffering;
indeed, having placed the host of ancestors within the offering-ball (piṇḍa) consisting of light and bliss, [one should perform it]. || 322 ||
From the inner realm of Māyā up to the end of Ākāśa, it is characterized by the exhaustion of all latent impressions (saṃskāra);
and it shines forth from its very root, with reference to the body above.
Just as the solar disc in the sky [appears] through the sequence of its rising, one should again dissolve that by means of the meditation on the moon. (324)
He does not return again to the field of karma with his fruit still remaining;
likewise, he who casts the funeral ball (piṇḍa) upon that which rests in the Brahma-field [is liberated]. 325.
O twice-born one, know that within the infinite, vast, and full nature of consciousness, there exists the unmanifest [Self];
it is the deliverer of one's own lineage and is devoted to knowledge and action. (326)
However, rare is that person for whom this realization of reality truly exists—one whose self is purified by devotion to the Blessed One and who is solely intent upon his mantra. (327)
Then, for the sake of accomplishment, one should proceed with the external śrāddha rite in the presence of the Lord of Mantras, the Fire, and the Brahmins, in their proper order.
O Blessed One, O Lotus-eyed One, this mantra known as Abhyarthāsana-karma, which has been brought down, indeed concerns my paternal lineage. 329.
Becoming yourself one whose soul is devoted to the ancestral rites (śrāddha), lift yourself up from the ocean of worldly existence;
enjoy [the fruits] yourself through devotion to Śakti, indeed by means of knowledge and the like.
For by means of the instrument, the web of enjoyments characterized by the three marks arises through power;
having thus petitioned and having resolved it with the mind. (331)
Then, having indeed uttered this entire group of ancestors in sequence:
"Oṃ Oṃ Oṃ Oṃ, O Supreme Lord, for the satisfaction of the ancestors. (332)
"Indeed, for the sake of deliverance, I perform sacrifice; Oṃ, Oṃ, salutations, salutations!
Having mentally uttered this once, fourfold, or ninefold," (333)
Recalling that which was placed within the Supreme Self while residing in the outer garment,
he then, with all his resources, offered the arghya and pādya offerings first.
O twice-born one, one should worship the Lord of Mantras with enjoyments ending with betel;
in this regard, the following is the general procedure for the act of taking up the enjoyments. (335)
And this mantra should always be recited during offerings made with faith:
"Oṃ vauṣaṭ! This [offering] has the luster of nectar and consists of strength and vigor. (336)
"Enjoy this stainless enjoyment whose nature is brilliance; salutations, salutations!
Having sprinkled the available food offering with the great [gaze]," (337)
Thus, that which is not large in form, having been placed in the hand, yet enters the vessel; likewise, that which does not exist [externally] but is held now by the mind—this is *dhāraṇā*. (338)
Having thus worshipped Mantreśvara for the satisfaction of the ancestors,
one should then offer that "body-sweetmeat" (dehamodaka) in the event of the loss of a blade of *darbha* grass.
Oṃ [k, kh, g, gh: Oṃ, you are ours]. Homage from us! O you who pervade the world, be pleased with our assembly of ancestors.
May this [offering] become inexhaustible for them, which has been made by you and taken into your own self. 340.
Thus, that very duty (kartavyatā) indeed leads one from the state of the ancestors to one's own self;
it impels the interior of the hair-pores of the Lord of Mantras like the rising sun.
One should sequentially visualize the host of ancestors in the region outside the heart-lotus;
then, one should indeed satisfy those established within the inner measure with offerings such as *arghya* and collections of enjoyments.
One should meditate upon [the deity] as white as the full moon, shimmering with a mass of rays, entering into the mantra-self by means of one's own power. || 343 ||
Within that host of ancestors consisting of radiant energy, one should indeed again meditate upon the assembly of the Pitṛs,
possessing the splendor of ten thousand midday suns, flashing with light, while remembering the Lord.

Then, once that activity has ceased, one should gradually imagine that [the breath] has entered the space of the lotus of the heart through the pores of the skin by means of those [channels]. || 345 ||
Having taken [the substance] from the mantra located near the seat with the thought that it is the moon,
he should then go to the vicinity of the fire and meditate there upon the Lord who has arisen therein.
Then, having gratified [the deity] with devotion according to the rule until the completion of the full oblation, the king of mantras is employed;
there, the sacrificial porridge (caru) is prepared as before, as well as the rice for the piṇḍas.

Then, having worshipped [the deity] with honey, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and *darbha* grass placed within a silver vessel, one should perform the striking and other rites while reciting the consecrated mantras.
Having established its faultlessness, one should afterwards cover it with a cloth or similar material;
then, preceded by meditative inquiry, one should worship the seat together with its common attributes.
Then, having sprinkled water mixed with sesame seeds over the kuśa grasses in sequence from bottom to top, according to their respective positions, while reciting the Praṇava; || 350 ||
There, one should first place the vessels made of gold and so forth in their proper order;
following the sequence beginning with the ancestors, they should be placed at the beginning, at the end, and in front of that. || 351 ||
One should deposit that [offering] with its name preceded by the mantra and followed by a salutation;
reciting "sesame, water, and tips of kuśa grass" and then "this is your arghya," one should offer it in sequence. (352)

O twice-born one, having thus prepared the ritual water-offering (arghya) extending as far as the great-grandfather, one may desire other offerings in this manner during the giving of the śrāddha, and likewise in other rites as well.

As before, having offered the arghya water into the vessels according to their names and lineages— as previously described— or separately for each vessel according to the number of seated twice-born, || 354 ||
Then, having brought the food prepared for each individual along with the sacrificial fee (sādhya),
he should place it, together with kuśa grass, into the hands of those who descend as far as the great-grandfather (prapitāmaha).
Having likewise offered the *arghya* water with a remainder in the hands of the others,
one should perform it within well-defined boundaries using the *arghya* waters.
When the water for the *arghya* offering has been given, he should offer the shape of the entire vessel;
then, with the ghee held in the hand of the Brahmin and with that *arghya* water, [he performs the rite].
Then, O twice-born one, having cast his own eyes into another vessel,
he should take that water in due order and proceed to the vicinity of the fire.
Then, having placed that vessel filled with sesame seeds and water before him,
one should mentally meditate upon the Supreme Lord Viṣṭaraśravas within it. (359)
Having divided the array of the ancestors there, one should meditate upon it with the syllable Oṃ,
situated in the stainless sky like a cluster of stars.
Likewise, O Kamalasaṃbhūta, while that remains steady within the other vessel,
one should contemplate the state of blissful activity in the space descended from the stainless one.
Then, having first performed worship of them with water-offerings, flowers, and perfumes, [he saw] the Lord, the Inner-Sovereign of all, vibrating with his own splendor.
There, one should place two blades of kuśa grass smeared with honey into water,
having covered them with another vessel made of clay.
The two vessels, Heaven and Earth, filled with seed-syllables, are to be understood;
having placed them and worshipped them according to their respective successive roots. || 364 ||

Within those [energies], one should utter the subtle manifestation of the Father (pitṛ) and meditate upon the Praṇava, which is the nature of universal consciousness and has attained oneness with the sound of the Tāra. || 365 ||
One should block [the breath] that has arrived by way of its own channel-path while seated on a kusha-grass mat;
there, one should contemplate it through its power according to the sequence already taught.

In some cases, however, when there is a single occurrence of the word "two" (dvi), one should recognize the ancestral state (paitrī sthitiḥ) as it was manifested in embodied form, arranged in a row and characterized by the previously mentioned definition. || 367 ||
Having filled the cupped hands from the *arghya* vessel with sesame-water, the twice-born should offer a continuous stream of it in succession while reciting that [mantra]. (368)
"O Name, you who are established in the Praṇava, may this water for the feet be yours.
Then, having prepared another vessel, he should offer it into the fire as before. || 369 ||
With his hand adorned with silver and provided with a sacred ring (pavitra),
he [should worship] the all-pervading nature of consciousness, which sustains the forms of the seven constituent elements (dhātus).
Having determined with the mind that the infinite is Brahman through meditative cultivation,
this is the support for living beings, this is the supreme nourishment.
It is the source of manifestation and the place of dissolution, characterized by supreme bliss;
therefore, one should first worship it, situated within the vessel, with offerings of water (arghya), flowers, and unguents.
Having worshipped with the *praṇava* and having likewise brought it down with that same [syllable],
one should mentally revolve that very [form] in the shape of a sphere while reciting it.
Since everything consists of all powers, they assume every form everywhere; yet, for the sake of the manifestation of their respective actions, they take on fixed forms.

With respect to all the ancestors, including those who share the same lineage and those who are not to be favored, one should worship them as desired with abundant enjoyments preceded by the offering of arghya and the lords of mantras.
Likewise, one should worship those [deities] who have assumed the form of food in due order;
for the vessel beginning with Alaka is filled with filtered water.
Having prepared food there mixed with honey, darbha grass, and sesame seeds,
one should indeed meditate upon the Lord of Mantras— formless and of immeasurable splendor— residing within the orb of the moon.
One should meditate on the pure, cool spray as it sprouts outside within oneself, being poured out from the pitcher along with that water.
Then, O twice-born one, having taken a sesame seed soaked in honey with both hands, and filling [the vessel] again and again with supreme faith for each one, (379)
With sesame seeds and water, accompanied by meditation, one should offer consecrated water in sequence to the ancestors for their satisfaction. (380)
Then, one should perform the rite for the foremost of the twice-born facing eastward, as before, yet with special care and endowed with faith during one's own śrāddha. (381)
The Brahmin should gradually perform the rite for all his limbs, from the feet up to the head,
with flowers mixed with water for the *arghya* offering and with ointments such as sandalwood.
Then,
having fanned them with the fans of their wings to stir up the wind,
he subsequently offered various garments scented with incense. (383)
Then, having adorned them according to one's ability with ornaments such as bracelets and the like,
one should immediately give them sacred threads along with upper garments.
Then white garlands for the head and neck-garlands, followed by divine fragrance and powdered incense mixed with camphor for the head. || 385 ||
Then, having indeed offered them the supreme collyrium for the eyes,
he should afterwards show them a mirror and scatter flowers before them.
Then, O Great-minded One, one should fumigate them in sequence with incense purified by fragrant smoke; they should be worshipped with a brightly shining lamp. (387)
Sandals for them, various umbrellas, wooden shoes, footstools, and those very seats. (388)
Having fashioned various beds, palanquins, horses, and so forth, as well as silver and other materials for all of them, they should be prepared. (389)
Alternatively, having offered that root [offering] to all according to one's ability, there is a communal assembly for the complete satisfaction of the minds of those who share in it. || 390 ||
Again, having placed water for the *arghya* offering in their hands while reciting the mantra,
one should perform their worship in sequence, just like the sacrifice to the Lord.
Then, with the honey-mixture (madhuparka), with various kinds of food offered with faith, and with pure snacks consisting of fruits and roots, as well as with refreshing drinks (pānaka). || 392 ||
It should be eaten first with fragrant *rasālā* and boiled milk,
or in small leaf-cups (*puṭa*).
For the pleasure of all the Brahmins, having made it equal and offered it,
he should give the arghya water into their hands as before, for them to consume.
Recalling the mantra mentally and receiving it from the twice-born with water, he remains before [the deity] with a single-minded focus, muttering and meditating upon the Astra-mantra.
Indeed, for their satisfaction, this Dharma-śāstra—which yields the great fruit of easy awakening and is superior to asceticism—is the most excellent of all, even more so than the Mokṣa-śāstra. (396)
Proclaiming his virtues, that which is suitable for him should be offered;
then, when the twice-born has been satisfied... || 397 ||
When the connection has been established as before, he should always offer water; indeed, O twice-born one, he should satisfy [the ancestors] once again. (398)
Together with the water and the food remaining from the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa), as well as with the honey-mixture (madhuparka), sesame, milk, clarified butter, and side-dishes. || 399 ||
Having filled his hollowed palms with water, he should then cast the piṇḍa outside,
in front of the twice-born, along with a stream of water.
One should cast it toward the northern direction and lead it to the abode of Antaka;
then, having discarded the *pavitraka*, one should discard the *pratiśāṭaka*.
Then, having changed that garment, or else while recollecting [the deity] above in his heart,
he should afterwards perform the sipping of water (ācamana) with his own mantra, and then with the Heart-mantra of the stainless Self.
"O sirs, may everything be complete!"—thus he should prompt those seated on their seats;
then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) to the twice-born who are restrained in mind, he should proceed. || 403 ||
Then, as before, the annual rite should be performed in due order;
it should be performed by all [the practitioners], except for those two facing east, while remaining standing. 404.

Then, having extracted all the stimulating substances from the ends of those two footprints, one should place them in a vessel along with fruits and roots, and infused with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds. (405)
(130) He should now make a request to the twice-born regarding the remainder of what has been eaten:
"O sirs, please state its application"; for they should speak without agitation. 406.
Indeed, our own vessel was taken out according to his desire for wealth;
then there was the ball of food belonging to the grandfather, which had been honored.
Having brought that [element] from his own body by means of the *recaka* breath alone, one should separate it like a spark and then indeed contemplate it.

Having meditated with the heart-mantra upon [the goddess] who resides within a vessel of nectar and is like the moon, and having performed the recitation twelve times for the sake of the twice-born woman who has prostrated, according to her desire; 409.
Having explained the remainder to his wife out of consideration for the Brahmin,
and having applied and concluded [the ritual], he offered [the oblation] into the fires of the twice-born among the cows and the waters.
Having first performed the fire-ritual for the food vessels, one should then place there, in front of the Blessed Lady, water together with sesame seeds. (411)
O Lotus-born One, one should gradually give gold to the ancestors for their gratification, and one must protect it from jackals at present. (412)

In this ancestral rite (*pitṛkarman*) performed for the mother, which consists of the proper placement of the vessels and the ritual actions, the *paiṇḍī* offering—accomplished with food and drink—is to be completed after the meal. (413)
One should not recite the "Akṣayyā" prayer even when the water-rite (udakakriyā) is performed for the sake of pleasure;
nor should there be the offering of the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), nor the ritual overturning of the water vessel (udakaparivartana). || 414 ||
Then, having opened the vessel belonging to the ancestors, one should extract from the lotus of one's own heart the mantra for the deity,
who possesses the brilliance of the fire of the sun at the end of an aeon, and offer it with food.

That vessel is in the expanse of space; at a distance of twelve finger-breadths from that, in the expanse of space, is the pitṛ-pātra (the vessel of the ancestors). Indeed, the dvādaśānta is unified with the vessel in due order. (416)
One should perceive them as those spoken of in the Saṃvīta, and with the mantra, one should meditate upon the Lords of Mantra and the ancestors with a meditative mind—
just as [one perceives] Pātaṅgin together with his strength, so too at night the mountain of blazing fire.
Thus, having attained oneness through that mantra,
they beheld Hari, the Lord of Mantras, who resembles a hundred moons.
Having dissolved the meditative powers that possess constituent parts into that [state], which is indeed pervasive,
the King of Mantras then causes it to become absorbed like the assembly of ancestors.

Having made it his own through the path of the fathers (*pitṛmārga*), and having released his eyes there with that water, the Lotus-born One (*abjaja*) was once again accompanied by his wife in his gaze.
Having cast into the water that which was previously offered along with the liquid,
and having approached the abode of worship where the deity has entered the fire of patience, || 421 ||
O twice-born one, having worshipped the Lord of Mantras as before, he should gratify him;
then, having performed its withdrawal, he should partake of his meal.
Then, O Pauṣkara, while meditating on the Lord of Mantras within the lotus-petal of the heart together with his kinsmen,
one should remain silent and consume morsels resembling nectar.
Once the ground has been cleared of remnants and thoroughly washed, whatever food with its side-dishes remains—[which is purified from the ocean of suffering by the hand]—should be offered. || 424 ||
Having brought that [food] and placed it in another vessel provided with darbha grass and sesame seeds,
one should set down a second lamp outside that [vessel], toward the south.
Then, reciting the mantra in a pure place and having spread a layer of darbha grass,
he should pass the night in appropriate religious discourses.
(131) O twice-born one, the *śrāddha* for the ancestors has been ordained by this rule;
it pacifies the suffering of saṃsāra and bestows liberation without delay. (427)
Having offered that which is of a single type, as well as that which consists of both [aspects], through faith,
it is employed by means of the fire of knowledge and action.
Abiding in worldly dharmas, she forms a latent impression (*vāsanā*) when [the goal] is fulfilled;
therefore, indeed, through that action, clarity of mind arises. (429)
Those who know the mantras should practice with effort for the sake of attaining expansion;
then, one should perform the mental purification (*manassaṃskāra*) for those who are accomplished, including the five [limbs]. || 430 ||

Now listen as I describe the ritual procedure known as the *aurdhvadehika*, which immediately follows [the previous rites] and is intended for the attainment of the results previously mentioned. (431)
And know that this too is twofold, O Lotus-born one;
it belongs to all those who have been initiated and liberated by means of the nectar and other [substances]. (432)

Indeed, when the mantra has been propitiated as before with faith, it bestows that very benefit constantly upon the states of activity such as the manifest (vyakta) and so forth, as if it were being granted.
O one of stainless gaze, until satiety and reaching the limit of the Lord’s pleasure,
the second [rite] is performed upon the tip of the stainless [vessel], once the Lord of Mantras has been made present.
Food consisting solely of boiled rice, free from the act of cooking, is always beneficial for all beings of little strength who are easily satisfied. (435)
Then there exists that which is situated within the blazing, unmanifest seed;
it is subtle, characterized by a gentle movement, and is the supreme vital breath (*prāṇa-śakti*) itself.
Indeed, having resorted to that external time characterized by days, which is a tenth part of that [total], the agent, possessing the corresponding ritual procedure, should act in due order.
Pervaded by portions of its vital breaths, it brings forth the manifest characterized by the senses from the unmanifest, indeed under the guise of the form of food.
The sense-faculties beginning with the ear and ending with the organ of generation— by relying upon these, one may swiftly attain [the goal] once ten days have passed.
O best of Brahmins, on the eleventh day, Śakti-hood itself indeed [is attained] here,
O Brahmin, by means of the thirty-third day, which is most manifest.

O twice-born one, by means of the *vināḍī* consisting of the preceding *satya*, and again by its portion of breath characterized by two *ṣaṭkalas*, the remaining group of principles (*tattva*) is [to be known]. 441.
But the darkness of the principle of intellect (buddhitattva) must be dispelled in due order;
first, O twice-born one, [one should meditate on] the intellect for one year, and then for a second year.
Then, from the subtle element of sound (śabda-tanmātra), the pentad of the five elements indeed arises;
thereafter, the group beginning with space (ākāśa) is manifested from those subtle elements.
Indeed, by a group of five months, one attains mastery over the earth and the five elements;
thereafter, having become clothless, one likewise consumes what has been discarded after eating at a sacred site.
When the tooth-stick has been sipped with water from the heart-mantra, and those [five products of the cow] have likewise been used according to rule,
while the mantra is recited in the proper place and one is similarly clothed in fresh garments.
Having sipped water (ācamana) with the *hṛdaya* mantra and then having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the root mantra upon the palm of the hand,
one should likewise perform the ritual of totalization (*sakalīkaraṇa*) of the body from the feet up to the head by means of that very same mantra.

Briefly, by means of the limbless [mudrā], the Brahmins, consecrated with the heart-mantra according to their respective lineages, [should act] out of a desire to bestow grace upon the deceased. (447)
O twice-born one, he should then offer three handfuls of water mixed with sesame seeds under that person's name, along with darbha grass and silver. || 448 ||
For the sake of purification, for the sake of auspicious peace, one should recite one hundred and eight times;
either one's own mantra, the weapon-mantra, or the general twelve-syllable mantra. (449)
Either the aggregate of the nine-fold self-seeds as one, or by the power of meditative cultivation, one should proceed according to the rule in the previously specified ritual action. (450)
O twice-born one, a deceased person’s Śrāddha performed by two [persons] at a sacred ford, at a river crossing, in a house, or in an auspicious sanctuary, brings exceedingly great merit. (451)

Having encountered the mass of obstacles, which consists of darkness and the like, such as [the lack of] radiance and so forth, it causes the obstruction of resolve and makes one's actions deficient. (452)
Therefore, by the power of the Brahma-mantra, one must protect one's own strength from its very root—driving away the form of darkness with radiant light. (453)
Having first propitiated all the items, such as sesame seeds and *darbha* grass, with the mantra, one should discard these;
then, standing up and facing the east, another rite should be performed.
Now, one should perform the appropriation of the site as common to all;
with the contemplation of Brahman, one should meditate upon the root mantra as omnipresent. (455)
O Lotus-born One, one should contemplate the form of the heart-mantra as radiant like the sun, situated within the eight directions between the earth and the sky.
Then, one should meditate on the entire sky as far as its limits with the head;
Śiva, who has become a pillar, is in the center, like the path of saṃsāra.
The pure and great nature of the Brahman-artery should be meditated upon;
one should place the reality that exists externally within the path characterized by conceptual construction.
In the perception of one another through the utterly pacified *karman* and *brahman*, one should there remember the eye as being like a window, serving as the gateway. (459)
One should then meditate upon the Aparājita [mantra], which has a thousand whirling sparks of fire, ending with the word *rājahaṃsa*; this brings about the complete destruction of obstacles. (460)
Thus have I declared this *āyatana*, the mantra-form and the mantra, for all rites and for the mantras beginning with the *ādhāra* and the *āsana*. (461)

For the sake of the accomplishment of those of purified self who have reached the ultimate goal of the *haṃsa*, one should not perform the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) there according to the prescribed rule, nor should one establish a fixed limit therein. (462)
Having sat upon a seat made of darbha grass, which has been permeated by the pervasiveness of the *praṇava*,
one should perform the three-fold breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) using the root mantra.
Then, by means of the two types of dhāraṇā, one should perform the purification of the body;
thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) as before upon the hands and the body.
Having obtained the *arghya* and *pādya*, one should sprinkle [the area] with that water;
having struck [it] with a blade of *darbha* grass while reciting the *sarvamantra*.
Beholding it there, one should utter [the mantra] and, with that brilliance, burn away the impurity;
then one should meditate upon it as having attained the splendor of the sun's orb by means of the root mantra.
One should sprinkle the hearth, together with its fire and fuel, with water consecrated by the *astra* mantra;
then one should kindle it with the *netra* mantra and subsequently awaken it with the *varma* mantra. (467)
Having washed the vessel with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra, one should strike it immediately thereafter;
then, having moistened it with the root of *darbha* grass, one should cover it with the armor-mantra.
Having washed the rice grains repeatedly with the Astra-mantra,
one should place them together with honey, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and cow’s milk while reciting the Mūla-mantra.
The knower of mantras should cook [the offering] with a ladle over which the weapon-mantra has been projected, using the heart-mantra;
thereafter, he should remove the cooked food with the root-mantra.
Then, having washed and smeared [the body] with the Netra-mantra,
one should apply vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on the directions with the Śikhā-mantra, and protect oneself from the front with the Kavaca-mantra.
One should establish it upon a well-smeared portion of ground provided with sesame seeds and unbroken rice grains, situated on a bed of kuśa grass presided over by the Praṇava.
Having thus prepared the *caru* while covering it with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*),
one should perform the rites of spreading the sacred grass (*brahmāstaraṇa*) at the time of the actual accomplishment.
One should employ the heart-mantra, reciting it with the mind according to the path of mantra;
thereafter, one should perform the rites for the deceased, or by means of that [wind], the worldly [rites]. (474)
There, in the divine [fire], having first performed the ritual worship as before,
one should duly offer enjoyments characterized as previously described, intended for the deceased.

Indeed, by merely eating from the vessel that has been turned on the wheel, one should fill it with all kinds of food, having first anointed it and so forth, while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra. || 476 ||
Having touched it with the fire of the gaze and having prepared it with its various condiments, one should offer it to the Lord,
as prescribed, out of a desire for His grace.

Having clearly visualized the form of the syllable *kha* or, alternatively, having drawn the deceased from the sky by means of the syllable *oṃ* and by his own name, one should place him within the space of the heart. 478.

And having contemplated it as having become like a tiny spark of fire with only a slight remnant remaining, [one sees] that it is joined with a small portion of vital energy (prāṇakalā) and that its karmas have been brought under control. || 479 ||
And having gradually led the mere existence of the particularity out through the path of fire,
the seer of the mantra, remaining established in his own place, abides within the object.

Then, O Brahman, one should meditate with the syllable Om upon that which is endowed with the multitude of powers of the principles (tattva-śakti), which rests upon the potency of food, and which is called Prāṇa, the imperishable. 481.
Then, by means of that path of heat, while recollecting the heart-mantra,
one should visualize the *preta* as having emerged [from the body], its vital breaths being obstructed within the sense of hearing.
Know, however, that the nature of the subtle state is colored by knowledge, and that it has attained, in reality, oneness with the departed spirit. (483)
O Brahmin, he should gradually contemplate whatever slight [vision] has entered his heart;
thus, through the sense of hearing, the singleness of the manifest vital breath (prāṇa) is attained by those [senses] that have reached it. || 484 ||
O Lotus-born One, now that the vital breath has arisen from its food and subsided, one should remember everything that is beneficial along with its root, just as one remembers the wind. (485)

But that which is formless, like a blow, impelled by the power of breath (*prāṇa-śakti*) and uttered by the twice-born, one should meditate upon with the heart as that sense organ which has attained the state of the Heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*). || 486 ||
Once you have been seated upon the throne, as before pervaded by [the deity],
one should subsequently worship you like a Lord of Mantras (mantreśa) with constant and auspicious offerings such as arghya and the rest.
O Lotus-born One, one should offer flowers, unguents, and incense up to the mother;
thereafter, one should indeed offer water with sesame seeds by means of the name, the lineage, and the heart-mantra.
Then, having satiated that sense-organ which resides within the locus of fire and has the heart as its form, according to the rule and by means of the previously mentioned sequence, (p. 134).
Then, having summoned [the deity], one should place the previously mentioned vessel, which consists of the Blessed One,
upon the seat remembered as before, in front of the Blessed One.
Having placed the mantra upon the heart with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should then worship it with water for honoring (*arghya*) and other offerings;
then, having sat down comfortably, one should proceed to the place of worship.

One should meditate upon Him with the heart in the sense-faculties according to one's own capacity, as He has attained a formal manifestation; yet He remains present within the power of food as the essence of taste, both through differentiation and non-differentiation.
One should meditate [as before], and the preta should be remembered as before by means of the *praṇava*;
having brought it forth and attained it through its state as the presiding deity of food. || 493 ||
And having performed the end of the mantra for the lord of the twice-born along with the arghya water,
he then attains oneness with that power of the vital breath through the heart-mantra.
O Lotus-born One, the offering (naivedya) [is dissolved] within that preta;
then, it [gradually] reaches the space of the heart along with the vital breath (prāṇa). || 495 ||
One should cause [the soul] to experience its departure during the activity of the sense of hearing for the sake of manifestation;
having thus established the self of the deceased within the previously mentioned body of the Brahmin. (496)
Then he should place water in the hand as before for the purpose of sipping,
and [he should do so] for that person who has begun eating and whose meal is subject to doubt.
Meditating with his intellect, he should stand before him; then, by the power of the vigor of the food, that [object] reaches its true state through the heart and the faculty of hearing.
O best of the twice-born, as soon as that lord of the twice-born had finished his meal, he emitted from his own body the sound of the *praṇava*, having exhaled it through the right channel. (499)

Having drawn in the preta into the space of the lotus of the brahman’s heart by means of that [mantra], one should, as if with the deceased, unite it with existence through one's own heart at the ear. (500)
O tiger among brahmins, when the leftovers have been removed, the propitiation of the Lord is performed as before; then the performer, having finished his meal, should proceed. (501)
For the sake of pacifying obstacles and other hindrances, one who possesses the mantra should recite the Astra-mantra one hundred and eight times;
then, being self-possessed, he should perform the worship of the Lord of Mantras at the place of practice along with its ancillaries.
Having withdrawn all the offerings, beginning with the arghya and flowers, ending with the vowels,
and having cast them into the reservoir, one should perform the *svāya* [rite].
Then, at the arrival of night, he should perform the concentration on the mantra and the recitation;
likewise, the fourfold group consisting of the eye, taste, and that which is known as the nose. 504.
O Mahāmati, the fourfold group of days should be manifested;
then the fivefold group beginning with speech, in sequence, by means of the head, O best of beings.
O best of the twice-born, for the sake of attaining welfare for the deceased, one who has attained existence should prepare a sacrificial oblation (caru) when the eleventh day has arrived. 506.

Provided with various foods, side dishes, and condiments, and well-prepared with faith, one should prepare the sacrificial porridge (*caru*). [The reason for the textual reading "one should prepare the caru" here must be sought.
Then, having washed his feet and sipped water according to ritual custom, he should be struck and gazed upon. (507)

Having placed [the disciple], who is purified by clear water and has bowed with the *praṇava*, and who is meditated upon as the reality of the Blessed One, into the seat-circle which has been worshipped and permeated by the state of pervasion. || 508 ||
Then, having anointed [the image] with devotion using ointments such as sandalwood and the like,
and having wrapped it in fine cloth, one should adorn it according to one's ability. (509)
With excellent ornaments such as golden bracelets set with gems, with garlands, sacred threads and the like, and with purifying head-cloths; || 510 ||
Having placed food and condiments in his hands, one should worship the Lord of Mantras with supreme faith, desiring to show grace to the deceased Brahmins.
Then, the root mantra is on both palms (or, according to manuscripts g and gh, on the surfaces of the hands); the heart and other limbs are on the fingers;
the eye is on the tips of all the nails; and thereafter, [the mantra] is on the body from the feet up to the head.
Having placed the feet at the end [of the mantra] in their respective locations, such as the heart and so forth,
one should meditate on the nature of the mantra, endowed with the pride of that very [mantra].
Having worshipped with the *praṇava* accompanied by the designation "Father," and with offerings such as water for the hands (*arghya*) and flowers, in a special manner as before; || 515 ||

Whatever is offered as a means of pleasing him after everything has been explained— whether it be ending with cattle, land, or gold— and whatever else brings him satisfaction, that indeed is the instrument for his delight.
The deceased becomes free from debt and attains the supreme state.
Then, he should be satisfied with food as prescribed, just as before. || 517 ||
One should meditate on the heart as being active, as before, by means of the root mantra;
however, that which resides within the group of sense faculties is indeed characterized by the presence of the consort (samāyā). || 518 ||
One should everywhere recollect the *praṇava* along with the root mantra as the deceased;
thus, having attained the state of *asmitā*, it is properly joined with the powers of the senses. (519)
Having placed this [mantra] ending with the earth-syllable (*dhara*), one should win over [the disciple] through acts preceded by wisdom;
there, for the sake of awakening, one should perform [the rite] and write [the mantra] with the *śikhā* mantra.
O twice-born one, the armor is prescribed for the manifestation of the mind itself, and then, in due order, for the manifestation of the five subtle elements (tanmātras). || 521 ||
Indeed, for one who constantly recites the weapon-mantra of the Bhūtas,
[the result is attained] in exactly twelve months, or even in ten or eleven.
Having indeed offered the funeral ball (piṇḍa) for the deceased when the thirteenth month has arrived,
O Lord, the joining [of the deceased] to the path of the ancestors must be performed within that which consists of the Blessed One.
Listen clearly as I speak of how that which is born from the lotus is accomplished:
first, the bath is fully described, and thereafter one should perform it accordingly. (524)

For the sake of the *śrāddha*, one should cause the best of the twice-born to sit down after they have sipped water for purification (*ācamana*), their feet have been washed, and they have been provided with abundant and well-prepared food served with faith. || 525 ||
[He should initiate] sons, those who know the rules (samayajña), practitioners (sādhaka), or teachers (deśika);
