whether they be householders, celibate students (brahmacārī), forest-dwellers (vanastha), or renunciants (yati). 526.
O best of the twice-born, having placed four facing north or two facing east in the presence of the Lord of Mantras, one should thus install them.

Of those two, the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa is indeed prescribed for one by means of the weapon-mantra (astra), and for the second, the rite of placement (nyāsa) is performed by means of the armor-mantra (varman). || 528 ||
O twice-born one, for the rite of placement (nyāsa) of the first [deity] facing northward, the eye is [placed]; above that, it is ordained by his head.
Then, for the second [deity], one should perform the placement on the hands and so forth belonging to the fourth [deity] by means of the heart-mantra and indeed the root-mantra.
p.
136) Then, having performed the worship of the Blessed One for the six [or nine], one should place the crest-mantra (śikhāmantra) in the void of the sky.
Then, having performed the worship of the Blessed One up to the abode of fire (agnibhavana), || 531 ||
Having performed [the rite] exactly as prescribed, one should indeed worship with special care;
then, O best of the twice-born, that which has been assigned to the weapon (astra) should be worshipped with the weapon-mantra.
One should perform the worship of the armor and the armored form, excluding the pair consisting of the name and the lineage;
thereafter, one should perform the worship for others by means of their own names and lineages.
There, one should worship the deceased twice-born man with his own respective mantra,
having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) on his eyes with that very same mantra.
Seated upon that, however, is situated the one characterized as the Pitṛ;
O twice-born one, his own head-mantra is prescribed for his worship.

O Brahmin, having worshipped the heart-mantra according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the worship of the deceased grandfather by means of his name, his lineage, and indeed with the heart-mantra.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the root mantra according to the prescribed rite, one should honor the great-grandfather by that very name together with his lineage (*gotra*).

O Brahmin, for those who have been honored at this time, the internal application of the rite intended for the ancestors, such as the *preta*s and others, should indeed be performed within their hearts. (Note: *cāntasya* is an alternative reading. || 538 ||
O Lotus-born one, understand from me how the destruction of the food offering occurs gradually for those whose nature is the essence of food, as previously described. (539)
Then, having mentally visualized the host of deities, one should meditate upon them with an even mind through the intellect;
without abandoning one's own locus, one should, through devotion, attain likeness to the full moon.
In the *sāmā* [the *svātaṃpaitre*], one should contemplate the mere food of the ancestors as the eye-mantra;
likewise, one should mentally recollect the arrived head-mantra (*śiromantra*). || 541 ||

Together with the power of vision, having taken up the two powers known as the Netra and the Upper [Mūrdhan] within the vessel consecrated by the Heart-mantra, he then assumes that which consists of the Heart.
One should indeed contemplate the Śakti, who is contained within the food offering (naivedya), by means of the root mantras;
through the very guise of the power of the mantra, she is present in the sacrificial food as the essence of the Praṇava.
And one should effect the unification of the mantra and the Brahman for that deceased person, O Pauṣkara;
then, having placed the vessel of the food offering (naivedya) upon this [altar], it should indeed be presented. || 544 ||
After the twice-born have been seated with various kinds of food, both solid and soft, he should give water into their hands, ending with a mere drop of cow’s milk. || 545 ||
O twice-born one, for the sake of the satisfaction of the ancestors, one should repeatedly ask those engaged in eating what each requires and give it to them.
Then, one should perform their placement there with those mantras ending in "svāhā. O Pauṣkara, according to this rule, one should effect the unification of the Śaktis.
Having now extracted the deceased from the two-fold body, as before, he who is endowed with the qualities of reality and power, blazing like the sun.
Having drawn that [deity] back again into the heart-lotus by means of the splendor of the mantra,
one should indeed perform what is more appropriate, having drawn it from there into the heart.
Then, having purified the paternal portion for the sake of increasing it upon the heart-lotus,
one should extract that which is fully satisfied from there and place it within the heart with the *hṛdaya* mantra.
Having placed [the two] within the range of the heart-lotus of the great-grandfather,
and having made it radiant with the mantra, Brahman, and kalās, one should bring it there into the heart.
Having dissolved [the food] with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), and then through the meditation on tranquility within the self—
having thus performed this mental connection (*anusandhāna*)— from that point forward, for him indeed... (552)

O tiger among the twice-born, the status of being a father [is attained] specifically at the Śrāddha performed after a year; it does not belong to other ancestors who long for the Śrāddha, nor to those beings whose state as a *preta* has been pacified, nor to one who remains in a waking state. || 554 ||
The state of being a father is attained and established in each successive stage, higher and higher than the last.
Thus it has been taught, O Lotus-born One, by means of the mantra together with its ancillaries.
Now, learn from me that ritual procedure known as *aurdhvadaihika* (the rite for the deceased) for those who are to come, which is performed with four mantras belonging to the fourfold nature. 556.
Having established the ten faculties, from the ear up to the organ of generation, by means of the mantra known as Vāsudeva over the course of ten days; || 557 ||
In this [rite], O Pauṣkara, one should perform [the manifestation] for the possessor of individuality (vyaktimat) with Sāṅkarṣaṇa;
in the principle of intellect (buddhitattva), one should manifest it with the third [mantra] together with Manas.
O Pauṣkara, when a year has passed in this manner, the letter *kṣmā* is to be manifested from the unobstructed subtle element of space (*ākāśatanmātra*), just as before.
O best among those who know mantras, one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite in sequence, beginning with Aniruddha and ending with Vāsudeva, using these four mantras.
O best of the twice-born, one who desires self-knowledge should thus perform this arrangement with the nine forms for the sake of attaining auspiciousness for his kinsmen.
Therefore, now listen with one-pointed attention to this in brief:
for the satisfaction of the sense organs, such as hearing and the rest, the mountain is prescribed. (562)
For those such as Bhūgā and others, Nṛsiṃha is indeed within this power upon the seat of the sky-goer;
for the sake of manifesting the reality of Brahman, it is beneficial for the intellects of those possessed of a mind. || 563 ||

O Mahāmati, having thus performed the recitation (japa) consisting of the retention of the mantras together with the subtle elements (tanmātra) and the primary elements (bhūta), and conjoined with the principles (tattva) and the digits (kalā); 564.
Then, after one year has passed, he should bring about the contemplation of the Pitṛs with the four [deities] beginning with Aniruddha, preceded by Varāha and the others.
By means of the previously described procedure, conjoined with knowledge and meditation,
and through divine, immutable action, [he performs] manifold accomplishments.
That second arrangement has been indicated by me;
having made it clearer as I speak, listen attentively. || 567 ||
Having performed all the previously mentioned procedures for the preparation of the sacrificial oblation (caru),
one should kindle the fire, consecrated with the purificatory rites as before.
Having meditated upon the Lord of Mantras within that [mandala], one should offer libations with sacrificial fuel sticks (samidh) in sequence;
then, having spread kuśa grass with their tips pointing south in front of that, as before, [verse 569].
Having meditated upon the seat of one's own abode, and above that the lotus seat,
one should place the food-ball (annagolaka) as before, joined with the primordial [syllables] and so forth.
Having performed everything previously mentioned in that regard, immediately thereafter,
he should offer handfuls of water with sesame seeds before it, using the name of the deceased.
Having given it, then withdrawn it, and cast it into the midst of the water, O twice-born one, he should then effect its assimilation into himself by means of the mantra. (572)

Having gathered everything into water and cast it away without fire, one should perform this for ten days; then, as before, on the eleventh day, having completed the rites... (as previously described).
One who knows the ritual procedure should perform the *śrāddha* preceded by the offering of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*),
once the year has been completed, for the purpose of effecting the attainment of the status of a progenitor (*pitṛtva*). (574)
The previously mentioned meditation, together with the mantra—and whatever else may be additional—becomes like a blazing sun, having attained a state of unified power. (575)

One should recollect that mantra which constitutes its presiding deity, characterized by the internal self (adhyātma), and having emerged as the physical form (piṇḍa) assumed as the external element (adhibhūta), situated within the mouth. 576.
One should observe its activity in the sky above that place;
thus, O Lotus-born One, it is led away as something distinct from food. (577)
Then, having taken a handful of food from that mass consisting of curd and flour with its mantra, as well as whatever fragments were there, [he should now offer them] by way of pervasion.
One should now properly remember the transformed [state] as all-pervasive;
then, O Lotus-born One, one should meditate upon the primordial state, both with respect to the internal self and the divine.
One should lead that food into the funeral cake (piṇḍa) for the ancestors, and then lead it upward from there.
Thus, when the deceased has attained oneness with the funeral pyre (cit), [he is united] together with the representative of the pyre.
Indeed, everything should be performed entirely as with the *piṇḍa* for the *preta*s;
then, after that, his worldly affairs, and thereafter those pertaining to the ancestors. || 581 ||
Therefore, that too—just as before—one should lead it to the state of supremacy (*paratā*) within this aforementioned ritual pertaining to Prajāpati, O best of the twice-born. (582)

From the day one is initiated as an *ādeṣṭṛ* (preceptor) up until the day one attains the status of a *pitṛ* (father), whatever remains that was previously mentioned, one should perform that first. || 583 ||
However, at the place of the meal, while the twice-born are seated upon their seats,
the word "Akṣayya" (inexhaustible) should indeed be uttered by them with water mixed with sesame seeds.
To this extent, the purport of this [treatise], known as the *Aurdhvadaihika*, has been correctly elucidated; it is characterized by the quality of sattva. (585)

When passion has arisen from the beginning, it flashes forth indeed in the heart, just as one remembers; and likewise, the two components of cognition, O Pauṣkara, are like two pieces of wood [rubbed together]. (586)

The food prescribed for them as an offering, along with the funeral cake (piṇḍa) accompanied by water, and likewise the rites for the deceased, should be performed at their respective times as is appropriate for the family. || 587 ||

O Lotus-born One, the prohibition of the four types of pride has been ordained during periods of birth-impurity and the like; indeed, for the householder, this prohibition lasts until the end of his life.

O best of the twice-born, for the lords of the twice-born, as well as for others who sacrifice solely to the fourfold Self, there is no [other deity] to be worshipped, because He is the source of all those worthy of worship. (589)

Therefore, one may indeed exercise authority during a period of impurity caused by death or birth, as well as in receiving or giving gifts, for that duration, provided there is no intermixture of castes.
Indeed,
for those who do not sacrifice to the gods and for those who sacrifice to the Blessed One, this innate practice is undoubtedly mutual.
But he who desires the path and wishes to follow it thus toward the Imperishable (Acyuta), should perform the ten-day rite once the period of impurity has passed. || 592 ||
Thus it was said by the Lotus-born One: "The supreme enclosure for the *śrāddha*, beginning with the formal offering (*saṃpradāna*), remains eternally established just as it is. (593)
Now, furthermore, out of context, learn the procedure for the optional *śrāddha* (*kāmya-śrāddha*),
which bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation upon devotees of purified soul. (594)
If a matter pending in a court of law has been abandoned by his kinsmen through the wisdom of the Teacher,
yet one person desires it himself, that individual may recover the entire debt after twelve days.
I shall now relate that matter briefly and exactly as it occurred: in the past, having accumulated the necessary provisions and being surrounded by excellent companions, [he set out]. (596)
Having placed before them either one or many twice-born men who produce clarity of mind, on a bright day prior to the fortnight of the ancestors (pitṛpakṣa), O twice-born ones. || 597 ||
Either during the rainy season or otherwise in the autumn, or in the month of Mādhava,
one should go to the abode of Viṣṇu, which is crowded with people offering flowers and incense.
Or the bank of a great river, or a mountain peak with its ridges and water, free from danger and not crowded by outcasts such as Śvapākas and Śabaras. (599)
Having approached that place, one should perform austerities and sacrifice according to the prescribed rules,
for the Gaṇas, at the abode of the Nāgas, for the Bhūtas, and for the Lord of the Forest (Vanaspate).

On the following day, one should indeed perform the worship of one's own mantra with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), according to one's ability, through the mouth of the resident of the sacred field (kṣetravāsin). || 601 ||
Or, having manifested it, one should then pray to that which is worthy of worship.
I bow to the Lord, the Supreme Overseer, who is endowed with the seed of his own consciousness;
he whose designation is both manifest and unmanifest, and who is the aggregate of the body and the senses.

I establish [the self], having joined it with its constituent principles according to the ritual rule; and out of compassion, I make the form of differentiation non-different from the mass of my own pure parts.
O Supreme Lord, for the sake of experiencing the fruits of my own well-performed deeds, the characteristic of the vital wind remains within me after it has departed from my body. (605)
Accompanied by suffering and longing, and shrouded by dense clouds, it arises filled with agitation, inexhaustible as if for a long time. 606.
And likewise, the power (*vaśā*) of a living being is inactive; whether by means of another body acquired at some time or after a long interval, it remains subject to the lack of autonomy. || 607 ||
That terrible and unbearable state, which in reality persists, goes to its destruction through your grace, O Lord; therefore, by means of food and water, [let it be quickly removed]. (608)
The aggregate known as the senses, which is to be produced, is free from disease;
it is without continuity, beyond doubt, devoid of desire, and situated within the web of karma. (609)
Having taken you as his object, who today acts for himself? You alone act as the protection for yourself—the supreme refuge for those fallen hell-beings who are devoid of hope. 610.
You alone are eternally capable of delivering those for whom the funeral cakes have been lost;
since you are that eternal one, beginning from that very eternity, you are the perpetual refuge.
O Blessed One, may the web of obstacles along with their latent impressions not approach me until the day of completion; may there indeed be the accomplishment of my task.
Having thus petitioned the Unborn One and filled the water-vessel with water,
one should complete it with the remainder of that [water] and maintain self-restraint until the conclusion.
Having set aside all worldly conventions characterized by dharma, pleasure, and wealth, as previously described, one should thereafter become fully attentive.
Then, having performed the worship of the deity according to one's preference, I shall perform the libation (tarpaṇa) either in front of him or to his right. || 615 ||
Then, having seated the lord of the twice-born and having performed everything according to the prescribed rite,
he [proceeded] with a mind free from doubt and with an intellect directed in that very same way.

One should meditate upon one's own consciousness as having arrived in the presence [of the deity] within one's own home; and one should remember that single, sinless state with the syllable Om (praṇava) at the appropriate time.
Having attained the great state of cessation as taught in the scriptures,
one who has performed the mendicant's duties and undergone the prescribed initiation should practice accordingly.
Having thus performed the collection of the bones according to the prescribed rite, O Lotus-born One, one should then perform the mantra-bath there indeed. (619)

Then, having been consecrated by the best of the twice-born who are versed in the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, he should perform the ritual bath with the principal mantras containing the word "water" (ab-liṅga). || 620 ||
From among the previously mentioned twelve-syllable mantras,
one who has been initiated should indeed recite only a single mantra that possesses the characteristics described above.
Whether by means of one's own mantra or the weapon-mantras (astra-mantras), once the bath has been performed in this manner,
one should again meditate upon one's own twelve-syllable mantra within the lotus of the heart.
With his mind focused on nothing else, he remains reciting [the mantra] for half a muhūrta, or for a full muhūrta, while his form shines with the luster of molten gold, or indeed remains formless.
O Brahmin, by this intention, the impurity arising from his own lineage— which would otherwise last for an eon— is brought to an end for those men who are qualified.
The reality is that for those things produced from the mind and for those produced from other causes, it occurs according to their respective order;
however, it is not so for all things produced from the All-Powerful One, nor for those produced within the fire of bliss (or the protector of bliss).

And for those twice-born who are qualified and possess that knowledge—[whether they are] those who have conquered their senses or those who are established in true knowledge—having thus purified his body, he should prepare food as before. (626)
Food fit for consumption, accompanied by condiments, was prepared specifically for the sacrifice to the Lord,
as well as for the libation to the Fire and for the offering of funeral cakes.
Just as the second body, the subtle vehicle (ativāhika), which is a form composed of the elements,
meets its destruction through ritual action— such as initiation— for those seeking liberation.
That which one has given oneself at this time through giving for ten days and so forth,
that body comes into existence for the sake of future assistance through those actions.
Through long-term practice over time, together with that [practice], one accumulates a great store of karma.
Truly, through the grace of the Lords of Mantras, there arises indeed tranquility for those beings;
and by that stainless deed, they are brought to the state of being fathers.

Furthermore, that which is even more weighty than this—whether it be self-acquired or otherwise—should indeed be made available for the benefit of men until the end of ten days and so forth. || 632 ||
When the daily [rite] has concluded at its end, one should then perform the dismissal of the deity to be worshipped,
having mentally resolved [to do so] either by oneself or through the mouth of the Guru. (633)
For, under the pretext of a funeral rite (śrāddha), one joins the future body— which is indeed the support of karma—
with the constituent parts of the principles of the Lord (īśvara-tattva-aṅga) that exist separately, because of the manifestation of the body.

Then, O Lotus-born One, having worshipped the Lord of Mantras as before with offerings possessing all the complete characteristics, ending with the ritual gift of handfuls of sesame seeds according to the rules.
Then, according to the previously mentioned procedure, with devotion and faith,
many Brahmins devoted to the five daily rites should perform [the rite] for one day.
For he who desires prosperity through the sacrifice to the Blessed One and other rites must first satisfy [the deities];
therefore, this is the cause for crossing over [to liberation], whether one is alive or dead.
I do not see any other means than this sacrifice preceded by mantras; for those who know the reality of origin and dissolution are devoid of the practice of worshipping with mixed [methods]. (638)
In this regard, those three vessels are eternally devoted to knowledge and ritual action;
they are intent upon the mastery of mantras—thus there is no deviation from what ought to be done.
Endowed with devotion and faith, it is the supreme raft for crossing over;
let it remain, O Pauṣkara, as the means for those who are free from sin.
The sacrifice consisting of Brahman is pure, even though it is forbidden by others;
however, because they have fallen, the offering of funeral cakes and water with sesame seeds must be performed for them.
And by the chanting of these names, they go to the supreme goal. One thing is said to be most excellent: valor that is free from worldly activity. || 642 ||
Or, O best of the twice-born, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance preceded by the establishment of the sacred fires,
up until the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, within ten days.
When the fire has been first gratified and the Lord of Mantras residing within it has been satisfied,
one should then perform the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having seated one Brahmin on the seat, or even many according to one's capacity,
they should be offered libations according to the rule for the sake of attaining the realization of the fundamental principles (tattva).
With fruits and roots for food, as well as various kinds of delicacies, and with diverse purifying drinks—both those to be licked, drunk, and sucked. (646)
With sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās), betel leaves accompanied by water-pots, umbrellas, sandals, vehicles, and other desirable gifts as are appropriate; || 647 ||
By means of which one indeed attains joy toward the assembly consisting of the Blessed One, having understood his resolve as well as the strengths and weaknesses of the place, time, and power. 648.
Out of greed for a worthy recipient (satpātra), he quickly desires to perform a *śrāddha* either ten days prior or until the point of attaining the status of a *pitṛ*.
O twice-born one, O Lord, if for many days no prepared food has been obtained, one should nevertheless perform the worship correctly with leaves, flowers, and other such offerings. (650)
Intent upon satisfying the fire for the sake of his own ancestors,
he should prepare a vessel completely filled with śāli rice drenched in honey and clarified butter.
Above the embodied form, it is adorned with fruits and roots; it is enriched with an upper garment and a sacred thread, and joined with a garland.

Having worshipped and offered [the vessel] which is filled with grain, provided with a single [piece of fruit], accompanied by a water-pitcher, and endowed with incense, lamps, and so forth; || 653 ||
Then, for the sake of the ancestors and for the sake of one's own self, one should offer water with sesame seeds;
this may be done for a single person or indeed for many.
Having offered the prepared food to the best of the twice-born who have been honored, it should indeed be presented in due order to the Lord for worship. 655.

Having prepared the rice-ball (piṇḍa) with grains sprinkled with honey and clarified butter as before, [he places it] before the Lord who has entered the womb of the fire, amidst the darbha grass... 656.

One should perform the offering of fragrances as before, with a perfectly pure intellect, according to the rite prescribed for the hungry ghosts (*preta*), by means of the self through the self. (658)
Having completed a year according to the prescribed rite preceded by mantras,
one should perform the annual śrāddha ceremony every year for as long as one lives.
Endowed with various kinds of gifts and adorned by sincere faith,
they should proceed according to the prescribed path, provided they belong to the appropriate lineage.
At the end of the mantra, they should be employed preceded by the word "sama.
O twice-born one, one should personally meditate upon one's own form, which is known as the pride of knowledge (jñānābhimāna). 661.
Therefore, [one should meditate on her] as pure and blazing in form, sometimes characterized by a specific shape,
and sometimes in the form of a sphere, resembling the midday sun.
In some cases, its light may be even fainter due to the influence of that activity;
having thus completed [the ritual] according to the rules, preceded by the sacrifice to the Blessed One.
Everything previously enjoined, up to the satiation of the Brahmins,
is concluded with the offerings of cooked rice, the funeral cakes (piṇḍas), and so forth, ending with the fire ritual.
O best of the twice-born, one should eat together with one's kinsmen (or, according to some versions, with those possessing wisdom) the food that has been offered and remains;
this applies specifically to the divine Prājāpatya rite and those preceded by the Aurdhvadehika.

In this activity accompanied by mantras, there is indeed accomplishment for those whose selves are enlightened; for those who are themselves the agents within their own selves, she [the Goddess] bestows both the states of being and the mantras.
And by means of that [method] by which the one who has ceased quickly attains accordance with reality,
there— having performed all [the rites] with the mantra deposited— one should act.
Having performed the propitiation of the lineage of waters, O one of stainless eyes, until complete satisfaction is reached,
one should perform everything according to the instruction, preceded by the recitation of mantras.
"Take it," "bring it," "hold it fast"—O twice-born one, one should indeed mentally recall every such activity from the beginning until the end of the meal. (669)

With the *praṇava*, one should visualize oneself entering the fire— characterized by that very form— which resembles the combined radiance of the sun, moon, and fire, and into which the mantra itself has dissolved.
Or, know that within the Supreme Self, which is divided, there exists the fourfold nature (cāturātmya);
it has the form of a Kadamba flower, possesses all powers, and is untainted.
Thus, O lotus-eyed one, this great procedure for the state after death of one who remains in the condition of a living being has been declared,
which is equal to the primary ritual manual.

In this matter, O Brahmin, that which was previously stated—both what has been explicitly mentioned and what remains unsaid—should be understood with a concentrated mind as culminating in the pleasure of the Blessed One. (673)

Whatever great rite consisting of offerings for the ancestors and the deceased one performs according to this rule, for the sake of their satisfaction in the hereafter, they bestow upon him an auspicious progeny. (674)

O twice-born one, even if incomplete in terms of ritual disposition, mantra, action, and material substances, this chapter on the *śrāddha*—when recited like a yoga—indeed [fulfills its purpose] for those who partake in the *śrāddha*. 675.
For by offering everything before [the deity] with devotion, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors;
how much more so, O high-minded one, regarding the mantra of Brahmā and the ritual of mantras?
Pauṣkara said:
O Blessed One, by virtue of this merit, may the Lord Brahmā...
The Blessed Lord said:
Just as the orb of the sun cannot be heard of without their vow,
so too is the form of the Blessed Viṣṇu, whose body consists of the six divine qualities.
Manifested previously as the essence of the supreme dharma, it exists by way of its own nature.
O Lotus-born One, these [qualities] are always manifested by none other than you;
for such is the distinction between the fourfold-formed Lord and the Supreme. (680)
Just as all various tastes, whether formed into a mass or distinct, and possessing diverse forms, exist within the powers of the pervasive Lord of All; so too do [all things] abide within Him. 682.
(There is a gap in the manuscript here) O Brahmin, the Lord Vāsudeva is the eternal soul of the universe. || 683 ||
Furthermore, those [energies], consisting of the density of consciousness, are properly employed for the sake of the ritual action of the letter *u*;
yet they all remain established as such within the Full Self (*pūrṇātman*), where they are conventionally designated by the names of the phonemes at their conclusion. || 685 ||
But those Kṛtyās perform their actions through the agent, by means of the power of manifestation and the power of that which belongs to the Lord. (686)
Inlaid with a web of rays, from the center of which, O Lotus-born One,
the Self was revealed together with the primordial principle (āditattva).
And the preparation for meditative concentration, whether in the attainment [of results] or in the practice of dhyāna, the all-pervading Supreme Self has arisen... || 688 ||
For this very reason, it is inferred by its mere self-luminous aspect;
likewise, the moon is indeed only a tiny fraction of the power of bliss. (689)
O lotus-eyed one, you should know that the supreme treasure belongs to him who is pleased.
For whatever other entities exist in this world, they are imitations of that;
even qualities such as knowledge and the rest are obtained from him, being born of his power and his portions.
In every respect, the Blessed One exists in this way as the universal;
this form is not of the nature of illusion, nor is it joined with the qualities of the power of insentience.
O Blessed One, O Lotus-born, for that which is dissolved within truly exists;
for when investigated by those who perceive the Imperishable, it is indeed eternal. (693)

The mantras that are prescribed for the funeral rites (śrāddha), as well as those declared for initiations (dīkṣā) and other ceremonies, become like the Lord seen in a dream when they reach the stage of non-existence.

And even in other activities, she likewise performs that which is endowed with such greatness, having understood through her intellect the activity enjoined by the scriptures and preceded by mantra. (695)
For indeed, through the nature of knowledge, he quickly attains mastery over the deeds of those foremost of the twice-born who are learned in the Vedas and abide in the stages of life for your sake.
Just as there is no fault in eating from the vessel of a Śūdra when one possesses the weight of knowledge, so it is indeed always for those who are naturally radiant and pure. 697.
Could it not be born of impurity? Could it not be a lack of purity due to being accepted by Śūdras?
For this very [scripture] belongs to the Śūdras because of the weight of their knowledge. (698)
There is no contradiction anywhere between the mantras and the [Tantric] observances (samayas),
for the mantras consisting of the three Vedas bestow the fruit of worldly activity (pravṛtti).
There exists [the place] called Ṣmāntadvijagraha. || 700 ||
O best of the twice-born, because it is not innate, their state is illuminated by Brahmanic splendor;
though they lack formal consecration, they are fully awakened,
and among them there exists only mutual service.
O Lotus-born One, for the lords of the twice-born, the lions among beasts, and the mantras, there is indeed a gradual resting point, proceeding step by step in due order. (703)
And in the fourth, known as Śūdra, O Pauṣkara, the Prabhākara and Vāha [mantras] are established; indeed, they are characterized by sharpness through the power of the path.
In that same way, O Brahmin, the three classes of fiery color likewise recede;
for the purpose of which they were indeed prohibited... || 705 ||
The mind alone is indeed the support for mantras such as the Ṛgveda and others;
know that their purity is the Sovereign of All.
And for those [mantras] whose doubts have been revealed, likewise [the endings] are svāhā, vauṣaṭ, and vaṣaṭ. || 707 ||
O Blessed One, those mantras which were previously prohibited by me for your sake, and the Praṇavas [and so forth]... || 708 ||
O twice-born one, although those [terms] are indeed common designations for the Omniscient One,
they nevertheless function as primary terms in the context of sacrificial rites.
By which, O Mahāmati, they do not possess the quality of luminosity, [as ordained] by the primordial Lord, the All-pervading One. || 710 ||
Within the threefold collection of sounds, people are transformed in three ways;
the Brahmins who do not worship other [deities] are [established] in the assembly of mantras, such as the Añcala and others.
The four [classes of] officiating priests—those of the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and * * * * * * * * * * —are mixed together in the seed, the mass, the word, and so forth. 712.
In the perfectly pure array of mantras, which is free from the influence of passion and delusion, there are indeed mantras of the rājasa and tāmasa types. (713)
Especially by one who is constantly well-restrained and devoted.
A Śūdra who knows the mantras must always maintain the three [Vedas]—
namely those designated as Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman— when they are employed in ritual action.

For it is established in heaven, supreme, fruitful, and complete with its limbs; likewise, for those who have mastered all-knowing mantras, [it bestows] the power of atomization (*aṇimā*) and so forth. || 717 ||
For it is always unrequested and conjoined with liberation;
for this very reason, it belongs to one who propitiates [the deity] in its entirety.
O Pauṣkara, that [practice] is employed for its accomplishment whose fruit consists of the powers such as *aṇimā*,
together with their constituent parts and the totality of conditions.
For the direct realization of that [mantra] yields the eternal fruit of absolute liberation (kaivalya),
O Great-minded One, even for those mantras that are rajasic or tamasic.
For this very self-cultivation, which is endowed with even slightly visible results and accompanied by excellence in rebirth, yields the fruit of excellence in the mind. || 721 ||
Among these, that which is the principal fruit in comparison with what has been stated is indeed that which pertains to the Sāttvika mantras and rests upon a single portion [of the path]. (722)
For the sake of the conditions for liberation, [the names] were proclaimed for the purpose of accomplishment;
the mantras are the makers of names, and their success arises from the power of those rites.
Action is understood from the scripture...
[it] would arise from association with the virtuous... would it not?
Of the six mantras of the best of the twice-born, and of the eternal rite.
O twice-born one, in some cases the fruit arises from the conjunction of the three; in other cases, the culmination of the ritual action is the greatness of the mantras.
O twice-born one, they remain with their own facial forms, stationed there by the power of mantra to exercise authority in certain places. (727)
Birth, excellence, and action arise together with the causal conditions;
knowing this, one must always indeed apply oneself to the devotees. 728.
But in the manifold array of mantras, O Brahmin, which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, [the truth is revealed].
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of Śrāddha," in the venerable Pauṣkarasaṃhitā of the venerable Pāñcarātra.
(Total number of verses: 729).

Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter. (There appears to be a textual gap here; in this chapter, significant omissions and transpositions are observed in the root manuscript collections, and in many places, even the comprehension of the subject matter is difficult.)

The Blessed Lord said: It is not for those devoted to the recitation of the Vedas, nor for those who sacrifice with the desire for liberation, nor for those intent on austerities, nor for those who practice only the duty of charity. (1)
O Pauṣkara, for all those devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice, it was thus declared by the Great One regarding that most venerable rite:
"In this way, how might the suffering of worldly existence not be pacified for men? (3)
(Here there is a significant omission in the text.
The Blessed One said: "It bestows the path to heaven and likewise grants the most excellent fruit."
And the Agnihotra alone belongs to the Brahmins who are exponents of the Vedas.
But those, O Brahmin, who remain therein, established in that which possesses the nature of that Dharma— in the worship, in meditative absorption, in the rite of recitation, and in praise— [5]
For those whose minds were uplifted, who understood the deeds of the Blessed One,
and who purified themselves through the study of the true scriptures, their abode was filled with fervor.
When performed with substances such as guggulu and others, together with complete oblations (*saṃpūrṇāhuti*) and secret mantras, it shall become a means of deliverance from worldly existence.
With sacrificial vessels made of *vaikaṅkata* wood, with various means of accomplishment, with wealth acquired through righteous means, and also with devotion and faith. (8)
Just as fire has been described as arising from various wombs,
you previously prepared the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) properly according to the ritual rules.
And having brought it down into the midst of that [lotus], which had arisen from various wombs—
[here the text is missing]— Pauṣkara said:
"O Blessed One, what are the origins of fire, and what is its knowledge?
The Blessed One replied:
The origin of fire is twofold: that which arises from the sun and that characterized by jewels."
From the contact with that hand-mirror, O Lotus-born One, the second [image] arises.
Therein, the womb of various types of birth possesses manifold characteristics.
She who is established in this world through the very process of churning—
she is sometimes [manifested] as Kaicakī, free from effort.
However, stone is of three kinds; among them, that which is produced solely from water is rare.
That which [arises] from entirely auspicious elements through mutual friction— // 15 //
And the *salohacātakī* is characterized by the index finger being bent down. || 16 ||
In the third pair of revolutions, there is the perfect union of iron and stone with one another, and likewise [the union] of those born from iron and stone.
The eighth [chapter] also briefly describes the single characteristic of the churning-stick (*manthāna*). || 18 ||
O Lotus-born One, there is nothing superior anywhere to that which has been described as the nature of the jewel. (19)
Even that which is most excellent must be understood as being within the time...
from the tip of the flame and from the flickering flame, its manifestation is at the summit...
[the fivefold station of these, ending with the Brāhmaṇa and so forth].
O Mahāmati,
that very power, endowed with manifestation through various deities, is filled with hosts of arrows and pervades the universal generality.
Therefore, the fire must indeed be brought forth by means of the power (*śakti*);
for just as it is with a householder, so too, in the case of a conflict between the two, [the ritual] does not arise.
Therefore,
the power of the lotus-born [Brahmā] is the source of all categories;
it is sung as being of four kinds, and furthermore, in seven ways.
O Lotus-born one, this narrative of yours is now being told.
O Lotus-born One, there are the Yākṣī, the Pārthivī, the Saurī, the Śaikhī, the Bhrāṣṭrī, the Kāpālī, the Khatantrā, and Agni; yet none of these exist without Him.
O Brahmin, their stability is further said to be of two kinds:
that called "seedless" (nirbījā) and that which has a seed (sabījā). First, the seedless is described.
The bhavani is of two kinds: that which is called "located therein" (tatsthānākhyā), and indeed the cakrī;
likewise, there are those with a base (*salo*) and those consisting solely of stone (*kevalāśmamayī*). || 30 ||
This is declared to be the seedless (nirbīja) [practice], and it is also described as the seeded (sabīja).
It consists of the Śaikhī, Bhrāṣṭrī, and Kāpālī, characterized by independent fire.
O Lotus-born One, that which was spoken by me to you as the "Hotṛ-conjunction" is, without distinction and with equal generality, always applicable to all. (32)
Even though you have arisen from a lotus, listen nevertheless to this which has been understood.
For celibate students (*brahmacārins*), the fire is characterized by iron;
for householders, it is known as the *ādhāna*; and for forest-dwellers, it is the *kaicakī*. (34)
And the Sāvitrī of the ascetics was indeed ordained for the propitiation of the Supreme Brahman; it was established as the two fire-drills (*araṇī*) for the leading of the Fire,
and by the king’s permission, it was divided twofold into the common and the celestial.
That [first], the permission for that [second], and the third—these three constitute the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*) for the Vaiśya caste;
and these three likewise for the Kṣatriya. || 37 ||
For the sake of achieving the proper sequence for a Śūdra, and specifically by the permission of that [preceptor], it should be performed for the best of the twice-born among the twice-born. || 38 ||
And the second belongs to the Śūdra; O Pauṣkara, it is different from that for any other [caste]. 39.
In times of distress, however, one should not give [the mantra] to anyone else, nor to a Śūdra, nor to another [unqualified person].
(In all four manuscripts, there is a gap in the text here. That which is primary [is the best]; transgression yields little success.
All the various wombs have been ordained for everyone according to the distinction of their fruits. || 42 ||
O you who have arisen from the eleven lotuses, listen attentively to how it was:
for those desiring land, [it was] made of jewels; for those seeking fire, it was indeed of bell-metal.
The Gopa, characterized by the absence of passion, bestows [these qualities];
she should be known as the Kaicakī womb, which grants happiness, good fortune, and nourishment.
The ground that bestows intelligence and vigor is known as Bhūyiṣṭhā; it is the destroyer of enemies, celebrated as the one adorned with iron and stone, and is the source, O Lotus-born One. 45.
The Śaikhī is Dharma, while the Bhrāṣṭrī is indeed the giver of land;
the Kāpālī has the womb of consciousness (saṃveda), O Lotus-born One, and she increases one's station.
In the Manu-kalpa, she is the auspicious source that brings about the pacification of diseases for those who desire it,
and likewise for the four stages of life (āśramas).
There is no contradiction regarding the state of being an egg-born [aṇḍaja] when there is mutual seizing;
for at the time of one’s will, all [beings] have access to all wombs. (48)
"For those who are devoted to the propitiation of mantras, these [rites] are indeed always unopposed;
O twice-born one, let that which occurred previously not happen again at this time, even if it were excessive. (49)
If, due to negligence, he has not become tranquil, he might again say, "My origin is another [origin is different].
This is neither by force nor by constraint, for one who abides in the state of gathering [disciples], nor out of reverence. (50)
One who has been accepted [as a disciple] should indeed perform the penance again; it should be performed with special care if the offense was public, but otherwise if it was private.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Classification of the Fire-Source," in the *Pauṣkara-saṃhitā* of the glorious *Pañcarātra*.

51) Now begins the twenty-ninth chapter;
the Blessed One said:
In the Prājāpatya and Daiśika [k:
* * * kara] rites, which are measured by the raised hands, one should gradually increase the field [k, kh: * * * nayet] by one finger-breadth at a time until it reaches its full extent. || 1 ||

To the extent that a field measuring eight cubits arises for the purpose of the sacrificial hearths (dhiṣṇya), so too, by way of measurement, would there be one hundred and eighty-one [cubits]. || 2 ||
The auspicious number of all the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*), situated in the eight directions, becomes eightfold. || 3 ||
O twice-born one, arising from the distinctions of the square and other shapes for the sake of rites performed for specific desires,
[the marks] possess the characteristics of a garland of excellent jewels, the Śrīvatsa, a crown, and armlets;
they resemble a conch, a discus, a mace, a lotus, a bow, and various arrows.
All [the pillars] together with their pedestals are fashioned with four, three, two, or one belt;
they are marked with the discus, lotus, mace, and conch, either individually or collectively.
Likewise, they arise beautifully from their own limbs, which flow through the eight sources,
according to the number of each respective poetic composition, namely two, two, two, and twelve.

Know that one part is one finger-breadth (aṅgula) for the sake of establishing all the limbs; indeed, this is so for all [the deities] according to the various requirements of their respective cavities.
But the division known as the manifestation of the unmanifest is remembered as being manifold;
it is the bondage characterized by worldly enjoyment, which yields infinite fruit for those who seek it. (9)
The Supreme Lord asks about the attainment of desires. [g, gh: He asks the Supreme Lord about the state of being. || 10 ||
O Mahāmati, according to the principle of the characteristic of illumination, those [measures] are independent;
the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*) are twelve finger-breadths wide, and those at the end of the hand are thirteen.
They possess all forms, are mobile, and are devoid of girdles. || 12 ||
In the case of a secondary alternative (anukalpa), however, mobile [images] are prescribed for the satiation of the mantra;
likewise, those measuring up to two cubits are characterized by great auspicious marks.

Having scratched lines upon the ground and filled them with grains, seeds, or even earth—whether due to a lack of materials or for the sake of completing the ritual constantly—one should proceed. (14)
But in the case of secondary or tertiary substitutes, one must always act without contradiction,
using [wood] that is endowed with bark, symmetrical, full, succulent, straight, and firm.
O twice-born one, for those [images] made of clay that are twelve finger-breadths in height and so forth— even those fashioned from minerals, or as some say,
from wood— the same procedure should indeed be followed when they are mobile and filled with oblations.
Since there is no oblation without a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that brings success to those who sacrifice with mantras,
therefore a pit should always be prepared— whether according to the Sūtras, or mobile, or fixed.
And due to the specific nature of the sacrificial ground, when it is yellow and twice as high, it may be two-sided, four-sided, eight-sided, or circular. || 19 ||
Having established the measurement of the excavation, it should first be raised to the desired height.
One may construct [the altar] with bricks, either unburnt or burnt, according to one's preference; or else,
they should be made equal and uniform, such that a portion of them remains levelled,
and each subsequent layer becomes two finger-breadths greater than the one before.
O Great-minded One, from the eastern edge of the boundary-line (mekhalā) to the point where the two doors are given,

the measurement of the rim (nemi) is three-quarters or half of that, according to one's own white [pure] nature; such is the true measurement and positioning of the twelve sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa), O Great-minded One.
O beautiful-eyed one, having divided those twelve [fingers]—each measuring twelve angulas—into four parts or three parts here at some time; 25.
The measurement of the rims (nemī) is equal to their height and also to their width;
it is always equal to that of the base (yoni), provided the latter is made from the rear side.
However, it should be raised by the measure of two finger-breadths at the back of the rim;
you should then gradually decrease it from the circumference according to proportion.
O Lotus-born One, the [three] finger-breadths should always be increased by one-third part from the measurement of the girdle, which is reduced by one-quarter.
Then, having divided that [line] into three parts and extended its tip,
one should [construct] the womb (yoni), the expansion and conclusion, and the sequence of the final squares in due order.
Having attained equality through non-falling away, smooth like the trunk of an elephant, and having resorted to its own manifold form characterized by the qualities (guṇas). || 31 ||
They flow through the night with a stream of awakening that resounds with the sound of *aṃ*;
yet they do not reach the fathomless ocean of the Puruṣa, which is the locus for the washing away of all things.
Having perceived the source [fallen] in the sky, with the dust of passion [dispelled],
he was freed from the two-fold wheel of existence through the two qualities of darkness.

(150) Precisely because its qualities are overwhelmed, [it appears as] that which possesses the state of a calf and a girdle; know that which is formless, the Supreme Brahman, to have entered into the ether. 34.
In the sacrificial fire-pan (dhiṣṇya) which has four girdles, within those four girdles,
he himself [established] the unmanifest fourfold Self there, prior to the enclosing sticks (paridhi).
For those whose forms are perfectly complete, there is that which arises from my liberation—
consisting of pairs of pairs of qualities, beginning with Acyuta, and manifesting as a triad in sequence.
Action that relies upon the flow [of consciousness] attains oneness with Brahman. || 37 ||
[She is] the one who has subdued the vast and infinite wombs of those whose forms are distant forests;
she who possesses earrings (or coils), whose limbs are extended, and who dwells in perfect stability.

For others who are intent upon the practice of *yoniśas* (proper method), there is contraction [of the breath] like that of the rims of a wheel; listen now to this regarding the appropriate time. O Brahmin, the husks [or impurities] consist of four parts, depending on whether they are superior or otherwise.

[The measurement] is indeed [determined] by five finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) less than the constant heat; and for those who are equal in measure, though possessing various forms as their own nature, it is equal in width and length... [and so forth].
One should bind those who are deficient [in limb] as witnesses...
[omitted] ...a height of two cubits; for others, it should be the same, up to a hundred [fathoms].
Having thus previously considered the factors such as place and time,
as well as his own capacity, he [performed] the layout of the lines for the *vyūha* (the ritual arrangement),
O Pauṣkara, including the moat, the eight girdles, and the womb of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), as before.
With her limbs extended and held in control, her girdle firmly positioned, she should cause him to fall with an upward gaze for a moment by means of the hollow of her swelling breasts. || 39 ||
Listen to this from me: for others who are diligent in the practice of *yoniśas* (proper reflection), there is contraction [of the lifespan] during the *anukalpa* (subsidiary aeon) of Kuṇḍanemi;
O Brahmin, it is divided into four parts in relation to the highest and other [categories]. 41.
One should measure it with a single finger for each cubit;
one should increase it by two cubits until it reaches the witness-mark.
And even those measuring all directions, lacking five finger-breadths, are of various forms in their nature, despite having constant breadth and measurement. (43)

For the sacrificial hearths (*dhiṣṇya*) that are equal in width and length, as well as for their girdles (*mekhalā*), those other than the central one should be two cubits high; the rest should be equal to that, or a hundred [units]. Having thus previously considered the influence of place, time, and so forth. (45)

Then, from its own power, the array (vyūha) falls there with splendor... [omitted]. O Lotus-born One, above the seats (pīṭhas), which are well-formed, eight-cornered, and four-wheeled, there is a cavity;
and the womb (yoni) of the seat, O Pauṣkara, is for the eight girdles.
Having made known the decrease and increase of the moon itself,
he, with a mind purified by knowledge, causes those things to be dissolved away by means of his intellect.
One should now lead [the offering] for the sake of satisfaction by means of the dual splendor within oneself;
for the power of the Lord’s fire, the supreme primordial nature consists of the flames and so forth. 49.
p.
151) Another [aspect] is that the various forms of the natural hearths arise from fire;
indeed, these very forms of fire exist in the state of the sacrificial pits for the sake of ritual action. || 50 ||
What was ordained for the mouth of the Lord and for the mouths of the Brahmins—that oblation which is indeed offered by the preceptor when it falls into the sacrificial pit—[is as follows]. (51)
Everything offered into the fire indeed grants success, for it consumes everything entirely;
having first properly [prepared], one's own strength gradually overcomes the obstacle.

Whatever substance is prescribed for an oblation, when offered into a smokeless, licking fire that is well-established and situated in its own place, it possesses a merit of ten million times ten thousand crores.
One should perform oblations numbering one hundred thousand, gathering the necessary materials;
this brings about the staff, the victory over the two wings, and inexhaustible, sustaining success.
Then, for others, it flows in a continuous stream;
O son, [place the deity] situated in the sky by means of yoga upon the lotus of the Mantra-Brahman. 55.

"But when the primary rite has been lost, O Lotus-born One, what is appropriate? [Tell me] concerning the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), their dimensions, and the lineage and potency of the bamboo [for the ladles], and so forth. (56)
It should be made of copper or iron, and its interior should be like the interior of a lotus. || 57 ||
By means of which one carries the other dharmas, yet does not cause them to fall to the ground;
one should then fashion the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as refined by the formative forces (saṃskāra) and deposit that [deity] therein. || 58 ||
And with many Ājyadoha hymns, for the purpose of satiating him with mantras. || 59 ||

O twice-born one, by the force of the syllable *oṃ* of the fire, one should quickly cause the essence of the milk of clarified butter to fall above, in the midst of the pervasive Lord who is the self of the mantra. (60)

And for the attainment of liberation and enjoyment, [one should meditate] thus upon the mouth of the *brahmarandhra* in sequence, endowed with fragrance and forests, complete and of equal radiance. (61)
O Brahmin, having performed the worship of the Lord of Mantras together with his retinue, his limbs, and his secondary limbs, as well as that of the Emblem and its enclosure; 62.

Then, having obtained the authority, one who is free from sloth should perform ten thousand or more repetitions of the mantra previously commenced for the sake of service, beginning with the Brahma-mantra.

For it is certain that, according to one's capacity, [this should be done] at dawn when the sun has set, or indeed at the midpoint of the night, in accordance with the injunctions of the scriptures. 64.
After the rite of preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is completed, for the sake of propitiating the one who has been worshipped,
when the recitation of one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) and so forth has been accomplished on a day of Brahmā (*brahmadina*), [the following occurs].
When that equal homa is completed, or if it is ordained otherwise by the Lotus-born One, one should offer grains,
seeds, sesame, or fruits, either in full measure or in a portion equal to a fraction.
O Pauṣkara, by means of the mudrā called Jalaja, which has the face of Hari as its arrow,
[one attains success] in six months, or twice that time, or even four times that, according to one's capacity and through the practice of yoga at intervals.
When the two and four are fully completed at the end of a hundred capable ones, [the assembly of] the Sami...
Reciting them correctly with the intellect, either together or individually according to one's own capacity. || 71 ||

One should lead the entire collection of mantras, even if divided, to joy through oblations of clarified butter; and indeed, from the *dhruva* vessel, [one should do so] with the consecrated [offering].
Next, I shall describe its characteristics, together with the measurements of the object to be measured:
it should be produced from a well-known sacrificial tree, free from defects, firm, and without blemishes. (73)
Having taken a very well-prepared piece of wood that is free from the fear of fire, [and] auspicious, [it should be] not stale and not kept overnight. || 74 ||
From the wrists up to the middle fingers of both arms,
one should again multiply that [measurement] by the breadth of the thumbs seven times.
Leaving off eight by eight, one should proceed; the remaining ones are increased by one.
These indeed are to be fully understood as the eight beginning with the Banner, in their proper order. (76)
In that regard, whatever remains is known as auspicious for the auspicious;
you [are so] from the remainder of the pair, and the Lord of Beasts (Mṛgādhipa) is from the third.
Four times its own increase is the vṛṣabha, said to be fivefold; from sixfold and the remainder, it is indeed the gaja, and from sevenfold? || 78 ||

Among these, the seven known as the "single" (ekākhyas) are considered pure and bestowers of auspiciousness; likewise, those beginning with Gaja, Indra, Siṃha, Vṛṣabha, and Dhvaja are granters of welfare. (79)

For the sake of averting misfortune, for the destruction of obstacles, for one's own welfare, and for the increase of prosperity, one should insert a length of one finger or joined fingers according to the proper method. (80)
One should divide that length into five parts, and its width should be made equal to a petal for the sake of success; therein, O Pauṣkara, the central region should be established.
The first, Kauśa, and the others, excluding the goat (agoḥ), follow their respective designations in sequence;
one should perform the reduction of the earth-elements according to the parts of the petals, filaments, and the wheel.
The ear-marks are to be fashioned from the space between the two, namely the wheel and the lotus.
Its length should be one-fifth [of the total], equal to its width;
and it should be joined at two parts, extending from the region of the branch to the tip.
Situated in the center of the irrigation channel of the plowshare, she is adorned with various karmas. || 85 ||
One should perform one's own respective ritual experience, and thereby the auspicious non-ritual [experience];
then, by means of the first portion situated in the center of the mandala of the earth.
Having fashioned a lotus endowed with its characteristic marks— consisting solely of sixteen petals, complete with a stalk, filaments, and a pericarp— 87.
It is seedless, with the calyx slightly adorned,
and either surrounded by Hetīśa, who is endowed with the characteristics as previously described, or otherwise.
One should fashion the ground as a wheel-base, marked on both sides at the corners;
the mandala should be adorned with kaustubha gems, svastikas, or conch shells and other such symbols. (89)
Or, [Tārāktā] Gaṇāḍhya...

[and so forth]. Therefore, for the sake of the subsequent proportion, one should again discard the eighth part situated in the two sides and perform a reduction so that it becomes like "elephant-trunk" (gajapāṇi). || 91 ||
The space between the two [boundary] earths should be measured by six parts;
it should be made equal to six parts in width, possessing auspicious characteristics.
Having divided that width into two or five equal parts,
one should further subdivide it as desired from the front for the sake of proportional measurement.
And there is another aggregate... [as before] ...
like a fish, marked with the insignia... in due order. (95)
From the two sides, one should lead the remainder from the exterior toward the interior by way of the throat;
so that there may be light in the cow’s-mouth [shape], this bestows great supernatural power (*mahaddhi*). || 96 ||
But for conchs and the like that lack a pedestal (*vedikā*), one should [measure] up to the end of...;
however, by means of the two parts of the earth (*vasudhāṃśa*) not included within the pedestal, one should divide [the remainder].
Starting from the shoulder and neck, one may extend three [verses] up to the neck as desired. || 98 ||
Having assigned the portion as previously described...
for one who has omitted the rite of the altar, there is indeed the statement of Śaṅkha: || 99 ||
One should construct it measuring five parts together with an additional quarter-part;
whether it is slightly more or slightly less in width, it shines beautifully as desired.
One should gradually reduce three parts of the pitcher and two parts of the base;
one should reduce [the height] of the broad-bellied conch by one-fifth.
Then, one should worship the region of the belly in two ways with garlands and other offerings.
For that which extends in length from the base consists of three parts. (102)
From the middle of that, having first projected the body toward the region of the throat as previously described,
one should then divide the remainder into ten parts and measure seven of those parts.
One should fashion a staff in the shape of a mace, expanded at the neck;
it should be of two kinds as specified, and at the end, it should be provided with salt.
In that context, the emanation is said to consist of exactly three parts;
one should construct it reaching up to the pedestal, occupying one part.
One should construct a svastika endowed with the proper characteristics, marked by a lotus in the center;
then, one should arrange the filaments (*karṇikā*) and the collection [of petals] at the end, part by part. || 106 ||

In the courtyard, with eight beautiful and auspicious pearl-oyster shells—well-proportioned, set within frames, endowed with the quality of water-streams, and accompanied by bracelets and yokes. || 107 ||

In this manner, according to the procedure for the arrangement of the streams (*dhārā*), once it is completed with the six pairs, it is circular and square, situated in the midst of the accumulation. 108.
One should grasp the handle with a fist characterized by the "muṣṭimīdṛg" [or "muṣṭimīdṛgrodapa"] mark,
and likewise extend the shaft externally so that it exceeds the length of the pole.
One should fashion a hundred-petaled lotus with its face turned downward, broad and with its pericarp facing upward;
it should have many petals and filaments, with the two hands held in fists at the limit of the weapon. (110)
Or else, one may cast it upon the altar; now hear another characteristic of the pedestal (pīṭha), which is prescribed in the Ardhakalpa, auspicious and comparable to the pedestal of the gods.

Having divided [the area] up to the edge of the crown (uṣṇīṣa-pada), the preceptor should previously establish the twelve parts with those respective portions; this is what is declared as the instruction. || 112 ||
The lotus, or the discus-lotus, is marked with the [auspicious] characteristics; however, listen further to its measurement and division according to the specific site. 113.
Having made the field extend as far as the Brahma-sthāna and divided it into six parts,
one should adorn two parts in the center for the purpose of establishing the position of the pericarp (karṇikā).

The enclosing rim (paridhi) is made with one-eighth part, the row of filaments (kesarāvali) with half [of that], the mass of petals with one and a half [parts], and the sky (vyoma) outside of that with half [a part]. 115.
O Pauṣkara, having reached these fields with their internal divisions, one finds a royal city endowed with various wonderful arrangements through its constituent parts. 116.
Having taken up small portions from each, one should place them in the various limbs; the verbal forms [should be arranged] in sequence, beginning with the syllable *brahman* at the feet. (117)
And one should slightly lower it from field to field as prescribed;
otherwise, having traversed the remainder, the noble one would be harmed.
Here, the measurement of the field for the whorl and filaments is as previously stated;
having completed the network of petals together with the sky [the pericarp], it is done by means of a fractional part.
Outside of that, one should construct the field characterized as previously described, with a circumference equal to the wheel and its rim plus half a part. || 120 ||
Behind him, one should fashion either a lotus with its stalk or a lotus alone;
the lotus and its mass of petals [should be fashioned] at the mouth... || 121 ||
This is the [treatment of] the construction of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

At that time, the object of cognition (*prameya*) must indeed be understood in this context for the sake of establishing the conceptualization and the accomplishment of ritual action (*karma*). || 122 ||
Ananta, in the form of a hundred-petaled lotus, holds the position of the fist here; by means of that fist, he is present here as the Endless One (*anantavat*).
Having remained within in the nature of the seed-syllable, he then rises with his face turned upward once more. || 123 ||
That great vital breath (prāṇa), which is the noble self-nature and moves with speed,
is impelled through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) again and again according to His will.
The seven netherworlds are its stalk and the skin; it is a lotus whose essence is the senses.
Resting upon this, the nectar remains like water within its own flow.

Abiding within the lattice of the arrangement of the wheel (*sacakraracanājāla*), you hold the form of the weapon (*astramūrtidhṛk*). Vāyu, whose vehicle is the sky (*ākha*) and who possesses the form of the conch (*śaṅkhavigraha*), is the deity of the sky (*kha*); he is truth, the immeasurable, and the manifest reality (*satyam bhūtamameyaṃ ca*). Having been projected by means of the time of refinement (*saṃskārakālena*), he holds the form of the sacrificial session (*satramūrtidhṛk*), and thereafter holds the treasury of the kingdom of wind (*vāyurājyakośaṃ ca khaṃ*). (Note: The text contains minor orthographic variations between manuscripts *g* and *gh*, which have been integrated for clarity.)

Seedless, unborn, unshakeable, and primordial, it is the presiding deity of the garland of deities; it is the reality that has become manifest, immeasurable, yet this very object of knowledge is the infallible.
But at the time of consecration, having placed it there, one should always perform the recitation and the libation; then, setting aside its length, one should take only the width of the altar.
One should construct it according to the specified proportions,
neither too thick nor too thin, but properly aligned with straight lines;
thus one should make it either consisting of material substances or composed of auspicious stones.
Now, the characteristics of the *sruva* and *sruc* ladles for the purpose of the fire-oblation (*homa*) are described:
having taken pure iron that possesses the previously mentioned numerical characteristics.
One should divide the length of the *sruc* into eight parts, excluding three;
by that measure of a part, its width is prescribed.

Having divided it into equal parts with clear lines according to the sequence, one should fashion the base from the root as an eight-part square. (If it says "one should fashion from the root," that is excellent. 133.
Then, having avoided excessive bulk, one should indeed fashion [the base] with half the width;
one should create a lotus resting upon its support, complete with its decorative arrangement.
That conch with its mouth wide open, possessing the Nandyāvarta design and auspicious marks, is said to be four parts in measurement, excluding the two side portions. || 135 ||
Bound in the middle like a noose, well-proportioned and circular,
the staff has four parts and its face protrudes from the mouth of the pitcher.
From the mouth of the conch, one should fashion a canopy joined with a triad [of elements],
and one should create two stalks for the stream [of water], measuring eight parts.
Having completed the square neck-pedestal (kaṇṭhapīṭha) like the [main] pedestal,
one should carve a lotus there, situated within a circular disc.
The thread [of the neck] should be like a net of pearls at the four corners of the conch-shell base;
the neck should be raised by one part and measured at two parts in width. (139)
Slightly curved, it should not be more than one-eighth of the height above the [lower] part;
the head should be like a lotus, with the neck as its stalk and the ears as its pericarp.
The forest of the pericarp is surrounded by the edges of infinite filaments;
outside of that is the mass of petals, which is equal in height to the filaments.
Without division, facing backward and sideways, one should place it within the center of the pericarp, sealed by means of a sphere alone. || 142 ||
It should be marked with the Kaustubha gem or with the foremost of the Saurabhīya [lineages],
and it is suitable for the oblation of clarified butter and substances according to the measure of the half-homa.

The definition [of the sacrificial ladle] has been fully proclaimed according to the authoritative means of knowledge; it is traditionally remembered as being for the purpose of the oblation of clarified butter. Now, understand the remainder.
Varuṇa is indeed the manifest embodiment of nectar, appearing in the form of the lotus;
and that weapon, established in the form of the stalk, causes fear to the obstacles.
The Moon, which brings nourishment to the world, is the lotus at the foremost place;
for that capacity known as bliss should be understood as the Supreme Lord. (146)
But the preceptor, being self-restrained and seeking to accomplish that installation, should rely upon this divine conceit and [the other qualities]. || 147 ||
But in the case of secret fire-rituals, all the implements and the noble ladies remain within their own respective substrates, situated in a single locus of their own instruments.
Therefore, one who is not qualified [for this] should instead be devoted to the deity of food. || 150 ||
One should resort to the supreme refuge;
the taking away of the body, though forbidden, is auspicious. || 151 ||
He who, established in a position of authority, attains the state [of perfection] bestows it upon those who have received his permission and upon your devotees. 152.
The vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) should be characterized by the Great Brahman;
one should fashion it with the interior of a lotus, auspicious for the purpose of the southern journey. || 153 ||
Having properly grasped the self and having honored it well, one obtains [the state] through fire;
at its root is the firm stalk of valid cognition, which possesses auspicious characteristics. || 154 ||
One should produce the stainless essence (*amalasāra*) from the seed-syllable; that which is capable of that is known as the stalk (*nāla*), served by the three [Śaktis]. (155)
Having prepared a divine lotus-pond with fully blossomed, half-blossomed, and budding lotuses,
as well as with lotuses interspersed among them.
And having a face four spans wide, with the interior of a full-blown lotus [between its parts]. || 157 ||
By means of a third part of the wheel-space, one should pierce the region of the throat with the wind-petal; having indeed completed one [breath], it becomes another. 158.
The crown, together with the utpala lotus, is perfected by fragrant sounds;
for them, that lotus with its stalk is the supreme vessel of the Lord. (159)
It is always known as the seat for reclining and an ocean of nectar;
it is filled with garlands and fragrant flowers, and situated between two stones.
Also those bowls which are excellent and so forth, and those suitable for drinking. 161.
All of those, joined with the conch, lotus, thunderbolt, and lordly [trident],
may be fashioned in various designs from metal, wood, or other materials.
One should fashion those [mandalas], such as the conch and the lotus, with measurements according to one's preference, like the lotus itself;
O Lotus-born One, these are for rites preceded by the propitiation of mantras. (163)

One should fashion everything with its characteristic marks, including the pedestal, the water-jars (*kalaśa*), and so forth; likewise, the pearl rings, the ornaments such as bracelets and the like, and all the headgear beginning with the turban (*uṣṇīṣa*) that adorns the upper body. || 165 ||
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Kuṇḍa," in the Pauṣkara Saṃhitā, a Great Upaniṣad within the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
(Total number of verses: 165) Now begins the thirtieth chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
O Blessed One, O Acyuta, when the loss of knowledge and so forth has occurred for those devotees who practice mantras, for one established in yoga, and for one whose activity is virtuous— || 1 ||
I now wish to hear the means of protection by which, when performed, devotees attain the fulfillment of their purpose. || 2 ||
The Blessed Lord said: "O Brahmin, how may one who is devoted to ritual action obtain the desired fruit within a year through that rite, without the worship of Pavitra?"
Just as the Aśvamedha sacrifice fulfills all desires for Brahmins and the Rājasūya sacrifice does for kings, so too is this the ornament for my devotees.
Just as the Kaustubha is known to be the most excellent ornament among all ornaments, so too is the Pavitraka to be understood as the preeminent among the entire web of enjoyments.
Since it eternally fulfills for devotees the supreme activity of the Lord for the attainment of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, what enjoyment could possibly be superior to that? (6)
To his devotees, he indeed grants eternal residence in the same realm through constant devotion;
and to those who are practitioners, he grants proximity, endowed with various supernatural powers. (7)
It bestows union with its own mantra-self upon the foremost of practitioners once the Uttarāyaṇa has passed and during the middle of the Cāturmāsya period.
O Lotus-born One, one should perform [this rite] at the beginning or at the end, on all twelfth lunar days (dvādaśīs), on all transits of the sun (saṃkrāntis), and on full-moon days.
On all new moon days, as well as on every third lunar day,
under the asterisms sacred to Viṣṇu, and at all such auspicious moments.
On the twelfth lunar day that marks the conclusion of the four-month period, which is the divine Ṣaḍaśītimukha, whoever should perform the ritual installation on that day— 11.
The purificatory thread (pavitraka) of the source of the universe purifies one's own lineage— past, present, and future.
There, the Lord Hari, the Supreme Self and the infallible Acyuta, being personally present with various manifested forms, is pleased with his devotees.
Although Nārāyaṇa, whose essence is the mantra, is himself eternally present and situated within the lotus-born [Brahmā] for the sake of his devotees. 14.
Nevertheless, because of the power of the desire for that [result] in that ritual act, the Lord, the King of Mantras, assumes proximity to the practitioners. || 15 ||
Just as the sun reaches its peak intensity upon the arrival of the summer season,
yet without abandoning its own essential nature, it becomes even more proximate to the All-pervading Lord.
Indeed, for the sake of the non-emission and the maintenance of the worthy recipient, the place, and the time, there is the *pavitraka* in that [night], because it is impossible in any other. (17)

The person who is devoted to knowledge and action, performing his duties with devotion through ritual acts, becomes one whose actions are unbroken; such a person is a performer of the undivided [sacrifice]. (18)
Endowed with devotion, faith, and likewise enthusiasm, and possessed of the powers of yoga, one attains identity with Brahman very quickly, O Pauṣkara. (19)
With his entire being, he always protects his devotees’ every auspicious activity born of mind, speech, and heart.
Therefore, its essential nature as it truly is must be fully understood, as well as the fruit that comes to devotees through the completion of that [practice]. (21)
That which is the uncut, white expanse of the infinite extension of the source of the world,
itself undergoes fragmentation through its own manifold nature by those of unrefined knowledge.

The "world-thread" (jagatsūtra), however, is its ritual procedure performed with golden threads and the like; it assumes the sixfold qualities and the sense of self-identity through the nature of the *pratisara* cord. (23)
And it is colored by the passion for knowledge, joined with the effects born of vigor,
enveloped by the fiery mantras, and further encircled by power.
When the occasion for ritual service has arrived, one should perform the imperishable rite of sovereignty according to one's capacity;
thus, O Lord, the Pavitraka ceremony has been fully explained, though it does not belong to the Prabhū. (25)
When Viṣṇu, the supreme lord of Brahman, is established as its very form,
that which is offered according to rule with devotion bestows the station of the Blessed One.
And just as that gross, distinct [self] is to be conceptualized by means of categories established in common usage, listen to how that is so. (27)
The thread should be fine, firm, white, and smooth, spun by a girl born of the Brahmin caste,
or by a disciplined elderly woman.
Whether it has been prepared by a pure widow or obtained in whatever manner possible, one should take it and purify it with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra). || 29 ||
O twice-born one, having gazed [at the image] and performed the recollection of the root-mantra fourfold,
or eightfold if there is consideration for the fourfold nature [of the deity].
