In the various forms of the Blessed One, however, it is characterized by distinctions divided according to the differences [of the stones],
being three or fourfold in its presiding nature within Keśava and the others.
One should avoid the *rājasa* sacrifice with uneven threads of Viṣṇu, because that *pāvitrika* rite is uneven and belongs to no one [in its true sense]. 32.
(158) Purificatory rites (pāvitraka) should be performed with threads spun from those [fibers],
first for the mantra, the weapon, and the water-pot, and then for the abode of the various mantras.
The splendors of the principal deity named Maṇḍala, of everything contained therein,
of that which resides in the pericarp, and of that which goes to the filaments and petals.

Of the one whose form is the array of emanations (vibhavavyūha), and of the two [deities] characterized by the emblems and weapons, there is worship with flowers upon the head, the throat, the two shoulders, and above on the ground. || 35 ||
According to the authoritative measurement, there are four [units] for the image of the Lord of the World;
two for the sacrificial pit and the fire; and two for the scripture and the pedestal. 36.
Of the Lord who is the essence of speech and the reality of phonemes, and of the great-souled components of ritual action, beginning with the bell and the rosary; || 37 ||
While his wife was bowed with devotion and intent upon the worship of Hari, as were his kinsmen, friends, and those who practice the dharma of the Blessed One. (38)
And of his subsequent companions, those servants who desired the fourfold self, who were well-disposed toward him, and who performed sacrifices to Puruṣottama. || 39 ||
For the increase and purification of women,
this beautiful purifying rite should be performed in the proper sequence.

For the worship of the four locations of him who is established in the six paths and the seats, who is the locus of various mantras, and who possesses the distinctions of qualities such as knowledge; || 41 ||
O Lotus-born One, one should fashion the ornament for the Lord Mukhyamantra with a thread increased by eight hundred [units], or with half, or even with a quarter of that amount.
For this very reason, the number of recitations, oblations, and so forth—whether complete or deficient—is balanced by that very Self for the sake of the devotees' mantras. (43)
With gold, excellent jewels, camphor, mālaya-fragrance, sandalwood powder, and saffron;
combined with all medicinal herbs and mixed with cinnamon, cardamom, and other ingredients. || 44 ||
One should fashion its interior construction using various purifying substances along with pure cotton, marked by the number of threads and the weight in palas.
O lotus-eyed one, it is like a citron, a fresh myrobalan, or a conch shell;
furthermore, the spaces between them are joined by an uncut thread.
For the purpose of understanding the divisions, one should arrange [the mantras] nearby;
then, having assigned others as desired for the remaining sacrifices (yājyās), [one should proceed]. 47.

One should provide a collection of ornaments for the disciple together with the *sūtra*, *bhrama*, and *samopeta* types of *garbhas*, and two ornaments along with the *garbha* for the venerable teacher.
O Blessed One, because of the placement of mantras and the cultivation of identity [with them], this has been ordained;
therefore, O Heroic One, the ritual arrangement for others should be performed without a womb.
One should fashion an embryo situated within [the womb], adorned with Bāhlīka;
and having decorated it with golden figures on top. (50)
[The image should be fashioned] with cuttings of leaves or made of gold, [adorned] with the conch, discus, mace, lotus, garland, śrīvatsa, and kaustubha [jewel]. (51)
[He was armed] with the discus, the conch, the mace, the Nandaka sword, the bow, the plowshare, and other weapons;
he resembled the Mandāra flower and was like the Pārijāta tree. || 52 ||

It was enriched with the Śrīvṛkṣa, the mountain, the lord of serpents, the svastika, chowries, and jars; it was further adorned with the flames of the sacrificial fire on the altar, with various emblems, and with parasols.
With the networks of coils belonging to the serpents who are the bulls of the rivers and oceans, [he supports] either one or many, according to their respective places. (54)
Having placed it in a copper vessel made of metal and covered with cloth,
one should further cover it from above with unwashed cloth that has been fumigated with incense.
Having performed his daily rites on the tenth day, the performer, being restrained and pure,
accompanied by the eminent preceptor, should be intent upon offering water for the guest-offering (arghya) and flowers for the purpose of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa).
Accompanied by the sound of the sacred Vedic chants and those reciting hymns of praise and auspicious verses,
he performed the worship of the door-keepers at the time of the moon's rising and entered.
Having sat down in a pavilion shaped like the world of Vairāja and adorned with ornaments, one should begin the internal sacrifice according to the prescribed rule. (58)
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) first, one should prepare the entire offering of water (arghyāmbu);
then, for the sake of attaining the fruit of being free from obstacles, one should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa.
One should perform the Brahmakūrca rite and then purify the ground;
this includes the installation of the arches and other structures, their worship, and the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
One should perform everything— the arrangement of the mantra, the weapon, and the pitcher, as well as the descent of the mantra upon those two,
and their worship and so forth— in the same manner as the procedure for initiation.
One should perform the divine practice while remembering the All-pervading Lord through *kumbhaka* [retention of breath];
since one cannot remain engaged [in this] incessantly, this is the prescribed remedy.
The mantra-practitioner should indeed visualize the sacrificial pit as a protective weapon;
then, having brought [the deity] down, the Blessed One should worship the seat upon the sacrificial ground.
Having performed the recitation without error until its conclusion, one should proceed to the presence of the image;
having prostrated with the eight limbs, one should offer the arghya water upon the head.
Then, with devotion, one should offer a beautiful handful of flowers accompanied by ointment and incense to Puruṣottama, together with his limbs and retinue.
Having set aside everything offered at midday, such as the flower-worship and other rites,
and having taken it up with his head, he bowed down and worshipped it thoroughly.
Then, having purified the water with the weapon-mantra of Viṣvaksena,
one should purify the image of the Blessed One along with its pedestal, and subsequently the temple.
One should bathe the Lord of the Gods with rites prescribed by the ritual manuals,
using ablutions such as the *brahmakūrca* and others, performed according to the application of mantras.

Then, one should worship according to the prescribed rite with fruits that correspond to the various ritual objects, which have been duly consecrated according to one's capacity and are accompanied by gems and other such items.
Having performed everything with devotion, including all natural enjoyments as prescribed in due order, one should conclude with prostrations and proceed to the sacrificial chamber.
There, having consecrated the fire, one should indeed perform the satiation with mantras by means of the fire consecrated by the water from the jar and the image.
One should cook the *caru* on the hearth with milk, ghee, and rice while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*;
having then lifted it out and purified it with ghee, one should present it in the proper sequence.
Then, one should offer a single portion of the oblations remaining in the vessel;
afterwards, one should give the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), filling the entire interval with sacrificial offerings (bali).
Having performed the libation with water-sprinkled offerings, one should then offer oblations in sequence;
likewise, having fully prepared the clarified butter, one should indeed perform the binding of the mudrās and so forth.
Having performed the prostrations up to the point of bowing down before the Lord standing upon the ground,
one should then consecrate the entire collection of ritual substances with the Astra-mantra.

Having established everything in the direction of the wind (the northwest) according to the sequence of the ritual lines, [he should do so] with a body clothed in white garments and protected by armor.
Having worshipped it with the weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should cover it with the armor-mantra (kavaca);
then, all eight arrows, together with their external feathers, [should be prepared].
Having offered clarified butter into the fire-altar while reciting the Astra-mantra in all directions and intermediate points,
[one should encircle it] with a firm five-colored thread or one that is very white.
Recalling the fourfold circumambulation, one should complete the armor;
likewise, one should encircle [the area] from the interior of the mouthful to its exterior. (79)
Facing east and seated upon his seat, he should drink the *brahmakūrca* poured from the hand of the Guru, and afterwards, he should eat the remainder of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
One should drink water infused with gold, gems, and kuśa grass, over which one has recited the heart-mantra; thereafter, one should consume betel leaf together with a tooth-stick.
Having sat upon a woolen rug provided with a blanket and a layer of kuśa grass,
one should recite the supreme mantra along with its ancillaries, while chanting auspicious, excellent hymns of praise.
Having performed the meritorious discourse concerning the Sovereign of All, having completed the mandala,
and having then carried out the remaining rites as prescribed for the ornaments, (verse 83).
On the eleventh day at dawn, having performed worship preceded by bathing, one should offer oblations according to the proper rite until the final complete oblation is given. (84)
Having approached the region of the water-pot (kalaśa), one should perform the offering; then, for the sake of inviting the Lord to the special enjoyments, [one should proceed]. 85.
A tooth-stick, betel with its accompaniments, mouth-perfumes, a mirror, sandalwood and other fragrant substances, and nutmegs and areca nuts; || 86 ||
Then, having placed before the Lord of the World on his right side,
he offered guggulu resin and refined incense, as well as a lamp in a copper vessel.
The ornament of the circle of light, a golden thread with a bracelet, and yellow pigment and collyrium in a metallic vessel filled with honey and clarified butter. || 88 ||
One should offer the six flavors to the Great Form, and white and red cloths to the eyes; then, one should likewise offer the water of a sacred river to the Lord in the western direction.

Whatever mountain-grown fruits such as bilva and the like, grassy plots, and blue darbha grass were intended for the purpose of enjoying the water of sacred fords and food, [he placed them] in a copper vessel for the crow. (90)
Then, O Puṣkara, one should offer to the Lord of Gods, the All-pervading One, garlands, medicinal herbs, the seven types of seeds, and fruits in the north.
Bowls of sesame seeds and rice, milk, the essence of curd, and clarified butter; fragrant substances such as cardamom and cinnamon; juices and minerals such as red ochre and the like. || 92 ||
The coconut fruit is fruitful, as is every product derived from sugarcane; these shine when placed in a bell-metal vessel, O Lotus-born One, provided they are available. (93)
Or, in the absence of these, the offering may be presented in a vessel made of sacrificial leaves;
for others, water with kuśa grass, betel leaf, and a tooth-stick [should be provided]. 94.
White garments, upper cloths, and sacred threads, along with sandalwood, saffron, agallochum, camphor, and white sandalwood, were all perfumed with these fragrances. (95)
One should offer a fragrant purifier to the one who has entered the four stations;
thereafter, one should present the water-offering (arghya), flowers, and incense, and perform the binding of the mudrās.

At the beginning, middle, and end, one should recite the supreme mantra together with its ancillaries for the sake of perfect, flawless peace; thereafter, with palms joined in reverence, one should recite [the following].
One should offer the first hymn-mantra with the knowledge of the Praṇava:
"O Infinite One, consisting of all mantras, eternally present and imperishable. (98)
O Lord of yoga, whose body is the enjoyment of creative contemplation, in whom qualities are both subordinate and primary;
O Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman, Lord of the vital breath, you who possess four forms! 99.
O All-pervading One, O You who have not fallen from Your true form, O Omniscient One, Supreme Person!
From this very moment until the day of Your departure—100.
O Lord, endowed with various groups of mantras,
grant your presence within my divine image, its physical form, the ritual pitcher, and the ground of the mandala.
In the counting-thread, in the rosary, in the fire, in the form of the Guru, in the bell, on the seat of the scriptures, and in the ritual implements for sacrifice; || 102 ||

In all matters such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, those who are single-mindedly devoted [to the Lord], and among the various attendants (*pārṣada*) of Viṣṇu who take delight in their births and duties (*carma-karma*). || 103 ||
Indeed, for those who are purified by faith, skillful, and have you as their sole refuge, [there is the fruit] of past actions such as ritual bathing and the like. 104.
For the sake of fulfilling the occasional and the obligatory rites that have remained incomplete,
and for your own pleasure, I shall today perform [this] today.
The ritual procedure for the purifier (*pavitraka*) and all rites [are completed]; therefore, this [text] has been honored as the essence of the oral tradition. 106.
Perform the preliminary consecration ending with the fire-oblation; make everything one's own. When the vigil has passed, [worship] you... || 107 ||

(161) O Blessed One, you have been requested here by means of the various sections of the Brahma-sūtras, which grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation; O Blessed One, you know everything that dwells within the heart. 108.
"Out of affection for me, your devotee, you should grant me favor this morning.
Having thus invited Him, one should prostrate on the ground with the eight limbs [of the body]. (109)

Having circumambulated [the deity] four times while recollecting the mantra in his heart, he should worship with songs, dances, and other offerings, accompanied by hymns of praise and the recitation of the Vedas. || 110 ||
One should pass the night in a vigil accompanied by shouts of "Victory!";
then, having bathed during the Brahma-muhūrta and performed the auspicious rites for the marriage-thread ceremony, [one should proceed].
First, one should perform the sacrifice at the gateway with great magnificence;
thereafter, O Pauṣkara, one should duly perform the sacrifice to the Blessed One.

By means of various tactile objects such as seats and other ritual implements, as well as those intended for pleasing the senses— produced in many varieties and known for their heart-pleasing qualities— (113)
With various kinds of foods to be chewed, eaten, licked, and sucked,
as well as all the auspicious vegetables, roots, and fruits produced in the six seasons.

With purifying items steamed over fire, accompanied by side dishes and the like, consisting of stable products derived from cows, served in bronze vessels filled with honey and clarified butter. || 115 ||

It was like the ocean with its various seas filled with juices, milk, and curds situated in every direction; it was provided with betel leaves and nuts in measured portions, along with appropriate inner furnishings.
Together with excellent beds, purifying objects dear to oneself, and natural pleasures arising from one's own country or foreign lands, [one should enjoy]. (117)

With vessels made of gold, adorned with perfumes, garlands, and other ornaments, one should perform [the rite] in this manner in the presence of the maṇḍala, ending with the recitation and the mudrās. 118.
Having performed the sacrifice to the Blessed One, especially in the temple of the deity,
one should then take up the vessel of ornaments, open it, and worship it.
Taking up the *pavitraka*, he should go to the vicinity of the water-jar (*kalaśa*),
for that collection of limbs of worship is indeed unmanifest and pertaining to the ultimate reality (*tattva*).

The third indeed consists of both; likewise, having integrated the triad beginning with the internal (ādhyātmika), one should indeed recollect it within that [Self] by means of the intellect from the heart.
Therein, the collection of eight times eight, which is unmanifest and comprises the gathering of enjoyments,
is proclaimed as the assembly of mantras and mudrās that pertains to the ultimate reality.
Vedic recitation, singing, instrumental music, vows, observances, gifts preceded by festivals, and various occasional rites; || 123 ||
These, possessing both forms, bestow the goals of human life and grant delight to Janārdana, the source of the universe, who is the very embodiment of mantra.
That which is radiant, consisting of consciousness, pure, and their imperishable form—subtle and like a lotus-petal, that should be contemplated within their wombs. 125.
O Great-minded One, that which resembles the sun, the moon, and fire, and is conceived as having a measurable extent, should be meditated upon within the locations of the multitude of knots. 126.
The gross, the conventional, and the third, which is universal—
these should indeed always be contemplated as the locus for the collection of the threads of reality.
Having thus characterized the internal pervasion, O Pauṣkara,
one should contemplate the mantric pervasion known as the "presiding deity," which moves within the mind.
That form which is inseparable from the four, comparable to nectar,
filled with a multitude of diverse appearances, both manifest and unmanifest, and imperishable— 129.
O great-minded one, one should constantly contemplate the presence of the three— the crown, the Śrīvatsa mark, and the Kaustubha gem— as the supreme deity.
The beautiful and auspicious form, produced from the union of the five elements—earth, water, fire, air, and ether—brings complete satisfaction to his devotees. 131.
And its status as the presiding deity over the elements should be understood within the range of a *yojana*.
Having meditated thus, O Lotus-born One, one should utter the end of the root mantra. (132)
With hands raised, he should recite that mantra adorned with the *praṇava*,
O Lord, which is the stainless, supreme knowledge that is the means for attaining you. (133)
Devotion accompanied by faith, along with the performance of sacred rites, reveals you;
indeed, you have declared that this is the means for the attainment of the indivisible perfection.
By your grace, I have composed this work called the *Pavitra*, according to my ability, for the sake of those devotees whose souls are purified and who are devoted to both knowledge and action. (135)
Now, meditate upon that Supreme Goddess as is appropriate;
for knowledge which is stainless is indeed a more auspicious action than that.
You alone are indeed the other injunction beyond the collection of mantras, the assembly of substances, the attainment, and the fulfiller of incomplete rites. || 137 ||
O Blessed One, by this truth, may every part of your ritual practice remain unimpaired for you, who are free from deceit and afflicted by the destruction of worldly existence. (138)
O Blessed One, I have made my request here; my longing for you is supreme, until my complete satisfaction through you, the bestower of perfect knowledge. (139)
But when a time of calamity has arrived, O Acyuta, ritual action and knowledge must not be abandoned intentionally; you know all this in its true essence.
O Lord, because you have not been properly honored by me with appropriate enjoyments at the proper time and in the proper manner, there is distress in my heart.
Worship with the enjoyment of sensory objects and satiation with the milk of sovereignty—none of this is of any use to those who have accomplished their purpose in you. 142.
"For this entire [teaching] of mine, sown in a fertile field, will bear fruit as immortality; indeed, knowing this, I [bestowed it] in the past. (143)
It was accepted from the mouth of my guru, O Lord, Sovereign of All; yet it does not flash forth clearly in my intellect as it truly stands, nor has it been fully realized.

From the activities of mind, speech, and body, from the time of night until dawn, [the self is not the agent] because of the lack of independence, the incapacity [of the body], and the instability of the mind. (145)
O Lord, due to obstacles such as cold, heat, wind, rain, and the like, as well as fevers and other ailments,
the constituent elements of the ritual— which correspond to Your own nature— fail to be fully realized.
The daily ritual (āhnika) culminates in the attainment of supreme bliss until the cessation [of worldly activity];
however, as it has been stated, this is not possible for the immortals (gods). 147.
To fulfill that [requirement], however, there is a most excellent worship called Pavitraka, which has been prescribed by you for every year. (148)

Whatever has been performed by me through direct perception and whatever has been worshipped that was not stainless, and whatever was incomplete due to a deficiency in ritual action—lead all of that to purity for me. (149)
Whether through knowledge or ignorance, whatever has been spoken by me as prescribed may all that be entirely fulfilled; may you always remain fully satisfied. 150.
O Imperishable One, Lord of the World, Eternal Form of Mantra!
Protect me, O Lotus-eyed One; forgive me, O Unborn One; be gracious, Om! (151)
Having thus uttered the root mantra together with the marks such as the heart-mantra and others, one should then place it upon the head of the Lord, whose essence is the mantra.
[He is] the embodiment of all-knowing wisdom, activity, enjoyment, and virtuous intention;
thus [he is visualized] both within the mandala and situated inside the temple. (153)
O Mahāmati, even for one situated in the midst of fire, having placed [the object] upon it,
by means of worship and enclosing it within a *puṭa*, it becomes purifying and sacred.
Then, having given the ritual implements to the teacher—who is the very self of the scripture—having placed him within his own heart and honored him like a deity; 155.
Then, being well-pleased, he [the sage] began with a blessing for the sake of his complete success,
as he stood near the sacrificial fire together with his wife.
Or at the conclusion of the oblation, or at the end of the recitation for others, according to the sequence;
then, with coverings and gifts gathered according to one's means. (157)

O Brahmin, [he should be honored] with sacred threads and upper garments, accompanied by umbrellas and sandals, with various kinds of food, incense, and offerings such as the touching of the body (ālabhana), and so forth. (158)
O Pauṣkara, one should honor all the brāhmaṇas as well as those ascetics who are well-versed in the means [of practice],
having concluded [the rite] after three nights or seven days.
Having first performed the great worship and concluding with the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti),
one should gradually withdraw [the ritual] either by oneself or through the Guru as one's own Lord.
Having taken the consecrated vessel and worshipped it according to the prescribed rite,
he should place his knees upon the ground and prostrate before the preceptor.
Having first honored him with offerings of water for the feet, flowers, and so forth, and having prostrated himself, he should present that vessel, saying: "O Lord, please grant your favor. (162)
The preceptor should pronounce a blessing for him, consisting of devotion to the Blessed One,
in accordance with tradition and scripture, through the grace of the Fourfold Self.
"O Brahmin, may that year-long [observance] be perfectly fulfilled for you while you remain seated upon the head of him who is thus proclaiming it. (164)
One should perform the dismissal of the Lord according to the sequence, preceded by worship, using the two mantras for the jars which bestow protection, good fortune, and liberation. (165)
One should worship Viṣvaksena along with his limbs (attendants), and immediately thereafter offer libations;
afterwards, having withdrawn everything, one should perform the formal dismissal.
Having arranged the drinking of Soma as before for the sake of achieving flawlessness,
[he should do so] in a vessel fashioned from gold, silver, or fine jewels, or one that is beautifully adorned.
Upon the base of the wheel, within the expanded interior of the jar, [is she] whose neck has the folds of the Pāñcajanya conch and whose face is as beautiful as a hundred-petaled lotus. 168.
O Lotus-born One, adorned by circles of moonlight garlands above and below, with the streams of nectar-water flowing from the mouths of the serpent Śeṣa in the form of a sea-monster! 169.
Adorned with rivers, oceans, śrīvṛkṣas, fish, and garlands—thus endowed with these marks—for the sake of propitiating the All-pervading Lord. (170)

In the offering of water for the feet, the arghya, the water for sipping, and the bath; likewise, during the annual festival and also during the ritual of consecration with a thousand jars (sahasrakalaśa). || 171 ||
Thus has been described the supreme Pavitrāropaṇa rite, O lotus-eyed one, which always protects the devotees on earth from deficiencies, excesses, and other such faults. || 172 ||
By performing its completion with devotion, a Brāhmaṇa becomes a knower of the Vedas;
a Kṣatriya indeed becomes illustrious, possessed of extremely fierce power, and endowed with unbroken progeny. || 173 ||
The Vaiśya shall be endowed with wealth and grain, and the Śūdra shall be possessed of happiness; indeed, such is the fruit of infinite gifts of cows, land, and gold. || 174 ||
A man shall obtain that same fruit by giving for a hundred years every day what was given throughout his entire life, once his maximum lifespan is complete.
When the time has arrived, having reached the abode of Hari by means of his own intellect,
he properly creates a body while correctly recollecting the Lord of Mantras.
Being fanned by vehicles resembling the moon and accompanied by celestial women,
he goes to heaven while being honored likewise by the immortals.
Having enjoyed vast pleasures arising from all the various worlds,
after a long time, one indeed returns once again to human birth.
He is born at an auspicious time, in an auspicious place, and into an auspicious family;
and when childhood has passed, his collection of faculties becomes manifest.
But when the principle of the intellect (buddhitattva) has been awakened through the power of practice over many births, one should become devoted to Nārāyaṇa in deed, mind, and speech. || 180 ||
The wise man is constantly devoted to ritual action, dedicated to Brahman, truthful in his prowess, unwavering, pure in soul, and free from the company of the wicked. || 181 ||
Freed from disease and grief, endowed with sons, wife, and other kin, and liberated from untimely death, he attains stainless knowledge. (182)
One attains Śvetadvīpa, which is very difficult even for the gods to reach;
having beheld the Lord of the Universe there, [one attains it] even more so than other wise men. || 183 ||
That person who is devoted to that ritual action attains the state of the Supreme Brahman;
those who behold the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) of the Lord of the Universe being placed [upon him] perceive it as such.
Likewise, others who rejoice in this also go to Amarāvatī;
so too those who hear this sacred rite which destroys all sins. (185)
And they indeed obtain whatever merit there is from sacrifices, charitable works, and the like—provided that the woman has no other refuge and is urged by her husband. (186)
Devoted to him, she was virtuous and chaste in deed, thought, and speech;
she was ever free from malice toward her husband and remained self-restrained in every limb.
The Lotus-born One also places the purifying thread upon the Source of the World;
by doing so, one shall indeed attain fortune along with prosperity before long.
At the end of her body, she attains the status of being worshiped by celestial women and gods;
she gazes downward at those headed by Arundhatī.
O Lotus-born One, at the end one attains that knowledge by which one goes to the imperishable state, and by which one delivers one's kinsmen from their evil deeds. 190.

O Brahmin, the mantra-practitioner, being the very self of the mantra, gives an ornament to the all-pervading Lord preceded by affection, under the names of the ancestors such as Janaka and others. (191)
Men who have bathed in the waters of the celestial river go from an evil rebirth to a happy one; for as is nectar to the gods, so is the water of the Gaṅgā to men. 192.
O Lotus-born One, just as the *svadhā* offering is for the ancestors who perform rituals, so too is the *pavitraka* for those rich in sacred rites; it is purifying and increases prosperity. (193)
It destroys all faults and fears, annihilates all calamities, bestows all happiness, and reveals all secrets. (194)
He who is a perfect devotee of the Blessed One, having undertaken the mastery of mantras,
proceeds in this very manner through constant worship, whether by inclination or through the habituation of birth.
Indeed, with single-minded devotion toward Viṣṇu, the supreme Parameṣṭhin,
one should strive with great effort to obtain such a teacher.
O Lotus-born One, due to the absence of one's own teacher and because he is not present, the initiation should be performed by another teacher who has been requested to do so. (197)
Neither by deed, nor by mind, nor by speech—nor by any other inferior means—should one who is established in another doctrine associate with my devotees who are devoted solely to me. (198)
For the spiritual teacher must be sought out for the performance of the *pavitrārohaṇa* and other rites, even though the internal witness knows me as I truly am. (199)
Because he was so devoted to one whose purpose was accomplished, I then considered him my guru;
I consider a guru who has arrived as a deliverer [only] through the power of devotion. (200)

Where there is such equilibrium of the mental fluctuations of these three—the disciple, the teacher, and the mantra—there is liberation according to the Tantra and the attainment of supernatural powers (siddhis). || 201 ||
He who, knowing this, nevertheless behaves toward devotees as one who is not devoted, and bestows mantras upon disciples—he, the lowest of men, goes to hell. (202)
Devotion previously accumulated gradually becomes manifest to devotees through contact with those [devotees], through their conduct, and by avoiding the censure of the mantra and the deity. (203)

Therefore, whatever [cognition] clearly arises from an object and has that object as its domain—whether belonging to others or to oneself—that is traditionally held to be the means for establishing it. (204)
Where the teachers possess unwavering devotion, and where the disciples likewise have the desire for worship, right there [should it be performed]. (205)
Then, O Lotus-born One, the supreme mantra (or lord of mantras), being pleased, becomes present.
Such is the activity of one who has attained perfection, possesses equanimity, and is indeed beyond action. (206)
Know that the ritual action of anyone other than this is preceded by devotion; and that devotion directed toward Him is considered equal to the conduct of a devoted wife. (207)
Possessing the eight characteristics, complete, purified by faith, and bestowing liberation;
other than this, success (siddhi) bestows only the fruits of deviation. 208.
I stand as a witness to all, and I know their inner disposition according to reality;
for when their devotion toward me is indeed unswerving, [by those two]. (209)
I favor the disciple through the essence of the mantra by means of the guru’s mouth;
therefore, one who is not a devotee should never be initiated, but only one who is devoted.
One who is not devoted should not be joined with one who is excessively devoted in your worship;
for those who are devoted, devotion toward one who lacks devotion toward the Guru leads to torment.
Physical and mental suffering increases moment by moment; through this, one's mental cultivation turns toward sensuality, whereby one goes to a most inferior state.
O Lotus-born One, for devotees who have no other refuge than the Guru,
the two-fold and three-fold defects quickly come to destruction.
He truly cannot endure great infamy or malice directed toward a guru who is worthy of favor, yet who is ungrateful, arrogant, and devoid of ritual action.
And for one who has been initiated, there is the presence of intolerable defects;
therefore, with every effort, [one should act] for the sake of attaining the unseen fruit. 215.
Whatever duty has been prescribed must be performed by both the disciple and the teacher;
one who lacks devotion does not attain true knowledge, nor does one who lacks devotion attain meditative concentration.
One who is not a devotee does not understand the proper ritual service; one who is not a devotee cannot be a knower of the scriptures.
Likewise, one who is not a devotee should not worship an image, perform a sacrifice, or offer worship to the sacred fire.
One should cause him to wear the *namudrā* and make him hear the *samayas*, provided he has not committed an offense out of greed toward those who lack devotion for the Teacher of the World. (218)
If a teacher, out of delusion, approaches those who understand the meaning of the contrary [teachings] and whose nature is devoted to derision, he goes to hell. (219)
"O Lotus-born One, regarding that which was asked by you, it has been stated: 'If one afflicted by suffering does not perform the previously mentioned expiation... (220)
For the benefit of his devotees, the auspicious Pavitrārohaṇa rite was performed when the rainy season had set in, for those dwelling within the belly of the three worlds.
It should be told to humans, gods, and siddhas who follow [the teachings]:
they indeed proceed with great speed through faith for every year.
In this great undertaking of the Supreme Lord, involving the Greatly Intelligent One,
while the All-pervading Lord remained in repose during that season abundant with flowers and fruits.
While the sky was being overspread by clouds accompanied by cranes, and the surface of the earth was adorned with white, blue, and red lotuses; 224.
In forests, groves, and gardens, provided with green grassy plots and the like, endowed with rice crops and other grains, and beautified by the waters of ponds; || 225 ||
The *pavitraka* rite performed for Viṣṇu, who resides within, bestows supreme satisfaction;
O Brahmin, his practice of sleeping [during the month] was previously ordained for him at all times. (226)
Then, O Brahmin, when that day has been completed by those two,
the ritual sacrifice (karmayāga) must certainly be protected by those devoted to the performance of rites.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Investiture of the Sacred Thread," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā of the Great Upaniṣad within the illustrious Prāñcarātra. || 30 ||
Now begins the thirty-first chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
O high-minded one, having performed the Pavitrārohaṇa rite during the Cāturmāsya period, [one should proceed as follows].
It is to be brought to completion through various observances honored by the world. || 1 ||
One should worship this bed of the God and Goddess; hear now the procedure for that:
[it should be] inlaid with gold and other gems, and adorned on all its parts. (2)
And upon a couch suited to the Blessed One, white as the moon, adorned with a white parasol, yak-tail whisks, and excellent small bells; || 3 ||
It was attended by the Vaijayantī host, adorned with golden staffs at its base,
decorated with a divine canopy, and embellished with saffron and other fragrant substances.
It was beautified above, covered with horizontal and vertical cloths,
and filled with nutmegs and the like, parched grain, and all kinds of seeds.
One should meditate upon him on this couch, which is provided with variegated cloths at its corners, strewn with heaps of excellent flowers, and furnished with jewel-lamps.

O high-minded one, [meditate upon] the Lord of Nagas, who dwells in the midst of the Ocean of Milk, whose crown consists of a thousand hoods, and who is as white as snow, the jasmine flower, and the moon.
Having visualized [the deity] with the syllable *praṇava*, one's own name ending in a consonant and accompanied by the nasal bindu (*m*),
and having worshipped, praised, bowed down, and propitiated [him].
Having placed upon it the image of the Goddess of Action (Karmārcā), adorned with necklaces and armlets, anointed with sandalwood, camphor, and bāhlīka, and encircled with flowers; || 9 ||
Having covered [the image] with a cloth over the eyes, well-perfumed with created forms, one should recite its own seed-mantra syllable: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Lord of Lakṣmī. (10)
Having mentally articulated the beautiful [mantra] in the sequence of its limbs and sub-limbs, together with the syllables of the twelve letters joined with the words of one's own name. || 11 ||
However, in the absence of an image made of ritual materials (karmārcā), one should place an auspicious seat made of darbha-grass clusters according to the prescribed injunctions.
Having placed that supreme mantra within it from the interior of the sky of one's own lotus,
[one perceives it] situated in the midst of the cage of all the Śaktis, beginning with Gaṇḍā, who are concealed therein.
Having led [the devotee] through the gift of the forms of the individual deities while absorbed in meditation,
[he should offer] a garment honored by the limbs of the gods, unworn and of pure nature.
Having offered and worshipped it above with flowers, incense, and ointments, one should deposit the power of consciousness (citi-śakti), which is the withdrawal of all principles (tattvas). || 15 ||
To the right, however, is the form named Abhimāna, holding aloft a chowrie;
likewise, on the left is Jñānaniśā, holding aloft a palm-leaf fan.
One should meditate on the supreme [form of] Nidrā, who delights in massaging the hands,
standing at the region of the lotus-feet and caressing them with her lotus-hands.
Having taken her two divine feet, Śrī herself stands in close proximity;
she is the bliss that is the form of Brahman, the deity of deities unto him. 18.
With eyes filled with wonder born from the bliss of remembering Him within, they should be worshipped with their own names, words, and mantras, preceded by the syllable Om (praṇava). || 19 ||
O Lotus-born One, having thus properly installed this bed for the God of Gods according to the prescribed rite, men who observe the Cāturmāsya vow [should do so]. (20)
Daily worship should be performed here, as well as cleaning and smearing with clay or mineral derivatives, or with fragrant substances such as sandalwood and the like.
The offering of incense and lamps, fanning with a fan to raise a breeze, and the hospitable service of cool water mixed with moon-fragrance and sandalwood. (22)
Having brought about the cessation of perspiration with plantain leaves, white water-lilies, and lotuses mixed with blue water-lilies, one should perform worship repeatedly. (23)
And there was singing with sweet tones, accompanied by flutes and lutes;
thus, when two months had passed, the roar of clouds arose from the sky.
O Brahmin, on the twelfth day of the month of Bhādrapada, at the onset of night,
the God of gods, Adhokṣaja, indeed resorts to a slight awakening.
For the sake of the stability of the immortals, one should perform the ritual rotation, leaving the supine position by means of the assembly of limbs on the right side. (26)
O Pauṣkara, resorting to yogic sleep and bringing about both manifestation and dissolution, [the Lord] dwells within the axle of the wheel of the vital breaths, which is the seed of the universe.
Then, from the lunar orb at Mūla, having drunk the covering waters,
this Supreme Lord [resides] on the twelfth day of the month of Āśvayuja when the sun has set.
He should abandon his divine bed during the night of Kārttika;
then, rising like the Lord of the Immortals, he should stride forth as the sovereign of birds.
For the sake of pacifying the defects of all the streets of the entire multitude of worlds,
he whose self is immeasurable wanders about, bringing joy to those beginning with the gods.
"Displaying his own path of dharma in this world, his great deeds should be performed by his devotees in this manner. (31)
Through various auspicious festivals, acts of charity, prayers, and vigils, accompanied by human songs and melodies, as well as playful diversions joined with laughter. || 32 ||
O Brahmin, they were always playing with joyful minds, self-restrained, bowed down before the Lord, standing in one place with their thoughts fixed on no other.
Indeed, for the remaining month, those capable great men devoted to austerity must once again protect it within their own hermitage or in the sacred field of Amarakaṇṭaka.
O Brahmin, [one may perform it] with a twelve-night rite, a six-night auspicious rite,
or, O Lotus-born One, if there is incapacity, with a three-night rite or even a single day and night.
Then these four auspicious vows should be observed by men who abstain from food at night,
who are devoted to month-long fasts, and who are supreme Vaiṣṇavas.
Beforehand, one should perform the vigil for Acyuta for three nights, two nights, or one night, with meritorious narrations and songs preceded by hymns of praise. (37)
With savory and sweet dances, with laughter that brings joy, with shouts of "Victory! and salutations accompanied by the clapping of hands; || 38 ||
One should worship Śrīnivāsa while offering oblations, meditating, and reciting prayers,
with abundant ritual services including enjoyments preceded by the six flavors.
On the twelfth lunar day, during the Brahma-muhūrta, one should worship Hari, who is the embodiment of the mantra, with water-offerings (arghya), ointments, garlands, and prepared incense.
O Great-minded One, [he was honored] with the sounds of conchs accompanied by the resonance of dundubhī and paṭaha drums, and with the various lofty words uttered by throngs of bards.
Then, having raised [the deity] from the bed with hymns characterized by awakening and with great shouts of "Victory! Victory! uttered again and again; 42.
Then, with great magnificence, one should worship in due order within the mandala and other [sacred sites],
preceded by a grand ablution and with all the aforementioned enjoyments in their fullness.
With many great lamps, along with clusters of seed-vessels containing sprouts, and fruits beginning with the jackfruit, all anointed with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds.

With flowers, water-offerings, sandalwood paste, and other such items, adorned with the sacred thread (brahmasūtra), and with clusters of blossoms from jasmine, Arabian jasmine, and other varieties; || 45 ||
With rafts provided with straight branches from the Kadamba, Cūta, and Śrīvṛkṣa trees, connected by cords, and well-worshipped with saffron and other offerings; || 46 ||

Having thus performed the sacrifice, including the concluding oblations (homa), with various gifts such as cows, land, gold, and the like, as well as auspicious upper garments, one may [bestow] a village, a city, or a house. (47)
By means of a vehicle equipped with a purifier (pavitra), beautiful wheels, and mantras, missiles, and a water-pot, or by means of its interior image; || 48 ||
Accompanied by the sound of Vedic chanting and provided with songs and instrumental music, the courtesans who were devotees of the Lord, together with the citizens, [performed]. (49)
Accompanied by wandering mendicants and celibate students devoted to silent recitation and praise,
he was escorted by a great procession adorned with banners and covered by white umbrellas.
Burning fragrant incense, as well as various types of *sāmya* and *guggulu*,
and having thus circumambulated the vehicle, one should bestow wealth upon those who seek it.
Then, having circumambulated him and prostrated four times with all his limbs like a staff upon the ground out of devotion to Puruṣottama, || 52 ||
While standing on the chariot or at the temple, praising him with his mind and reciting prayers,
he should scatter parched grain, white mustard seeds, and fruits upon the arghya-water and flowers.
Just as one visualizes the deity of a particular direction, so too should one visualize all directions;
by means of this, one should traverse the entire abode and indeed bind the stability [of the mandala]. 54.
For His devotees, the Blessed Lord is not obstructed by space, time, or other such factors during their devotion;
this is what is called "circumambulation," common to all embodied beings. (55)
When thoroughly practiced and fully mastered, it bestows the imperishable state;
one should perform it with both knees and hands, or with the two knees alone. (56)
Once at the end of the year, or on the three junctures and the twelfth days of the lunar fortnights, or likewise at the conclusion of a sacrifice, with the head bowed down; 57.

Having thoroughly honored [the deities], he then bestows the fruit of the dispositions and actions of practitioners without delay; at the end of the body, the majestic worlds are attained in succession.
Having performed the sacrifice with supreme devotion, he thus bowed down to Adhokṣaja,
who was to be honored with circumambulations accompanied by prostrations.
Indeed, by visiting all sacred fields and wandering to all holy fords,
the Blessed One bestows the fruit upon the devotee who worships his feet.
By whomsoever the form of Hari, whose self is mantra, has been circumambulated,
he has been left behind by the defects born of worldly existence after they themselves have circumambulated him.
For those devotees of purified soul who are dedicated to the service of the Blessed One,
this southern activity on the auspicious path is most excellent.
Because it is equal to the sphere of gnosis and because it revolves like a wheel,
it bestows constant auspiciousness and exhausts the accumulation of afflictions.
For those who are devoted to the service of the Blessed One, for those dwelling in temples, or for others who are devotees, [the offering] consists of the faculties of action and speech. (64)
In the inner sanctum of Viṣṇu, or in the pavilion for the removal of the image from the womb,
one should perform a series of prostrations without a series of circumambulations.
Since the sight of the back of the hand of the pervasive Lord residing within the fire causes defects,
so too does the body of those whose form is mantra cause a lack of accomplishment.
Having performed a circumambulation of the knees while remaining close to the Lord within,
O Brahmin, there is no other conduct more contrary for devotees than wandering about his feet.
Likewise, those mounted on sandals or shoes, or wearing umbrellas and turbans;
those seated in vehicles, horses, or palanquins; and those chewing betel and the like. (68)
Carrying a plaything, a bird, a stick, a mirror, or a cosmetic implement, he may laugh, or rejoice, or sigh with delight, or chatter much. (69)

One who, with a provoked mind, engages in playful dalliance and amorous sport, yet wanders about seeking auspicious results, shall not obtain fruit from this tree, even though he is filled with haste. (70)

Therefore, one who desires what is auspicious should always perform [this rite] with a mind focused on nothing else, with an inner self absorbed in that, whether at home, in a temple, or on a mountain. (71)
O Mahāmati, because the single-liṅga (ekabera) bestows abundant fruit with little effort,
is infinite, and is the supreme means for bringing about great liberation.
Having thus circumambulated [the deity] and offered a handful of flowers,
one should then cause [the deity] to descend from the chariot, preceded by the mantra-consecration of the wheels.
Then, having again performed worship with the hands joined in the *mudrā* gesture,
one should offer libations of clarified butter and other substances, and finally present the auspicious *pūrṇāhuti*.
One should ask forgiveness from Puruṣottama by offering the guest-water (arghya), incense, and other such items;
likewise, one should present a boat and an umbrella along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
O Brahmin, having prostrated before his own guru, or in his absence before the twice-born, he should place both knees upon the ground and, with palms joined in reverence, recite this: || 76 ||
O Lord, Sovereign of All, by this rite may all people attain an entirely auspicious state; may you, for your part, experience supreme delight.
Thereafter, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas with various kinds of food and drink, along with gifts of dakṣiṇā given with faith for the sake of the satisfaction of the lineage of the ancestors. (78)
Then, accompanied by his kinsmen and servants, he should perform the concluding sacrifice (anuyāga);
or, if he possesses the means, O Lotus-born One, it should be performed in this manner by those who are unperturbed.

The Lord should be beheld by the immortal gods as situated in the Brahma-chariot within the sacred field, or as the Master stationed in a village, an urban site, or a celestial chariot (vimāna). || 80 ||

Thus has been described the ritual for devotees known as the Kaumudī, the fruit of which—beginning with residence in the same world [as the deity]—is established according to one's inner disposition. (81)
And all that has been told regarding the Pavitrārohaṇa and other rites for devotees of purified soul, exactly as it was spoken by you, O Lotus-born One—[all this has been heard]. 82.
O twice-born one, due to lack of independence, lack of capability, or lack of wealth, one may perform this in the same manner during all other twelfth days within the year. (83)
Even when prohibited during the night, or during the Cāturmāsya period of restraint,
the concluding rites at the end of the Tulā portion must nevertheless be carried out by the devotees.
If [the moon] were to be eclipsed before [the time], and the eclipse has passed by the twelfth day,
one should perform the entire rite during the night, because that is the period of supremacy for that lunar day.
One should likewise observe this excellent vow for five days during both [the months],
from the end of the eleventh day until the full moon, specifically from the month of Tulā until the month of Vṛścika.
The renunciation of honey and meat, the avoidance of liquor and women, as well as the killing of various species of wild animals and the cutting down of trees; || 87 ||
The burning of forests, the digging of the earth with spades and other tools, the beating of cattle and goats, and the killing or binding of human beings; 88.

One should carefully avoid the nocturnal wandering of those of low caste, as well as any social dealings with them; one should also diligently avoid fine rice and everything involving the use of ointments for anointing the body. 89.
O Lotus-born One, on the day following the day of conclusion, this is ordained for the year for devotees and those possessed of faith. (90)
The consecration must be performed for the sake of attaining well-being, peace, and auspiciousness;
therefore, it should be carried out by an excellent preceptor with a mind intent on bestowing grace. (91)
In the absence of the guru, the practitioner may [perform the rite] with his mother, his father, or with officiating priests (ṛtvij) who are older in age, or with other practitioners (sādhakas). 92.
Then, having placed [the deity] upon an auspicious seat marked with a svastika and a lotus,
one should [place him] upon a lotus with nine centers that has been delineated with threads, or else upon an eight-petaled lotus.
When it has been drawn with saffron and other pigments, or well-filled with flowers, covered with a cloth for the eyes, and prepared with the prescribed powder; || 94 ||
(170) It should be joined with bells that are either already present or new ones according to the ritual rules,
along with bowls containing seeds that have sprouted and marked with auspicious, full ears of barley. || 95 ||
With curd, mirrors, white umbrellas, flowers, and auspicious rings;
with all kinds of seeds and the like, all fragrant substances, and bilva fruits and the like—96.
Accompanied by auspicious songs and musical instruments, together with the chanting of the Vedas,
there were preceptors learned in the Pañcarātra who were devoted to meditation and silent recitation.

Accompanied by the sounds of lutes, flutes, and water-drums, as well as the resonance of flutes and bells, [the assembly] remained established in the doctrines of the true Vedas concerning the origin and dissolution [of the world].
In the sacrificial hall, adorned with various forms of maidens, there were flames, flowers, full water-pots, and beautiful clusters of trees.
It was surrounded on all sides by cows and young calves, including bulls chewing upon *dūrvā* grass and other fodder, and it was crowded with throngs of bards and Brahmins.
But for the sake of increase, one attains supreme fortune endowed with all powers;
and for the sake of attainment, one reaches Acyuta, the true, eternal, and imperishable state. || 101 ||
O Pauṣkara, this method of bathing has been prescribed for devotees;
having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) according to the previously mentioned ritual in due order, [one should proceed].
Nine water-filled jars, adorned with gold and gems and arranged according to the previously described method, should be placed there.
First of all, Varuṇa should be meditated upon by everyone as seated upon a chariot drawn by serpents,
with hands granting boons and fearlessness, and vomiting forth the essence of nectar.
That which is called *Svādva* and known as *Kṣīra* has attained a state of oneness;
it is mounted upon a variegated sea-monster (*makara*) and holds a jewel-vessel raised in its hand. 105.
One should meditate everywhere upon Varapāṇi and Samudra as being like water;
she is born from the foot of Nārāyaṇa and, in the east, carries a jar of water.
In the southeast, one should place Yamunā, who is mounted upon a tortoise and worshipped by the gods;
and in the south, Sarasvatī, seated upon a frog and a lotus.
[He saw her] slowly [attaining] the state known as the Flow, which releases one from the bondage of the noose;
she was situated on a bull in the southwest and had a lion's face in the west.
One should place Airāvatī, seated upon an elephant, in the pitcher in the northwest;
and here, in the center of the northeast lotus, one should place Vitastā, riding on a fish, in the pitcher.
The Narmadā, mounted upon a buffalo; the Samaṅgā, worshipped by the gods;
the Vṛṣadvatī and the Devikā; and the Paroṣṇī, also called Baḍabā.
Sindhu is in all eight Kakubhas, surrounding them in due order;
or else, all [the goddesses] are situated upon lotuses in the secondary jars (upakumbha), holding water-pots raised aloft. 111.
Adorned with clusters of flowers, they should be filled with water that has been consecrated one hundred and eight times by means of the mantras of the deities beginning with Vāsudeva.
Having worshipped [the deities], one should bestow the consecration (abhiṣeka) for the attainment of all fruits,
having meditated upon the lotus situated within the wheel, resting upon a foundation such as gold.
It was as described for the rivers, seas, and Varuṇa, previously fashioned, enriched with excellent pearls and gems, and adorned with svastikas and other auspicious signs. || 114 ||
In the month presided over by the lords of the months beginning with Keśava among the twelve spokes,
it is established, endowed with deities in all its limbs, and consecrated with mantras.
Or one may perform the auspicious purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) with that water;
by daily placing that water upon the head and by offering salutation [to it], [one attains the same merit]. 116.

One is liberated from all defects and attains auspiciousness and prosperity [by bathing] at the group of holy fords (tīrthas), including those by the oceans and the assembly of rivers such as the Gaṅgā. (117)
One whose self is purified and who takes refuge in Acyuta obtains the fruit arising from the ritual bath;
and when the concluding avabhṛtha bath has been performed, the practitioner then becomes fully satisfied.

For the sake of accomplishing the state of the Blessed One, one should oneself [sprinkle] with the water from the feet of the Guru using the right hand alone, while mentally recollecting one's own mantra. (119)
Having sprinkled [the water] on the head with the mudrā called the conch (*śaṅkhā*) and with its opening facing upward,
and having discarded the garment moistened by the water, one should then put on another garment. (120)
Having first adorned the body with flowers, perfumes, and ornaments beginning with the uṣṇīṣa as before, one should then sit upon a seat.
Then, one should perform the rebuke with the weapon-mantra as previously described;
having offered praise and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should present the auspicious water-offering (arghya) and other honors.
Having received all the royal regalia, ending with the parasol and the fly-whisks,
from the hand of the supreme preceptor, he then rose from his seat.
Having paid homage to the Lord of the World, the Supreme Lord, the Imperishable One,
he reached Anālālaya together with the preeminent teacher.
Having filled his joined palms with flowers, garlands, perfumes, incense, fruits, or seeds,
he performed worship of the Lord within the fire-chamber.
Recalling the Lord of Mantras within his heart, he should sit facing the fire;
then, with a seat consecrated by the recitation of mantras and sprinkled with water, [he should proceed].

As before, one should touch everything up to the crown of the head with a mind focused on meditation, remaining pure; then, having visualized the mantra within the palms of the hands, one should perform the ritual of the infused body.

One should offer that [garland], accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and arghya, upon the head and at the heart; or else, one should offer a garland of flowers made of darbha grass, consecrated with the mantra of the [respective] colors.
Having properly placed it upon his own garment, his girdle-string, his sacred thread, or his upper arm,
he should first place it into the lotus-hand of the disciple.
Having thus brought about unification with the fire possessing qualities,
this is for the sake of attaining the presence of all perfections until liberation.
The preceptor should again perform the fire sacrifice (homa) up to its conclusion,
using seven types of fuel-substances mixed together and combined with sugar.

O Brahmin, one should offer one hundred, or a thousand, or ten thousand oblations into the fire, accompanied by the eight-syllable mantra of the central form of the deity; thereafter, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
One should place the *sruva* with its bowl facing downwards upon the *sruc*;
then, having worshipped the *sruc* filled with clarified butter with flowers and other offerings, one should proceed. (133)
One should perform worship with fragrant flowers and waterless *arghya* offerings;
thereafter, one should offer clarified butter (*ājya*) in the number previously stated, or half of that.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should again offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) as previously described—whether by the hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, or lakhs, O fair-eyed one. (135)
The essence of knowledge (jñānātman) constitutes one-fourth of each of the preceding forms individually;
it is equal to that in the heart and other limbs, and likewise in all the upper parts.
In the case of the consorts of the Supreme Lord, however, according to the Pauṣkara [Tantra], one should offer all the marks, ornaments, and so forth, in sequence, with half that amount. 137.
The libation for the six mantras of the shared seat, which embody the nature of Time, as well as for the Guru and the others, is prescribed as half [of the standard amount]. || 138 ||
O Lotus-born One, having offered oblations to the weapons, the world-protectors, and the door-keepers,
according to the lineage of gurus and in due order, one should offer half and half respectively.

O best of Brahmins, for an oblation of ghee that is not accompanied by a full offering, the number [of repetitions] should be made one more than even; likewise it is for lotuses and other such offerings.
These sacrificial fuels, produced from the tree of the Brahmayajña and arising from the tree of purified knowledge,
are likewise [offered] from milk-trees, drenched in the three sweets.
The mantra-practitioner should offer oblations according to the prescribed rule, bringing forth the collection of mantras in sequence,
providing satisfaction through the offering of full oblations and by performing oblations for each respective part.

O twice-born one, having offered oblations according to the number of one's own intellect, one should indeed satisfy one's own limbs—conquering all obstacles—until the final full oblation; thus at the end, the fire [is satisfied].
When the array of mantras has been performed in the heart, one should bring it to satisfaction with the *pūrṇāhuti* (the final oblation).
Once the fire-sacrifice (*homa*) has been thus completed, one should then offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*).
One should apply a *tilaka* or an *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* with ashes upon the child at the appropriate locations, using the *hṛdaya-mantra*, the *varma-mantra*, and the *śiras-mantra* respectively. (145)
The Heart-mantra should always be employed in all rites;
one should always perform all actions with that mantra. (146)
One should perform the ritual procedure exactly as prescribed for that which is called "the essence of all mantras.
When this has been performed, drops of water fall from the mouth of the funnel.
Then, one should place [the water] from the praṇītā vessel upon the head with the hand;
this is the oblation prescribed for the seeker of liberation who is free from desire, as previously described.
For one who possesses desire yet seeks liberation, and who is adorned with ornaments, the Omniscient One dwelling within the heart does not grant permission for what is craved. (149)
Since he bestows even heaven upon his devotees without being asked, what indeed is there that he cannot give? Therefore, one should abandon all entreaty.
O one of great intelligence, this much alone is to be sought from the supreme Lord Acyuta by a living being who has performed worship at all times. 151.
Grant me supreme devotion by which you may be pleased with me;
O Lord of Gods, when you are propitious, what on earth is not attained by me? 152.
Having been told this, O lotus-eyed one, once the rite of consecration is completed,
he shall become qualified for hearing the scripture of the Blessed One.
He attains the divine station of Viṣṇu through supreme devotion, by which he delivers himself from the perils of saṃsāra. (154)
O Pauṣkara, once the offering of the water-pot has been performed, one should then offer groats, meat, and so forth,
starting from the outside of the mandala and proceeding in a clockwise direction.
O Blessed One, having offered oblations to all the quarters along with water, accompanied by sesame-water, honey, clarified butter, fragrance, and flowers. || 156 ||
The rite for the ancestors should be performed as before with cooked rice in front of the fire;
once the offering of the bali has been made from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) outside the mandala, [the following should be done].

Having sipped water for purification and worshipped the goat from the pitcher, the sacrificial pit, and the mandala, he should then eat with forbearance for the sake of the worship, being honored according to the prescribed rule. (158)
Having fumigated [the deity] together with the limbs and the retinue in due order, one should then offer the request for forbearance with waterless flowers and so forth. (159)
Having completed the worship of the fire and having prostrated according to the rule,
one should internalize its power within oneself by means of the heart-mantra and the mudrā of withdrawal.

Having set aside the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, one should perform the sprinkling with water upon the sacrificial ground and on one's own head, using the water that has been brought forward and then raised.
Then, having withdrawn that Acyuta residing in the heart by means of the two [fingers] joined together,
and having performed the withdrawal of the sacrificial bed, one should then [bathe him] with honey, milk, and water.
O Lotus-born One, having reached the sacrificial ground Āmalī as well,
he cast everything into the water and collected it back, beginning with the offering of arghya.
For the sake of favoring the disciple, one should perform the secondary sacrifice (anuyāga);
that sacrifice of the guru must indeed be performed in the same manner as the sacrifice to the Lord (bhagavadyāga).
Having bestowed [the initiation] upon the disciple, one should then depart once the self-sacrifice has been performed;
from this day forward, one should practice the propitiation of the mantra according to the rule.
O son of the Lord, one should not, with a conscious mind, abandon the worship [of the deity] due to faults such as delusion or laziness. (166)

Likewise, during the recitation of mantras, in the fire-chamber, at the time of bathing, in giving gifts as prescribed, in the chanting of hymns, in reflecting upon the scriptures, and even in listening to them; || 167 ||
Having performed a prostration at his feet, he offered his head to receive the command of Nārāyaṇa-ratātman, whose intellect was capable of providing explanations for those who were worthy. 168.
Then one should perform the sustenance of life by consuming the food offering (naivedya) and so forth;
those who have observed the fast and partake of the supreme Lord’s meal [attain the highest state]. (169)

And those men whose bodies have been purified by what remains from the sacrificial gift (sampradāna) are indeed worthy of being saluted by men and worthy of honor due to their continuous succession of spiritual accomplishments (siddhi). || 170 ||
The reality of the self (ātmatattva) is to be known as that which is eternally ordained for him;
and by means of that food, he performs the sacrifice with his own self for the sake of accomplishing the self. 171.
Know that the subsequent sacrifice (anuyāga) is that which is performed by oneself within the self, using the water and fruits remaining from the sacrificial feast. 172.
Those who daily perform the consumption [of food] before eating do so either to grasp that power through the vital breaths, or out of necessity for the sake of sustaining life.
Those endowed with devotion in thought, established on the true path, and firm in their vows,
go without effort to the imperishable state at the end of the body.
Those men of meritorious deeds who possess this divine vow stand at the head of all observers of vows who sacrifice with ritual offerings.

One should understand that whatever auspicious thing is properly offered according to the rules to Viṣṇu—the Self who is both Mantra and Brahman—is for his sake; furthermore, one should consider this [offering] to be a well-dug well. 176.
This is that immortal Brahman; this is imperishable life;
this is knowledge, this is vigor, and this indeed is the splendor of Viṣṇu.
This moon, remaining unbroken, exists itself in the form of food;
and for the sake of the perfection of that which resides in the condiment, the Lord Parjanya [is present]. (178)
The Supreme Lord, as the presiding overseer, experiences [the world] through the nature of the fire within the heart;
because he is favored by that power, he is the Person who has entered into primordial nature (prakṛti). || 179 ||
In this way, the giver of food is to be known as the eater of food, and the food stands before him;
through the external offering of one's own clarified butter, it attains full awakening.
Just as the powerful digestive fire residing within the body is activated by water,
so too does it act upon the sixfold essence of the six types of food.
Then, from that [state], one becomes Ātma-Brahman; by means of that slight cause, having brought oneself face-to-face with it, one should then slowly offer the food as an oblation.
First, one should offer four oblations with the outer joints, having regard for the fourfold nature; then, by virtue of regarding the fourth alone, one should offer three oblations.
Then, with a focused heart, he should eat morsels with the root mantra;
finally, with mouth and hands purified, he should drink water consecrated by the mantra.
Or else, that water may be [the one] flowing from the lotus-feet of his meditation, or it may be that which was previously consecrated for him who bears his form. (185)
Since it encompasses all that, it brings about the destruction of all defects, pacifies all afflictions, and always bestows all happiness. (186)
O Lotus-born One, it is more purifying than all sacred fords and mantras;
therefore, indeed, after the meal, one should first perform the satiation of the fire within the heart.
Constantly devoted to heartfelt devotion, one should drink [the water] like the milking of clarified butter;
then, at the Brahma-tīrtha, one should recite [the mantra] twice or four times in succession while drinking.
Thus, the incomparable greatness of that food known as Prāpaṇa, which was given as a remnant, should be understood exactly as it has been described. 189.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, one should always offer libations to the ancestors and give offerings to the worthy devotees of the Supreme Lord for the pleasure of the All-pervading One.
He who knows thus the greatness of both the food offering and Acyuta,
and partakes of it according to the prescribed rule, attains equality with Acyuta.
By one who knows the vow, and especially by a devotee of the Source of the World, [the teacher] must indeed always be protected like one's own life, even more so than life itself. 192.
Through this proper procedure, beginning with the gift of food and according to one's capacity, the Supreme Lord indeed attains supreme delight toward him. (193)
He who offers food, which is the supreme Brahman in embodied form, when honored, has effectively given everything to those who know the true nature of the Lord. (194)
But at the conclusion of the vow, in sacred places such as temples and the like, during auspicious moments determined by favorable lunar days and astrological ascendants, || 195 ||
Having performed [the rite], that which is given to the Blessed One becomes inexhaustible;
and when it is before worthy recipients, by that Adhokṣaja is satisfied. (196)

One who is intent upon his own spiritual practice must strive with great effort to avoid those who are unworthy recipients, those who do not partake in the sacred rites, atheists, and those of evil nature. 197.
For women, Śūdras, animals, and especially for laborers—whether acting with desire or without desire—the knower of mantras, established in the true vow, [should perform this]. (198)

For he who offers as an oblation that which is purified by mantra but consists of forbidden substances—even one who has attained perfection (siddha) falls into degradation, let alone one who merely desires to ascend [the path]. 199.
Pauṣkara said:
O Lord of Gods, I desire to know that compendium of the duties of the Blessed One which you have designated as worldly; please explain it to me in brief.
The Blessed One said:
Whether with abundant wealth or even a small amount acquired through righteous means, having dedicated it to the infallible Lord (Acyuta), whether it be auspicious or inauspicious— (201)

When performed for the pleasure of the Blessed One by those who are absorbed in Him, together with the members of the assembly, these [rites] yield small fruit like ordinary sacrifices; yet they are traditionally held to bestow heaven. (202)
For those who possess desire, even there, they indeed grant that fruit by means of it;
but for devotees who are free from desire, they surely grant the world of Acyuta.
Various austerities such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances were performed for the pleasure of the Blessed One, and they granted whatever was desired.
Whatever is indeed desired by these [disciples] for as long as they live, that which is pleasing to the Supreme Lord, is accepted [by the teacher] without causing weariness. (205)
Having reached that meritorious field and arrived there, that imperishable [being] indeed bears fruit before long through its divine nature of knowledge.
Or if a practitioner, with single-minded devotion, constantly worships [the deity] on land with leaves, flowers, and so forth, then at the end of his body, that embodied soul— || 207 ||
By the grace of the God of gods, universal stability shall prevail;
he shall receive worship like that of Viṣṇu for as long as he lives.
At the time of the body's end, the wise man— devoted to devotion and faith, and solely intent upon Nārāyaṇa— proceeds to Śvetadvīpa.
And by those celestial chariots, O Mahāmati, they proceed along the path beginning with the Radiant (arcis).

With well-known, fragrant flowers and fruits... [From this point onward, a mutual transposition of the textual sequence is observed in the manuscript collections (*mātṛkā-kośa*): Manuscripts *k* and *kh* constitute one group (*varma/varga*); manuscripts *g* and *gh* constitute another group (*varga*). In the first group, the first collection begins from the start of the chapter up to "O Great-minded One, the Arcirādi [path]," forming the first set. Subsequently, beginning with "The array of manifestations (*vibhava-vyūha*)" and ending with "But the chewing of sesame and good fruit preceded by the water at the feet of the Lord," there are nineteen and a half verses, forming the second set. Then, starting with "Suprasiddhaiḥ" and ending with "Shown as such by that being, O Sage, not by the Great One," there are twenty-two verses, forming the third set. From here onwards, beginning with "Having made and having smelled," up to the end of the chapter, is the fourth set. In the second group of manuscripts, the first, second, and third sets are written as before; however, the commencement of the fourth set differs. Specifically, after the third set, the second set is written again to its conclusion, and the third set is omitted; instead, the fourth set is written in its entirety as a continuous sequence. In both groups of manuscripts, the reason for the inversion is precisely the writing of the second and third sets out of order. Here, the resolution is as follows: the arrangement of the second and fourth sets, with their unobserved junctions, maintains the continuity of the text's sequence and does not disrupt it. On the other hand, the third set, which has intruded in between, cannot be connected in any way with the fourth set; rather, it forms a perfectly joined connection with the first set and finds its proper place there. Beyond this, the second set provides a correct introduction and sustains the order of the work. Therefore, the textual sequence has been arranged according to what has been shown; let the wise be the final authority. ...with pleasant, auspicious flowers and fruits. (210)
He who worships Acyuta with devotion in a forest or in the midst of mountains attains many desired objects, even those not sought after. (211)
At the end of the body, he will be worshipped like the Blessed Lord by Indra and the other gods,
either in a divine Vaiṣṇava temple, or in one perfected by a Siddha, or even in one built by a human being.
One should perform the great ritual action with devotion and wisdom, such as bathing with milk and other substances, and anointing with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and bāhlīka. (213)
O twice-born one, there is indeed an encircling with divine, immeasurable cloths that are white, yellow, and reddish,
along with an auspicious upper garment and a sacred thread.
When wealth is available, one should then adorn [the deity] up to the feet with golden ornaments set with gems, as well as with flowers and excellent garlands.
One should fumigate with auspicious guggulu resin sprinkled with clarified butter,
and with many great lamps filled with sesame oil and clarified butter.
Immediately thereafter, one should worship it with interwoven cloths that are unwashed, unblemished, very white, and dyed,
and which contain cardamom, cinnamon, and other ingredients within their folds.
Then, having worshipped the Lord with curds mixed with honey and clarified butter, along with various pure offerings of food, including fruits and roots; (218)
With pure, cooling, and sweet beverages, purified by water and mixed with cinnamon, cardamom, and other spices, ground and scented with incense and camphor; || 219 ||
Immediately thereafter, [the deity] should be satiated with coconut water;
furthermore, excellent scented water is for the purpose of the food offering and the rinsing of the mouth. (220)
Then [he should wear] a white garment that has not been worn or washed, or one from which the male organ has been removed;
furthermore, it should be perfumed with camphor powder and rubbed with sandalwood paste.
And having offered excellent betel leaf with areca nut, as well as rice, pulses such as *śimba*, grains, sesame seeds, and white mustard; 222.
Rocanā, the śrīphala fruit, flowers, dūrvā grass, the dhātrī fruit, curd, new white silk, and a white lotus with a clockwise whorl.

Having placed it in a vessel made of metal, wood, or even leaf, covered with leaves such as those of the *tāla* tree, and enriched with water for honor (*arghya*) and flowers, one should then set it down in the center.
Having placed his knees upon the ground and bowing his head low, he should offer gold or very pure bullion according to his own capacity. (225)
Having taken it with both hands turned upward and offered it to the Lord of the World,
O best of the twice-born, for the sake of fulfilling all enjoyments.
By which [means] there is the attainment of all future desires for those seeking the fruit of reality;
indeed, by which [means] those who are free from desire are joined with the Supreme Self.
Chowries, fans, and other articles of enjoyment, as well as beds, seats, and stringed musical instruments; || 228 ||
Having properly observed with his own intellect those great objects, extending as far as kettledrums, clay drums, and musical ensembles, which bestow joy upon the mind; || 229 ||
