When all [the materials] are available, one should worship with the mind; when they are unavailable, one who worships with the most excellent of immortals (gods) through the power of faith and devotion— || 230 ||
Having enjoyed pleasures according to their desire in the realms of heaven and other true abodes, they shall,
after a period of time, [return] by the power of the Goddess's will.
O Sage, by means of that very great path through which reality is seen,
he remains for many hundreds of kalpas amidst the worlds of the manifested arrays (*vibhavavyūha*). (232)
Having attained knowledge there, and then descending to the surface of the earth,
he suddenly enters into dissolution within the Blessed One, the immeasurable Self.
The worship of the Immovable One according to the power of sacred fields, abodes, and holy fords has been described in brief, for the sake of quelling the worldly existence of devotees. 234.
Now, listen to the worship of Hari based on [the divisions of] time, for the sake of destroying the worldly existence of devotees whose souls are solely intent upon Viṣṇu. (235)
Furthermore, one should worship with abundant, purifying enjoyments acquired through righteous means,
with faith and devotion, on auspicious days.
At the prescribed times for occasional rites, one should always remain undisturbed,
even during auspicious planetary configurations (lagna) and moments (kṣaṇa) known as celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial.
Especially on the twelfth days of both fortnights, and on those days well-known in the country—[in some places it is read as "diśi ruddheṣu"]—as understood from other scriptures. (238)
On days such as the *parividdha* or *ardhavāsara*, one should avoid honoring other deities with offerings that are respectful yet not prohibited, or with water, roots, fruits, and the like. (239)
Then, for the purpose of cleansing the stomach, one should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) contained in a leaf-vessel,
consecrated by the water from the feet of the image of the Blessed One.
Together with water purified by gold, darbha grass, and excellent jewels,
and having likewise observed the fast, he should worship Keśava as before.
Having gratified the lotus-eyed Acyuta with gifts of gold, food, water, cows, land, black antelope skins, and other such offerings, he presented them to Him. (242)
Having taken that command upon his head, whoever bestows it upon one who is absorbed in that [deity],
shall surely attain the state of the Blessed One through devotion, even if seeking a fruit.
Furthermore, O Mahāmati, for one who seeks the fruit, after many hundreds of millions of eons, it bears fruit quickly as the fruit of divine existence— that is to say, as divine enjoyment.
And for one endowed with long life, health, good servants, sons, and a wife, whatever astrological rite or auspicious momentary act has been forgotten shall be made true. (245)
Having first completed the preliminary rites with a vigilant mind, one should complete the remainder of the ritual when the auspicious hour has arrived. || 246 ||

Having offered water for the feet, flowers, and other items until the completion [of the rite], along with golden cows and the like, for two days, one day, or three nights, or indeed for six days; || 247 ||
Having completed the twelve-day rite, which lasts for two fortnights, according to the prescribed rule,
prior to the day concluding the vow, one should perform the all-night vigil and other such rites.
It should be spent without indolence through recitation, fire-offerings, worship, meditation, prostrations, circumambulations, sacred narratives, and meritorious hymns of praise. (249)
Then, at the time of dawn, or at night, or on an auspicious day, one should perform the rites beginning with the bath and ending with the fire-oblation of the vital breaths (prāṇāgnihotra). || 250 ||
O twice-born one, it is constantly forbidden to eat at night without the rising of the sun;
however, one may prepare prepared food for the twice-born accompanied by water.

And one should offer before the Blessed Lady well-prepared oblations mixed with clarified butter, preceded by water from the feet of the deity, along with sesame seeds and the chewing of excellent fruits. (252)

Having performed this and having smelled [it]—[that which is to be known here has been explained in the commentary on the verse "of the numbered [mantras], by those well-known"]—one should then touch the food offering (*naivedya*) once again;
indeed, before eating, one should consume it for the sake of destroying inauspiciousness. 253.

This should always be honored by those who know the vows and are absorbed in the Blessed One, for the sake of attaining bliss, happiness, and good fortune, and indeed for the dawning of the future day.
From the day the vow is undertaken, this must be done; likewise, on the day of the vow, one who desires a happy rebirth for their offspring should avoid [certain things] with great effort. (255)
A day free from causing harm to others is always to be accepted as pure;
however, that which is joined with a portion of the preceding day is even more weighty.
If the day of fasting is joined with even a slight portion of the preceding or following day,
it is always established as such in the world.
But for those devoted to fasting, that [offense] shall not result in any fault;
for this vow belongs to devotees who are free from desire, O you who are yourself dedicated to vows. || 258 ||

For those seeking fruits, who are subject to rebirth and whose minds are devoted to the machinery of karma, fasting is prohibited; yet it is also established that eating is permitted during the fast. || 259 ||
Then, for the sake of bowing, they attain the state of being limbs for the devotees;
by means of this, no turbidity arises in the mind during the worship of Acyuta.

For those who are unable even to observe a fast, yet whose souls delight in ritual action and the Veda, know that every gift is equal to the avoidance of harming others; such a person should always practice all forms of giving.
On another day, like one who has fasted, the worshiper whose nature is the Blessed One, being capable of the required ritual actions, should worship the Guru as soon as he has arrived. || 262 ||
Having indeed gratified and requested the World-Teacher for forbearance for the sake of his livelihood, [one should perform it] for half a day, or less than that, or more. (263)
It is proper that, having first performed the preliminary rite on the very first day,
one should always observe the vow of eating only at night if one intends to undertake the formal resolve.
An extraordinary fruit arises for him from fasting;
having brought it to its conclusion at the end of all acts of giving on the day of the vow.
On that very day, one who observes the fast should perform the sacrifice to the Self through the constant worship and other rites dedicated to Viśveśa until the end of that day.
Whatever remains [to be done] on the following day shall indeed be accomplished then;
otherwise, know that it would cause conflict for the embodied being who has already fulfilled his purpose.

Through the renunciation of what is inexhaustible and through the power of non-grasping, one should thus [determine] what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted regarding those who are afflicted by the lunar days, as was done in the past.
Having understood this, Vāsudeva, the infallible Lord whose self is the Master of the lunar days (Tithīśanātha),
is indeed to be worshipped at the beginning of the festival and other occasions by those observing fasts, in due order.
On both fortnights, or indeed on the bright fortnight according to one's wish,
the Lord whose self is the Grandfather (Brahmā) is born from the lotus there on the first day.
And he should be worshipped according to the rules with a mind endowed with devotion; thus, in two years—or in two fortnights, or even by worshipping for one fortnight. (271)
Having duly exhausted [the effects of karma] through gifts and fire-oblations according to his capacity,
the Creator himself becomes Hari on the second and third days.
Then, on the fourth day, one should honor him whose self is restraint (saṃyamana);
on the fifth, the one whose self is nectar (amṛta); and on the sixth day, Śaktīśa. || 273 ||
On the seventh day he is indeed Jñānamūrti, and immediately after that, Viśvātmā;
on the ninth day he is Siddhātmā, and thereafter the Lord Dharmātmā.
Then on the thirteenth day, O high-minded one, he is the self of Īśāna, the lord of gods; the self of Sūrya, the illuminator of the quarters; the self of Kāma, and then the self of Kalā.

The Blessed One is the Self conceived as the Father; these various manifestations belong to the Lord of the World for the sake of engaging in optional rites and for the constant attainment of desired goals. (276)
He should be worshiped with offerings such as water for the hands (*arghya*) and flowers, accompanied by ritual acts;
for the sake of worship on the first day, one should sacrifice to Brahmā for a year.
Thus, one who desires the power of speech should worship the immutable Lord Dhātṛ, as well as Hari, for the sake of destroying obstacles to liberation and for the attainment of that [speech]. (278)
Then, for the pacification of unrighteousness, one should worship Yama, the master of self-restraint;
and on the fifth lunar day, for the sake of increasing longevity and health, one should worship Amṛteśvara.
One should worship the infallible Śaktīśa on the sixth lunar day for the sake of the power of one's own capacity;
furthermore, on that very day, one should properly worship the Lord of that day (Taddinēśa) for the attainment of self-consciousness.

Then, for the sake of abundance among the three kinds of accomplishments, the Universal Soul [worships] the Lord of the Ninth Night for the purpose of attainment; thereafter, he effects the acquisition of the true Dharma.
On the tenth day, O high-minded one, one should worship the Sun, the object of adoration;
and on the eleventh day, the seeker of knowledge should worship the Great Lord, the Master of Sciences.
On the twelfth day, for the sake of great splendor and power, one should worship her Lord;
and on the thirteenth, for the sake of obtaining various women and jewels, one should worship her husband.
Then, for the sake of victory over the arts, the self, time, and death, one should always worship;
and for the pacification of the threefold debt, one should worship the Supreme Lord.
Thus, the lord of the fifteenth day (the Moon) is always to be honored;
even though, O twice-born one, it has been stated that the lords of the lunar days are to be worshipped on those respective lunar days.
That [observance] is ordained for those twice-born who are single-mindedly devoted and who do not seek rewards;
indeed, it applies to them on the eleventh day of both fortnights.

And that which causes affliction to others—whether prescribed as such everywhere (though in some places "paripīḍa" is seen instead), or dedicated to them, or turned away from them—even though two lunar days have been mentioned by means of the two lords of the lunar days. 287.
O best of the twice-born, although Ekādaśī and the like are likewise [prescribed], they are secondary and not primary; therefore, Acyuta is the primary [object of worship].
For not only that, O Pauṣkara, but the entire web of other objects as well, and even the mental beings who are the teachers of this phenomenal world [are included]. 289.
Thus, everything has been set forth out of a desire to show grace to devotees;
it is proclaimed as consisting of the Perfectly Full (supūrṇamaya), arising from the state of the Lord of Fullness (pūrṇabhāveśvara). || 290 ||
For one who has made a sincere vow for the sake of the fasts of the year, preceded by the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) and the casting of water; || 291 ||
In the twelfth month of that [year], on the twelfth lunar day, everything prescribed for the conclusion of the Anuyāga should be performed; otherwise, the fruit of the entire year is lost.
Indeed, worship performed on the thirteenth day comes to be fruitless;
one should rather perform it on the eleventh day, as desired.

O Brahmin, for the sake of attaining the fruits of the three aims of life (trivarga), one devoted to vows should perform a vow lasting one night or more with devotion, even without [seeking] those specific fruits. (294)
Because he is unattached to all things, no fault arises for him;
he should perform sacrifice and the self-sacrifice on the thirteenth lunar day with a joyful mind.
Or, O twice-born one, when the time from the end of the previous watch until the twelfth [watch] is mixed with dharma, yet the watch is either deficient or excessive; || 296 ||
O Mahāmati, on the thirteenth day, having especially avoided [the practice] through lack of exertion or desire, it attains the status of being an auxiliary limb.
On the thirteenth day, one should perform the prescribed duties with one's own intelligence; for a Vaiṣṇava who fails to do so, there is indeed a great transgression.
For one who knows the mantras, the propitiation of the twice-born is superior even to that of the gods;
for one who knows the mantras, there is worship, fire-offerings, recitation, and giving according to one's own capacity. (299)
Full of joy, one should exert effort; being observant of vows and intent on ritual action, one should always perform the entire procedure according to the primary rule.

For those who have accepted [the practice] with devotion, free from deceit and illusion, the secondary alternative (anukalpa) is considered equal to the primary rule for practitioners, provided it is properly observed. || 301 ||
Lord Hari, the sovereign of all, truly dwells within the heart of everyone;
He knows the inner disposition for the sake of truth and bestows a fruit corresponding to it.
Gold, jewels, water, the six flavors, sesame seeds, clarified butter, a sacred thread, an umbrella, sandals, clothing, cows, and land. (303)
Garlands, perfumes, lamps, grain, and excellent fruit—these are the objects of desire;
by offering them collectively, they become the givers of all desires.
Therefore, on the twelfth lunar day falling on a Thursday, he should be propitiated with jars of *kāmadhenu* [cow's milk] upon the earth where rivers meet the ocean. (305)

For the attainment of all desires, for the welfare of all beings, for the sake of destroying all dualities, and for the satisfaction of the ancestors, [one should offer] the water-pot to the God. (306)
By this gift known as the "wish-fulfilling cow," the Supreme Lord, who is intent upon the upliftment of the world, attains supreme delight. (307)

Having considered the place, time, and other factors, one should worship Acyuta with faith either at home or in a temple; that which is thus offered should be consumed according to the prescribed rule.

If there is no devotion to the sacred sites (*bhāvabhakti*), yet by the power of devotion to the sacred sites one regards even a mere portion of water as a holy place (*tīrtha*), such as where the two waters meet at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā; || 309 ||
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Dharma of the World," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, a great Upaniṣad within the glorious Pāñcarātra. 31.
(Total number of verses: 309) Now begins the thirty-second chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, what would happen for men who perform sacrifices with excellent mantras if they were to intentionally abandon that worship? (1)
The Blessed One said:
"O one of great intelligence, having first made a formal resolve accompanied by mantra during the worship with mantras, one should continue without despondency for as long as one lives."
And whatever has been assigned to the deities, that must be diligently accomplished through action, mind, and speech, according to one's power and according to one's own means.
When birth-impurity (sūtaka) or similar conditions have arisen due to lack of independence or incapacity,
one should then worship the Guru according to the rules, preceded by formal prayer.
Whether it be a self-restrained son of the guru, a brother who has been initiated together, or one who is younger or older—O Lotus-born One, there is no exception to this. (5)
There would be a severe expiation prior to the examination of the initial resolve;
for that purpose, others indeed have their own respective mantras, mudrās, and so forth. (6)
When the time for secrecy has arrived, those who have attained perfect accomplishment must not speak;
yet he who, out of delusion, reveals his own mantras, mudrās, and so forth [to others], (7) [is at fault].
O twice-born one, for those others who are not devotees, Mantreśvara,
together with the host of Siddhas, approaches with his face turned away.
And having caused great suffering, the officiating priests must therefore, with great effort,
keep their own mantra secret along with its prescribed ritual procedure.
Except for the guru, the son, the wife, and a sincere disciple,
one should not perform the ritual of satiating the mantra and its worship in the presence of others.
Even there, the one born from the lotus (Brahmā), intent on ritual action, should recite the mantra mentally, but he should conceal the visualization of the mantra.
In the same way, one who possesses the mudrās and the rosary will indeed attain success;
for it is exactly so for one who, without these, undertakes the mastery of mantras.
Having consecrated an image of the deity with devotion and installed it in one's own home,
one should apply oneself to its worship, provided that one possesses the necessary capability and other requisite qualities.
A lord of the twice-born, knowing the five times of ritual and devoted to the six duties, should, when possible, maintain this as his eternal livelihood.
That by which your fruit in this world and the next becomes eternal—[that you should speak], otherwise not out of constraint, nor out of fear, nor out of deceit. (15)

A wise person should worship the deity, whether on a regular basis or even on an occasional basis, for the attainment of perfectly complete results—this is the true conduct of those with pure vision, O one of stainless eyes. (16) [Note: The text in brackets indicates a portion that has been displaced due to a scribal error in the manuscripts *ka* and *kha*. It reads: "But on an occasional basis, or regularly, for those engaged in the worship of twice-borns, whether they are established outside or installed within the home."]

Therefore, he by whom worship was previously undertaken as a constant duty shall indeed become a partaker of the fruit of that omission—the sin resulting from its neglect—which leads to falling into the world of spirits. || 17 ||

Therefore, one who desires auspiciousness should not speak thus [of the cessation of the deity], for there is no loss of function for those engaged in worship, whether that worship is occasional or constant. (18)

O Mahāmati, whatever means of subsistence one enjoys from anyone, whether that person is established outside [the community] or has been installed within a household, and for whatever purpose it is intended— [that sustains him]. (19)
From that as its cause, his entire fruit arises from mere volition alone;
therefore, one who is devoted to worship should not neglect this mode of life.
O twice-born one, having understood through the mind the true state of the hearts of householders who seek the mantra-form [of the deity], the deity indeed [responds] to both.
It duly bestows the fruit or produces an obstacle;
knowing this, O Lotus-born One, one should apply oneself with effort to the true nature of the scriptures.

No form whatsoever belonging to the fourfold nature of the Lord—whether it be his personal form or his majestic manifestation—should be disregarded with a mind that is deliberate and full of pride. (23)
But the image (arcā) made of stone or wood, or painted on cloth or a wall, may always be worshipped according to one's own capacity during periods of impurity and so forth. 24.
Having understood that the time has come for the preservation of the lineage, and having performed their respective duties with a mind purified by faith, they marked [the vessel]. || 25 ||
One should worship until the stainless time arrives;
for the sake of atonement, one should perform worship again, preceded by a bath.

Having offered oblations into the fire according to the rules with devotion, and having given sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and others, there shall indeed be atonement for the one who worships the Veda; otherwise, a Brahmin would incur sin.
Because men do not worship the deities who have been installed within their homes, nor do they worship the deities who are manifest [in the world]. (28)
O Lotus-born One, this indeed bestows auspiciousness; how much more so when performed according to the rules, in its entirety, and endowed with all necessary materials? (29)

O twice-born one, indeed, through the attainment of enjoyments accompanied by faith, through devotion accompanied by faith, and through an intellect that is perfectly pure and situated on the path of right conduct; || 30 ||
The worship of deities through mantra, mudrā, posture, and meditation, which accomplishes their specific purposes, is performed by the officiating priests according to the established rules. (31)

Knowing this, O Lotus-born one, one who fears saṃsāra should not harbor pride; however, in the case of non-worship of the gods during rites performed for specific desires or occasional rites, [there is no fault].
And especially every day, may there be an obstacle for you, as well as for the Brahmins and other devotees, through separation and the like. (33)
O Pauṣkara, having performed the bath appropriate for the gods and the ancestors,
one should thereafter perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) and recitation (japa), primarily for those who abide in the presence [of the Lord].
And from the practice of those great mantras and of the scripture known as the Siddhānta, the most excellent fruit is obtained. (35)
And so, O Lotus-born One, it is seen in this world that the conduct of gods, asuras, and humans arises from their own inherent nature.
All those belonging to the various castes and stages of life were endowed with their own innate qualities as prescribed by birth;
they were masters of the Purāṇas and Smṛtis, and knowers of the Vedas and Vedānta.
O Mahāmati, even sages who are devoted to the dharma of their own karma do not attain supreme accomplishment without the adoption of mantra.
What more need be said of those men of dull intellect who, for the sake of worldly gain and delusion, fail to follow the Siddhānta practice and do not serve its adherents? (39)
Having understood this, one should exert effort in the practice of mantra-adoration, in propitiating the gurus, and in delving into the Siddhāntas and other scriptures. (40)
O one of stainless vision, because those who are devoted to that [scripture] attain perfect liberation directly, whereas for others—those whose nature is addicted to dry logic—it is not so. (41)
And for those devoted to knowledge and action, various perfections arise here;
yet they attain liberation in every way through the perpetual exhaustion of the body. (42)
Pauṣkara said:

O Lord, I now desire to know the true nature of ritual action (karman) for those who possess knowledge, as well as that which bestows great supernatural power (maharddhi) upon practitioners of mantra.
The Blessed Lord said:
Whatever ritual acts and so forth are contained within the final syllable of the mantra indeed become auxiliary limbs for the practitioners of mantra within the web of enjoyments.
At the beginning of each [of these], it must always be thoroughly understood by the practitioner as being the nature of pure consciousness, vibrating with its own radiance. (45)
It is perfectly filled with the powers of differentiation known as the objects, the senses, and the elements,
which are fully awakened yet mutually subordinated.
And that which manifests in the form of the conceited self and in enjoyment does so indeed by itself for the sake of attaining both further experience and liberation.
Well-known by its very characteristic form to those who sacrifice with mantras, it enters into the state of being a constituent limb; such is the nature of its eternal abiding.
And now, O lotus-eyed one, by those who have awakened, that [notion] must be discarded; for it depends upon mental cultivation, and in reality, it does not exist at all.

(182) For those for whom the word of the authoritative teacher is paramount and whose souls delight solely in scripture, existence may be established through the mantra of being; however, the means [to that] is the realization of true existence. (50)

For those whose minds have been purified by the devotion of one who has truly passed away, it is indeed impossible through any logical arguments to establish that fire possesses the nature of water. || 51 ||
In this way, the nature of fire can never arise from water,
nor can a reversal of these two ever be observed by a practitioner of mantra.
That is indeed a magical net of mantras, originating from the Lotus-born [Brahmā], which impels devotees toward the auspicious path and is characterized by various forms of conviction. (53)
The Blessed One, whose very form is knowledge, out of a desire to bestow grace upon his devotees,
indeed enjoys [the world] himself by means of a portion consisting of the nature of enjoyment.
For the liberation of the sacrificers, however, there is a twofold collection of objects;
therefore, one should constantly practice according to these two divisions. (55)

Indeed, the agent is endowed with knowledge; thus, action itself is of a distinct nature—that which has been received from the mouth of a realized teacher and rendered certain through the sacred tradition (āgama). || 56 ||
O one of great intelligence, the mantra that has been duly obtained through requests and other means is accompanied by mudrās and adorned with the sense of existence.

Due to that negligence, for those who were unenlightened and whose minds were intent on other activities, it became corrupted by the transposition of phonemes and so forth, or was lost through the omission of vowels and such. (58)
O Lotus-born One, such a person always brings about even greater misfortune for practitioners of mantra;
that too occurs very quickly, O Lotus-born One. (59)
Through the power of extreme devotion, it is employed in rites such as bringing the multiform object of speech face-to-face.
By virtue of His power to bestow grace, He grants the desired object to those beings who possess true devotion and have surrendered to Him, even without following the prescribed sequence.
The Lord of Mantras becomes gracious toward those who have cultivated devotion for even a short time;
how much more so, O Pauṣkara, toward those who are perfected in ritual action and knowledge? 62.
And for those who are devoted to faith and have been enlightened by their teachers, [he spoke] without words of pride, but with speech that gladdens the heart. (63)
And the great means of the ocean-like mantras, which was previously established, as well as the eternal lineage of gurus transmitted through succession. || 64 ||
Then, O twice-born one, there is the state of eternal optimism for its recipient, followed by self-restraint preceded by devotion and accompanied by ritual action. (65)
And then, having understood the meaning of the scriptures as well as one's own subsequent realization, one should again proceed with various means preceded by devotion. (66)
One who knows the authoritative scriptures (āptasadāgama) should indeed always be served by one who is constantly devoted to mantras and seeks both visible and invisible fruits. 67.
O Pauṣkara, when such a person exists, one should properly attend to all their needs, such as security and well-being, every day according to one's own capacity.
For in this very cycle of existence, the Supreme Lord Acyuta has been set in motion as the Guru, acting according to the will of Īśvara. 69.

O Greatly Wise One, for one who desires to proceed by means of that [disciple], his own mantra—[which arises from the lotus-born of meditation]—should first be given to him for the sake of devotion. || 70 ||
Or else, out of devotion to His son, one should always offer the first portion of cooked food during the performance of the secondary sacrifice (anuyāga), with a completely satisfied mind.
Let it be, O one of great intelligence, whether he be his own guru or his son;
or another who knows the sequence [of initiation], is learned in the Agamas, is single-mindedly devoted, or is composed of the three Vedas. (72)
Having performed his daily rites, well-contented, with a peaceful mind and free from agitation, he was indeed exceedingly devoted and had been entreated for a long time, O high-minded one. (73)
Or else, one should employ the mantra known as *svamantrasādhana*, which consists of twelve, eight, or six syllables;
it is designated as *jitaṃta*, has the *praṇava* at its beginning, and contains the seed-syllable at its end. (74)
In this way, it should be joined together in one place, like a heap of embers above;
having placed it with its limbs upon the palm of the hand, one should [dissolve it] into the body by means of that consciousness and so forth. (75)
Taking that ego as his support, he who eats in whose house with favor,
for him indeed that [merit] becomes infinite at that very moment.

O Lotus-born One, the Lord of Mantras is not so gratified by all desired enjoyments in the mandala and other rites, nor even by offerings of clarified butter and the like in the midst of the fire, as he is when propitiated [in this manner].
It attains supreme joy, just as [joy arises] when it has entered the body of the teacher;
therefore, having relied upon the causal sign, one should practice within the intervals between the opposing factors. (78)

Likewise, O Lotus-born One, having specially worshipped one's own mantra in the presence of the Guru—whether for a month, a year, or a period of six months—one should perform the rite within that time. (79)
Thereafter, for the satisfaction of the ancestors and indeed for his own welfare,
he should worship the preeminent teacher until the end of the night.

Having propitiated [the preceptor] with enjoyments beginning with water for the feet and respectful offerings (arghya), ending with the massaging of his feet, and having offered wealth according to one's ability, one should present the mother’s property.
Having followed him as he departed for his own home and so forth, O one of great intelligence—those who have thus committed themselves to the rite of mantra worship; 82.
The castes, beginning with the foremost of the twice-born— the Brahmacārins at their head and ending with the mendicants—
all indeed attain perfection.
Pauṣkara said:

O Lord of the World, in former times, within the cave of that [heart], there exists the mantra-form of the deity, which is both one and arises in manifold divisions, characterized by its reflected image. (84)
O twice-born one, [the image] may have been previously accepted out of devotion, or installed by oneself or by ancestors, or consecrated with mantras, or even deposited by another. (85)

Or else, having obtained it from another who was unqualified, such as a thief or the like, through wealth, it has now been received from one's own guru for the sake of attaining success in both the seen and the unseen worlds. (86)
The mantra produces clarity of mind and removes the suffering of saṃsāra;
it is employed for that purpose, complete with its limbs and its retinue. (87)
"O Blessed One, please instruct me on what is ordained for the seeker, or whether it is not so.
The Illustrious Lord said:
"O Brahmin, O twice-born one, that which is self-manifested as well as by the hosts of immortals—"
It was established by those accomplished in mantra who are identical with the Blessed One in form.
O Lotus-born One, the application of mantras presided over by Him, together with His own, has been ordained for the sake of attaining the presence of the Lord for human beings. (89)
Thus, one's own mantra, along with its retinue, should not always be kept in the house;
rather, it should be applied to other mantra-forms, such as the words and so forth.
O twice-born one, it should be worshipped with its own mantra accompanied by the [deity's] insignia and limbs;
and the mantra should be both enclosed within the *bimba* and released from it.
O Mahāmati, indeed, for all those [mantras] that are self-manifested and complete, the arrangement of the mantras with one another brings about excellent qualities. 92.
But he whose mind is constantly intent on the practice of mantra-attainment shall exhaust the remaining impermanent bonds of karma residing within his body.
It is forbidden to apply [the power] of one's own mantra to others, except in the case of all beings who are equal and especially those regarding mantras; otherwise, it is prohibited. 94.
O twice-born one, because for someone, in some place, and in the proper manner of mantra practice, one's own self becomes gracious even without the arising of pure knowledge. (95)
(184) Worship performed with one's own mantra is not prohibited anywhere else;
however, according to the primary rule of one's own path, it should be done at home or elsewhere within a maṇḍala. 96.
When there is worship according to the mantra and tantra, no fault exists in using what has been gathered for the sake of worship with one's own mantra; the same applies to sacred shrines.
When a maṇḍala of images has been consecrated there by means of a mantra that opens the path, then indeed the vision [of the deity] is accomplished.
O Lotus-born One, the offering of flowers is performed with one's own mantra, which is all-pervasive and pure in nature, for mantras are indeed of the very essence of pure consciousness. 99.
For the universal, consisting of the Śabdabrahman, is indeed without distinction;
however, their mutual differences arise from meditation, ritual placement (nyāsa), and so forth. 100.
It arises as variegated and formidable, bestowing the fruits of malevolent rites;
yet it is one's own mantra, intent on grace and consisting of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman). 101.
O Lotus-born One, it enters into the relationship of sacrificer and priest;
likewise, although that [Self] is restrained there, it remains without the cognition of the power of manifestation.
But it exists as the very self of the Word-Brahman; since there is identity with that, how could there be destruction?
Just as there is no destruction of fire without the two individual manifestations of the cloth [or jar], so too there is no destruction of this without their unity.
Thus, through the two forms of sound itself, there is unity by way of grace;
and so too is there a noble birth for the agitation, even without a special sacrifice. (104)
In one's own home, in a mandala, in a sacrifice, or even in a divine abode and so forth.
Pauṣkara said:
O you who consist of the universe, I do not perceive any higher path in this world than that which has Vāsudeva as its essence, for all things, both moving and unmoving, are composed of him. (105)
The Blessed One said:
"This is true, O one of great intelligence, exactly as you have urged.
However, for a living being who is engaged in ritual action and devoted to bhakti," (106)
That place where the heart finds rest in the ultimate sense is indeed the true path for the Vaiṣṇava sacrificer; for he is truly one of sattvic nature.
Spontaneously engaged out of a desire to favor the world,
he exists through the manifestation of his power and array, with a pure essence and a self endowed with the six qualities.
O Brahmin, know that to be the true path by which one serves him through scripture or ritual action—a path that eternally bestows the manifestation of Brahman. (109)

The all-pervading Lord, abiding in the state of both manifestation and dissolution, by His own will expands that which is composed of the qualities (guṇas) and characterized by divinity, having resorted to the field (kṣetra) created by Prakṛti. || 110 ||
Know that [the principle] consisting of māyā is permeated by qualities such as complete knowledge and the like;
however, that which consists of the [three] guṇas is variegated and not entirely pure.
For that scripture which reveals it, as well as the prescribed procedure (itikartavyatā), O Brahmin, you should know to be a false path when viewed in light of the former [the true path]. (112)
Therefore, that which is known as the Vibhava and Vyūha is remembered as the supreme cause for attaining the highest state— the eternal and infallible form.
To those who have quickly sought refuge through action preceded by knowledge—those practitioners whose selves are purified—he grants the attainment of the true state. (114)
O Lotus-born One, when the attainment of desired fruits through ritual actions is at hand, I consider there to be no other means for those who constantly long for enjoyments. (115)

Having abandoned the manifestation of the most subtle array [of the world] belonging to those who sacrifice to the True Brahman, the worldly fruit characterized by the attainment of heaven and so forth must be renounced. (116)
For [the goal] is not attained even by constantly seeking it through sacrifices and other such means;
therefore, the host of deities within the realm of Māyā is not to be propitiated.
But since the true path has been correctly explained by those who have entered it rightly,
therefore, O Kamalasaṃbhūta, you should always indeed apply yourself with effort. (118)
One should indeed perform the propitiation of these mantras with devotion for even a moment;
through their grace, the threefold suffering comes to an end. (119)
O Lotus-born One, [these are] the physical, the internal, and the divine.
Pauṣkara said: "O Blessed One, regarding the constant worship of mantras by their worshippers with offerings such as leaves and flowers at all times, what is the fruit of such worship?"
"What is the fruit for the officiating priests from performing their worship in detail with many flowers and other offerings? In this matter, I have a great doubt. (121)
The Blessed Lord said: O best of the twice-born, equality of fruit is established for poor devotees even without fruits, flowers, and so forth, by virtue of their internal devotion. (122)
Whatever fruit is obtained from honoring those who are rich in Vedic knowledge yet devoid of food,
that same fruit is obtained by honoring devoted followers who are always wealthy through fire-offerings (homa) and other rites.
Know this: for poor devotees who worship with flowers and such, a single day and night is always to be understood as being equal to a mere moment. || 124 ||
O Lotus-born One, understand also the true nature of that time which pertains to kings and the poor, and which is dependent upon ritual action. 125.
O Pauṣkara, one should perform the dhāraṇā and meditation of the mantras together with whatever pure collection of enjoyments has been obtained. 126.
Indeed, through the extensive practice of the union of the oceans, the sacrifice performed by those who offer it constantly bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation before long. (127)
That which is contracted by means of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) and so forth, and which has been performed, yields no enjoyment;
whereas that which is [contracted] through enjoyments along with concentration and so forth is indeed achieved only after a long time.
And he bestows upon his devotees the supreme state, devoid of worldly enjoyment;
therefore, for those constantly seeking the highest good, it leads to the attainment of the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 129.
With an undisturbed mind and devotion, relying upon a portion of time and free from other activities, one should perform it according to the prescribed rule. || 130 ||
Indeed, the sacrifice is fully perfected through the extensive practices beginning with dhāraṇā;
even if it is complete with enjoyments, it is truly a source of prosperity for men.

Nevertheless, O Pauṣkara, there is a superiority among those devoted to ritual action (karmaniṣṭha), for it brings about both enjoyment and liberation; yet, through deceit, that [superiority] is obscured, and only becomes manifest when that deceit is removed.
The enthusiasm of the officiating priests may indeed diminish; therefore, one should never abandon the ritual of mantra-adoration, even in the absence of an abundance of wealth. 133.
O Pauṣkara, for one whose nature is otherwise, who is intent on the fruit of attaining enjoyments— that multitude of pleasures— for such a person of unrefined self, this [path] is primary.
Furthermore, for those of true discernment, there is no swift refutation of that action which is eternally rooted in liberation and bestows the supreme goal of human existence. (135)
Pauṣkara said: For those worldly devotees whose minds are intent on various activities and whose hearts are constantly distracted by the burden of supporting sons, wives, and other kin— (136)
O Acyuta, how is their worship accomplished in detail?
For by failing to worship them, the excellent fruit prescribed by you results in deficiency. (137)
The Blessed One said:
Indeed, that action which is performed according to the proper sequence brings about the highest good for human beings.
Therefore, that [teaching], whether concise or extensive, should not be abandoned.
O Lotus-born One, for what reason can equality be established between the primary ritual, which is extensive, and the secondary ritual that follows it? (139)
And even there, for those who are free from guile, devoted, and purified in soul, worship with leaves, flowers, and the like, along with enjoyments and words, has been prescribed. (140)
But without the continuity of actions over time, O Great-minded One, there would be no earth, water, fire, air, or that which belongs to space (ether). (141)
From the fivefold dhāraṇās, two [practices] have been prescribed in brief—
namely those called burning and nourishing— for the sake of the complete purification of the body.
And from meditation on the nature of both the supreme and the non-supreme, one [attains] the single, supreme, great heart-mantra among all mantras for the performance of ritual services. (143)
O Mahāmati, that which is accompanied by ritual action and the mind, beginning with the *praṇava*, is indeed the single mudrā to be propitiated; it is known as the mantra of yoga. (144)
Through recollection, one should perform the utterance of the partless [deity] between the eyes;
and that which is the worship by means of one's own names, containing the *natipraṇava* (the syllable *namaḥ*). || 145 ||
The supreme [form] of the mantras, which are embodied according to the prescribed rule, is known as "swift" (kṣipra);
that second [form], distinguished by seed-syllables (bījas), has the characteristic of being subtle (sūkṣma). || 146 ||

O Lotus-born One, all ritual action of the mantras, together with the sacrificial balls (piṇḍas) consisting of the nectar of their specific characteristics and their names, ending with the recitation (japa), is remembered as the "Great" (bṛhat).

O Lotus-born one, through the first [method], absolute liberation is attained quickly; however, through the second, it is attained after some interval of time, by means of the sequence of conscious effort.
O one of stainless vision, it bestows the six qualities beginning with knowledge right here and now as the first [result], and the eightfold power beginning with atomization (aṇimā) as the second.
But indeed, O Pauṣkara, the third [state] is the sovereignty over all worlds; however, it is equal to the attainment of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) for all. 150.
Indeed, even though the mantra known by its own name is great, it [is mastered] quickly through the threefold time preceded by the [correct] characteristics. 151.
Nevertheless, O Lotus-born One, in the worship beginning with the eastern direction and so forth,
one should recollect either the seed-syllable (bīja) or the body-mantra (piṇḍa-mantra) following the Praṇava.
O Lotus-born One, having likewise propitiated the heart-mantras and others of the Lord of Mantras, as well as other mantras known as "inner," [one attains success]. 153.

O Lotus-born one, there is no contradiction between those who abide on the lotus-seat and possess the characteristics of the Pradhāna and other [deities], provided they are without seeds or physical bodies.
[The worship] of those residing at the gates—beginning with Vighneśa, who is called Tathāsanaka, and [the others] such as Lokeśa marked with the vajra and those bearing his weapons. || 155 ||
This applies to the celibate student, the householder, and even the independent ascetic;
how much more so, then, for the householder who is devoted to worldly activities? (156)

This indeed is for the lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika) whose souls are devoted to that [state], for the practitioners (sādhaka) who possess consciousness, and for those who dwell in solitude; it is for their benefit. || 157 ||
He who, being intent on devotion and faith, correctly grasps [the mantra] and practices it, receives therein the twofold fruit previously described from the essence of the mantra. || 158 ||
Together with the accomplishments of the practitioner, O Great-minded One, it shall be free from obstacles.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "An Inquiry into the Omission of Worship," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, a Great Upaniṣad within the illustrious Pāñcarātra.
(Total number of verses: 160) Now begins the thirty-third chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
The worship of the Ninefold Form has been previously understood by me for the sake of various [worldly goals], but that of the Fourfold Self for the sake of liberation has not been known.
The Blessed Lord said:
"From the worship of the solitary God, whose nature is never abandoned and who possesses four aspects, liberation arises; that [liberation] results from that twofold worship."
O Brahmin, for the attainment of various fruits, listen further to the worship of Him who assumes diverse forms according to their multiplicity, exactly as it is established. || 3 ||
One should worship the all-pervading Supreme Self, the primordial deity Adhokṣaja, who is to be honored everywhere— at the beginning, at the end of the worship, and also in the middle.
Then, by means of the yoga of emanation, one should worship the eastern petal and the others,
beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa and ending with Nārāyaṇa, in their proper sequence across the four [petals].
Furthermore,
by means of the method of descent (ayayoga), one should indeed worship [the deities] beginning with Nārāyaṇa and ending with Saṅkarṣaṇa, up to the station of the Lord of the Bound (bandhyeśa).
Likewise, in the fire-lotus, the four beginning with Pradyumna—
extending from Śabdabrahma to the end of the deities— are indeed always to be worshipped.
On the right, however, beginning with Aniruddha and ending with Garuḍa as the seat,
the arrangement is established, characterized by its origin and dissolution.
Then, one should worship [the deities] ending with Nārāyaṇa and Nṛsiṃha within the lotus of the Rākṣasa;
and in the lotus situated in the western direction, one should worship [the deities] beginning with Brahmā and ending with Kṣmādhara.
Ending with Saṅkarṣaṇa, beginning with Viṣṇu, and situated in the wind and the lotus;
[one should meditate on] Nṛkesarin and Varāha, [arising] from knowledge and so forth, [and] from water and water. 10.
The triad beginning with Saṅkarṣaṇa, and that which begins with Īśāna and Kṣmādhara,
are to be honored in sequence through their very emergence and dissolution.

O Brahmin, that which was proclaimed first as this "ninefold" [great reality consisting of nine forms], its power arises for him through worship according to that sequence. (12) *Note: The text provided contains a lacuna; the portion from "navasaṃkhyamidam" up to "bhāvitātmanām" is missing in manuscript g and gh, replaced instead by an additional verse. This translation reflects the available Sanskrit text.*
It bestows the fruit of the fourfold self and the four aims of life upon those who have cultivated their inner selves.
And for those seeking fruits, the attainment of various fruits arises without delay through the constant worship of these fourfold beings independently. (14)
Whichever [deity] among the fourfold forms is first proclaimed,
its specific power arises through worship according to that sequence.
For this much indeed has been stated as the fruit by virtue of its arrangement;
because through it, power and sovereignty over the origin and dissolution of beings become unimpeded.
O Brahmin, that mantra of the Lords of the World, whose form is the mantra, possesses incomparable radiance; it is infinite, self-luminous, and peerless. 17.

When there exists [this knowledge] through the thorough understanding of the forms of the Supreme Lord, He who is without beginning or end and infinite manifests for the realization of those engaged in action. 18.
In order to accomplish their deliverance from that [suffering], he himself has manifested as the Vyūhas;
through his fourfold nature consisting of Prāṇa, Icchā, Śabda, and Kāla, there are nine [forms]. (19)
Of that very Great Soul, the God, whose nature is without distinction, who possesses all powers eternally present, and who is ever-arisen; || 20 ||
And for those who have been led by the specific joys arising from the knowledge of sound,
I have declared this yoga for the sake of quelling the worldly existence of living beings.
The phenomenal world (prapañca), though not to be abandoned and non-different from the Supreme Self—
which is of the nature of reality— is indeed a complete agitation that bestows the highest bliss.
The wheel of worldly illusion belonging to him, which has emerged again by the power of his will,
is that wherein sages, gods, and men alike become deluded.
As long as we have not been favored by this supreme one of fourfold nature, who possesses the form of the six qualities and is manifested through the individuality of the Guide.

At the time of his worship, however, one should vividly recollect him—resplendent with the six attributes—as manifesting like a *kadamba* flower, either externally or within the sky of the heart. (25)

And by means of a worshipper who consists of many selves, who is composed of the four castes, and by means of the sound alone—consisting of vowels and consonants together with the *bindu*—[he should worship]. || 26 ||

However, by means of some well-known external ritual accessory (upacāra), which is primary, intended, and pleasing to the mind—[g, gh: along with the ritual accessory and its name]—[one should worship]. || 27 ||

O Lotus-born One, having first performed the placement (nyāsa) of one's own limbs upon it, complete with all their qualities, one should worship it with its own mantras alone, without any distinction of location.
Now, within that mantra-sphere resembling a *kadamba* flower, [one should meditate] by means of the twelve-syllable mantra, which is indeed non-different [from it]. (29)

Having indeed brought it to manifestation within that [image], one should again establish the placement of the limbs and sub-limbs according to the sequence of colors in their respective locations, such as the heart and so forth.
Then [one should place them] on the heart, the head, the crest-lock, the two shoulders, the middle of the hands,
the eyes, the belly, the back, and the two arms.
Then, on the two thighs, the pair of knees, and subsequently on the two feet—there, preceded by the Praṇava, the six syllables are considered to be the ancillary limbs (aṅga-mantras). || 32 ||
There are others called the six Upāṅgas; hear their characteristics:
that which is well-established, pure, common, and unobstructed. (33)
Awakened, luminous, and eternal, that knowledge is directly the Imperishable (acyuta),
by whose power the entire collection of its own powers [is sustained].
Furthermore, as the cause of arising, persistence, and dissolution,
it attains a state of differentiation through its own limbs, yet without ever abandoning its essential nature.
O twice-born one, it is the heart of the infinite powers of the mantras of Mantreśa, possessing various capacities and colors, like a jewel-lamp.
And likewise, that [nature] is the self-revealer of strength and the other [qualities];
it is the sovereignty that transcends all, which is the quality belonging to the Supreme Lord. (37)
That head of all mantras bestows glorious enjoyment and liberation;
it is indeed the supreme power of the Lord, filled with manifold energies.
Carrying the fire upwards, pure, and according to the ritual rules—that indeed is the mantra-crest-lock (śikhā).
That which is fortitude, other than the unswerving persistence characterized by steadfastness, is not [true fortitude]. (39)
Know that very thing to be the armor of mantras, for it is their essential strength—that irresistible valor, sovereignty, and the power of both origin and dissolution. (40)
O Brahmin, that which is the infinite luminosity of the Lord of the universe—beyond comparison—is the weapon of those whose forms are composed of mantra, possessing peerless radiance. (41)
O Great-minded One, through the thorough knowledge of that eye, the supreme abode is perceived; and for some, it is completely dissolved along with the heart.
O twice-born one, having indeed abandoned his own field, he kindled the established knowledge; for, by the power of the Lord’s will, he became the eye-mantra of all mantras.
In some places, the semi-vowels (*antasthā*) of the fourfold group of limbs possess a radiance like that of the letter *ña*;
they abide upon the preceding [consonants], like a support resting upon jewels. (44)
Therefore, without a speaker, their light consisting of ignorance cannot be fully understood;
those skilled in the Lord’s work must recognize them as being devoid of true worship. || 45 ||
Thus, O one born from the manifested lotus, the bodily disposition has been explained for every act of ritual placement; now hear the certain conclusion regarding the ancillary [disposition]. 46.
For by means of that quality of knowledge, it always embraces—whether externally or internally—a small object, its secondary parts, and its belly. (47)
O Mahāmati, others also [attain] perfection through figurative usage;
furthermore, according to the nature of the means, there is attainment of both success and liberation. || 48 ||
And that which follows after all giving, consisting of the fruit of sovereignty, is known as the "pṛṣṭha" (the following); O one of stainless eyes, that is the second Upāṅga.
O twice-born Sūtikṣṇa, that which is the manifestation of the two-fold nature of the Lord, whose essence is Power—
both fierce and gentle— is the secondary limb (upāṅga) known as the arms.

That which is the great essence consisting of potency, belonging to the manifested power of manifestation and possessing manifold seeds—that is the field known as the thighs, whose nature is that very essence. (51)

That which is the body consisting of both knowledge and ignorance belonging to the All-Knowing One—or rather, that which provides the occasion for the manifestation of His power—is indeed proclaimed as the fifth subsidiary limb (upāṅga) called Jānu. || 52 ||
O Lotus-eyed One, that power of sustaining the state of the Imperishable, which indeed possesses a quality distinct from its own, is declared to be the name of Your feet. (53)
In the placement (nyāsa) of the Lord regarding creation, maintenance, and withdrawal, or within one's own self,
there is the conceptualization of the primary limbs and secondary parts preceded by the twelve syllables.

Furthermore, O Supreme Lord, although it consists of syllables that are few in number and others that contain more, and although its form is deficient or excessive, it is nevertheless composed of those very same constituent parts.
Thus they constantly worship me for the sake of ritual practice; moreover, one should worship [me] in one's own fields by name, with a prostration and the *praṇava*.
One should perform this among the secondary limbs (upāṅgas) of mantras that have an excess of syllables;
the utterance [of the mantra] occurs together with twelve measures (mātras) and the syllable.

Indeed, by virtue of being a general term, she remains as the "consisting of water" (ammayī), whether through the vowels beginning with *a*, or through the consonants beginning with *ka* together with the bindu. 58.
O best of the twice-born, in the ancient cities, the gift of individualized forms was established by the hand, which is formed as a mass through the mixture of vowels and consonants.
Pervasion should be understood as consisting of the primary and secondary limbs (aṅga-upāṅga), or else it has another characteristic:
it is free from the primary and secondary limbs of cognition and consists of the radiance of mantra-knowledge.
That which is the supreme nature, the supreme speech, whose form is consciousness, stainless and transcendent,
is filled by the Great Self, who is partless and possesses the state of the presiding witness.
Just as the body is distinct from the living soul, [the subtle body] is distinct from the gross and the subtle;
therein, the gross consists of the elements, while the subtle is designated as the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka).
Just as the principle of the Self residing in the body experiences enjoyment born of sense objects, so too does the Lord, having attained full manifestation, take [upon Himself] that same experience.
In every way, one should worship that Lord of Mantras, established in his form, with his own mantra, through enjoyments, recitations, various hymns, and libations into the fire.
Through specific acts of giving and sacrifices, concluding with the libations to the ancestors,
one should lead [the deceased] to incomparable joy by means of these ritual applications accompanied by recitations.
Thereafter, O Pauṣkara, one should perform the worship of the Mantreśas in due order;
for these are indeed the honors paid to the Mantreśas who express their respective forms. (66)
O twice-born one, even for those who bear the marks associated with the internal limbs of yoga,
when they are in that form in the land of enjoyment, they are indeed [placed] in the forest of enjoyment.
All [deities] possessing the characteristics as previously described should be meditated upon in sequence,
within the mantra-body and the embodied form, blazing with radiant rays. (68)
Furthermore, that supreme mantra-nature, due to its universal form, manifests as various names and syllables, and likewise possesses various forms. (69)
Therefore, O Brahmin, the gift of an image is not prescribed separately for each [deity],
just as other mantras are not [prescribed] with letters separate from the root mantra.
Some have emerged from the Cause, endowed with individuality, power, and qualities;
others, consisting of distinct manifestations, are Lords of Mantras by His will. (71)
The one, all-pervading Lord Ananta, out of compassion for living beings,
established himself by his own will in various forms of mantras, just as he desired.

O Brahmin, though by nature she is one, she indeed becomes many for the sake of the great-souled ones who are to be supported; by the will of the Lord of the World, O Brahmin, she is established in manifold ways.
That which is the supreme mantra-nature, characterized as Vāsudeva,
whose form consists of the six qualities (ṣāḍguṇya), and who is endowed with all powers, principles, and attributes.
Having become a treasury, she herself is characterized by bliss within her own subtle mantra-body, whose sole nature is luminosity. (75)
Through the recitation [of its mantra], through the remembrance, and through the worship of that which resides within one's own manifestation,
the practitioner of its vow attains that supreme, peaceful state which is non-different from it.
Thus, for one who worships the all-pervading Acyuta who has attained oneness,
both worldly enjoyment and liberation— whose nature is eternally accomplished— rest in the palm of his hand.

However, for the sake of manifesting those whose nature is pure consciousness, who possess qualities such as knowledge, and who are the arrays of the power of their own mantras, the Supreme Lord [acts]. (78)
O Lotus-born One, by Your own will, You have manifested Your own power of sound, whose characteristic was previously unmanifested, and within which Your body consists of mantra.
Then, endowed with the qualities of omniscience and mantras possessing the characteristics as previously described, they establish a firm state for the sake of favoring living beings. (80)
But in the arrangement of letters, which consists of various seed-syllables and clusters, whether solitary or mixed, and numbering many, it is essentially recitation. (81)
The purity of the knower, presided over by Consciousness and honored by the immortals, is proclaimed as the very essence of the ritual mantra from its very root. (82)
Furthermore, these mantras, whose bodies are sound and whose nature is contemplation,
do not deviate from their essential form, yet they assume manifoldness.

It is manifold indeed due to the power of various forms, also due to the power of various sentient beings, due to the power of various faiths and devotions, and again due to the power of various fruits. (84)
Furthermore, O Brahmin, due to various castes, various regions, and various times, and through the exertion of various means, [the teachings differ]. (85)
And for the sake of self-realization for those men solely intent on liberation, and for the welfare of living beings whose minds are distracted by sense objects; (86)
Pauṣkara said:
"O Acyuta, you have described the sacrifice for the Blessed One intended for a practitioner of pure being,
one who has conquered the senses, a devotee, and one who has attained perfection in mantra."
I wish to understand again the yoga for the sake of conquering reality;
by knowing it according to the prescribed rule, the knower of mantras attains the stable state.
In the supreme state of Samādhi belonging to the Lord, which resembles a lamp in a windless place that does not flicker.
The Blessed Lord said:
"I have taught you the yoga of the primary [path] immediately after the yoga of action;
that is prescribed for the householder and the sage, but not for one who sacrifices to another."
Likewise, for the Paramahaṃsa who stands outside the world,
I shall describe the yoga of reality according to the characteristics distinguished by the stages (bhūmikās). (90)
O Pauṣkara, for one who has received initiation for the purification of all principles, there is the constant direct perception [of them] through the various supernatural powers (siddhis). || 91 ||
For the sake of attaining liberation and for the pacification of the veil of ignorance,
he abides in the Supreme Self by virtue of his nature as pure consciousness.
O high-minded one, he abides as the essence of mantra, whose nature is the light of consciousness,
remaining concealed by his activity through the yoga of the manifestation of his powers.
O Lotus-born One, that which is to be perfectly awakened to always remains veiled by the Supreme, the all-pervading Lord who consists of all powers. (94)
It is unconfused and innumerable, perfumed by hundreds of latent impressions (vāsanās), belonging to one who is favored by the Guru and solely devoted to the mantra. 95.
That entire web of reality ceases to exist in no other way; therefore, one who has attained the goal and is devoted to the system of action [should proceed]. (96)
One must constantly practice the conquest of the principles (tattvajaya) for the sake of attaining one's true nature;
having meditated upon and propitiated the all-pervading Lord, who consists of all powers.

One should understand [the sequence] from the feet to the head by way of the presiding principles (tattva) according to the distinction of locations, as it has been taught in the context of initiation (dīkṣā). || 98 ||
Then, O twice-born one, like a plantain leaf-cup and then like a sweetmeat, having thus practiced yoga threefold for the sake of that victory, it becomes pure. (99)
But now, O Lotus-born One, one who is equal to both [of them] falls into delusion, characterized by sleep, lethargy, exhaustion, labored breathing, and a vacant gaze. 100.
Know that the six sheaths (ṣaṭkośa) are characterized by obstacles; they belong to you through your own self.
One should conquer them with certainty through the meditation on this weapon-mantra and also through its recitation. 101.
Having first achieved mastery over the vital winds, such as prāṇa and the others,
and being seated in a comfortable posture, one should indeed mentally salute the feet of the Guru.

Having worshipped [the deity] by means of its pervasiveness and having projected it into the body composed of forms, one should then practice with the mind directed toward the external, relying upon identity with that [deity]. || 103 ||
O twice-born one, within the center of the heart-lotus, in the interior of the world,
resides the Supreme Brahman, consisting of all powers, by means of the syllable Om (praṇava).
O twice-born one, having practiced through the yoga of repeated application, one should first cultivate that; indeed, one should perform the practice of conquering the principles by this very method.
Or else, with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) enclosed at the beginning and end by the Praṇava, or with the name-word,
one should indeed meditate upon the thousand-rayed sun and the net of principles individually.
Through the practice of *japa*, that ignorance gradually dissolves into the knowledge of reality.
Then, having first taken the *praṇava*—the sound that is the foundation—as the heart-mantra, one becomes absorbed in that. (107)
In reality, one should dissolve the word "bhava-hṛt" (the heart of existence) along with its designation into the interior of the Praṇava;
and the Praṇava itself, as sound, into Hari, who consists of the bliss of the Self.
In this manner, O twice-born one, he should gradually effect the conquest of the elements beginning with earth, as well as their respective mantras,
and achieve the complete mastery over his own organs and senses.
Thus, having conquered the thirty-three [gods] by means of the imperishable among the principles (tattvas),
he then [conquered] the mind, the ego, the intellect, and the collection of qualities in succession.
Having meditated upon and recited [the mantra] that is designated as consisting of *tamas*, *rajas*, and *sattva*, one should abandon it;
for the subtle [self] is designated as distinct from its constituent aggregates and is characterized differently from its own qualities. (111)
Then, having realized and abandoned even the unmanifest (avyakta), one should thereafter conquer that which is the cause of this aforementioned phenomenal world and of the other.

For one who is intent upon various doctrines and arisen from his own conceptual constructions, the reality of time—which consists of the past, the future, and the present—should be contemplated. (113)

O Great Buddha, having thus meditated upon that which purifies the infinite, as well as the characteristics of existence and non-existence, and the manifold world of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), one should abandon this triad.
The characteristic of the means is indeed the Dharma consisting of four characteristics;
it is eternal, known by the names of the powers of knowledge, action, will, and vital breath. (115)
One may realize it through recitation, meditation, and the higher practice of yoga;
therefore, O Brahmin, one should grasp that which is to be accepted—the pervasive and eternal aggregate.

The divine state, characterized by the seven notions (or numbering seven), should be meditated upon for the pacification of karma; it should be known as the cessation of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman) and as eternally manifest. 117.
The existence of the supreme Self, who is the very nature of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman), who is formless yet possesses that form, consists of six attributes. (118)
Having thoroughly practiced the Śabdabrahman, immediately after the six qualities, one should recite that which is beyond syllables, unobstructed, and devoid of sound.
That indeed expresses the true Brahman; it is beyond the realm of speech and is imperishable.
While vowels and consonants are the expressers of all forms, they are themselves the expressers of the Formless.

And due to their own specific qualities, there are many [mantras] characterized by ten features, consisting of the nature of syllables, vowels, consonants, names, sounds, resonances, and tones. || 121 ||
O Mahāmati, there is sound (*dhvani*), the peak-syllable (*kūṭa*), and that which ends with the explosive release (*visarga*);
from these, which possess mixed forms, the essence of the sentence arises through effort. (122)
One who bestows all accomplishments until liberation shall himself partake in those accomplishments;
for the meditator who is proficient in this attains the supreme Brahman.
Then, through practice and by pleasing the one who is easily propitiated, he understands it correctly;
and that meditation, O Lotus-born One, is distinct from ordinary meditation and is meditative absorption pertaining to the inner self.
And that which appears externally as manifold within the nature of light and bliss—those two are the waves and the subtle self-nature of the Lord who is denoted by the word "Sat. (125)
Together with her, the knower of reality proceeds to the imperishable state; having thereby attained self-realization from the Supreme Lord, who is higher than the high. (126)

And it shall always belong to those who delight in knowledge and action, who practice faith and self-restraint, who are believers, who have conquered their senses, and who are devoted to the True Being.
This should never be spoken to one who is not a devotee, nor to an atheist, nor to one whose mind is fixed on fallacious reasoning, nor to one who has abandoned both ritual action and Brahman. 128.
From dawn until the end of night, this activity of the Supreme Lord is what reaches the hearts of those Brahmins who have transcended the world.

Many others, established in worldly conventions, are not [true] lords; they are devoted solely to the void or Brahman, yet remain possessed of the intellect that proliferates through the elaboration of speech. (130)
Pauṣkara said:

"O Eternal One, I desire to know, according to the prescribed rule, the characteristics of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted through the various divisions of the collection of principles; please explain this to me."
The Blessed Lord said:
Just as the oil of milk does not exist apart from it, know that in this same way the Supreme Lord is present within all principles (tattvas). || 132 ||
One should practice as taught in meditative absorption (samādhi) through both unity and diversity; for indeed, that which was previously agitated becomes solitary upon its attainment. 133.
The group of organs known as the senses, along with the entire phenomenal world extending up to the highest manifest being— that imperishable aggregate— is withdrawn.
Indeed, the field of enjoyment for those bound by karma is designated as having manifold forms;
it is endowed with the qualities of pleasure and pain, and is firmly composed of delusion and illusion. (135)
Ignorance, however, increases moment by moment through attachment to that [object];
it dissolves through knowledge. Therefore, O twice-born one, one must always [cultivate] that [knowledge]. (136)
Although the means to be contemplated through the meditation on what is to be abandoned is indeed clear,
even that remains unstable when it comes to the actual attainment of the accomplishments (siddhis).

Therefore, O best of those endowed with sattva, having extracted the essence from that, one should employ the means for the perfection of yoga: namely, mind, intellect, ego, and the quality of sattva. (138)
This fourfold unmanifest state ceases through the attainment of Brahman;
thereafter, there is the divine instrument characterized by the five powers.
O Great-minded One, that which is known as time, knowledge, action, will, and vital breath is the supreme, non-abandonable, eternal [Self], which effects the accomplishment of all ritual acts. (140)
For the victory over the multitude of principles, for the attainment of the six qualities,
for the thorough knowledge of the fourfold self, and indeed for the realization of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman).
But for the attainment of the bliss of light and for reaching the state free from conceptual construction,
one should first receive this ninefold method from the mouth of the Guru.

By means of the natural state associated with Acyuta, which consists of the objects of attainment and the means of attainment, there is nothing that the practitioner does not directly realize through that realization. (143)
Accomplished meditation always bestows its own respective fruit through victory;
for this reason, that which is to be accomplished is the means for accomplishing another object to be accomplished.
And that group of six beginning with knowledge is distinct from the reality of Brahman;
likewise, the eightfold power beginning with atomization (aṇimā) is so, as well as whatever else is different from this. || 145 ||
Origination and dissolution, as well as sovereignty facing every direction—the spiritual, the divine, and that pertaining to the elemental self, O twice-born one. (146)

However, regarding the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) on the practice of reality (*tattva*), those who contemplate reality should know that the collection of principles begins from the word "Śabdabrahman" and ends with "Earth. (147)
Know that the supreme Brahman within is always the universal;
likewise, that which pertains to the divine is to be known as the Praṇava together with its Lord. 148.
O lotus-eyed one, the respective nature of everything—whether gross, subtle, or supreme—is to be known as the *adhibhūta*. 149.
This general method of meditation, preceded by internal [contemplation], applies everywhere;
now I shall speak of it with its specific details—listen with a one-pointed mind. (150)
O twice-born one, the supreme Brahman, which is waveless, is to be understood as the inner self (adhyātma) within the uncreated Śabdabrahman through many millions of mantras.
By virtue of their divine nature, they are eternally established in that very [state], O twice-born one;
however, that which consists of the collection of the principles of speech should be understood as the elemental (adhibhūta). || 152 ||

The Śabdabrahman, as it has been described, which is known by the name of the six internal qualities, should be fully understood as the fourfold self (cāturātmya), which is beyond form with respect to the divine realm. 153.
That which they proclaim as the innumerable array of powers (śakti) arising from the qualities (guṇas), know that to be the specific nature of the objective sphere (adhibhūta). || 154 ||
Indeed, whatever sixfold quality belongs to the vital power (prāṇa-śakti) with respect to the internal self, that is the eternal,
lotus-eyed Vasudeva with respect to the divine.
The vital breaths, beginning with apāna, which sustain the universe, constitute the *adhibhūta* (the elemental).
The two powers of knowledge (*jñāna*) and strength (*bala*) abide as being superior to the power of will (*icchāśakti*). 156.
That which is to be known as the presiding deity (adhidaiva) is the Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa, the Imperishable;
and that which is the capacity (sāmarthya) resting upon all the principles (tattvas) is indeed the objective element (adhibhūta). || 157 ||
O Pauṣkara, know that these two, called Sovereignty and Heroism, belong to the internal [self];
but the presiding deity of the power of action (kriyā-śakti) is the supreme lord Padmapna. || 158 ||

O one of stainless vision, the pervasive expansion of great light is the *adhibhūta*; it is the ever-arisen power of fire (*tejaḥ-śakti*), which is the unmanifest (*avyakta*) within the twice-born as the *adhyātma*.
O high-minded one, the triad of the sun, the moon, and fire is proclaimed as the presiding deities; the three unconfounded qualities (guṇas) are the objective sphere (adhibhūta). 160.
Furthermore, the respective functions of the three qualities (*guṇa*) within the internal self are as follows:
the deity of *sattva* is fire; for *rajas*, it is the state of immortality. (161)

The sun is the presiding deity of *tamas*, while Viṣṇu is the presiding deity of *sattva*. O Great-minded one, non-attachment to *rajas* is to be understood as its presiding entity (*adhibhūta*). (162)

For great delusion (mahāmoha) is proclaimed as the presiding deity of darkness (tamas); the conscious principle (cetana) is the internal attribute of the intellect (buddhi), and its presiding deity is always [the god] Sadāśiva. 163.
O Lotus-born One, passion is indeed his *adhibhūta*, consisting of the power of the twice-born;
that which is called *ahaṅkāra* is his *adhyātma*, O lotus-born one. (164)
With respect to the divine, the great Vaiśvānara of Time is to be fully known;
and now, the greatness of the mind is explained with respect to the elemental.

Internally, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) is the Boar in the form of the ego (ahaṅkāra); he is to be known as the deity presiding over the divine (adhidaiva), and his will (saṅkalpa) constitutes the elemental state (adhibhūta). || 166 ||

But for the five sense-faculties, the mind is traditionally held to be the internal [deity]; know that Time, the Self, and the Divine are the presiding deities, while pleasure and so forth are their corresponding objective domains. (167)
That which consists of speech and the other [organs], pertaining to the twice-born as the internal self (adhyātma), is the group of sense organs;
however, that which pertains to the divine (adhidaiva) should be understood as the infallible one named Viśvarūpa.
O one of stainless vision, that which consists of the eight wombs—namely, activity and the objective world—is indeed the internal state of the subtle elements together with the gross elements. 169.
Understand the extremely subtle array of instruments as the presiding deities;
O Lotus-born One, know this manifold manifestation of the Lord's power to be His divine array.

For those seeking victory over the stages of reality, that triad which was previously described—beginning with the *adhyātma*—is for the sake of attaining yoga; [namely] that which is to be awakened (*voddhavya*) and the objective world (*adhibhūta*). (171)
O Four-faced One, that [state] is attained by all yogins through the power [of practice], gradually indeed, and by means of gradual absorption through repeated cultivation. (172)

[Extending] from the earth (*ākṣiteḥ*) to the limit of the plane of the Self of all powers (*sarvaśaktyātmapadaparyanta*), which is imperishable—this practice of yoga is remembered for the purpose of dispelling the notion of [independent] reality (*tattva*) and [false] bondage. || 173 ||
For those who seek the fruit, the reality (tattva) would be distinct from the fruit due to the conquest of reality.
