Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Principles," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, a Great Upaniṣad of the glorious Pāñcarātra.
(The cumulative number of verses is 174) Now begins the thirty-fourth chapter;
the Blessed One said:
In a sacred field, a divine sanctuary, a place crowded with holy sites, or in a beautiful grove or forest free from small creatures; || 1 ||
In an underground chamber, on a mountain peak, in a secluded temple,
or in a cow-pen belonging to a brahmin, one should consider oneself secure in a solitary spot.
O Lotus-born One, when the time has passed midnight,
one should practice the cultivation of reality (tattvābhyāsa) right before one's own mantra.
There, O Great-minded One, once fatigue has been overcome, having offered the *arghya* at the head of the mantra and having offered incense accompanied by the sound of a bell— || 4 ||
Having offered praise and performed circumambulation, one should [place it] on a clean spot provided with a covering,
such as a black antelope skin, a *kutapa* woolen cloth, or a blanket.
O Brahmin, having indeed abandoned sleep and remained upon the purifying bed,
one should rise during the Brāhma-muhūrta and perform the five-limbed bath.
O twice-born one, having performed the twilight ritual according to the rules while floating or standing in the midst of the water, he should sit before it with a stainless mirror.
Having displayed and then withdrawn the mantra into the interior of the heart-lotus,
one should perform the rites for those consisting of land and water, excluding the mantra that is eternally established [therein].
Immediately thereafter, having withdrawn the mantras constricted by the limbs of the ritual action,
one should [dispose of] all the remaining offerings, such as the *arghya* and so forth, together with that which has already been consumed.
Having offered [the remainder] to Viṣvaksena with his hand filled with water,
and having cast it into the water as before, he should then collect all of that together.
O best of Brahmins, one should also perform the withdrawal of the mantras from one's own body into the Self by means of the mind; thereafter, one should effect the acquisition of enjoyment.
For the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice to the Blessed One, one should indeed solicit from pure Vaiṣṇava recipients with clean wealth, and not otherwise.
Pauṣkara said:
O Lord of the World, you praise again and again the offering of incense accompanied by the sound of a bell over all other enjoyments. (13)
I wish to know the greatness, the measurement,
and likewise the characteristics of the incense burner and the bell, as well as those of the one who holds the incense fire, exactly as they are.
Let the essential nature and characteristics of incense smoke be set forth.
The Blessed One said:
O Lotus-born one, understand now the definition, the most pure means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge belonging to that which has the Śabdabrahman as its single body. 15.
Know that the equal, the half-equal, the superior, the extended, the first, and the middle are [the divisions];
and know that which is one-third of that to be the equal, while the fourth part is the inferior. 16.
The width is prescribed as being threefold according to the measurement of its height, increased by one-twelfth part—or, according to another reading, decreased by one-tenth part. || 17 ||
Having first demarcated the site with cords running east-west and north-south, one should thus establish the field as a long square. (18)
Having divided and filled it with threads extending horizontally and upwards, one should then place five vertical threads and eleven [horizontal ones]. (19)
Now hear from me the division of those known as the arms:
the field of sound (śabdakṣetra) is prescribed with five and a half parts.
There, having visualized the wheel and the lotus as all-visible, one should likewise visualize,
in sequence, the conch, the lotus-born [deity], the pearl necklace, and so forth.
One should fashion a perfectly circular pearl necklace situated within three concentric circles;
having left half of the portion at the front, one should leave half of that half above it.
With the remaining large portion, which is half of that part above it,
a twelve-spoked wheel is prescribed, provided with the region of the navel.
O Brahmin, it may consist solely of chisels, or be mixed with earth according to necessity;
it may have sixteen spokes, or a hundred peaks, and be beautiful to behold.
Then, O Lotus-born One, having fashioned a twenty-four-petaled lotus with its pericarp and filaments using one part and the upper portion [of the remaining material], || 25 ||
Having mentally excluded the space between the hub of the wheel and the tips of the petals, one should fashion it according to the desired measurement, made very smooth and free from flaws. (26)
One should fashion a beautiful mass of filaments situated within the center, or one that is attached to the pericarp, elevated, and well-compacted.
Then, above, by means of the two paths and a portion, there is the auspicious mark;
the king of conch shells rests upon the base of the pericarp and is visible as a half-moon.
Adorned by the power of the series of worlds,
the *kumbha* (vessel) is equal in measure to a portion of that [universe], appearing in the form of the whirlpool of the syllable *Oṃ*.
Then, by means of half a part,
one should gradually reduce the pitcher from the opening of the hole down to its base.
O Brahmin, up to the limits of the conch and the pitcher, one should shave from two directions;
likewise, the mark of the fish should be shaved half by half from two feet.
The first series of worlds has an extent of four and a half parts;
the second is reduced by one part, and the third is measured by one part.

O Lotus-born One, by means of one's own intellect, from the top down to a point slightly above the end, the field is prescribed as being diminished everywhere according to the force of the proportional measurement (anupāta). || 33 ||
O Great-minded One, understand how it should be fashioned upon the conch: its height should be four and a half parts.
O twice-born one, the width of the portion designated as the *muṣṭi* on the mace-base should indeed be made one and a half parts, and its height should be one part.
It should be either square or smooth and adorned with artistic work;
in the case of a circular [mandala], it is remembered that the square is for the circular one, and the four-cornered for the round one.
For that which is of equal form, O Brahmin, or has a hand-hold there, or is pointed at the top like a spearhead, or is circular—it is remembered as being common in all respects. (37)
One should raise the fist upward and perform the "club-stiffening" (gadāstambha) as before;
know that it has seven joints and is provided with knots and shells (śukti).
It is adorned with strings of pearls, possesses sharp edges and a square shape,
and is endowed with the form of a bracelet as well as a cluster of stars.
Having completed it as circular with a multitude of shells, or as a simple square, smooth and devoid of ornamentation. (40)
One should construct a pillar for the mace (gadāstambha), either octagonal or perfectly circular, marked according to its own proportions; then, upon its summit—
One should fashion [the image] with two parts elevated, having either two arms or four arms;
its limbs are divided as previously described, and it is adorned with a circle of eyelashes.
O twice-born one, one should make the wings as wide as that [central part] and equal to a fourth part;
and the two tails and the two wings should indeed be extended by a third part.
The pair of primary hands should indeed be extended equally and joined together like a casket, arising from the forehead.
Spreading like wings, situated in the sky, marked by the study of the Vedas,
and indeed devoted to the collection of mantras— this should be performed, or else in full detail.
Then, having spread it out upon the surface of the earth according to this procedure,
the craftsmen themselves must examine it along with the measurements and the unfinished forms.
Whatever is deficient or excessive due to this reason, one should personally rectify it before that [deity], by means of the heart alone, through one's own intellect and action. 47.
O Lotus-born One, the moving embryo, made of sharp iron,
measures half a part more than the field and is the manifester of sound.
Thus far has been described the great primary fiery creation,
wherein manifest time is supported, O Lotus-born One, residing in the navel.
And therein, the group of spokes is remembered as twelve;
that very same [wheel] has sixteen spokes along with the neuter vowels. (50)
O Lotus-born one, the threefold form of all phonemes is established in the state of Vaikharī, preceded by Paśyantī, O Lotus-born one. (51)
Indeed, that supreme nature of speech which resides in the six-spoked [wheel] supported by the spokes,
is present in that very sixteen-spoked [wheel] and likewise in the *akartarīs*.
For it exists eternally indeed in the form known as the Middle;
beyond this is that which possesses twenty-four syllables as its quality.
O Mahāmati, that lotus which is the lattice-work should be fully understood;
know that the color designated as "prakāra" is the pericarp of the lotus.
The conch is the letter *ya*, while the mace is held in the clenched fist;
the seven letters beginning with *ra* and ending with *ha* constitute the joints of the mace. (55)
"O Lotus-born One, know that patience is thus;
and the bell has the nature of the Sound-Brahman (śabdabrahman) as its defining characteristic. (56)
The power of the Blessed One is indeed to be known as being contained within the six qualities;
it is endowed with a multitude of splendors and assumes the form of that substance which is splendor itself.
Know this to be the one called Ghaṇṭā, the dual quality pertaining to the presiding deity;
it is that which resides within the space of the heart and is to be abandoned for the sake of attaining Śabdabrahman.
It is eternally manifest, incomparable, and beyond the range of the mind;
therefore, it is not possible to teach it to others who lack devotion. || 59 ||
O Lotus-born One, this is the characteristic of mantras consisting of the nature of others:
that which exists within the tenfold sound beginning with the letters and ending with the visarga.
And it abides in the nature of the mantra, consisting of the form of the phonemes;
it is the mantra that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, which has been received from the mouth of a true Guru.
The object of knowledge situated in five locations should be worshipped by devotees intent on divine rites:
externally in an image and the like; on the tip of the tongue; and in the lotus of the heart.
And within the crest of incense smoke and the auspicious sound of the bell,
their true nature as light remains established, illuminating the heart.
O Mahāmati, know that in its intermediate form it is uninterrupted;
furthermore, it rests upon the smoke of incense and possesses the body of Vaikharī speech. (64)
When the bell is being rung for the sake of uninterrupted experience, those who abide by relying upon it must indeed always be known [as such]. 65.
At the time of daily worship, however, practitioners desiring success should [meditate on] Ananta,
accompanied by Kāla and Vaiśvānara, as the impeller of sound.
The conch rests upon a necklace of pearls, situated in the mouth of the bell;
O one of great intelligence, it is firmly established there, and above that, it rests in the sky.
In whichever region of the body the twelve-fold sun is situated as the wheel (*cakra*),
that very same [sun] abides within the *kartarīs* by way of the nature of the months. (68)
The moon indeed consists of sixteen digits and has a body composed of those digits;
in all the circular fields, Varuṇa himself is present.
The individual soul (jīva) indeed rests upon the unmanifest lotus-petal interwoven with the principles (tattva),
while the Lord (Īśvara) rests upon the pericarp (karṇikā) within the filaments of that lotus.
Know that the syllable Om (praṇava) is placed upon the conch, and the Vidyā is situated on the mace;
likewise, Garuḍa is the presiding deity of the vital breath—thus is the host of deities.
Having meditated upon her and worshipped her with the initial offerings of water (arghya) and so forth, and having fumigated her according to the prescribed rite,
O Lotus-born One, one should establish her upon the pedestal at the proper times.
Listen as I speak of those [rites] that must be performed among the Vedic rituals:
thereafter, during the worship of the deities situated within the seat of Gaṇeśa.
Especially at the time of the oblations and the mantras, during the offering of incense, at the conclusion of recitation and praise, and when the satiation of the fire has commenced; || 74 ||
At the offering of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), at the dismissal of the mantras, at the time of worshipping Viṣvaksena, and in the presentation of his worship; || 75 ||
For one desiring success, the prescribed movement must not be otherwise;
it should be accompanied by the authoritative means, the defining characteristics, the object of knowledge, and the presiding deity. (76)
And learn from me his other forms, which are mere semblances of the primary one. || 77 ||
By means of the five [mantras] mentioned, beginning with the discus (cakra) and ending with Garuḍa. || 78 ||
O Brahmin, the arrangement of the water for the feet is prescribed for all of them. || 79 ||
It is broad, with long petals, and endowed with a mass of filaments. || 80 ||
O twice-born one, one should place the triad beginning with the conch upon its pericarp;
or else, near the line of the mouth, one may place the disc alone.
Having first formed that triad beginning with the conch and followed by the lotus, and having subsequently completed everything as it was described, ending with Garuḍa at the rear; || 82 ||
O Lotus-born One, O Four-faced One, having fashioned a conch, a mace, and the king of birds upon the lotus of the field whose wheel is liberated; 83.
Upon the door-panel is a lotus with a long petal, facing downwards;
it is devoid of the conch-mark and endowed with the stalk of a mace and a sword. (84)
Having fashioned the conch as described for the earth with its equal [measure], a mace should then be made above it, provided with the enemy of serpents (Garuḍa). 85.
Alternatively, one should fashion a lotus with its face turned upward and its stalk directed toward Garuḍa;
or rather, a lotus with its own face [turned upward] is prescribed in that location.
And having likewise obtained a conch shell with a clockwise spiral, adorned with three folds—one for each [hand], excluding the discus, the conch, and the lotus. (87)
A bell that is very smooth and round, with a face like a cluster of pearls and stars, and free from any blemish, shall become a refuge for those who face obstacles.
O Brahmin, for she indeed dispels obstacles when accompanied by a mark;
therefore, she must certainly be made with a mark in order to obtain the fruit of her husband. 89.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Incense Bell," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, a Great Upaniṣad within the Śrī Pāñcarātra. || 34 ||
(Total number of verses: 89) Now begins the thirty-fifth chapter;
the Blessed One said:
Thus has been described the characteristic of the incense bell, which increases prosperity,
O twice-born one, when it is rung during the offering of incense.
The mantra constantly attends upon the worshipper here [in this presence].
Now, one should construct the measurement of the path using either one’s own fingers or those consisting of the [standard] measures. (2)
O Brahmin, with twenty-four [units], one should prepare the supreme incense-burner; its length should be made by craftsmen using pure iron, as previously described.
O Lotus-born One, having made that square face, which rests upon fire, circular or octagonal by means of a measurement equal to one-fourth of its own size; 4.
In the center of this eight-sided [mandala], one should indeed fashion a wheel together with a lotus;
or a lotus accompanied by the Lord of Weapons (the trident), or a svastika, or a house of jewels? || 5 ||
It is properly adorned with a turban-band and a conch-shell at its upper edge;
now hear from me concerning that wheel, which is both square and circular.
For the characteristic, O Mahāmati, according to its state, is distinguished;
having made the field either square or equally circular. (7)
In that space, one should fashion a lotus arising from a lotus, adorned with lotus stalks;
it may be simple or provided with a wheel, according to rule and distributed for enjoyment.
Having first divided that [circle] into eight equal parts up to the center, one should then draw a circle with a radius of six parts, starting from the hollow of the pericarp.
O twice-born one, as it revolves within the cavity of the pericarp, one should bring it to a state of depression;
one should know that its measurement is equal to half a sphere, just as when it is sealed.
With one-third of that [measurement], the height of the pericarp (karṇikā) is formed around the six-fold division;
it is well-surrounded by filaments (kiñjalkas) characterized by that same measurement.
That which remains from the seventh part, outside the row of filaments,
consists of two parts by which the network of petals is completed.
Having likewise prepared the wheel outside of that, divided into as many sections as desired and adorned with strings of pearls, just as before; || 13 ||
O twice-born one, having taken a fourth part from the eighth part of the field according to the stated measurement, one should designate it for the purpose of the altar (vedi).
One should fashion four conch shells in the four corners of the altar;
this square altar, as previously described, is adorned with conch shells.
O Lotus-born One, this configuration of the field of activity (vṛttakṣetra) is not prescribed as fixed;
it may emerge from the back of the lotus in whatever circular shape is desired.
It should extend as far as the edge of the altar-ground or up to the rim of the wheel;
it may be shaped like a face or perfectly circular, according to the specific requirement of that site.
For the purpose of supporting the altar, two lotuses are raised up;
in their center stands [the deity], endowed with the auspicious marks, seated in the lotus posture or other such postures. (18)
One should assume the form of Agni; indeed, that pair of feet should be outstretched, and one's own mouth raised up toward the region of the ears.
O twice-born one, having fashioned [the image] at the end of the stalk upon a pericarp-lotus,
it should be adorned with lotus petals that are half-blown and likewise with Tathāgatas.
O Mahāmati, at its base one should construct a foundation exceeding that [in height] and equal to it in width; the ground-plot should be provided with a svastika, well-perforated, and very firm.
Then, at the back of the lotus, one should fashion the wind-element (marut-kṣetra) together with its bindu;
it serves as the support and is equal in height to the earth-element (kṣmā-kṣetra).
Together with the diameter and breadth of the earth, it is equal to that or twice as large;
resting upon the rim of the wheel, it is dissolved and easily bent.
Or else, the first [feature] is a network of small bells, which is supreme for dispelling obstacles;
thus indeed has the specific characteristic been fully described. (24)
Now hear from me the general description of the incense burner for the mantra-practitioner:
within its circular interior, there is a lotus provided with a pericarp and filaments.
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus adorned with a circular perimeter representing the sky,
it may be provided with a string of pearls, or likewise constructed with an altar.
Then, in the middle, one should fashion [the mandala] with a twelve-spoked wheel together with a lotus, or otherwise [with other designs],
extending with variously colored petals up to the back boundary.
In the place where the petals are fully blossomed, it is adorned with a turban and a cloth,
serving as a resting place for the face, and provided with a supporting rim.
Pure, with a very smooth stalk, and freed from the fibers of the lotus—thus should the form be conceived according to the desired measurement. (29)
O Lotus-born One, that which is fashioned from all metals according to one's own capacity indeed bestows happiness upon ministers, virtuous householders, and devotees. (30)
I shall describe the characteristics of that which is called the *samudgara*; let it be understood:
a hollow, circular cavity according to the dimensions specified for its width. (31)
Having first made them perfectly equal, like a lotus bud with its stalk,
one of those two should be placed above the other in the center.
O Lotus-born One, it is covered by a fully blossomed lotus with its face turned downward, and by a second lotus with its face turned upward. (33)
Indeed, that stalk which stood above, joined with a multitude of seeds and possessed of gaps,
was grasped by Vinata from its base with her trunk, which resembled the leg of an elephant.
And having employed two [teeth] reaching to the region of the nose for the sake of stability, thus has the characteristic of those in full bloom been described. (35)
Now listen, O Great-minded One, to the characteristic of those [lines] as they have been requested, according to their arrival: it is one-fourth of the previous length in terms of its breadth.
Having laid out a quadrangular field upon the surface of the earth,
one should then divide that length into eight equal parts.
O Lotus-born One, one should then construct a pedestal four times as wide [as the base],
elevated by one-eighth part, and endowed with the arrangement previously described.
Extending from the feet up to the uṣṇīṣa, it should be spread out according to its width;
it should be raised by half the height of the pedestal and measured as three parts of that width.
One should fashion a lotus in the center of the pedestal with two pericarp-sections,
possessing eight petals and filaments, and adorned by a circular space.
It should be broad by half a part from its width, and again, its height should be four and a half parts; it may be either octagonal or perfectly circular.
Or it may be beautiful and square, provided with that same arrangement; for the pillar should be established in this manner, O Lotus-born One, according to one's desire.
That which is circular among these is indeed endowed with various artistic arrangements;
it rests upon the top of the pillar and is generally measured by one part.
Equal in width to the pedestal, it is adorned with twelve spokes, provided with a hub and a broad rim, and decorated with pearl necklaces and other ornaments.
O Lotus-born One, having fashioned the wheel with its small bells as before,
it should be fixed within the middle of the axle and elevated by one and a half parts.
From the top, it should be equal to the pedestal; in thickness, it should be commensurate with the wheel;
in width, by half its portion; and it should be narrow at the eight designated points.
And by means of gradual progression, its expansion is thus prescribed;
having thus prepared the mouth of the smoky fire. (47)
Always, at all times, in the act of worshipping the All-pervading Lord, [he offered] water-born flowers, land-born flowers, and living beings born of the sky as well as those grown on earth. (48)
And with canopies of leafy creepers, along with conch shells, svastikas, and lotuses;
with clusters of pure flowers, and with Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others. (49)
And outside, in all directions, there should be a residence for the celestial nymphs;
this applies to one who possesses such a palace and whose face is a circular pedestal.
O Lotus-born One, I shall duly explain the arrangement of the seat, which is joined with three offerings and resembles the face of a conch shell. (51)
O Lotus-born One, one should fashion a lotus that is elevated with pride upon the seat; it should be a variegated support for the pillar, divine, and made of *āmalasāra* wood.
Then, one should erect a pillar fashioned with artistic designs and previously smeared with red [pigment],
or one resembling a series of coils, upon the three-fold base of the pillar-shaft.
O Brahmin, one should fashion a lotus wheel with filaments and twelve petals;
its pericarp should be broad, and above that, one should place a face as described previously.
It was arranged according to the description given above, circular on all sides,
adorned with strings of pearls, and hung with a network of tinkling bells.

O Lotus-born One, regarding these, one specific ritual procedure has indeed been taught; furthermore, I have composed this arrangement concerning the nature of water-born and land-born beings. || 56 ||

And having thoroughly reflected upon it, O Lotus-born One, that [measurement] should always be performed for all [limbs], when the body is properly formed and the internal parts are clearly manifested. || 57 ||
Thus has been stated in brief, as well as in detail,
the characteristic of the act of burning incense and of that which assumes various forms.

Having thus accomplished [the rite], consecrated it, and led it to the state of ultimate reality, one should again empower it with its own mantra and worship it as it rests within the support. || 59 ||
At the base, in the place of the svastika, know the earth-element (kṣmātattva) to have five characteristics;
the water is the lotus, and the fire is the wheel of great luster.
Within the pericarp [is] the sky with its network of bells moved by the wind;
thus indeed is it accompanied by the adhibhūta and the adhidaivata. 61.
That which was previously declared as the object of meditation for the accomplishment of all rites is the entire form of the wheel, consisting of the nave, spokes, rim, and circumference. (62)
That which is partless and perfectly round is indeed celebrated as the "orb of space" (vyomavṛtta);
one should worship the incense burner endowed with such characteristics.

Having performed the consecration according to the rule, one should proclaim the lineage of one's own family; having marked it with one's own name and offered it, O high-minded one, [one should recite]. 64.
In the divine abode of Hari, frequented by gods and Siddhas,
one should perform offerings at the three times of day, together with incense smoke.
One should cause a pleasant-sounding bell, accompanied by the sounds of kettledrums and other instruments, to be rung;
and with hymns of praise, one should perform many circumambulations of the divine temple.
O Great-minded One, having heard from outside the sound of a bell— the single seat of the Śabdabrahman— there arose great satisfaction for the assembly of Siddhas stationed there.
Whose is this unstruck sound that has now suddenly become manifest, by whom it was projected outward for the sake of instructing those capable of liberation? (68)
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Incense Burner," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, a Great Upaniṣad within the glorious Pāñcarātra. || 35 ||
Now begins the thirty-sixth chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to know that which has been uttered by you."
And it was marked by the characteristics of a great-souled being. || 1 ||
Whatever divine abode or perfected sanctuary there may be, it serves as a means for men—whether they be ignorant or even wise—to attain [liberation]. (2)
O Lord, for those who practice mantras preceded by propitiation,
there is constant favor from the deity as well as great victory over reality.

For those who have completed their studies, for celibate students, for ascetics free from attachment, and for those who have desisted from the householder's life, it quickly becomes free from obstacles.
The Blessed Lord said:
This world, extending as far as the primordial earth (Ākṣiti), is indeed differentiated by duality and consists of illusion (māyāmaya).
It is composed of the principles of the Lord (bhagavat-tattva) known as the fields (kṣetra), together with the lords of the fields (kṣetranātha). || 5 ||
Furthermore, he himself [manifests] through those whose forms consist of various manifestations, preceded by an array of pervading bodies,
and who possess the eternal and stainless embodiment of the six divine attributes.
For the sake of favoring those living beings who are ungrateful and of little intelligence—whether they be devotees, non-devotees, or even atheists. (7)
When the island has moved to the axle of the earth-wheel,
that field which bestows the fruits of one's own karma— though it be ancient and renowned— is indeed limited in its merit for a person.
For the sake of favoring human beings, [the Lord], though formless, has presided over various locations through his own names out of compassion, by means of the most excellent sacred fields (kṣetra).
Likewise, O Lotus-born One, [the deities] were joined with their lords of the fields in embodied form;
or else, having established themselves upon the earth in the state of seeds, they remained there. || 10 ||

[He is endowed] with knowledge and the rest, with the powers such as atomization (vāṇimā) and so forth, with the unmanifested elements such as earth, fire, and the rest, in the form of the principles (tattva), seeds (bīja), and digits (kalā), all united with the existence of Brahman.
Having descended into this world, they indeed manifest themselves prior to creation;
then, by their own essential nature and out of a desire to favor all beings, they proceed.
At the time of the withdrawal of the circle of the earth, together with the most excellent fields,
he brought under his control those who possess mastery and excellent bodies, as well as the preeminent sages.
For in each respective field that bestows security and a favorable rebirth,
there exists a state of mind characterized by various desires, as well as a state of self-conceit.
Having indeed manifested his individual form through the supreme and other means of knowledge, according to the appropriate times, by means of the essence of Vāsudeva’s grace; 15.
Therefore, the lords of the fields on earth are indeed renowned by that very form and name;
others are likewise famous under similar names, while the deity himself is the abode.
In this way, the land of action is presided over by the lords of the fields and the fields themselves—
both by the formless fields which are of the nature of consciousness, and likewise by the embodied lords of the fields.
Thus, those leaders of fields who have descended individually into the fields,
they too, after a period of time, will themselves become like stone due to their own defects.
O twice-born one, having perceived this, they disappear due to the ruin of the country and other such calamities;
yet, through abundant deliberations, they once again attain manifestation as before. (19)
And having descended by himself, he should impel [them] through his own power,
just as the ocean, being impelled by the mass of clouds, acts [upon them]. (20)
Thus do my representatives speak— whether in a dream or even in direct perception—
concerning welfare, security, and so forth, either on their own initiative or because their very selves have become absorbed in Me.
O Lotus-born one, it shall always exist for the sake of the welfare of those who are devoted to that truth; however, for others, it serves no purpose other than untruth.
Thus, our excellence is endowed with the existence of [this world];
the latent impression of nihilism exists for the purpose of refuting those who are not devotees. (23)
Indeed, for the satisfaction of the believers and for the accomplishment of the holy sites and other rites,
those Lords of the Field (Kṣetrapālas), Vāsudevas, and Aṣudevās, are stationed within the hollows of the stones.
In some places he appears directly in the form of the discus, conch, lotus, and mace;
especially so on Mount Trikūṭa and indeed on Mount Raivataka.
O twice-born one, [these are found] at Sālagrāma, on the Sahya mountain, likewise at Viṣṇupada,
at Vyāvarta, at Kṛṣṇāśva, and on the slopes of the Himālaya.
On Mount Mahendra, Malaya, Vindhya, or Ṛṣabha; or on Hastidanta, where Satyavrata resides, or on the excellent mountain Vikaṭa. || 27 ||
O Lotus-born One, [this is] on the sacred and most enchanting field of Siṃhācala, presided over by Vāsudeva. || 28 ||
Those who, by their own intellect, go to a field fashioned without effort by some single being of manifold forms and distinctions; || 29 ||
Having taken refuge in the Lord of the Field, those who dwell there in the [outer] regions, or at the end, or others in the middle portion of the earth; || 30 ||
Or else, at first, they are seen by the gods; then they gradually proceed toward that Lord of the Field who has truly entered into the earth.
But that [state of] being in the same world, proximity, and union is for those who are free from attachment yet devoid of discernment—people who lack vision. 32.
But even if one has previously been an atheist who has come for refuge, O Pauṣkara, if he now stands in my presence with faith and is free from worldly activity, [he shall attain success]. 33.

O Lotus-born One, when he was unconscious and being led away by his kinsmen, they cried out "Save him! to the Lord of the World, casting themselves down along with the women, children, and others. Then, knowing that he had been liberated from the body together with the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), [they were released].
Having indeed placed [him] upon that excellent chariot with the great sound of musical instruments.

Having forcibly conquered the fierce soldiers of Death here by means of the servants of the Lord of the Field—namely Nṛsiṃha, Kapila, Kroḍa, Vāmana, Aśva, Śiro-mukha, and others—[he entered]. || 36 ||
With gentle faces, they hold the lotus, discus, and mace;
they bear the plow, the Nandaka sword, the thunderbolt, the noose, the goad, and the bow.
Having been brought by those with faces like Garuḍas, who hold pestles and other such weapons as well as staffs in their hands,
they approach the Lord of the Field and cause him to descend.
"O King, in this field belonging to you, his body composed of the five elements has been abandoned today; he is now without a protector. Perform for him the funeral rites as is appropriate. (39)
But the Lord of the Field, having heard what was uttered by the Gaṇa— [the deed of the virtuous]—
regarded him with a gaze imbued solely with compassion.
Indeed, whatever sin was committed previously in that sanctuary remains as a residue of fault for one who has returned to his own place. (41)
Having brought about the dissolution of all associations through these two methods over the course of time, whatever else was made one's own has likewise been so transformed.
Having drawn forth the latent impression (tapas) from his own body by means of his power and according to the influence of his characteristic marks,
and having ascertained its fitness for refinement, he indeed acts for the attainment of perfect knowledge.

But he grants birth in the land of action (karmabhūmi)—[according to another reading: "therein, at the beginning of his practice"]—into a family of those who perform virtuous deeds, whether in his own field or in another's field; for that is indeed what constitutes being in the same world (sālokana).
Having attained his authority in due time and having performed, in brief, the pervasive practice as appropriate— the auspicious [rite] of thirteen kinds— (45)
By that [means] one becomes one who has accomplished their purpose; by half of that, another;
and the third, O Lotus-born One, is joined with perfect knowledge.

For indeed, through time and by means of the manifestation of the senses characterized [by their objects], one who has previously observed the vow himself should, with deliberate intent, [perform it] in that sacred field as before. (47)
Thereafter, with intense devotion, one should abandon the body through vows and other means in the presence of the Lord of the Field; thus, that person becomes free from all defilement.

Having made the individual body the fire-drill, when knowledge—which is stainless and auspicious—is produced, O lotus-eyed one, he instructs him in that very place in the sacrificial clarified butter (ājya). 49.
O Brahmin, having reached that supreme abode known as Vāsudeva, the merits of the sacred pilgrimage sites of the yogins do not even come near it.
For even those who possess knowledge, by always serving as a support, indeed attain the status of being constituent parts [of yoga], and they too reach the most excellent state of supreme yoga. 51.
O Brahmin, through this supreme means for living beings, they attain that which is eternally filled with knowledge, free from all obstacles. 52.
Since it exists, for this reason it must indeed always be cultivated, just as rays [are drawn] from a pure seed of noble birth. (53)
And they destroy the power that gives rise to growth through suffering;
for indeed, at present, it is exactly thus, without any loss of its own nature.
Indeed, by his own power and through the auspicious rays of his own energy,
he completely purified the field of the inhabitants of that field, having destroyed all their impurities.
Thereafter, they bestow grace upon that person whose sins have been exhausted,
by means of earth, water, fire, wind, and the characteristics of the sky.
For that which is established here is constrained; hear now from me that which is unestablished:
that which arises from the abandonment of food and water is known as *vāta* (wind). [g, gh: *tadvāda*] || 57 ||

O Pauṣkara, having correctly understood that the supreme non-appearance arises through the obstruction of all doors, or [having understood] the time of the falling away of the body, one should exert effort here. (58)
One who desires auspiciousness should strive with effort and devotion toward the attainment of that goal;
yet even if it is not attained through such effort, it is surely obtained through the practice of previous births.
By which [means] do they indeed go to dissolution? Save me, birth after birth, from the exceedingly powerful sin of a man who has made up his mind [to commit it]. (60)
O Lotus-born One, even if the attainment of that [state] has not yet arisen, one who does not possess the terrible teaching of the Ender (Antaka) is not a fit vessel for it. 61.
He is to be honored even by the messengers of Yama, like a man who performs sacrifices;
for let alone human beings adorned with restraints and other virtues. (62)
Other living beings there as well, who are enriched by a particular devotion to the [deity], are born again in another birth due to the power of their prior latent impressions (saṃskāra). || 63 ||
O Brahmin, those who are devoid of right discernment do not attain [this], nor do my devotees; yet he who finds [this] among these [others]—[attains it]. 64.

Among men, he is indeed blessed and is not greatly oppressed by his evil deeds; for although there is no destruction of actions that have not been experienced [through their results], [he is spared]. 65.
They attain attenuation through the power of the greatness of the sacred field;
indeed, the destruction of karma occurs solely by virtue of the practice [of that place] over successive births. (66)
O Mahāmati, by virtue of the power of the lords of the fields together with their fields, those who give gifts to supplicants in such fields as these [attain great merit]. (67)
Or, for the sake of propitiating the All-pervading Lord, they perform austerities with devotion;
they master the Lord of Mantras and offer libations with sesame seeds and other substances.
O Lotus-born One, those who worship the gods with sacrifices obtain the full fruit [of their actions] through the well-known [mantras] preceded by the twelve syllables. (69)
Having received from the mouth of the Guru the *jitantā* mantras ending with the *mantrānta*,
or else by means of his own principal mantra, one should worship the Supreme Lord according to the prescribed rule.

And whatever is situated in the venerable sacred site (ārādhyāyatana) is given to those who hold authority—the foremost of the twice-born and the best of brahmins—who follow the five-fold ritual (pāñcakālin). || 71 ||
That [merit] is to be understood as inexhaustible for those who still desire worldly existence and enjoyments;
however, for those whose passion has ceased through giving, it leads further to the attainment of liberation.
Those who dwell within villages, districts, or other regions,
having given [land] to many [servants] equal to themselves— for their own prosperity (or, according to another reading, for death)— enjoy freedom from disease.
Know that, through one's own power, this [merit] becomes complete in birth after birth, eternally, and from that divine abode, it leads to infinite existence. (74)
O Brahmin, it should be understood that from the Siddhāyatana, one attains a hundred thousand births; however, from the one ordained by the most eminent of Brahmins, one attains a thousand births.
Know that what is performed by a Kṣatriya yields ten-fold results, while that which is prepared by a Vaiśya yields half of that.
O Brahmin, O best of the twice-born, a gift given to a temple constructed by a true Śūdra should be known as yielding sixteen-fold fruit.
Is the fruit indeed the same when a gift is given to a sanctuary for the foremost of the twice-born, which has been designated for those castes who have no other refuge? || 78 ||
But those who have constructed temples with materials from mixed castes give, in due order, half of what was previously mentioned. (79)
O Pauṣkara, for those who desire results and those who are free from desire,
the Lord dwells in all abodes and is present within all forms.
Whether existing within another form or appearing as an incarnation,
he bestows the supreme state through his activity at the conclusion of each manifestation.
Therefore, O twice-born one, you must perform this with great effort, preceded by the propitiation of the mantra, through ritual action characterized by the mark of purity. 82.
Therefore, for those men who are liberated from passion and who offer sacrifices unto the Imperishable,
the unborn and all-pervading Vāsudeva, abiding within the functioning of their own self, is revealed.
But when one whose mind is presided over by that [Brahman] performs sacrifice externally wherever it may be, there and then the eternal Brahman is manifested for them. 84.
Pauṣkara said:
I wish to know the destiny of those men born in a temple who have performed inauspicious deeds, once they have died there—whether it be within or elsewhere. (85)
The Blessed One said:
O Lotus-born one, it is due to some previous impure karma that the intellect indeed repeatedly commits evil deeds.
Even though he knew the greatness of the sacred field, due to being helpless and by the force of his past habituation, he remained there as he was dying.
And in the field of those who have committed evil, for the sake of eternally pacifying their misdeeds, he [the Buddha] acts through means that are not overly harsh, even unto the very end. (88)
Are you alone among them [who act thus] in Kuru? For that which remains after eating is indeed a stain;
it pacifies [the effects of] whatever inauspicious they have performed almost immediately. (89)
Furthermore, O high-minded one, having received that command with his head bowed, he accepted our possession of the body (or enjoyment). || 90 ||
With a mind accompanied by compassion, they purify themselves;
thus, freed from faults, they proceed after the lapse of time. 91.

(206) Through the shared world (*sālokya*) with the *sāmīthīnas*, through the totality of their wisdom, and especially through association with the virtuous, those whose impurities have indeed been destroyed surely return to the Vedic path once more. (92)
They practice that very thing by which they indeed attain union (sāyujya).
Pauṣkara said: "If those born therein, being most wicked, should indeed perish here..."
What is the destiny of those men who are extreme sinners? || 93 ||
The Blessed One said:
At the end, Death purifies their evil deeds through no other means of instruction;
for then, once their faults have been removed, they return again to human birth.
O Lotus-born One, when the mind is intent on the destruction of the body with intense resolve, it attains purification as before, just like men who have committed evil deeds. 95.
Those born there who are free from defects, having gone elsewhere to their dissolution,
now indeed proceed by celestial chariots to the abode of Antaka.
Having honored them, he should then speak with palms joined in reverence:
"O Blessed Ones, please proceed to your respective places and abodes; may you indeed depart. (97)
That state known as sālokya, which is stainless and brings about the destruction of the bonds of worldly existence,
is attained solely by this virtuous path shown by me.
As you set forth, there will be prosperity for you, just as it is for the other inhabitants of that place who know the true nature of the Blessed One. (99)
Thus, for men who lack discernment, the fruit arising from the lotus may come from the sense-base; how much more so, then, for others? 100.
The earth is his feet, his own self is his navel, heaven is his head, and the moon and sun are his eyes; the worlds preceded by the Mahat are the hair upon the body of that All-pervading Lord.
The cardinal directions are his ears, and all the intermediate directions are indeed his arms;
his extension reaches down to the netherworlds, as far as the foundational power (Ādhāraśakti).
The station of that all-pervading, resplendent, and great-souled Lord, who possesses eternal form, is in the region of the soles of his feet. || 103 ||
Since everything consists of the nature of the Word (pada), for that very reason,
O twice-born one, there is indeed no place without a sacred abode for the faithful among the believers.
For those who deny the existence of the afterlife, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is composed of darkness;
however, O Great-minded One, let it be well known that the state of the virtuous remains established for now. (105)
In whatever place it has been installed with devotion by the best of Brahmins and others—whether immovable or movable, beautiful, and made of clay, wood, or stone—[it is to be honored]. 106.
Whatever image of Hari is made from metals such as gold and other ores, for those people who have perished there, it is indeed by virtue of its majesty [that they attain liberation]. (107)
Their residence in the triple heaven is characterized by no great excellence;
at the end, when they have fallen away, their rebirth occurs in various abodes.
O Great Buddha, this [action] should indeed be fully understood in its proper sequence by those devoted to me;
the direct manifestation of the Lord of the Twice-born arises in various fields and sub-fields. 109.
O you born from the lotus, your birth was from the abode of a Kṣatriya fashioned by Brahmā; your birth occurred in a place prepared by a virtuous Vaiśya. 110.

O Lotus-born One, in the abode of Acyuta established by the sages, a man shall not undergo rebirth from the lineage of Maudgalya through his worship; [in another reading: he attains Nārāyaṇa]. || 111 ||
A great sanctuary was fashioned by that man who had attained success through mantra;
for it brought about an excellence of enjoyments for men, and likewise after the lapse of time. (112)
O twice-born one, as far as the sphere of existence conceived by those who know the mantras, there is the eternal destruction of evil; and immediately after that, O Kṣatriya, there is another. (113)
Gradually, O Pauṣkara, by means of a canopy that is not too large, there shall indeed be a complete destruction of those defects over the course of time. (114)
O Lotus-born One, having subsequently descended to the earth, he quickly consumes his remaining food right there and, through religious observances, exhausts his prior misdeeds.
As previously stated, those who proceed in due order reach the supreme state;
and those who have been designated here for the auspicious rite of casting off the body [attain it] in the same way.
For the discerning, no other expiation has been prescribed than this very [practice], for the destruction of the misdeeds accumulated from birth until now. (117)
When those [sins] have been completely burnt away by them, they attain the imperishable state at the end of the body;
therefore, having reached this sacred field, one should perform expiation. 118.

Having personally understood the fruit of evil and having resorted to the eternal essence, one whose mind and intellect were previously contrary [to the truth] thereby attains a state of auspicious stability. (119)
Even if a field is powerful—indeed, even if it is a field that bestows auspicious rebirths upon men—it does not abandon its own capacity, which is discernment, the second [essential factor]. (120)
The group of mind, intellect, and senses, together with the collection of instruments,
is completely purified from its very root to its end by means of great austerity.
The shrines and other such objects constantly bestow their favor upon him—whether that living being remains in the state of life or has gone to the next world. (122)
Even the virtues of the earth are not to be taken everywhere due to the weight of the prescribed rule, just as suppliants do not take [wealth] from high-souled men. 123.
One who perceives food and drink for their own sake abandons the one who knows their quality even if they are devoid of merit,
and likewise, the one devoid of merit abandons the one possessed of merit or otherwise.

Having thus understood the greatness of this sacred field, one should bring it to the highest state of splendor through austerity, meditation, recitation, and the like, as well as by the satisfaction of action, speech, and mind.

The Blessed Lord said: [A loss of text is perceived here; for prior to this, there is the question of Pauṣkara: "If those most sinful who have been born here should perish, what is their destination? (verse 93). As an answer to this, the text proceeds by describing the good destiny of those whose sins have been purified by Antaka, beginning with: "Wherever there is any image of Hari, for men who perish there, by the power of its majesty, their residence shall be in Triviṣṭapa" (verses 106–109), and so on. Following that, the majesty of the sacred field (*kṣetra*) under discussion is concluded by the Blessed Lord with the passage ending: "He should bring it to the highest splendor" (verse 125). Then, abruptly, after citing the heading "The Blessed Lord said," and beginning with "By the four [attendants], Vāsudeva and the others," another subject is introduced. The statement of Pauṣkara’s question that prompts this is not seen; without the prompting statement, the connection of the matter about to be commenced is not established. Therefore, it is certain that the statement of Pauṣkara’s question has been lost.]
By means of the four forms beginning with Vāsudeva previously mentioned,
then by the twelve beginning with Keśava, and thereafter by the ten beginning with Matsya.
The group of principles previously mentioned, numbering twenty-six including the earth (kṣmā) and ending with Īśvara, exists together with the twelve [deities]. || 127 ||
The ten [circles] are surrounded by that which is suitably proportioned and well-formed;
having reached each respective principle (tattva) together with Vāsudeva and the others.
(208) For such is the abiding state of all the gods for the sake of the pacification of existence;
it is the universal form endowed with the six qualities, O Great-minded One. 129.
For they always manifest solely by virtue of their own activity, indeed,
solely through the power of grace and by the will of the All-pervasive Lord.
The surface of the earth is always pervaded by all [beings] who constantly assume various forms; yet each individual manifestation possesses the nature of Ananta through its own majesty.
Thus they proceed with various forms, distinguished by their vehicles, weapons, and emblems; for this is according to the will and sovereign power of the Lord of the World. (132)
Indeed, the status of all beings within their own natures is of various kinds,
even though it is fixed for those who possess weapons and those who bear emblems.
Nevertheless, O Brahmin, all [these] are traditionally held to be common to all embodied beings; even so, understand from me regarding that matter as well.
Nor is it for the sake of pacifying the delusions of others that [the Buddhas] manifest with specific marks, insignia, and banners;
rather, their manifestations are to be understood as occurring through the power of their own activity.

Likewise, due to the power of the various manifestations of that portion, some are the protectors and supports of the primordial forms, while others are distinguished by banners and emblems. || 136 ||
In this way, O twice-born one, the supreme group of manifestations of the three is indeed equal; others, such as Keśava and the rest, likewise bear it equally. (137)
Together with its forms and characteristics, indeed along with its specific distinctions.
Pauṣkara said:

"O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the marks and other characteristics of all [the deities], as well as the specific distinctions you have indicated for the sake of the liberation from worldly existence of those subject to rebirth. (138)
The Blessed Lord said:
Listen, O pure-eyed one, as I describe to you correctly and in due order, beginning from the Primordial God, the arrangement of the marks. 139.
Of the four hands, the first on the right should be meditated upon, O one of stainless vision, as bestowing fearlessness or granting boons to devotees.
Know that the left [hand] carries a conch shell across all four positions;
however, for the first [deity], it is again on the left and right sides relative to the two rear [positions].
Understand that Acyuta holds the Kālacakra and a heavy mace in his left hand, together with a plow and a pestle in his right hand. 142.
In his two western arms, O Pauṣkara, are a drawn bow and arrow, as well as a shield accompanied by the sword Nandaka; such is the form of Aniruddha.
"With the two rear hands starting from the middle hand"—
thus indeed [is the procedure] for the fourfold form, and likewise for other forms.
Listen to the description of the abodes of those marked with the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus;
first, the stations of the three deities belonging to the Primordial Goddess (Ādidevī) shall be told. (145)
Know that there is a discus in the left rear hand and a conch in the right;
in the principal right hand there is a lotus, and in the one following it, a mace.
For in this manner the Blessed Keśava holds the lotus and other objects;
indeed, with his two principal hands, the right and left, he holds the mace and the lotus.
He holds the conch and the discus in his two left hands and likewise in the pair of his two right hands;
know him as the Blessed One named Nārāyaṇa, and now learn of the one named Mādhava.
In the primary right and left [hands], the Lord holds the conch and the mace;
in the two front arms, however, he holds the lotus and the discus.
These three divine forms, radiant as jasmine, the moon, and crystal, together with the Blessed Vāsudeva, constitute his fourfold nature. (150)
O Lotus-born One, the thorough knowledge of these three bestows liberation for some and the enjoyment of worldly existence for others; they belong to the three gods who protect desire. 151.
"In the principal left hand there is a lotus, and indeed in the other right hand there is a mace; such is described as the form of the Lord known as Govinda. (152)
Now, learn of the arrangement of Viṣṇu’s marks:
in his left and right hands, in front, there are a conch and a lotus.
Thus, with his two rear hands, he holds a discus and two kaumodakī clubs; now hear the description of the one known as Madhusūdana. (154)
The lotus is in the primary hand, while the Pāñcajanya conch is in the left;
the mace is in the right, the discus is behind in the right, and the other [attributes] are on the right side. (155)
Thus, indeed, this triad belongs to the gods who possess the form of knowledge;
but the second [form], due to its fourfold nature, has the brilliant luster of a ruby.
Now, the sequence of the three Pradyumna deities is described;
listen to the description of their emblems along with their respective colors. (157)
In the front left hand there is a discus, and in the other [right] hand a mace;
in the back left hand a conch is prescribed, and in the one following that a lotus. || 158 ||
Understand the form of the Lord known as Trivikrama, the Dwarf (Vāmana):
a mace is in his left hand, while the discus is in his primary right hand. (159)
In the left hand, which is the rear one, there is a lotus, and in the right hand there is a conch;
for Śrīdhara, the mace is proclaimed to be in his primary left hand.
In the front, on the right side, is a discus; on the left, at the rear, is a conch;
and on the other [side], the supreme lotus and a discus with a brilliance equal to ten million suns.
O twice-born one, these three forms together with the Lord should be known as possessing the luster of molten gold, existing in a state of fourfold nature.
Therefore, understand also the triad of those whose forms are unceasing,
along with their bearing of emblems and their distinction by color.
In his left hand he holds a lotus, while in the second [left] hand he holds the king of weapons;
and in his two right hands, starting from the one furthest back, they hold [their respective objects] in sequence. (164)
Let one understand Padmanābha as holding a lotus bud and a heavy mace;
in his foremost left hand is the king of discs, and in his other principal hand is a lotus.
Dāmodara holds a mace in his left hand, while in the one following it he holds the king of conchs;
in the leftmost hand he holds a beautiful mace positioned at the front.
The conch is in the front on the left side, while the discus is in the back on the right;
the lotus, radiant as the sun, is in the back on the left side.
This group of forms is remembered as resembling the flax flower;
it too possesses a fourfold nature along with the god Aniruddha. (168)
Listen now to the abiding of the weapons—both formless and embodied—of Viṣṇu, the Lord of All, for the sake of stability within these three worlds. (169)
O Great-minded One, with both hands they stand separately on either side, pressing down upon him; they gaze at his face, holding a mace and a discus.
And Śaṅkhapāṇi and Śaṅkheśa, with another pair of weapons; whatever collection of two or more hands there may be, that is endowed with various [implements]. (171)
He is joined with the noose, goad, lotus, and other excellent weapons;
now hear concerning the sixteen forms of these various manifestations. (172)

O best of the twice-born, having meditated upon the Pāñcajanya conch in the form of a discus within the primary hand, one should likewise contemplate the mace and the discus pervading the entire body.

With both hands pressed against the face of the All-pervading Lord, as if drinking it in—[here, at this point, a comparison with the interior of a lotus bud is necessary]—as if drinking from an earthen vessel; this must be remembered by those devoted to Him. 174.
(210) Now, attend to this form of the formless mantra;
it should be recollected according to one's desire, even by virtue of its beautiful playfulness. 175.
Just as the condition of people in various lands has existed since the beginning of creation, the maintenance of both the formless and those with forms is now described from the very root. 176.
With his two rear arms,
he holds a pair of well-fashioned [objects] that extend from the region of the head, gazing at the face of the Lord.
Or with the hand awaiting a command, or that hand holding a fan and such;
or with the hand tucked inside the armpit, or else with the gesture of wonder (vismayamudrā). || 178 ||
It is joined with the mudrā known as *sampuṭa* or born from the lotus;
indeed, it has four faces and feet, and its established form is that of one absorbed in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). || 179 ||
O Brahmin, [the rites] for all [beings] are prescribed according to the requirements of the purpose, as well as by the will of the practitioner and indeed by the power of time. (180)
Having been requested, they sat down upon couches of enjoyment;
then, seated upon lotus-thrones marked with wheels, he [the practitioner] should meditate upon the heart as endowed with the three abodes.
Or with the previously mentioned twelve-syllable designations, or with the six general mantras of the twice-born characterized by the six political expedients (ṣāḍguṇya). || 182 ||
Whoever worships with devotion, according to their own capacity or wealth, being freed from all defects, attains that respective state which is free from suffering.
In whichever manifest field it has been personally brought down externally, there the practitioners achieve success through the specific name of that accomplishment. || 184 ||
O Lotus-born One, those who recite their own mantras, who are devoted, eternally pure, and intent on ritual action [attain this], as do those of other forms and deities. 185.
Listen as I declare to you that which begins with the Banner and the convention thereof;
I shall speak of this triad, O Goddess, which is proclaimed as beginning with Keśava. (186)
It was adorned with a great Garuda-bannered flag,
a large palm-tree banner, and a lotus-emblemed plow-sign.
O twice-born one, the triad beginning with Govinda, which is indeed adorned by the banner known as the Makara and by Pradyumna, must be understood.
The triad beginning with Trivikrama is eternally adorned by the deer-marked moon alone, and marked by Aniruddha. (189)
Indeed, there are three [names] ending with Dāmodara and beginning with Hṛṣīkeśa,
belonging to the all-pervading Lord Viśveśvara, who assumes forms according to his will.
All these have indeed been ordained together with the sovereignty of their forms by the gods who are lords of the three worlds, beginning with Varāha, Narasiṃha, and others. || 191 ||

O Lotus-born One, [the Lord manifests] through Keśava and the others, who possess various manifestations, are radiant with all virtues, and are the fourfold self (cāturātmya) as is appropriate, even though [the source] is non-existent.

O Brahmin, [the images] should be fashioned according to their prescribed characteristics— namely those known as the Swan, Fish, Horse, Tortoise, Lion, and Boar— either according to one's capacity or as produced through ritual consecration.
In this world, for the sake of their livelihood in the acts of worship and meditation,
[he was appointed] by the ascetics who were free from attachment, the perfected ones (siddhas) residing in the sacred field.
Thus, by means of those human bodies with faces as previously described, having great arms, known as Nṛvara, Ahaṇa, and Nṛsiṃha, and designated as having the faces of a man and a horse; || 195 ||
O one of stainless vision, this region of the earth was pervaded by the Lord Vāmana, who assumed a dwarf form, out of a desire to bestow grace. (196)
And he was like a *snātaka* celibate student, adorned with the marks [of his stage], appearing in a different form that bestowed happiness upon all joys. (197)
By the Lord known by the name Trivikrama, whose form traversed the three worlds,
and who is designated as Rāma with a flaming axe in his hand.
O best of the twice-born, by these and other qualities to be described hereafter, he has repeatedly performed the removal of the burden from the earth. (199)
Indeed, that entire collection of cosmic eggs, together with all their various manifestations and all the twice-born beings, is pervaded both internally and externally by the two.
Through the lords of the gods, both primary and secondary, who are characterized by their origins and dissolutions,
[the Lord] never abandons His own nature, even as He assumes various other forms of manifestation. (201)
That reality which arises from a portion [of the Absolute] is indeed a distinct manifestation;
and that which is endowed with various manifestations is the supreme collection of manifestations.
Listen to me as I speak correctly of those by whom the entire world is pervaded:
another Rāma, born of the kṣatriya caste, together with his brother and three divisions. (203)
He who, remembering "I am a man," was the slayer of the Rākṣasas;
he who, having accomplished his purpose, knew his own divine and supreme nature. (204)
Rāma, whose arms were indeed long and who, together with the soul of Kṛṣṇa, assumed the state of childhood and performed great divine deeds; (205)
And know that the Lord Viṣṇu as Kalki, who manifests for the sake of restoring lost dharma, will slay the hosts of Mlecchas upon the earth in the Kali age.
The Lord Viṣṇu, whose nature is dharma, is eternal;
for it is from him that the manifestation has indeed arisen, beginning with Nara and ending with Kṛṣṇa.

He who always protects [the community] in this way—endowed with the five times and the six duties, possessed of his own specific dharma, and accompanied by recitation and meditation—[attains success]. || 208 ||
O Brahmin, the Lord Hari, Nārāyaṇa, who consists of four forms,
became known by the name Kṛṣṇa after the manifestation of the All-pervading One.
It has been revealed by you in four ways; therefore, understand it as something else:
the Blessed One is the Universal Form, characterized by many bodies. (210)
Among them, O Pauṣkara, one is indeed called Antarā, belonging to Kṛṣṇanātha;
and three are the primordial, imperishable [forms] of him who has descended into human existence.
The glorious one has a thousand faces, as well as a thousand feet and hands;
he who bears both the manifest and the unmanifest, and maintains the collection of immortals within the lineages.
And he is the great Lord of manifestation, whose navel is like a lotus in the water;
he brings about both origin and dissolution through various yogas practiced in many different ways.
And know that the slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha was another manifestation of that Lord, Padmanābha, the All-pervading One. || 214 ||
You are the god who caused the Mandara mountain to rise, as well as the one who brought back the nectar;
you are the bearer of the jar of ambrosia, and your body takes the form of a woman.
Furthermore, he severed the head of that Rāhu into yet another form;
thus, O Mahāmati, this very Blessed One became fourfold.
Endowed with various manifestations, he is the supreme manifestation among all;
the Lord of Lakṣmī, the highest Master, is the treasury of all auspiciousness.
The second [form], with a serene soul, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men;
he is endowed with four forms of Lakṣmī and has Garuḍa as his seat. || 218 ||
Furthermore, that seat, endowed with glory, is of eight other varieties; it fulfills the mental dispositions of the gods and others, preceded by enjoyment. || 219 ||
He is the possessor of enjoyments, the slayer of Kālanemi, whose vehicle is the lord of birds;
he has a thousand spokes on his hands, is glorious, and is marked with the auspicious Śrīvatsa sign.
Is Kālavaiśvānara the lord of Śālīna, residing in the waters?
He is the knower of the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) of the formless and all-pervading Lord. || 221 ||
He who indeed exists as the body of egoity through various distinctions,
and who is the liberator of the lordly elephant from the crocodile of saṃsāra characterized by the [six] rasas, || 222 ||
The Lord Kapilākṣa, Adhokṣaja, is the instructor of knowledge;
and Brahmā, the embodiment of wisdom with four faces, is indeed worshipped by the worlds. || 223 ||
He is indeed that constituent part which perfectly possesses the characteristics of all manifestations;
he is the one who always effects the dissolution at the end of the age.
Indeed, that was another manifestation of the Great Rudra named Śaṅkara,
who exists as the support of all for the god Analaśāli.
Lokeśvara, whose body is peaceful, whom others know as the Buddha—
he is the one who transcends the qualities of the intellect and is the reviler of the fault of violence. (226)
Know that the Sun and the Moon are the two embodied lords who serve as the eyes of the Supreme Self, the deity known by the name Agni-Soma.
The supreme lord Agni, the consumer of oblations, always takes that mouth and that other deity, having purified them with mantras, once the offering preceded by clarified butter has been presented.
The presiding deity named Vāyu, who is indeed the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti) of Viśveśa, constantly satisfies the entire world-system of Brahmāṇḍa.
And indeed, as the sustainer of the world through the nature of various aggregates, these forms of the Blessed One abide within this triple world. (230)
Through various forms of dress and various characteristics of physical constitution, indeed by virtue of various functions and by virtue of various appearances. || 231 ||
Thus, by means of fabricated sounds and so forth, the Blessed One, in that very moment,
appeared to those devoted to the recitation and meditation [of his mantra] in a form identical to his own.
In its intended form, endowed with the six qualities,
having the nature of consciousness, eternal, and possessing a stainless essence as its own nature.
O Mahāmati, with the desire to bestow grace upon all, he fills everything by means of exhalation and inhalation; that which exists everywhere among all those aforementioned beings— || 234 ||
The eternal universal form of the manifestations beginning with Vāsudeva [is manifested] through the power of yogic sovereignty and also by the will of Acyuta. (235)
O Lotus-born One, having understood this, you should not harbor any astonishment in your heart regarding that which is manifest in various forms, endowed with diverse names. (236)
He was seen in the form of the Blessed One, both as one self-manifested and so forth,
and as one descended into the midst of the earth by the path previously described.
In all the designated holy fords (tīrtha), in various sacred fields (kṣetra), on delightful mountain peaks, and in the caves situated amidst them; || 238 ||
In forests rich with groves, in the regions of the netherworld,
in other worlds situated above, [he was honored] by gods and the most excellent of Gandharvas.

Atheists, who have transgressed the boundaries of conduct and are defiled by delusion and illusion, are possessed by the faults of conceptual construction; their intellects are bewildered and rendered dull. || 240 ||
Those base individuals who touch the stalk of the lotus-feet sink into a terrible hell along with their ancestors for a long time.
Those whose minds are corrupted by conceptualization, who indeed seek the root of the six sense-bases of the gods, shall suffer the severing of their heads. (242)
The root, consisting of the power of steadfastness, is difficult even for the gods to perceive;
how then could it be perceived by the deluded, since it has attained the state of a material substance? (243)
And the system of the sixfold reality (ṣaṭtantra) consisting of means of knowledge and objects of knowledge, which is supreme...
by those [deities] born from the feet of Kṣetreśa who abide within this middle hexad. || 244 ||
That state which exists when the Lord of the World himself descends, endowed with divine qualities and powerful natural attributes.
Once grasped, it becomes perfectly stable and is even fashioned by those who have attained mastery;
yet, through defects such as the divisions of the directions and so forth, it passes into a state of otherness.
Due to the greatness of his eternal presence, time proceeds in this world in an ever-increasing sequence until the end of the kalpa.

O Great-minded One, she who grants the pacification of the wicked through her power, and who bestows accomplishment (siddhi) together with it, is also [the source] of the bases of human effort (pauruṣāyatana) known as the "accomplished ones" (siddha). 248.
Therefore, even for the lords of reality who have descended themselves upon the earth,
as well as for the devotees who fear saṃsāra, [this is the path] of the Lord of All.
They are to be honored by those who visit them until the end of their lives, and they must be constantly attended by those residing there who follow the stages of life (āśramas). 250.
By men who have attained their qualification through rites such as initiation and sacrifice,
[the state] endowed with qualification belongs precisely to those for whom initiation has been performed. (251)
However, for the sake of propitiating Acyuta and for the attainment of the state of supreme beatitude, even the worship of other deities is prohibited. (252)
For this is indeed the supreme commitment (samaya) of those whose nature is immeasurable joy;
it is well-known as arising from the manifest form of the Supreme Lord.
Except for the manifestation arising from the *vyūha* or that known as the *vibhava*, which was previously described, there is no other form residing on the earth to be worshipped by the wise. (254)
O best of the twice-born, in some places earthen lingas are seen presided over by manifestations that are portions of the Blessed One, and they are also heard of.

Even though this may be so regarding the Vaiṣṇavas, O Great Buddha, nevertheless they are not to be worshipped because of their hostility; for that Vaiṣṇava affiliation is merely a limiting adjunct (upādhi).
Even those who were brought down by the Self-Existent One— whosoever they may be,
such as Skanda, Rudra, Mahendra, and others— are prohibited from being worshipped.
And Puruṣottama is the inner controller of all the gods; although his form is unmanifest, he manifests his respective powers within each individual being. || 258 ||

O Brahmin, because of the power of internal devotion and even from the attainment of one's own ritual duties, having understood this, one should certainly not create such a confusion of devotional practices. || 259 ||
One who desires the supreme goal should avoid [these] with effort;
those Brahmins known as Ekāyanas are truly devoted to Acyuta.

Those who are single-mindedly devoted to the truth, who do not worship other deities, and who perform the sacrifice to Viṣṇu as their duty without seeking any reward, do not depart at the end of the body [to rebirth].
And at the end of their bodies, O Lotus-born One, they attain the state of Vāsudeva;
others, however, who perform sacrifices with mixed motives, are remembered as mere semblances of devotees.
O Brahmins, these [impurities] are to be fully understood through the worship of the various hosts of paths;
therefore, one whose body has been perfected by the rite known as initiation (dīkṣā) [is liberated].
Until the completion of the recitation, he should remain devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
intent on the acts of recitation and fire-offerings, he remains seated, dedicated to hymns of praise.
At the end of the body, he shall indeed attain the world of Viṣṇu,
and having obtained an excellent birth once again, O best of the twice-born, [he remains so] from childhood onwards.
One should become proficient in the deeds of the Blessed One, devoted to them, and absorbed in them;
indeed, one should do so even when faced with times of adversity, without aiming for any fruit.
Having abandoned the body, O Pauṣkara, one shall not undergo rebirth here again.
Pauṣkara said:

O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, [I ask about] the compendium of principles (tattvasaṃgraha) extending to the end of the earth, together with the sacred fields (kṣetra) and the most excellent of fields, and that by which all is pervaded in its ultimate extent.
Beginning indeed from the true reality of Brahman known as Vāsudeva, you should explain it to me in its proper sequence, out of a constant desire to bestow grace upon all.

The Blessed One said: "O twice-born one, by means of my own self consisting of the fourfold nature, established within the body known as the sixfold qualities (ṣāḍguṇya), I have pervaded everything up to the end of heaven with my own state as the supreme deity. (269)
That which is indeed the sovereign power called Īśvarī, the illuminator, [is endowed] with the primordial fourfold nature, distinguished by the divisions of knowledge and the rest. (270)
And she is pervaded by the Great Self (mahātman), whose form is light and whose mark is unmanifest;
she is the supreme divine Prakṛti, characterized by the single quality of sattva.
O Lotus-born one, Pūrṇā is manifested through the multitude of Vaibhavī powers,
together with another form and likewise as another manifestation.
Through seeds consisting of manifestations, in a fourfold aggregate,
there is the imperishable name [of the Self] known as Jīva, Kṣetrajña, and Ātman. (273)

Indeed, by the will of the Lord, that very state always proceeds, having reached its support—the eternal, so-called Unmanifest (avyakta), which is the equilibrium of the three qualities (traiguṇya). || 274 ||

Therein resides the Supreme Lord, the master of the world, who possesses a fourfold nature (*cāturātmya*) that is clearly manifest yet distinct from the unmanifest, appearing in the form known as the ego-principle (*abhimāna*). || 275 ||
Two-armed and possessing a human form, [he is] resplendent like the sun, with banners, ornaments, and emblems marked by the conch, the discus, and other such signs. || 276 ||
He is established in the unmanifest principle of the intellect (buddhitattva), yet he is more manifest than the manifest;
he is all-pervading, possessing four forms, four faces, four arms, and four states of existence.
O Lotus-born One, having resorted to ego, [the unmanifest] is joined with imperishable and manifest marks extending as far as the banners. (278)
All those beginning with Keśava are indeed remembered as abiding in various forms;
and those beginning with Haṃsa, which I have described as consisting of six, possess the characteristics of their respective perfections.

O Brahmin, having attained the principle of the mind (manas), these six, endowed with the qualities of perfect knowledge, again become otherwise, possessing the qualities of the sense organs (buddhīndriya). || 280 ||
Having assumed human bodies, these supreme lords remain established;
they are the lords of the twice-born, such as Vāmana and others, who have Kalki as their ultimate goal and possess six arms.

But those qualities beginning with dharma and ending with the universal form (viśvarūpa), which are endowed with all attributes, always remain supported by the collection of the organs of action. || 282 ||
O Lotus-born One, the five subtle elements (tanmātra-pañcaka) exist by depending upon the group of elements beginning with space (ākāśa), which consists of both the eatable and the eater. 283.

O one of great intelligence, those foremost of the wise mentioned previously are indeed established by relying upon these, together with the remaining manifestations that have yet to be described. (284)
