Just as [the sun], having reached its eclipse, comes into contact with a single region throughout the three worlds, so too does the confluence of sacred fords come together at Kurukṣetra. || 285 ||
And with a supreme mind intent on bestowing grace, O twice-born one, at the time of death, he should recollect the Buddhas pervaded by the gods. (286)

Those who possess the presiding deity, the earth as their limit, the body as their form, and the compendium of the principles, being endowed with the relationship between the signified and the signifier, also attain the supreme goal. (287)
O twice-born one, because it is through the power of the Blessed One known as compassion that he enters the affectionate kinsmen of a living being for the sake of achieving their association.
O Mahāmati, by this method he indeed brings about auspiciousness for one who is unconscious at a sacred ford, a sanctuary, or a field. 289.
Pauṣkara said:
O Lord, please now point out that [place] which has been occupied here for the sake of favoring living beings, together with the sacred fields and their presiding deities.
The Blessed One said:

"In the land of action (karmabhūmi), there are certain fields that are auspicious for human beings; indeed, even those places which are inaccessible to them, except for the hosts of gods and siddhas."
Now, listen to me with constant and one-pointed attention:
in the region of the earth known as Āryāvarta, which is designated as meritorious. (292)
In the vicinity of the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa), established on all four sides,
at the edge of the ocean’s waterline, within that great expanse at its boundary.
All the gods, beginning with Ādideva, who have descended since the beginning of creation along with their respective presiding deities (svādhiṣṭhānas), are characterized by manifest forms.
In whatever region of the earth, whichever universal form [of the Lord] has come from this or that [source] and remained established since the beginning of creation; || 295 ||
p.
215) And likewise, it is indeed accompanied by Kṣetreśa and Tīrtheśa;
for from the vicinity of the temple, when the lotus-born [fire] is blown [into flame], || 296 ||
As long as there is penetration by sound from existence, that is called a "field" (kṣetra);
it is the imperishable interval between the divine abodes and so forth. (297)
By this measurement, that which is one krośa or slightly more or less is to be known as Antarvedī for those whose souls are devoted to Nārāyaṇa. || 298 ||
In performing sacrifices, offering ancestral rites (śrāddha), giving gifts, departing [from this world], or in worship;
in recitation, meditation, austerity, and sacrifice; and by the satiation of the sacred fires—299.
O best of the twice-born, just as the light of a lamp situated in one place illuminates the region of the earth beyond it, so indeed does it [the self] act.
Having approached one's own field and the lord of that field, the embodied beings attain success both in this world and in the next. (301)
In that regard, first of all, attend now to the arrangement of the four forms and the group of other forms upon the earth.
Residing at the sacred field of Puṣkara under the name Puṇḍarīkākṣa,
the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva remains eternally present there.
Thus, having arrived at all the excellent fields himself, the Lord of All,
manifesting in four forms, established the stability of the sacrifice for the foremost of the twice-born from the very beginning of creation.
Ascertain the arrangement of those twelve-fold divisions of the four forms, along with their sacred fields and holy fords.
Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, dwells on earth in a dual form;
as Govinda, the Supreme Person, he exists with a manifested form.
He remained stationed on a portion of the earth in the place called Naga.
O Lotus-born one, even in the place called Vṛndāvana, Viṣṇu remains in two ways, O Brahmin: as Viṣṇu and as the Foot of Viṣṇu (Viṣṇupada). || 308 ||
And having reached the mountain named Mandara, Madhusūdana descended and remained there for the sake of compassion toward all living beings.
Resorting to the waters of the Yamunā, Trivikrama, the God of gods, stands there; O Lotus-born One, he bestows a good state of existence upon men. || 310 ||
O Lotus-born One, another form known as Vāmana has come from its own essential nature and rests upon the Sahya mountain for the sake of pacifying the sorrow of living beings. (311)
Having reached the water known as the Narmadā, which destroys all sins,
the Lord Śrīdhara is established there, as is Kauṇḍale together with Śrī.
The Blessed Lord Hṛṣīkeśa, though established upon the earth by his own nature,
resides in the field known as Dhvajā on Dharādhara, and in Kubjāmraka, O Lotus-born One.
Padmanābha, the Lord of Mādhya, having descended,
remained stationed in the southern direction, near the land at the edge of the ocean.
O Brahmin, the blessed Lord Dāmodara has come from his own essential nature and resides on Mount Raivataka for the welfare of those whose minds are purified.
O best of the twice-born, having reached the temple of the universe together with these other forms and their manifestations, [one should understand] the arrangement of those others as well. (316)
Understand this, O one of great intelligence, with an attentive mind:
know that the King of Swans (Haṃsarāja) was worshipped by the Siddhas and immortals in Śvetadvīpa. || 317 ||
The Lord, whose self is the fish, was in the waters; whose self is the horse, at Vaḍavāmukha;
whose self is the tortoise, in Rasātala; and whose self is the lotus, in the Vindhya forest.
The soul of the Lord of Beasts, the destroyer of the sins of all embodied beings, is to be known there in that very field in the form of a boar. || 319 ||
On the auspicious bank of the Ganges, frequented by gods and *siddhas*, the Lord, whose eyes are like the finest gold, dwells within the great golden mountain. (320)
The Lord Mīnavaktra resides at Naubandhana-giri;
the god Aśvaśiras is at Kṛṣṇāśva; and [the Lord] is at Kṣitikṣetra, which is honored by the earth.
On the coastal region bordering the salt ocean, frequented by the Siddhas,
the Lord Kūrmavaktra is stationed, bearing the conch and the discus.
O twice-born one, when the purification has been performed, Nṛhari likewise remains in three ways in the city of Ujjayinī, in the place known as Viśākhamūla.
At Kokāmukha he is Varāha; at Vārāha, the best of mountains;
at Kandamāla, he is Vivīta; and at Kulakukṣi on the Himācala mountain.
And [he saw] Vāmana, of dwarfish form, established in his universal manifestation (vaiśvarūpya);
and at Pauṣkara in Kurukṣetra, on the banks of the Gaṅgā in the Middle Country.
Having reached the bank of the Yamunā, he manifested another great incarnation known as Trivikrama, whose body traversed the three worlds.
O twice-born one, on that best of mountains called Mahendra,
the Blessed One known as Rāma, who bears an axe in his hand and is the destroyer of the kṣatriyas, is established.
On Mount Citrakūṭa, the great Rama, the destroyer of demons,
whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals, remains established there.
Rāma, the wielder of the plow, indeed remains as another [incarnation] among auspicious human lands, causing the waters of the Yamunā to whirl.
Furthermore, on that island in the ocean known as Dvārakā, which is worshipped by the immortals,
dwells the Blessed One Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord who is the Self of all.
The Lord Kalkī Viṣṇu, being praised by the twice-born,
remained there with a restrained mind after reaching the river Vipāśā.
The great-souled one, whose very form is Dharma, dwells in Dharmāraṇya, which is honored by the gods;
intent on bestowing grace, he remains there, worshipped by the worlds.
Known as Narasaṃjña, the Lord of the World remains eternally present among the Siddhas who have performed worship and in delightful regions upon the earth.
On the mountain named Govardhana, the Lord Hari, the Sovereign of All, resides; he is worshipped in that sacred place during the processions of the cows.
And in Sāligrāma, O twice-born one, the Blessed One resides in the forest named Rājendra;
likewise, he dwells in the portion of the earth known as Devavrata.
O Brahmin, another Kṛṣṇa, possessing four forms, descended to the surface of the earth and remained at Piṇḍāraka, liberating people from their evil deeds.
O Lotus-born One, the Lord Viśvarūpa resides on Śvetadvīpa, at Kurukṣetra, on the Himavat mountain, at Vedikā (or Devikā), and on its banks. || 337 ||
In the ocean of milk, Hari—lying upon the serpent Śeṣa (an alternative reading is *śeṣāhiśayanaḥ*)—is situated;
and from his navel-lotus was born the Grandfather (Brahmā). || 338 ||
Relying upon form in four ways, she alone exists within this entire universe; understand correctly how she acts for the welfare of all the worlds. (339)
O Brahmin, having reached his bed situated at the bottom of Pātāla,
he assumes the Agneya form at the end and withdraws the universe.
Having resorted to the foot of a banyan tree at Prayāga, which is worshipped by the gods, he made the entire world a single ocean and reached that divine tree. (341)
O twice-born one, that Blessed One remains on that shore upon the earth;
one should meditate upon Him as He reclines beneath the banyan tree, the bestower of divine states. (342)
On a lofty portion of the Himālaya known as Bhṛgu,
he who is the slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha remained established upon the surface of the earth.
In the field of the earth consisting of milk and water, frequented by gods and asuras,
the Lord whose hand is Mount Mandara dwells, worshipped by the gods.
In that very place resides the god Amṛtajit, served by the Siddhas;
he assumes a beautiful form and likewise holds a vessel of nectar. (345)
The Conqueror of Death stands amidst the Siddhas, Munis, and gods;
he is the god who, accompanied by his host, splits [the world] in two and has Garuḍa as his vehicle.
The Lord resides at Sāligrāma in the region of the Sāla trees,
upon the ridge of Mount Trikūṭa, which is accessible to those who travel through the sky.
Under the very pretext of lifting the elephant, the Lord who dwells in Śvetadvīpa, known by the name Aprameya, descended and remained there.
At the delightful spot on earth where the Gaṅgā meets the ocean,
at Naimiṣa, which is honored by the Siddhas, the Lord, the divine enjoyer of sacrifices, [resides].
The Lord Ananta resides taking refuge in the Saindhava forest,
while the Lord of Gods, holding the Śārṅga bow, dwells in the region known as the Daṇḍaka forest.
And he who is known as Śauri, that Acyuta, stands in the region of Utpalāvartaka for the sake of those desiring victory over the host of Rākṣasa clans. 351.
On the earth, at the confluence of the ocean and the Sindhu river, frequented by the Siddhas,
the Blessed One resides as a teacher of knowledge for the sake of pacifying suffering.
Having reached the field of Sūkara, the Lord whose vehicle is Garuḍa remained mounted upon Garuḍa, marked by the Pārijāta tree held in his hand. || 353 ||
O Pauṣkara, together with the Siddhas and hosts of gods, he who is named the Lord of the God of Gods also resides in the sky upon the summit of Hastiparvata.
O high-minded one, having reached a single spot, the Bestower of Boons, Vaikuṇṭha, stands over the whole of Magadha with a garland and water-pot in his hands at Gayā.
Having ascended to the region of merit, the Supreme Person resides there;
then the Blessed One, whose nature is inconceivable, dwells upon Mount Gandhamādana.
The God, established in the vow of Śipiviṣṭa under the name of Śipiviṣṭa, [resided] on that auspiciously marked land extending as far as the ocean. || 357 ||
Having assumed the form of Kapila, the Lord Vāsudeva remained there;
and having descended from his own essential nature, he became the Prajāpati known as Brahmā.
O Brahmin, having reached Maṇibandha, he remains eternally present in the region of Magadha, residing upon the earth of Great Enlightenment (Mahābodhi).
O twice-born one, Janārdana, the god of gods whose self is the Lord of the World, is established as the embodiment of the ego within the right eye of the god.
The Lord known as Sūrya is situated upon the Golden Mountain; Acyuta, the all-pervading one whose body is composed of self-conceit (abhimāna), resides in the left eye.
The Blessed One, known as Soma, resides in the hermitage of Somatīrtha;
moreover, he exists in the form of fire within the submarine fire (Vaḍabānala), O unconquered one.
O Brahmin, the Lord who brings an end to the asuras shines in the sky as the soul of all things;
furthermore, that god, adorned with many weapons, appears again under the name of Viṣṇu.
Jayākhyam resides indeed in Ujjayinī for the conquest of the sins of men, while [the form] named Cakradhara is situated in the sacred region of Kāśmīra, in the field known as [Cakrapura]. (364)
The Blessed One Cakrapāṇi stands there as the bestower of liberation upon his devotees;
at Pauṣkara, he is known by the name Surottama and holds a mace in his hand.
Know that he is always present at Gaṅgādvāra together with the gods;
he is four-armed, four-formed, four-faced, and possesses four modes of movement.
The eternal Lord Viṣvaksena resides at Piṇḍāraka,
as well as in the city of Prāgjyotiṣa, having taken up his auspicious station on that portion of the earth.
Having come from her own domain to where the Lord named Viśveśvara resides,
she arrived there in that sacred field (nābhi-kṣetra), which was filled with perfected beings and Vidyādharas.
The Lord of the World, known as Svāmī, resides on the bank of the Mandākinī;
in the great yoga at Bhallātaka, he bestows liberation upon those who meditate.
O Brahmin, in the subterranean realm (rasātala) known as Nṛsiṃha, situated on the bank of the Devikā, the Lord resides under the name Ripukṣaya, the Sovereign of All.
On the portion of the earth known as Śaṅkara, which is frequented by all the gods, Jagan-nātha, the embodiment of knowledge, resides, bestowing auspiciousness upon men. (371)
O Brahmin, on this earth, in the field of the ancestors (Pitṛkṣetra), the Blessed Lord, the Soul of the Universe, resides under the name Janārdana, liberating beings from the three debts.
O Lotus-born One, these incarnations have been described to you in brief;
by them, the surface of the earth has been pervaded by you yourself again and again. (373)
O Lotus-born One, with the intent of showing favor to worldly beings,
one should constantly perform the chanting of the names of those who are otherwise inaccessible during the three junctions of the day.
And he set his mind upon visiting and even beholding those Mlecchas in those regions who were on the earth in sacred fields and other such places. (375)
For it is always to be seen, free from any confusion, by sages, gods, and perfected beings in their own great hermitages. (376)
In sacred reservoirs of water and in various places upon the earth,
all [these forms] have the appearance of the Blessed One, characterized by the manifestations of his majestic power.
Those who have been liberated and those others who, having reflected by their own intellect, have been duly installed with mantras and possess true valor; || 378 ||
Through their persistence, those things which are of various kinds— designated as past, future, and so forth—
are indeed determined by their configuration, whether they are called gentle, fiery, or both.
Together with the manifestation of various weapons and emblems held in his arms, which consist of divine play and bestow happiness upon the mind. 380.
And the ground was likewise adorned by men who were devoted and favored, as well as by Siddhas and others, just as it had been described. (381)
These, beginning with Ādideva, are declared to be the lords of the principles (tattveśas);
however, they abide non-differently within the supreme principle of the Lord (bhagavattattva).
Just as the rays of the sun, just as the multitude of flames from a fire, and just as the waves of the ocean, so it is with you, O Lotus-born One.
The common aspects of consciousness are eternally pure, all-pervasive, and supreme lords;
resting upon the existence of reality, they are adorned with knowledge and other qualities. (384)
Endowed with the eightfold powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā), they indeed abide by their own nature and eternally maintain their presence throughout all the paths and grounds.
For the liberation of all beings, especially on this earth,
[this was taught] beginning from the time of universal origin until the end of the dissolution.

In sacred fields and on the banks of holy fords, by means of the mantra— which consists of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman) and which manifests as its own transformation— one [should worship] even in a general manner.
Then, for the benefit of all worlds, he assumed a form that was both manifest and otherwise, composed of earth, descended yet imperishable. (388)
In this [world] known as the Jagatī-āyatana, yogins attain success;
provided that, after some time, the immersion of individual manifestations occurs. (389)
And there, the lords of yoga, the gods, and the perfected ones (siddhas) always maintain their presence through their power, remembering that form as being identical with Him.
And they establish an image made of stone, clay,
wood, or metal, wherein those who possess the power of mantras perform the ritual piercing (anuvedha).
Whatever other station is indeed remembered by the name Acyutīya,
that is the form of Him who is present there and who bears a body of sound.
When mantras— whether they are of diverse natures, manifest in their own forms or unmanifest, restrained, or functioning according to one's will— are [employed], || 393 ||
Due to its form and configuration, it belongs to the Supreme Lord;
otherwise, in this world, that which is known and unknown would be permanent in a different way. (394)
In this way, O Pauṣkara, the permanence of the sense-bases (āyatana), as well as their beginninglessness, incalculability, and vastness, have been fully revealed.
O twice-born one, those who have arisen as my manifestation are indeed well-known through the power of individualization;
yet, apart from that nature of individualization, I exist even as sound, with an imperishable essence.
For, O Brahmin, other excellent sages, having seen that delightful place elsewhere as consisting of both natures—the nature of sound and the nature of manifestation—[attained realization]. (397)
Having established a firm stability there through both action and mind, one should [use] the faultless, pure water, which is filled with trees and medicinal herbs. (398)
Having observed a stone of auspicious characteristics brought from elsewhere,
one should then give instructions to an artisan born of the lineage of Viśvakarman.
And having fashioned a beautiful impression of the lotus feet of Viṣṇu, the source of this world and the Lord of all, upon this stone; || 400 ||
In this way, O Mahāmati, there are other sages in their respective abodes who bear the marks of Hari, beginning with the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus. (401)
Having established their residence there through actions purified by devotion, other excellent twice-born ones likewise had their minds nourished by devotion. (402)
And out of a desire for the welfare of their devotees,
they establish dwellings in the previously mentioned regions and in those consecrated by the Siddhas and others.

And among the sealed [teachings], such as the multitude of seals beginning with the thousand-spoked wheel, and during the worship of the Great Buddha through stones or by means of emanations; || 404 ||
Having performed the appropriate ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in the form of consecration (*saṃskāra*),
they perform the daily worship according to the rules at the three times of day.
With mantras preceded by the Ṛg and Sāma Vedas, endowed with twelve syllables, for the sake of attaining the state of the Blessed One and for the disciples and others to obtain auspiciousness. (406)
In this way, O Puṣkarasambhūta, all the villages and territories, as well as the cities and towns of kings that are renowned and auspicious upon the earth, [were established]. || 407 ||
It was brought forth by the seers and pure men, and by the Lord himself, out of compassion for his devotees who are devoted to the path of merit. || 408 ||

O twice-born one, [the deity] abides through the differentiation of the array of manifestations (*vibhava-vyūha*), and likewise by the will of placement (*nyāsa*) and the desire to bestow grace; yet, in the event of harm from thieves and the like, [one should take refuge] within the *Antarbhāgavata*. 409.
The mantras, such as the previous mantras and others, which were previously obstructed there,
remain having abandoned their forms in the space of the aperture of Brahmā (brahmavivara).
As long as no consecration has been performed, that which was previously declared to be stable increases;
the great defect grows for half a day, and otherwise for a full day. || 411 ||
Therefore, for all the practitioners born in that region, as well as for the king, [the task] should be performed by the best of the twice-born and others, or by merchants or householders. (412)
The guide, the lord of men, must perform the rite that destroys fear—that which consists of a collection of mantras for the pacification of all sins. (413)
Whoever should constantly perform the installation of individual images in deserted temples for the sake of all beings' welfare and for the purpose of Dharma, [attains great merit]. || 414 ||
The pacification of its defects shall result in the destruction of all suffering, and for those beings who have not yet attained perfection, it serves to destroy great delusion. || 415 ||
Indeed, that which is the imperishable form, characterized by its sovereignty over Brahman,
is endowed with specific qualities and possessed of portions of divine glory.
Prajāpati, having approached him as he was reflected upon the mirror of his intellect, brought him within the range of his hearing, even for his own son, the artisan. (417)

And for one who has been perfected and consecrated by the teachers through fire-oblations and other rites, that which is transferred there before long—that secondary form of Īśvara—is indeed the primary reality. 418.
At the time of its formal assignment by the great-souled reciter,
there is likewise this beginninglessness regarding the generic forms belonging to the various substances.
Indeed, one whose vision perceives perfected prosperity on the ground at the same time does not fall into forgetfulness regarding the universe, as it rests upon the intellect of the artisan.
For he assumes a form endowed with auspicious marks for his devotees,
according to the specific desire of each, indeed, by the power of their heartfelt devotion.
Having personally seen the manifest form on earth, O wise one,
know that great and imperishable image to be indeed named Brahmā, Rudra, and the Sole Sun. (422)
O lotus-eyed one, that which was described as abiding in various arrays and endowed with various forms must indeed be worshipped in that very manner through the intellect. 423.
Whether seated or risen during worship or meditative concentration,
others stood in various postures, established within forms of darkness.
It bears a wondrous mark; indeed, by its own will, it possesses two marks: through both hands, it displays four [fingers] hanging down. 425.
By means of gathering the primary weapons— the conch, discus, mace, and lotus—
in the very order previously specified among the World-Guardians and others.

If the bow and other weapons are held by others according to their will or speech, with arms extended horizontally, they indicate the attainment of prosperity for those who are exceedingly devoted, through the state of having uplifted arms.

But for those whose devotion is weak, by means of those situated in the form of animals, the great divine state of the Self—which is established within the heart through spiritual attainment—is attained. || 428 ||
For those men who possess devotion mixed with other [motivations] while performing sacrifices, their attainment of heaven is described by Bhuja-bṛndā and others from his own mouth. (429)
O Brahman, although I am always equal toward all beings,
those who are my devotees attain prosperity if I indeed instruct them with diligence.
Or images duly consecrated by others belonging to the eight castes, such as the Brāhmaṇas and so forth, or by the best of kings; (431)
When one causes a reflection-like manifestation to move by oneself or by Acyuta, even without the defect of decay, that is an inauspicious shaking. (432)
An injury caused by portents and other such defects brings about the destruction of the king;
however, once those whose mantras have ceased are re-established, [the kingdom is restored]. || 433 ||
O Pauṣkara, their arising occurs constantly for the sake of peace; however, according to how they are meditated upon by the lords of teachers, they resemble the sun, the moon, and fire. (434)
And the lords of mantras, perfected through the sound of the *praṇava*, enter;
after a short period of time, they draw forth their own supernatural power (*vibhūti*). || 435 ||
Indeed, having had their defects destroyed, they were rendered free from obstacles and pure;
furthermore, they were established by the highly perfected ones in sacred fords, holy fields, and forests.
Those who, out of delusion, deny the configuration, measurement, and form existing at a particular time within the manifestations of the array of emanations; [they fall into error]. (437)
Therefore, at the time of death, those with meager wealth and possessed of little understanding sink into a terrible and unbearable darkness. || 438 ||
Those who desire their own welfare must avoid the god without him [the Lord],
just as the Lord of the World himself descended and remained no longer as he was before.

Thus, when these [cognitions] have been grasped as being stable, they are conceived by the opponents as being free from defects such as doubt, hesitation, and the like; yet they do not undergo any change [into falsity].
Due to the greatness of his eternal presence, time proceeds in this world in an ever-increasing succession until the end of the kalpa.
She who, together with prosperity, splendor, fame, and immeasurable action,
grants the pacification of the wicked and bestows accomplishment through her power.
And, O Mahāmati, there are those known as Siddhas who possess the bases of human power, who have themselves descended here upon this earth as lords of reality. || 443 ||
Thus, O Lotus-born One, I have [described] the lords of the fields together with their respective fields.
Both the revealed and the secret have been disclosed by me for the enjoyment of living beings.
For those living beings who seek the fruits [or knowledge], who serve the Lord of the Field in every field,
they attain their desired goal right here in this very world, and it shall be imperishable.
Now, those great [powers] born upon the surface of the earth in the [age] called Pralaya— learn the secret concerning the lords of the fields in each respective field. (446)
By means of knowledge and the rest, as well as the unmanifest powers beginning with *aṇimā* and ending with the earth,
which are the seeds of the principles (*tattva*), which are to be accepted, and which are endowed with the reality of Brahman.
Or, having descended into the world, they indeed manifest themselves before creation;
thus, out of a desire to favor all beings, they appear spontaneously in the form of objects.
At the time of the withdrawal of the circle of the earth, together with the sustainers of the field (kṣetradharas),
they abide within the principle of Īśvara by His will.
And at the time of the manifestation of the universe, they speak of a prior manifestation,
along with birth from the genus, as well as suffering arising from the body and its location.
How is one liberated from such defects as mental afflictions and physical diseases that are difficult to endure, and others like these? (451)
Those who possess right knowledge may manifest devotion either through the grace of the Field-born (the Buddha) or through the grace of intense devotion and so forth. (452)
And at the end, O twice-born ones, the realization arises in men regarding the field, the Imperishable;
yet those who are not devotees, the foremost among atheists, do not desire it amidst their conceptual constructions. || 453 ||

Discrimination regarding the Puruṣa and other principles, as well as the attainment of the fruit from the Lord, and the renunciation of the purpose of the Puruṣa—these must certainly not be abandoned by one who has been awakened. 454.
And in this world, life is joined with the ritual acts of Brahmins;
yet the Lord is capable of removing that [bondage] through various kinds of sacrifices. (455)
Then, those best of men who are faithful and devoted obtain its existence from the mouth of the Guru, conjoined with the direct experience thereof. (456)
Then, one should know the Self by means of the self as the omniscient Lord;
[one must likewise understand] that beginningless conceit which is both material and born of the quality of sattva.

The characteristic of *asmitā*—the mark of "I am" everywhere—is terrible, yet it always bestows what is desired; it should be understood by the self through the self until one has attained full awakening. (458)
For just as seeds that have spread according to their season yield little fruit, so it is because of the diversity of activities in various fields and abodes. (459)
Furthermore, through the power of practice throughout successive births, the exhaustion of karma will surely occur.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Investigation of the Abode," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, a Great Upaniṣad within the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
(Total number of verses: 461) Now begins the thirty-seventh chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
And, O Lord of the World, the placement of stones marked with footprints, as well as those marked with wheels and lotuses, preceded by the ritual consecration. || 1 ||
O Lord of the World, I now desire to know about these supports as well as others, and likewise about the stones that have been established since beginningless time. (2)
And by householders or forest-dwellers who have obtained the marks of the Supreme Lord, such as the conch and other emblems, for the purpose of worship. || 3 ||
Furthermore, for the successful completion of sacrifices such as these,
you must instruct me on the arrangement of both mobile and immobile objects.
The Blessed Lord said: Previously, the material was prepared by a self-restrained artisan,
having been purified through consecration with substances previously empowered by mantras.
O Lotus-born One, wherever [a placement] is appropriate, one should perform that placement there, up to the limit of the power of grace (anugraha-śakti) within the Akṣiti [cakra].
The presence of the mantras should be effected upon the mobile seat alone;
however, the temporary restriction and the worship therein are prescribed for that specific occasion.
O Pauṣkara, beginning from the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti), the complete restraint of the entire collection of mantras is always ordained for all [of them] when they are well-stabilized.
Having invoked [the deity] there, one should worship with the mantra and then dismiss it again;
for the mantra of the object of worship is not beneficial apart from the time of worship, O Lotus-born One.
Because it is accomplished through a cause, its cessation occurs here by means of knowledge;
at the time of bringing flowers and other offerings, the Supreme Lord is present every day.
But he who is intent on bestowing grace remains right there, like the sound of an echo;
or rather, he has attained a state of identity with the moving image. || 11 ||

The arrangement of mantras on the pedestal (pīṭha) is prescribed as being like that of a movable pedestal; this applies whether the pedestal is very stable or has a single source, and also in the case of a very stable one when it is separated [from its original location].
O Pauṣkara, the placement (nyāsa) of the mantras prescribed for the stable seat is indeed performed from the feet up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) for one whose form is unsteady. 13.
One should indeed effect the arrangement of the primary principles (tattvas),
beginning with earth and ending with the feet, from the Unmanifest (avyakta) down to the end of the earth.

Either the mantra consisting of all the principles (tattvas) or his [the deity's] own mantra alone should be applied in the heart as the primary [mantra], inseparable from the cause that is the principle.
Then, when the occasion for worship has arrived, one should employ the system of mantras and tantras for the sake of removing the insentience of the multitude of principles and mantras.
O Brahmin, having invoked that mantra—which is the living soul, eternally pure and ever-risen—and which is adorned with its limbs, marks, and so forth; || 17 ||
Having withdrawn [the deity] established therein, or when the ritual worship (arcana) has been completed,
one should perform the withdrawal of the mantra-arrangement (vinyāsa) that was previously described.
The expulsion of those who possess holy fords, sacred fields, or lands is ordained, even if the image is permanently installed in a temple or in one's own home. (19)
Otherwise, one should perform its confinement (*nirodhana*) upon the tongue, the ear, and so forth,
together with their own respective foundational seat-mantras (*ādhārapīṭhamantra*) and marks (*lāñchana*).
One should perform this specific rite for unstable foundations once the consecration has been completed and the Supreme Lord has been installed as prescribed. (21)
Then one should perform the secondary piercing (anuvedha), starting from the base up to the crest-lock (śikhā), according to the method for the crest-lock,
by means of the thread of the power of capability and by the imperishable Lord.
When [the disciple] is present, for one whose [impurity] has been removed by that [initiation] and who is endowed with the [deity's] forms and so forth,
the multitude of mantras does not abandon him, even after a long period of time.
Whether unawakened or awakened, whatever man installs another image—whether made of material substance or otherwise—in that very shrine; || 24 ||
And immediately thereafter, that [consciousness] arises permeated by that cognition;
for such is the nature of this knowledge in these three worlds, O Lotus-born One. (25)
By virtue of being the sense-bases (*āyatana*), it exists as far as the moon and stars; therein lies the arrangement of the world-realm where the perfected ones (*siddha*) dwell. (26)
Therefore, one should not allow those who are unestablished in this to lead it to a different state;
rather, one who knows that, who knows the truth, is devoted, faithful, and always a believer—[should do so]. || 27 ||
Having recognized that this single reversal of the earth arises from a change in time and can be effectively treated with efforts made out of fear of its disappearance, [one should act]. (28)
Having received that command regarding the observance of the vows from the gracious [deity],
one should perform the worship preceded by the Mahāyoga [or perhaps "preceded by the Mahāyāga"], beginning with the Praṇava and ending with the Pūrṇāhuti.
Having performed the ritual gift and having seated him upon a supreme seat, otherwise a doubt arises therein regarding the Supreme Lord. || 30 ||
Accompanied by disease, thieves, famine, and the destruction of the kingdom,
there shall be future and present calamities such as the ruin of the country.
If the shifting is performed according to the prescribed rules, it shall not bring about any undesirable result;
one may then perform the re-consecration either elsewhere or in that very same place.

According to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, one should properly awaken the mantra with a preceding festival; however, one should not awaken the tantra without its proper ritual performance.
One should rely upon the state that is both stable and tranquil when it has become inexhaustible;
for there is a fault for the one who causes movement due to being devoid of the prescribed method.
However, regarding the offerings, worship, and gifts for that [image], one should bring them to equality prior to its installation;
having made the image very firm or immovable, one should then set it down there.

One should perform the gift of cows, land, and gold according to one's capacity; likewise, [images] made of metal, clay, stone, or wood, as well as those fashioned from cloth and other materials, should be offered. 36.
If the image of the Blessed One suddenly assumes a state of withered appearance, it is due to a reversal in procedure, the omission of ritual acts, or worship performed at an improper time. (37)
There will be great danger for the kingdom, for the worshiper, and for the people;
therefore, [one should practice] that which is the excellent mantra, complete with its ancillaries, and purified according to the tantra.
One should perform libations for seven days in succession upon the water-pot, the mandala, and the fire;
during the seasons of Hemanta and Śaiśira, one should worship the divine image made of stone.
Having bathed and worshipped her according to the prescribed ritual,
and having wrapped her in fine garments, one should then [anoint her] with the sacrificial product of a cow (gavya-havis).

Having brought it to a state of solid mass from the base of the pedestal, one should color it with sandalwood paste and the like, as well as with flowers made of leaf-cutting (patraccheda) or fashioned from cotton-wool (picu), such as white ones and so forth. || 41 ||

And with other auspicious materials originating from various regions—white, yellow, and so forth, or [according to g and gh] originating from the east and other directions—dried by shade and wind, green, and combined with various distinct varieties. || 42 ||
Having performed the worship as prescribed, along with various ornaments,
he should cover [the image] with a thick, white cotton cloth.
With pure saffron, or with a woolen blanket, white, very thick, unwashed, and new. || 44 ||
When the cold season has indeed passed, having removed the woolen blanket for the sake of purifying the best of the twice-born, kings, and those of purified soul, (45).

He should grant the requests made in due order by his devotees, such as the Nāgaras and others, for their prosperity, for the pacification of inauspiciousness, and for protection, according to the sequence of their petitions. (46)
For the victory over untimely deaths and for the pacification of diseases, during the onset of the summer season, one should perform this daily with cool water. (47)
One should perform the bath according to the prescribed method in due order,
using lentils, black gram, and wool, as well as turmeric and rice.
Having massaged and washed him, and having made him clean with a cloth using clarified butter for anointing and so forth, as well as white sandalwood paste; || 49 ||
Then that dwelling should be washed with cold water;
having swept it, one should apply an external coating of cow dung.
Having scattered leaves, flowers, water-lilies, blue lotuses, and red lotuses,
one should fan the image of Acyuta with palm-leaf fans moistened with water.
Having praised him with various hymns in a loud voice,
O Lotus-born One, he then circumambulated him twice or four times.
Neither one, nor three, nor five in number, nor anything that is an uneven count;
for the Blessed Lord Hari is indeed equal toward all.
The renunciant (saṃnyāsī) should perform prostrations like a staff in every direction,
accompanied by circumambulations, rising up many times before [the teacher].
For those such as the *snātaka* and others, this very same [practice] is prescribed; indeed, it is performed with a mind endowed with devotion together with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). 55.
A householder should daily perform prostrations accompanied by circumambulation, with his back, head, knees, forehead, chest, and hands touching the ground. (56)
Mentally recollecting the eight-syllable mantra repeatedly upon the expansive ground,
he stood before the Blessed One on that narrow stretch of earth.

But as for how one should perform it with devotion: having joined the palms together in a hollowed cup at the region of the heart and the head, one should, while shaking them, remember the Lord of All.
By performing this rite according to his own ability, whether with offerings or otherwise, a man devoted to the practice of devotion attains his desired fruit. (59)
Free from desire, those who behold the Lord of the World with devotion, honored by His devotees, shall attain the eternal abode worshipped by the gods. (60)
Those who rejoice with faith also partake in that fruit;
for those engaged in action, the destruction of the cycle of existence—which is otherwise inexhaustible—comes to pass.
For it is by means of two methods, and not otherwise in any way, that [the goal is attained]:
from the complete section on ritual action (kriyākāṇḍa) together with the mantras, which possesses five characteristics. || 62 ||
Through the thorough knowledge of perfect awakening and through being colored by devotion to the Blessed One,
he who is eternally absorbed in the Blessed One in deed, mind, and speech— 63.
But one who is truly qualified for the teaching shall abide in its reality;
he understands the supremacy of this scripture, which bestows liberation and is imperishable. (64)
He attains purification from previously accumulated evil deeds before long.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Investigation of the Sanctuaries," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, a Great Upaniṣad within the venerable Pāñcarātra.
(Total number of verses: 64) Now begins the thirty-eighth chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
The re-establishment of those infinite forms that existed on earth in various fields and were subsequently lost over time.
The gods and the Siddhas perform [this rite] by repeatedly remembering His form;
how can a dwelling be constructed by means of unreal things that possess the nature of mortals? || 2 ||
For the sake of uplifting his own family, and also for the sake of his own fame.

The Blessed One said: "O Pauṣkara, by means of the mantra together with its ancillaries (sāṅga), accompanied by knowledge and meditation, joined with the worship of the temple, and indeed with recitation (japa)..."

And that which is the application of mantras to substances, beings, and forms— that indeed is the established consecration (pratiṣṭhā) prescribed for practitioners of mantra, characterized by its attainment.
O twice-born one, at the end, the mantra bestows the eternal perfection of mantras;
O Pauṣkara, this is for those who have died due to the lack of capacity among those who know mantras.
And by his sons and others, O high-minded one, impelled by the Teacher with a benevolent intention,
[the rite was performed] according to the prescribed rule and with that mantra.
Together with the mantras known as Ṛk and Sāman, which are joined with his own pervasive power,
and with a mind that is attentive and engaged in worldly activity.
That which is performed as the middle [practice] is indeed the foundation that bestows only slight enjoyment;
yet at the end of the body, it grants a stainless and auspicious state.
Mental concentration (dhāraṇā) is indeed achieved through the exclusive use of Vedic mantras characterized by their appropriate occasions,
together with meditation on the Lord and the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa).
The leader of teachers should indeed perform [this rite] for his devotees toward the Supreme Lord;
it should be understood as common [to all], bestowing the enjoyment of heaven like a sacrifice.
O Lotus-born One, honored by the world, it should be understood that the fruit of mantras— whether pertaining to this world or the next— is dependent upon the teacher in this world.
Therefore, O Pauṣkara, he who knows reality, who is learned in the scriptures, devoted to right action, knows the six paths, and is undeluded, [should act] with his whole being.
Established by that, O Lotus-eyed One, the deity—whether moving or perfectly steady and vast—is there firmly restrained by the mantra. 13.
Through the distinction between the mobile and the stable, it should always be present.
Pauṣkara said:
O Lord, over the course of time, even a substance undergoes the nature of decay;
for the essence of mantra, though worshipped by the worlds, is indeed imperceptible to people.
Why is it awaited by those who know reality? Herein lies my great doubt.
The Blessed One said: Having separated [the soul] from the bondage of karma, the Lord, appearing in the form of a teacher, [acts].
To those who have surrendered through various forms of devotion, as well as to those seeking various fruits [of their practice]. || 15 ||
O high-minded one, having ascended that great power of fame belonging to those who perform deeds—which fills the temple of the universe and is free from all defects—[you shall attain your goal]. (16)
By means of the rays of power, she is permeated through the methods consisting of both divine mantras and the substances of worldly activity, by means of her steadfastness.
And she remains there for the sake of bestowing grace; thus it is celebrated as "Pratiṣṭhā.
Such is the arrangement consisting of material substance where the Lotus-born One resides. (18)

That rite known as *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration) constantly brings benefit to both [the devotee and the deity], is characterized by compassion and devotion, and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (19)

And that, O one of pure vision, is eternally forbidden as something to be performed for the sake of self-realization by the twice-born who are established in the True Brahman; it is forbidden in every respect, O one of pure vision. (20)

And because of that fault, there is indeed no deliverance for them except through the falling away of the body; for no other means of their downfall exists, as such a downfall would cause excessive sin.
Therefore, from the very beginning, that [act] must not be performed by those who have disciplined their souls;
for it is always forbidden to those four who have undertaken such actions.
One should always perform one's duty properly for the sake of establishing others and with a benevolent mind, never out of a nature of obstruction, nor through greed, nor out of pride. || 23 ||
O Lotus-born One, when an accidental affliction such as a broken limb occurs, for the sake of compassion toward devotees, [one should act] with divine mantras, powers, and so forth. (24)
When those [mantras] preceded by the twelve syllables— which are characterized by having liberation as their sole fruit—
are fully worshipped, offered in sacrifice, and recited, they always effect purification.

Therefore, O best of the twice-born, this [rite] should be performed with every effort by those possessing the three Vedas, by Kṣatriyas, by Vaiśyas, or by Śūdras who are absorbed in the Blessed One. (26)

Indeed, those who possess desire or are free from desire, being intent on the propitiation of mantras, should always perform the installation of the image of the Blessed One while remaining as *snātakas*. (27)
Formerly, a preeminent twice-born follower of the Pāñcarātra, having first made a formal request, [appointed] one worthy of propitiation who was established in a position of authority. (28)
He who is the knower of the manifest Supreme Self, preceded by its ritual array (vyūha),
is always authorized to perform the installation of the images of other deities.
Bestowing grace, establishing [the devotee], and defining their authority—these are said to be the duties toward those devotees who are endowed with no other [refuge]. (30)
They were non-different [from him], knowers of the five times, who were not separate from him in the past;
born from his mouth before creation, they were contemplators of the twelvefold inner self.

Those for whom the origin and dissolution [of all things] proceed through the supremacy of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha), perform the renunciation of even their actions through the supervision of the Lord in due order.
Therefore, another person who possesses supremacy toward that [goal] is even more difficult to find;
for such a one, there is a pure and manifest culmination of the object of knowledge, and a firm abiding in its practice. (33)
Those situated on other paths do not accept the supremacy [of the Lord] among one another;
and for those who do accept it, there is no stability in that form of the Lord.

One who has transcended the [limited] office, who has attained the true aim, who is unartificial, devoted to the five times (pañcakāla), pure, and has reached the further shore of the Tantric Siddhāntas—him indeed [one should honor]. || 35 ||
Therefore, indeed, the injunction for all three types of Vedic mantras must be performed for every ritual act,
according to the characteristics of the appropriate occasion.
Because, whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, in the rites of constant propitiation within the activities of the mandalas and so forth arising from the lotus [of the heart], || 37 ||
O Pauṣkara, even though that form and its orientation are eternally established, it will grant its presence to one who possesses [that] reality within their heart. (38)
The Lord of the Universe, the Supreme Self, the infallible Master, who is the very form of mantra—even for the pleasure of your mind, O Brahmin, he does not do so without great eagerness. (39)
O twice-born one, that [ritual] is prescribed for him for the sake of attaining desires or for the sake of fame,
whether performed with the necessary means in a temple or in his own home. (40)
Thus has the primary ritual procedure been correctly explained; hereafter, learn in brief that other secondary procedure which exists therein.

By twice-born ones who had previously received initiation, who were established in the dharma of the three Vedas according to rule, and who were devoted to the constant worship of the Lord as His bhaktas; 42.

By those who have attained the essential mark (*lakṣya*) through the prior practice of retention (*dhāraṇā*) and meditation (*dhyāna*), and who have exerted themselves in the rites of mantras, maṇḍalas, sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), weapons (*astra*), mudrās, and so forth; (43)

By those who are established in the pervasion of the six paths, who possess the habit of renunciation, who are free from envy, who do not abandon the proper sequence, who are skillful, and who protect their own duties; || 44 ||

When the consecration has been performed by those who are celebrated for their good reputation in the world and likewise excluded from ill repute, the performer attains established status through them. (45)
O Lotus-eyed One, therefore this great festival called Pratiṣṭhā is always forbidden for others, as well as for those who perform sacrifices with mixed rites.
Pauṣkara said:
"O Lord, the sacrifice involving mixed [elements] has been repeatedly forbidden;
yet, you have previously declared that the performance of the sacrifices already mentioned is accepted."
You ought now to dispel this doubt that has arisen regarding those very principles.
The Blessed One said: "O one of great intelligence, this which has been urged by you is true;
however, when another course of action is available, there is no fault for those who possess the requisite qualification."
For all other deities possess an imperishable state of supremacy with respect to Acyuta, because they are dependent upon him; indeed, it is through the worship of him that other gods are worshipped.

For there is no fault in honoring one's wives who are lawful spouses, whether in their presence or in their absence, just as there is none in honoring one's brothers or groups of servants in the world. (50)
Furthermore, those who abide in worldly dharmas, who have abandoned the state of equanimous wisdom,
and who lack discernment regarding the Blessed Lady, [act] constantly only out of necessity.
For they indeed proclaim the superiority of all [others] by mere words,
those who, lacking the requisite qualification, are here impelled toward the worship of deities.
Thus, out of greed for remaining on the path, having understood their intention, those who practice a mixture [of doctrines] are established in a state of downfall. (53)
Those who act in such a manner are surely led to hell; but this is not so for those purified by true devotion, whose souls are dedicated to Vāsudeva.
O one of great intelligence, let it be that he sometimes commits a fault or even inflicts injury; nevertheless, service should be performed with devotion. (55)
Indeed, for those devoted to the mantra through faith,
if during the performance of the recitation of that mantra a syllable undergoes a change of phoneme or is omitted due to that particular vowel, [the rite remains effective].
Furthermore, O Lotus-born One, although it is always augmented by vowels and other elements, it bestows the single goal of the mantra upon its practitioners before long. (57)
And by the power of excessive devotion, He bestows what is desired;
for to those who have taken refuge and are purified by true devotion, [He grants it] without [waiting for] the prescribed sequence.
The Lord of Mantras quickly bestows his grace upon those who have cultivated their selves;
how much more so, O Pauṣkara, for those who are perfected in both ritual action and knowledge? 59.
And for those who are devoted to faith and have been awakened by their teachers, therefore, O Mahāmati, they are perfectly serene in this teaching.

All rites such as initiation and so forth are performed for devotees by those who are affectionate toward their devotees; and he who, though not yet fully realizing Me, performs these acts for the sake of attaining Me.
For those of dull or middling devotion whose minds are intent on the enjoyment of desires, for such worldly beings,
my initiation— or the rite of installation and so forth— may be performed out of delusion. (62)
Indeed, along with the seed of devotion for him, his own web of ritual actions will quickly perish,
and even the supernatural powers (siddhis) will turn their faces away.
O lotus-eyed one, having committed such great evil, he shall quickly fall into a terrible hell at the end of this very life, even though he has attained a good rebirth. 64.

Indeed, by the greatness of the Blessed One’s mantra and through the power of its application, the sin arising from association perishes; yet, it may arise again due to the force of prior latent impressions (saṃskāra). || 65 ||
Having further performed difficult penances, he may again obtain a human body;
he should exert himself in virtuous conduct by which he may attain peace. (66)
He certainly attains that preceptor who is full of ego, devoid of devotion, and lacking authority; he shall surely obtain a state in hell according to his desire.
O twice-born one, although the essence of mantra is omnipresent and bestows grace upon all, even so, it does not manifest its presence there [in an unworthy vessel]. 68.
Whether one truly enters me at the end of the body after worshipping my image, or whether one does not enter me, in either case,
ghosts and vetālas cause the destruction of wealth and other possessions at that very moment.
O Lotus-born One, those who are established in other philosophical systems are not to be favored;
likewise, by one who fears the terror of saṃsāra, such a teacher is certainly not to be rejected.

O one of great intelligence, for this very reason, by one who is solely devoted to right devotion and free from hypocrisy and attachment, the supreme sacrifice known as Pratiṣṭhā [should be performed]. (71)
Indeed, that which must be returned by the Vaiṣṇavas should be done so by the Vaiṣṇavas themselves, down to the very root.
Pauṣkara said:
O Lord, for the benefit of the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas who are devoted to the Blessed One, I desire to know the very method of creating the image. (72)
The Blessed One said:

For the sake of the gods, for the purpose of a journey to the forest, or for auspicious acts such as protection, when one has reached a region of the forest and performed the worship of its presiding deities; (73)
One should carry away a stone or a tree from the edge of a forest with a perfectly pure mind, preceded by a sacrifice to the Blessed One, as an eternal [offering]. (74)
Together with those who knew the Pañcarātra, as well as those devoted to the Ṛg and Sāma Vedas,
and with pure and humble artisans intent on their duties.
Those who are self-restrained and initiated should first collect materials such as trees, stones, minerals, or earth; however, those containing living organisms should be sprinkled with water.
A small collection of minerals produced from forest lands, consisting of earthy substances, has been prepared; that should be mixed with the cow dung. (77)

And for the purpose of fashioning the image, when there is a collection of auspicious great clay, [one should perform the rite] with the Heart-mantra over those images made of mineral substances or those containing a core of clay. || 78 ||
O Lotus-born One, the application of powders derived from pearls, gold, and copper is always prescribed for the pacification of the burning sensation caused by the power of mantras. (79)
Everything from the charcoal and wood up to the edge of the forest is utilized;
all of that, when gathered according to the prescribed rule, shall bring about success.
Having thus previously taken [the clay] from a forest or a grove of trees,
one should perform the fashioning of the image (bimbāpādana) there or in the vicinity of one's own house.

Having been commanded by the Guru, one should perform the sacrifice according to the rules in the ritual hall; afterwards, one should worship the artisan, the master, and oneself, following the sequence arising from one's own [tradition].
A wise sacrificer should abandon from the very beginning any rajasic or tamasic disposition toward this most excellent undertaking. (83)
(229) "O Lotus-born One, that [attainment] surely does not come to those of defiled intellect;
or even if it were complete, it would be agitated by hundreds of obstacles and defects. (84)
O Lotus-born One, even for one of a sattvic nature, a deficiency of limbs arises through past karma alone, causing mental distress. (85)
Now, learn from me the procedure prescribed therein for the multicolored image, using pigments and water that has been strained and so forth. (86)
And the joining of the prescribed parts is performed with perfumed pigments,
such as white, red, and others, which are purifying and consecrated by mantras.
With clay mixed with honey, ghee, and milk, combined with silk-cotton powder, and sprinkled with golden water, [one should prepare] images made of clay. || 88 ||
O lotus-born one, when a split occurs in something made of wood, or when it breaks,
a rite preceded by pacification is prescribed using a cloth and a weapon.
For those born of stone, a large wound is always prescribed to be treated by excision;
indeed, when even a slight wound has occurred, it should be treated with a probe of precious gems.
When the rubbing on a whetstone is performed with a golden [tool],
and an equality of marks is produced, the image will be endowed with excellent qualities.
The installation of those [images] that have sustained injury certainly brings death to the preceptor, the patron, the foremost artisan, and the people of the region. (92)
A wound located on the circle of the sense organs (the face) brings misfortune to the perpetrator;
one situated from the ear to the navel causes the death of a son. (93)
In the latter two parts of the wife's body, the region from the buttocks to the anus brings about the destruction of brothers;
up to the waist, it results in the loss of sisters. (94)
And wherever there may be a wound from the base of the thigh to the knee, it causes the destruction of wealth, grain, and cattle before long. (95)

And for the sake of compassion toward all, he should proclaim [the merit] from the knees down to the soles of the feet, even if it brings faults upon his circle of servants, as well as for his own sake. 96.
O Lotus-born One, the maker should lead the image—which is being fashioned and freed from beeswax—to a state of flawlessness. || 97 ||
Indeed, when a deficiency of limbs occurs, listen now to this secondary rule (anukalpa).
In the commencement of a physical conflict, there is the fault of injury;

however, when devotion to the Blessed One has arisen, even if that [conflict] occurs, abandoning it and [suffering] destruction are each more contradictory [to that devotion] than the one preceding it. (98)
Indeed, when compared with large images and the like, the relinquishment of the material substance is not appropriate, especially in the case of superior metals such as gold and others. (99)
O Lotus-born One, when a deficiency of limbs occurs, one should perform a sacrifice for the sake of pacification;
having restored that limb once more, O Lotus-born One, according to the specific injunction.
One should apply as much pure gold and gold-mercury as is available to the wound; likewise, one should apply all types of powdered gems consecrated with the twelve-syllable mantra. (101)
O Mahāmati, in this manner and likewise for those arising from other elements, one should fill it with its own element mixed slightly with gold. (102)
O Pauṣkara, if by performing this rite according to the prescribed rule the purity of mind does not arise, another practice must be undertaken.
Having first performed worship as before for the authorized elders and the gurus, they indeed cause [the deity] to be directly perceived; then one should lead it back again to the formless state.
Furthermore, another [image] should be produced by that same material substance, unimpaired, complete in all its limbs, captivating, and of a distinct character. || 105 ||
Since that [lotus] exists eternally even without the passage of time,
O Kamalasambhūta, it arises perpetually from mere volition alone.
When she reaches that place, his ancestors say, "She has arrived," while those beginning with the great-grandfather dispute among themselves. (107)
"Having been freed from faults for the most part through our lineage, we shall attain the state of Vāsudeva, provided that he desires it. (108)
Then, for the pleasure of the fourfold Self— the complete knowers of reality— he quickly undertook the great sacrifice known as Pratiṣṭhā.
O Lotus-born One, [you are the source] of the sages, the gods, the ancestors, and of human beings and all creatures dwelling within the belly of the three worlds. || 110 ||

O twice-born one, when an image made of metal has been broken and arises from a different scriptural tradition, one should fashion another image; in this way, the benefits for the next world and so forth will be secured.
Therefore, that very [action] is prescribed, or its specific variety, because through its connection one attains great merit arising from both worlds as the agent. (112)
For those who reside in their own country and have been provided for with wealth and other means,
the measurement of the property should be carried out, divided according to the aforementioned categories.
O Lord, he who makes an image of the All-pervading One for the sake of his kinsmen and others, being liberated from all defects, goes to the world of Viṣṇu. || 114 ||

O Brahmin, a divine image may be self-manifested, or established by perfected adepts (siddhas), or installed by the wise; however, it must not be one that has been set up by those other than brahmins and the like. 115.
The mantra that has been deposited there, together with the limb-mantras and their respective marks,
departs to its own abode, leaving behind the image even without ritual action.
Having cursed the preceptor, as well as the agent for whom it was established, the Piśācas, Bhūtas, Vetālas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas likewise [were affected]. (117)
The site, the pedestal, the image, and everything up to the flagstaff—knowing this, O Great Buddha, one who desires auspiciousness should act accordingly. (118)
Just as auspiciousness is accomplished for a consecrated image through worship, fire-offerings, and gifts, accompanied by musical instruments and songs; || 119 ||

In their own homes, devotees should, at all times and according to their ability, perform the worship of the mobile image with flowers, incense, and other offerings for the attainment of auspiciousness. (120)

For as long as life lasts, one should worship one's own mantra during the three periods of the day upon a stable image that has been consecrated with the mantras of reality; however, if the image is mobile, the practitioner of mantra should worship it at the time [of practice]. || 121 ||
Or rather, previously, the Guru deposited the common [mantra] consisting of twelve syllables for the benefit of those devotees who had attained [the path], out of a desire for their welfare. (122)
Having thus withdrawn [the offerings] according to the scriptures with devotion for the attainment of the fruit of enjoyment,
one should offer them together with the *mātrās* to one's own guru for the sake of the pacification of worldly existence.
Placing his hands at his feet, he made this request with his head bowed:
"At the time of your abandonment of the body, [please grant this] to me, who am worthy, or [to someone else]."
Filled with [the mantra], it should indeed be placed by the Vaiṣṇavas out of a desire for my grace, at the time of the disciple's renunciation of the body, out of compassion for him. 125.
In this way, O high-minded one, the teacher should give instruction to another who is fit; and by him, in turn, it should be given to another self-restrained disciple at the end of his body.
O Great-minded one, O Brahmin, because of the absence of that [devotion] for a devotee who is otherwise hospitable, a householder must ensure his residence in a temple.
But if one does not obtain enjoyments, one should completely renounce food and drink for the sake of propitiating the All-pervading Lord, being pure, bathed, and clear-minded. (128)
Having offered water for the arghya on the head, either with flowers or alone, this is indeed the primary worship with water;
for it is the very root of all enjoyments.
Since all things consist of rasa, and that rasa is the Supreme Lord, the Blessed One named Nārāyaṇa; therefore, that is remembered as the most excellent arghya offering.
One should then place the entire network of enjoyments at the feet, for by so doing,
one attains the state of being situated within the cavity of its own cause.
Not long after, although the devotees, the ministers, and the performers of ritual sacrifices possessed the power of earth, fire, ether, and wind, [they were nevertheless overcome]. (132)
Flowers, incense, and other such enjoyments are proclaimed to end with the mantras;
even there, their manifestation is rooted in taste, for they are of that very nature. (133)

O Lotus-born One, he by whom everyone is seen as a connoisseur of rasa everywhere, through the state of abiding bliss and the essence of those very [senses] such as taste—[he is the true knower]. 134.
Thus, O Lotus-born One, the arrangement of the human deities—both those that are mobile and those that are immobile—has been fully described. 135.
Except for the worship of the supreme twice-born (the Brāhmaṇas), one should certainly avoid any other unstable Vaiṣṇava image;
there should be no installation in the house of the Blessed One of images belonging to the Sun, Rudra, or Indra.
That which is prescribed for the images also produces negligence;
however, the forms of the deities who possess other forms are not characterized by such [static] manifestations.
Those situated within the worlds must be fashioned by a firm ritual procedure,
as must the various manifestations and their respective appearances.

Building in walls that have been prohibited is forbidden, as is constructing a house on elevated ground, except for the dwellings of the gods; furthermore, it must not exceed the height of the adjacent structure.
As it has been said: "Indeed, one who desires to perform the ritual in reverse from the primary method, out of necessity for the ground, should do so preceded by faith and devotion. (140)
First, the worship and the fire-oblation (*pūjāhavana*), as well as the instruction of the teacher (*daiśikī*), and likewise [the other rites]...
He was never a source of opposition toward the gods who are worthy of worship, nor toward the protectors of the earth who follow the path of devotion. (142)
And for those sacred seats (pīṭhas) whose forms have not been seen, there will be inauspiciousness;
likewise for those situated in sacred sites (āyatana) that have been occupied by those dwelling within. 143.
When there is worship of the mantra-forms whose bodies are the manifestations of emanation, the acquisition of wealth by Vaiṣṇavas and Brahmins and others is indeed ordained. || 144 ||
At the outset, however, for the sake of propitiation, one should indeed perform the entire rite ending with the mantra as the primary method;
for in the secondary alternative (anukalpa), it may be done by means of other materials such as a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and so forth.
Even when the web of enjoyments is less than eight times eight, and when no further enjoyment is possible, for all enjoyments and karmas, O lotus-born one, [this is the case]. (146)

One who desires auspiciousness should constantly perform the supreme rite of pacification, characterized by the sacrificial procedure of the Blessed One, which encompasses both deficient and abundant extensive purposes. (147)
Pauṣkara said:
O Lord of the World, please instruct us regarding that supreme goddess of mantras, the pacifier of all defects, and how she should be employed by the teachers. 148.
The Blessed Lord said:
For those devotees of purified soul, the previously described lotus-wheel, which is free from a dwelling place, is beneficial and pacifies all defects. 149.
Or rather, because the worship beginning with the pedestal (pīṭha) and ending with Viṣvaksena is indeed not effective there without the worship of Sarveśvara.

For those who are free from expectations, the placement [of the deities] should be performed by one who knows the ritual rules—some being distinct, some without support, and others situated in the sky; thereafter, one should cause the recitation of the Ṛgveda hymns.
Having fashioned the seat (pīṭha) together with its limbs and the city (pura) together with its feet,
one should perform there the previously mentioned nyāsa, beginning with the ādhāra.
Having perceived [the deity] as being like one's own body, and having remembered it as revealed by the presiding witness,
one should now [unify it] with the universal consciousness (citsāmānya) that expresses the form.
And just as here, having recollected [the state] with sensation and so forth, one is joined with one's own body;
for when there is supervision by direct perception, there is no fault of confusion.
In the same way, the worship beginning with the Foundation Power (ādhāra-śakti) and ending with Viṣvaksena is faultless within the maṇḍala, provided it is preceded by the word "Bhagavat. (155)
Having uttered the name of every [deity], at the end one says "namas ātmane" (salutation to the Self);
in this manner, there is the worship of the deities of the seat, beginning with Dharma. 156.
And thereafter, O Pauṣkara, having performed the worship of the mantra-forms that have been invoked within the maṇḍala according to their respective positions, [one should proceed]. (157)
That which is complete leads to peace, while that which is incomplete leads to a lack of peace;
therefore, for the sake of peace, one should always perform the gift of a cow and the libation of fire according to one's own capacity.
But prior to the sacrifice to the Blessed One, [the ritual] is always prescribed everywhere;
and that is performed with rites permeated by knowledge, together with the arghya and other offerings. 159.

Having understood that from which it correctly arises, as well as the auspicious reality established therein, one perceives its beginninglessness and non-difference from the seed and the sprout. (160)
O Lotus-born One, for those in this world who desire the fruit in order to attain that fruit, knowledge and action indeed exist in a state of mutual interdependence. (161)
This should be understood through the perfectly pure intellect, even by means of discernment, as belonging to the Supreme Self known as the Blessed Vāsudeva. (162)
For the sake of bestowing grace, [he taught] the radiance endowed with knowledge and action,
together with mantra and mudrā, out of compassion for those engaged in ritual practice.
Endowed with the power of reality (tattva-śakti), possessed of qualities such as knowledge and the rest,
and accompanied by the eightfold [powers] beginning with atomization (aṇimā)— the very seeds of supernatural accomplishment (siddhi).
For the pacification of all faults and for the perpetual attainment of the supreme state.

O best of the twice-born, the "Effulgence of the Supreme Lord" (Pārameśvarollāsa) is to be understood as non-different from the Supreme Lord himself, just as the auspicious flames of a smokeless fire are non-different from the fire itself. 165.
Just as the waves of the ocean and the rays of the sun [arise from their source],
so too do [the mantras] arise from the heart-lotus like the sun, through the power of devotion preceded by volition.
He constantly brings about the arising of the intellect of the fortunate one at the great festival;
having worshipped with sacrifices characterized by ritual intentions and enjoyments, as before. (167)
O Lotus-born One, he is subsequently gratified with more auspicious external offerings such as clarified butter and other substances, according to the prescribed rite upon the support of fire.
And the guide, in the form of a brahmin, having been brought to the highest satisfaction with food, drink, wealth, and other gifts, indeed bestows supreme peace. (169)
Pauṣkara said:
"O Lord, regarding the performance of rites such as the Śāntika and others, and concerning the mandalas and so forth, I desire to know the meditation upon this Sustainer of the World. (170)

The Blessed Lord said: O Lotus-born one, whatever manifestation is worshipped, it should be known as being endowed with qualities such as knowledge and so forth; it is the eternal [form] of the All-pervading Lord, O Lord, to be known through the self of all. (171)

For the sake of pacifying the suffering of saṃsāra, or for the complete pacification of that which arises from it, one should indeed offer [the sacrifice] after making it the object of focus, with devotion and firm faith. (172)
For the constant attainment of one's desired goals, [the deity] should be worshipped with twelve-syllable and other mantras by the reciters,
appearing in various forms and adorned with weapons, limbs, garments, garlands, ornaments, and so forth.
Thus, being perfectly filled with powers purified by ritual and with his own other means of accomplishment,
Acyuta manifests a form consisting of pure consciousness.
One should remember [the Lord] in his human form for the attainment of the state of the virtuous,
with a body that is beautiful, divine, and immutable. (175)
For those who perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and meditate, great knowledge—characterized by light—arises effortlessly from the body, emitting a radiance that is the very nature of wisdom. 176.
Endowed with garlands, garments, and ornaments that are peerless and suited to themselves—consisting of pure consciousness, self-luminous, and mutually delighting one another. (177)

He should gladden those who are afflicted by the fires of past karma and who do not practice meditation, by means of a multitude of cows arising from the mass of his own bestowed moonlight, in order to pacify their weariness.
O Lotus-born one, know that the two powers called Vidyā and Kalā— consisting of knowledge and action and conjoined with will— unite like a conch and a discus.
The Blessed One possesses infinite power and is remembered as having infinite qualities;
he is distinct from the principles of the sun, moon, and fire, which serve as examples for the perceptible world.
By the very means of his own awakening, the extent of this [Lord] is established;
he is indeed everything, so what more could there be beyond all? (181)
When that which is to be meditated upon shines forth within his own self, that is knowledge established in the Self;
through devotion and appropriate meditation, from this very state comes peace.
In this way, understand his supreme form, which is indeed the highest bestower of bliss upon those meditators whose intellects are focused on the Supreme. 183.
With [hair] resembling crushed black collyrium, thickly curled and dark-blue, greyish-white as camphor, divine, and with their interiors interspersed with flowers; || 184 ||
It was adorned with beautiful hair crowned by a diadem and tiara,
possessing the radiant luster of ruby and resembling land-lotuses and kāśa flowers.
With palms and soles of feet red, with faces beginning with the lower lips, with the interiors of nostrils and ear-holes, and with teeth appearing like pearls; (186)
With eyes like slightly reddish cow’s milk and pure blue lotuses,
one should thus first [visualize] the lotus-eyed Acyuta within the heart-lotus.
The meditation on the splendor and light of various mantras shall grant all desires;
indeed, meditation upon the external maṇḍala brings the suffering of existence to an end. (188)
It exists as non-different from the supreme reality of the Blessed One; established herein is the externally cognizable array of mantras, which is ever-arisen. (189)

Indeed, that which bestows liberation upon living beings through the nature of various individual manifestations must first be thoroughly understood in its successive stages, as previously described. (190)
O Brahman, the powers of the Boars have been described according to their characteristics;
their manifest meditation has been duly explained previously in due order. (191)
O Lotus-born One, the eternal, pervasive, and stainless form of the Supreme Brahman known as Vāsudeva indeed exists in a state of non-difference [from Him]. 192.
Just as the flame, the disc, and the radiance of fire, the moon, and the sun exist,
so too does He assume by His own will the form known as the ego (abhimāna), as has been described.
O Blessed One, it is indeed for the sake of bestowing grace that the powers of mantra manifest their own supreme, conceited form. (194)
By taking this as the object of focus, through recitation, meditation, and worship, the knower of mantras who remains established in devotion to this hymn attains everything without delay. (195)
O Lotus-born One, that which is innate, natural, and born of karma— the bondage of action— is indeed established just as impurity (kālikā) exists within the ore of copper.
Having herself become the power of omniscience through the nature of the supreme mantra,
she gradually effects the piercing of the principles of action and the self.
