Those who constantly attain that which is endowed with devotion and free from obstruction drink the supreme Brahman, the Lord, for the sake of attaining the nature of the Mantra.
Having obtained their respective offices in succession upon reaching the station of their own Lord, they proceed by the power of mantra; because of that, they do not return again. (199)

O Lotus-born One, having understood this, those mantras which are the most preeminent, as well as the forms of the Lord of the World, are indeed to be meditated upon and worshipped in that very same way. (200)
Through propitiation, recitation, meditation, and thorough knowledge,
they bestow their own auspicious state— that which is imperishable and infallible.

O Lotus-born one, having understood this, those who are well-established in the means of expression [should know] that the great web of karma belonging to those whose nature is karma is burned away like fire. 202.
With those [mantras] preceded by twelve syllables and followed by six or eight syllables,
known by their own names or by their own seed-syllables (bīja), as received from the mouth of the teacher.
The supreme lords known as Vāsudeva are to be meditated upon in two divisions;
and there are four [others] ending with Aniruddha, according to the arrangement of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha). || 204 ||

In this same way, other [forms] such as Varāha and the rest, together with the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha), as well as those celebrated as the twelve beginning with Keśava, [are likewise established]. || 205 ||
The worship of the fourfold Self, whose essential nature is never abandoned, who possesses manifold forms, and who exists in various states of transformation.
But that which is for the sake of accomplishing various goals, as well as for attaining qualities according to one's inclination—
having correctly understood the sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya), there is the supreme tranquility of majesty.
O Pauṣkara, that which a wise person desires to attain quickly must be worshipped according to its actual state, for it is indeed nothing other than the perceptible reality. (208)

As before, with respect to the fivefold manifestations (pañcavyūha) and so forth of the forms of the Lord’s manifestation, he desires the sixfold qualities beginning with sovereignty, as well as the fourfold nature (cāturātmya) and the rest. (209)
One should worship the foremost [deities] beginning with Vāsudeva, who has Pradyumna and Acyuta as his presiding overseers;
furthermore, he who desires the great multitude of qualities should worship them preceded by their specific forms.

All various perfections of will, such as the power of atomization (aṇimā) and others, as well as the Lord of All, must be understood; yet, up to the level of the Presiding Deity (adhyakṣa), He is indeed the Imperishable (acyuta).
However, for one who constantly practices meditation and worship, it is beneficial to focus primarily on Pradyumna as the foremost, for he is the collection of qualities beginning with motion. (212)
The face of the Guru appears resplendent once again in his worship, following the sequence beginning with Vāsudeva and Acyuta, and ending with Pradyumna. (213)
But he who desires the attainment of the group of six preceded by vigor, should then worship that Acyuta, the presiding lord, who is not Pradyumna.
For one who desires the sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya) preceded by power (tejas) through worship,
the triad beginning with the supervisor (adhyakṣa) is further prescribed for that worship.
Whether prior to the worship of the deities' forms or through worship alone,
the knower of mantras shall attain the state of liberation, which is the reality of the Blessed One.
Although that triad of forms exists at its end as all-pervading,
nevertheless, the Lord is truly the sovereign who, by his very nature, is the source of the universe's manifestation.
Having thus understood that he alone is to be worshipped immediately thereafter,
you, together with your lordly self, [should worship] the Lord who is the witness of the waking state.
By worshipping first the triad beginning with Acyuta,
one should gradually propitiate the triad of the Ādideva within those respective stations.
Listen attentively to how the practitioner of mantras should perform the worship of the qualities in this manner, according to the rule of the fourfold nature.
Knowledge, power, sovereignty, and valor—this fourfold set, when differentiated, brings about accomplishment instantly through sacrifice. (221)
Strength, sovereignty, heroism, and splendor—this quartet culminates in brilliance;
whatever one desires, that which is most cherished, one shall obtain through thorough knowledge.
O Lotus-born One, this quartet—splendor, power, knowledge, and strength culminating in valor—is indeed desired; it bestows these upon the practitioners of mantra.

Having uttered the auspicious word beginning with the *praṇava* for the one whose nature is knowledge (*jñānātman*), exactly as it was stated for the quality of knowledge, so indeed it is for all [the other qualities]. || 224 ||

Worship for the attainment of liberation and enjoyment is thus remembered as being of various kinds, performed either according to the unswerving sequence or by means of the aforementioned reversal. (225)
Furthermore, one should worship the world-source, though divided by distinctions,
as non-dual within the great twelve-spoked wheel and within its interior of innumerable petals.
But the Lord who has transcended the qualities (guṇātīta), as before, is within the pericarp;
indeed, he is on the petals by means of the twelve-syllable mantra and its constituent letters. (227)
Salutation to those who are restrained by the *praṇava* (Oṃ), proceeding clockwise from the eastern quarter;
for the attainment of the qualities that have come to be yours, there is indeed that which is joined with the sixfold [set]. 228.
One should worship, in sequence, the threefold movement of the divine Cāturātmyas, as well as the other triad consisting of the Guṇas, and the forms [of the deities]. || 229 ||
Therefore, for the sake of attaining the fruit through those means, one should perform sacrifice with desire,
by means of action preceded by knowledge and endowed with devotion and faith.

O twice-born one, together with the dharma of your own caste and stage of life, and through perfect meditative concentration, [you should practice] until the time of your final liberation, for as long as you live.
And because [the afflictions] have been pacified by its intense power, through the attainment of knowledge,
and by means of this very body— or indeed by either one of these two— [liberation is achieved].
By virtue of his gentle and slow nature, and by virtue of his disposition, he is worshipped by the immortals;
indeed, whoever performs worship under his authority [attains this]. (233)

Then, through the aforementioned pure enjoyments and various ritual acts, once the constituent parts of the rite have been accomplished, one should offer the *arghya* with the heart-mantra and the weapon-mantra to one's own self. (234)
Having offered various divine enjoyments and imagined objects of worship, using words preceded by the syllable *praṇava* (Om) and ending with a word of salutation (*namaḥ*). || 235 ||
Thinking "I offer," one performs the acquisition of the rules for their enjoyment;
the offering of them with the intellect and with the head bowed low [is the ritual]. (236)
That which is to be known during the offering [of the breath] by the reciter from the Lord of the Heart— namely,
those [elements] previously drawn in by inhalation that were situated outside, [is to be offered] in due order.
The fivefold offering, beginning with the arghya, known as "heart-pleasing," is performed with the añjali mudrā by one whose mind is purified by faith. (238)
The offering should be presented in many ways, or indeed just as is possible,
having relied upon the Supreme while remaining restrained with the senses.
Having covered the nostrils of the face with a cloth,
O Lotus-born One, it shall not be afflicted by one's own breath.
Just as there is no further germination of seeds that have been thoroughly roasted,
so too is there no [rebirth] from the first fruit of ritual action resulting from the worship of Acyuta.
O one of great intelligence, let that which is designated as "karma" rest for now; for is it not known to be fallen from wisdom?
Indeed, being devoid of fruit, it brings about the supreme destruction of existence from its very root. (242)
Sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha certainly bestow the fruits of ritual action;
yet even they do not yield their own fruit to those who possess devotion to the true mantra.
But sacrifices whose nature is knowledge, having correctly understood the intention of Parāśara, bestow supreme peace upon those who know the reality of the Blessed One. (244)

O Lotus-born One, for others, the desired fruit is heaven and the like, while the sought-after result is the enjoyment of mortal existence; indeed, the fruit may be either pertaining to the hereafter or to this world.
Having established this in one's intellect, O best of Brahmins, one should perform the recitation of mantras and other rites with faith,
together with a sense of purpose purified by devotion.

Having thus worshipped the unborn and imperishable [Lord], together with his limbs and retinue, according to the sequence of the primary forms through the differentiation of powers and manifestations; 247.
Indeed, He alone is to be worshipped with the *Ṛgveda* and the *Yajurveda*;
through the mantras in the state called *Acirā*, by means of the tantras, for the attainment of one's desired goal. (248)
It is the supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, the pure, and the supreme Lord;
by its power it is the infallible one, which is designated by the eyes as well as by name. (249)
Clearly, the Supreme Brahman is perceived by him somewhere through the characteristic of his eyes;
for those whose mantras are hidden within, it exists elsewhere, indeed, on the outside.
Therefore, O Mahāmati, the six limbs and the five limbs are indeed the designators (vācaka) and the designated (vācya), for they are properly joined through the act of propitiation.
When the reality of the Lord known as Netra transcends the [other] limbs, it resides in the head and in space for all mantras, whether they be primary or secondary. (252)
First, for the sake of stability, one should employ one's own seed-syllable, which is of the nature of light;
then, one should meditate upon the Lord of the Direction situated therein, in his form as both the transcendent and the immanent.
But by means of the yoga of arising, having summoned the mantras from the supreme state according to their sequential positions for the occasion of worship, [one proceeds]. (254)

And having installed [the deity] according to the scriptures, with the weapons and armor as the final [elements], when the sacrifice had been completed according to the rules for Hari, the Lord of All; || 255 ||
The practitioner desiring success should effect a gradual dissolution [of the elements].
Thus, indeed, is the power of the Controller, the supreme lordly energy known as Netrā. (256)
By virtue of being the radiance of the mantras, she exists as their very essence;
she should be remembered externally in the lotus, or within the heart, inside the letter A.
By means of the seed-syllable called *niṣedha* together with the anusvāra and the letter *kha*,
she shines with the brilliance of ten thousand fires, suns, moons, and boars.
Indeed, through the union of the signified and the signifier, it is always to be honored;
by the sound of the *sṛṣṭi* [syllable] alone, everything desired is produced in creation. || 259 ||
Furthermore, through worship, he bestows the unbroken seed of enjoyment, which is contrary to the ministers, and which is eternally accomplished through ignorance.
At the time of concluding the daily recitation of mantras, as well as at the beginning, one should first understand the mantra exactly as it stands in its proper sequence. (261)

The seed-syllable, the cluster, that which is called the word, and likewise the mantra with its characteristics—this indeed is the classification of mantras, accompanied by a corresponding variety of results. (262)
Since the Lord of All exists in the form of various denotable objects,
He is figuratively designated by four kinds of pure designators.
For thus there exists a mutual manifoldness of dependence between the denoters and the denoted, provided that the established rule [of their relationship] is maintained. (264)

O Brahmin, even without the syllables of the *piṇḍa* known as names and characterized by words, one should effect the conceptualization of the signified meaning through its own seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*). (265)

Of the twelve ancillaries (aṅga) together with their sub-ancillaries (upāṅga), [the recitation] is by their own names; of the six alone, however, it is indeed by name, and of the five as well, according to one's wish. || 266 ||
All of these, joined with the anusvāra and placed within the Praṇava (Oṃ),
should be employed by one who is established in the self of the Nyāsa, during the supreme general worship of the mental form.
At the conclusion, however, one should place the salutation and so forth in accordance with the action;
likewise, when aiming for a specific result, the salutation is proclaimed [to be performed]. (268)
Upon the attainment of the powers beginning with *aṇimā*, one should utter *svāhā*;
but for nourishment, O Lotus-born One, one should indeed utter *vauṣaṭ* in all cases. (269)

The utterance *huṃ phaṭ* is prescribed for the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*), as well as for causing enmity (*vidveṣa*) and the rite of destroying the wicked (*uccāṭana*); whereas *vaṣaṭ* is for mutual affection (*anyonyaprīti*).
O Brahmin, for the sake of satisfaction, in the offering of oblations (bali), and for the increase of splendor,
one must indeed recite [the mantra] preceded by the Praṇava and ending with the word of salutation (namaskāra).
There are other classes of mantras that effect the renunciation of karma;
these are prohibited for men who follow established philosophical tenets (siddhāntins), as they entail their respective fruits. (272)
O Lotus-born One, [this is for] those who know the mantras and the Siddhāntas, especially those who possess knowledge of the mantras, as well as for practitioners who are learned in other Tantras.
These are permitted for those who seek the fruits [of their actions] and whose minds are devoted to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures. || 274 ||
O you of great austerity! Those which are the garland-mantras and so forth, as well as those known as hymn-mantras that are endowed with Vedic mantras; || 275 ||
O Lotus-born one, those who offer the piṇḍa of renunciation, beginning with the *praṇava*, constantly win over the minds of the wise. (276)
Of those mantras with their various meanings, there is indeed the power of the Supreme Lord—eternally manifest, subtle, called "Being," and characterized by knowledge. (277)
O Lotus-born one, O virtuous Brahmin, their will must be made the means for accomplishing [their goals];
it causes [the lotus of the heart] to blossom through the granting [of gifts], even for the sake of liberation. (278)
And for the benefit of those devoted to acts of devotion who serve [the deity] constantly, the wise one, according to the prescribed rule, [offers] medicinal herbs whose roots grow upward. (279)
On this earth, those who have correctly understood the ritual procedure perform [the rite] even by means of burnt fire;
how much more so, then, those who know the scriptures, performing it with devotion according to the prescribed rules? (280)
The teacher of the awakened ones brings about what is beneficial for the mind;
for them, all secret discourse and the entire ostentation of words, beginning with "bound" (baddha), has ceased. (281)
Having relied upon the sequence of the words and mantras that are beneficial, one should proceed in due order.
Pauṣkara said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to know, according to the distinctions of time, the true nature of the perfected mantras and the established state of the Āgamas. (282)
The Blessed Lord said:
O best of the twice-born, time is one; yet, due to the influence of its own functions, it appears as if divided to those agents who are destined for the state of the Lord.
That which is indeed measured by nāḍikās constitutes a day and night consisting of six seasons;
having divided that from dawn into five unequal parts, [one should proceed]. (284)
Having reached the hour of Brahmā, the knower of mantras, being restrained and pure,
should purify his own body by means of the āyāma and other practices as prescribed.
Then, one should perform the worship of the mantra arising from the body invested with mantras,
continuing until the conclusion of the recitation and hymns, or until the sight of the sun.
Thereafter, one should perform the worship of enjoyments, such as flowers, roots, fruits, and so forth;
when the eighth part of the day has passed, one should perform it preceded by a bath.
As before, one should perform the propitiation of the mantra until the end of the third watch;
thereafter, in the fourth watch, one should engage in the study of the scriptures. (288)
Having performed reflection accompanied by hearing and exposition according to the desire of one's own intellect,
and after the sun has set, one should enter the hall of worship.
One should properly perform the worship of the mantra, accompanied by recitation and meditation;
thereafter, having taken to the bed, one should remember the Lord of Mantras within the heart.
Having passed the portion of the night and then rising from his bed,
he should indeed practice the mantra-yoga within the lotus of the heart as before.
Having returned to his bed and awakened once more, O Lotus-born One,
he should rise, leave the couch, and then perform what was previously prescribed.
Know this to be the distinction of time; now the distinction of the scriptures is being stated:
that in which the fourfold nature (cāturātmya) is worshipped as something to be performed.
O Pauṣkara, know that the Āgama which was previously [taught] by the Brāhmaṇas through their own traditional designations is called the Siddhānta. 294.
The definition of the established doctrine [k: these syllables are present here]:
namely, the ten forms together with their various manifestations, as well as the multitude of incarnations accompanied by other forms. (295)
It is joined with the intermediate manifestations, encompassed by the heart-lotus and so forth,
along with Lakṣmī and the others, those known as the conch and the discus, Garuḍa, and the lords of the directions.

O Lotus-born One, know that [treatise] which is accompanied by its ancillaries and established in the science of weapons, known as the *Mantrasiddhānta*, to be the scripture that bestows all fruits. (297)

Where, in the absence of the fourfold form, another [form] is metaphorically attributed, the form of the Blessed One is [visualized] solely through the mantra, conjoined with the sacrifice [or, according to an alternative reading, "conjoined with the limbs"]. || 298 ||
O Pauṣkara, he is joined with the very array of his beloveds, such as Śrī and others, and is surrounded by various ornaments and weapons that possess embodied forms. (299)

(238) That scripture known as the *Tantrasiddhānta*—[there is an alternative reading: "for that scripture is known as *Tantra*, O Lotus-born; it should indeed be fully understood"]—bestows both worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*).
In that [scripture], lions and other [creatures] appear according to the distinction between the primary and the secondary applications. || 300 ||

When [the deity] has been worshipped by means of the yoga of four, three, two, or more [limbs], they—whether surrounded by their respective retinues or established individually—are indeed [present]. (301)
Know that whatever is propitiated according to one's capacity belongs to another tantra;
thus, always understand this to be the commonality among the various scriptures. (302)
And in the Pauṣkara [Tantra], it is stated that there are two names for the Siddhānta, namely Pañcarātra;
each one exists with many divisions from its very root. (303)
According to the power of various dispositions, [the teaching] has been manifested by the Siddhas and others as concise, as detailed, and thirdly, as possessing both characteristics. (304)

It is traditionally taught that those who have attained perfection through tens of millions of births by means of the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and the Vedas together with the Vedānta, find their abode here. (305)
Therefore, from this scripture, the supreme, imperishable Brahman known as Vāsudeva is attained through action preceded by knowledge. || 306 ||
For this very reason, O Brahmins, the designations of the Siddhāntas are meaningful;
[they include] the Purāṇa, the Vedas and Vedānta, as well as others born of Sāṅkhya and Yoga. (307)
It should be known as being of five kinds, O Lotus-born One, wherein one remains for five nights;
it is traditionally called Pañcarātra precisely by virtue of the excellence of its fruit.
The root known as the True Tradition (Sadāgama) indeed reveals the Supreme Brahman;
it bestows divine perfections and brings peace to those whose actions are obstructed by impediments. || 309 ||
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Determination of Qualifications," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, a great Upaniṣad within the glorious Pāñcarātra.
(The cumulative number of verses is 313) Now begins the thirty-ninth chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
O Supreme Lord, I desire to know eternally the authority of the scriptures along with their designations, as well as the relationship between them and the gods and other beings. (1)
The Blessed One said:
It is concise, of three types— inferior, middling, and superior—
and it is composed in the Anuṣṭubh meter, consisting of one hundred verses.
For that treatise known as the Mūla consists of two hundred verses, each verse being defined by its four quarters;
that which consists of one hundred and fifty verses is remembered as the Uddhāra.
These three types of deficiency, along with their variations of decrease and increase, are manifold for all [beings]; yet their designation does not change again. (4)
That which is to be fully known consists of two hundred and fifty;
and that which is known as the Bṛhaduttara is double this amount.
That is declared to consist of one thousand and five hundred kalpas;
furthermore, the deficiency or excess of these three should be understood gradually.
In this way, O Lotus-born One, there are many other scriptures with different names; all of them are but portions of the Kalpa, and thus they should be fully understood.
From three thousand five hundred up to six thousand one hundred,
and extending as far as twelve thousand, that scripture is known by the name Saṃhitā.
And those others which indeed occupy the intermediate space by more than a hundred scriptural topics—
all of these should be understood, O Lotus-born One, as being designated as *saṃhitās*.
And those scriptures extending up to one hundred and twenty-five thousand [verses], as well as those exceeding that by measures of hundreds and thousands, have been revealed. || 10 ||
All of these, however, should be understood in sequence from the aggregate of eons (kalpaskandha),
consisting of many thousands increased by hundreds and exceeding one hundred thousand.
And that scripture known as the Tantra, consisting of three and a half crores,
is said to be the ninefold division of these three.
Therein proceeds an incalculable enumeration of intermediate numbers,
through an awakening that follows the sequence of the ages and is empowered by the three qualities.
Through the manifold relationship beginning with the divine and ending with the intermediate, there is an immeasurable designation; henceforth follows the union.
That which issues forth from the Supreme Lord together with Time is indeed immeasurable;
it is firmly established in the hearts of the perfected ones (siddhas) who have known all that is to be known.
By the measure of his own awakening, he has illuminated ten million [teachings], whose various divisions ending in the word *pāda* have been proclaimed in succession. || 16 ||
Wherever it has arisen according to one's desire, along with various sectarian differences,
there are many other rites that are pure, as well as those characterized by passion (rājasa) and darkness (tāmasa).
O Lotus-born One, the Sātvata [scripture] is the first of all scriptures, the tradition of the Supreme Lord, purified by valid means of knowledge, and beneficial.
In the Siddhānta, those who know the reality of the Blessed One attain, from the perspective of ultimate truth,
that which has come down through the lineage for the liberation of living beings.
Pauṣkara said: O Lord, by whomsoever this supreme scripture of the Supreme Lord was first received—immeasurable, vast, infinite, and like unto the sky—[by him it was taught]. (20)
The Blessed Lord said: [I shall describe] the scripture named Aprameya, concerning Vāsudeva— the Lord of all, the pervasive, the imperishable, the infallible, and the one who is to be expressed.
O twice-born one, know that the sound of the self is not a separate characteristic;
O twice-born one, the self, which is designated as the nature of knowledge, is indeed led by its own will.
For him who has attained his desires by nature and is self-dependent,
this great [ego], consisting of the power of the qualities and called "conceit," arises through a portion of his knowledge.
Having assumed for himself a form consisting of sound, that Blessed One, who is beyond the senses and imperishable, approached of his own accord by his own will.
But that all-pervading Saṃkarṣaṇa is rested within the embodiment of knowledge;
he himself is infinite potency, merged with the embodiment of knowledge.
His form, consisting of the power of qualities (*guṇa-śakti*) and called "Light" (*prakāśa*), is the eternal Pradyumna, characterized by self-conceit (*ābhimānika*) and imperturbable. (26)
By that great being, the scripture, blazing with the luster of lightning,
was breathed forth; indeed, he who is the embodiment of valor entered it of his own accord.
Then, O Brahmin, he who possesses an imperishable body knows that great fiery expansion produced by the nature of vigor, and he sustains it as Aniruddha.
Endowed with qualities, powers, and virtues, unconquered and imperishable,
this scripture was abandoned by the high-souled Pradyumna like a belch.
Having taken up that which was held within his heart by the self of Aniruddha,
the Lord created the deity Vāgīśa, who consists of the manifestation of the qualities (guṇas).
Then Aniruddha, whose nature is imperishable, attained that pair of goals through the scripture;
it was free from agitation, beyond doubt, and thereafter reached a state of immortality.
O Embodiment of Knowledge, that which was known from a portion [of you] has indeed been made imperishable within your own primordial form by the Embodiment of Knowledge.
And the state of being of equal flavor (samarasatva) has been set forth in various treatises by the Siddhas, having been extracted from Vāgīśvara exactly as it was taught. (33)
Having correctly collected [the essence] like butter from the ocean,
this [teaching] of the all-pervading Brahmā, the presiding deity of knowledge, has been revealed.
O twice-born one, [this was done] by those impelled by the gods headed by Rudra, Āditya,
and Indra, as well as by the portions of Rudra and others who had arisen from their own parts for the sake of those who sought [their aid].
It was revealed by Brahmā to his own sons, Nārada and others, and from them it was passed on to the sages of purified souls residing within the three worlds. (36)
It is solely by the power of his own intention, as well as by the power of various times, various places, and various castes. || 37 ||
Thus, O one of great intelligence, this connection of the scripture has been told to you exactly as it is, along with its secret; indeed, it should be understood according to its true meaning. (38)
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Traditions," in the *Pauṣkarasaṃhitā*, a great Upaniṣad within the illustrious *Pāñcarātra*.
(Total number of verses: 38) Now begins the fortieth chapter.
Pauṣkara said:

"O King, I have understood that great pacification of faults, which is supreme for bringing peace; indeed, through its application, it produces a state of well-being even when things have gone awry. (1)

Through your grace, as a consequence of this context, [I have explained] everything up to the connection with the scripture, as well as the foundation of various dharmas for living beings and that which bestows heaven. (2)
Now, therefore, I wish to learn from you in brief the characteristics of the images and other details, along with their secret doctrines, concerning the Source of the World.
The entire procedure known as *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration), which was previously enjoined, [applies here];
furthermore, regarding the defects of the images, there are the rites involving beeswax that have been described.

O God, those [characteristics] were previously described by you as being without measurement or proportion; indeed, this characteristic extends from the hair at the top of the head down to the feet. (5)
O Lord of the World, I did not understand this with full precision as it truly is.
The Blessed One said:
O Pauṣkara, having first established the various dharmas,
one should perform the pure, supreme installation of Acyuta for the sake of liberation.
On a ground-site possessing auspicious characteristics, having first [prepared it] with cow-products and food,
you [should consider] the characteristics of the earth together with the attainment of success in the eastern direction.
That very purpose for which the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) was clearly stated must indeed be understood;
it concerns the ground, such as a reservoir of water and so forth, which is adorned in various ways. (8)
Together with forests, forest-dwellers, villages, cities, and so forth,
he should accept the gift for the purpose of installation according to the previous rules and ritual procedures.
Having prepared an extensive area extending as far as a grove of flowers,
the preceptor should then perform the excellent concluding rite of the forest procession.

And by means of the ascendant beginning with the hour (horā), by the auspicious moment (muhūrta) that has been honored, and when the bird (śakuna) is in the sky and Mars (bhauma) is auspiciously bestowing happiness upon the mind; || 11 ||
When only a short distance remains, one should dwell outside the forest on an auspicious planet,
a favorable lunar mansion, and on a propitious day.
And having performed a sacrifice there to the forest deities, he should enter the forest,
taking with him a stone marked with auspicious signs, such as white and other colors.
One should [select] a tree that is very glossy, pleasant, pure, free from defects such as cracks and the like, endowed with auspicious marks, uninjured, straight, and firm.
The fruit should be large, yielding blossoms, milky, or even devoid of them; it may be of various species, fit for ritual use, and conducive to the excellence of the sacrificial components.
Having first performed the offering of oblations to the presiding deity beginning with Sattva,
and having performed the dismissal, the preceptor, with [the sacrificial post] smeared with honey and clarified butter, [should proceed].
Then the artisan should strike with a tool;
there, one should [use] sandalwood, syandana wood, and likewise fragrant sandalwood.
Agaru, karṇikāra, kāśmarya, and red sandalwood; bilva, āmalaka, and mango; as well as tāla, varṇaka, and siṃhaka. || 18 ||
Śrīparṇī, coconut, nāgamātṛkā, and pīnaka;
cow’s milk, wood-apple, as well as camphor, tāla, and tamālaka. (19)
The jujube tree, the acacia, the phalgu, the madhūka, the kiṃśuka tree, the phālaveta, the date palm, the nīpa, the nāraṅga, and the śiṃśupa [kh: nārada-śiṃśupa]. || 20 ||
The great Pippala tree, the Aśvattha, the Pippalī branch, Suradāru, Harītakī, Vakula, and also Udumbara. || 21 ||
Kālākhyam, Puṣpakūlam, and another tree called Vaira;
Phālasyam, the Bhūrja tree, Palāśa, and Kṛtamardaka. || 22 ||
The *tinduka*, the heartwood of seeds (*bījasāra*), the great *mātuluṅga* tree, the *rājavṛkṣa*, the *kohitaka*, the *sunābhi*, the *kuṭaka*, and the *arjuna*. (23)
Sarala, kuṭaja, śāka, śamī, śrīveṣṭa, ketakī, asana, spandana, and the term stabaka (used both singularly and in the plural). 24.
Those sacrificial trees that are full of pith, well-proven, and honored by the world—
all these excellent trees are to be taken for rites such as the installation ceremony.
By increasing the distance by one tāla at a time up to the limit of the dvādaśānta, there are thus sixteen images; this indeed is the other [classification].
(242) It is solely by virtue of necessity that these trees have been assigned in sequence to the task of providing images, from those of very small size up to the great. (27)
Some are prescribed solely by virtue of their results for those seeking results; others are prescribed for those free from desire, and all bestow every kind of fruit.
With these seven components previously mentioned, auspicious archways (toraṇas) should be constructed;
indeed, the sacrificial ladles (sruva) and other implements suitable for the fire-ritual have also been described.
O Puṣkara, the firewood, the fuel-sticks, and the enclosing logs in the fire are for the purpose of propitiating the mantras; they are auspicious seats.
All the forms of the mantras, as well as their seats (pīṭhas), and the various temples and so forth, together with their enclosures; || 31 ||
Beds, seats, and other such items, as well as divine implements, chariots, and so forth for the purpose of chariot processions during festivals dedicated to Viṣṇu [should be provided]. (32)
One should procure long flagstaffs for the tops of the spires according to the scriptures, ensuring they are made of wood that has been dried in the shade.
One should certainly not take [wood] that has been defiled by cracks, splits, worms, holes, or marks from the claws of lions or bears, nor by defects such as lightning strikes and the like.
Pauṣkara said:
O Blessed One, [please describe] the characteristics of the auspicious seats (bhadrapīṭha), the images,
the pedestals for the goddesses, and likewise the temples.
I wish to know the true nature of the chariots and other vehicles, as well as the dimensions of their flagstaffs and those who decorate the pavilions. (36)
The Blessed Lord said:
On an auspicious day favorable to oneself and approved by one's gurus, one should everywhere contemplate [the deity] together with the artisan, beginning from the month of Māgha. || 37 ||
Then, together with Suniveśa, he should indeed bring about everything;
O Brahman, those places of manifestation belonging to the All-pervading Lord which were previously mentioned.
O Lotus-born One, among those two, the non-artificial auspicious seat is more excellent; it is endowed with honor, weight, and measure, and possesses a divine form.
In that regard, first, images made of highly auspicious metals such as gold are prescribed;
immediately thereafter, those fashioned from stone are considered auspicious, provided they possess the form of the Blessed Lord.
Wood, plaster, and likewise painting are desired according to one's material resources;
therein, the residence of the worthy among the worship of the twice-born is traditionally taught for the attainment of liberation.
For the sake of the prosperity of those trustworthy ones devoted to service who offer oblations to the spirits,
and for the sake of attaining divine seats in heaven for those intent on sacrifices and fire-offerings, || 42 ||

O Brahmin, for ascetics who are free from attachment, there is nothing more excellent than Hari, the Lord of all, residing within their hearts; yet, O sage, a place of worship with auspicious characteristics is also highly esteemed.
Wherein one attains incomparable clarity of mind through worship,
having attained it with effort and consecrated it with Vedic mantras.
One should perform the rite with very pure primary substances such as earth, ashes, water from sacred fords (tīrtha),
and so forth, using vessels made of gems, gold, silver, or copper, and not otherwise.

Together with the networks of channels and their vital airs, which are to be accepted as one's own body, and with the constituents, and the qualities such as innate knowledge, along with the moon, sun, and fire. || 46 ||

That which is other than the collection of principles (tattvas), extending down to the earth, arises by depending upon substance (dravya) as its cause; this great reflected image indeed exists [therein]. (47)
There, in the space of the heart-lotus, that which is placed by means of the meditation on Brahman— blazing with the light of the jewel of the mantra— bestows its corresponding fruit.
For those agents who are devoted to faith, it always brings about a stable fruit, namely the supreme realization of Brahman, in every respect. (49)
In the end, by the power of the virtuous, one attains the knowledge that illuminates the self;
therefore, understand now the measurement according to the proportions. 50.
One should decrease it by one finger-breadth at a time from the measure of a palm tree, down to a limit of four finger-breadths; such is the measurement thereafter.
O Brahmin, for movable images, one should increase the height by one finger-breadth at a time up to the limit of tranquility (twenty-four fingers),
reaching a maximum elevation of two tālas.

For stationary [images] intended for the worship of the twice-born, one should increase the measurement by two finger-breadths at a time, up to a limit of four śamās; beyond that, one should proceed accordingly.
One should increase each [measurement] by one *tāla* up to the limit of the "end-maker" (*dvādaśāntakara*),
and from there upwards, one should increase it by one *tāla* plus a quarter (*sapāda*).
From the excessive worship of the twice-born, another fourfold result arises;
one should give that again when it has increased, for the sake of further growth, starting from twelve finger-breadths.
One should give a third part from the third part of the three images, and furthermore,
one should give half a *tāla* or even a full *tāla* for their height.
For the second type of images, however, the height should be one cubit (śama);
beyond that, one should increase it for the purpose of measurement. || 57 ||

One image may be of a single *tāla*, while another should be increased from this point upward, gradually reaching up to one hundred *tālas* by means of fractional *tālas*, O best of the twice-born. (58)

For the sake of achieving the desired height and for the attainment of one's wishes, one should repeatedly effect an increase [of the image] according to the requirements of its manifestation and form. (59)
Furthermore, the greatness [of the image] in the rite of the *bimba* is prescribed according to purpose, and also sequentially, along with its respective measurements and so forth. (60)
Likewise, it should indeed be understood by one seeking results according to the nature of those results;
and for those free from desire, everything has been taught for the attainment of all fruits. (61)
Thus, O twice-born one, it has been declared that there are many varieties according to the class of image, whether they are made of metal, clay, stone, or wood, as available.
Having ascended, their bodily parts are arranged with various pigments produced from their own trees, and they are endowed with bound weapons, garments, and other accoutrements. || 63 ||
O Lotus-born One, just as the bodies of living beings are composed of distinct sinews, bones, flesh, and so forth,
so too is the manifestation of mantras known to consist of the constituent elements (dhātus) and other such parts.

By both the unawakened and the awakened, she is worshipped with various enjoyments for the sake of attaining the fruits of the four aims of life; thus, through internal worship, there is external worship as well.
O Brahmin, apart from that great image made of variegated stone, how else could one fashion an image made of clay, metal, or wood? (66)
O Brahmin, this image, though devoid of distinct parts purified by valid means of knowledge, has been described as being merely a measure.
For those devoted to devotion and faith, [the image] is indeed movable or immovable for the purpose of worship; therein, it is movable when going on a pilgrimage to shrines and holy places. (68)
And one should give [the image] to those who are diligent in their practice, provided it is free from defects and the like;
when worshipped, it bestows success both in this world and in the hereafter. (69)
Therefore, for images that are movable, whether situated on separate seats within one's own hermitage or in another hermitage,
a distinct pedestal is conducive to auspiciousness.
Indeed, everything has been prescribed according to the distinction between mobile and immobile [forms];
those made of clay have been described in brief, while the peripheral pedestals (pīṭhas) are mentioned exclusively.
Now I shall describe in detail, specifically from the *Bhaṅgāsana*,
the characteristics of the auspicious seats (*bhadrapīṭhas*) made of wood.
For that which is pervasive among others— consisting of stone, gold, and so forth—
is, O Mahāmati, from a measure of twelve finger-breadths up to two cubits.
One should construct the auspicious group of Bhadrapīṭhas by increasing the measurement by one finger-breadth (aṅgula),
using the three types of aṅgulas as previously described according to their desired characteristics.
All [images] up to a limit of twenty-four finger-breadths (dvādaśāṅgula) are characterized as "abbreviated" (saṃkṣipta);
those that terminate at exactly one cubit (hasta) are proclaimed as "medium" (madhyama). || 75 ||
Beyond this, they are recorded as being spread out to a measure of two cubits;
know that the first image follows this sequence, with each subsequent one possessing greater preeminence.
Due to the abundance of fruits and because of worship with arghya, flowers, and other offerings,
all [the vessels] were provided with conduits, possessed four legs, and were adorned with excellent craftsmanship.
Those who stand on one foot with only a single garment, who are to be understood by kings as being without [a water] channel, yet are adorned with feet and limbs; || 78 ||
O Great-minded One, the remaining [deities] should be fashioned like the surface of a mirror, accompanied by crescent moons resembling strings of pearls and provided with mirrors. (79)
It was interspersed here and there with swans and vidyādharas, who were endowed with outspread tails like filaments and possessed the gait and grace of lotuses.
Having thus completed it according to what was appropriate for its beauty,
the extensive base of the auspicious throne is now adorned with a drainage channel.
One should always place that which is to be worshipped to the north of oneself;
now, its characteristic mark on the southern side of one's own self is described.
In the center of the broad *bhadrapīṭha*, [the throne] should be made with a third part [of its width],
according to the length previously specified, smooth or adorned with artistic designs.
One should then bury that which shines forth like the appearance of a bath,
having divided it into three equal and perfectly level parts, with one portion at the front.
Having cleared away two parts from the outside, starting from the base at the region of the throat,
one should make the tip threefold from the base, with the middle part extending out through the opening.
Know that even for one who delights in the enjoyment of water, above the two parts, the Karmāṇinī—whose arrangement has been indicated above—should be fashioned. 86.
She, who has the form of a crocodile's face and possesses the characteristics of Kapila, is to be abandoned;
she extends one-third of her width into the ground, with a continuous line of feet.
One should certainly not construct it with an abundance of ornamentation;
rather, it should be like the Sarvatobhadra image, provided with limbs in the center.
One should adorn the various parts of the body with flowers, leaves, or even sprouts,
or else with marks in the shape of the crescent moon, according to one's own ingenuity.
To the north of that, one should fashion a lotus together with a wheel, or a lotus alone;
one should make it inclined outward, or else a great, expansive face.
Then, the face should likewise be joined well with the end of the northeast portion,
and its extension should be fashioned according to the characteristic of a clockwise rotation.
The arrangement of the limbs and the body parts together with the minor members, as well as the auspiciousness of the palace—concentrate your mind on these one-pointedly. 92.
From half of the arghya-pīṭha, the area extending toward the back should be made square,
while the left side should be well-rounded.
One should place the head [of the pillar] upon that [base], which is broad and wide;
the pillar should be well-rounded, fashioned, smooth, or square.
Alternatively, it may have eight corners or be fashioned with beautiful designs;
the encirclement of the pillars is prescribed to be three times longer than their thickness.
It was filled with forests and groves rich with the foliage of spreading creepers,
and with the lords of sages intent on meditation and devoted to the study of the Vedas.

O Mahāmati, [the worship] is performed by perfected ones (siddhas) who are identical with the Blessed One, appearing in embodied or unembodied forms bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, or holding a rosary and a water-pot.
O Lotus-born One, one should thus fashion these [deities], or others as well, with full-blown lotuses provided with filaments and pericarps. (98)
Or rather, by those who are utterly deluded, this very [body] must be treated like a garland on a stick through their successive actions; it is not fit for the auspicious throne.
On the back part, however, that which has been conceived as the circle and so forth is by nature the support of the wheel, having the essence of an upward-facing lotus. (100)
Having led [the deity] outside of that, one should fashion a wheel marked with all the limbs;
one should make four pillars as a supreme support, like a tortoise. (101)
O Mahāmati, the width of that which is to be seated with equanimity is indeed ordained to be one and a half times its [own] width. 102.
In the forest of the earth, [the site] may be shaped like the Maheśvara-maṇḍala, circular, level, or narrow due to a gradual slope from the top. || 103 ||
Having made the base area three-quarters or equal [in measure] from the bottom region,
and having performed the consecration as before, it should be provided with a temple.
Having brought the Lord of Mantras near for the sake of attaining liberation, one should worship with supreme devotion or according to one's own capacity for the attainment of results. 105.
O Lotus-born One, these eight varieties of his, which are octagonal, were fashioned by the practitioners residing in their own homes with great magnificence.
They may be hexagonal, circular, or even square;
one should fashion that which is square so as to be provided with its own petals.

Therefore, O Mahāmati, for the sake of establishing the existence of this [soul], it has always been established by means of the measures (pramāṇa) taught in accordance with the specific philosophical systems. || 108 ||
Having indeed completed it by arranging the composition and bringing it to its conclusion.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Auspicious Seat," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, a great Upaniṣad within the glorious Pañcarātra.
(Total number of verses: 109) Now begins the forty-first chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
The ritual installation of mantras has indeed been indicated by the path already described;
I now wish to know it exactly as it has been taught.
The Blessed Lord said:
For men who are worshippers, whose souls are solely devoted to the mantra, and who have awakened to the form of the mantra, worship performed in secret is beneficial. (2)
Now, with a concentrated mind, learn of the arrangement and configuration of the wooden structures and other elements, including their pillars, as they stand upon the foundation.
Likewise, for pillars that are free from stiffness and whose bases rest upon the ground,
their thickness is traditionally held to be equal to one-third of their own width.
The water-channel should be equal to that [foundation] in length, or measured as half [of it] in width;
having divided it into well-equal parts, the lowest [type] should first be made strong.
The short [lines] consist of twelve syllables, while the middling ones consist of fourteen; those that are extensive consist of sixteen syllables, and among these, the first ones are in the middle.
The pedestal should be fashioned with six parts, smooth, level, and auspicious;
it may be perfectly circular or square, or simply its own lotus shape.
Alternatively, it may be provided with wheels and lotuses;
its height is prescribed as half [of the base], while its thickness, including the lotus-base, is one and a half times that.

O best of Brahmins, the previously mentioned characteristics apply equally to those two types of lotuses together with their circles; however, for the square [mandala], one should fashion it as follows.
O Lotus-born One, you should not construct conch-shapes in the corners, nor should you make a group of four starting with the conch for a circular [mandala].

O Lotus-born One, regarding that which was stated concerning the wheel and the lotus— the height of half [the diameter] for both the wheel and the lotus, which are devoid of the circle and have a square base.
Is the mantra not prescribed for the solitary [deity] and for the one accompanied by the assembly?
One should bury that lotus from the center, two parts at a time, all around.
The excavated portion is made equal and half as wide as its length;
the water-retaining wall all around the excavation is equal in height to the slope on the outside.
And the sacred thread (sopavīta) is prescribed as being situated within the supporting lines;
this is the calculation of the twelve parts (dvādaśāṃśaka), and thus this is the calculation of the parts everywhere. || 14 ||
O twice-born one, the measurements for the groups of wooden parts as well as those made of stone were previously ordained according to divisions and portions based on their proportions. 15.
In the center of that, one should perform everything previously mentioned according to the portions [assigned] by the sages;
furthermore, one should gradually bury two portions each around it.
The birth-support (janmāśraya), however, is recorded as being surrounded by one and a half parts;
whatever measurement was stated above that, it is indeed prescribed there.
Having divided that into sixteen parts, one should perform everything as before using eight parts in the center, together with a quarter of a part.
O Brahmin, one should dig a trench all around with two parts;
the reservoir is prescribed to be three-quarters or two-thirds of that size.
Having prepared the wheel as previously described, beginning with the lotus and so forth as stated,
one should fashion a seat consisting of nine lotuses for the placement of the Lord during worship.
And in whatever manner one has calculated the expansion, in that same manner,
taking [the earth] from the previously dug-out places, one should join it together in the middle region.
By which the field and the lotus are divided for you, as well as the nine lotuses based upon the excellent mantra. (22)
Just as a lotus is appropriately joined with its common stalk when worshipped, so too should the division of the extensive portions be made exactly as described. (23)
Then, having prepared it, one should diligently construct an abundance of girdles and other ornaments, starting from the water-reservoir and proceeding in order according to its layout.
Having cleared away the majority [of the obstructions] from the four directions by means of the *anupāda* [formula],
one should then divide [the remaining area] starting from the tail, three, four, five, or six times.
Divided into three parts, it is adorned with a crown (*uṣṇīṣa*), a lotus, and three girdles (*mekhalā*);
divided into four parts, the crown is situated amidst six girdles. (26)
One should indeed fashion an auspicious lotus pond with two networks of tinkling bells;
O Lotus-born One, when there is an abundance of devotion to the sages, it should be sixfold.
One part should form the uṣṇīṣa section, which should be like a loose hair-tuft;
below that, the thread is prescribed to be cut into the shape of a pearl-shell (śuktikā).
Below the portion of the oyster-shell [design], one should fashion a circle provided with a pericarp;
and a circular seat is prescribed, as well as a square one on all sides. (29)

One should fashion three girdles below that, possessing auspicious characteristics; they should be slightly larger than the stated proportions, increasing gradually in sequence by one-quarter [of the measurement].
The stability [of the temple] is established according to the intermediate sūtras, which is beneficial as it generates the divisions;
having abandoned the portion of the uṣṇīṣa-pīṭha and the Garuḍa with palms joined in reverence. (31)
One should perform [this] with one's own face joined with another [face], or with two hands; I consider this to be the Bhadrāsana posture, performed either with the front or the back [hands].
Between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, one should fashion Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures,
in the middle of that [space], on its northern side, upon the auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha).
On both sides of the measurement, one should fashion an ocean encircled by jeweled vessels, containing a gentle-formed [deity] along with divine aquatic creatures. (34)
Then, the remaining four directions should be filled with clusters of small bells,
whether in a mobile image made of material substances or one fashioned from finger-measurements (aṅgula).

Now, for the sake of the fame of kings and others who desire auspiciousness, as well as other wealthy persons, I shall describe various types of dwellings that are beneficial for those above [the commoners]. (36)

One should first perform [the rites] there for those established in various dharmas—whether it be a king, a practitioner, or anyone else—for that which indeed bestows worldly prosperity and heaven. (37)
Having quickly brought about the cessation of that ritual through the fruit of the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga),
he should thereafter indeed perform the re-installation of Hari once again.
In that state where the accumulation of specific karmas has indeed ceased, one does not encounter even the slightest unrighteousness through mere volition alone. || 39 ||

For by that very same [practice] which has been correctly completed, in another birth he shall indeed attain the supreme knowledge born of solitude, which grants the accomplishment of liberation. || 40 ||
For supreme peace is not produced by any other action, but by an action free from poison; such an action, governed by Dharma, bestows imperishable results. || 41 ||
Pauṣkara said:
O Blessed One, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, I wish to know from you the foundation of the various dharmas, so that my doubt may be pacified. (42)
The Blessed One said: Having first constructed an auspicious temple for the five deities, with a mind that is indeed stainless and free from desire, (one should proceed). 43.
In that [city], one should establish a city for the twice-born, founded upon righteousness and purpose;
it is common to all worlds and brings about the destruction of all defects.
It is indeed the supreme among all dharmas, always bestowing all desires;
it is the most excellent assembly of those who know the five times, consisting of the Blessed One himself.
Having recognized him as one devoted to the six duties, dedicated to the dharma of the three Vedas, pure among kinsmen, and free from mutual dualities; (46)
Devoted to his wife and the agnihotra fire, and intent on the study of the Vedas, [he should dwell] in a place endowed with rivers, mountains, and forests, and free from wicked creatures. (47)
In a region rich with crops, rice, and fruit, abounding in lush young grass, provided with sweet water, and adorned with excellent ramparts; (48)
Having reached that auspicious place there and having worshipped the Lord of the World, he then bathed, was anointed, and adorned with garments and ornaments. (49)
Having first presented a copper plate and having seated a Brāhmaṇa,
one should worship him as he sits upon his seats with water for the feet, respectful offerings, and flowers.
And with fragrant incense and betel leaf, O Mahāmati, one should give water with kuśa grass into the hand at the places prescribed in due order. (51)
One should cause [the disciple] to recite, "I shall not be negligent" with the twelve-syllable mantra;
then one should perform the Sāman chant "pratiṣṭhāsi" as a prayer.
O lotus-eyed one, out of a desire for my grace, you should worship me as I truly am in your own home by means of the rites arising from your own lineage. (53)
Together with his partner in the practice of the True Dharma, he should perform the rites on the prepared altar according to the scriptures,
offering sacrificial fuel and other materials for the fires or for the single fire, as his capacity allows.
This must be performed throughout the three periods of time; let your own duty be fully observed. No entry should be granted to those who have committed evil deeds.
One's own sons, daughters, servants, ministers,
and those born of one's own lineage should be consecrated through the Vaiṣṇava rite so that they may become identical with the Blessed Lord.
For a moment, from the time of Brahma until the appearance of the sun,
one should perform the twilight ritual (sandhyā) with bathing, worship, recitation of mantras (japa), hymns of praise, and the study of sacred texts.
Immediately thereafter is the acquisition of the means for sacrifice and enjoyment;
then follows the bath, performed according to the prescribed rule as beneficially ordained.

Then, following the internal sacrifice, one should perform the purification of the elements (ābhūtaśuddhi) in the evening and subsequently carry out the external worship according to the prescribed rule.
Then he should perform the fire-oblation, followed by the rites for the ancestors,
the offering of bali to the spirits, and the honoring of guests.

Immediately after his own sacrifice, accompanied by kinsmen and servants, he performed the private recitation of the Vedas, beginning with the Ṛg and Sāma Vedas, and reflected upon the Itihāsas and other sacred texts. 61.
Then, one should practice meditative concentration within the lotus of one's own heart;
thus is described the daily rite consisting of thirteen limbs, which is identical with the Blessed One.
Indeed, as the night approaches and [the body] is wasting away, one should daily perform this duty with devotion;
furthermore, one should practice renunciation and indeed undertake its formal acceptance once more.
Having thus received this command from the mouth of the preeminent teacher for the sake of householders,
the officiant should indeed depart from that place and perform a circumambulation.
Thus has the ritual procedure for the installation of Brahman been recounted to you;
it should be observed by Vaiṣṇavas and by lords of men for their own spiritual success. 65.
Now, listen to the establishment of our own doctrine:
having constructed a monastery and a temple, provided with a natural means of livelihood and preceded by proper conduct. (66)
It was filled with merchant families and laborers, as well as groups of servants;
and there stood ponds and water-mills situated near the windows.
There, having first bathed together with the preceptor, one should prepare in abundance various kinds of food, including rice accompanied by condiments, snacks, and other edibles. (68)
Having first performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the body with mantras consisting of twelve syllables,
the wise one should worship the Lord of the World, the Supreme Lord, the Infallible One.
Having summoned the Brahmins who had arrived and were masters of the Vedas, [he said]:
"This is that immortal food; this is the life-span bestowed by Prajāpati. (70)
This is Viṣṇu, this is Prāṇa, this is Jīva, and this is the Supreme;
for the sake of the welfare of all beings, the Anuyāga has been established. || 71 ||
O Janārdana, you who consist of food, the source of the world of the five elements;
remain present here until the time of the dissolution of all beings.
One should first invoke the Ṛṅmayas as before; then two other Śrutis known as Sāman;
and the Guru, together with his family, must indeed be requested [for initiation] beforehand.
Furthermore, it must be engaged in and maintained together with the assembly of guests and others by means of a mind that is receptive to my grace. (74)
Then one should satisfy them with food, indeed with food that has been honored;
thereafter, one should purify the remains from the assembled group once they have sat down.
Having circumambulated the assembled group of guests, he should depart;
this is declared to be the establishment of the food for those who perceive the Imperishable.
It is the supreme means of deliverance and likewise the bestower of all happiness.
p.
249) Now, understand this foundation of gnosis, this very foundation of gnosis.
By performing which indeed arises that knowledge accompanied by discernment. || 77 ||
Having collected the five pure collections of scriptures, including the *Sadāgama* and all others, together with the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. (78)

[He taught] those [teachings] endowed with the Smṛtis and other Smṛtis, accompanied by the Itihāsas, and integrated with the sciences of logic (ānvīkṣikī) along with the science known as grammar (śabda). || 79 ||

Having filled various collections of colors with the colors of the *nadīnāgaraka*—[this term refers to the *nadīnāgaraka* colors because it is an adjective qualifying "colors"; it should perhaps be read as *nandināgarakaiḥ*]—and having deposited them into inexhaustible caskets, [he placed them]. (80)
Having tied it with a very firm thread, such as black silk or the like, [one should place it] in a location that is very stable,
well-known, and frequented by kings and citizens.
In that place, inhabited by twice-born men, mixed with various peoples, and protected by a multitude of the virtuous,
there was nearby a stone house equipped with iron engines.
It was provided with doors and bolts, whitewashed and auspicious,
adorned by the Goddess of Speech (Vāgīśvarī) seated upon a lotus and decorated with various ornaments.
With that [hand] raised, holding a conch, discus, mace, and lotus,
she likewise bears a rosary, while her other hand holds a collection of scriptures.
[One should worship] with her who bestows boons and fearlessness, or with Siddhas and others;
then, as before, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), wearing white garments and being pure.
Having placed the books containing the collection of scriptures in due order upon that iron vehicle, which is presided over by the syllable Om and duly honored, (86)
Having worshipped them, anointed them, and covered them with cloths for their eyes, and having performed worship with the twelve-syllable mantra, one should recite this: || 87 ||
To Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, whose body is pure knowledge—to you, who are the essence of the scriptures, may this [image] remain well-established, imperishable, and present here indeed. 88.
For the sake of benefiting the ignorant and for the purpose of generating awakening, the gods and others, being subject to decay, have left you alone, who are thus imperishable. (89)
Having spoken thus, one should worship again the embodiment of the Vedas and Vedāntas,
adorned with the sacred scriptures (Sadāgamas) and the Purāṇas of the Lord.
Every day, with supreme devotion, [one should worship] the seat consisting of the Śabdabrahman before the Vidyāpīṭha, upon the auspicious seat previously described.
O best of the twice-born, one should appoint a vigilant person for the act of worship;
then, having circumambulated and offered incense, one should ask for forgiveness.

In the matter of providing for those in need, he should accumulate there a store of goods; and he should ensure his livelihood is well-provided for, being firmly rooted in the protection of the Teaching. 93.
Having performed that rite, he should entrust [the scriptures] for the preservation of the treasury of knowledge;
thereafter, in that temple, he should cause those who observe the vow of celibacy (brahmacārins) to recite them.
One should oneself recite the two mantras previously mentioned with palms joined in reverence for the sake of people who are blinded by the darkness of ignorance and lack discernment. (95)
From the establishment of the seat of the scriptures, stainless knowledge arises;
and by the great fruit arising from this very [knowledge], Hari [is attained]. 96.
May he attain supreme joy; no fruit of mine is required, for this establishment of the Seat of Knowledge has been perfectly revealed. (97)
For those seeking fruits, devotion to knowledge bestows the desired fruit;
it also grants the liberation of ponds, wells, tanks, and groves.
Indeed, for those seeking fruits, the installation [of an image] preceded by consecration bestows heaven;
but for those who have renounced ritual action, that same act of Viṣṇu grants his own supreme state.
The cause of the worlds, the Lord of all beings, the Sovereign of all, the Infallible One—formless yet consisting of sound, characterized by the nature of both knowledge and action. (100)
Having attained its own true nature, it abides in the world,
having taken recourse to a body composed of that [nature], which is the supreme bliss of truth. (101)
O Mahāmati, for gods, sages, and humans,
she is thus a power consisting of various flavors, having the form of a branch.
What is the female elephant situated in the forest fire? [It is she] who is composed of various manifest sounds, mixed with coral, leaves, flowers, wind, and water. || 103 ||
The first portion of the earth is indeed immobile, known as the "footed" (the ground), which bestows leaves, flowers, and fruits; it is the form of the gods, worthy of being honored. (104)
Then, having taken refuge in another mobile form consisting of a cow,
[he was filled] by those [rays] arising from it, which consisted of the five Upaniṣads.

With the five consecrated mantras, beginning with the Ṛgveda and Sāmaveda verses, together with cow-dung and other substances in their proper order, and accompanied by water infused with *kuśa* grass.
Furthermore, for the sake of purification, one should first sprinkle water around that excavated pit,
and afterwards lead it to a state of sanctity by filling it completely with water.
Or else, O twice-born one, with this water that has reached the earth—now cool, free from salt, and only slightly agitated by my anger—[wash your feet]. 108.
When it is available, [one may use] gold according to the requirements of place and time,
whether it be purchased, obtained from a *tāṭaka*, or extracted from a sprout.
Having gone to the vicinity of cows and Brahmins, he cast a hundred paces or more into the middle of the pit; thus that pit became vast and great.
One who dwells in water for a long time should be made as extensive as desired and accessible from all directions, so that no fixed boundary arises.
One should always make it two bow-lengths in width, while keeping it deep by the same measure, so as to greatly increase the affection of elderly women of noble family.
It may be equal to one and a half bows, or even ending at a single bow;
starting from two bows up to indeed a hundred bows.
Once the width of the excavation has been determined, thereafter, according to your [requirements], there shall be the earthen, the airy, the lunar, and the fiery [elements]. (114)
Having made it square and elongated, endowed with auspicious characteristics,
and adorned with a multitude of pathways according to the requirements of the site, || 115 ||
It was endowed with trees, creepers, and groves, adorned with grassy plots, provided with resting places for travelers, and likewise furnished with pavilions for repose. || 116 ||

Having acted thus according to the instructions, and having determined and maintained [the proportions] upon that ground where the body of the cow is situated, she should effect the reduction of the excavation.
They satisfy that water until the conclusion of the ritual proceedings;
having thus consecrated it, he then gazes toward the eastern direction.
The officiant, standing on the western side together with the Brahmins, [should perform the rite] now with water drawn from that [well], or otherwise with other [water]. (119)
At that time, one should smear the ground with clay mixed with cow dung,
using the twelve-syllable Gāyatrī, the Sāman, or the Vāsudeva mantra.
And having stationed, in due order, those who recite the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda in the eastern, southern, and northern directions respectively for the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa).

On dry land, in pools belonging to children, or in very beautiful ponds, [one should perform the rite] with the twelve-syllable mantra or with one's own [mantra] for which the ritual placement (nyāsa) has been performed. || 122 ||
Having taken a single lump of clay from the middle of the excavation,
he should place it upon a seat provided with silk and flowers.
Above that, however, is a golden-bellied jar filled with water,
properly wrapped in cloth and smeared with saffron and other unguents.
One should place a garland of flowers, flower-clusters, dūrvā grass, darbha grass, seeds, fruits, and water; as well as a white sacred thread, a bright eye-ointment, and one who wears a turban.

One should meditate upon the pervasive Lord Acyuta with the syllable of Earth (la), which is void yet endowed with life, accompanied by the nasal bindu, and joined with his name and the nectar (amṛta). 126.
One should meditate upon Nārāyaṇa as the supreme form arising from the sweet sound; at the end of these three seed-syllables, the lotus should be employed.
"O Blessed One, salutations then to Nārāyaṇa, the self of all beings.
The installation preceded by ritual bathing should be performed according to the prescribed rule. (128)
Having performed the sacrificial rite ending with the *pūrṇāhuti* by means of the twelve-syllable mantra, or indeed the eight-syllable or six-syllable mantra. (129)
Having honored, according to his ability, the best of the twice-born beginning with his guru,
he then took a full pitcher filled with water from a pond.
The performer should first place a lump of clay inside the mouth of the lotus;
then, having poured water from the jar, he should utter this mantra: || 131 ||
O formless Lord, O Protector Vāsudeva, whose nature is nectar, remain well-established for as long as the moon and stars endure. 132.
O Lord, grant immediate protection to me and my followers;
may the gods, the ancestors, along with the Sādhyas and all beings, be forever nourished.
May you attain supreme joy through this fruit produced here;
may there be satisfaction for all beings dwelling within the belly of the three worlds.

Having spoken thus, he should cause those best of Brahmins who are knowers of the Sāman to chant the Sāman beginning with "dhruva ā dyauḥ" and then the Ṛk verses, followed by the Sāman beginning with "pratiṣṭhāsi. (135)
Afterwards, with various kinds of offerings,
he should satisfy all the brāhmaṇas and all those who performed the excavation, along with water.
Having propitiated the guides with gifts when one possesses wealth, as well as the poor, the helpless, and one's servants, for the sake of attaining infinite fruit. (137)
One should perform the gift of gold and land according to one's capacity, as well as the gift of a maiden and the release of a bull, preceded by the ancestral śrāddha rites. (138)
The fault arising from execution or imprisonment, as well as that arising from fines and penalties, must be investigated by petitioning the lord of men on behalf of the people. (139)
However, this alternative piercing is prescribed when possible:
[one should pierce] either a tree that bears the primary fruit or an Ashvattha branch. 140.
Having established the grove, having performed the rites of consecration and bathing,
having anointed it and adorned it well, he brings [the image] forward according to the prescribed rule.
Having wrapped it in a cloth and adorned it with a garland of flowers,
one should perform everything up to the end of the fire-oblation (homa) as before, accompanied by the mantras.
By that means, the agent goes to the further shore, the opposite bank of the ocean of saṃsāra.

The foundation of fruits, roots, food, and so forth is the foundation of fruits, roots, and food; listen, for I shall speak of it for those who seek its fruit. In the three worlds, no gift is found superior to the gift of food. (143)
It is proclaimed that the taste of food provides immediate gratification, is pleasing to the heart, and even bestows life upon living beings, both at its production and during its preparation. (144)
From food beings arise; therefore everything is established in it.
And that [food] is established by means of which [the Self]; therefore everything is established in That. || 145 ||
Together with his own self, he shall dwell in this world, in the heavenly realm known as Brahmaloka,
for as long as he lives, free from disease and devoid of suffering.
Through sons, wives, wealth, and food, he attains increase moment by moment;
he receives supreme honor from the most excellent, even greater than before. (147)
The deities, sages, and perfected beings constantly contemplate for him supreme increase in lifespan as well as exaltation.
Then, having become joyful and nourished, he is forever satisfied;
after enjoying vast pleasures, he finally reaches the abode of Nārāyaṇa.
He travels in celestial chariots resembling the moon, fashioned by the gods;
having remained in all the worlds, beginning with heaven, for many hundreds of kalpas.
Furthermore, in due course of time, he returns here to this most excellent and auspicious land;
having attained birth in a family of the virtuous, he achieves a great and supreme state of being.
He is born handsome, eloquent, and devoted to learning and wisdom; he is always honored by all, even his enemies, and is ever beloved. (152)
Virtuous, endowed with heroism, possessed of fortitude and energy, always devoted to the twice-born and the gods, he is a donor intent on the welfare of all beings. || 153 ||
Devoted exclusively to the Dharma, indeed a knower of the Dharma, and solely intent upon Nārāyaṇa, he enjoyed the entire threefold aim of life according to his desired characteristics. || 154 ||
Having performed auspicious karma practiced throughout many births, which yields infinite merit, one attains knowledge by means of which one proceeds to the supreme state. || 155 ||
Indeed, there is no worship of wells, ponds, or fragrant flowers;
for one should bestow pure [offerings], as that constitutes identity with the deity, and perform every prescribed rite accordingly.
And having brought the herd of cows into the state of being limbs within this abode of the Blessed One,
through the fire-sacrifice to the All-pervading Lord preceded by bathing and enjoyment— 157.
For the sake of pleasing the cows, however, the teaching should be imparted;
that fire, accompanied by a herd of cows and provided with lamps of ghee. (158)
It must be protected like a deity as long as the moon and stars exist,
and it shall dwell there perpetually, blazing with light, together with its laborers.

Having prepared an auspicious sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) at home according to the divine Vaiṣṇava rites during the meritorious period beginning with the Ṣaḍaśītimukha, [one should perform the rite]. || 160 ||
Or even when the collection of Dharma was formerly established by himself,
with auspicious Vaiṣṇava hymns and the twelve-syllable mantra and others.
Once the rite for pacification has been performed, the Hotṛ priest should likewise recite slowly the thousands of Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman verses that praise the God of gods.

Having consecrated the fire and the sacrificial pit with ghee and other offerings, with unbroken grains, and with yellow, white, and black sesame seeds, according to the rite dedicated to Prajāpati; || 163 ||
One should offer oblations beginning with a thousand and ending with ten thousand,
or beginning with a hundred and ending with a thousand, using a ladle made of copper.
Then one should offer clarified butter with an eighth part of the *pālīya* measure;
whether free from desire or possessed of desire, one should then offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
But Nārāyaṇa, the soul of the Vedas, through the mouth of the Vedas,
indeed grants all desired objects by means of the ultimate method.
When this has been performed, one should bind [the vessel] above the horns from whatever materials have been prepared;
and for seven nights, or alternatively for three auspicious nights, one should perform the *vasudhārā* rite.
Now, the procedure for performing it for a single day according to one's own capacity is described:
in a smokeless, wide sacrificial pit, using firm pieces of wood fit for sacrifice, (168)
Having made the fire-altar on the ground of the girdle (mekhalā) higher than a palanquin,
or else two bow-lengths high, one should spread a copper plate above that.
A cauldron should be placed upon a firm wooden ring with four sturdy bamboo legs, capable of supporting its weight.
Then, it should be raised by four finger-breadths measured by the span;
one should take a golden rod made from a measure of gold, uniform throughout.
One should perform the piercing with iron in a medium-sized crucible equipped with the proper measurements; then, having covered it with cloth, one should extract [the substance]. || 172 ||
Having poured into a cauldron ghee that was free from impurities, fragrant, possessing auspicious characteristics, and fit for oblation,
he exerted himself until it was completely exhausted.
Starting from what has been said thus far, [he spoke of] the flowing time of day and night, which is remembered as threefold, and the divine Self who is beyond the senses. (174)
Or else, until dawn today, he shall seize the watch that has been held,
or perhaps two watches, or even three watches.
Or there may be four *praharas*, depending on one's own capacity;
for it begins at a measure of six *prasthas* and indeed ends at four *prasthas*. (176)
One should draw forth the flow according to one's capacity, or a *pālika* measure of clarified butter;
