having strewn it with the [mantras] rich in the adhibhūta and adhideva, one should contemplate the clarified butter as the adhyātma.

The purifier, the nectar, the Brahman, and the clarified butter are indeed the supreme Self (adhyātma); the fire is the deity (adhideva), and the herd of cows is the elemental substrate (adhibhūta). (178)
For it is said that I alone am the wealth, assuming my own essential form;
thus, by means of its extent and as a ritual injunction, it proceeds.
By whose power this entire world is indeed rendered destitute,
having placed a cauldron upon a wide-open vessel.
And the Blessed One, Puruṣottama, is to be worshipped as a deity;
now, with offerings of water for the feet, flowers, and so forth, within a vessel filled with wealth.
He himself remains a bestower of grace upon faithful men, from the very commencement until the completion of their auspicious deeds. (182)
Having worshipped and paid homage to Acyuta with the twelve-syllable mantra,
one should then offer unguents, as well as flower garlands and incense.
He offered a great oblation of food, including honey-mixture (madhuparka) and various edibles along with fruits;
then, with devotion, he [worshipped] the Lord of All, the omnipresent one, stationed within the temple.
Having performed the rite preceded by bathing with great magnificence,
he worshipped according to the rules with excellent and authentic hymns.
Preceded by the secret mantras consisting of eight and twelve syllables,
one should touch the ground with both knees and remain with the head bowed before him.
Having first established this for the sake of singular security, one should recite:
"O supreme wealth, you are ghee; you have completely filled everything. (187)
This supreme power, Tāreya, is indeed worshipped as the Lord himself;
by [offering] garments and so forth, one obtains a fruit equal to that of the Agni sacrifice.
Having completed that village, which was situated within his domain and endowed with a very large herd of cattle, by means of an edict issued to the Brahmins who were its guardians; 189.
In such a way that his great fame and supreme righteousness are not cut short,
so must this be performed by the king for the increase of his glory and merit.
That which exceeds sixfold and so forth, as well as the three auspicious things proclaimed—
namely, the cow-pen, fire, and the lamp— these are the limbs within the sanctuaries.
And it must be protected by those who know the Dharma so that there may be no interruption;
for through the mouth of the Fire alone, [the offerings reach] thirty-three crores [of deities]. (192)
And every day they attain incomparable satisfaction for the gods with various products derived from cows, beginning with curd, milk, and clarified butter. (193)
The Blessed One attains delight through offerings that are characterized by purity;
like the supreme sun, he illuminates everything with his splendor.
And by the power of the lamp that is always present,
he who, presiding over the Lord of the World, [recites] during the sixty-six [auspicious] occasions— || 195 ||
On the lunar days, the Blessed One is to be worshipped in the water-pot, the mandala, and the fire;
[the worshipper], having fasted, being pure, bathed, and having performed the auspicious marriage-thread ceremony, [should perform the rite].
With devotion, by means of this mantra beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*, may the Lord of Gods, Vṛṣākapi, the presiding authority over dharma, be pleased with me. (197)
He is the benefactor of cattle, the lord of cattle, the protector, and he stands encompassing everything.
Therefore, on a smeared portion of ground, why is there only a *kutapa* [woolen blanket]? || 198 ||
Having spread out a pure, unworn, and large cloth, together with sesame seeds and unbroken grains (akṣata), all kinds of seeds, kuśa grass, and white mustard seeds; || 199 ||
Outside of that, one should offer the full oblation starting from the east in sequence;
[one should prepare] eight vessels with milk, rice, sesame seeds, curd, unbroken grains, juice, and sesame.
With clarified butter, all types of seeds, and cloths, there should be a curtain outside;
along with arrows, threads, peacock feathers, and well-prepared seats.
There were also bowls containing sown seeds placed upon the mouths of full jars, as well as branches laden with fruit, adorned with the branches of trees. || 202 ||
Having placed [the vessel] in the directions along with lamps blazing with the Rigveda and other [Vedas],
he then brings it down into the center of that mandala prepared by Surabhi.
Adorned with ornaments and cloth, decorated with bells and chowries, possessing gems, gold, and white lotuses, and embellished by its horns. || 204 ||
(254) His beloved has a tail of pearls and coral, silver feet,
a mirror upon his forehead, and is endowed with great splendor through her beautiful garlands and crown. 205.
In this very manner, O Vīryadhvaja, you shall see Surabhi, adorned with ornaments,
standing in the prime of youth and unassailable, on the left side of the bull.
[One should give] a cow equipped with a bronze milking vessel, consecrated on the previous day, and accompanied by the four cows named Nandā, Sunandā, Surabhi, and Śītalā. (207)
Four milch-cows should be stationed there facing [the deity] in the east and other directions;
they should be endowed with great power and wealth, capable of yielding milk, and auspicious.
Now, indeed, with reference to the directions and to one's chosen deity, [one should offer] cows that are pregnant, those with calves, and those that have recently calved, each one by one. (209)
One should also apply his own sandalwood paste along with the earth from the field of Vṛṣṇi; however, if these are unavailable, one may indeed use other materials.
One should provide assistance according to one's ability, but its price must not be calculated;
having established the four Agnihotra fires, they should be maintained outside [the village]. 211.
Provided with clothing and ornaments, along with fragrant incense and its value,
as well as land for the sake of wealth, or whatever implements belong to the bull.
Having prostrated with devotion to the Guru, one should release the bull and Surabhi at the right shoulder region, using the weapon as desired.
It should be sealed in an instant with iron heated by fire;
having performed the renunciation of the bull in this manner, specifically for that purpose, once again— || 214 ||
One should give abundant gifts of food, accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā),
whether for one's own sake or for the sake of another, dedicated to the Lord of Mantras.
Indeed, he who performs the rite of releasing a bull goes to the world of Brahmā;
for the bull is the Lord Dharma himself, who in this world binds together desire and worldly prosperity.
By that which has been renounced, the eternal suffering of birth is indeed completely abandoned;
for Prakṛti, along with its eternal fragrance, is truly perishable.
And due to its particularization, there are three powers whose nature is passion (madanātmikā):
the first is the intellect (buddhi) with the thought "I am," and the next is the five sense organs. || 218 ||
All those who abide by relying on the spiritual lineage (gotra) turn back from [samsaric existence], together with the establishment in various dharmas through the release of the bull. 219.
It has been spoken; now, O one born from the lotus, take to heart that divine [teaching] which bestows liberation and has been indicated again and again. (220)
O lotus-eyed one, the installation of Acyuta bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Establishment of Various Dharmas," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, a Mahopaniṣad of the glorious Pāñcarātra.
(Total number of verses: 221) Now begins the forty-second chapter. The Blessed One said:
In ancient times, the Lord of All, at the commencement of all undertakings preceded by the acquisition of the earth,
[was worshipped] with mantras beginning with the twelve syllables.

The Blessed One should be propitiated with devotion on an altar, or upon a water-pot, or on the ground; having gratified Him with devotion through oblations of clarified butter and other offerings, accompanied by mantras consisting of the Vedas.
The Blessed One, whose self is Viśvakarman, should cause Gaṇeśa to be worshipped with various services,
such as flowers, incense, and ointments.
O Lotus-born One, when Viṣṇu has been dismissed along with the fire,
those artisans who are skillful therein are to be honored immediately thereafter.
And with minds ever purified by serene faith, they constantly perform these rites;
by them, being self-restrained and bathed, their own husband should be gratified with libations.
Therefore, O twice-born one, you should accept a field that is desired by you—
whether it be uncultivated or cultivated— and characterized by the virtues of the earth.
Having taken up [the site] which is free from thorns, favorable, approved by architects,
and as extensive as desired for the purpose of consecration, || 7 ||
Mahendra, the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa), Vāyu, and Vittapa (Kubera) shall likewise occupy their stations in the directions of Īśāna and so forth,
having established themselves in divine abodes and the like.
But first, there is a great and auspicious temple of the gods with five shrines;
from the path of one's own self that leads to accomplishment it is attained, but from the wrong path it leads to non-attainment.

This much has been stated regarding those who are liberated from their desires; however, for others, it results in fault, even though Hari is omnipresent within both their own path and the supreme path.
While that [insight] flashes incessantly in the intellect, one should, by means of the scriptures, oneself [recognize] that Guru;
then, on an auspicious and favorable lunar mansion, having paid homage to the omnipresent Lord Acyuta, || 11 ||
O twice-born one, having first warded off all obstacles eternally,
he should perform the worship together with others who follow the Ekāyana path and those who recite the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
They were adorned with ornaments, wearing turbans and white garments,
anointed with unguents, garlanded, decorated, and wearing finger-rings.
With the sounding of conch shells and musical instruments, with auspicious songs, and with hands holding fruits, flowers, unbroken grains of rice, nets, white mustard seeds, and so forth; (14)
O twice-born one, having undertaken the rite with purity and accompanied by the preceptor, the performer should reach the site for all [the rites] while remembering Vāsudeva in his heart. (15)
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), and having recited the three *gāyatrīs* and so forth, as well as the *Śākuna Sūkta* and the *Śivasaṃkalpa*, || 16 ||
Accompanied by the Śrīsūkta and the excellent Bhadraśrīsāman,
one should indeed recite "Svasti bhoḥ" along with the commencement of the ritual action.
Then, having recited the six *camasas*, and immediately thereafter the [mantras] beginning with *śānti*,
the officiant, standing while muttering the eight-syllabled mantra, shall then become your preceptor (*deśika*).
O Lotus-born One, having constructed outside the sacrificial field, either in the northeast or in the east,
a beautiful leaf-hut that is capable of withstanding wind and rain, (verse 19)

There, having prepared flowers, water for honor, incense, and so forth, one should indeed proceed to the auspicious pedestal after having prepared the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) together with various mantras.
Having brought the image of Nārāyaṇa into proximity within an auspicious golden vessel filled with water from river-tīrthas, he worshipped it.

Having completed the arrangement with golden vessels filled with all the [substances], accompanied by a bundle of *darbha* grass and a garland, and having performed the rite with the two jars of the mantra and the weapon (*astra*), the supreme [practitioner] proceeds. || 22 ||
Having understood that the common seat belongs to those two, one should perform its worship;
having worshipped the Lord of Mantras together with his weapon in the heart according to the rule. (23)
It should be placed upon the golden seat together with the vital breath and the mind;
then, by way of the lunar channel, the King of Mantras, the *Hrdayamantra*, [should be established].
Then, having caused the blazing form of the Lord— which burns away the multitude of obstacles— to descend by the southern path into the vessel placed on the left, [one should proceed].
O twice-born one, the triad of mantras is prescribed as common everywhere:
that which consists of six syllables, eight syllables, and likewise twelve syllables.
That thousand-spoked weapon, Hetīśa,
which has been obtained from a highly gracious guru by one who has undergone initiation, is to be thoroughly understood as a divine armament.
Having brought this auspicious and distinguished weapon, together with its ancillaries (aṅgas),
into his body, and having worshipped it along with its ancillaries using enjoyments ending with the sacrificial portions (mātrās), [he should proceed].
Then, with the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman hymns characterized by their appropriate occasions,
which reveal the Lord of All, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa).

The preceptor should thus perform [the rite] with a thousand or a hundred measures of sesame seeds, complete with unbroken rice grains, purified by the mantras of the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) and the weapon (astra).
Having first established four attendants of his own, who are experts in mantra and adorned with ornaments, upon pillars made of sand and other materials in the east and the other directions; || 31 ||
Those four [Vedas] beginning with the Ṛgveda, which extend from Īśa to Vāyupatha,
are to be worshipped with devotion by those intent on ritual action for the purpose of oblations during the collection of the sacred field.
One should offer abundant clarified butter and other substances with those mantras that do not contain the *amiliṅga*,
using the four mantras pertaining to the fourfold self, preceded by the twelve syllables.
The other brahmins, remembering Hari, the Lord of All,
should offer oblations while he stands as the supervisor in the fourth corner, having assigned one [brahmin] to each [corner].
For the sake of the fire-oblation in all the sacrificial pits, [they should be] those who have invested their bodies with the mantras,
who are pure, self-controlled, skillful, and who have exerted themselves in the science of architecture (vāstu-śāstra).
Having summoned those born of the lineage of Viśvakarman and seated them in front,
he should sprinkle them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances, while they are indeed clad in white garments.
Having observed those whose fingers and other limbs were adorned with garlands, sandalwood paste, and turbans,
and having purified them, he took them along with the water-pot.
One should place a very firm cotton thread, consecrated with the Sahasrāra mantra,
into the hands of the architects along with a single measuring rod.
Having sprinkled them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and consecrated them a thousand times with mantras,
he scattered seeds mixed with parched grain and accompanied by white mustard.
While reciting the Astra-mantra, one should perform three circumambulations clockwise around the discus,
from the first step back to that same spot, accompanied by the auspicious sounds of the bell.

Then, having taken the measurement of the site according to the desired cubits, by means of the portions belonging to the disciple, the preceptor, and the agent, or else by the portions of Viśvakarman; || 41 ||
Having extended that thread from the northeast corner and so forth toward the four directions,
one should mark the eight directions with stakes made of sacrificial wood.
Then, the wise one should offer the *bhūtabali* in a clockwise direction,
consisting of sesame flour, powder of turmeric, parched rice, curd, and barley meal.
It is declared as "bhūtakrūra"; with that, one should offer the bali-oblation to the spirits (bhūtas).
Whatever beings or even Rākṣasas dwell here— || 44 ||
May all those [obstacles] depart today; I shall prepare this place for Hari, having woven together trees with arrows, cane-sticks, creepers, bundles of hides, and other materials. (45)
[He should take] spades known as *kuddāla*, which are shaped like the upper part of a drum (*mṛdaṅga*), capable of holding white clay, not too heavy, and not sharp. (46)
Standing upon the sacred site (kṣetra) at the Brahma-pada, facing whichever direction one desires, one should worship the very firm elephant-footprints arising from the sacrificial wood. 47.
Having recollected [the mantra] with its twelve syllables, the Blessed One, the creator of beings,
should meditate upon that which is characterized by the adhyātma, known as the adhibhūta and the adhideva.
Therein, [he visualizes] the earth consisting of the seven continents, together with the oceans and so forth,
along with the seven netherworlds, and endowed with the elements beginning with the moving [beings]. (49)
She is completely surrounded by all powers residing in the Word,
together with the letter *la*, which is joined with the seed-syllable of Brahman and the nasal bindu.
Having first honored [the deity] with one's own mental conception,
and having meditated upon the state of the adhibhūta, one should thereafter recollect the ādhidaiva.
The power of the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the sovereign of all,
is the supreme form of the inner self, the great Vārāha manifestation belonging to Viṣṇu.
This much has been stated regarding meditation in general for the acquisition of land;
one should also recall here the specific [meditation] according to the nature of the temple site.
Having meditated upon the manifestation of the fourfold form within the square [mandala],
one should contemplate the divine, elongated square known as the Vidyāgama.
One should meditate on the wheel whose spokes have ceased and arisen, with its parts fully enclosed;
one should contemplate the Lord reclining upon Ananta within that circular and elongated abode.
The pure city of eight constituents (puryaṣṭaka), which bears the body of the lotus of time,
arose from the navel-cavity of Viṣṇu and abides as the essence of the eight directions.
In the temple, one should meditate upon the earthly abode as having eight corners;
having thus contemplated it repeatedly with the twelve-syllable mantra.
Having restrained [the breath] with the six-syllabled mantra and having bound the mudrā for the twice-born Acyuta,
he remains in meditative absorption and concentration until the presence of the water-pot.
Then, as before, one should worship with extraordinary enjoyments using the eight-syllable mantra;
together with the Brahmins, he himself should again offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) into the fire.
For the sake of completing all rites, once the site has been consecrated as a sacred field,
one should indeed perform the installation of the feet on another, most auspicious day.
Then, skillful laborers should be appointed in due order;
indeed, by satisfying them with food, drink, and other necessities, they will attain contentment. (61)
The Blessed One said:
When a portion of the earth has been thus acquired and cleared of thorns,
and when it is accessible, free from pebbles, young, pure, and rich in wealth, it is a gift of land endowed with treasures.
Did you perhaps seek some artificial purity by abandoning that grove, which was filled with great trees long established there? (63)
It was crowded and pervaded by its incessant roots produced from that [tree];
yet it was known that even this was in a state of infancy, for its purity was destined to come to pass.
Cities, villages, and regions are not abandoned by the currents of rivers,
because they repeatedly shatter their hopes while seeking great purity.
Having bathed and indeed having cast away all worldly attachment,
one approaches the auspicious, white, sugarless, and smooth [state], or [one should bury it] at the edge of the water.
Having seen the water and worshipped it, one should offer libations to the Lord of Aquatic Creatures (Varuṇa),
who is accompanied by the lords of the Nāgas and surrounded by hosts of gods standing nearby.
For the sake of stability, it is filled with all kinds of stones and earth; and having been filled with both earth and stones, it is then smeared with that glossy [mud] for the various castes.
Having repeatedly pounded [the ground] with water poured from a jar, one should level it, smear it, and then settle the herd of cows there. || 69 ||
It was filled with young calves together with herds of lordly bulls,
possessed of watered rice fields, and abundant stores of grass.
Having scattered sesame seeds there and cleared away the cow-dung and other debris, he should afterwards drive away the herd of cows and smear the ground once more. (71)
Having worshipped [the deity], one whose nature is the Sun should perform the accomplishment of the directions as before;
O Lotus-born One, [he should worship] the temple together with the form of the Blessed Lord. (72)
Having first determined the direction facing one's preference,
one should then construct the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa) on that plot of ground.
If that is not obtained in the three directions, then [the site] should extend toward the north or south,
for the sake of suitability, purity, comfort, and freedom from obstacles.
It should be covered with *śara* grass, *kāśa* grass, reeds, or *kūrca* grass, or even by other materials, without being cut.
There, five royal seats are prescribed with intervals between them.
Then, it may be seven, six, or five cubits according to one's means;
or indeed four cubits, or even four and a half cubits.
O best of Brahmins, having excluded all the intermediate spaces by means of one-sixth of their respective extensive dimensions, one should then proceed with their height.
O Mahāmati, one should adorn all the corner pillars with their own respective twenty-fourth part of the width and height.
Having erected them according to that measurement upon the tops of the pillars,
other rods, arranged in a decorative pattern, are extended crosswise.
All [the gateways] arise from the large lotus and are provided with arches (toraṇa) on the four directions;
the width of the arches shall indeed be one-third of the pedestal (pīṭha).
The height of all [the deities] is prescribed as three parts of their respective width; all of them, including Cakra and Garuḍa, are [measured] by a count of three, four, or five [parts]. 81.

All the arches, together with their pillars, should be set upon the ground according to the measurement of the intervals between them, ensuring that they all possess excellent auspicious characteristics.
Furthermore, O twice-born one, the regions are square, while those in the middle are octagonal;
the upper portions are circular, all divided into equal parts. || 83 ||
The eastern and western portions of the street are equal to both pedestals;
each of the southern and northern sections is the extent of one pedestal.
Having thus completed the sacrificial pavilion for the Lord through every ritual action,
one should construct an altar marked with a lotus above the northern seat.
It should be circular or square, well-proportioned, and known as "illuminated" (prakāśa), possessing auspicious characteristics;
its ground should be adorned with a girdle and marked with the symbols of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
For the purpose of consecrating the ritual substances,
one should perform the worship of the mantra, the weapon, and the water-pot upon the central seat within the mandala on the ground situated near them.
A set of four bathing jars containing medicinal herbs should be placed in the chamber;
elsewhere, one should place the bed upon that very bathing pedestal.
Know that the fifth pedestal, provided with the materials for bathing, should be well-honored with sand and placed near the bathing pitcher. (89)
Having thus prepared the great circular enclosure with its gates, windows, doors, and bolts for the purpose of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), || 90 ||
Having abandoned the measurement of the temple site situated all around it,
one should draw an eightfold sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the cardinal directions, complete with its boundary line (mekhalā) and pedestal (pīṭha).
In the alternative procedure (anukalpa), however, one should indeed construct [the pavilions] outside the eastern circle, or in the western part;
they should have a single pedestal and be provided with archways (toraṇa).
Or they may have six pillars, each with its own separate pedestal, and be distinct from one another;
on the eastern side is the one called Cakrapadma, and on the southern side is Kevaleśvarī.
Or, O Lotus-born One, it may be fashioned as a square with a gada for its girdle;
a lotus in the northern quarter and a conch in each of the four corners. (94)
O Brahman, this is recorded as the arrangement of the sacrificial pits for the installation rite of deities such as the Cāturātmya in the consecration of the pedestal.
Listen to the arrangement of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in various directions and intermediate points, for the increase of great prosperity, good fortune, longevity, and health. 96.
Know that for the accomplishment of all rites and the removal of obstacles, there is a reversal of results; however, for liberation, it is equanimity.
O Brahmin, it is endowed with two pairs of maces in the eastern direction and the fourth [northeastern] quarter; the discus is in the southern direction, and the conch is in the western direction.
In the northern direction, there is a lotus with petals as desired; having prepared the southeast fire-pit in the shape of an aśvattha leaf. (99)
One should make a triangle with its apex pointing east, a circle as before,
and for the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa), an eight-sided pit (kuṇḍa) in the northwestern direction, at the station of Vāyu.
Having first drawn the seat known as Śrīvatsa, characterized by a crescent moon as described before,
one should mark it with the appropriate signs in the northeast.
Therefore, attend with one-pointed concentration to another arrangement:
in the eastern quarter, there is a station situated in the shape of a Kaustubha gem in the south-eastern direction.

The discus is in the southern direction, while that in the north-western direction has the shape of a Śārṅga bow; the one in the western direction has the form of a mace as before, and the one called Mālā is in the position of Vāyu.
The form of the northern direction is that of a lotus, and the form of the Lord (Īśa) is that of the Śrīvatsa;
indeed, for all [of these], the measurement is prescribed as being equal to their width.
As before, having rubbed down the half of the lip to one-twelfth [of its width],
one should fashion the binding of the girdle so that it is perfectly level and equal in extent to its own width.
O twice-born one, all [the lines] including the girdle are indeed uneven, as previously stated;
the yoni should be fashioned according to the prescribed characteristics, resembling a leaf of the Pippala tree.
In the middle of the area, one should draw a well-rounded fourth [line] marked with the Śrīvatsa;
this is on the ground of the temple site, or rather, that very same [line] is outside in the northeast quarter.
O high-minded one, having performed the libation for all rites accompanied by honorific offerings, as well as for the deities who are the limbs of the site and for the world-protectors; 108.
O Lotus-born One, the temple for the sacrifice, along with its sacrificial pit, should be constructed in this manner for Vighneśa, the door-keepers, Kṣetreśa, and likewise for the Earth.
Then, both from within and from without, one should adorn the *ūrja* with various beautiful banners and those multitudes of lovely *vaijayantī* flags.
With lofty plantain-like tree trunks that were pure and firm, with clothed vessels full of water, and indeed with clusters of flowers and blossoms; || 111 ||
Indeed, without a fire-house, there are various kinds of canopies;
with arrows having peacock feathers, and with threads representing the presiding deities of the elements.

[He was honored] by the world-protectors and others who had arrived beforehand, by the doorkeepers, by the pavilions on the ground of the sacred field, by mirrors, by variegated fly-whisks, and by clusters of bells resonant with sound. || 113 ||
With bronze vessels completely filled with honey, clarified butter, curd, and milk, and with clusters of green *pālikā* containers placed upon the mouths of the jars; || 114 ||
With vessels of śāli rice accompanied by gold and filled with fruits, along with parched grain, white mustard seeds, and seed-vessels provided with the six flavors; || 115 ||
Then, with fragrant substances such as cinnamon and cardamom, with vessels and betel nuts, and with madhūka, jujube, lac, sugarcane, and the three myrobalans; || 116 ||
Just as with the many flowers produced by them that form various clusters,
so too with various such multitudes of purifying enjoyments. (117)
The ritual grounds (bhūmis), however, are outside the pedestal and surround it on all sides;
having brought all the abundant materials accumulated there into that place, [one should proceed]. || 118 ||
Then, when the planet is auspicious and the lunar mansion is favorable and stable,
and when the ascendant is fixed, situated in a fixed division, completely pure, and endowed with excellent qualities.

For the purpose of establishing the foundation of the temple’s base, the patron, who is indeed composed of the Lord, having performed the *āhuti* oblations together with the foremost of the twice-born and accompanied by the preceptor, [proceeds]. (120)
Accompanied by the sounds of kettledrums, tabors, musical instruments, conchs, and the like,
he should recite the excellent Vedic hymns, beginning with the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
Having performed the worship of the gatekeepers and entered the sacrificial hall,
one should remember the pervasive presence [of the deity] in one's own seat, perform worship, and sit down.
Near the central pedestal, on the western foot, one should place [the image] facing east;
and on the eastern side, facing west, one should join them upon earthen seats.
One should employ the Yajurvedins at the northern and southern directional instruments; and having stationed those who know the Sāmaveda facing east in the western part.
And together with the brahmins of the Ekāyana school, who were characterized by the designation "Mūrti," he [then] [established] those devoted to their daily rites in the northern direction.
Then, having established the portions of the Atharvaveda in pairs,
he remained with his excellent assistants behind him, awaiting perfect knowledge.
And the instructor of the mantras, during the worship of the twice-born and others,
should place him to his own right, single-minded and composed.
Then, having mentally grasped the power of the deity who presides over the mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the twelve-syllable form.
Then, with the previously mentioned eight-syllable mantras consisting of Vedic verses,
one should first offer water for the feet (pādya) using a golden pitcher (bhṛṅgāraka) according to the ritual procedure previously described.

Having prepared water for the feet and the arghya offering, as well as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and having honored the twice-born with unguents, flowers, and so forth, along with garments and ornaments for the fingers.
Having fumigated [the area] in due order with purifying materials rich in gold,
the master builder, being diligent and accompanied by assistants, should cause [the image] to be seated.
Then, having granted the command of Māna, he established [the images] made of gold, silver, or even new copper upon the field of action.
O Lotus-born One, in the secondary ritual (anukalpa), one may use earthen jars made of stone or clay;
among them, the central jar should measure twenty-four finger-breadths.
It is broad in the middle and rises two finger-breadths at each [side];
the face is six finger-breadths [in length], and its mouth is traditionally held to be three finger-breadths.
O Lotus-born One, it should be known that above the girdle, the height is three finger-breadths;
and those lotuses of the directions are equal [in width] when raised by half of this amount.
Having filled [the vessels] with various fruits and indeed with earth,
and having pounded them together with strong wood of the *khadira* tree, they were gathered in water.
Having dug a pit for the sake of filling it completely,
and having leveled and smeared it, the practitioner should then perform the accomplishment of the directions as previously described.
One should adorn it with various banners and hoist victory standards;
one should beautify it with sturdy, purifying tree parts, such as plantain stems and the like.
With garments, full jars, flowers, silken cloths, and clusters of blossoms;
when the planet is auspicious, the lunar mansion favorable, and the aspect is propitious—139.

When the ascendant is fixed, situated in a fixed degree, completely pure, and endowed with auspicious qualities, the builder, indeed absorbed in the Divine (Bhagavanmaya), proceeds for the purpose of constructing the base of the temple. (140)

Having performed his daily rites, accompanied by the foremost of the twice-born and the Preceptor, [he proceeds] amidst auspicious sounds such as the beating of kettledrums, tabors, and other musical instruments. (141)
(261) While auspicious hymns are being sung by groups of bards,
he should cause the praised Vedas— beginning with the Sāman, Ṛg, and Yajus— to be recited. 142.

Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the form of the twelve-syllable mantra, he should enter the ground prepared by the earth itself, which has been fashioned from the accumulated provisions.

Then, having prepared water for the feet, the arghya offering, and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) together with the mantras beginning with the eight-syllabled one and those consisting of the Vedas, he should worship the most excellent of the twice-born.
The master builder (sthapati), with offerings of water for honor (arghya), flowers, and other items, should proceed with the auspicious rite;
he should cause each twice-born man to recite the Gāyatrī preceded by the syllable Oṃ.
Having first recited the Gāyatrī Sāman and then the Kanikranda,
one should likewise perform the commencement of the ritual immediately following with the syllable Oṃ.
Thereafter, one who knows the Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda should recite the Ekāyana, the Śivasaṃkalpa, the Bhadra, and the Naṃ-samudīrya. (147)
Bhadraśrīsāmasāmajña, who knows the duties of a hundred [others] and understands the dharma of what is to be done,
having divided the field as before and now purified it— 148.
With all the purifying Vedic mantras and those of the Pāñcarātra,
he should place the girl in the northern direction or in the northeast within the enclosure.
Having constructed a square maṇḍala on a level earthen pedestal, it should be inauspicious [in form], "Sarvatobhadra" [in name], and provided with two houses for subjugation (vaśya). || 150 ||
Having placed him upon a noble seat and having adorned two water-pitchers with garlands and other ornaments, one should perform the ritual practice (*sādhana*) in one of them.
With the twelve-syllable mantra and with the principal mantras declared in the Vedas, the Blessed One, Puruṣottama, [was invoked] into that supreme vessel for the weapon.
Having reached the front of the pavilion with the mantras and the weapons and liṅgas arising from the four Vedas, one should perform the worship that brings about the state of the Heart.
Having brought [the deity] down, one should perform the external worship as previously described;
then, having offered libations according to the rule into the fire, excluding the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
One should indeed worship Vāstu, the foremost among men, along with the host of deities as its limbs;
one should complete the rite with a hundred, fifty, or even twenty-five oblations.
Immediately after that, [he should offer] sesame seeds sprinkled with clarified butter and clarified butter itself,
with Vedic mantras for the Vāstu-deity and the mantras beginning with Devavrata.
Furthermore, there should be a set of nine water-pots made of metal, perfectly level, according to one's capacity, but certainly not less than twelve finger-breadths in size. (157)
It should be made of stone or clay, well-baked, very firm, and auspicious;
it should be shaped like a water-pot (bhṛṅgāra), octagonal, or like a conch, and elevated. || 158 ||
One should perform the ritual bathing for the purification of all [the deities], characterized by the removal of offerings, the absence of attachment, and the withdrawal of materials. 159.

O twice-born one, having accepted [the invitation], whether immediately or on another day, he should gradually fill the vessels covered with cloths with the appropriate materials while reciting Vedic passages containing their respective names. || 160 ||
With the eight-syllable Gāyatrī and the twelve-syllable Vidyā, [one should worship] with golden sands, gems, pearls, and so forth. || 161 ||
With all the minerals, grains, and other substances such as pārata and the like, along with seeds including white mustard, and grains beginning with nīvāra; || 162 ||
One should adorn the exterior with camphor, sandalwood powder, saffron, and agallochum, as well as with silk garlands, sandalwood paste, and other such items.

Having thus worshipped and consecrated her, one should place Lakṣmī, seated upon a lotus throne and surrounded by the treasures (or, according to another reading, surrounded by the oceans), in the midst of the four.
Then, for the other four [jewels], the king of gems known as Kaustubha,
together with the Lord of Treasures, is empowered by means of the mantra and his own name. (165)
The Blessed One, whose self is all-powerful, should contemplate within himself the partless embodiment of sound by means of the six-syllable mantra. 166.
One should lead the four-footed Brahma-field by means of the eight-petaled [lotus];
having placed the pot of the Lord of All in the center, within the interior of the pericarp.
O twice-born one, [place] four jeweled jars in the eight directions of the circle of directions, starting from the eastern portion in clockwise order, or [recite] the worldly mantras.
The target is the group of four jars extending from the northeast to the northwest;
having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should then perform the worship of the central [deity].
One should indeed worship the fourfold [deities] beginning with the Heart-mantra located within the jewel-pitchers;
however, one should worship the single mantra for all four using the Śrī-pitchers.
Having thus performed the placement of the partless (niṣkala) mantra upon the eyes with the eye-mantras and upon that central jar, one should then perform it for all [the other jars] at once.
One should provide nine vessels made of either copper or stone, which are equal [in size],
well-rounded or square, very solid, and twelve finger-breadths in length.
And there, within the central jar, the four powers are restrained;
that power which is the Supreme Goddess (Parādevī), capable of sustaining the entire universe.
One should remember Prabhāsā, Vaiśvarī, Jñānaśakti, and Amṛtā in the cardinal directions,
and Ānandalakṣaṇā in the collection of jars located in the intermediate directions.
The power called Kriyā is the unswerving energy that bestows birth upon the capable one;
having thus performed the placement (nyāsa), one should perform the worship of Śrī and the others by their respective names.
Thereafter, one should worship the mantra of the treasures and their lords along with its ancillaries;
then one should display the mantra-mudrā, which is characterized by all-pervasive power.
One should perform the recitation with the twelve-syllable mantra and carry it out with complete restraint; [this] is not [attained] through the six-syllable [mantra]. || 177 ||
Then, having urged the knower of the Yajus-sacrifices, "Let the Yajus be joined," and [having urged] the knower of the Sāmans, "The Puruṣa-sūkta, which is the Ṛc, is named Viṣṇu. || 178 ||

Then, with the six-footed hymn beginning with "atharvāya," he should thereafter perform the emanation of the self (ātmavyūha) for the twice-born who have reached the single path (ekāyana), consisting of the fourfold mantras of designation (saṃjñā). || 179 ||
Then, having chanted the Sāman Rathantara accompanied by the Namaskāra, he should indeed proclaim the Ṛgveda with great joy. || 180 ||
The Sāman is indeed established in the knower of the Sāman; then he should utter it.
Thereafter, however, [is the interval] of the pitchers... || 181 ||
Then, having applied a coating of white plaster to all [the directions],
the eight directions of the field should be sealed with the eight Śaktis.
By means of the complete suppression within the stone, or even if the stones are not equal, all [the lines] should be made equal above, possessing the characteristics of the Sarvatobhadra. || 183 ||
Having first been consecrated by bathing and other rites, adorned with garments, garlands, and colors,
and seated upon a throne of the eight jewels, she should be well-disposed toward the eight [deities].

One should indeed place the eight [syllables], distinguished by their phonemes and preceded and followed by the *praṇava* (oṃ), starting from the east and ending in the direction of Īśa (northeast), manifesting them individually. || 185 ||
O Great-minded One, with the syllable *praṇava* and her own name ending in *namaḥ*, she is eternally possessed of strength and vigor; she is named Anantā, steadfast and immutable. (186)
The eighth among the twice-born is named Sandhyā, known as Dhṛti and Sthiti;
she proclaims the beginning and end of the Vedas along with the observances of the Yajurveda.

O Lotus-born One, one should then recite the Vidyā-mantras and the Ṛgveda hymns, and subsequently the Ekāyana; or else, having offered oblations with "yad vāyo" and so forth, [one should proceed]. (188)

Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, the preeminent teacher, the performer of the rite, should recite whatever mantra is to be proclaimed, while recollecting the collection of mantras (*mantrasaṃhitā*). || 189 ||
Accompanied by all the name-mantras beginning with Nyastaśrī,
one should recite this mantra of the Ekāyana, which consists of seven types of intellect.
One should offer all the oblations for the fulfillment of the rites.
Thus much, O lotus-eyed one, has this primary ritual procedure been described by me to you. (191)
I shall now describe the secondary rite (anukalpa), which brings benefit to all;
in this jar, everything worshipped by the hosts of other sacred fields is present. (192)
One should install the array of mantras as prescribed, including those for Sthalaga and Gopala,
as well as the single, supreme power of the Lord which consists of all powers.
Having placed [the vessel] in the center of that [area], one should fill it with nectar and other substances;
then, one should draw a lotus above that with pigments such as saffron and the like.

One should then level the remaining excavated portion of the ground on all sides, using the same method as before—starting with the striking and so forth—with arrows made from all [the prescribed] materials. (195)
With a five-colored thread and firm stakes made of sacrificial wood,
the knower of mantras should then recite the Jīmūta [mantra] while employing the Astra-mantra.
Having sipped water and bowed down, one should indeed offer the aforementioned *bali*—consisting of four squares and sandalwood—to the [deities] of the directions as desired. (197)
The king of mantras, abiding in the three places by means of the twelve-syllable mantra, having then granted forbearance and withdrawn [the deity] as before, preceded by worship; || 198 ||
He acted as the external overseer for all those belonging to the cycle of worldly existence,
placing Viśvakarman at the head of the other flesh-eaters.
He should provide food, sacrificial fees, and other gifts to the foremost of the twice-born, as well as food and monetary gifts to other supplicants according to his own capacity. (200)
Furthermore, one should construct the house and the seats in this manner according to various regions; likewise, the temple should be fashioned in diverse ways, endowed with distinct divisions.
Then, having analyzed the sequence ending with the seat of the banner by means of one's own intelligence.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Installation of the Base of the Temple," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, a great Upaniṣad within the glorious Pāñcarātra.
(Total number of verses: 201) Now begins the forty-third chapter. The Blessed One said:
Starting from a corner of the palace residence, according to one's preference,
one should construct a courtyard on all sides and fashion a surrounding wall.
In a temple with four gates, adorned with four forms, there should be a courtyard for the planets and a main street, either entirely on one side or accompanied by the left side.
O Great-minded One, one should construct two pairs of gates for the city streets facing the walls, and four or eight palaces for the [royal] residences.
For it appears as either a single form or manifold characteristics by the power of the Blessed One;
and according to one's own inclination, it is merely a manifestation appearing as a palace.
O Brahmin, if one intends to arrange eight [shrines], then a group of four should be established there in each of the four corners, made of baked bricks, stone, or wood.

Then, one should arrange two temple-faces facing each other at two locations near the entrance; furthermore, one should place pairs of temples with intervals between them in the three remaining directions.
O high-minded one, the height of the door is declared to be equal to the measurement of the deity including its pedestal; this is the proportion for deities who are elevated in stature.
One should bring about the elevation by means of a pedestal for those [liṅgas] of various short dimensions;
[such a pedestal], through its breadth and height, is free from the restriction of specific characteristics.
The gateway is easy to enter, brings virtue even in times of distress, is well-constructed and purified, and is followed by the lunar mansion. || 9 ||
Having taken the continuous sequence of finger-breadths for both the width and the length,
one should multiply them by each other for the sake of auspiciousness and the attainment of stars.
Or, for the sake of gain, one should purify [the breath] by means of fist-closures while the fingers remain in place;
the counts of one, three, five, and seven are indeed auspicious, while all others are remembered as inauspicious. || 11 ||
The banner, the tiger, the bull, and the lordly elephant are beneficial in their respective order;
thus, for the sake of obtaining the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), one should again beautify that position.
From the Ādeka up to twenty-seven, one should joyfully perform the remaining rites;
or, with great effort, one should choose an increase of even a single finger-breadth for the two feet.

Having first deliberated thoroughly in this manner for the sake of attaining an auspicious constellation from the heap of finger-measures, one should properly construct the temple of the Earth-god (Brahmā). 14.
For the Lord seated upon a couch or a seat, or standing upon Garuḍa,
there should be one [deity] in each of the three desired directions, or three [deities] in those three directions.
Seated in the southern direction, with its face turned toward the western quarter,
the Garuḍa-throne is situated at the southern door of the temple in the northern direction.
Regarding that which is proclaimed as the fourfold set of the four corners:
there, in the southeast (anale), the first [corner] is situated toward the north at the northern gate, while the last is toward the east.

It is remembered that those called "limited" (iyattā) are attached to parts by virtue of their own measure of consciousness—or according to another reading, by transformation—and by what is considered as existence, through the power of delimitation. (18)
O Lotus-born One, that specific distinction known as the *āsthāpana* [rite] occurs when the consecration of the *brahmapāṣāṇa* and the *paiṭhika* [stone] has been completed. (19)
When bathing alone has been performed for the sake of pacifying defects in craftsmanship by means of rubbing with unguents, earth, ashes, cow dung, and so forth, [the following should be done]. (20)
Once the gift of the eyes has been completed and the supreme ritual bath has been performed,
the Guru and others should be raised up by force by many attendants under the supervision of the guardians of the image.
O Pauṣkara, because the mantra has now been variously established through its placement, and because the triad has attained oneness as if with adamantine cement, [the result is secured].
When the rising of the ascendant has been declared, one should indeed perform the ritual placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa),
through the contemplation of which power the establishment of that [deity] in its proper state is likewise accomplished.
On the inner walls of the palaces and so forth, the lords of practitioners have inscribed [the names] for the sake of success, up until the time of their attainment of siddhi. (24)
O twice-born one, the mantra and the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Kalabimba and indeed of Sāsana are for the purpose of constant propitiation, even in the case of ritual worship.

O Brahmin, that [earth] which is known as "moving" (calana) and also as "stabilizing" (sthitisthāpana), and which is excessively corrupted by defects such as the breaking of the ground and the flooding of waters; || 26 ||

Having lifted [the image] from there and placed it in this location characterized by auspicious marks, its re-installation is declared to be the "perfect re-establishment" (saṃsthāpana) due to its being correctly established once again. || 27 ||
One should always remain seated on a faultless seat, free from the defects caused by lightning strikes and other such calamities that may have previously defiled it.
O Mahāmati, an image that is equal to that [original] and rich in auspicious marks should be honored;
or else, it may be placed upon another new pedestal. (29)
One must understand its specific distinctions, as well as its placement and elevation;
for it is devoid of the assembly of [ordinary] knowledge and is perceived as being uniform in a single direction.
Furthermore, the circle of directions is [perceived] here primarily through the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) associated with one's own limbs,
and also by virtue of the states of lying down, sitting, standing, and moving or remaining still.
And there are many specific types known as *pratiṣṭhā* which bestow all perfections (*siddhi*),
due both to their general configuration and to their particular qualities.
The common worship performed with pure and imperishable [materials] by those seeking fruits is established;
its equality of fruit should be understood, however, as occurring in another birth. (33)
The establishment in the fourfold self bestows eternal knowledge, having attained which a man shall not undergo rebirth again. || 34 ||
But he who, desiring the fruit, should perform the installation of the four forms with supreme faith and devotion, O Lotus-born One, [attains success] simply through his intense resolve. (35)
The paternal, the maternal, and that which is called the wife—these seven lineages—he uplifts when he attains birth upon this earth once again. (36)
O Lotus-born One, one who takes refuge in devotion to Hari endowed with righteousness shall attain [the fruit],
just as one born on the third lunar day [of the month] attains it when possessed of true discernment.
"By means of this, O best of the twice-born, one indeed crosses over from the terrible straits of saṃsāra; thus has the form of the primordial foundation been described. (38)
Now, however, understand that after having enjoyed the desired fruit among the divine worlds, [one returns] from those specific arrangements.
Having attained an excellent birth, one should indeed practice once again that divine state established in Brahman which was [attained] in a previous birth. 40.
Consciousness proceeds as before until it reaches the state of the Supreme Lord;
this much is the difference stated, O Great-minded One, while there is equality in the rest.
O Lotus-born One, [this is the fruit] of the supreme, divine, fruitful sacrifice,
which is directed toward Acyuta— the imperishable one who brings about the end of worldly existence.
Understand that distinction which exists even among mere entities—such as [those of] the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, and those whose souls are devoted to the householder stage of life. (43)

O Great-minded One, for those who have been initiated, O Brahmin, for those who are terrified of death and the like, and for those established in worldly affairs, the rites of installation and so forth [are prescribed]. (44)
Those who have been freed from the hindrances bestow the fruit as described by me,
for they have been initiated into Nirvāṇa by their Guru and know the Imperishable One.
For those who have attained their qualification through devotion, who are constantly engaged in worship,
who are firmly established in perfect meditative concentration, and for whom this birth is the last, (46)

O Lotus-born One, you have established a foundation for those whose minds are exhausted by conceptual construction, for the sake of protecting your own family and others, and because of the arising of infinite beings. (47)
O best among the wise, their observance is indeed prescribed for a period lasting as long as life, for the sake of the complete satisfaction of the intellect.

Having understood this, and having completed everything up to the conclusion of the banner with wealth and power acquired through righteousness, one should indeed conclude by means of the "seizing" (ākṣepa) rite.
Seated with his face turned toward the south, dwelling in the abode that is the refuge of all,
he is stationed upon a throne at the eastern gate in the house of Nirṛti.
Thus, situated upon the back of the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) in the temple of the quarter of Vāyu (the northwest),
one attains the fruit of divine enjoyments together with the celestial realms.
Having attained the status of Prajāpati by being situated in the directions as described,
she established the eternal stability of the three worlds and all that follow above them.
By means of this vehicle, a person attains divine movement through the sky;
for those devotees who desire fruits, there are rewards such as specific stations and lands. (53)
All those established in the initiation for results (phaladīkṣā) belong to cities seeking results;
however, their birth is preceded by an excellent birth and is self-revealing. 54.

Know that, O Lotus-born One, for the sake of the pacification of worldly existence, [this should be done] very soon by establishing [the deities] in the three directions according to the sequence already specified.
Or, O Great-minded One, the forms of Nṛsiṃha, Kapila,
and Kroḍa are prescribed in sequence for the four intermediate directions as before.
One should place the horse-faced [deity] as the residence for pearls, lions, and the like;
or alternatively, one should establish tortoises and others in the three directions.
For the sake of attaining the prior fruits for the gods who are lords of the Fish and the Dwarf incarnations,
[the mantras] should be applied in the intermediate directions according to the sequence as prescribed.
The Supreme Lord, whose form is the universe and who embodies all the gods, holds the axe-weapon in his hand as Trivikrama and wears the head of his beloved upon him.
Therefore, O lotus-born one, all other manifestations whatsoever that have not been mentioned in this rule are likewise [to be understood]. || 60 ||
One should employ only those approved by the gurus, and not those who perform sacrifices for others;
for then one may construct a beautiful and desirable hut together with the gods. || 61 ||
In front of the door, one should construct a structure resembling a pavilion, provided with a flight of steps and adorned with an altar; it stands as the locus for worship.

O Lotus-born one, for the stability of other enjoyments, and for the purpose of establishing the foundations of the palaces, one should then construct an auspicious structure capable of withstanding wind and rain.
Whether five or nine [liṅgas] are placed within a single pot of water, or even one,
which is filled with all kinds of jewels, that supreme Lord is established there.
One should worship that [deity] every day, together with its limbs, its marks, its mantras, and its retinue, and likewise adorned with one's own [inner] power.
For the purpose of consecrating the mantra-image and for the pacification of obstacles at the proper time;
otherwise, O Great-minded One, an unavoidable obstacle arises. (66)
Mantras always attain their presence through worship performed at the three times of day;
through lack of worship, they bestow sorrow wherever they are obstructed. (67)
O Lotus-born One, the measurements for the forecourt and the placement of the deities have been described; now, please pay close attention.
In the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa), however, on that ground, within the desired and extensive palace, it is established under various names solely by virtue of its arrangement. || 69 ||
The characteristic of the investigation of the fourfold Self, who stands upon the pedestal of the power of Brahmā and gazes toward the four directions, is as follows: 70.
That which is to be awakened is her foundation, filling the array of the directions;
she exists in the form of the power of steadfastness (dhṛti), being formless and of a transcendent nature.
(267) For stability and for the sake of ritual practice, there is the state of being a Brahma-stone and copper;
O Lotus-born One, everything up to the limit of the senses is established upon the Brahma-stone. 72.
Furthermore, that formless [principle] indeed pervaded everything from the very root,
having assumed the characteristics of both material and immaterial substance, like a pillar.
The uninterrupted persistence of a single, undecaying seed, established within each distinct object, is indeed firmly rooted.
O twice-born one, [this concerns] the manifestation of the multitude of forms—whether divided into various arrays, or as a single whole, or as groups of two and so forth. 75.

When the abiding of a single [deity] upon a single universal pedestal occurs by its own will, that specific distinction known as *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration) is designated as *sthāpana* (installation). || 76 ||

And the unmanifest, which comprises all principles and is permeated by the power of consciousness (cicchakti), is brought into a state of oneness with the form of substance called "motion" by means of the intellect. 77.
O twice-born one, at the time of consecrating the image, during that which is called the "impregnation" (adhivāsa),
one should [fix] the excellent mantra with immobility, and again with the contemplation of movement.
Having indeed fashioned it with its limbs and its characteristic marks according to his own intention,
he then placed that [mantra], which was fixed in his heart, within his own heart for the sake of propitiation.
One should gather [the fruits] because the purpose has been accomplished, either constantly or at another time;
this is the reality known as "Existence" (Sadākhyam), which is devoted to the proclamation of existence.
Likewise, it possesses various perceptions and is of diverse measures;
indeed, it is colored by various and manifold arrangements.
It is adorned with many variegated stages (bhūmikās), and it is appropriately proportioned from the soles of the feet up to the cranial aperture (brahmarandhra). 82.

One should perform [the rite] progressively higher and higher with various clusters of blossoms arising from the worlds beginning with Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, consisting of both stationary and moving beings, as well as perfected ones (siddhas).
It was graced by lords of serpents, by Nāga kings, by beautiful lotus groves,
and by divine bowers of various creepers bound together with cords like drums.

Likewise, there were multitudes of living beings born in water such as crocodiles and others, as well as those born in forests and on mountains, headed by the king of beasts (the lion) and his like. || 85 ||
There were elephants and Śabaras, together with lotuses resembling swans,
and other aquatic flowers such as conch-shells, svastikas, and kahlāras.
With delightful manes like joyful lotuses rising up, with yak-tail whisks adorned with small bells, with parasols, banners, and other such regalia; || 87 ||
Together with all those dwelling on the earth and those not dwelling on the earth, along with the oceans and rivers,
with the nine types of divine implements, and with the gods such as the Moon, the Sun, and Fire.
[He saw it] with divine manifestations accompanied by other manifestations, with islands together with other islands, and with subterranean realms (pātālas) along with their inhabitants. || 89 ||

O Brahmin, [it was filled] with great people, ascetics, and lords of the worlds of truth who possessed great splendor; with those devoted to meditation and silence, and with twice-born ones accompanied by the sacrificial fires and the gods.
O Lotus-born One, one should thus adorn the auspicious pillars of the legs with these and other [ornaments], together with nose-ornaments for all directions.
From the center of the space within the inner sanctum, one should fashion [the area] marked with wheels and lotuses,
together with the gods beginning with Pitāmaha, as well as the Siddhas and Vidyādharas.
With attendants bearing flower garlands and waving whisks and fans, and with the splendors of the forest garland, mace, conch, discus, lotus, and other emblems; 93.

[The enclosure] consists of the Sva, Ga, Īśa, Veda, and Vedāṅga [squares], marked with rosaries in their hands, standing outside the Cakra and Brahmā [enclosures] as the outer covering (āvāraka). || 94 ||
One should adorn the interior wall-section with hosts of all the gods, daityas, and others, as well as with Nārada and other celestial beings intent upon dance and song.
Having indeed restrained that mantra there with the syllable *praṇava*, his own name, and the word signifying prostration, he placed the world of the living beings (*bhūloka*) at his foot.

In this manner, one should place the Bhuvarloka exactly as it exists upon the pedestal of the temple, the Svargaloka upon the shaft (jaṅghā), and the Maharloka within the region of the great spire (śikhara). 97.
*Stambha*, *talapa*, *caraṇa*, and *jaṅghā*;
*sthāna*, *sthūṇa*, and *pāda*—these are synonyms. (98)
Janaloka is within the knot of that [crown-lock], and the one called Tapas is the staff;
and the world called Satya is at the crest of that [lock] in the abode of the gods.
And one should meditate upon the supreme pervasion thus, O Brahmin, extending through the seven worlds and upwards beyond the worlds, within the chosen temple.
It is permeated by other things such as trees and so forth, which possess their own respective natures, and by the characteristics of the "other" which pervade everywhere in mutual relation. (101)
O Brahman, it was indeed devoid of a portion of the earthly realm (bhūrloka) and likewise abandoned by others,
because of the predominance of rajas and tamas and the presence of only a slight degree of the quality of sattva.

For this very reason, for others whose forms consist solely of the quality of *sattva*, the world of earth (*bhūrloka*) exists separately as the first stage of the series of paths beginning with the feet. || 103 ||
When the jewel-installation (ratnanyāsa) has been performed, the three stages beginning with waking should be placed upon the tuft (śikhā) known as Kūrma, Brahmā, and Ātman. 104.

Endowed with the state of the Fourth Brahman (turyabrahma) upon the seat that is the reflection of the path of mantra (mantrādhva), he [the Guru] places his foot upon the other's foot; this is the arising of desire for that reality (tat-tattva). 105.
Then, one should meditate upon the path of the digits (kalādhvan) from the navel up to the crown of the head;
that [path] is characterized by the mantra-brahman within the lotus of the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). || 106 ||
In the pericarp is the Supreme Brahman, the universal, eternal, and all-pervading;
at the time of initiation, the state consisting of the paths has been described by me to you.

O Mahāmati, that perfection belongs to temples ending with the pinnacle, as well as to images together with their pedestals, characterized by the presence of presiding deities and other such features. (108)
In that regard, the Blessed One is indeed the internal, embodied, peaceful, and infallible Self;
for He alone is the Virāj-Self, the imperishable one who exists as the presiding deity.
The *adhibhūta* is the unmanifest (*avyakta*), O twice-born ones; for it consists of all the *tattvas*, together with the others such as *vidyā* and *kalā*, which exist for the sake of another.

O Great-minded One, just as [the elements] are established in their dissolution along with their seeds through the stages of the subtle and so forth, so too do the principles beginning with sound rest upon the intellect (buddhi). 111.

In the same way, O Brahmin, those [deities] are remembered as presiding over the body of the temple, which consists entirely of power and is pure, characterized by the quality of goodness (sattva). || 112 ||
The mantra was prescribed by the omnipresent Lord of All, who is omniscient, all-pervading, and the sovereign creator of everything. (113)

Know that the house of the mantra-form is likewise [to be treated] through ritual service; therefore, having consecrated it along with its pedestal according to rule and with great effort, [one should proceed]. 114.
The installation of that [image] born of a virtuous being is ordained to be like that of a deity;
it should be provided with a flight of steps and a well-characterized pedestal (jagatī).
And that pedestal of the temple should be understood as being of the same nature [as the deity],
having attained a state of oneness through coatings of white lime mixed with mercury.
It was constructed with baked bricks, as well as with firm clay and stones,
endowed with the correct proportions and characteristics, and fashioned according to the instructions of the Omniscient One.
O twice-born one, that which is colored by the web of passion yields eternal fruit;
and because it has been worn out, it must be performed again through the Svayambhū and other rites.
O Great-minded One, when various images that are indestructible and worthy of worship are honored, the doer obtains a fruit multiplied a thousandfold.
The trees, the fields, and the lotuses—those who desire water repeatedly offer these with true devotion for the pacification of their misdeeds. (120)
O Lord of Men, those who have been lost through the influence of beginningless ignorance and the power of time are protected by you through worship and other such means. (121)
At the end of their bodies, they go to heaven, unobstructed by the defects of kingship;
returning from heaven after time has passed, they attain stainless knowledge.
By this, the suffering of saṃsāra becomes endurable and goes to its destruction;
indeed, such is said to be the fruit of entering a temple of the gods. (123)
O Lotus-born One, let there be for those devotees who possess knowledge and even for kings a celestial abode endowed with the contemplation of all paths. (124)
The teacher, by means of his unconditioned will to grasp, brings about the pervasion consisting of the path of the worlds from the Absolute alone; he should demonstrate this to his devotees.
O twice-born one, the builder who is endowed with auspicious marks, possessed of fortune, and free from deceit, obtains the previously mentioned fully complete fruit. (126)
Indeed, whatever fruit the builder obtains from palaces built without mantras by his own hand or by the hands of artisans—namely gold, land, food, and so forth—that [fruit] he receives. (127)
One obtains the fruit resulting from the gift of all one's possessions according to the prescribed ritual;
whether small, middling, or great, it is achieved by means of clay, wood, bricks, and so forth.
Whether it be a celestial abode filled with gods and endowed with the characteristics of valid means of knowledge as described,
or a village dwelling known as a hut, provided it possesses the aforementioned qualities.

Whether from the cardinal and intermediate directions, from the exterior, or from other established [sources], by means of others designated as the *vibhava* and *vyūha* [emanations], or indeed through various other manifestations; || 130 ||
If, even after a long period of time, the wealth-earning activities of those who have bathed are shaken by defects such as earthquakes and the like, [then they must act]. (131)
One should perform the extraction of the preceptors' [debts] properly with their consent;
or else, a king, his minister, or another person devoted to the virtuous may do so by the king's command. (132)
Having obtained the supreme permission from the Lord for the performance of vows, worship, and other rites,
one should meditate upon the All-pervading Lord as lying supine upon a bed of darbha grass on the Ananta-śayana.
With the twelve-syllable mantra, the Lord Hari [bestows] lordship over heaven;
[this is achieved by reciting it] ten thousand times, or five thousand times, or even one hundred and fifty times.
Then, under an auspicious constellation favorable to both the king and the city,
for the sake of pacification, [he installed] that which is the living soul, bearing the qualities and the form of the Lord of Mantras.
Having worshipped Traiguṇya according to the prescribed rite and having offered libations with many pieces of sacrificial wood in due order, he extends his hand at the end of his life.

Just as the power (śakti) consists of the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) and the collection of manifest entities as previously described, so too does the pentad consist of the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), the collection of words (padasaṅgha), and existence itself (sattābhūta). 137.
Having gratified and honored them, along with the elements and the presiding deities (sādhibhūtādhidaiva),
as well as the host of elemental powers (bhūtaśaktigaṇa) and that which is indeed the other, the most subtle [principle], 138.
O Brahmin, one should duly construct the abode of the divine pedestal, having recognized it as equal to the rising sun by means of its own specific names and mantra-words. (139)
O Blessed One, protect once again this multitude of mantras, beginning with the *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*, which reside in manifest form and are indeed without foundation. 140.

Indeed, that which measures half a *udumbara* in extent and occupies the cardinal and intermediate directions is pervaded by *darbha* grasses situated upon the qualities of the intellect (*buddhi-dharma*), characterized by the power of discernment (*viveka*).
One should perform the continuous connection because of the lack of full comprehension of that;
however, at the time of its arousal, one should now perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
And by means of the signs of extraction (upoddhāra) and the eight-limbed Vedic [mantras],
having made each one manifest as the Self through the *pūraka* breath-retention, like the orb of the sun.
Then, having placed it within a well-esteemed and honored water-pot (kumbha) filled with water—or within an image made of gold and other materials—one should worship it every day. || 144 ||

Having correctly introduced [the disciple] for the sake of the perfection of arising, one must indeed again perform the re-establishment of the refined [consciousness], just as it was extracted. (145)
For the increase of kings, rulers, nations, places, cattle, and the twice-born,
and for the eternal attainment of that state by everyone, including all their companions.
O twice-born one, the restoration of palaces and images, as well as that of cows, land, gold, and so forth, and of the kingdom together with its king, should be performed in this same manner. (147)
It arises for the sake of auspicious peace in this world and the next;
otherwise, O Lotus-born One, a great fault would surely occur. (148)
And for those who seize palaces, whether outside or inside,
by means of mantras such as the eight-syllabled one, the images are set in motion.
One should perform the withdrawal of one's own mantras already deposited as before,
just as fire is drawn from the sun by means of a sun-crystal gem. (150)
O Pauṣkara, when the mantras have been collected and are being recited, if a breakage occurs among the images due to the force of karma or through negligence, [the following should be done]. (151)
Then, due to that very past sin, one should perform an expiation that produces clarity of mind and indeed brings about fame and well-being. (152)
In that regard, one should perform the vow for one night, three nights, six days, or twelve nights, according to one's own capacity. (153)
And by performing with focused attention the rites beginning with bathing and ending with the fire-oblation,
one should give gifts of sesame seeds along with gold and silver.

O high-minded one, one should provide food—consisting of rice with ghee and milk and so forth—to many eminent brahmins according to one's ability, preceded by the recitation of peace-mantras (śānti). 155.
Having thus completed this vow arising from the preceptor and others, one should dwell taking refuge in a well-known sacred field frequented by the Siddhas. (156)
Or else, at a well-known sacred site (tīrtha), reciting the great twelve-syllable mantra repeatedly for one day or three days, || 157 ||
One should perform the rite at the time known as a muhūrta, specifically during the three junctions (saṃdhyā), in a divine or perfected sacred site (āyatana). || 158 ||
When there is indeed equality in devotion, this expiation is prescribed as common to all castes; however, it is declared that for one who acts openly, the penance is tenfold.

In the rite of recitation, a progressive increase in merit is indeed prescribed for the devotees of the Śūdra, Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, and Brāhmaṇa castes, provided they do not worship through other [means]. (160)
For it has been stated in the *Prakāśa*: "Now, for as long as clarity [of mind] persists, one should recite the mantra during that time; it is considered purifying to consume [the substance]. (161)
As long as one's own intellect, together with the mind, attains clarity,
[one should recite] the twelve-syllable mantra and indeed that which is the eight-syllable mantra in a place free from light.
O best of the twice-born, one should perform the three daily junctures (sandhyās) in sequence with the six-syllabled mantra;
having bathed as prescribed, one should remain standing within the water and recite it.
At the time of bathing, with single-minded concentration and according to one's ability, one should recite the mantra accompanied by the three mantras—
specifically the eight-syllable mantra— the prescribed number of times in the morning and at midday.
One should indeed perform the time and place [preparations] once for each bath;
the five-limbed consecration (pañcāṅgābhiṣeka) and the remainder should be performed daily at the junctions of the day (saṃdhyā). || 165 ||
Having thoroughly washed the lower part of his body down to the hips with nectar-water,
he discarded his lower garment and took up a clean cloth.
Three days, six days, eight days, and twelve days—
this is beneficial for those from Śūdras up to the twice-born (dvijas), each succeeding one being more so than the last.
O one of great intelligence, this sequence is the cause for the purification of the mind;
it is further accompanied by its fruit, and now another injunction is being stated.
The field, which is concise, common to all, situated on whichever level is desired, and measuring from four cubits up to twelve, is the [sacred] field. 169.
Successively decreasing from the two preceding ones, down to the minimum limit,
[the number of devotees] ranges from five hundred up to the gods, according to their enjoyments.

The walls consist of two parts each; the space between the five members (pañcāṅga) is indeed [one part]; the inner sanctum (garbha) is three and a half parts from that, and the walls are one and a half parts.
Know that the layout of the ground measuring six cubits consists of divisions reduced by one-eighth; the central sanctum (garbha) indeed occupies seven of those parts.
That which is to be fully known consists of four remaining parts as the walls;
with four parts and eight-and-a-half parts, it reaches the tip of the eight cubits.
One should complete the arrangement of the walls with three and a half parts;
the womb-area (garbhakṣetra), including its limbs, shall consist of five cubits from the nine-square grid.
The remaining collection of cubits is prescribed for the walls;
the width of the womb-chamber (garbhakṣetra) of a ten-cubit [temple] is six cubits. || 175 ||
By means of two cubits alone, the assembly of walls is established;
from a field of eleven cubits, the inner sanctum (garbha) is six and a half cubits.
The measurement of the wall is declared to be four cubits and a half; from twelve parts of the site, it is seven parts less one quarter. (177)
The temple should be understood as being three-quarters of four cubits;
and the walls should likewise be constructed by dividing that very measurement in the same manner.
Having made the fruit-bearing walls with thirteen parts,
when nine parts are filled by the sky (the void), the temple of the Lord should be constructed.

Having brought about success for the sake of auspiciousness with a distance of two finger-breadths or one finger-breadth, one should direct the mind toward the wall [of the temple] which contains a portion of their grace. 180.
Having discarded excessive measurement, one should apply it to the fields;
how much more so for measurements such as the finger-breadth and the like, which are equal to an atom? || 181 ||
Since it brings prosperity to men, yet its decline is inauspicious, that [lotus] must indeed be preserved with great effort, O Pauṣkara. (182)
It is endowed with architectural designs and fashioned with four faces;
when considering the nature of the Four-Selfed One, it has one or more doors as appropriate.
Facing whichever direction one desires for the sake of attaining various fruits of accomplishment, one seeking long life should face the east, and one seeking fame should face the south. (184)
One should construct it facing west for the sake of livelihood in a self-supported [temple];
and a temple facing north bestows wealth and grain. (185)
O Pauṣkara, know that this much has been stated as the supreme worldly fruit for all [the goddesses], consisting of various enjoyments. (186)
In one's own field, which is vast and delightful, or on the ground of one's own lap, independently; or together with a previously established [image] in a temple of Hari. (187)

This is remembered as the primary ritual procedure (mukhyakalpa) in the Svāyambhuva or Siddha-tantras; elsewhere, O assembly of the wise, it should be understood as a secondary procedure (anukalpa). || 188 ||
On the ground spread out and shaded by the shadow of the flagstaff of the eastern palace, which has been purified from defects with bricks and lime-powder; (189)
Having established that [image] within that interval, one should perform the rites beginning with the fire-oblation (homa) as prescribed, along with the offering of food (sonnatam);
and the image, together with its pedestal (sapīṭha), should be made according to the measurements of the temple door, being all-pervading and imperishable.
Endowed with all the complete marks for the sake of his fame reaching to the ends of the ocean,
and for the upliftment of his own lineage, both past and future.
The very moment this resolve is formed, "I shall establish [the image]," at that very instant his fame attains unshakable stability.
What need is there to mention all other places, such as the world of the earth and so forth, for he who performs the consecration of the Source of the Universe through his own splendor? (193)
He who performs the Vaiṣṇava consecration for those whose fathers and others have passed away, or for any other [deceased], according to his own capacity or his wealth; || 194 ||
Before long, they constantly go to the abode of Antaka;
and thereafter, after some time, they reach the supreme station of Viṣṇu.
Having encountered a favorable portion of the earth, together with [virtues] such as noble lineage and good character, they practice what is auspicious by which they attain rebirth. (196)
Out of compassion, he who performs the consecration for himself, for his kinsmen, or for others, shall obtain the fruit arising therefrom. || 197 ||
And the lords of mantras, perfected through the resonance of the Praṇava, enter [the body] and, after a short period of time, draw forth their own divine power. (198)
Indeed, having had their faults destroyed, they were established again— free from obstacles and pure—
by the perfected ones and others in sacred fords, holy fields, and forests.

Those who, out of delusion, seek to obstruct the manifestation of the array of emanations within the forms [of the deities], [denying] their configuration, measurement, appearance, or the defects arising at a later time—[they are hindered]. (200)
The supreme lords, beginning with Vāsudeva, are to be meditated upon in two divisions;
there are four, ending with Aniruddha, according to the arrangement of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha).
In this way, others such as Varāha and the rest [are worshipped] together with the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha);
likewise, those beginning with Keśava are worshipped either with all [four] or with one or another of them.
O you who are worshipped by the immortals, he who performs worship according to his own capacity, even with very slight or even more slight devotion, [attains success]. (203)
Then, through the aforementioned pure enjoyments and various ritual acts,
once the constituent parts of the rite have been accomplished, the King of Mantras [should offer] the arghya water with the heart-mantra and the weapon-mantra.
And having offered the various honored enjoyments of the Lord as prepared, with [the mantra] beginning and ending with the Praṇava... [only this much of the text was obtained]. || 205 ||
